This encyclical letter was issued by the Synod of Antioch around 268–269. That synod condemned and deposed Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, for his teaching about Christ and for his conduct. The letter was drafted by Malchion, a presbyter and teacher of rhetoric at Antioch, who had exposed Paul's views in a public disputation. It is addressed to Dionysius of Rome, Maximus of Alexandria and the whole Church. Eusebius preserves extensive extracts in his Ecclesiastical History, and fragments of the acts of the disputation survive in later writers.

The Martyrdom of the Holy and Glorious Apostle Bartholomew is an anonymous apocryphal account of the apostle's final mission and death. It survives in Greek and is closely related to a Latin passion; it probably dates from somewhere between the fifth and seventh centuries. It describes Bartholomew's preaching in "India", where his presence silences the demon worshipped in the temple of Astaruth. He converts King Polymius and his household, and the king's brother Astyages then has him put to death. The text is an important witness to the legends about Bartholomew that shaped his later veneration.

The Martyrdom of Ignatius is an anonymous Greek hagiographical account of the death of Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, whom it calls a disciple of John the apostle. It tells how Trajan, in the ninth year of his reign, condemned Ignatius at Antioch. He was taken to Rome, meeting Polycarp at Smyrna on the way, and was thrown to wild beasts in the amphitheatre. The narrative claims to be by companions who saw these events. Most scholars, however, date it well after the second century, perhaps to the fourth or fifth. It shaped later tradition about Ignatius's martyrdom.

The Martyrdom of Justin and his companions, also called the Acts of Justin, is an anonymous Greek account of the trial and execution of the Christian philosopher Justin Martyr and several fellow believers at Rome. They were tried before the urban prefect Junius Rusticus, who held office around 162–168. The text is largely a record of questions and answers in which Justin states his faith and refuses to sacrifice. It survives in several recensions and is valued as one of the earliest and most sober martyr acts.

The Martyrdom of Polycarp is a Greek letter from the church of Smyrna to the church at Philomelium and to all churches. It describes the arrest, trial and execution of Polycarp, the aged bishop of Smyrna, usually dated to around 155–160, though some scholars place it later. It is the earliest surviving Christian account of a martyrdom outside the New Testament. It presents Polycarp's death as an imitation of Christ's passion and gives early evidence of honouring martyrs' relics and anniversaries. It is traditionally grouped with the Apostolic Fathers.

This is a collection of short passages from the lost writings of Melito, bishop of Sardis in Asia Minor in the later second century. They survive as quotations in later authors such as Eusebius and Anastasius of Sinai, in catenae and in Syriac translations. They include passages from his Apology addressed to Marcus Aurelius, from the Extracts to Onesimus with its early list of Old Testament books, and from works on soul and body, the cross and faith. The authenticity of some pieces is disputed. Together they show Melito's paradoxical rhetoric about the incarnation and the passion of Christ.

Against Porphyry was a Greek treatise by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. In it he answered the Neoplatonist philosopher Porphyry, whose attack on Christianity, Against the Christians, was widely read. Jerome mentions the work, but it is lost apart from a few short excerpts. These are moral and theological reflections: that true excellence is what God values, that repentance works best when it is immediate, and that human good lies in resembling God.

The Banquet of the Ten Virgins is a Greek dialogue by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. Its title and form deliberately echo Plato's Symposium. Gregorion tells Euboulios about a banquet held by Arete (Virtue) in a garden, where ten virgins give speeches in turn praising chastity and virginity. They draw heavily on allegorical readings of Scripture. Thekla gives the fullest speech, and the work ends with her hymn to Christ the Bridegroom. It is Methodius's only work to survive complete in Greek and an important early Christian treatise on virginity.

Concerning Free-Will, also known as De autexusio, is a Greek theological dialogue by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. It is a debate between an orthodox speaker, Orthodoxus, and a follower of Valentinian Gnosticism. The work argues against the view that matter is eternal and is the source of evil. Instead, it traces evil to the misuse of the free will that God gave to created beings. It is an important early Christian treatment of the origin of evil and of human moral freedom.

This Greek fragment argues that matter is created and is not the cause of evil. It rejects the idea that two uncreated substances, God and matter, could exist side by side. Eusebius quoted it in his Preparation for the Gospel under the name of Maximus, traditionally identified as a late second-century bishop of Jerusalem. The same passage also appears in the Dialogue of Adamantius against the Marcionites. Most scholars, however, think it actually comes from On Free Will by Methodius of Olympus (died c. 311). The work is an early Christian contribution to the debate over the origin of evil.

The Discourse on the Resurrection, also known as Aglaophon, is a Greek dialogue by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. It argues against Origen's teaching on the resurrection body. Methodius rejects the view that the "coats of skins" of Genesis are bodies, and he insists that the same flesh will rise. He holds that God is not the author of evil, which instead comes from the misuse of free will. The Greek original survives only in substantial fragments, chiefly those quoted by Epiphanius and Photius. A fuller version is preserved in Old Slavonic.

The Fragments are a collection of passages attributed to Methodius of Olympus, a bishop, theologian and martyr who died around 311. They survive as quotations in later writers and anthologies, and they come from works that are lost or only partly preserved. They include an allegorical reading of the story of Jonah, drawn from his treatise On the Resurrection. In it the whale signifies time, Jonah stands for Adam, who lost immortality through sin, and the storm-tossed ship is present life. The fragments add to what is known of Methodius's teaching on bodily resurrection and his allegorical reading of Scripture.

These are short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Job, preserved in the catenae (medieval chains of patristic commentary) under the name of Methodius, usually identified as Methodius of Olympus (died c. 311), bishop and martyr. Their authenticity cannot be fully confirmed, as is often the case with catena material. The fragments discuss Job's speeches to his friends. They argue that true wisdom, joined to piety, is beyond human discovery and comes only as God's gift through revelation. This is why Greek philosophers seeking God by their own strength failed.

This short Greek fragment comes from a lost discourse on martyrs attributed to Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and Church Father who died around 311. Only a brief passage survives, preserved as a quotation by later writers. It praises martyrdom as so admirable and desirable that Christ himself honoured it. Citing Philippians 2:6, it presents the Son's self-emptying descent to humanity as the source of this gift. The passage is a small witness to pre-Nicene reflection on martyrdom as an imitation of Christ, from the era of the last great persecutions.

On Things Created (De creatis) is a Greek theological treatise by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. The full work is lost. It survives only in a summary of excerpts made by the ninth-century patriarch Photius in codex 235 of his Bibliotheca. The surviving passages argue against Origen and his followers. They criticize his allegorical reading of texts such as "cast not your pearls before swine" and dispute his view that the created world is coeternal with God. The work is an important witness to early opposition to Origen.

Octavius is a Latin dialogue defending Christianity, written by Marcus Minucius Felix, a Roman lawyer, probably in the late second or early third century. Its exact date and its relation to Tertullian's Apologeticum are disputed. Set on the beach at Ostia, it records a debate between the pagan Caecilius Natalis and the Christian Octavius Januarius, with Minucius as judge. Caecilius attacks Christian beliefs and rumoured practices, Octavius refutes him, and Caecilius is converted. Its polished Ciceronian style makes it one of the earliest and most elegant works of Latin Christian apologetic.

The Muratorian Canon, or Muratorian Fragment, is an anonymous Latin list of New Testament books that may be the oldest of its kind. Ludovico Antonio Muratori published it from an eighth-century codex that came from Bobbio Abbey. It is usually dated about 170–200 and thought to translate a Greek original, but some scholars place it in the fourth century. Its opening and ending are lost. The surviving 85 lines comment on the Gospels, Acts and the epistles, and name the books accepted, disputed or rejected by the churches the compiler knew.

The Narrative of Events Happening in Persia on the Birth of Christ is a legendary Greek account attributed to Sextus Julius Africanus, the third-century Christian chronographer. Scholars have long rejected that attribution, and the work probably dates from between the fifth and seventh centuries. It describes miraculous signs at a Persian temple announcing Christ's birth, followed by the Magi's journey to Bethlehem and their report on their return. It is an example of the apocryphal tradition that grew up around the Nativity and the Magi.

The Narrative of Joseph of Arimathaea is an anonymous Greek apocryphal text belonging to the literature that grew up around the Passion and Pontius Pilate. Its date is uncertain and is usually placed somewhere between late antiquity and the early Middle Ages. Joseph, who asked Pilate for Jesus' body, tells the story in the first person. He describes the crimes of the two robbers crucified with Christ, Gestas and the penitent Demas, along with his own imprisonment, and expands on the Gospel accounts of the crucifixion and its aftermath.

The Narrative of Zosimus, also known as the History of the Rechabites, is an anonymous apocryphal text that survives in Greek, Syriac and other languages. It tells of Zosimus, a desert hermit who, after forty years of strict fasting, is guided by an angel to the land of the Blessed. These are descendants of the Rechabites of Jeremiah 35, who live a sinless life apart from the world. Its date and origin are disputed. Some scholars see an early Jewish core, which was later reworked by Christians, possibly between the first and sixth centuries.

The Nicene Creed is the profession of Christian faith first adopted by the First Council of Nicaea in 325 against Arianism. It affirms that the Son is "begotten, not made" and "of one substance" (homoousios) with the Father, and it ends with anathemas against Arian formulas. According to tradition, the First Council of Constantinople expanded it in 381, mainly the article on the Holy Spirit. This Niceno-Constantinopolitan form remains the most widely shared creed among Eastern and Western churches.

De bono pudicitiae (On the Good of Chastity) is a short Latin treatise in the form of a pastoral letter. It came down among the spurious works of Cyprian of Carthage but is now generally attributed to Novatian, the Roman presbyter and rival bishop of the mid-third century. The author writes to his congregation while absent from it. He commends chastity as the Church's adornment and treats it in its forms of virginity, continence and marital fidelity, with biblical examples such as Joseph and Susanna. Together with De cibis Judaicis, it shows Novatian's moral teaching and rigorist outlook.

On the Jewish Meats is a Latin pastoral letter by Novatian, the Roman presbyter and later rival bishop of Rome. He wrote it to his community while away from them, probably in the 250s. It follows two earlier letters against the Jews on circumcision and the Sabbath, which are now lost. Novatian argues that the Mosaic food laws taught moral lessons through symbols, and that in Christ all foods are clean. He still warns Christians against gluttony and against eating food offered to idols.

De Spectaculis is a short Latin treatise in the form of a pastoral letter. It was handed down among the works of Cyprian of Carthage, but scholars generally attribute it to Novatian, the Roman presbyter and rival bishop, and date it to the mid-third century. The author warns Christians against attending the circus, theatre and gladiatorial games. He answers people who defended these shows from Scripture by arguing that every such spectacle is devoted to idols. The treatise draws heavily on Tertullian's earlier work of the same name.

De Trinitate is a Latin theological treatise by Novatian, a Roman presbyter who later led a rigorist schism and was considered an antipope. It is usually dated to about 240–250, before his break with Pope Cornelius in 251. In thirty-one chapters it follows the rule of faith, treating in turn God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Against the Monarchians and docetists, it argues that Christ is truly God and truly human and distinct from the Father. It draws heavily on Tertullian and is one of the earliest major works of Latin theology written in Rome.

Against Celsus is an apologetic treatise in eight books by Origen of Alexandria, written around 248 at the request of his patron Ambrose. It refutes The True Word, an attack on Christianity by the second-century pagan philosopher Celsus. Origen answers him point by point, defending faith, the identity of Jesus, allegorical reading of Scripture and Christianity's relation to Greek religion. It survives complete in Greek and is among the most important works of early Christian apologetics. It also preserves most of what is known of Celsus's lost work.

This is a large Greek exegetical work by Origen of Alexandria, written for his patron Ambrose. He began it in Alexandria around the early 230s and continued it after moving to Caesarea. It originally ran to at least 32 books, but only a few survive, among them books 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 19, 20, 28 and 32. Origen reads the Fourth Gospel at both a literal and a spiritual level. He often argues against the Gnostic commentary of Heracleon, which makes this one of the earliest surviving Christian commentaries on John.

This is Origen of Alexandria's verse-by-verse exegesis of the Gospel of Matthew, written in Greek at Caesarea late in his life, around 246–248. It originally ran to twenty-five books. Only books 10 to 17 survive in Greek, covering roughly Matthew 13:36 to 22:33. An anonymous early Latin translation preserves much of the rest, and a few fragments survive in other writers, including Origen's account of the order of the four Gospels. The commentary combines literal and allegorical interpretation and is a major witness to early Christian biblical scholarship.

On First Principles (Greek Peri Archon, Latin De Principiis) is a theological treatise in four books by Origen of Alexandria. He wrote it at Alexandria around 220–230, and it is regarded as the first systematic exposition of Christian theology. It covers God, the Trinity, rational beings, the world, free will, and how to interpret Scripture. Only fragments of the Greek original survive, mainly in the Philocalia. The full text comes down in Rufinus's Latin translation of 397, which softened passages thought unorthodox. Its teachings fuelled the later Origenist controversies.

This Greek letter is Origen's reply to the Christian chronographer Julius Africanus, written from Nicomedia, probably around 240. Africanus had objected that the story of Susanna in the Book of Daniel was a late forgery. He pointed to Greek wordplays that could not have existed in a Hebrew original and to features he found implausible. Origen defends the story's place in the Church's Scriptures and discusses differences between the Hebrew and Greek texts of the Bible. The letter is one of Origen's few complete surviving letters and an important early witness to debates over the biblical canon and textual criticism.

The Letter to Gregory is a short Greek letter by Origen, probably written in the 230s or 240s. It is traditionally addressed to his pupil Gregory Thaumaturgus, though some scholars question whether this is the same Gregory. Origen urges the gifted young man, who could have become a lawyer or philosopher, to turn his talents to Christianity. He should take from Greek philosophy and the liberal arts whatever helps in understanding Scripture, just as the Israelites "spoiled the Egyptians" (Exodus). The letter survives in the Philocalia and is an early statement of how Christians might use classical learning.

The Letter to Gregory is a short Greek letter by Origen, probably written in the 230s or 240s. It is traditionally addressed to his pupil Gregory Thaumaturgus, though some scholars question whether this is the same Gregory. Origen urges the gifted young man, who could have become a lawyer or philosopher, to turn his talents to Christianity. He should take from Greek philosophy and the liberal arts whatever helps in understanding Scripture, just as the Israelites "spoiled the Egyptians" (Exodus). The letter survives in the Philocalia and is an early statement of how Christians might use classical learning.

These are short Greek passages attributed to Pantaenus, the second-century Christian teacher at Alexandria. He was remembered as Clement of Alexandria's master and as a missionary to "India." Pantaenus is not known to have left any complete writings, so only these scattered sayings survive, quoted by later authors. One comments on Psalm 19:4, "In the sun hath He set His tent," and on how the prophets use verb tenses. Another concerns how God knows created things. They are a rare direct glimpse of the earliest Alexandrian Christian teaching.

The surviving fragments of the Exposition of the Sayings of the Lord, a Greek work in five books by Papias, bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia. It was written in the early second century, with dates proposed from about 100 to 140. The work itself is lost. Its excerpts survive as quotations in later writers, chiefly Irenaeus and Eusebius. Papias collected oral traditions from the "elders" who had known the apostles. The fragments matter most for their early and much-debated statements about how the Gospels of Mark and Matthew came to be written.

The Passing of Mary is an anonymous apocryphal narrative surviving in two Latin recensions, part of the wider Transitus Mariae tradition, generally dated between the fifth and seventh centuries. It tells how Christ promises his mother advance notice of her death and how the apostles are miraculously gathered to her bedside. It goes on to describe her burial and the bodily taking up of Mary into heaven. The second form is ascribed to Melito of Sardis, though the attribution is spurious. These texts strongly shaped later Western belief and art concerning the Dormition and Assumption.

This anonymous Latin martyr account describes the deaths of Vibia Perpetua, a young noblewoman, the slave Felicitas and their companions, who were executed in the arena at Carthage in 203. At its core is Perpetua's own prison diary, written in the first person and recording her visions, together with a vision narrated by her fellow martyr Saturus. An editor framed these with a preface and an account of the martyrdom. Some have identified the editor as Tertullian, but this is disputed. The work is among the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman. A Greek version also exists.

This short anonymous Latin martyr account tells of Symphorosa, a Christian widow, and her seven sons. They are said to have been put to death at Tibur (Tivoli) under the emperor Hadrian. According to the story, pagan priests accused her when Hadrian ordered religious ceremonies for his new villa there. She refused to sacrifice to the gods and was drowned, and her sons were executed the next day. Manuscripts attribute the text to Julius Africanus, but this is doubtful. Its date is uncertain, and it is probably a later composition.

The Passion of the Scillitan Martyrs is a short anonymous Latin account of the trial of Christians from Scilli in Roman North Africa. Speratus and his companions were tried before the proconsul Saturninus at Carthage on 17 July 180 and beheaded. The text consists mostly of the court interrogation, in which the accused refuse to swear by the emperor's genius. Speratus also mentions "books and epistles of Paul." It is the earliest dated Christian document from Latin Africa and among the most reliable of the early acts of the martyrs.

The Canonical Epistle is a set of penitential rules by Peter I, bishop of Alexandria (300–311). It was written in Greek around 306, at the "fourth passover" of the Diocletianic persecution, and is preserved as part of his treatise or sermon on penitence. Its canons lay down graded penances for Christians who had lapsed under persecution, depending on whether they gave way under torture or imprisonment, through fear, by trickery, or by sending substitutes. Received into Eastern canon law, it was later commented on by the Byzantine canonists Theodore Balsamon and John Zonaras.

This is a collection of surviving fragments from the writings of Peter I, bishop of Alexandria from 300 until his martyrdom in 311, during the persecutions under Diocletian and his successors. It includes a letter warning the Alexandrian church against Meletius, who had ordained clergy in Peter's absence, the beginning of what became the Meletian schism. It also includes a passage on the Godhead and the Incarnation. Its best-known part is the Canons from his treatise on penitence, which set the terms for readmitting Christians who had lapsed under persecution. These canons were later received into Eastern church law.

This is a short letter from four Egyptian bishops, Hesychius, Pachomius, Theodorus and Phileas of Thmuis, to Meletius, bishop of Lycopolis. It was written about 305–307, while the authors were imprisoned during the Great Persecution under Diocletian. The bishops rebuke Meletius for ordaining clergy in dioceses outside his own jurisdiction. They appeal to the ancestral law of the Church, under which each bishop acts only within his own see. The letter is an early witness to the Melitian schism in Egypt. It was probably written in Greek but survives only in Latin.

This Greek letter was written by Phileas, bishop of Thmuis in Lower Egypt, to the Christians of his own city during the Great Persecution under Diocletian. Phileas wrote it while imprisoned at Alexandria, shortly before his own martyrdom around 306. The surviving passages, preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea in his Church History (Book VIII), describe the tortures suffered by the martyrs of Alexandria. They praise the martyrs' steadfastness and present it as an imitation of Christ's self-emptying. The letter is a valuable eyewitness account of the persecution in Egypt.

Codex 119 of the Bibliotheca, the ninth-century collection of book reviews by Photius, patriarch of Constantinople, describes a twelve-book work by Pierius, a presbyter of Alexandria. Pierius was said to have headed the Alexandrian school and taught the martyr Pamphilus. Photius praises his clear, easy style and wealth of argument. He also notes opinions that stray from later Church teaching: his talk of "two substances" in Father and Son, which Photius reads as meaning persons, and a view of the Holy Spirit as lower in glory. The entry is a key witness to Pierius's lost writings.

This short Greek exegetical fragment comes from a lost commentary on Paul's First Epistle to the Corinthians by Pierius, an Alexandrian priest and teacher of the late third century who was known as "Origen the Younger." It survives because Jerome quoted it. Jerome places Pierius alongside Origen, Dionysius, Eusebius, Didymus and Apollinaris as major interpreters of the epistle. Commenting on 1 Corinthians 7:7, "For I would that all men were even as I myself," Pierius says that Paul here openly preaches celibacy. The fragment is a small surviving witness to early Alexandrian biblical interpretation.

The Epistle to the Philippians is a Greek letter by Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, and his presbyters, written to the church at Philippi in the first half of the second century. Many scholars think it combines two letters written at different times. It urges faith, righteousness and good conduct, warns against greed and docetic error, and draws heavily on New Testament writings. It also mentions the letters of Ignatius of Antioch. Irenaeus praised it, and it is Polycarp's only surviving writing and one of the Apostolic Fathers.

Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, wrote this synodal letter to Victor, bishop of Rome, around 190 during the Quartodeciman controversy over the date of Easter. Writing for the bishops of Asia gathered in synod, he defends their custom of keeping the Pascha on the fourteenth day of the lunar month. He appeals to the tradition of the apostles Philip and John, and of Polycarp, Melito and others. He also notes that seven of his relatives had been bishops and that he had served the Lord sixty-five years. Fragments survive in Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History.

The Life and Passion of Cyprian is a Latin hagiographical account of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, who was martyred in 258. It is attributed to Pontius, a deacon who served under Cyprian and accompanied him into exile. He wrote it shortly after Cyprian's death. It covers Cyprian's conversion, his time as bishop, his work during the plague at Carthage, his exile to Curubis and his execution under Valerian. It is often regarded as the earliest surviving Christian biography in Latin, and it praises its subject in a rhetorical style.

The Protevangelium of James is an anonymous Greek infancy gospel from the second century. It presents itself as the work of James, the brother of the Lord. It tells of the miraculous conception of Mary to Joachim and Anna and her upbringing in the Temple. It goes on to her betrothal to the elderly widower Joseph, the birth of Jesus in a cave near Bethlehem, and the events that followed. It is the earliest surviving text to assert Mary's perpetual virginity. Although the Latin West condemned it as apocryphal, it shaped Marian feasts, art and devotion, especially in the East.

The Two Epistles Concerning Virginity are early Christian letters falsely attributed to Clement of Rome. They were probably written in Greek in the third century, likely in Syria or Palestine. The complete text survives only in Syriac, with Greek fragments preserved in later anthologies. Addressed to male and female ascetics, the letters praise virginity, which they say must go together with good works. They also condemn men and women ascetics living together and give rules for wandering ascetics' conduct. They are important evidence for early Christian asceticism.

The Contestatio (Diamartyria) is a short Greek text that, together with the Epistle of Peter to James, comes before the Pseudo-Clementine Homilies. It is falsely attributed to Clement of Rome and its date is uncertain. In it James reads Peter's letter to the elders and lays down how the books of Peter's preachings may be handed on. The recipient must be a faithful, circumcised man who has been tested for six years. Standing beside living water, he makes a solemn adjuration to keep the books secret. The text shows the Jewish-Christian setting of the Clementine literature.

The Epistle of Clement to James is a pseudonymous Greek letter that serves as a preface to the Clementine Homilies, part of the Pseudo-Clementine literature, and probably dates from the third or fourth century. Written in the name of Clement of Rome to James, "bishop of bishops" at Jerusalem, it reports Peter's death at Rome. It then describes how Peter ordained Clement as his successor and records Peter's instructions on the duties of bishop, presbyters, deacons and catechists. The letter is an early witness to the idea of Roman episcopal succession from Peter. Rufinus translated it into Latin.

The Epistle of Peter to James is a short pseudepigraphal letter that opens the Pseudo-Clementine Homilies. It is a Greek work wrongly attributed to Clement of Rome. In it, Peter asks James, bishop of Jerusalem, to entrust "the books of my preachings" only to tested and worthy people. He takes as his model Moses handing on his teaching to the Seventy, and he complains that his doctrine has been distorted. Scholars often link the letter to a hypothetical earlier source, the Kerygmata Petrou, which may date from the second century. The surviving text belongs to the fourth-century Clementine literature.

The Clementine Homilies are a Greek Christian romance in twenty books. They claim to be by Clement of Rome but are pseudonymous and were probably composed in the fourth century. Clement narrates his youthful questions about death and the world, his conversion, and his travels with the apostle Peter. These lead to Peter's discourses and debates with Simon Magus and finally to Clement's reunion with his lost family. With the related Recognitions, the Homilies reworked a lost earlier source. They are an important witness to Jewish-Christian thought and were translated into Syriac and other languages.

The Recognitions is a fourth-century Christian romance falsely attributed to Clement of Rome. It is one of two surviving versions of the Pseudo-Clementine writings, alongside the Clementine Homilies. It tells of Clement's conversion, his travels with the apostle Peter, Peter's debates with Simon Magus, and how Clement was reunited with his scattered family. The Greek original is lost. The text survives complete in Rufinus of Aquileia's Latin translation of about 406, and in part in an early Syriac version. It is an important source for Jewish-Christian traditions.

The Exhortation to Repentance (Exhortatio de paenitentia) is a short anonymous Latin work that was long transmitted among the writings of Cyprian of Carthage. It is now counted among the Pseudo-Cyprianic texts. Its date is uncertain and is generally placed between the mid-third and fifth centuries. It is a collection of biblical testimonia, mostly from the Psalms and the Prophets, set out like Cyprian's own proof-text collections. Its stated purpose is to show that all sins may be forgiven to anyone who turns to God with his whole heart.

De laude martyrii (On the Glory of Martyrdom) is an anonymous Latin treatise that came down among the works of Cyprian of Carthage but is not by him. It was probably written in the mid-third century, during a time of persecution. Some scholars, notably Adolf von Harnack, have attributed it to Novatian, though this is disputed. In a rhetorical style, the author explains what martyrdom is, how great it is and what it gains. He urges readers to accept death for Christ gladly and argues that Christ's propitiation crowns martyrs without further purgation.

This is a collection of Greek writings that have come down under the name of Gregory Thaumaturgus, the third-century bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, but whose authenticity is doubtful or rejected. It includes a fragment on the Trinity, a treatise on the soul addressed to Tatian, homilies, a discourse on all the saints and a comment on a passage of Matthew. Their dates and authors are uncertain. Some pieces probably belong to later centuries, as their developed Trinitarian and Christological language suggests.

The Kata meros pistis, or Sectional Confession of Faith, is a Greek doctrinal statement handed down under the name of Gregory Thaumaturgus, the third-century bishop of Neocaesarea. Most scholars regard it as a fourth-century work, and since Hans Lietzmann's study it has usually been assigned to Apollinaris of Laodicea or his circle. Written as a series of condemnations, it rejects those who say the Son was made from nothing or became divine by grace, and those who call the Spirit a created being. It sets out the Trinity as one Godhead and explains how Christ became incarnate.

The Twelve Topics on the Faith is a short Greek doctrinal treatise attributed to Gregory Thaumaturgus, the third-century bishop of Neocaesarea. Its authenticity is generally rejected, and it is usually dated to between the later fourth and the fifth century. It sets out twelve anathemas on the person of Christ, each followed by an explanation. They condemn claims that Christ's body was uncreated or of the same substance as his divinity. Its insistence on both his full divinity and his real humanity reflects the Christological controversies that followed Apollinarianism.

Against Beron and Helix is a Greek theological treatise on the divine nature and the Incarnation, written against two otherwise unknown heretics. It survives only in fragments and was once attributed to Hippolytus of Rome. Modern scholars regard it as pseudonymous and much later, perhaps from the seventh century or after. The fragments argue that the infinite God cannot change. They also hold that the Word became truly man without any conversion of his divinity, with each nature keeping its own properties and activity.

The Discourse on the End of the World is a Greek eschatological sermon that names Hippolytus of Rome, bishop and martyr, as its author. It is generally regarded as spurious and much later than him; its date is uncertain, but it is often placed between the seventh and ninth centuries. Drawing heavily on Hippolytus's genuine treatise On Christ and Antichrist, it uses the prophets and Revelation to describe the signs of the last times, the rise and deceptions of Antichrist, the second coming of Christ and the final judgment, and it urges repentance.

The Discourse on the Holy Theophany is a Greek homily for the feast of the Theophany (Epiphany), which celebrates Christ's baptism in the Jordan. It has come down under the name of Hippolytus of Rome, but its authenticity is widely doubted and its date is uncertain, probably between the fourth and sixth centuries. The sermon begins by praising the goodness of creation and the life-giving power of water. It then reflects on Christ's baptism by John and the descent of the Spirit, and ends by urging its hearers to seek rebirth through baptism.

This pair of short Greek lists is falsely attributed to Hippolytus of Rome. The first, on the Twelve Apostles, says briefly where each apostle preached, how he died and where he was buried. The second names the Seventy disciples of Luke 10 and usually gives each one's episcopal see. The date and author are unknown, and the lists are generally placed somewhere between the seventh and ninth centuries. They are close to the similar lists ascribed to Pseudo-Dorotheus. They show how Byzantine tradition told the story of the apostles' missions and the founding of churches by apostles.

This is a group of Greek letters falsely attributed to Ignatius of Antioch, the early second-century bishop. They are addressed to the Tarsians, the Antiochians, the deacon Hero and the Philippians, and they include an exchange with Mary of Cassobola, called Mary at Neapolis. They were composed in the later fourth century, probably in Syria, alongside the interpolated long recension of the genuine letters. The compiler is often identified with the author of the Apostolic Constitutions. The letters attack docetism and promote church order, and their Christology has been called subordinationist.

This group of Latin letters and decrees is attributed to the third-century Roman bishops Zephyrinus, Callistus, Urban I, Pontianus, Anterus and Fabian. They are forgeries from the False Decretals, a large canon-law collection put together around the mid-ninth century in Carolingian Francia under the pseudonym Isidorus Mercator. The author's identity is unknown. The letters set out rules for trying accused bishops, including strict requirements for witnesses and appeals to the Roman see. Their aim was to protect bishops and strengthen papal jurisdiction. They shaped medieval canon law until they were shown to be forged.

The Discourse to the Greeks (Oratio ad Graecos) is a short Christian apologetic treatise in Greek. It was handed down under the name of Justin Martyr, but scholars do not accept it as his work. It is usually dated to the first half of the third century. In five chapters the anonymous author explains why he turned away from Greek religion. He attacks the immorality of the Homeric heroes and of the gods in the poets. He then urges his fellow Greeks to follow him in turning to Christianity. A Syriac version was made before the seventh century.

The Hortatory Address to the Greeks is an anonymous Greek Christian protreptic in thirty-eight chapters. It was long attributed to Justin Martyr, but it is now generally regarded as the work of a later writer. Its date is disputed and is usually placed in the third century or later. The author argues that Greek poets and philosophers contradict one another and are of little use as guides to religion. He holds that whatever truth they reached was borrowed from Moses and the prophets, who were older, and he urges his Greek readers to accept the true religion.

On the Sole Government of God (De monarchia) is a short Greek apologetic treatise attributed to Justin Martyr but generally regarded as the work of an unknown later author, probably of the third century. It argues that there is one true God and that idolatry arose through forgetfulness and custom. It makes its case almost entirely through quotations from Greek poets and philosophers, some of them spurious, including a Pseudo-Orphic poem. Eusebius mentions a work by Justin under this title, but whether it is the same text is doubtful.

The Key (Clavis Scripturae) is a Latin glossary of biblical symbolism attributed to Melito of Sardis. The attribution draws on Eusebius, who lists a work by Melito called "The Key", but that work is lost. The surviving Latin text is generally regarded as a later medieval compilation, probably from the early Middle Ages, though its exact date is uncertain. It is arranged by subject. Each entry takes a scriptural term, such as the head, eyes or right hand of the Lord, gives its spiritual or allegorical meaning, and supports it with biblical quotations.

This apologetic discourse survives in Syriac and is presented as an address by Melito, the second-century bishop of Sardis, to "Antoninus Caesar." Scholars generally regard it as pseudonymous and distinct from Melito's lost Greek apology to Marcus Aurelius. Its date and original language are uncertain, though it is usually placed in the late second or third century. The speaker urges the emperor to turn from error to the knowledge of the one true God. He attacks idolatry and explains pagan deities as deified human beings. It is an important witness to early Syriac Christian apologetic.

The Oration on the Palms is a Greek festal homily for Palm Sunday, celebrating Christ's triumphal entry into Jerusalem. Its preacher calls the faithful from the Lenten fast to rejoice, and draws on the prophets and the Gospels to praise Christ as the victorious King. It has come down under the name of Methodius of Olympus, the bishop and martyr of the early fourth century. Scholars generally regard the attribution as spurious, and its true author and date are unknown. It is probably a later work, perhaps from between the fifth and seventh centuries.

The Oration on the Palms is a Greek festal homily for Palm Sunday, celebrating Christ's triumphal entry into Jerusalem. Its preacher calls the faithful from the Lenten fast to rejoice, and draws on the prophets and the Gospels to praise Christ as the victorious King. It has come down under the name of Methodius of Olympus, the bishop and martyr of the early fourth century. Scholars generally regard the attribution as spurious, and its true author and date are unknown. It is probably a later work, perhaps from between the fifth and seventh centuries.

This short Greek text summarises the Acts of the Apostles chapter by chapter. It belongs to the Euthalian apparatus, the body of prologues, chapter lists and reading aids attached to the Acts and Epistles in many New Testament manuscripts. It has sometimes been attributed to Pamphilus of Caesarea, but the attribution is doubtful, and the date of the apparatus is disputed. Its author follows Luke's narrative, marks whole chapters with letters of the alphabet and marks their subdivisions with asterisks. The work shows how early Christian scholars divided the biblical text and made it easier to consult.

Against All Heresies (Adversus omnes haereses) is a short Latin catalogue of thirty-two heresies, long transmitted as an appendix to Tertullian's De praescriptione haereticorum. Scholars agree it is not by Tertullian. Its author and date are uncertain, and Victorinus of Pettau has been suggested. After briefly setting aside Jewish sects such as the Sadducees and Pharisees, it summarizes Christian heresies from Simon Magus onward, including the Gnostic teachers. It is widely thought to depend on Hippolytus's lost Syntagma, which makes it an important witness to early heresiology alongside Philastrius and Epiphanius.

This anonymous Latin poem retells the opening chapters of the Book of Genesis in verse, starting with the six days of creation. It was handed down among works wrongly credited to Tertullian, and is sometimes called the Carmen de Genesi. Who wrote it is uncertain. At one time it was credited to Juvencus. It is also often linked with Cyprian the Gaul, an early fifth-century poet who put the first books of the Bible into Latin hexameters. It belongs to the late antique tradition of biblical epic, which retold Scripture in the forms of classical poetry.

A Strain of the Judgment of the Lord (Carmen de judicio Domini) is an anonymous Latin poem in hexameters. It has been handed down among the works wrongly attributed to Tertullian, and its real author and date are unknown. It is generally placed somewhere between the fourth and sixth centuries. The poem opens with a classical appeal to the Muses and goes on to praise God as Creator of nature and humanity. It then turns to death, the resurrection and the final judgment, with the rewards of the righteous and the punishment of the wicked.

The Carmen adversus Marcionitas is an anonymous Latin poem in five books of hexameters against the teachings of Marcion and his followers. It was long transmitted among the works of Tertullian but is not by him. Its author and date are uncertain: it is usually placed between the fourth and fifth centuries, and some scholars have suggested Commodian. The poem defends the unity of God, the resurrection of the flesh and the harmony of the Old and New Testaments. It also gives a list of the early bishops of Rome.

The Carmen de Iona et Ninive, also called De Iona propheta, is a short Latin poem in hexameters retelling the story of the prophet Jonah. It was once transmitted among the works of Tertullian but is not by him. Its author and date are uncertain; some scholars attribute it to Cyprianus Gallus. It opens by recalling the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, then describes how God sent Jonah to warn sinful Nineveh. Jonah tries to flee, fearing that God's mercy will make his prophecy come to nothing. The poem is often grouped with the companion Carmen de Sodoma.

The Carmen de Sodoma (Poem on Sodom) is an anonymous Latin poem in hexameters retelling the destruction of Sodom from Genesis 19. It has come down among works wrongly attributed to Tertullian and Cyprian. Its real author and date are uncertain, though some scholars attribute it to Cyprianus Gallus. The poem notes that after the Flood God promised never again to punish by water. It then describes how Sodom's renewed wickedness was punished by fire, which it presents as a foreshadowing of the final judgment. It is an example of early Latin biblical epic.

The Apology of Quadratus is the earliest known Christian apology. Quadratus wrote it in Greek and addressed it to the Emperor Hadrian, probably around 124–125, when Hadrian visited Athens. Only one short passage survives, quoted by Eusebius in his Ecclesiastical History. In it Quadratus argues that the Saviour's miracles were real and lasting: people Christ had healed or raised from the dead stayed alive long after his time on earth, and some survived into the author's own day. It is uncertain whether this apologist was the same person as Quadratus, bishop of Athens.

The Report of Pilate (Anaphora Pilati) is an anonymous Greek apocryphon from the Pilate cycle, preserved in two forms and usually dated, uncertainly, to the fourth or fifth century. It is presented as a letter from Pontius Pilate to the emperor in Rome, describing the miracles of Jesus, his trial and crucifixion at the demand of the Jews, the darkness and earthquake that followed, and his resurrection. It often circulates with the Acts of Pilate and the Paradosis Pilati. Together these texts reflect a growing early Christian tradition that presented Pilate as a reluctant witness to Christ.

The Greek Apocalypse of Ezra is an anonymous Christian pseudepigraphon attributed to the prophet Ezra (Esdras). Its date is very uncertain, with estimates ranging from the second to the ninth century. It draws heavily on the Jewish apocalypse known as 4 Ezra. After fasting, Ezra is taken up to heaven, where he argues with God for mercy on sinners. Angels then guide him through the punishments of the damned, and he is shown a description of the Antichrist. The work belongs to the tradition of Christian apocalypses that describe journeys through heaven and hell.

The Revelation of John, also called the Apocryphal Apocalypse of John, is an anonymous Greek apocalypse falsely attributed to John the Apostle. Its date is uncertain, with proposals ranging from late antiquity to the early Middle Ages. Set on Mount Tabor after the Ascension, it is written as a dialogue in which John asks Christ about the end of the world. It covers the Antichrist, the resurrection, the Last Judgement and the fate of creation. It survives in Greek and was widely copied in Byzantine circles.

The Apocalypse of Moses is the Greek version of the Life of Adam and Eve. It is an anonymous apocryphal narrative presented as a revelation given to Moses through the archangel Michael. It tells of Adam and Eve after their expulsion from paradise, including Abel's murder, Adam's final illness, Eve's own account of the Fall, Adam's death and burial, and the promise of resurrection. Its date and origin are disputed. Some scholars see a Jewish work of the first century, while others regard it as a Christian Greek composition from as late as the fifth century.

The Apocalypse of Paul, also called the Visio Pauli, is an anonymous apocryphal apocalypse probably written in Greek in the late fourth century. It claims to be a revelation found under Paul's house in Tarsus in the reign of Theodosius. It expands on 2 Corinthians 12 and tells of the apostle's journey through heaven and hell, describing the judgment of souls and the rewards and punishments that follow. The Greek original survives only in part. Through Latin and other versions it became widely read and shaped medieval ideas of the afterlife.

Rhodon was a Greek Christian writer of the late second century, active around 180–200. Only small fragments of his work survive, all preserved by Eusebius in his Ecclesiastical History. Rhodon was a pupil of Tatian in Rome. The main passage comes from a treatise against the followers of Marcion, addressed to Callistion. It describes divisions among them: Apelles taught a single first principle, while Potitus and Basilicus held two. It also recounts Rhodon's conversation with the aged Apelles. Rhodon also said he meant to answer Tatian's "Problems". Jerome attributed an anti-Montanist work to him, but that ascription is doubtful.

Rufinus of Aquileia wrote this Latin preface around 397–398 for his translation of Origen's treatise On First Principles (Peri Archon). In it he places his work in a line of Latin translations of Origen. He praises, without naming him, a "brother and colleague", clearly Jerome, who had translated Origen's homilies on the Song of Songs for Pope Damasus. He also explains that he altered or left out passages he thought heretics had added to the text. Because he invoked Jerome's earlier praise of Origen, the preface set off the bitter quarrel between the two men over Origen.

The so-called Second Epistle of Clement is an early Christian sermon in Greek, usually dated to the mid-second century. Its author is unknown. Tradition attributed it to Clement of Rome, but scholars generally reject that attribution. The text begins by urging its hearers to think of Jesus Christ "as of God," the judge of the living and the dead. It then calls for repentance, self-control and steadfast faith in view of the coming judgment. Often counted as the oldest surviving Christian homily, it appears alongside 1 Clement in Codex Alexandrinus and is grouped among the Apostolic Fathers.

The so-called Second Epistle of Clement is an early Christian sermon in Greek, usually dated to the mid-second century. Its author is unknown. Tradition attributed it to Clement of Rome, but scholars generally reject that attribution. The text begins by urging its hearers to think of Jesus Christ "as of God," the judge of the living and the dead. It then calls for repentance, self-control and steadfast faith in view of the coming judgment. Often counted as the oldest surviving Christian homily, it appears alongside 1 Clement in Codex Alexandrinus and is grouped among the Apostolic Fathers.

Two Greek fragments by Serapion, bishop of Antioch from about 190 to 211, survive because Eusebius quoted them in his Ecclesiastical History. The first comes from a letter to Caricus and Pontius. It condemns the "New Prophecy", or Montanism, and sends along letters by Claudius Apollinaris of Hierapolis. The second comes from a treatise on the Gospel of Peter, written for the church at Rhosus. Serapion had first allowed that gospel to be read there. After examining a copy from Docetist circles, he rejected it. The fragments are important early evidence for how Christians judged which writings were authentic.

The Sententiae episcoporum is the Latin record of the council of North African bishops that met at Carthage under Cyprian on 1 September, usually dated to 256, though some headings give 258. After letters exchanged with Bishop Jubaianus were read, Cyprian and each of the eighty-seven bishops from Africa, Numidia and Mauritania gave a short opinion in turn. All held that heretics joining the Church must be baptized. The record opposed the position of Stephen of Rome and was later debated in Augustine's writings against the Donatists.

The Shepherd of Hermas is an early Christian apocalyptic and moral work written in Greek in Rome, probably in the first half of the second century. Its narrator, Hermas, a former slave, receives revelations from an aged woman representing the Church and from an angel dressed as a shepherd. The book has three parts, the Visions, Commandments (Mandates) and Similitudes (Parables), and its central concern is repentance after baptism. The Muratorian fragment names its author as a brother of Pius, bishop of Rome. It was widely read in the early Church, and some treated it as scripture.

The Address to the Greeks is a Greek apologetic treatise by Tatian, a second-century Syrian Christian who had studied under Justin Martyr in Rome. It was probably written around the 160s or 170s, though the exact date is disputed. The work fiercely attacks Greek religion, philosophy, morals and learning, arguing that the Greeks took their arts from "barbarians". It sets out Christian teaching on the Logos, creation, the soul and demons. Its argument that Moses lived before Homer influenced later Christian apologists and chronographers.

The Diatessaron is a gospel harmony made by Tatian, a second-century Christian apologist and ascetic from the Syriac-speaking East, around 160–175. It weaves Matthew, Mark, Luke and John into a single continuous story of Jesus's life, opening with the prologue of John. Scholars disagree on whether Tatian first wrote it in Syriac or Greek. It was the standard gospel text in Syriac churches until the fifth century, when the separate gospels replaced it. The original is lost and is known through later translations and commentaries, including a medieval Arabic version.

This is a collection of passages from lost writings of Tatian, the second-century Syrian Christian apologist known for the Address to the Greeks and the Diatessaron. The passages survive only as quotations in later authors such as Clement of Alexandria and Jerome. They include lines from his treatise On Perfection according to the Saviour, which presents marriage as an obstacle to prayer. Jerome's reports call Tatian a leader of the Encratites who condemned all sexual union and held that Christ's flesh was only apparent. The fragments are important evidence for the strict ascetic views of Tatian's later years.

Ad Martyras (To the Martyrs) is a short Latin exhortation by Tertullian of Carthage, written for Christians held in prison and awaiting martyrdom. It is usually dated to around 197–203, though the exact date is uncertain. Tertullian urges the prisoners to keep peace among themselves and not to grieve the Holy Spirit. He presents prison as a place of spiritual retreat and their suffering as a contest like an athlete's or a soldier's. He also offers pagan examples of endurance. It is one of the earliest Christian writings addressed directly to confessors.

Ad Nationes ("To the Nations") is a Latin apologetic treatise in two books by Tertullian of Carthage, written around 197 and addressed to pagan readers. The first book argues that hatred of Christians rests on ignorance. It rebuts the popular charges against them and turns those accusations back on their accusers. The second book attacks pagan religion and draws on Varro's division of theology into physical, mythical and civil kinds. Its material closely parallels Tertullian's more polished Apologeticum from the same year, and it is often regarded as a preliminary version of that work.

Against Hermogenes is a Latin polemical treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in the early third century. It attacks Hermogenes, a contemporary painter and Christian teacher who held that God formed the world out of eternal, uncreated matter. Tertullian argues that an eternal matter would be equal to God and so destroy his uniqueness and sovereignty. Working closely through the opening verses of Genesis, he defends the creation of all things out of nothing. The treatise is an important early statement of the doctrine of creatio ex nihilo.

Adversus Marcionem is a Latin polemical treatise in five books by Tertullian of Carthage, written against the teachings of Marcion of Sinope. By the author's own account, it is the third version of the work. Book I refers to the fifteenth year of Septimius Severus, which dates it to about 207–208. Tertullian rejects Marcion's split between a good, unknown God and the Creator, and argues that Christ fulfilled the prophets. He then goes through Marcion's Gospel and his Pauline epistles. Because the work quotes them so closely, it is the main source for reconstructing Marcion's canon.

Against Praxeas (Adversus Praxean) is a Latin theological treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, probably written around 213 during his Montanist period. It attacks the Monarchian teaching of Praxeas, an opponent of the New Prophecy from Asia Minor. Praxeas stressed God's unity so strongly that he identified the Father with the Son and said the Father himself was born and suffered. Tertullian answered that he had "crucified the Father." Against this view, Tertullian defends one divine substance in three persons and uses the term trinitas. The work strongly shaped the language later Western theology used for the Trinity.

Against the Valentinians (Adversus Valentinianos) is a Latin polemical treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in the early third century. It attacks the Gnostic school of Valentinus by summarizing and mocking its elaborate myth of the Pleroma, its paired aeons and the fall of Sophia. Tertullian compares the sect's secrecy to the Eleusinian mysteries and ridicules its many-storeyed heavens as a kind of apartment block. He names Justin, Miltiades, Irenaeus and Proculus as his authorities, and the work leans heavily on the first book of Irenaeus's Against Heresies. It is an early Latin witness to Valentinian teaching.

Adversus Judaeos is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, usually dated to around 200. It says it was written after a public dispute between a Christian and a Gentile convert to Judaism. It argues that Gentiles share in God's grace and that the Mosaic law, including circumcision and the sabbath, has been superseded by a new law. It also argues from prophecy, including Daniel's seventy weeks, that Jesus is the promised Christ. The later chapters closely parallel the third book of Against Marcion, and whether Tertullian wrote them is debated.

The Apologeticum is a Latin defence of Christianity written by Tertullian of Carthage around 197. It is addressed to the magistrates of the Roman Empire. Tertullian protests that Christians are condemned for the name alone, without a fair hearing. He answers the charges of secret crimes, atheism and disloyalty to the emperor, and argues that Christians should be legally tolerated like other groups. Its material overlaps with his earlier Ad nationes and with Minucius Felix's Octavius. The work is best known for the line "the blood of Christians is seed."

De cultu feminarum is a Latin treatise in two books by Tertullian of Carthage, written around the beginning of the third century; its exact date is uncertain. Addressed to Christian women, it urges simplicity in dress and condemns jewellery, costly fabrics, dyed hair and cosmetics as vanity and a danger to chastity. Book I traces such adornments to the fallen angels and defends the authority of the Book of Enoch. It is often quoted for its harsh description of woman as "the devil's gateway".

De Corona (The Chaplet) is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, usually dated to about 211, during his Montanist period. It defends a Christian soldier who refused to wear the laurel crown when an imperial donative was handed out, and who was imprisoned for it. Tertullian argues that wearing garlands is rooted in idolatry and is improper for Christians, and he questions whether military service is compatible with faith. The work is often cited because it appeals to unwritten church tradition, describing early baptismal, eucharistic and other customs such as making the sign of the cross.

De Fuga in Persecutione (On Flight in Persecution) is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage. It is usually dated to about 208–212, during his Montanist period. He addresses it to a Christian named Fabius, who had asked whether believers may flee when persecuted. Tertullian argues that persecution comes about by God's will to test the faithful. He therefore condemns both flight and buying immunity with bribes. The rigorist position he takes here was later rejected by the wider Church.

De Spectaculis (The Shows) is a moral treatise in Latin by Tertullian of Carthage, written between about 197 and 202. It is addressed to catechumens and baptized Christians, and argues that they must not attend the circus, theatre or amphitheatre. Tertullian traces these entertainments back to pagan festivals and idolatry, and says they stir up dangerous passions. He ends by setting the far greater spectacle of Christ's return and the Last Judgement against them. It is an important early witness to Christian attitudes toward Roman public life.

De exhortatione castitatis is a short Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in the early third century and usually placed in the period when he was coming under Montanist influence. He addresses a fellow Christian whose wife has died and urges him not to marry again. Tertullian sets out three kinds of virginity: from birth, from baptism, and continence after marriage. He treats second marriage as a concession that falls short of God's will. The work is an important witness to early Christian debates over remarriage. It is also notable for arguing that lay people share in the priesthood.

De patientia is a short moral treatise by Tertullian of Carthage. It is usually dated to around 200–206, before his turn to Montanism. He opens by admitting that he is unfit to write on patience because he is so impatient himself. He then presents God and Christ as models of patience and traces impatience back to the devil and to the fall of Adam and Eve. The treatise also covers patience under loss, injury and persecution. It is the earliest Christian work devoted to this virtue, and Cyprian drew on it for his own De bono patientiae.

De Baptismo (On Baptism) is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage. It is usually dated to around 200, before his turn to Montanism, and is the oldest surviving Christian work devoted to baptism. Tertullian wrote it to answer a woman of the Cainite sect who rejected water baptism. He defends the power of water as God's chosen means and explains the rite. He also discusses John's baptism, martyrdom as a "baptism of blood" and who may baptize. He advises delaying baptism for young children and the unmarried.

De ieiunio adversus psychicos (On Fasting, against the Psychics) is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage. He wrote it during his Montanist period in the early third century. It defends the stricter fasting of the New Prophecy against the mainstream Christians, whom Tertullian calls "psychics", or merely carnal believers. These practices included xerophagy (eating only dry food), extended station fasts and additional fasts. Tertullian links gluttony with lust and with repeated marriage, and he answers the charge that such fasts were innovations. The treatise is an important witness to early Christian fasting practice and to the conflicts over Montanism.

De idololatria (On Idolatry) is a Latin moral treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in the early third century; its exact date is disputed. It presents idolatry as the chief crime of humanity, one that contains all other sins. It then sets out how far Christians may take part in the life of a pagan society. Tertullian condemns trades that serve idol worship, such as making images, astrology and selling incense. He also rejects pagan festivals and oaths, public office and military service. The work is an important source on early Christian attitudes toward Roman civic and religious life.

De Pudicitia (On Modesty) is a Latin polemical treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in his Montanist period in the early third century. It attacks an edict by a bishop, ironically called "pontifex maximus", which granted forgiveness to penitent adulterers and fornicators. The bishop has traditionally been identified as Callixtus I of Rome, though some scholars suggest Agrippinus of Carthage. Tertullian argues that grave sins such as these cannot be remitted by the Church. The work is an early witness to debates over penance and church authority.

De Monogamia (On Monogamy) is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage. It comes from his later Montanist period and is usually dated to the second decade of the third century. Calling himself and his fellow believers the "Spiritual", as people who recognise the new prophecy, he attacks both the heretics who reject marriage and the "Psychics", meaning mainstream Christians, who allow a second marriage. He argues that Christians may marry only once, even after a spouse dies. The work takes a harder line than his earlier writings on the same subject, To His Wife and An Exhortation to Chastity.

De Oratione is a short Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, usually dated to about 200, during his early, pre-Montanist period. It is the oldest surviving Christian commentary on the Lord's Prayer. Tertullian explains each petition and calls the prayer a summary of the whole Gospel. He then turns to the practice of prayer: forgiveness and a clean conscience, posture, kneeling, the kiss of peace, fasting on station days, the veiling of virgins and the hours of prayer. The work later shaped Cyprian's treatise on the Lord's Prayer.

De Paenitentia (On Repentance) is a short Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage. It is usually dated to around 200–206, before he joined the Montanists. He first contrasts pagan regret with Christian repentance, which he grounds in reason and God's will. He then urges catechumens to repent truly before baptism. Finally, he allows one further repentance for serious sins committed after baptism, through public confession and penance (exomologesis). It is one of the earliest witnesses to the Church's penitential discipline. Its relatively lenient position contrasts with his later, rigorist De Pudicitia.

De Carne Christi (On the Flesh of Christ) is a Latin polemical treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, usually dated to the early third century, around 206–212. It defends the reality of Christ's human body against Marcion, Apelles, Valentinus and others, who denied his flesh or claimed it was of a heavenly or psychic nature. Tertullian argues that Christ was truly born of Mary and truly suffered and died. Its companion work is On the Resurrection of the Flesh. The treatise is an important early witness to the developing doctrine of the incarnation.

De Pallio (On the Pallium) is a short rhetorical treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, usually dated to the early third century, though its exact date is debated. Addressing the citizens of Carthage, who had mocked him for giving up the Roman toga for the Greek pallium, the cloak of philosophers, Tertullian defends his choice. He builds a wide-ranging argument about change in nature, in history and in human dress. Its ornate, allusive style makes it one of his most difficult works. It ends by presenting the pallium as the garment fit for a Christian.

De Anima (On the Soul) is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, usually dated to around 210–213, during his Montanist period. It is his longest single work and is often called the first Christian study of the soul. Tertullian follows an earlier dispute with Hermogenes about the soul's origin and argues mainly against the philosophers. He holds that the soul is corporeal and is passed on from parents to children, a view called traducianism. He rejects pre-existence and transmigration. He also discusses sleep, dreams, death and the soul's state before the resurrection, drawing on the physician Soranus.

The Prescription Against Heretics (De praescriptione haereticorum) is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, usually dated to around 200. Rather than refute heretical teachings point by point, it argues on legal grounds, borrowing the Roman idea of a "prescription," that heretics have no right to appeal to Scripture at all. Scripture, he holds, belongs only to the churches founded by the apostles, whose unbroken succession of bishops guarantees the true rule of faith. The work strongly shaped later arguments about tradition and apostolic authority.

De Carnis Resurrectione is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in the early third century. It defends the bodily resurrection against Gnostic and Marcionite opponents. These opponents held that the creator of the world was opposed to the supreme God, that the flesh was worthless, and that only the soul would be saved. Tertullian argues from the dignity of the body as God's creation, from the Old Testament prophets and from Paul's letters. It is among the most thorough early Christian treatments of the resurrection of the body.

Scorpiace ("Antidote for the Scorpion's Sting") is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, written in the early third century; its exact date is disputed. It is aimed at Gnostic teachers, likened to scorpions, who spread their "poison" in times of persecution by telling Christians that martyrdom was needless and that God could not want the death of the innocent. Drawing on the Old and New Testaments, Tertullian argues that God commands and rewards martyrdom and that confessing Christ publicly is a duty. The work is an important early defence of the theology of martyrdom.

De Testimonio Animae (The Soul's Testimony) is a short Latin apologetic treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, usually dated to about 197–198, soon after his Apologeticum. It expands on that work's idea of the soul as "naturally Christian". Tertullian sets aside learned appeals to philosophers and poets and turns instead to the plain, untaught soul. He argues that its everyday sayings, such as "God grant it" and "God sees", show that people naturally know the one God, demons, and judgment after death. It is an early Christian argument that knowledge of God is natural to every person.

Ad Uxorem (To His Wife) is a Latin treatise in two books by Tertullian of Carthage. It is usually dated to around 200–206, generally before his Montanist period. Written as a kind of spiritual testament to his wife, the first book urges her not to remarry if he dies first, and praises widowhood and continence. The second book allows that if she does remarry, she must marry a Christian. It warns against marriage to pagans and ends with a well-known description of Christian marriage. The work is important evidence for early Christian views of marriage and family life.

Ad Scapulam (To Scapula) is a short open letter by Tertullian of Carthage, addressed to Scapula, proconsul of Africa, and usually dated to about 212, during a local persecution of Christians. Tertullian says Christians do not fear persecution and pray even for their enemies. He argues that worship cannot be compelled, since each person should worship according to their own conviction. He also warns the governor of divine judgement, pointing to recent portents and to the misfortunes of earlier persecutors. It is an early Christian appeal for freedom of religion.

De virginibus velandis (On the Veiling of Virgins) is a Latin treatise by Tertullian of Carthage, usually dated to the early third century and assigned to his Montanist period. Tertullian notes that he had already treated the subject in Greek. He argues that unmarried women who have reached maturity must be veiled, especially in church, against local custom that let them go uncovered. He draws on 1 Corinthians 11 and on nature, and claims that truth outranks custom. He also argues that discipline grows more complete under the Paraclete while the rule of faith stays unchanged.

The Testament of Abraham is an anonymous pseudepigraphic work, probably composed in Greek in the first or second century AD, likely by a Jew living in Roman Egypt. It survives in a longer and a shorter recension. God sends the archangel Michael to announce Abraham's death, but the hospitable patriarch refuses to give up his soul. He is given a heavenly journey showing the judgment of souls, and in the end Death takes him by deceit. Christians transmitted the work, and it was later translated into several languages.

The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs is a pseudepigraphal work presenting the deathbed speeches of Jacob's twelve sons to their descendants. Each patriarch reflects on his own life, warns against a particular vice or praises a virtue, and foretells the future of Israel. It survives in Greek and took its final form around the second century AD. Scholars still disagree about its origins. Some see it as a Jewish work later expanded by Christians, while others think it was composed by Christians drawing on older Semitic material.

The Hypotyposes, or Outlines, was a theological treatise in seven books by Theognostus of Alexandria. He was a late third-century teacher in the Origenist tradition, said to have led the Alexandrian school. The work itself is lost. It is known from Photius's summary and from a few short fragments, chiefly quoted by Athanasius. These passages teach that the Son comes from the Father's substance, as a ray from the sun, without dividing it. They also comment on the sin against the Holy Spirit. Photius criticised parts of its teaching about the Son.

This short Greek fragment comes from the synodal letter of a council held at Caesarea in Palestine in the 190s, during the controversy over the date of Easter. Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea, presided, with Narcissus of Jerusalem, Cassius of Tyre and Clarus of Ptolemais. The letter backed keeping the Paschal feast on Sunday, against the Quartodeciman custom of Asia Minor. The surviving passage, preserved by Eusebius in his Church History (5.25), asks that copies be circulated among the churches. It also notes that Alexandria keeps the feast on the same day, and that the two churches exchange Paschal letters.

To Autolycus is a Greek apology in three books by Theophilus, bishop of Antioch, addressed to a learned pagan friend and written shortly after 180. It is his only surviving work. Theophilus defends the Christian name, attacks idolatry and Greek myths and philosophy, and explains the Genesis account of creation. He also builds a world chronology to show that Moses and the prophets are older than Greek writers. The work is notable as the earliest known Christian use of the word "triad" (trias) for God, his Word and his Wisdom.

This Latin poem by Venantius Fortunatus is addressed to Felix, bishop of Nantes. It was written in the second half of the sixth century, while Fortunatus lived in Merovingian Gaul. It opens with a long description of nature reviving in spring: sun, stars, flowers, crops, vines, trees and bees. This renewal of the world is then celebrated as a sign of Christ's resurrection and triumph over hell. Lines from the poem were later taken into the liturgy as the processional hymn "Salve festa dies", which was sung widely in medieval Easter celebrations.

Victorinus, bishop of Poetovio (modern Ptuj, Slovenia), wrote this Latin commentary on the Book of Revelation in the later third century. He died as a martyr around 304. It is the earliest surviving Latin commentary on Revelation and works through the book's visions and symbols in sequence. Victorinus read the visions as recapitulation: the same events are retold in different images, not given in strict chronological order. The commentary openly teaches millennialism. Jerome later produced a revised version that softened its chiliastic passages, and that revision circulated widely.

On the Creation of the World (De fabrica mundi) is a short Latin treatise, surviving only as a fragment, by Victorinus, bishop of Poetovio (modern Ptuj, Slovenia), who was martyred around 304. It reflects on the six days of creation and the seventh day of rest in Genesis. It draws out the symbolism of the number seven and links the days of creation to events in Christ's life. It is an early example of Latin biblical exegesis and of millenarian thought, and is one of the few works by Victorinus to survive.

The Apocalypse of Paul, known in Latin as the Visio Pauli, is an anonymous apocryphal apocalypse probably written in Greek in the late fourth century. It builds on Paul's rapture to the third heaven in 2 Corinthians 12 and describes his guided tour of heaven and hell, the judgement of souls at death, and the punishment of sinners, including unworthy clergy and monks. A prologue claims it was found in Paul's house at Tarsus under Theodosius. Latin, Syriac and other versions made it widely read in the Middle Ages, and Dante probably knew it.

The Apostolic Constitutions is a Greek church order in eight books. It claims to give the apostles' own instructions, handed on through Clement of Rome. It was actually compiled around 375–380, probably in Syria, perhaps at Antioch. The compiler is unknown but is often identified with the interpolator of the Pseudo-Ignatian letters. The work reworks earlier sources, chiefly the Didascalia Apostolorum and the Didache. It covers Christian morals, clergy, liturgy and church discipline. Book 8 includes a complete eucharistic liturgy and the Apostolic Canons, which makes the collection valuable for the history of early Christian worship.

The Badarak (Classical Armenian Patarag, "offering") is the eucharistic liturgy of the Armenian Church. It is anonymous and grew over several centuries. Tradition links its beginnings to Gregory the Illuminator and Nerses the Great, and its fuller arrangement to the fifth-century scholars who translated the Bible into Armenian. It draws on Cappadocian and Byzantine models, including the liturgies associated with Basil and John Chrysostom, and its anaphora bears the name of Athanasius. Its exact date of composition is uncertain. It is still the central act of worship in Armenian Christianity.

1 Chronicles is the first half of the Book of Chronicles, a Hebrew scriptural history that the Septuagint divided into two books and called Paralipomenon. Tradition ascribed it to Ezra. Modern scholars instead attribute it to an anonymous priestly author, "the Chronicler," writing in Jerusalem in the Persian or early Hellenistic period. It opens with genealogies from Adam to the exiles who returned from Babylon. It then narrates the death of Saul and the reign of David, stressing the ark, the Levites and the preparations for the Temple.

The First Epistle to the Corinthians is a letter of the New Testament written in Greek by the apostle Paul, with Sosthenes named as co-sender, to the church he had founded at Corinth. It was probably written from Ephesus around 53–57. Paul responds to reports of factions and to questions from the community about sexual morality, marriage, food offered to idols, conduct in worship, the Lord's Supper and spiritual gifts. It includes the celebrated hymn to love (chapter 13) and the earliest extended teaching on the resurrection (chapter 15).

1 Esdras, also called Greek Esdras or 3 Esdras (its Vulgate title), is an anonymous book of the Septuagint. It retells material found in 2 Chronicles 35–36, Ezra and part of Nehemiah: from Josiah's Passover, through the return from exile and the rebuilding of the Temple, to Ezra's reading of the Law. Its best-known addition is the contest of three guards at the court of Darius, which Zerubbabel wins. It is probably of the second century BC. Eastern churches accept it as canonical, but in the West it is counted among the apocrypha.

The First Epistle of John is a New Testament writing in Greek, the first of the three Johannine epistles. It names no author.
