Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is disputed, and many scholars place it within the Johannine community around 85–100. It reads more like a homily than a letter. It teaches that God is light and God is love, and that believers must confess their sins and love one another. It also rejects those who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. Its theology of love and fellowship has strongly shaped Christian thought.

1 Kings is the first half of the Book of Kings in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint and Vulgate tradition calls it 3 Kingdoms (Regnorum III). The anonymous work belongs to the Deuteronomistic history. Scholars generally date a first edition to the late seventh century BC and a final edition to the mid-sixth. It tells of David's death and Solomon's accession and reign, including the building of the Jerusalem Temple. It then covers the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam and Jeroboam and the later kings of Israel and Judah, ending with Elijah's conflict with Ahab.

1 Maccabees is an anonymous historical book, probably written in Hebrew in the Hasmonean kingdom in the late second century BC. The Hebrew original is lost, and the book survives in the Greek of the Septuagint. It begins with Alexander the Great's conquests and goes on to tell of Antiochus IV Epiphanes' decrees against Jewish practice and the revolt led by Mattathias and his sons, chiefly Judas Maccabeus. It ends with Simon as high priest, about 134 BC. Catholic and Orthodox churches accept it as deuterocanonical scripture, but it is not part of the Hebrew Bible.

The First Epistle of Peter is a letter in the New Testament, one of the Catholic Epistles. Its author presents himself as the apostle Peter, writing from "Babylon", probably meaning Rome. Many scholars, however, think it came from a Roman Christian circle linked to Peter, sometime around 60–90. It is addressed to Christians scattered across Asia Minor who were suffering persecution. The letter urges them to keep hope, holiness and patient endurance, modelled on the sufferings of Christ. It also gives household instructions and contains a famous passage on Christ preaching to the "spirits in prison".

1 Samuel is the first half of the Book of Samuel in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint calls it 1 Kingdoms and the Vulgate 1 Kings. It is anonymous. Jewish tradition credits it to the prophet Samuel, with additions by Gad and Nathan. Modern scholars see it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, put together from older sources around the seventh to sixth centuries BC. It tells of Samuel's birth to Hannah and his career as a prophet, the fortunes of the Ark of the Covenant, Saul's anointing and rejection as Israel's first king, and David's rise.

The First Epistle to the Thessalonians is a letter of the New Testament sent by the apostle Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, to the Christian community he had founded at Thessalonica in Macedonia. It was probably written around 50–52, most likely from Corinth. Scholars widely accept it as authentic, and it is often regarded as the earliest surviving Christian writing. Paul gives thanks for the converts' faith under persecution and defends his own conduct among them. He urges them to live holy lives and addresses the fate of believers who have died before the Lord's return.

The First Epistle to Timothy is a New Testament letter written in Greek and addressed by the apostle Paul to his co-worker Timothy, who had been left at Ephesus. With 2 Timothy and Titus it forms the Pastoral Epistles. It warns against false teachers, gives directions on prayer and worship, and sets out qualifications for bishops and deacons and rules on widows and elders. Pauline authorship is disputed. Many scholars date it to the late first or early second century. It was important for later teaching on church order and ministry.

2 Chronicles is the second half of the Book of Chronicles in the Hebrew Bible, which was divided into two books in the Septuagint. Greek and Latin tradition calls it Paralipomenon. It is anonymous. Tradition credited it to Ezra, but scholars attribute it to an unknown "Chronicler" writing in the Persian or early Hellenistic period. It tells the story of Solomon's reign and the building of the Temple, then follows the kings of Judah to the Babylonian exile. It ends with the edict of Cyrus allowing the exiles to return.

The Second Epistle to the Corinthians is a New Testament letter written in Greek by the apostle Paul, with Timothy named as co-sender. It is addressed to the church at Corinth and the Christians of Achaia, and is usually dated about 55–57. Paul writes about comfort in suffering and defends his apostolic ministry. He also urges a collection for the church in Jerusalem and confronts rival "super-apostles." Many scholars think it combines parts of several letters. It was translated early into Syriac, Latin, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian and Georgian.

The Second Epistle of John is a short New Testament letter. Its author calls himself "the elder" and writes to "the elect lady and her children", which most readers take to mean a local church. Tradition ascribes it to the apostle John, but the authorship is disputed. It is usually dated to the late first century. The letter urges mutual love and obedience to the commandments. It warns against deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh and forbids welcoming them.

2 Kings is the second half of the Book of Kings in the Hebrew Bible. In the Septuagint and later Greek and Latin tradition it is called 4 Kingdoms. The anonymous work closes the Deuteronomistic history. It runs from Elijah's last days and Elisha's ministry through the fall of Samaria to Assyria and the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah. It ends with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and Jehoiachin's release in exile. Scholars generally date a first edition to the late seventh century BC and a final edition to the mid-sixth.

2 Maccabees is an anonymous Jewish history written in Koine Greek, probably in Hellenistic Egypt in the late second century BC. It presents itself as an abridgement of a five-volume work by Jason of Cyrene. Two prefatory letters urge Egyptian Jews to keep the feast of the Temple's purification. The book then tells of the persecution under Antiochus IV Epiphanes and the revolt of Judas Maccabeus, ending with Nicanor's defeat in 161 BC. Its martyr stories, and its teaching on resurrection and prayer for the dead, influenced Christian thought. It is deuterocanonical in Catholic and Orthodox churches.

The Second Epistle of Peter is a short letter in the New Testament. Its author presents himself as the apostle Simon Peter, but most modern scholars consider it pseudonymous and date it to roughly 80–120, which may make it the latest New Testament book. It urges believers to grow in virtue and become "partakers of the divine nature," warns against false teachers, and defends the expectation of Christ's return. It overlaps closely with the Epistle of Jude, and its place in the canon was disputed in the early Church.

2 Samuel is the second half of the Book of Samuel in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint and Vulgate count it as the second Book of Kingdoms or Kings. It tells of David's reign, from his lament for Saul and Jonathan to his rule over Judah and Israel, his capture of Jerusalem, God's promise of a lasting dynasty, his sin with Bathsheba, and Absalom's revolt. Jewish tradition credits it to Samuel, Gad and Nathan. Modern scholars treat it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, compiled about 630–540 BC from older sources.

The Second Epistle to the Thessalonians is a short letter of the New Testament. It names Paul, Silvanus and Timothy as its senders and is addressed to the Christian community at Thessalonica in Macedonia. It encourages believers suffering persecution and promises God's just judgement when the Lord Jesus is revealed. It corrects the claim that the day of the Lord has already come, describing a "man of lawlessness" who must appear first. It also warns against idleness. Scholars disagree about whether Paul wrote it. Dates proposed range from about 50 to near the end of the first century.

The Second Epistle to Timothy is a New Testament letter. It is one of the three Pastoral Epistles and is presented as written by the apostle Paul to his co-worker Timothy. Many scholars think it was written by a later follower of Paul in the late first century, while others accept that Paul wrote it during his final imprisonment in Rome. It is framed as Paul's last charge: Timothy should endure hardship, guard sound teaching and resist false teachers. It contains the statement that all Scripture is inspired by God, and Paul's farewell, "I have fought the good fight."

The Third Epistle of John is the shortest book of the New Testament. It is a private letter from an author who calls himself "the elder" to a Christian named Gaius. Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is debated, and it is usually dated to the late first century. The elder praises Gaius for welcoming travelling missionaries and condemns Diotrephes for refusing to receive them and for seeking preeminence. He also recommends Demetrius. The letter sheds rare light on authority and hospitality in the early church. Some early churches questioned whether it belonged in the canon.

3 Maccabees is an anonymous Jewish work composed in Koine Greek, probably in Egypt during the first century BC. Despite its title, it has nothing to do with the Maccabean Revolt. It tells how Ptolemy IV Philopator, after his victory at Raphia, was prevented by divine power from entering the Jerusalem Temple. He then turned against the Jews of Egypt and ordered them trampled by elephants, but God delivered them, and a festival was founded in thanksgiving. The book is regarded as scripture in the Eastern Orthodox, Armenian and Syriac churches.

The Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament. It forms the second half of a two-volume work with the Gospel of Luke and is addressed, like that Gospel, to Theophilus. Tradition names Luke, a companion of Paul, as its author, though scholars disagree about this; it is usually dated around 80–90. Acts begins with Christ's ascension and Pentecost and describes the early Jerusalem church. It then follows the spread of the gospel to the Gentiles, mostly through Paul's missionary journeys, and ends with his imprisonment in Rome.

Amos is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is the third of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew order and the second in the Septuagint. It is attributed to Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah. He preached in the northern kingdom of Israel around 760–750 BC, under Jeroboam II and Uzziah. Its nine chapters announce oracles against the surrounding nations and then against Israel itself. They condemn oppression of the poor, empty worship and injustice. Scholars debate how much of the book's account of the prophet is historical.

The Book of Baruch is a short book of Jewish scripture attributed to Baruch son of Neriah, the scribe of the prophet Jeremiah. Its real author is anonymous, and scholars date it to roughly the second century BC. It is set among the Babylonian exiles and contains a confession of sin, a poem in praise of wisdom identified with the Law, and words of comfort to Jerusalem. It survives in Greek, though parts may have been translated from Hebrew. Part of the Septuagint, it is canonical for Catholic and Orthodox Christians but counted among the Apocrypha by Jews and Protestants.

The Epistle to the Colossians is a New Testament letter addressed to the Christian community at Colossae in Phrygia, Asia Minor. It names Paul and Timothy as senders, but many scholars doubt that Paul wrote it, and its date is uncertain. It is usually placed between about 58 and 80. The letter presents Christ as supreme over all creation and powers. It warns against a local "philosophy" involving ascetic and ritual practices and gives instructions for Christian households. Its close parallels with Ephesians have long attracted scholarly attention.

The Book of Daniel is a biblical apocalypse set during the Babylonian exile in the 6th century BC. Most scholars date its final form to about 167–163 BC, during the persecution under Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Its six court tales (chapters 1–6), written mostly in Aramaic, tell of Daniel and his companions at the Babylonian and Persian courts. Four visions follow (chapters 7–12), written mainly in Hebrew. The Greek versions, the Old Greek and Theodotion, add Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, and the Prayer of Azariah. Daniel strongly shaped Jewish and Christian apocalyptic thought.

Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Torah and of the Christian Old Testament, is presented as Moses' farewell speeches to Israel on the plains of Moab before they enter the Promised Land. It reviews the wilderness wanderings, restates the law, and calls Israel to stay faithful to God. It ends with the Song and Blessing of Moses and his death. Tradition credited Moses with writing it, but most scholars date it to the 7th–5th centuries BC. It contains the Shema (6:4), which Jesus quoted as the greatest commandment.

Ecclesiastes (Hebrew Qoheleth, "the Preacher" or "Teacher") is a book of wisdom literature in the Ketuvim of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. Tradition attributes it to Solomon, but most scholars date it to roughly the fifth to second centuries BC, partly because of its late Hebrew and Persian loanwords. Its speaker reflects on how fleeting and "vain" human toil, wisdom and pleasure are "under the sun," since death comes to all. He recommends enjoying life's simple gifts from God, and the book closes by urging the reader to fear God and keep his commandments.

The Epistle to the Ephesians is a New Testament letter written in Greek and addressed under the name of the apostle Paul to Christians at Ephesus. The words "at Ephesus" are missing from some early manuscripts. Many scholars think a later disciple wrote it, perhaps around 80–90, while others hold that Paul wrote it during his imprisonment around 60–62. Its main themes are God's eternal plan to unite all things in Christ, the Church as Christ's body, and the reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles. It ends with moral teaching, including household codes and the image of the "armour of God."

Esther is an anonymous book of the Hebrew Bible, one of the Five Scrolls (Megillot) among the Writings, and part of the Christian Old Testament. Its date is uncertain, usually placed in the Persian or early Hellenistic period. Set at the court of the Persian king Ahasuerus, it tells how the Jewish queen Esther and her cousin Mordecai foil Haman's plot to destroy the Jews, and it explains the origin of the festival of Purim. The Hebrew text never names God explicitly. The Greek version adds several passages, including prayers, that are accepted as canonical in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

Exodus is the second book of the Bible and of the Pentateuch. Tradition ascribes it to Moses, but modern scholars think it took shape from earlier sources and oral traditions during and after the Babylonian exile, with final revision in the Persian period. It tells how the Israelites were enslaved in Egypt and freed under Moses. It goes on to describe the covenant and the giving of the Law at Mount Sinai, and the building of the Tabernacle. Passover and the crossing of the Red Sea became central images for Jewish and Christian interpreters alike.

The Book of Ezekiel is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It follows Isaiah and Jeremiah among the major prophets. It presents itself as the visions and oracles of Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, dated between about 593 and 571 BC, though its final form reflects a longer process of composition. It has three main parts: judgment on Israel, oracles against the nations and promises of restoration. These include the valley of dry bones and the new Temple. Its throne-chariot vision shaped later Jewish mysticism and Christian apocalyptic and exegetical tradition.

The Book of Ezra is a book of the Hebrew Bible and Christian Old Testament, written in Hebrew and Aramaic and originally joined with Nehemiah as a single work. Its author is unknown; tradition credits Ezra himself. It tells how Cyrus allowed the exiles to return from Babylon in 538 BC and how the Temple in Jerusalem was rebuilt and dedicated in 515 BC. It then follows the scribe and priest Ezra's mission to reform the community, including his campaign against marriages with non-Jews.

The Epistle to the Galatians is a letter of the apostle Paul to the churches of Galatia in Asia Minor, written in Greek around the middle of the first century. Its exact date and the location of its recipients are disputed. Paul defends his apostolic authority and his gospel against teachers who urged Gentile converts to be circumcised and keep the Mosaic law. He argues that people are justified through faith in Christ, not works of the law. A central text for Christian ideas of grace and freedom, it was translated early into Syriac, Latin, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian and Georgian.

Genesis is the first book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, and the opening book of the Torah, or Pentateuch. Tradition names Moses as its author. Most modern scholars instead see it as an anonymous composite work that took its final form during or after the Babylonian exile, perhaps in the fifth century BC. Its first part (chapters 1–11) tells of the creation, the fall, the flood and the early history of humanity. Its second part (chapters 12–50) follows the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. Church Fathers wrote many commentaries and homilies on it.

The Book of Habakkuk is the eighth of the Twelve Minor Prophets of the Hebrew Bible. It is attributed to the prophet Habakkuk and is usually dated to the late seventh century BC, probably during the reign of Jehoiakim of Judah (609–597 BC). In the first two chapters the prophet speaks with God about injustice and the coming Chaldean (Babylonian) invasion. The third chapter is a liturgical prayer, and scholars disagree about whether it has the same author. Habakkuk 2:4, "the just shall live by his faith," became central to Christian thought through Paul's letters.

The Book of Haggai is a short prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible. It is the tenth of the Twelve Minor Prophets. Its two chapters contain oracles that the prophet Haggai delivered in Jerusalem in 520 BC, the second year of the Persian king Darius I. Haggai addresses the governor Zerubbabel, the high priest Joshua and the people who had returned from exile in Babylon. He urges them to rebuild the ruined Temple and blames the land's poor harvests on their neglect of it. He also promises future glory for the Temple and for Zerubbabel.

The Epistle to the Hebrews is a New Testament book written in highly polished Greek, usually dated between about 65 and 90. It does not name its author. It was long attributed to Paul the Apostle and placed among his letters, though this was doubted in antiquity and most modern scholars regard the author as unknown. Its sermon-like argument presents Christ as the Son, superior to the angels and Moses, and as the eternal high priest of a new covenant. It urges its readers to persevere in faith despite persecution.

The Book of Hosea is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is traditionally first among the Twelve Minor Prophets and is attributed to Hosea son of Beeri, an eighth-century BC prophet of the northern Kingdom of Israel. Its fourteen chapters condemn Israel's worship of other gods. They compare the people's unfaithfulness to Yahweh with the infidelity of Hosea's wife Gomer, and they promise eventual reconciliation. Much of the book probably dates to the time of Jeroboam II, though scholars dispute how far later editors shaped it.

The Book of Isaiah is the first of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the first of the major prophets in the Christian Old Testament. It is attributed to Isaiah son of Amoz, an eighth-century BC prophet in Jerusalem. Most scholars think much of it was written later, during and after the Babylonian exile. Its oracles of judgment and restoration focus on Judah, Jerusalem and the nations. Christian writers read its prophecies of Immanuel and the Suffering Servant as foretelling Christ, and quoted it more often than almost any other book.

The Epistle of James is a New Testament letter written in Greek and addressed "to the twelve tribes which are of the Dispersion." It names its author as James, traditionally identified with James the brother of the Lord, who led the church in Jerusalem. That attribution is disputed, and proposed dates run from the mid-first century to its end or later. Written in the manner of wisdom literature, it urges endurance in trials, care for the poor and control of the tongue, and teaches that faith without works is dead. Early Christians long debated whether it belonged in the canon.

The Book of Judith is an anonymous Jewish narrative, probably composed in Hebrew around the second or first century BC. It survives mainly in the Greek Septuagint, and Jerome made a freer Latin version from an Aramaic text in the late fourth century. It tells how Judith, a devout widow of Bethulia, beheads the Assyrian general Holofernes and so saves her people. The Catholic and Orthodox churches accept it as deuterocanonical. It is not part of the Hebrew canon, and Protestants count it among the Apocrypha.

The Book of Jeremiah is the second of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and one of the major prophets of the Christian Old Testament. It collects the oracles, laments and life story of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, a priest from Anathoth, who preached in Judah from the reign of Josiah until the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC. Jeremiah's followers, perhaps including his scribe Baruch, and later editors expanded the book. It warns of judgment for idolatry and promises a new covenant. It survives in two forms: the Hebrew text and a shorter Greek Septuagint version.

The Book of Job is an anonymous book of the Hebrew Bible. It belongs to the Ketuvim (Writings) and is the first of the Poetic Books of the Christian Old Testament. Its language points to composition in the Persian period, though the date is uncertain. A prose prologue and epilogue frame poetic dialogues between the righteous Job, who has lost his wealth, children and health, and his friends, followed by Elihu's speeches and God's reply from the whirlwind. The book's treatment of innocent suffering and divine justice made it a major subject of Jewish and Christian theology and exegesis.

The Book of Joel is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and one of the Twelve Minor Prophets. It names its author as "Joel the son of Pethuel", of whom nothing else is known. Its date is disputed. Many scholars place it in the Persian period, partly because it alludes so often to earlier prophetic texts. Starting from a devastating locust plague, it calls the people to repentance and announces the coming Day of the Lord. It also foretells the outpouring of God's Spirit on all people, a prophecy Peter quotes in his Pentecost sermon in Acts 2.

The Gospel of John is the fourth of the canonical Gospels of the New Testament. Tradition attributes it to the apostle John, though modern scholars dispute who wrote it. It is usually dated to about 90–100. It opens with a prologue on the divine Word (Logos) made flesh. It then tells of Jesus' signs, long discourses, farewell teaching to his disciples, passion and resurrection. Its strong emphasis on Christ's divinity made it central to early Trinitarian and Christological debate. Origen, John Chrysostom, Augustine and Cyril of Alexandria all wrote major commentaries on it.

The Book of Jonah is an anonymous Hebrew narrative and one of the twelve Minor Prophets in the Jewish and Christian Old Testament. It tells of the prophet Jonah, son of Amittai, who flees God's command to preach against Nineveh. A great fish swallows him during a storm. After he is released he preaches, the city repents, and God spares it. Most scholars date the book to the postexilic period. Jesus' "sign of Jonah" led early Christian writers to read Jonah as a type of Christ's death and resurrection.

Joshua is the sixth book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It tells how Joshua son of Nun succeeded Moses and led the Israelites across the Jordan. It narrates their campaigns to conquer Canaan, the division of the land among the twelve tribes, and Joshua's closing call to remain faithful to the Law. Jewish tradition attributes the book to Joshua himself. Modern scholars treat it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, with an early form probably written in the late seventh century BC and completed during or after the Babylonian exile.

The Epistle of Jude is a short letter of 25 verses and the penultimate book of the New Testament. It names its author as Jude, "brother of James," traditionally taken to be a brother of Jesus. Its date and authorship are disputed, though it is usually placed in the late first century. The letter urges readers to contend for the faith against false teachers. It recalls examples of divine judgment and quotes the Book of Enoch, and it alludes to a dispute over the body of Moses. It closes with a well-known doxology.

Judges is the seventh book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is anonymous: Jewish tradition attributed it to Samuel, while modern scholars see it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, with the main editing often dated to the 7th century BC and later. It covers the period between Joshua's conquest and the monarchy. The book follows a repeated cycle in which Israel is unfaithful, is oppressed, repents and is rescued by a leader. These leaders include Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson. Its closing chapters look ahead to the coming of kingship.

Lamentations is a book of the Hebrew Bible made up of five poems mourning the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians in 586 BC. Four are alphabetic acrostics. Tradition ascribes them to the prophet Jeremiah, and in Christian Bibles the book follows his. Most modern scholars reject this authorship but date the poems to shortly after the city's fall. The poems personify Zion as a bereaved widow and present the people's sin as the cause of divine judgment. Jews read the book on Tisha B'Av, and Christians read it during Holy Week.

Leviticus is the third book of the Torah (Pentateuch) and of the Old Testament, traditionally ascribed to Moses. Its anonymous text probably developed over a long period, and many scholars think it reached its present form in the Persian period, though this is disputed. Set at Mount Sinai, it consists mostly of divine instructions given to Moses for the Israelites and the Aaronic priests. These cover sacrifices, priestly ordination, purity laws, the Day of Atonement and the Holiness Code (chapters 17–26). Christian interpreters read its sacrifices and priesthood typologically.

The Gospel according to Luke is the third of the canonical Gospels of the New Testament, written in Greek, probably around 75–90. Tradition attributes it to Luke, companion of Paul, who also wrote the Acts of the Apostles, but the work itself is anonymous. Addressed to Theophilus, it tells of Jesus from the births of John the Baptist and Jesus to the resurrection and ascension. It is noted for its infancy narratives, its parables, and its concern for the poor and outcast.

Malachi is the last of the Twelve Minor Prophets and, in Christian Bibles, the final book of the Old Testament. Its author is unknown: "Malachi" means "my messenger" and may not be a personal name, and Jewish tradition identified the writer with Ezra. The book mostly dates from the Persian period, perhaps around 500–450 BC. It is written as disputes between God and the people, and it rebukes careless priests, corrupt sacrifice, divorce and unpaid tithes. Christians long read its promise of a coming messenger and the return of Elijah as foretelling John the Baptist.

The Gospel according to Mark is the second book of the New Testament and is generally thought to be the earliest of the four canonical gospels. Most scholars date it to about 65–75. Tradition attributes it to John Mark, a companion of Peter, but the authorship is uncertain. Written in Greek, it is a short, fast-moving account that runs from John the Baptist's preaching through Jesus' ministry in Galilee to his passion in Jerusalem and the empty tomb. Matthew and Luke drew heavily on it. It was soon translated into Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian, Georgian and Slavonic.

The Gospel of Matthew is the first book of the New Testament and one of the three Synoptic Gospels. It was written in Greek, probably between about 70 and 100, and is traditionally attributed to the apostle Matthew, although its author is unknown. It opens with Jesus' genealogy from Abraham and goes on to tell of his birth, ministry, teaching, death and resurrection. It includes the Sermon on the Mount and stresses Jesus as the fulfilment of Jewish scripture. In the early Church it was the most widely cited gospel.

The Book of Micah is the sixth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is attributed to Micah of Moresheth, a Judean prophet active in the late 8th century BC under kings Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. Its seven chapters alternate oracles of doom against Samaria and Jerusalem with promises of restoration. Micah condemns corrupt leaders and defends the poor. Christians read 5:2 as foretelling the Messiah's birth in Bethlehem. Scholars debate when the book reached its final form, possibly in the Persian or Hellenistic period.

The Book of Nahum is the seventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It has three chapters and is attributed to the prophet Nahum the Elkoshite. In vivid poetry it foretells the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, as God's judgement on an oppressor of Judah. Its date is debated. Many place it between the sack of Thebes in 663 BC and Nineveh's fall in 612 BC, though other dates have been proposed. The book survives in the Septuagint, the Peshitta and other ancient versions.

Nehemiah is a book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, written in Hebrew. In Jewish tradition it originally formed a single book with Ezra. Much of it is a first-person memoir by Nehemiah, the Jewish cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes. He was appointed governor of Judah and, around 445 BC, led the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls despite local opposition. The book also covers the public reading of the Law under Ezra, the renewal of the covenant, and Nehemiah's religious and social reforms. Its final form probably dates from the late fifth or fourth century BC.

Numbers is the fourth book of the Hebrew Bible and of the Pentateuch, traditionally attributed to Moses. Scholars think it has a long, complex history, and its final form probably comes from a Priestly editing in the early Persian period. It is named after the two censuses of Israel that it records. The book follows the Israelites from Sinai through their wanderings in the wilderness. It tells of their rebellions, the sending of the spies and the Balaam episode, and ends on the plains of Moab before Canaan.

The Book of Obadiah is the fourth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible. Tradition attributes it to the prophet Obadiah, of whom nothing else is known. It is a single chapter of 21 verses, the shortest book of the Hebrew Scriptures. It announces divine judgment on Edom for its pride and its betrayal of Judah, and it foresees the restoration of Israel on the day of the Lord. Most scholars date it shortly after the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC. Others think it took shape through later editing during the Persian period.

The Epistle to the Philippians is a letter of the New Testament written by the apostle Paul, with Timothy named as co-sender, to the Christian community at Philippi in Macedonia. Paul wrote it while imprisoned, possibly in Rome around 60–62, though Ephesus and Caesarea have also been proposed. Its central themes are joy, partnership in the gospel and humility. It thanks the Philippians for their gift and warns against opponents. It is especially valued for the Christ hymn (2:6–11), which describes Christ's self-emptying and exaltation and was central to later Christological debate.

The Epistle to Philemon is a short letter in the New Testament written by the apostle Paul, with Timothy named as co-sender, while Paul was in prison. It is usually dated to the late 50s or early 60s, but the place of writing is disputed. Paul addresses Philemon, a Christian whose house was used for church meetings, and asks him to receive back his slave Onesimus as a beloved brother. Onesimus had become a Christian while with Paul. Its authenticity is almost universally accepted. The letter has been central to Christian discussions of slavery, reconciliation and fellowship.

The Book of Proverbs is a book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, and a classic example of biblical wisdom literature. Tradition ascribes it to King Solomon. Scholars instead see it as a "collection of collections" from different periods, with the final redaction often placed in the Persian or Hellenistic era. In short sayings and longer discourses it sets wise conduct against folly. It teaches that "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge" and personifies Wisdom as present at creation. Christian writers widely read Proverbs 8 in a Christological sense.

The Book of Psalms, or Psalter, is an anthology of Hebrew religious poetry in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It has 150 psalms in Jewish and Western usage, with a few more in Eastern churches, and is divided into five books. It includes hymns of praise, laments, royal psalms and thanksgivings. Many psalms are traditionally attributed to David, but scholars doubt this. They were composed over several centuries, before and after the Exile. The Psalms were central to Jewish and Christian worship, and early Christian writers commented on them extensively.

Revelation, also called the Apocalypse, is the last book of the New Testament and its only full apocalyptic work. Its author calls himself John and says he received his visions on the island of Patmos. Tradition identifies him with John the Apostle, but this has been disputed since antiquity. It is usually dated to about 95, under Domitian, though some scholars prefer an earlier date. It contains letters to seven churches in Asia and visions of judgement, the defeat of evil and the New Jerusalem. Its place in the canon was long contested, especially in the East.

The Epistle to the Romans is a letter of the apostle Paul to the Christian community at Rome and is part of the New Testament. Paul probably wrote it from Corinth around 55–58, before a planned visit to Rome and a journey on to Spain. It is the longest and most systematic of his letters. It sets out his teaching on sin, justification by faith, the place of Israel in God's plan, and Christian conduct. Romans has deeply shaped Christian theology, from Origen and Augustine to the Reformation. It was translated early into Syriac, Latin, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian and Georgian.

The Book of Ruth is a short anonymous Hebrew narrative in the Hebrew Bible. It is one of the Five Megillot in the Writings, while the Greek and Christian canons place it after Judges. The date is uncertain, but many scholars assign it to the Persian period. It tells how Ruth, a Moabite widow, stays loyal to her mother-in-law Naomi, goes with her to Bethlehem and marries their kinsman Boaz. Their son Obed became David's grandfather. Ruth appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, and the book is read in synagogues at Shavuot.

Sirach, also called Ecclesiasticus or the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach, is a Jewish wisdom book. Jesus ben Sira, a scribe in Jerusalem, wrote it in Hebrew around 196–175 BC. His grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt after 132 BC and added a prologue. The prologue is an early witness to the threefold division of the Hebrew scriptures. The book offers ethical teaching, praise of wisdom and a hymn to Israel's famous ancestors. Judaism excludes it from the Hebrew Bible, but it is in the Septuagint and was widely read in the early Church.

The Song of Songs, also called the Song of Solomon or Canticle of Canticles, is a book of Hebrew love poetry, one of the five megillot in the Ketuvim. Its superscription links it to Solomon, but its real author is unknown and its date is debated; many scholars place it in the Persian or Hellenistic period. In dialogues, dreams and rich imagery, a woman and her beloved express their desire. Jewish tradition reads it as an allegory of God and Israel. Christian commentators, from Origen onward, read it as an allegory of Christ and the Church or the soul.

The Epistle to Titus is a short New Testament letter written in Greek. It presents itself as Paul's letter to his co-worker Titus, whom he had left in Crete to organise the church there. Whether Paul wrote it is disputed: many scholars see it as a later pastoral letter, dated anywhere from the 60s to around 100. It sets out qualifications for elders and bishops, warns against false teachers, and urges sound doctrine and godly conduct. Together with 1 and 2 Timothy, it is one of the Pastoral Epistles.

Tobit is an anonymous Jewish narrative from the Second Temple period, usually dated to the 3rd or early 2nd century BC and probably first written in Aramaic or Hebrew. It tells of the pious, blinded exile Tobit in Nineveh and his son Tobias, who travels guided by the angel Raphael. On the way Tobias frees Sarah from the demon Asmodeus and marries her, and Tobit's sight is restored. The short recension, preserved in Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus, is one of several ancient forms of this deuterocanonical book.

The Wisdom of Solomon, or Book of Wisdom, is a Jewish wisdom book written in Greek, probably by an Alexandrian author. Most scholars date it to the first century BC, though proposed dates vary. It speaks in the voice of Solomon and urges rulers to love righteousness. It praises wisdom as a divine spirit present with God from eternity, defends the immortality of the righteous, and retells the Exodus. It is part of the Septuagint and is counted as deuterocanonical by Catholic and Orthodox churches. Protestants class it among the Apocrypha. It shaped early Christian theology.

The Book of Zechariah is the eleventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is attributed to Zechariah, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, a prophet active from about 520 BC under the Persian king Darius I. Chapters 1–8 contain eight night visions and oracles urging the returned exiles to repent and rebuild the Temple. Chapters 9–14, often assigned by scholars to later authors, hold oracles about a coming king and the future of Jerusalem. Christian writers frequently read these passages as messianic prophecy.

The Book of Zephaniah (Latin Sophonias) is the ninth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible, a short prophetic book of three chapters. It is attributed to Zephaniah, who prophesied in the reign of Josiah of Judah (640–609 BC). Many scholars date it to that period, though others think an original core was later expanded. It announces the coming "day of the Lord" as a day of judgement on Judah and the nations, and ends with promises that a humble remnant will be restored. Its imagery inspired the medieval hymn Dies irae.

Aldhelm is a short anonymous Old English poem from the tenth century. It is macaronic, mixing Old English verse with Latin and Greek words. The book speaks in its own voice and praises Aldhelm (d. 709), abbot of Malmesbury and bishop of Sherborne, as a holy and learned author and a noble poet of the English. The poem survives with a copy of Aldhelm's prose De virginitate, which it seems to have introduced. Its showy, learned vocabulary reflects the "hermeneutic" style admired in late Anglo-Saxon England.

Alms-Giving is a short anonymous Old English religious poem of only a few lines, preserved in the Exeter Book, a late tenth-century anthology of vernacular verse. Its date of composition is uncertain. The poem praises the generous-hearted man, who wins the highest honour in the world and the best judgement before the Lord. Its central image compares almsgiving to water putting out a raging fire that threatens towns: in the same way, alms drive away the wounds of sin and heal souls. The image echoes Ecclesiasticus 3:30.

Andreas is an anonymous Old English verse hagiography of about 1,700 lines, preserved in the Vercelli Book. Its date is uncertain, but it is usually placed in the ninth or tenth century. It retells the apocryphal Acts of Andrew and Matthias: the apostle Andrew sails to Mermedonia, a land of cannibals, to free the imprisoned Matthew. He endures torture there and finally converts the people. The poem was once attributed to Cynewulf, but that view is now generally rejected. It is notable for presenting the apostles as heroic warriors and for its many verbal parallels with Beowulf.

Azarias is an anonymous Old English poem preserved in the Exeter Book. It retells the apocryphal additions to Daniel 3. In the fiery furnace of the Chaldean king, Azarias prays for God's mercy on Israel, which has been scattered for its sins, and asks him to keep his promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The poem then gives the song of praise of the three youths and their rescue. Much of it closely matches a passage in the Old English Daniel, so the two poems' relationship has been widely discussed. Its date is uncertain.

Bede's Death Song is a short Old English poem of five lines on the soul's departure. It reflects that no one is wiser than they need to be in thinking, before death, how their soul will be judged for good or evil. Cuthbert's Letter on the Death of Bede reports that Bede recited it in his final days at Jarrow in 735, though it is uncertain whether he composed it. It survives in many manuscripts in Northumbrian and later dialect forms and is among the earliest recorded English verse.

Bede's Death Song is a five-line Old English poem said to have been spoken by the Venerable Bede shortly before his death at Jarrow in 735. It survives in the letter of his disciple Cuthbert describing Bede's last days. Whether Bede composed it or only recited it is uncertain. The poem says that before the "inevitable journey" no one is wiser than he needs to be when he considers what judgement, good or evil, his soul will receive after his death-day. This is its Northumbrian form. It survives in more copies than any other Old English poem.

Bede's Death Song is a five-line Old English poem traditionally said to be the last words of the Venerable Bede, who died at Jarrow in 735. It is preserved in Cuthbert's letter describing Bede's death, which says Bede recited it. Whether Bede composed it himself is uncertain. It survives in more manuscripts than any other Old English poem, in Northumbrian and West Saxon forms. The poem says that no one is wiser than they need to be when considering, before death, how their soul will be judged.

The Brussels Cross is an Anglo-Saxon reliquary cross, usually dated to the late tenth or early eleventh century and now kept in Brussels. It carries a short Old English verse inscription in which the cross speaks: "Rood is my name. Once, trembling and drenched in blood, I bore a mighty king." The lines closely echo The Dream of the Rood. A dedication follows, saying that the brothers Æthelmær and Æthelwold had the cross made to praise Christ and for the soul of their brother Ælfric.

Cædmon's Hymn is a nine-line Old English alliterative poem in praise of God the Creator. It is attributed to Cædmon, a cowherd at Whitby Abbey under Abbess Hilda. According to Bede's Ecclesiastical History, he received the gift of song in a dream. If Bede is right, the poem dates from between about 658 and 680, making it the earliest securely dateable Old English verse. This Northumbrian version is the earliest dialect form. The poem survives in many manuscripts of Bede's History.

Cædmon's Hymn is a nine-line Old English alliterative poem praising God as Creator of heaven and earth. It is attributed to Cædmon, a cowherd at the monastery of Streonæshalch (Whitby) under Abbess Hilda. According to Bede's Ecclesiastical History, Cædmon received the gift of song in a dream. If Bede's account is accurate, the poem was composed between about 658 and 680. It is the earliest securely datable Old English verse and an early example of traditional Germanic poetic form used for Christian themes. Its many manuscript copies survive in both Northumbrian and West Saxon dialect forms.

Christ and Satan is an anonymous Old English religious poem of 729 lines of alliterative verse. It survives only in the Junius Manuscript in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, and its date of composition is uncertain. The poem has three parts. The first gives the laments of Satan and the fallen angels in hell. The second deals with Christ's harrowing of hell, resurrection, ascension and the Last Judgment. The third retells Christ's temptation in the wilderness. Throughout, it contrasts Christ's power and glory with Satan's pride and misery.

Christ I, also called Christ A or the Advent Lyrics, is an anonymous Old English poem preserved in fragmentary form at the opening of the Exeter Book, a manuscript of the later tenth century. It runs to about 439 lines in twelve sections. Most sections expand on the Latin "O" antiphons sung at Vespers in the days before Christmas. They meditate on Christ's coming, the Incarnation, the virginity of Mary and the hope of redemption, using images such as the cornerstone the builders rejected. It is regarded as one of the finest works of Anglo-Saxon religious verse.

Christ II, also called The Ascension, is an Old English religious poem by Cynewulf, who probably flourished in the ninth century. It is one of four poems signed with his name in runes. It survives in the Exeter Book as lines 440–866 of the Christ sequence, between the Advent lyrics and the poem on the Last Judgment. The poem has five sections and is homiletic in character. It meditates on Christ's Ascension and draws mainly on Gregory the Great's Homily 29 for the Feast of the Ascension.

Christ III, also called Christ in Judgement, is an anonymous Old English poem of about 800 lines on the Last Judgement. It is preserved in the tenth-century Exeter Book, where it follows Christ I and Christ II. Scholars once read the three as a single poem. Its date of composition is uncertain. The poem describes Christ's sudden coming like a thief in the night, the trumpets at the four corners of the earth and the rising of the dead. It also shows the separation of the righteous from the damned, and Christ addresses sinners by recalling his Passion.

The Creed is an anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse that paraphrases the Apostles' Creed. It dates from the late tenth or early eleventh century. Each article of the Latin creed is quoted and then expanded in Old English, covering God the Father as creator, the Incarnation through Gabriel's announcement to Mary, the Passion under Pilate, the Harrowing of Hell, the Resurrection and Ascension, and belief in the Holy Spirit. It survives as part of the Old English "Benedictine Office", together with verse paraphrases of other liturgical texts. It is a witness to late Anglo-Saxon teaching in the vernacular.

Daniel is an anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse, generally dated between the eighth and tenth centuries and preserved in the Junius manuscript. It is a free paraphrase of the first five chapters of the biblical Book of Daniel. It begins with Israel's prosperity after the Exodus and its fall into pride and drunkenness. It goes on to tell of the Babylonian captivity, Nebuchadnezzar's dreams, the three youths in the furnace and Belshazzar's feast. Its version of the Prayer of Azarias and the Song of the Three Youths is closely related to the Exeter Book poem Azarias.

The Descent into Hell is an anonymous Old English religious poem preserved in the Exeter Book, a manuscript copied in the later tenth century. Its date of composition is uncertain. It opens at dawn with the grieving women going to Christ's tomb and then tells of the Resurrection and Christ's descent to break the gates of hell. John the Baptist welcomes Christ there and gives a long speech pleading for the captive souls, with prominent imagery of baptism. The poem is an important vernacular treatment of the Harrowing of Hell. Damage to the manuscript has left gaps in the text.

The Dream of the Rood is an anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse and one of the earliest examples of dream-vision poetry in English. The narrator describes a dream in which the cross of Christ appears, shifting between jewelled splendour and running blood. The cross then speaks and tells of its own felling and of the Crucifixion, where Christ appears as a young warrior-hero going eagerly to battle. The full text survives in the tenth-century Vercelli Book. Lines related to the poem are carved in runes on the eighth-century Ruthwell Cross, which suggests an earlier origin.

Elene is an Old English poem of 1,321 lines by Cynewulf. It is the longest of his four poems signed in runes, and its date is uncertain: it was probably written in the ninth century. Based on a Latin legend, it tells how Constantine won his victory under the sign of the cross. It then follows his mother Helena to Jerusalem, where she makes the Jew Judas reveal where the True Cross lies buried. It is the earliest English account of the finding of the Cross and survives in the Vercelli Book.

Exodus is an anonymous Old English poem of about 590 alliterative lines. It is often dated to the eighth century, but its date is uncertain. It retells the Israelites' departure from Egypt under Moses, ending with the crossing of the Red Sea and the drowning of Pharaoh's army. Along the way it includes a digression on Noah and on Abraham's sacrifice of Isaac. Its dense, heroic language presents Moses as a war-leader. The poem is valued for its vivid imagery and for reading the Exodus as a figure of Christian salvation.

The Fates of the Apostles is a short Old English poem of about 122 lines in alliterative verse. It survives in the Vercelli Book and is one of the four poems signed by Cynewulf, whose name is woven into it in runes. Its date is uncertain, probably the ninth century. Speaking in the first person, the poet briefly tells where each of the Twelve Apostles preached and how each died after Christ's Ascension. He closes by asking the reader to pray for him. This brief verse martyrology may have been written as a teaching aid.

The Fortunes of Men is an anonymous Old English poem of about a hundred lines, preserved in the tenth-century Exeter Book. Its date of composition is uncertain. It follows parents raising a child whose future only God knows, then lists the deaths and misfortunes some people meet: wolves, hunger, war, a fall from a tree, exile, hanging, fire and drunken quarrels. It then turns to the skills and blessings God gives to others, such as wealth, learning, music and craftsmanship, and closes by thanking God for his care of humankind.

Genesis is an anonymous Old English verse paraphrase of the biblical Book of Genesis. It runs from the praise of God and the fall of the rebel angels to Abraham's sacrifice of Isaac, and it survives in the Junius manuscript. It was once attributed to Cædmon. The poem has two parts. The longer Genesis A is usually dated to the eighth century. Genesis B is a later section translated from an Old Saxon poem and inserted into it. Genesis B is known for its vivid, heroic picture of Satan and of the temptation of Adam and Eve.

The Gifts of Men is an anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse, preserved in the Exeter Book. It was written before about 975, but its exact date is uncertain. The poem lists the varied talents God gives to people, including wealth, strength, beauty, poetry, eloquence, hunting, warfare, counsel, building and other crafts. Its point is that no one is left wholly without a gift and no one receives so many that pride follows. It recalls the Pauline teaching on gifts and is often read alongside the companion poem The Fortunes of Men.

The Gloria I is an anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse, probably composed in the late tenth or early eleventh century. It is a poetic paraphrase of the Gloria Patri, the Lesser Doxology, not the Gloria in excelsis. Each Latin phrase of the doxology is quoted in turn and expanded in English with praise of the Trinity, God's creation of the world in six days, and the hallowing of Sunday. It is one of several Old English verse paraphrases of liturgical texts that show how vernacular poetry was used in late Anglo-Saxon devotion.

The Gloria II is a short anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse. It is usually dated to the late Anglo-Saxon period, roughly the tenth or early eleventh century, though the date is uncertain. In a single sentence it gives glory and honour to the "Lord of hosts" and Father, together with the Son and the true Spirit, and ends with "Amen." In this way it echoes the Trinitarian doxology of the Gloria Patri, the Lesser Doxology. It shows how Latin liturgical formulas were adapted into vernacular verse.

Guthlac A and Guthlac B are two anonymous Old English poems in alliterative verse about Saint Guthlac of Crowland (674–714), a Mercian hermit of the Fens. They survive one after the other in the Exeter Book, copied in the later tenth century. Their dates of composition are uncertain. Guthlac A tells of the saint's life as a hermit on a fenland barrow and his struggles against demons. Guthlac B, which draws on Felix's Latin Life of Guthlac, describes his illness and death. Together they are important examples of Anglo-Saxon verse hagiography.

Homiletic Fragment I is a short anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse. It survives in the Vercelli Book, a late tenth-century manuscript, with its beginning lost. The poem has the tone of a sermon and condemns deceitful people who speak fairly but hide malice in their hearts. It draws on Psalm 27(28):3 and compares such people to bees, which carry honey in the mouth and a poisonous sting in the tail. It ends by urging its hearers to reject the corrupt world and hope for the light of heaven. When it was composed is uncertain.

Homiletic Fragment II is a short anonymous Old English religious poem of about twenty alliterative lines, preserved in the Exeter Book. Its date of composition is uncertain. It urges the listener to rejoice in God and hold firm in mind, because earthly friendship and promises fail as the world passes away. It then echoes Ephesians 4:5–6 in praising the one faith, one baptism and one eternal Father. The poem ends with the Incarnation: the Holy Spirit dwelt in the young Virgin, through whom the source of all light shone forth.

Judgment Day I is an anonymous Old English religious poem preserved in the Exeter Book, the late tenth-century anthology of Old English verse. Its date of composition is uncertain. The short homiletic poem describes the end of the world, when fire will consume the earth. It sets the endless torments of hell, where daylight never shines, against the joys of heaven prepared for the pure in heart, and urges its hearers to repent before the final reckoning. It is called "I" to set it apart from the unrelated Old English poem Judgment Day II.

Judgment Day II, also known as Be Domes Dæge, is an anonymous Old English poem of about three hundred lines, probably composed in the late tenth or early eleventh century. It is a free verse rendering of the Latin poem De die iudicii, traditionally attributed to Bede. The speaker sits alone in a grove beside flowing streams and is moved to remember his sins. He calls on himself to repent with tears and confession. The poem then describes the terrors of the Last Judgment, the torments of hell and the joys of heaven.

Judith is an anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse. Its date is uncertain and is usually placed somewhere between the ninth and tenth centuries. It survives only in the Beowulf manuscript, and its beginning is lost. Drawing on the deuterocanonical Book of Judith, it uses the diction of heroic poetry to tell how the devout Judith beheads the drunken Assyrian general Holofernes after his feast, and how the Hebrews then defeat his army. The poem is valued for its vivid style and its picture of a holy woman as warrior heroine.

Juliana is an Old English verse saint's life by Cynewulf, one of the four poems carrying his runic signature. It probably dates from the ninth century. It tells of Juliana of Nicomedia, who was martyred under Maximian. She refuses to marry the pagan prefect Heliseus, resists torture, argues with a devil in her prison cell and is finally beheaded. The poem has about 731 alliterative lines. It probably adapts a lost Latin passio and survives only in the Exeter Book, where two gaps interrupt the text. It is one of the few Old English poetic saints' lives.

The Kentish Hymn is an anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse, written in the Kentish dialect and usually dated to the tenth century. It is a free paraphrase of the Latin Gloria in excelsis, the hymn of praise sung at Mass. It opens with the angels' song of glory to God and peace on earth, then praises the Father, Christ as the Lamb who redeems humankind through his Passion, and the Holy Spirit, and closes on the Trinity. It is a rare surviving verse adaptation of a liturgical text in Old English.

The Latin-English Proverbs are a short anonymous Anglo-Saxon text that sets two Latin sayings beside Old English renderings. Its date is uncertain but is usually placed in the late Anglo-Saxon period, perhaps the tenth or early eleventh century. The first proverb lists things that decay: heat cools, brightness fades, love turns hateful and light grows dark. The second concludes that everything not eternal grows old. The Old English versions use alliteration and rhyme, so the piece shows how Latin wisdom literature was turned into English verse.

The Lord's Prayer I is a short anonymous Old English poem, a verse paraphrase of the Pater Noster in alliterative lines. It is conventionally numbered to distinguish it from other Old English versions and is usually dated to the late Anglo-Saxon period, though the exact date is uncertain. The poem keeps the order of the prayer's petitions, from the hallowing of God's name to deliverance from evil. It also adds traditional poetic epithets for God, such as "saviour of men" and "ruler of peoples." It shows how Anglo-Saxon poets turned core liturgical texts into vernacular devotional verse.

The Lord's Prayer II is an anonymous Old English alliterative poem that paraphrases and expands the Pater Noster. It was probably composed in the late tenth or early eleventh century. Each Latin phrase of the prayer is quoted and followed by a lengthy vernacular meditation in verse, praising God as ruler, judge and redeemer, and asking for forgiveness and eternal life. It is one of several surviving Old English verse renderings of the Lord's Prayer and shows how late Anglo-Saxon poets adapted liturgical texts for devotional use.

The Lord's Prayer III is an anonymous Old English poem, probably composed in the late tenth or early eleventh century. It is a verse paraphrase of the Pater noster. Each Latin petition is quoted in turn and then expanded in alliterative Old English verse. The poem adds devotional and doctrinal comment as it goes, explaining for example that the "daily bread" is Christ himself, sent to heal human souls. It is one of several Old English poetic versions of the Lord's Prayer. These show how Anglo-Saxon poets adapted core liturgical texts to the vernacular tradition of verse.

Maxims I is an anonymous Old English gnomic poem preserved in the Exeter Book, copied in the later tenth century; its date of composition is uncertain. It is sometimes divided into three sections, known as Maxims I A, B and C. It opens with an invitation to exchange wisdom and praise of God the Creator. It then strings together short, proverbial statements about God, human society, marriage, death, nature and right conduct, often in the form "X shall be…". It is a key example of Anglo-Saxon wisdom poetry, which blends Christian and Germanic traditions.

Maxims II, sometimes called the Cotton Maxims, is an anonymous Old English gnomic poem of about sixty-six lines. It survives in British Library, Cotton Tiberius B i, where it comes just before a version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. Its date is uncertain. Using the formulas "sceal" ("shall") and "byð" ("is"), it sets out how things naturally are and where they belong: kings, seasons, beasts, weapons, dragons, God and fate. It ends by reflecting on the mysteries of God's judgement and the afterlife. Like Maxims I, it is a key example of Germanic wisdom poetry blending traditional and Christian ideas.

The Menologium is an anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse, usually dated to the late tenth century. It survives alongside a copy of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. It describes the Christian year as observed in England, starting with Christmas and the start of January. It names the Latin and Old English names of the months, the major feasts of Christ and the Virgin, the days of apostles and English saints such as Gregory and Benedict, and the beginnings of the seasons. It shows how Anglo-Saxon England blended the liturgical and the natural calendar.

The Meters of Boethius are Old English alliterative poems that render the verse sections of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy. They belong to the Old English Boethius, an adaptation made between about 880 and 950. Only one of its two surviving manuscripts gives the poems in verse. One manuscript attributes the translation to King Alfred of Wessex, and this was long accepted, but the attribution is now considered doubtful. A proem presents Alfred as the teller. The first meter adds historical framing about the Goths, Alaric and Theodoric.

The Metrical Epilogue is a short anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse. It survives as a scribal colophon in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MS 41, an eleventh-century manuscript of the Old English translation of Bede's Ecclesiastical History. The scribe asks every reader, from the ruler of the kingdom down, to support the man who wrote the book "with both his hands". It prays that he may finish many more books and praise God until the end of his days. It is a rare example of a scribe writing about himself in vernacular verse.

The Metrical Epilogue is a short Old English poem in alliterative verse appended to the translation of Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care (Regula pastoralis) made under King Alfred of Wessex in the 890s. It is usually attributed to Alfred himself or to his circle. Its central image is a body of water. The Holy Spirit is the wellspring of wisdom, and through Gregory's book the Lord's well has been brought to the readers' doors. Readers are urged to draw from it carefully, mending any leaking bucket so that the water of life is not lost.

The Metrical Preface is a short Old English alliterative poem attached to King Alfred's translation of Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care (Regula pastoralis), made in the 890s. The book itself speaks. It tells how Augustine brought the work over the sea from Rome and how Gregory, the wise pope, composed it. It then says that King Alfred turned every word into English and sent copies south and north to his bishops, because some of them knew little Latin. The poem is a key witness to Alfred's programme of translation and learning.

This short anonymous Old English poem, composed around 890–900, introduces a copy of Bishop Wærferth of Worcester's translation of Gregory the Great's Dialogues, which was made at the request of King Alfred. The book speaks in the first person. It promises readers that the examples of the saints can lead them to the heavenly home. It also asks them to pray for the bishop who had the copy made, named here as Wulfstan, and for Alfred, praised as the best of treasure-givers. It is a rare verse witness to Alfred's programme of translation.

The Order of the World, sometimes called "The Wonders of Creation", is an anonymous Old English poem of about a hundred lines preserved in the Exeter Book, a manuscript copied in the later tenth century. Its date of composition is uncertain. The poem begins by urging an eager listener to question a wise, well-travelled poet about creation. It then praises God as maker of heaven, earth and sea, describes the ordered course of the sun and the harmony of nature, and ends by urging its hearers to obey the King of heaven and seek the heavenly kingdom.

The Panther is an anonymous Old English allegorical poem preserved in the Exeter Book. It is the first of three animal poems, with The Whale and The Partridge, known together as the Old English Physiologus, and it draws on the Latin Physiologus tradition. It describes the panther as a gentle, many-coloured beast, friend to all except the dragon. After eating, it sleeps for three days, then rises and gives out a sweet voice and fragrance that draw other creatures to it. The poem reads this as an image of Christ's resurrection and his victory over the devil.

The Partridge is an anonymous Old English religious poem preserved in the Exeter Book, a manuscript copied in the later tenth century. Its exact date of composition is unknown. It is the third and last part of the Old English Physiologus, after The Panther and The Whale. These poems draw Christian moral lessons from animals. Because a leaf of the manuscript is lost, only a short fragment survives. It records God's promise to return to those who turn to him in faith and calls the faithful to repent and earn a place in heaven.

Pharaoh is a short anonymous Old English poem preserved in the Exeter Book, a manuscript copied in the later tenth century. The poem's date of composition is uncertain. It is a question-and-answer dialogue of a few lines, similar to the learned catechetical exchanges found in works such as Solomon and Saturn. One speaker asks how large Pharaoh's army was when it pursued the people of God. The other replies that it numbered six hundred chariots of armed men, echoing Exodus 14:7, and that the angry waves destroyed them all. Damage to the manuscript has left parts of the text incomplete.

The Phoenix is an anonymous Old English poem of about 677 lines that survives in the Exeter Book. It was probably composed in the ninth century, though its date is uncertain. Its first part freely adapts Lactantius's Latin poem De ave phoenice. It describes a paradise in the East where seasons and decay never touch the land, and tells of the bird's fiery death and rebirth. The second part reads the phoenix as an allegory of Christ and of the resurrection of the faithful. It is a major example of Christian allegory in Anglo-Saxon verse.

A Prayer is an anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse, usually dated to the late tenth or early eleventh century. It is a penitential address to God. The speaker confesses a soul wounded by sin and asks Christ, the best of all physicians, to heal it. He contrasts the wretched man who serves the devil day and night with the blessed man who obeys the Lord. The poem then praises God's greatness, which neither all humanity nor the hosts of angels could ever fully tell. It belongs to the small body of Anglo-Saxon devotional verse.

Precepts, sometimes called "A Father's Instruction", is an anonymous Old English didactic poem preserved in the Exeter Book. It is usually dated to sometime between the eighth and the late tenth century. In it a wise father teaches his son ten times, and each lesson is introduced by a counted formula. He urges the son to do good and honour his parents and teachers. He warns him against sin, betraying friends, drunkenness, lying, anger, envy and lust for women. The poem mixes Christian morality with traditional Germanic wisdom literature and belongs among the Exeter Book's gnomic and instructional poems.

"A Proverb from Winfrid's Time" is a short anonymous Old English verse saying. It survives among the letters connected with the Anglo-Saxon missionary Boniface, whose birth name was Winfrid, and dates from the eighth century. It is written in an early Anglian spelling and is usually translated along the lines of "Often the sluggard puts off glory, every victorious undertaking; therefore he dies alone." It is a warning against putting off worthy deeds. The proverb is one of the earliest recorded pieces of English alliterative verse and an important witness to the early vernacular.

This anonymous Old English poem, often called the Kentish Psalm 50, was written in the tenth century in the Kentish dialect. It is a verse paraphrase of the penitential psalm Miserere mei, Deus, which is Psalm 50 in the Septuagint and Vulgate and Psalm 51 in Hebrew numbering. It opens with an introduction praising David as king, warrior and harpist, then tells of his sin against Uriah and Bathsheba and the prophet's rebuke. It then expands each Latin verse in alliterative verse as David's prayer of repentance.

Resignation is an anonymous Old English poem preserved in the Exeter Book, a tenth-century anthology of vernacular verse. Its date of composition is uncertain. It opens as a penitential prayer in which the speaker commits body, soul, words and deeds to God, confesses his sins and asks for mercy, patience and understanding. Later the tone shifts to a personal lament on exile, hardship and the speaker's sorrows, close to the elegies. Because of this shift, many scholars treat it as two separate poems, often called Resignation A and B.

The Rewards of Piety is an anonymous Old English didactic poem, probably composed in the late tenth or early eleventh century. It is written as a teacher's instruction to a beloved pupil and urges humility, almsgiving, wise speech, vigils and frequent private prayer. Fear of the Lord is presented as the beginning of wisdom. The poem warns that the world is nearing its end and that wealth given away after death cannot redeem a soul. It is a good example of late Anglo-Saxon vernacular moral and penitential verse.

The Riming Poem is an anonymous Old English poem of about eighty-seven lines, preserved in the Exeter Book. Its date is uncertain. It is unusual for combining traditional alliterative verse with sustained end-rhyme and internal rhyme. The speaker, who seems to have been a lord or king, looks back on a life of feasting, wealth and honour, then laments his present grief, old age and the decay of the world. The poem ends with a Christian exhortation to seek lasting joy in heaven.

The Rune Poem is an anonymous Old English poem in alliterative verse. It has 29 short stanzas, one for each rune of the Anglo-Saxon futhorc, and each stanza opens with the rune whose name it explains. The date is uncertain; scholars usually place it in the eighth to tenth century. The stanzas mix gnomic wisdom with Christian references to God and the Lord, and likely served to help readers remember rune names and their order. The only manuscript, Cotton Otho B.x, burned in 1731. The text survives only through George Hickes's printed edition of 1705.

"The Seafarer" is an anonymous Old English poem of 124 lines. It survives only in the tenth-century Exeter Book, and its date of composition is uncertain. A first-person speaker describes the hardships of a lonely winter voyage on icy seas, cut off from kin and the comforts of the hall. The poem then turns to a Christian meditation on how short earthly glory is and on hope for a heavenly home. It is usually classed among the Old English elegies, and scholars still debate whether it should be read literally or allegorically.

The Seasons for Fasting is an anonymous Old English religious poem, probably composed in the late tenth or early eleventh century. Unusually, it is written in eight-line stanzas. It begins with the fasts and sacrifices of Israel under Moses and moves on to Christian fasting. It then sets out the dates of the four Ember fasts and urges the English to keep the dates handed down from Rome rather than continental practice. It ends by condemning priests who eat and drink straight after Mass. It survives only in an early modern transcript.

Solomon and Saturn is an anonymous Old English verse dialogue, probably composed between the ninth and tenth centuries, although its date is uncertain. Saturn, presented as a learned prince of the Chaldeans, questions King Solomon. In the first poem, Solomon praises the "palm-twigged" Pater Noster, describing the Lord's Prayer as a power that opens heaven and fights the devil. The work belongs to a wider group of Solomon and Saturn texts in verse and prose. It is considered among the most enigmatic and difficult poems in Old English.

Soul and Body I is an anonymous Old English alliterative poem preserved in the Vercelli Book, a manuscript of the later tenth century. The poem's date of composition is uncertain. In it, a damned soul returns to its decaying body every seven nights and bitterly blames it for indulging the flesh. A shorter, incomplete address by a blessed soul follows. A related version, Soul and Body II, survives in the Exeter Book, making this one of the few Old English poems preserved in two copies.

Soul and Body II is an anonymous Old English homiletic poem preserved in the Exeter Book, copied in the later tenth century. Its exact date of composition is uncertain. A related version, Soul and Body I, survives in the Vercelli Book. In the poem, a damned soul returns every seventh night to its decaying corpse and bitterly blames it for indulging the desires of the flesh, while worms consume the body. Unlike the Vercelli text, it lacks the speech of a blessed soul. It urges readers to think about their soul's fate before death.

A Summons to Prayer is a short anonymous Old English religious poem, probably composed in the late tenth or early eleventh century. It is macaronic: each Old English half-line alternates with a Latin half-line, and the two languages together keep the alliterative pattern. The poem addresses a person, named only by the placeholder N., and urges them to pray to God, Christ and the Virgin Mary and to ask all the saints to intercede for their soul, so that it may reach the heavenly kingdom.

"Thureth" is the name editors give to an anonymous eleven-line Old English poem from the first half of the eleventh century. It survives only in British Library MS Cotton Claudius A. III, at the start of the pontifical known as Claudius Pontifical I. The book itself speaks the poem, calling itself a "halgungboc", a book of consecration. It asks God to protect Thureth, who had it richly decorated in honour of the Creator, and promises him eternal reward. It is a rare Anglo-Saxon example of a particular, identifiable book that speaks in its own voice.

Vainglory is an anonymous Old English didactic poem of about eighty lines, preserved in the Exeter Book. Its date of composition is uncertain. The speaker reports the teaching of a wise man learned in books, who explained how to tell God's own son from the sinner. The poem describes a proud man at a drinking feast who boasts, envies his betters and shoots arrows of malice, and sets him against the humble man. It is a notable vernacular treatment of pride, one of the principal vices of Christian moral teaching.

The Wanderer is an anonymous Old English elegiac poem of about 115 lines, preserved in the Exeter Book, a manuscript copied in the later tenth century. When it was composed is uncertain. A lone exile, having lost his lord and kinsmen, travels the wintry sea, remembers the joys of the mead-hall and reflects on the passing of all earthly things. He concludes that true security lies only with the Father in heaven. It is often read alongside The Seafarer and is valued for its blend of Germanic heroic values and Christian consolation.

The Whale is an anonymous Old English allegorical poem preserved in the Exeter Book, a manuscript copied in the later tenth century. Its date of composition is uncertain. It is the middle poem of the Old English Physiologus, between The Panther and The Partridge, and draws on the Latin Physiologus tradition of animal lore with Christian interpretations. The poem tells of the huge whale Fastitocalon, which sailors mistake for an island. When they land and light fires, it dives and drowns them. The whale stands for the devil, who deceives people and drags them down to hell.

1 Chronicles is the first half of the Book of Chronicles, a Hebrew scriptural history that the Septuagint divided into two books and called Paralipomenon. Tradition ascribed it to Ezra. Modern scholars instead attribute it to an anonymous priestly author, "the Chronicler," writing in Jerusalem in the Persian or early Hellenistic period. It opens with genealogies from Adam to the exiles who returned from Babylon. It then narrates the death of Saul and the reign of David, stressing the ark, the Levites and the preparations for the Temple.

The First Epistle to the Corinthians is a letter of the New Testament written in Greek by the apostle Paul, with Sosthenes named as co-sender, to the church he had founded at Corinth. It was probably written from Ephesus around 53–57. Paul responds to reports of factions and to questions from the community about sexual morality, marriage, food offered to idols, conduct in worship, the Lord's Supper and spiritual gifts. It includes the celebrated hymn to love (chapter 13) and the earliest extended teaching on the resurrection (chapter 15).

The First Epistle of John is a New Testament writing in Greek, the first of the three Johannine epistles. It names no author. Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is disputed, and many scholars place it within the Johannine community around 85–100. It reads more like a homily than a letter. It teaches that God is light and God is love, and that believers must confess their sins and love one another. It also rejects those who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. Its theology of love and fellowship has strongly shaped Christian thought.

1 Kings is the first half of the Book of Kings in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint and Vulgate tradition calls it 3 Kingdoms (Regnorum III). The anonymous work belongs to the Deuteronomistic history. Scholars generally date a first edition to the late seventh century BC and a final edition to the mid-sixth. It tells of David's death and Solomon's accession and reign, including the building of the Jerusalem Temple. It then covers the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam and Jeroboam and the later kings of Israel and Judah, ending with Elijah's conflict with Ahab.
