De aeternitate mundi is a Greek philosophical treatise by Philo of Alexandria, the Hellenistic Jewish writer of the early first century AD. It asks whether the cosmos can be destroyed. It sets out the opinions of earlier thinkers, including Aristotle and the Stoics, who held that the world periodically perishes in fire. It then gathers arguments that the world is indestructible. The work seems incomplete, since its closing words promise a reply to the opposing arguments. Its authenticity has been questioned but is now widely accepted. It is a valuable record of Hellenistic debates about the cosmos.

Against Flaccus (In Flaccum) is a historical and polemical treatise in Greek by Philo of Alexandria, the Hellenistic Jewish philosopher. It was written shortly after the events it describes, around 39–41 CE. It tells how Aulus Avilius Flaccus, Roman prefect of Egypt, enabled the anti-Jewish riots in Alexandria in 38 CE. It then follows his arrest, exile to Andros and execution, which Philo presents as divine punishment. With the Embassy to Gaius, it is a key eyewitness source for these events.

The Legatio ad Gaium, or Embassy to Gaius, is a Greek treatise by the Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria. It was written shortly after the emperor Gaius Caligula died in 41 CE. Philo recounts the delegation of Alexandrian Jews he led to Caligula in 40 CE, after the anti-Jewish riots in Alexandria. He also describes the emperor's attempt to have his statue set up in the Jerusalem Temple. Philo presents these events as proof of God's providence over the Jewish people. With its companion piece, Against Flaccus, it is an important eyewitness source for Jewish life under early Roman rule.

This anonymous Greek apocryphal narrative tells of John the Apostle's exile and death. It begins with Vespasian's capture of Jerusalem and Domitian's persecution, when Jews in Rome denounce the Christians to the emperor. John is then brought before Domitian, banished to Patmos, and later returns to Ephesus, where he dies peacefully. Its date is uncertain, but it is a later telling that draws on the older Acts of John, especially the account of the apostle's "departure" (metastasis). It shows how the legend of John grew and spread in Byzantine tradition.

This is an anonymous Greek apocryphal narrative about the apostle John, called "the Theologian", and is a later reworking of traditions found in the Acts of John. It tells how officials in Asia denounced John to the emperor for drawing the Ephesians away from their ancestral religion. In this version the emperor is named as Hadrian. Soldiers arrest John at Ephesus and take him to Rome, impressed by his humility and his long fast on the way. A companion of the apostle narrates the story in the first person. Its date and authorship are unknown.

The Protrepticus, or Exhortation to the Greeks, is an apologetic treatise written in Greek by Clement of Alexandria, probably near the end of the second century. It is usually seen as the first part of a trilogy with the Paedagogus and the Stromata. It exposes and ridicules the myths, mysteries and idol worship of Greek religion, and urges pagan readers to turn to the divine Logos, Christ, the "new song." Its many quotations from classical poetry and philosophy make it a key witness to early Christian engagement with Hellenistic culture.

The Paedagogus ("Tutor" or "Instructor") is a Greek treatise in three books by Clement of Alexandria, written around the end of the second century. It forms the middle part of a trilogy, coming between the Protrepticus (Exhortation to the Greeks) and the Stromata. It presents the incarnate Logos as the tutor who trains converts in Christian living. Book one sets out the religious basis of Christian morality. Books two and three give practical guidance on food, drink, dress, adornment, sexual conduct and social behaviour, drawing heavily on Stoic ethics, especially Musonius Rufus. The work ends with a hymn to Christ.

The Eclogae propheticae (Prophetic Extracts) is a collection of short exegetical and theological notes in Greek by Clement of Alexandria, written in the late second or early third century. It survives alongside the Excerpta ex Theodoto, after the eighth book of the Stromata. The notes are loosely connected. They comment on scriptural passages, especially from the prophets, and on topics such as creation, baptism, angels and spiritual powers. They cite texts like Enoch and the Apocalypse of Peter. Their exact purpose is uncertain, and they may be preparatory notes.

A Greek treatise or homily by Clement of Alexandria, written around the turn of the third century, though its exact date is uncertain. It interprets the Gospel episode of the rich young man in Mark 10:17–31. Clement argues that wealth does not of itself exclude anyone from salvation. What matters is the soul's freedom from greed and passion, and the right use of riches, especially in almsgiving. The work ends with the story of the apostle John and the young robber, which Eusebius later preserved. It is an important early Christian statement on wealth.

The Excerpts of Theodotus are a collection of notes by Clement of Alexandria, probably made around 200. They quote and summarise the teaching of Theodotus, a Valentinian Gnostic of the Eastern school, and of other Valentinians. Clement often adds his own critical comments. The notes cover the Pleroma, the Saviour, the origin of the world, the classes of humanity and baptism. They are among the most important first-hand evidence for Valentinian thought. They survive alongside Clement's Prophetic Eclogues, a related set of notes on Scripture, and some translations have printed the two together under one title.

These Greek fragments are ascribed to Gaius (Caius), a learned Roman churchman of the early third century. Most of them come from his Dialogue against Proclus, a Montanist, written at Rome under Bishop Zephyrinus and preserved only in quotations by Eusebius. They point to the "trophies" of Peter and Paul on the Vatican and the Ostian Way, attack Cerinthus's earthly millenarianism, and count only thirteen Pauline epistles, leaving out Hebrews. Excerpts from the "Little Labyrinth", a work against the adoptionism of Artemon, are also attributed to him, though its authorship is disputed.

The First Apology is a Greek defence of Christianity written by Justin Martyr, a philosopher from Flavia Neapolis in Palestine. It was addressed to the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius and his adopted sons, and is usually dated to about 150–155. Justin argues that Christians should not be punished for the name alone. He defends their morals, presents Christ as the incarnate Logos and appeals to the fulfilment of prophecy. The work contains some of the earliest descriptions of Christian baptism and the Eucharist, and it is a founding text of Christian apologetics.

The Second Apology is a short Greek defence of Christianity by Justin Martyr. It was probably written in Rome in the 150s and is traditionally said to be addressed to the Roman Senate. It was prompted by the execution of the Christians Ptolemaeus and Lucius under the city prefect Lollius Urbicus. Justin protests that Christians are condemned for the name alone and blames such persecution on demons. He also develops his teaching on the "seminal Logos" present in philosophers such as Socrates. Scholars still debate whether it was a separate work or a supplement to the First Apology.

The Dialogue with Trypho is a Greek apologetic work by Justin Martyr, generally dated to about 155–160. It presents a debate over two days between Justin and Trypho, a Jew who fled the recent war in Judaea. Eusebius places the conversation at Ephesus. The work opens with Justin's account of how he moved from philosophy to Christianity. It then argues from the Hebrew Scriptures that Christ has replaced the Mosaic Law, that prophecy is fulfilled in Jesus, and that Christians are the new Israel. It is the earliest surviving full-length Christian work addressed against Judaism.

The Epistle to Diognetus is an anonymous Greek apology for Christianity, addressed to an otherwise unknown enquirer named Diognetus. It survived among the works of Justin Martyr, but he is not thought to be its author. Estimates of its date range from about AD 130 to the later second century. The writer rejects Greek idolatry and Jewish worship and explains God's plan of salvation through his Son. The epistle is best known for its description of Christians as living in the world like the soul in the body. Its closing chapters may have been added later.

This is an anonymous Greek treatise against Montanism, the "new prophecy" from Phrygia. It survives only in fragments quoted by Eusebius in his Ecclesiastical History (book 5). The author addresses it to Avircius Marcellus, often identified with Abercius of Hierapolis. He describes preaching against the movement at Ancyra in Galatia and attacks the ecstatic prophecy of Montanus, Maximilla and Priscilla. The work is usually dated to the late second century. Its ascription to Asterius Urbanus comes from a modern editor and is not generally accepted. It is an important early witness to the Montanist controversy.

The Legatio, or Plea for the Christians, is a Greek apology by the Athenian Christian philosopher Athenagoras. It is addressed to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus and is usually dated around 176–180. The work answers three charges commonly brought against Christians: atheism, cannibalistic "Thyestean feasts" and "Oedipean" incest. It defends monotheism by drawing on poets and philosophers and argues that Christians should not be punished for their name alone. It is valued for its early account of God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit and for its strict Christian moral teaching.

The Legatio, or Plea for the Christians, is a Greek apology by the Athenian Christian philosopher Athenagoras. It is addressed to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus and is usually dated around 176–180. The work answers three charges commonly brought against Christians: atheism, cannibalistic "Thyestean feasts" and "Oedipean" incest. It defends monotheism by drawing on poets and philosophers and argues that Christians should not be punished for their name alone. It is valued for its early account of God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit and for its strict Christian moral teaching.

On the Resurrection of the Dead is a Greek philosophical treatise traditionally attributed to Athenagoras of Athens, the Christian apologist of the late second century. Some modern scholars dispute this attribution. It defends the resurrection of the body using reason rather than appeals to Scripture. It has two parts. The first answers objections, including the problem of human bodies being eaten and absorbed by other creatures. The second makes the positive case from God's purpose in creating human beings, from human nature as a unity of soul and body, and from divine judgment.

On the Resurrection of the Dead is a Greek philosophical treatise traditionally attributed to Athenagoras of Athens, the Christian apologist of the late second century. Some modern scholars dispute this attribution. It defends the resurrection of the body using reason rather than appeals to Scripture. It has two parts. The first answers objections, including the problem of human bodies being eaten and absorbed by other creatures. The second makes the positive case from God's purpose in creating human beings, from human nature as a unity of soul and body, and from divine judgment.

The Epistle of Barnabas is an early Christian Greek treatise in letter form, probably written between about 70 and 135. Early writers such as Clement of Alexandria ascribed it to the apostle Barnabas, but most modern scholars think an unknown teacher wrote it. It reads the Hebrew Scriptures allegorically, arguing that the Jewish law always pointed to Christ and properly belongs to Christians. It ends with a section on the "Two Ways" of light and darkness. Counted among the Apostolic Fathers, it was sometimes treated as scripture and appears in Codex Sinaiticus.

A letter in Greek from the church of Rome to the church of Corinth. It names no author, but it is traditionally attributed to Clement, bishop of Rome, and most scholars accept this. It is usually dated to about AD 96, although some scholars place it before 70. Members of the Corinthian congregation had deposed their presbyters, and the letter urges them to repent and to restore these leaders, who had been appointed in succession from the Apostles. One of the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament, it was read aloud in churches and copied into some biblical codices.

The so-called Second Epistle of Clement is an early Christian sermon in Greek, usually dated to the mid-second century. Its author is unknown. Tradition attributed it to Clement of Rome, but scholars generally reject that attribution. The text begins by urging its hearers to think of Jesus Christ "as of God," the judge of the living and the dead. It then calls for repentance, self-control and steadfast faith in view of the coming judgment. Often counted as the oldest surviving Christian homily, it appears alongside 1 Clement in Codex Alexandrinus and is grouped among the Apostolic Fathers.

The Epistle of Peter to James is a short pseudepigraphal letter that opens the Pseudo-Clementine Homilies. It is a Greek work wrongly attributed to Clement of Rome. In it, Peter asks James, bishop of Jerusalem, to entrust "the books of my preachings" only to tested and worthy people. He takes as his model Moses handing on his teaching to the Seventy, and he complains that his doctrine has been distorted. Scholars often link the letter to a hypothetical earlier source, the Kerygmata Petrou, which may date from the second century. The surviving text belongs to the fourth-century Clementine literature.

The Contestatio (Diamartyria) is a short Greek text that, together with the Epistle of Peter to James, comes before the Pseudo-Clementine Homilies. It is falsely attributed to Clement of Rome and its date is uncertain. In it James reads Peter's letter to the elders and lays down how the books of Peter's preachings may be handed on. The recipient must be a faithful, circumcised man who has been tested for six years. Standing beside living water, he makes a solemn adjuration to keep the books secret. The text shows the Jewish-Christian setting of the Clementine literature.

The Epistle of Clement to James is a pseudonymous Greek letter that serves as a preface to the Clementine Homilies, part of the Pseudo-Clementine literature, and probably dates from the third or fourth century. Written in the name of Clement of Rome to James, "bishop of bishops" at Jerusalem, it reports Peter's death at Rome. It then describes how Peter ordained Clement as his successor and records Peter's instructions on the duties of bishop, presbyters, deacons and catechists. The letter is an early witness to the idea of Roman episcopal succession from Peter. Rufinus translated it into Latin.

The Clementine Homilies are a Greek Christian romance in twenty books. They claim to be by Clement of Rome but are pseudonymous and were probably composed in the fourth century. Clement narrates his youthful questions about death and the world, his conversion, and his travels with the apostle Peter. These lead to Peter's discourses and debates with Simon Magus and finally to Clement's reunion with his lost family. With the related Recognitions, the Homilies reworked a lost earlier source. They are an important witness to Jewish-Christian thought and were translated into Syriac and other languages.

The Two Epistles Concerning Virginity are early Christian letters falsely attributed to Clement of Rome. They were probably written in Greek in the third century, likely in Syria or Palestine. The complete text survives only in Syriac, with Greek fragments preserved in later anthologies. Addressed to male and female ascetics, the letters praise virginity, which they say must go together with good works. They also condemn men and women ascetics living together and give rules for wandering ascetics' conduct. They are important evidence for early Christian asceticism.

This Greek work is an epitome, or abridgement, of the Pseudo-Clementine Homilies. Those homilies form an early Christian romance falsely attributed to Clement of Rome, and they recount his travels with the apostle Peter. Like its source, it opens with a letter from Clement to James, bishop of Jerusalem. It then describes Clement's youthful anxiety about death and immortality, and how his search for truth led him to Peter's preaching. The epitome was made in the Byzantine period, but its exact date and compiler are uncertain. Abridgements like this one helped the Clementine legend reach later Greek readers.

This Greek abridgment of the Pseudo-Clementine Homilies is known as the second epitome. The Homilies are a novel-like account of the travels and preaching of the apostle Peter, attributed to Clement of Rome but written by an unknown author, probably in the third or fourth century. The epitome opens with Clement's letter to James of Jerusalem. It then tells of Clement's youthful anxiety about death and the origin of the world, which led him to Peter. Its date and compiler are unknown. Byzantine epitomes of this kind usually add an account of Clement's martyrdom.

The Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, is a short anonymous Christian treatise in Koine Greek. Most scholars date it to the late first century, though some place it in the second. It opens with the "Two Ways" of life and death, a moral teaching probably adapted from a Jewish source. It then gives instructions on baptism, fasting, the Lord's Prayer and the Eucharist, and on church order, covering itinerant apostles and prophets as well as local bishops and deacons. It is the earliest known church order and an important witness to early Christian practice.

These are the surviving fragments and summaries of letters by Dionysius, bishop of Corinth around AD 170. Eusebius preserved them in his Ecclesiastical History. Dionysius wrote "catholic epistles" to churches in Sparta, Athens, Nicomedia, Gortyna, Amastris and Knossos, and to a woman named Chrysophora. In them he opposed Marcion and heresy, gave guidance on marriage and urged mercy toward penitents. His letter to Bishop Soter of Rome praises Roman charity and mentions that Clement's epistle was read in church. It also links Peter and Paul with both Corinth and Rome, which makes it an important early witness.

The Shepherd of Hermas is an early Christian apocalyptic and moral work written in Greek in Rome, probably in the first half of the second century. Its narrator, Hermas, a former slave, receives revelations from an aged woman representing the Church and from an angel dressed as a shepherd. The book has three parts, the Visions, Commandments (Mandates) and Similitudes (Parables), and its central concern is repentance after baptism. The Muratorian fragment names its author as a brother of Pius, bishop of Rome. It was widely read in the early Church, and some treated it as scripture.

The Epistle to Polycarp is one of the seven letters Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote in the early second century while under guard on his way to martyrdom in Rome. It is his only letter to an individual. Ignatius writes to Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, urging him to preserve unity, pray without ceasing, endure hardship like an athlete and care for every member of his flock. He also gives counsel on widows, slaves and marriage. The letter survives in a shorter, authentic recension and a longer, later interpolated recension.

This is a group of Greek letters falsely attributed to Ignatius of Antioch, the early second-century bishop. They are addressed to the Tarsians, the Antiochians, the deacon Hero and the Philippians, and they include an exchange with Mary of Cassobola, called Mary at Neapolis. They were composed in the later fourth century, probably in Syria, alongside the interpolated long recension of the genuine letters. The compiler is often identified with the author of the Apostolic Constitutions. The letters attack docetism and promote church order, and their Christology has been called subordinationist.

Against Heresies, originally titled Refutation and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So-called, is a five-book treatise by Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, written in Greek around 180. It sets out and refutes the teachings of various Gnostic groups, especially the Valentinians. Against them it defends the one God who created the world, the unity of Scripture, and apostolic tradition handed down through the succession of bishops. Only fragments of the Greek survive, but there is a complete early Latin translation. It is a key witness to second-century theology and to the fourfold Gospel.

These are passages from a letter that Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, wrote around 190 to Victor, bishop of Rome, apparently for the churches of Gaul. It concerns the Quartodeciman controversy. Victor had threatened to cut off the churches of Asia Minor, which kept Easter on the fourteenth of Nisan. Irenaeus urged peace. He pointed out that customs of fasting had long varied, and that earlier Roman bishops from Sixtus to Anicetus had stayed in communion with those who kept a different practice. The surviving text is preserved mainly in Eusebius's Church History.

1 Enoch, also called the Book of Enoch, is an ancient Jewish apocalyptic work attributed to the antediluvian patriarch Enoch. It brings together several sections written between about the third and first centuries BC, probably first in Aramaic and perhaps partly in Hebrew. It tells of the fall of the Watchers, the origin of the Nephilim and of evil, the coming judgement and Enoch's heavenly journeys. Aramaic fragments were found at Qumran, Greek portions survive, and the complete text exists only in Ge'ez. The Epistle of Jude quotes it, and the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Churches treat it as canonical.

The Martyrdom of Polycarp is a Greek letter from the church of Smyrna to the church at Philomelium and to all churches. It describes the arrest, trial and execution of Polycarp, the aged bishop of Smyrna, usually dated to around 155–160, though some scholars place it later. It is the earliest surviving Christian account of a martyrdom outside the New Testament. It presents Polycarp's death as an imitation of Christ's passion and gives early evidence of honouring martyrs' relics and anniversaries. It is traditionally grouped with the Apostolic Fathers.

The Sibylline Oracles are a collection of prophetic oracles in Greek hexameter verse. They are attributed to the Sibyls, the inspired prophetesses of Greek and Roman tradition. The surviving twelve books were written by Jewish and Christian authors over several centuries, roughly from the second century BC to the early centuries AD. Their contents mix apocalyptic prophecy, sacred history, moral teaching and attacks on idolatry. Early Christian writers such as Lactantius quoted them widely as pagan witnesses to Christian truth.

The Fragmenta are passages of the Sibylline Oracles, a collection of Greek hexameter prophecies attributed to the pagan Sibyls but largely written by Jewish and Christian authors. They do not survive in the manuscript books of the collection and are known only through quotation by early Christian writers, chiefly Theophilus of Antioch in To Autolycus and Lactantius. The longest fragment condemns idolatry and sacrifice to demons and proclaims one uncreated, invisible and all-ruling God. Their date and exact origin are uncertain.

The Epistle to the Philippians is a Greek letter by Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, and his presbyters, written to the church at Philippi in the first half of the second century. Many scholars think it combines two letters written at different times. It urges faith, righteousness and good conduct, warns against greed and docetic error, and draws heavily on New Testament writings. It also mentions the letters of Ignatius of Antioch. Irenaeus praised it, and it is Polycarp's only surviving writing and one of the Apostolic Fathers.

Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, wrote this synodal letter to Victor, bishop of Rome, around 190 during the Quartodeciman controversy over the date of Easter. Writing for the bishops of Asia gathered in synod, he defends their custom of keeping the Pascha on the fourteenth day of the lunar month. He appeals to the tradition of the apostles Philip and John, and of Polycarp, Melito and others. He also notes that seven of his relatives had been bishops and that he had served the Lord sixty-five years. Fragments survive in Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History.

This is a set of anonymous Greek exegetical fragments on the Psalms, preserved in Byzantine catenae and attributed to the "Seniores Alexandrini" ("Alexandrian Elders"), meaning unnamed interpreters of the Alexandrian tradition. Their date and authorship are uncertain. The surviving passages offer Christological readings of the Psalms. On Psalm 37, for example, the title's reference to the Sabbath is taken as pointing to Holy Saturday, and the psalm is read as Christ speaking in the person of humanity and bearing its sins. The fragments are evidence of early Alexandrian allegorical exegesis.

This is a collection of fragments from several unnamed early Christian teachers, the "elders" or presbyters, preserved by Irenaeus of Lyon in his Against Heresies, written around 180. Irenaeus presents some of these figures as people who had heard the apostles or their disciples. He refers to them with phrases such as "one better than us" or "a certain elder." The sayings cover the deceptiveness of heresy, the interpretation of Scripture and points of doctrine. They are valued as rare traces of second-century tradition, though it is uncertain how closely Irenaeus kept to their exact words.

The Testament of Abraham is an anonymous pseudepigraphic work, probably composed in Greek in the first or second century AD, likely by a Jew living in Roman Egypt. It survives in a longer and a shorter recension. God sends the archangel Michael to announce Abraham's death, but the hospitable patriarch refuses to give up his soul. He is given a heavenly journey showing the judgment of souls, and in the end Death takes him by deceit. Christians transmitted the work, and it was later translated into several languages.

The Testament of Abraham is an anonymous pseudepigraphic work, probably composed in Greek in the first or second century AD, likely by a Jew living in Roman Egypt. It survives in a longer and a shorter recension. God sends the archangel Michael to announce Abraham's death, but the hospitable patriarch refuses to give up his soul. He is given a heavenly journey showing the judgment of souls, and in the end Death takes him by deceit. Christians transmitted the work, and it was later translated into several languages.

To Autolycus is a Greek apology in three books by Theophilus, bishop of Antioch, addressed to a learned pagan friend and written shortly after 180. It is his only surviving work. Theophilus defends the Christian name, attacks idolatry and Greek myths and philosophy, and explains the Genesis account of creation. He also builds a world chronology to show that Moses and the prophets are older than Greek writers. The work is notable as the earliest known Christian use of the word "triad" (trias) for God, his Word and his Wisdom.

This is a Greek recension of the Lives of the Prophets, an anonymous collection of short biographical notices on the Old Testament prophets. The underlying work is often dated to around the first century AD, though its origin, Jewish or Christian, is debated. This version is traditionally ascribed to Dorotheus, bishop of Tyre, but the attribution is pseudonymous and its date is uncertain. Each entry gives the meaning of the prophet's name, the passages read as foretelling Christ, his tribe and birthplace, and where he died and was buried. Its strongly Christian reworking shows how Byzantine readers used the prophets.

The Lives of the Prophets is an anonymous Greek collection of short notices about the biblical prophets. It records where each was born, how he died and where he was buried, and adds legends and miracles. The account of Isaiah, for example, says he was sawn in two under Manasseh and links him with the spring of Siloam. Its origin is disputed. Some scholars date it to the first century AD as a Jewish work, while others regard it as later and Christian. Several Greek recensions survive, and this anonymous form is generally considered the earliest.

This is an anonymous Greek collection of short biographies of the Hebrew prophets, known as the Lives of the Prophets (Vitae Prophetarum). This recension was transmitted with scholia on the prophets attributed to Hesychius and other Church Fathers. Each entry explains the prophet's name and gives his tribe and birthplace, along with legends about his miracles, death and burial place. The core material probably comes from Jewish tradition of around the first century, though its date is disputed. It was later reworked by Christians and survives in several Greek recensions.

This anonymous Greek list names the apostles and the Seventy disciples of Christ. It is traditionally attributed to Dorotheus of Tyre, a long-lived bishop whom the preface describes as martyred under Julian, but the attribution is generally regarded as spurious and its date is uncertain. The list belongs to the same tradition as the Lives of the Prophets. It names each disciple, often with the see he held and the place of his death, beginning with James the brother of the Lord. Such lists shaped later Byzantine and Eastern traditions about the apostles.

The Address to the Greeks is a Greek apologetic treatise by Tatian, a second-century Syrian Christian who had studied under Justin Martyr in Rome. It was probably written around the 160s or 170s, though the exact date is disputed. The work fiercely attacks Greek religion, philosophy, morals and learning, arguing that the Greeks took their arts from "barbarians". It sets out Christian teaching on the Logos, creation, the soul and demons. Its argument that Moses lived before Homer influenced later Christian apologists and chronographers.

This anonymous Latin martyr account describes the deaths of Vibia Perpetua, a young noblewoman, the slave Felicitas and their companions, who were executed in the arena at Carthage in 203. At its core is Perpetua's own prison diary, written in the first person and recording her visions, together with a vision narrated by her fellow martyr Saturus. An editor framed these with a preface and an account of the martyrdom. Some have identified the editor as Tertullian, but this is disputed. The work is among the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman. A Greek version also exists.

The Preparation for the Gospel is a Greek work of Christian apologetics in fifteen books by Eusebius of Caesarea. He began it around 313 and dedicated it to Bishop Theodotus of Laodicea. It argues that Christians were right to give up pagan religion and philosophy for the Hebrew Scriptures. It surveys Phoenician, Egyptian and Greek theology and claims that Greek philosophers owed a debt to the Hebrews. It was written as a companion to the Demonstration of the Gospel, and it is valued for preserving many passages from authors whose works are otherwise lost.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek account in ten books of Christianity from its beginnings to the early fourth century. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, wrote it and revised it in several stages, finishing around 324–325. It traces the succession of bishops in the major sees and covers Christian writers, heresies, the fate of the Jews, persecutions and martyrdoms, ending with the Great Persecution and Constantine's victory. Because it quotes many earlier documents that are otherwise lost, it is a key source for early Christianity. An early Syriac translation also survives.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek account in ten books of Christianity from its beginnings to the early fourth century. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, wrote it and revised it in several stages, finishing around 324–325. It traces the succession of bishops in the major sees and covers Christian writers, heresies, the fate of the Jews, persecutions and martyrdoms, ending with the Great Persecution and Constantine's victory. Because it quotes many earlier documents that are otherwise lost, it is a key source for early Christianity. An early Syriac translation also survives.

The Martyrs of Palestine is a Greek account by Eusebius of Caesarea of the Christians who died in Palestine during the Great Persecution. It begins with Diocletian's edicts of 303 and continues to the persecution's end about 311. Eusebius lived in Caesarea at the time and witnessed many of the events, including the sufferings of his teacher Pamphilus. The work survives in two forms. This shorter recension is attached to Book VIII of some manuscripts of his Ecclesiastical History. A longer version survives mainly in Syriac. The work is an important eyewitness source for the last Roman persecution.

The Proof of the Gospel (Demonstratio evangelica) is an apologetic treatise in Greek by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, probably written in the 310s. It is dedicated to Theodotus, bishop of Laodicea, and follows his fifteen-book Preparation for the Gospel. Eusebius uses the Hebrew prophecies to argue that Christ and the Church fulfil the Scriptures, and explains why Christians follow the faith of the patriarchs rather than the Mosaic Law. Of the original twenty books, only the first ten survive, along with a fragment of the fifteenth. It is a major source for early Christian interpretation of prophecy.

Against Marcellus (Contra Marcellum) is a polemical treatise in two books by Eusebius of Caesarea, usually dated to about 336–337, after Marcellus of Ancyra was deposed by a synod at Constantinople. Eusebius attacks the book Marcellus had written against Asterius the Sophist, in which he criticised Eusebius himself and other eastern bishops. Eusebius accuses Marcellus of envy, careless use of Scripture and a Sabellian theology that denied the Son a distinct existence. The treatise preserves many fragments of Marcellus's lost work, and Eusebius followed it with his Ecclesiastical Theology.

The Letter to Flacillus is a short dedicatory letter in Greek by Eusebius of Caesarea, addressed to Flacillus, bishop of Antioch. It introduces Eusebius's three books On Ecclesiastical Theology, written in the late 330s near the end of his life. He explains that his two earlier books against Marcellus of Ancyra had simply quoted Marcellus's own words to expose them, while the new work refutes them directly. Eusebius accuses Marcellus of denying the Son a distinct hypostasis and presents his own account of the Trinity. He asks Flacillus to correct anything lacking.

On Ecclesiastical Theology is a Greek dogmatic treatise in three books by Eusebius of Caesarea, written late in his life, around 337–339. It follows his earlier two books Against Marcellus and continues his attack on Marcellus of Ancyra, whom he accuses of reviving the teaching of Sabellius by denying that the Son exists as a distinct being. Eusebius sets out what he presents as the Church's teaching on the Father and the Son. The work is an important witness to the theological disputes that followed the Council of Nicaea.

De ecclesiastica theologia (On Ecclesiastical Theology) is a Greek polemical treatise in three books by Eusebius of Caesarea, written in the last years of his life, around 337–339. It is dedicated to Flacillus, bishop of Antioch. It follows Eusebius's two books Against Marcellus, which mostly quoted Marcellus of Ancyra's own words. This work goes further and refutes them. Eusebius rejects Marcellus's teaching that the Word has no distinct existence from God and defends the Son as a real, distinct being. The treatise is an important source for the fragments of Marcellus and for the Trinitarian debates after Nicaea.

The Theophania, or "Divine Manifestation", is an apologetic treatise in five books by Eusebius of Caesarea. It was probably written in the later years of his life, though its exact date is disputed. The Greek original survives only in fragments, but a complete early Syriac translation is extant. The work argues against atheism and polytheism and presents the divine Word as creator and governor of the world. It then treats the incarnation, Christ's teaching and miracles, and the fulfilment of prophecy. Much of its material overlaps with Eusebius's Demonstratio Evangelica and his oration in praise of Constantine.

The Onomasticon, more fully On the Place Names in Holy Scripture, is a gazetteer of biblical place names in Palestine and Transjordan. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, compiled it and dedicated it to Paulinus. It is traditionally dated to before 324. The entries are arranged alphabetically and grouped by biblical book. Each gives a site's location and its name in Eusebius's own day. Jerome translated and revised it in Latin as the Liber de situ et nominibus locorum Hebraicorum. It is a key source for the historical geography of Roman Palestine and influenced the Madaba map and early pilgrim accounts.

The Life of Constantine is a Greek work in four books by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, written in honour of the emperor Constantine the Great. Eusebius composed it after Constantine's death in 337 and left it unfinished when he died in 339. It mixes panegyric and biography. It presents Constantine as a model Christian ruler and recounts his conversion, including the vision of the cross, his wars, his church building and his religious policy. It is one of the fullest sources for the religious history of his reign, and it quotes several imperial letters and documents.

The Oration to the Assembly of the Saints is a Greek speech attributed to the emperor Constantine the Great. Eusebius of Caesarea preserved it as an appendix to his Life of Constantine. The speech was given on Good Friday. Scholars disagree about its date and place, and they once doubted that Constantine wrote it, though many now accept it as his, probably translated from Latin. It attacks pagan polytheism and fatalism and defends divine providence and Christ's work. It is especially known for reading Virgil's Fourth Eclogue and an acrostic of the Erythraean Sibyl as prophecies of Christ.

This Greek panegyric by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, was delivered in Constantinople in 336 to mark the thirtieth anniversary of Constantine the Great's reign. Eusebius presents the emperor as the earthly image of the divine Logos and his monarchy as a reflection of God's heavenly rule. It also praises Constantine's suppression of polytheism and his support for the Church. Its later chapters are generally thought to come from a separate speech on Christ's sepulchre. The work is an important early statement of Christian imperial ideology, which later shaped Byzantine political thought.

The General Elementary Introduction is a Greek work in ten books by Eusebius of Caesarea. Its date is disputed: it may come from before the Great Persecution of 303 or from somewhat later. Only books six to nine survive, known as the Prophetic Extracts (Eclogae propheticae). They gather Old Testament prophecies about Christ, arranged by scriptural book and given brief commentary. They follow earlier books that argued for the faith without relying on Scripture. The work is an early source for Eusebius's exegesis and apologetic method.

The Ancoratus ("The Well-Anchored") is a Greek doctrinal treatise by Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia (Salamis) in Cyprus. He wrote it around 374 at the request of presbyters in Syedra in Pamphylia, whose letters stand at its beginning. It explains Christian teaching from Scripture and tradition: the consubstantiality of the Trinity, the full incarnation of Christ, and the resurrection and judgment. It argues against pagans, Jews and heretics, and lists the eighty heresies that Epiphanius later treated in the Panarion. It ends with two creeds, one of which closely resembles the creed associated with the Council of Constantinople of 381.

The Panarion ("medicine chest"), later known in Latin as Adversus haereses, is a Greek treatise against heresies by Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis (Constantia) in Cyprus. He began it around 374–375 at the request of the Syrian archimandrites Acacius and Paul and finished it about three years later. It describes and refutes eighty sects and schools of thought, from the time of Adam to the late fourth century. The work preserves many otherwise lost documents and reports, including fragments of Jewish-Christian gospels such as the Gospel of the Ebionites.

The Anacephalaeosis ("Recapitulation") is a Greek epitome of the Panarion, the great catalogue of eighty heresies by Epiphanius of Salamis (d. 403). It is transmitted under his name, but its authorship is doubtful, and it is often treated as the work of a later hand. Tome by tome, it gives brief summaries of each heresy. It begins with the primal "mothers" of error, Barbarism, Scythism and Hellenism, which it traces through biblical history from Adam onward. It served as a convenient reference guide to Epiphanius's heresiology and circulated widely.

Christus patiens ("Christ Suffering") is a Greek religious drama of about 2,600 verses on the Passion, death and resurrection of Christ. Much of it is a cento, built from lines borrowed chiefly from Euripides. The Virgin Mary is the central speaker, and the cast also includes Christ, the Theologian, Joseph, Nicodemus, Mary Magdalene and Pilate. Manuscripts attribute it to Gregory of Nazianzus, but most scholars think it is a later Byzantine work, sometimes assigned to the twelfth century and possibly to Constantine Manasses. Its authorship and date are still disputed.

Oration 27 is the first of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople in 380, while he led the small Nicene community there. It serves as an introduction to the series and is aimed at the Eunomians, radical Arians known for their skill in dialectic. Gregory does not yet discuss the Trinity itself. Instead he asks who may speak about God, when, before whom and how far, arguing that theology requires purity of life, quiet and restraint rather than clever debate.

Oration 28 is the second of the five Theological Orations by Gregory of Nazianzus. He preached them in Constantinople around 380, when he led the small Nicene community there against the Eunomians, who claimed that God's essence could be fully known. The first oration set out who may practise theology and under what conditions. This one argues that God's nature cannot be grasped by the human mind. Using the image of Moses on Sinai seeing only God's "back parts", Gregory shows that creation reveals that God exists, not what God is. The work is a classic statement of divine incomprehensibility.

The third of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople around 380 against the Eunomians and other Arian groups. After setting out the monarchy of the Father, Gregory defends the full divinity of the Son. He argues that the Son is eternally begotten without time or passion, and answers his opponents' arguments from the terms "begotten" and "unbegotten." The oration closes with a set of antitheses contrasting Christ's human lowliness with his divine glory. Oration 30 continues the argument with a fuller treatment of the disputed passages of Scripture.

Oration 30 is the fourth of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus delivered in Constantinople around 380 against the Eunomians and other Arians. It is his second discourse on the Son. Gregory answers, one by one, the scriptural texts his opponents used to make the Son subordinate, such as "The Lord created me" (Proverbs 8:22) and "the Father is greater than I." He assigns the exalted expressions to Christ's divinity and the lowly ones to his assumed humanity. The oration ends with a discussion of the titles of the Son.

Oration 31 is the last of the five Theological Orations that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople, probably in 380, against the Eunomians and the Pneumatomachi, who denied that the Holy Spirit is fully divine. Gregory openly calls the Spirit God and consubstantial with the Father and the Son. He separates the Spirit's procession from the Son's generation and answers the objection that Scripture is silent on the matter with a theory of progressive revelation. The oration was an important statement of Cappadocian Trinitarian theology shortly before the Council of Constantinople of 381.

This short Greek poem by Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390) belongs to his moral poems (Carmina moralia). It is a series of one-line maxims in iambic trimeter, arranged as an alphabetic acrostic: each line begins with the next letter of the Greek alphabet. The maxims urge the reader to make God the beginning and end of all things, to control anger, speech and the flesh, to honour strangers, and to accept everything from God with thanksgiving. It shows how Gregory used classical gnomic verse for Christian moral teaching.

On the Incarnation of the Word is a Greek theological treatise by Athanasius of Alexandria. It is the second part of a double work that opens with Against the Pagans, and both are addressed to a certain Macarius. Its date is disputed: some place it before the Arian controversy, around 318, while others place it in the 330s. It explains why the divine Word, through whom the world was made, took a human body to restore humanity from corruption and death. It also answers Jewish and pagan objections and remains a classic of Christian thought on the incarnation.

De Decretis is a Greek treatise in the form of a letter by Athanasius of Alexandria, usually dated to the 350s. It is written to an unnamed correspondent who had argued with supporters of Arius, including friends of Eusebius. Athanasius answers the Arian objection that the Council of Nicaea (325) used unscriptural terms, "of the essence" and "one in essence" (homoousios). He argues that these words express the meaning of Scripture about the Son's true divinity. The work is a major early defence of the Nicene formula. It also preserves documents connected with the council.

The Fourth Discourse Against the Arians is a Greek theological treatise that has come down with the three Orations Against the Arians of Athanasius of Alexandria (4th century). Most scholars doubt that Athanasius wrote it, and its true author and date are uncertain. It is a series of short arguments rather than a continuous discourse. Using Scripture, it argues that the Word is substantial and is the Father's own Son, and so preserves the single "Monarchy" of the Godhead. It attacks Arian teaching, and also views that separate the Word from the Son or merge Father and Son into one.

The First Discourse Against the Arians is the opening book of Athanasius of Alexandria's Greek polemical treatise against Arianism. Its date is disputed: scholars place it either around 339–346, during his exile in Rome, or in the later 350s. Athanasius argues that the Arians are sectaries named after their founder rather than Christians. He attacks the teaching of Arius's Thalia and defends the eternity of the Son and his unity of essence with the Father. He also begins interpreting disputed biblical texts such as Philippians 2:9–10 and Hebrews 1:4. It is a central text of Nicene theology.

The second of the Orations against the Arians is a Greek theological treatise by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. Its date is debated, though it is often placed in the late 330s or 340s. It continues his defence of the Nicene faith by examining scriptural texts that his opponents used to argue that the Son of God is a creature. These include Hebrews 3:2, "faithful to him that made him", and Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created me a beginning of his ways". Athanasius reads such passages as referring to the Son's incarnation rather than to his eternal being.

The third of the Greek Orations (Discourses) against the Arians by Athanasius of Alexandria, generally dated to around 340, though the exact date is debated. Its authenticity was questioned in modern scholarship but is widely accepted. Continuing the earlier discourses, it explains texts used by Arian opponents such as Asterius the Sophist, starting with John 14:10, "I in the Father and the Father in me." It argues for the mutual indwelling of Father and Son, who share one essence. It then attributes the Gospel accounts of Christ's ignorance, growth and suffering to the humanity the Word took on.

The Acts of Thomas is an anonymous apocryphal narrative, probably composed in Syriac in the early third century, likely at Edessa. It survives in Syriac and Greek versions, and scholars disagree about which is closer to the original. It tells how the apostle Judas Thomas was sold as a carpenter to the Indian king Gundaphoros, how he preached and worked miracles in India, and how he was martyred. It strongly favours sexual renunciation and includes liturgical prayers and celebrated poems, notably the Hymn of the Pearl. It is the chief source for the tradition of Thomas's mission to India.

The Fragmenta are the surviving remains of the writings of Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra (died c. 374), a supporter of the Council of Nicaea and opponent of Arianism. Most come from his treatise against Asterius the Sophist, written around the early 330s. They survive almost entirely as quotations in Eusebius of Caesarea's polemical works against him, with a few more in Epiphanius's Panarion 72. The fragments set out Marcellus's theology of the Word, which his critics condemned as Sabellian, and they are central to the history of the Arian controversy.

Against Celsus is an apologetic treatise in eight books by Origen of Alexandria, written around 248 at the request of his patron Ambrose. It refutes The True Word, an attack on Christianity by the second-century pagan philosopher Celsus. Origen answers him point by point, defending faith, the identity of Jesus, allegorical reading of Scripture and Christianity's relation to Greek religion. It survives complete in Greek and is among the most important works of early Christian apologetics. It also preserves most of what is known of Celsus's lost work.

This is a large Greek exegetical work by Origen of Alexandria, written for his patron Ambrose. He began it in Alexandria around the early 230s and continued it after moving to Caesarea. It originally ran to at least 32 books, but only a few survive, among them books 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 19, 20, 28 and 32. Origen reads the Fourth Gospel at both a literal and a spiritual level. He often argues against the Gnostic commentary of Heracleon, which makes this one of the earliest surviving Christian commentaries on John.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Gospel of John, preserved in the catenae: medieval chains of excerpts from earlier commentators arranged verse by verse. They are attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253), whose large Commentary on John survives only in part. Catena attributions are often unreliable, so some passages may come from other writers or may have been reworded by later compilers. The fragments deal with themes such as the eternal Word, creation and the incarnation. They add to what is known of Origen's lost exegesis.

The Exhortation to Martyrdom is a Greek treatise by Origen of Alexandria, generally dated to about 235, during the persecution under the emperor Maximinus Thrax. It is addressed to his patron Ambrose and to Protoctetus, a presbyter of Caesarea, who were both facing arrest. Drawing heavily on Scripture, Origen urges them to stand firm, to reject idolatry and apostasy, and to see suffering for Christ as a contest that leads to glory. It is one of the most important early Christian writings on the meaning of martyrdom.

On Prayer (Peri euchēs) is a Greek treatise by Origen of Alexandria, usually dated around 233–234 and addressed to his patron Ambrose and to Tatiana. It is the earliest surviving systematic Christian study of prayer. Origen asks why prayer is worthwhile if God already knows all things, explains the kinds of prayer named in 1 Timothy 2:1, and argues that prayer in the strict sense should be offered to the Father through the Son. He gives a long commentary on the Lord's Prayer and ends with advice on posture, place and times for prayer.

Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) preached this series of sermons on the Book of Jeremiah at Caesarea in Palestine, probably in the 240s. Twenty homilies survive in Greek, which is unusual because most of Origen's preaching is known only through Latin translations. Jerome translated some of them into Latin. Working through the biblical text passage by passage, Origen reads the prophet's warnings as signs of God's patience and his call to repentance, and he moves from the literal history to spiritual and moral interpretation. The homilies are important evidence for early Christian preaching and for Origen's exegetical method.

This is a collection of short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Jeremiah, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts in the Byzantine catenae on the prophets, the chains of patristic comment arranged verse by verse. Some may come from Origen's lost homilies or notes on Jeremiah, though catena attributions are not always reliable. The fragments show his usual allegorical and moral reading, applying the prophet's images to sin, temptation and the soul's struggle, and they add to the Greek homilies on Jeremiah that survive in full.

These are Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Lamentations, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) and preserved in the Byzantine catenae on the Prophets. They are thought to come from his lost commentary on Lamentations, which Eusebius says he wrote at Alexandria. The fragments explain the alphabetic acrostic structure of Jeremiah's laments. They read the captivity in Babylon allegorically as the soul's bondage to the devil and hostile powers, from which Christ sets it free. They are typical of Origen's spiritual method of reading Scripture.

This short Greek exegetical fragment is attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). It comes from his lost commentary on Lamentations and survives only because it was quoted in a catena, or chain of patristic comments, on the Octateuch. The passage looks at the phrase "justly pursue what is just" and separates four cases by asking whether the act itself is right and whether the intention behind it is sound. Joseph, hypocritical almsgiving and Paul's zealous persecution of the church serve as examples. It is one witness to Origen's largely lost exegesis.

De Engastrimytho (On the Witch of Endor) is a homily by Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) on 1 Samuel 28, where the medium at Endor calls up Samuel for King Saul. It is one of the few homilies by Origen that survive in the original Greek. Four passages had been read, and the presiding bishop chose this one for the sermon. Origen reads the story literally and argues that Samuel really appeared and prophesied. He also holds that the souls of prophets, like Christ, went down to Hades. Eustathius of Antioch later wrote a treatise attacking this reading.

These are short Greek exegetical fragments on the First Book of Kingdoms (1 Samuel), attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) and preserved in a Byzantine catena on the books of Samuel and Kings. They comment on individual verses, among them the fate of Eli's sons, the capture of the ark and the fall of Dagon. One passage explains that the Bible's human language about God is figurative: God's "wrath" is discipline and his "repentance" is a change in his dispensation, not a passion. Attributions in catenae are often uncertain, so the authenticity of individual fragments may be questioned.

This short Greek exegetical fragment on the Song of Hannah (1 Samuel 2) is attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). It survives in a catena, or chain of excerpts, on the Song of Songs. Ascriptions in catenae are often unreliable, so the attribution is not certain. The fragment reads Hannah's song as teaching that whoever approaches God should place all hope in him alone and practise humility rather than boasting. God knows everything, judges each person by their conduct, and rules over life and death. People come to know him through good works.

The thirty-nine homilies on Luke's Gospel were preached by Origen of Alexandria, probably at Caesarea in the third century. They survive complete only in a Latin translation by Jerome, made around 390 at the request of Paula and Eustochium, while the Greek original is preserved only in fragments. Most of the homilies treat the first four chapters of Luke, especially the infancy narratives, and a few cover later passages. They are an important witness to Origen's preaching and exegesis and to Jerome's activity as a translator.

These are Greek exegetical fragments on the Gospel of Luke, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) and preserved in later catenae, the chains of excerpts from earlier commentators. They may come from his lost commentary on Luke or from his homilies on the Gospel. Not every catena attribution is certain. The comments follow the Gospel verse by verse. For example, on Christ rebuking the fever of Peter's mother-in-law, Origen asks whether harmful powers can afflict the body. The fragments keep some of Origen's Greek exegesis that would otherwise be lost.

The Philocalia is a Greek anthology of extracts from the writings of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). The Greek text names Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen as its compilers, probably working in Pontus around 358–362. This attribution is widely accepted, though some scholars question it. It has twenty-seven chapters with titles added by the compilers, dealing with the inspiration and interpretation of Scripture, free will and providence. About a fifth comes from Contra Celsum. Because many of Origen's works are lost, the anthology also preserves Greek passages of On the First Principles.

Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) preached this series of sermons on the Book of Jeremiah at Caesarea in Palestine, probably in the 240s. Twenty homilies survive in Greek, which is unusual because most of Origen's preaching is known only through Latin translations. Jerome translated some of them into Latin. Working through the biblical text passage by passage, Origen reads the prophet's warnings as signs of God's patience and his call to repentance, and he moves from the literal history to spiritual and moral interpretation. The homilies are important evidence for early Christian preaching and for Origen's exegetical method.

This is Origen of Alexandria's verse-by-verse exegesis of the Gospel of Matthew, written in Greek at Caesarea late in his life, around 246–248. It originally ran to twenty-five books. Only books 10 to 17 survive in Greek, covering roughly Matthew 13:36 to 22:33. An anonymous early Latin translation preserves much of the rest, and a few fragments survive in other writers, including Origen's account of the order of the four Gospels. The commentary combines literal and allegorical interpretation and is a major witness to early Christian biblical scholarship.

This is Origen of Alexandria's verse-by-verse exegesis of the Gospel of Matthew, written in Greek at Caesarea late in his life, around 246–248. It originally ran to twenty-five books. Only books 10 to 17 survive in Greek, covering roughly Matthew 13:36 to 22:33. An anonymous early Latin translation preserves much of the rest, and a few fragments survive in other writers, including Origen's account of the order of the four Gospels. The commentary combines literal and allegorical interpretation and is a major witness to early Christian biblical scholarship.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the whole Psalter, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Most survive only as excerpts in later catenae, the Byzantine anthologies of biblical commentary. Origen wrote extensively on the Psalms, but compilers of catenae often confused or merged authors. Some material under his name is probably by others, such as Evagrius Ponticus, so the authenticity of individual fragments is doubtful. The comments read the Psalms morally and spiritually. Their opening reflection on Psalm 1 presents turning away from evil as the first step of the soul's progress toward God.

This Greek letter is Origen's reply to the Christian chronographer Julius Africanus, written from Nicomedia, probably around 240. Africanus had objected that the story of Susanna in the Book of Daniel was a late forgery. He pointed to Greek wordplays that could not have existed in a Hebrew original and to features he found implausible. Origen defends the story's place in the Church's Scriptures and discusses differences between the Hebrew and Greek texts of the Bible. The letter is one of Origen's few complete surviving letters and an important early witness to debates over the biblical canon and textual criticism.

Selecta in Genesim is a collection of Greek fragments of Origen of Alexandria's (c. 185–c. 253) exegetical writings on Genesis. Most survive in later catenae, the chains of excerpts that Byzantine compilers made from earlier commentators. Origen's own Commentary on Genesis, written in Alexandria, is largely lost. The collection opens with a passage from its third tome, preserved by Eusebius, on where the apostles went to preach. The other excerpts discuss particular verses: grammar, punctuation, the blessing to increase and multiply, and the creation of humanity in God's image. They are an important witness to Origen's lost interpretation of Genesis.

The Selecta in Exodum are Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Exodus attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive only in fragments, mostly preserved in later catenae (chains of excerpts from biblical commentators), and their exact relation to Origen's lost commentaries is uncertain. They comment on selected verses. A notable passage deals with the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, where Origen distinguishes between a heart described as "hardened", "strengthened" or "made heavy". This question of divine action and human free will recurs elsewhere in his writings.

Selecta in Leviticum ("Selections on Leviticus") is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Leviticus attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like other fragments of his biblical commentary, they survive mainly as excerpts in later catenae, so how much of the wording is Origen's own is uncertain. The comments explain the book's title and defend its laws on priesthood and sacrifice against critics who thought them unworthy of the Creator. Drawing on Paul's statement that "the law is spiritual," they read the ritual prescriptions as hidden teaching worthy of God.

The Selecta in Numeros ("Selections on Numbers") is a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Numbers attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). The notes survive as fragments, mainly through the catenae, the medieval chains of patristic commentary, and their authenticity is not always certain. They comment on individual verses, including the meaning of the word "manna", the prophesying of the seventy elders, Miriam's exclusion from the camp and the sending of the spies. They also read Joshua, son of Nun, as a type of Christ. The notes add to Origen's better-known Homilies on Numbers.

Selecta in Deuteronomium ("Selections on Deuteronomy") is a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Deuteronomy attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). The notes survive as fragments rather than as a continuous commentary, mostly drawn from later catenae, and the authorship of some passages is uncertain. They comment briefly on individual verses. Topics include Moses as the prophetic voice of God, Joshua as his successor, the inheritance of Reuben and Gad, and how the divine "voice" at Sinai should be understood without suggesting that God has a bodily nature.

The Selecta in Jesum Nave are short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Joshua attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts, mainly through catenae, and so their exact wording and authenticity are not always certain. The notes comment on individual verses and mix literal remarks with allegorical readings. Rahab, for example, is presented as a figure of the Church gathered from the nations, and her lowering of the spies through the window is compared to Paul's escape from Damascus.

Selecta in Judices ("Selections on Judges") is a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Judges attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as fragments, mainly in exegetical catenae, so how much of the material is genuinely Origen's is uncertain. The notes take up individual verses. They discuss whether the Spirit was behind Jephthah's rash vow, the "shibboleth" password test, Samson's Nazirite hair, the ephod and teraphim, and the defeat of Benjamin. They also add to what survives of Origen's Homilies on Judges, which are preserved in Latin.

The Selecta in Job is a collection of short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Job attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like other Origenian "selecta", the comments survive as fragments rather than a continuous commentary. They are mostly preserved in later catenae, so some attributions are uncertain. The notes explain individual verses, often morally or allegorically. For example, they read Satan's attacks on Job's household as possible only through drunkenness, and they treat harsh words from Job's friends as a heavy burden on the soul.

The Selecta in Psalmos are a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Psalms attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive mainly as excerpts in later catenae, and their authenticity is doubtful in part because some passages may come from other writers, such as Evagrius Ponticus. The opening gathers philosophical definitions of "end" from Aristotle and Stoic sources to explain psalm titles. Even so, the fragments remain an important witness to Origen's lost commentaries and homilies on the Psalter.

The Fragmenta in Ezechielem are short Greek comments on passages of the Book of Ezekiel attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts in later manuscript collections rather than as a continuous work. Origen wrote a long commentary and homilies on Ezekiel, most of which are lost in Greek, so these pieces help preserve his exegesis of the book. They show his allegorical method, treating Pharaoh as a symbol of the devil and the closed eastern gate as God's mysteries. They also comment on the meaning of Hebrew words.

The Adnotationes in Genesim, headed in Greek "Eklogai eis tēn Genesin" (Selections on Genesis), are short exegetical notes on passages of Genesis attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like many such fragments, they come down mainly through later catenae, so it is uncertain whether particular notes are genuinely his. The surviving comments deal with episodes such as the Flood. They explain, for example, that God's "repentance" means a change in his plan of salvation, not a human emotion, because the divine nature is free from passions. They help preserve Origen's largely lost commentary work on Genesis.

Adnotationes in Exodum is a set of brief Greek exegetical notes on selected verses of Exodus, headed "Eklogai" ("selections") and attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like many of his lost commentaries, the material survives only in fragments, mostly from catenae, and the authenticity of individual pieces is uncertain. The notes explain why God tests his people, distinguish an "idol" from a "likeness" and worship from service, and comment on the high priest's vestments and the forty days of the giving of the Law.

This is a collection of short Greek exegetical notes on Leviticus attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts in later catenae, the anthologies of patristic comment arranged verse by verse. The comments cover passages on unintentional sin and sin offerings, which they connect to Christ offered for the sins of all. They also discuss childbirth, presenting the Virgin Mary as free from ritual impurity, and the laws about leprosy. Origen's surviving Greek commentary on Leviticus is very fragmentary. As with many catena excerpts, the attribution of individual fragments may be uncertain.

The Adnotationes in Numeros are a set of brief Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Numbers attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like many surviving fragments of his biblical scholarship, they come down as excerpts rather than a continuous commentary. They comment on selected verses from chapters 11 to 24. Topics include the manna, compared with the readings of Aquila and Symmachus; Miriam's leprosy as a warning to the people; and Balaam's oracles. They link Balaam's prophecy of the rising star to the Magi who came to Bethlehem.

The Adnotationes in Deuteronomium are short Greek exegetical notes on Deuteronomy attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive only as fragments in catenae, the Byzantine chains of excerpts from earlier commentators, so how much is authentically Origen's is uncertain. The notes compare readings such as Aquila's translation and give typological interpretations. Moses' exclusion from the promised land, for example, is read as a sign that the law cannot bring things to perfection. Joshua's succession to Moses is likened to Elisha receiving Elijah's spirit.

These are short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Joshua, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) and preserved as excerpts in later biblical catenae. They comment on individual verses. One question is why Jericho was placed under the ban: its spoils are explained as a firstfruits offering, and the city fell to trumpets without weapons as a sign of divine power. The notes also explain why plunder was allowed at Ai. Catena attributions are often uncertain. The fragments are separate from Origen's Homilies on Joshua, which survive mainly in Rufinus's Latin translation.

The Adnotationes in Judices, titled in Greek "Eklogai eis tous Kritas" (Selections on Judges), are short exegetical notes on the Book of Judges attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253). They survive as fragments, mostly from catenae, and comment on individual verses. Examples include the water that sprang from the jawbone in Samson's story and the war against the Benjaminites. The notes reflect on divine justice and read Jacob's blessing of Benjamin as a prophecy. Whether every fragment truly comes from Origen is uncertain.

These are exegetical fragments on the Book of Job attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They are traditionally linked to his lost homilies on Job, which Jerome lists as twenty-two in number. The fragments survive only as excerpts in Byzantine catenae, anthologies of patristic comment arranged verse by verse, so how far each one is authentic is uncertain. Short notes on individual verses dwell on the devil's assault on Job and the protection God gives the righteous. They help show how Job was read in early Greek Christian exegesis.

The Excerpta in Psalmos is a collection of short Greek exegetical notes on individual verses of the Psalms, handed down under the name of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253). Its authenticity is doubtful. Like much of Origen's lost Psalm commentary, the material survives as excerpts in later compilations, and parts may come from other authors. The notes read the text allegorically and morally: "the world" is the Church, Zion is the watchful soul, and God's judgment calls believers to avoid ungodly deeds and thoughts.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Proverbs, preserved in the catenae (chains of excerpts from biblical commentators) under the name of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Origen's full commentary on Proverbs is lost. The fragments explain the sayings of Solomon allegorically and morally, treating wisdom as spiritual knowledge and instruction as the governing of the passions. Their authenticity is uncertain, because modern scholars have shown that many scholia once ascribed to Origen belong to Evagrius Ponticus.

The Scholia on the Song of Songs are short Greek exegetical comments on the Song of Songs attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as fragments in a catena, the epitome of commentary that goes under the name of Procopius of Gaza, where they appear alongside excerpts from other Fathers. Origen reads the Song allegorically as the love between Christ the Bridegroom and the Church or soul as bride. These fragments supplement his Commentary and Homilies on the Song, which survive chiefly in Latin translation.

The Scholia in Matthaeum are a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Gospel of Matthew, handed down under the name of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like many fragments ascribed to Origen, they survive mainly through catenae, the medieval chains of commentary on Scripture. Their authenticity is uncertain, and some passages may belong to later writers. The notes go through Matthew verse by verse. They open with a theological distinction between Christ's "genesis" and "gennesis," comparing the incarnate Word to speech made visible in writing.

These Greek exegetical fragments on the Gospel of Luke are attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253) and survive in catena manuscripts rather than as an independent work. They comment verse by verse on the Gospel. On Luke's prologue they contrast the four Gospels accepted by the Church with writings such as the Gospels according to the Egyptians, of the Twelve, of Thomas, of Basilides and of Matthias. They also reject docetic views of Christ's incarnation. Attributions within catenae are often uncertain, so the authenticity of individual fragments varies.

This is a large Greek exegetical work by Origen of Alexandria, written for his patron Ambrose. He began it in Alexandria around the early 230s and continued it after moving to Caesarea. It originally ran to at least 32 books, but only a few survive, among them books 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 19, 20, 28 and 32. Origen reads the Fourth Gospel at both a literal and a spiritual level. He often argues against the Gnostic commentary of Heracleon, which makes this one of the earliest surviving Christian commentaries on John.

These are Greek passages from Origen's homilies on Jeremiah that survive as excerpts in the Philocalia, the anthology of his writings traditionally said to have been compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen. Some overlap with homilies that survive elsewhere. Others, including material from the thirty-ninth homily, are known only through this anthology. The extracts deal with how Scripture should be read. They warn against rash speculation about God's hidden wisdom and insist that no stroke of the inspired text is empty, because every part comes from the divine fullness.

These are Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Job attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive in the catenae, the chains of patristic comment that Byzantine compilers arranged verse by verse. Origen is reported to have preached a series of homilies on Job, but the full series is lost, and the attribution of individual catena excerpts is often uncertain. The fragments comment on Job's righteousness, his losses, his wife's temptation and human life as a trial. They read the text morally and spiritually and stress endurance and the knowledge of God.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in nine books by Sozomen, a lawyer at Constantinople. He wrote it around the 440s and dedicated it to Emperor Theodosius II. It was meant to continue the work of Eusebius and covers events from the 320s to the 420s. The ninth book seems unfinished and stops short of the end date the author announced. Sozomen drew heavily on Socrates Scholasticus but added much material of his own, especially on monasticism, missions and the Church outside the empire. It is a key source for fourth- and early fifth-century Christianity.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in seven books by Socrates of Constantinople, also called Socrates Scholasticus. It was written in the 440s and continues Eusebius's history, covering events from 305 to 439: Constantine's conversion, the Arian controversy, the councils, and the affairs of the churches of the eastern empire. Socrates aimed for a plain style and drew on documents and on eyewitnesses. Sozomen used the work as a source. In the sixth century it was put into Latin as part of the Historia Tripartita, which carried it into the medieval West.

The Ecclesiastical History of Philostorgius (368–c. 439), a Cappadocian historian who followed the Anomoean teaching of Eunomius, was written in Greek in twelve books and appeared between about 425 and 433. It covered church history from the Arian controversy into the early fifth century from a non-Nicene point of view. The original is lost. It survives mainly through the epitome made by Photius of Constantinople in the ninth century. Photius summarised the work critically, but his epitome keeps a rare account of the period from the side of the losing party.

The Refutation of All Heresies, also called the Elenchus or Philosophumena, is a long Greek polemical treatise from the early third century. It is traditionally attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, but some scholars assign it to an unknown "Pseudo-Hippolytus", and it was once credited to Origen. The work argues that Christian heresies come from Greek philosophy, the mysteries and astrology. It surveys pagan thought and then describes some thirty-three Gnostic and other systems, which makes it a major source for early Christian heterodoxy. Books II and III are lost. Books IV–X were rediscovered at Mount Athos in 1842.

The Refutation of All Heresies, also called the Elenchus or Philosophumena, is a long Greek polemical treatise from the early third century. It is traditionally attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, but some scholars assign it to an unknown "Pseudo-Hippolytus", and it was once credited to Origen. The work argues that Christian heresies come from Greek philosophy, the mysteries and astrology. It surveys pagan thought and then describes some thirty-three Gnostic and other systems, which makes it a major source for early Christian heterodoxy. Books II and III are lost. Books IV–X were rediscovered at Mount Athos in 1842.

The Chronicon Paschale, or Paschal Chronicle, is an anonymous Greek world chronicle written in the seventh century, probably at Constantinople during the reign of Heraclius.
