Its author called it an epitome of the ages from Adam to the seventeenth year of Heraclius. Its name comes from its dating system, which follows the Christian Easter cycle. It opens with a discussion of the date of Easter that cites Philo and Peter of Alexandria. Although much of it draws on earlier works, it is an important independent source for events of the late sixth and early seventh centuries.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in six books by Evagrius Scholasticus, a lawyer at Antioch and aide to Patriarch Gregory of Antioch. He completed it around 593–594. It continues the histories of Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret, covering the period from the First Council of Ephesus in 431 to the reign of Emperor Maurice. Written from a Chalcedonian standpoint, it is a major source for the Christological controversies after Chalcedon, for imperial and Persian affairs, and for the plague of the 540s, which Evagrius survived.

This Greek church history in three books was written around 475 by an anonymous author, the son of a presbyter of Cyzicus, who worked in Bithynia. Following Photius, it was long misattributed to Gelasius of Cyzicus. Book I covers Constantine's reign up to 323, Book II the Council of Nicaea and Book III its aftermath. It draws on Eusebius, Rufinus and other historians, as well as on a parchment book that had belonged to Dalmatius of Cyzicus. The author aimed to show against the Eutychians that the Nicene Fathers did not teach Monophysite doctrine.

This Greek hagiography is attributed to Mark the Deacon, who presents himself as companion and deacon of Porphyry, bishop of Gaza from 395 to 420. It tells of Porphyry's ascetic life, his ordination, and his campaign to Christianize pagan Gaza. With imperial support, this ended in the destruction of the Marneion temple in 402. It is a vivid and detailed account of a city's Christianization, but its historical reliability is debated. Versions also survive in Latin and Georgian, and the Georgian may derive from a lost Syriac original.

The Acts of Philip is an anonymous Greek apocryphal work about the missionary journeys of the Apostle Philip. It was probably written in the mid-to-late fourth century. It was originally made up of fifteen separate episodes followed by a martyrdom account, and it mixes miracle stories with elements of heroic romance and ascetic teaching. In its best-known section, Philip preaches with Bartholomew and his sister Mariamne at Hierapolis (Ophioryma) in Asia. There he defeats a serpent cult and is martyred by crucifixion. The text matters as evidence for later apostolic legend and the ascetic piety of Asia Minor.

The Acts of Barnabas is an anonymous Greek apocryphal work, also called the Journeyings and Martyrdom of Barnabas. It claims to be written by John Mark, the companion of Paul and Barnabas. It tells of Mark's conversion and of Barnabas's split from Paul. It then follows Barnabas's mission through Cyprus, his martyrdom at Salamis and his burial by Mark. The work is usually dated to the fifth century. It is thought to reflect the Cypriot church's claim to apostolic foundation and independence from Antioch.

The Banquet of the Ten Virgins is a Greek dialogue by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. Its title and form deliberately echo Plato's Symposium. Gregorion tells Euboulios about a banquet held by Arete (Virtue) in a garden, where ten virgins give speeches in turn praising chastity and virginity. They draw heavily on allegorical readings of Scripture. Thekla gives the fullest speech, and the work ends with her hymn to Christ the Bridegroom. It is Methodius's only work to survive complete in Greek and an important early Christian treatise on virginity.

Concerning Free-Will, also known as De autexusio, is a Greek theological dialogue by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. It is a debate between an orthodox speaker, Orthodoxus, and a follower of Valentinian Gnosticism. The work argues against the view that matter is eternal and is the source of evil. Instead, it traces evil to the misuse of the free will that God gave to created beings. It is an important early Christian treatment of the origin of evil and of human moral freedom.

On Things Created (De creatis) is a Greek theological treatise by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. The full work is lost. It survives only in a summary of excerpts made by the ninth-century patriarch Photius in codex 235 of his Bibliotheca. The surviving passages argue against Origen and his followers. They criticize his allegorical reading of texts such as "cast not your pearls before swine" and dispute his view that the created world is coeternal with God. The work is an important witness to early opposition to Origen.

Against Porphyry was a Greek treatise by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. In it he answered the Neoplatonist philosopher Porphyry, whose attack on Christianity, Against the Christians, was widely read. Jerome mentions the work, but it is lost apart from a few short excerpts. These are moral and theological reflections: that true excellence is what God values, that repentance works best when it is immediate, and that human good lies in resembling God.

These are short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Job, preserved in the catenae (medieval chains of patristic commentary) under the name of Methodius, usually identified as Methodius of Olympus (died c. 311), bishop and martyr. Their authenticity cannot be fully confirmed, as is often the case with catena material. The fragments discuss Job's speeches to his friends. They argue that true wisdom, joined to piety, is beyond human discovery and comes only as God's gift through revelation. This is why Greek philosophers seeking God by their own strength failed.

This short Greek fragment comes from a lost discourse on martyrs attributed to Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and Church Father who died around 311. Only a brief passage survives, preserved as a quotation by later writers. It praises martyrdom as so admirable and desirable that Christ himself honoured it. Citing Philippians 2:6, it presents the Son's self-emptying descent to humanity as the source of this gift. The passage is a small witness to pre-Nicene reflection on martyrdom as an imitation of Christ, from the era of the last great persecutions.

This is a small collection of short Greek fragments of uncertain origin that later writers handed down under the name of Methodius of Olympus, the bishop and martyr who died around 311. They are not assigned to any known work, and their authenticity is doubtful. They include sayings on justice, described as the fulfilment of all the commandments and as "square", equal on every side. One passage, reporting Methodius's view, treats Adam, his begotten son and Eve, who "proceeded" from Adam, as types of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in five books by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was written around 449–450 and continues the history of Eusebius of Caesarea. It begins with the rise of Arianism under Constantine and ends in 429, with the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Theodoret writes from a firmly Nicene and Antiochene viewpoint and focuses on the struggle against Arianism. He quotes many letters, creeds and synodal documents in full. Along with the histories of Socrates Scholasticus and Sozomen, it is one of the main sources for fourth-century church history.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in five books by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was written around 449–450 and continues the history of Eusebius of Caesarea. It begins with the rise of Arianism under Constantine and ends in 429, with the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Theodoret writes from a firmly Nicene and Antiochene viewpoint and focuses on the struggle against Arianism. He quotes many letters, creeds and synodal documents in full. Along with the histories of Socrates Scholasticus and Sozomen, it is one of the main sources for fourth-century church history.

The Historia Religiosa, also called the Philotheos Historia ("History of the Lovers of God"), is a Greek hagiographical collection written by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, around 440. It gives thirty accounts of ascetics of Syria and Mesopotamia, beginning with Jacob of Nisibis. Among them is Symeon the Stylite, who was still living when Theodoret wrote. Theodoret knew many of these monks personally, and he tells of their hardships, miracles and teaching. A short treatise on divine love closes the work. It is a key source for early Syrian monasticism.

Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch from 412 to 444, wrote this Greek commentary on the twelve Minor Prophets, from Hosea to Malachi. It is usually dated to the earlier part of his episcopate, before the Nestorian controversy. The preface admits that many have already explained the prophets but argues that further interpretation still helps readers. Cyril reads each prophet first in its historical setting and then spiritually, as pointing to Christ and the Church. It is the fullest surviving patristic commentary on these books.

The Catena on Matthew is an anonymous Greek commentary on the Gospel of Matthew. It belongs to the Byzantine genre of the catena, or "chain", in which excerpts from earlier Church Fathers are arranged verse by verse along the biblical text. The text is divided into numbered chapters (kephalaia) on episodes such as the Magi, the Beatitudes and the healing miracles. Among the Fathers it quotes, John Chrysostom's homilies on Matthew are especially prominent. Neither the compiler nor the date is known. Such catenae matter because they preserve fragments of patristic exegesis that are otherwise lost.

The Catena in Marcum is a Greek catena, or chain of excerpts from earlier Christian writers, that works through the Gospel of Mark passage by passage. It opens with a list of the traditional chapter headings (kephalaia) of Mark. It is traditionally attributed to Victor of Antioch, a presbyter of the fifth century, but who compiled it and when are uncertain. It draws heavily on earlier writers, especially John Chrysostom. It is often counted among the earliest surviving commentaries on Mark and is valued for comparing the Gospel accounts.

This is an anonymous Greek compilation that supplements John Chrysostom's homilies on the Gospel of Matthew and records variant readings of them. It survives in the tradition of the New Testament catenae, anthologies of patristic comment on Scripture. It opens with a list of exegetical questions arranged in the Gospel's order. They include why the Gospel is so called, the women in Christ's genealogy, the star of the Magi, the flight into Egypt and Christ's baptism. Its date and compiler are unknown.

The Catena on Luke is an anonymous Greek commentary on the Gospel of Luke. Like other catenae, it is a "chain" of excerpts from earlier Church Fathers, arranged passage by passage along the biblical text. It opens with the traditional list of the Gospel's chapter headings (kephalaia), covering episodes such as the census, the shepherds, Simeon and the Temptation. The compiler and the date of compilation are uncertain. Catenae of this kind matter because they preserve fragments of patristic exegesis, including passages from commentaries otherwise lost.

The Catena on John is an anonymous Greek catena, or "chain", of patristic commentary on the Gospel of John. It sets out the Gospel passage by passage and attaches excerpts from earlier Greek interpreters to each one. The commentary draws above all on John Chrysostom's homilies on John, and it opens with his account of the evangelist as an unlettered fisherman of Bethsaida. A list of chapter headings precedes the commentary. Neither the compiler nor the date of compilation is known. Like other catenae, it is valuable because it preserves fragments of early exegesis, some of which survive nowhere else.

This anonymous Greek collection supplies additional material and variant readings for a catena, or chain commentary, on the Gospel of Luke. Catenae are Byzantine compilations that set excerpts from earlier Church Fathers beside the biblical verses they explain. The collection is titled "Interpretation of various [Fathers] on the Gospel according to Luke". It opens with a list of numbered chapter headings covering episodes such as Luke's prologue, the Annunciation, Simeon and Anna, Christ's genealogy, and the parables. Its compiler and date are unknown. Texts like this matter because they keep fragments of patristic exegesis that are often lost elsewhere.

This is an anonymous Greek supplement to a catena on the Gospel of John, giving additional material and variant readings from a manuscript in the Bodleian Library, Oxford. A catena is a running commentary assembled from excerpts of earlier Church Fathers. This one opens with a list of chapter headings taken from John Chrysostom's homilies on John. The headings follow the Gospel's episodes, from the eternal generation of the Word through the Samaritan woman and the feeding of the five thousand to the man born blind. Its compiler and date are unknown.

The Catena on Acts is an anonymous Greek catena, or chain commentary, on the Acts of the Apostles. Its heading calls it an interpretation of Acts "by Chrysostom and various others". It follows the biblical text passage by passage and sets beside each one extracts from earlier interpreters, drawing above all on John Chrysostom's homilies on Acts. A prologue presents Luke as an Antiochene physician and disciple of Paul. The compiler and date are uncertain. The work matters because it preserves fragments of patristic exegesis, some of which survive nowhere else.

This anonymous Greek catena on Paul's Epistle to the Romans belongs to the type named after its Vatican manuscripts. A catena is a running commentary built from excerpts of earlier interpreters arranged verse by verse. Its compiler and date are unknown. It begins with a prologue that summarizes the letter. The prologue says Paul wrote it from Corinth and treats the calling of the Gentiles, the end of circumcision, and the undoing of Adam's transgression through Christ. Catenae of this kind matter because they preserve fragments of patristic exegesis that are otherwise lost.

This is an anonymous Greek catena on Paul's Epistle to the Romans. A catena is a running commentary built from excerpts of earlier Church Fathers, each set against the verse it explains and labelled with its author's name. This form of the catena takes its name from a manuscript held in Munich. The surviving section begins at Romans 7:7 and opens with an excerpt from John Chrysostom on whether the Law is sin. Its compiler and date are unknown. Catenae of this kind matter because they preserve comments by Greek exegetes whose own works are partly or wholly lost.

The Catena on the First Epistle to the Corinthians is an anonymous Byzantine Greek commentary. Like other New Testament catenae, it strings together excerpts from earlier Greek interpreters, with John Chrysostom usually the main source, and arranges them verse by verse alongside Paul's letter. It opens with a summary of the letter's occasion: factions at Corinth, a case of incest, disputes over marriage and celibacy, food offered to idols, spiritual gifts and the resurrection. The compiler and date are uncertain.

This anonymous Greek catena on Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians is a running commentary built from excerpts of earlier Church Fathers, arranged verse by verse. Its compiler and date are unknown. It opens with a summary of the letter's occasion. Paul writes from Macedonia after the Corinthians have disciplined the man who took his stepmother, and he urges them to receive him back now that he has repented. The summary also notes Paul's teaching on letter and spirit, the new creation in Christ, the collection for the saints, and his defence against false apostles.

The Catena on the Epistle to the Galatians is an anonymous Greek compilation of exegetical excerpts on Paul's letter to the Galatians. It belongs to the Byzantine catena tradition, in which compilers set extracts from earlier Church Fathers alongside the biblical text as a running commentary. Its date and compiler are unknown. The opening explains the occasion of the letter: Jewish-Christian teachers were pressing the Galatians to keep the Mosaic law and were questioning Paul's apostolic authority. Collections like this one are important because they preserve fragments of patristic commentaries that are otherwise lost.

The Catena on Ephesians is an anonymous Greek commentary on Paul's Letter to the Ephesians. Like other catenae ("chains"), it strings together excerpts from earlier Church Fathers, each marked with the name of its source. It opens with John Chrysostom's introduction to the letter, which describes Ephesus as the leading city of Asia, a centre of the cult of Artemis and of philosophy, and presents Paul writing as a prisoner in Rome. When and by whom the compilation was made is uncertain. It is valuable for preserving passages of patristic exegesis, including fragments of commentaries that are otherwise lost.

The Catena on the Epistle to the Philippians is an anonymous Greek exegetical anthology, a "catena" or chain of excerpts from earlier Church Fathers arranged to follow the text of Paul's letter verse by verse. Compilations of this kind were produced in the Byzantine period, but this one's compiler and exact date are unknown. It opens with an introduction to the church at Philippi and the circumstances of Paul's imprisonment, drawn from John Chrysostom's homilies. Catenae are valuable because they preserve patristic interpretation, sometimes including fragments of commentaries otherwise lost.

This anonymous Greek catena on Paul's Epistle to the Colossians is a running commentary built from excerpts of earlier patristic interpreters, arranged verse by verse. Its compiler and exact date are unknown, though such catenae belong to the Byzantine period. The opening passage draws on John Chrysostom's homilies on Colossians. It discusses the letter as one Paul wrote in captivity and places it in sequence with Romans, Philemon, Philippians and Timothy. Catenae like this one matter because they preserve fragments of patristic exegesis, some of which survive nowhere else.

This anonymous Greek catena on Paul's First Epistle to the Thessalonians is a chain of exegetical excerpts from earlier Church Fathers, arranged as a running commentary on the biblical text. Catenae of this kind were compiled in the Byzantine period, and the compiler and date of this one are unknown. It opens with an introduction to the letter: Paul writes from Athens and sends Timothy to strengthen the Thessalonians in affliction, console them about the dead, and teach about the resurrection and the uncertain day of Christ's coming. Catenae preserve patristic interpretations that are otherwise lost.

This anonymous Greek catena is a chain of commentary on Paul's Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, presented as a volume of "exegetical selections". Like other New Testament catenae, it gathers excerpts from earlier Greek Church Fathers and arranges them verse by verse. Its opening draws heavily on John Chrysostom's homilies on the epistle. It explains that Paul wrote again because he could not visit, and to correct those who claimed that Christ's coming and the judgement were already at hand. The compiler and date are unknown.

The catena on the First Epistle to Timothy is an anonymous Greek commentary on Paul's letter. Like other catenae, or "chains", it is made of excerpts from earlier Church Fathers arranged in order along the biblical text. Its compiler and date are unknown. It opens with an introduction on Timothy as Paul's disciple, drawn from Acts. It explains why Paul wrote only to Timothy and Titus, then lists the chapter headings of the epistle, covering prayer, the qualities of bishops and the Incarnation. Catenae like this one preserve Greek exegesis, including passages from works that are otherwise lost.

This is an anonymous Greek catena, or "chain" commentary, on Paul's Second Epistle to Timothy. It is one of the Byzantine catenae on the New Testament. It presents exegetical extracts from earlier Greek writers verse by verse, with each excerpt attributed to its author, such as John Chrysostom and Theodore. Its opening asks why Paul wrote a second letter, explaining it as consolation for Timothy written near the apostle's death. Its compiler and date are uncertain. Catenae like this one preserve fragments of patristic commentaries that are otherwise lost.

The Catena on the Epistle to Titus is an anonymous Greek catena: a running commentary on Paul's letter to Titus built from excerpts of earlier patristic exegetes, arranged verse by verse. Its compiler and date are unknown, although Byzantine catenae of this kind were generally put together between about the sixth and tenth centuries. The opening comes from John Chrysostom's homilies on Titus. It discusses Titus's standing among Paul's companions, his charge over Crete, and why the letter is so short. Catenae like this one matter because they preserve fragments of commentaries that are otherwise lost.

This anonymous Greek catena, or chain of commentary, on Paul's Epistle to Philemon gathers excerpts from earlier Church Fathers and arranges them verse by verse. It opens with a prologue that draws heavily on John Chrysostom's homilies on Philemon. The prologue tells how Onesimus, a runaway slave who had stolen from his master, was baptized by Paul in prison in Rome. It also defends the short letter's place in Scripture, arguing that it teaches care for slaves and for small matters. The compiler and the date of compilation are unknown.

This anonymous Greek catena on Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews is a chain of commentary in which brief excerpts from earlier Church Fathers are set beside the biblical text, passage by passage. Its prologue asks why Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, wrote to Jewish believers, probably in Jerusalem and Palestine, and how this fits his imprisonment in Rome. Such compilations were made in Byzantine times. Their compiler and date are uncertain. They matter because they keep fragments of patristic exegesis that would otherwise be lost.

This is an anonymous Greek catena, a chain of excerpts from earlier Church Fathers, on the Epistle of James. It belongs to a larger Byzantine commentary on the Catholic Epistles, and its date and compiler are uncertain. A prefatory summary sets out the epistle's themes: kinds of temptation, faith shown in works, the treatment of rich and poor, Job's patience, and anointing the sick. The comments cite Eusebius on doubts about the letter's authenticity and draw on Didymus the Blind and unnamed interpreters. Much patristic exegesis survives only through compilations like this one.

This anonymous Greek catena on the First Epistle of Peter is a running commentary built from excerpts of earlier Church Fathers, arranged verse by verse beside the biblical text. It opens with a summary of the letter's argument. The summary presents Peter writing to Jewish believers of the dispersion, and it touches on Christ's preaching in Hades and on readiness for judgement. The material is then grouped under chapter headings. Its compiler and date are unknown. Like other New Testament catenae, it matters chiefly for preserving fragments of patristic exegesis that are otherwise lost.

This anonymous Greek catena is a Byzantine commentary on the Second Epistle of Peter. Its date and compiler are unknown. Like other catenae, it arranges the biblical text with excerpts from earlier Greek Church Fathers. It begins with a hypothesis, or prefatory summary, which presents the letter as Peter's reminder of earlier teaching before his approaching death. The summary notes the letter's warnings against false teachers and scoffers who deny the Lord's coming. It also notes the letter's teaching that a thousand years are as one day before God.

This anonymous Greek catena on the First Epistle of John is a chain of commentary that sets excerpts from earlier Church Fathers beside the biblical text, verse by verse. It opens with a prologue, or hypothesis, presenting the letter as the work of the evangelist John. The prologue sums up its themes: the eternal Word made manifest, God as light, mutual love, children of God and of the devil, the discernment of spirits, and sin unto death. Neither the compiler nor the date of compilation is known.

This anonymous Greek catena, or "chain" commentary, covers the Second Epistle of John. It sets brief excerpts from earlier Greek interpreters alongside the biblical text. It opens with a summary of the letter's occasion. The Elder writes to the "elect lady" and her children, praises their faithful conduct and urges love. He warns against deceivers who deny that Christ came in the flesh and forbids receiving them. The comments ask whether the "lady" was a church or an actual woman. Such compilations preserve fragments of patristic exegesis that are otherwise lost.

This anonymous Greek catena on the Third Epistle of John is a chain of exegetical comments drawn from earlier Church Fathers and arranged alongside the biblical text. It is part of the Byzantine catena tradition on the Catholic Epistles, and its date and compiler are uncertain. It opens with a summary (hypothesis) presenting the letter as a teaching on hospitality. The comments praise Gaius for welcoming travelling brethren, condemn Diotrephes for hindering such charity, and commend Demetrius. The text is divided into chapters with headings and explains why the letter is so brief.

This is an anonymous Greek catena, or chain of commentary, on the Epistle of Jude. It follows the biblical text section by section and sets excerpts from earlier Greek patristic interpreters beside it. An introductory summary (hypothesis) says Jude wrote to believers to warn them against intruders who taught that sin was a matter of indifference and who denied the Lord. The comments that follow deal with Christology, the fallen angels and the judgement of the ungodly. The compiler and date are unknown. Byzantine catenae like this one preserve exegetical material that would otherwise be lost.

This is an anonymous Greek preface to a Byzantine compilation of explanations of the Book of Revelation, gathered from earlier Church writers. In the manuscript tradition it is ascribed to Oecumenius, bishop of Trikka in Thessaly, and to Arethas of Caesarea, but it is not by Oecumenius, so it is known as Pseudo-Oecumenian. The preface defends the Apocalypse as inspired and as the genuine work of John the Evangelist. It cites Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, Methodius of Olympus, Cyril of Alexandria and Hippolytus in support, and presents John as a prophet as well as an apostle. Its exact date is uncertain.

This is a Greek commentary on the Book of Revelation attributed to Arethas, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia in the early tenth century and a leading Byzantine scholar. It relies heavily on the earlier commentary of Andrew of Caesarea, which it abridges, supplements and sometimes corrects. It works through the Apocalypse in numbered sections, beginning with the prologue, the letters to the seven churches and the opening of the seals. Its interpretation is mainly spiritual and ecclesial. The work is a witness to how Revelation was received in the Byzantine Church.

This Greek commentary on the Book of Revelation is by Andrew, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and dates from the late sixth or early seventh century. It explains the Apocalypse verse by verse, mainly through spiritual and moral readings, and often draws on and corrects the earlier commentary of Oecumenius. Andrew divided it into twenty-four discourses and seventy-two chapters. It became the standard Greek interpretation of Revelation and helped the book gain acceptance in the Eastern Church. It also shaped how the Greek text of Revelation was handed down.

The History of the Franks is a Latin history in ten books, properly titled Decem Libri Historiarum. Gregory, bishop of Tours (c. 538–594), wrote it between about 573 and 594. It starts with the Creation and a short account of world and church history, then covers Gaul. Most of it describes the Merovingian kingdoms of the sixth century, many of whose events Gregory saw himself. It is often the only source for the period. Its lively and sometimes partisan stories have earned Gregory the title "father of French history."

The Etymologies (Etymologiae, or Origines) is a Latin encyclopedia compiled by Isidore, bishop of Seville, in Visigothic Spain during the early seventh century. It was still unfinished at his death in 636, and his friend Braulio of Zaragoza arranged it into twenty books. It covers the liberal arts, medicine, law, chronology, Scripture and the Church, languages and peoples, animals, geography, building, warfare and everyday objects. It explains things mainly through the supposed origins of their names. Drawing on many classical and Christian authors, it became one of the most widely copied reference works of the Middle Ages.

This Greek hagiography is attributed to Mark the Deacon, who presents himself as companion and deacon of Porphyry, bishop of Gaza from 395 to 420. It tells of Porphyry's ascetic life, his ordination, and his campaign to Christianize pagan Gaza. With imperial support, this ended in the destruction of the Marneion temple in 402. It is a vivid and detailed account of a city's Christianization, but its historical reliability is debated. Versions also survive in Latin and Georgian, and the Georgian may derive from a lost Syriac original.

The Missale Gallicanum Vetus is an anonymous Latin sacramentary from Merovingian Gaul, usually dated to the eighth century. It survives only in fragments. It holds prayers for parts of the church year, including Advent, Lent and the Easter Vigil, together with baptismal rites. It is one of the few surviving witnesses to the Gallican liturgy before Carolingian reforms replaced it with Roman usage. It is also one of the earliest sources for the Easter proclamation known as the Exsultet.

The Missale Gallicanum Vetus ("Old Gallican Missal") is an anonymous Latin liturgical book from eighth-century Francia. Despite its name, it is a sacramentary: it gives only the celebrant's prayers. It survives incompletely and gathers material from several sources. It opens with a Mass for Germanus of Auxerre, and its other formularies cover feasts and seasons of the church year. It is one of the few surviving witnesses to the Gallican rite used in Gaul before Carolingian reforms brought in Roman liturgical books, so it is important for studying early Western liturgy.

The Missale Gothicum is an anonymous Latin sacramentary of the Gallican Rite, compiled around the late seventh or early eighth century and usually linked with Burgundy, probably Autun. It was once called "Gothic" because scholars thought it came from Visigothic territory. The book is incomplete at its start. It gives the variable prayers of the Mass for the liturgical year, beginning with the Eve of the Nativity, and some of its collects are borrowed from Roman sources. It is one of the main surviving witnesses to the Gallican liturgy before Carolingian Romanization.

The Mone Masses are a group of anonymous Latin mass formularies of the Gallican rite. They survive in a palimpsest manuscript from the abbey of Reichenau, which is why they are also called the Missale Richenovense. They are named after Franz Joseph Mone, who discovered and published them in 1850. The manuscript is usually dated to the seventh century, but when the prayers themselves were written is uncertain. They include Sunday masses and a mass for Saint Germanus of Auxerre. They are among the earliest surviving witnesses to the liturgy of Merovingian Gaul.

The Bobbio Missal is an anonymous Latin liturgical book of the Gallican tradition, usually dated to the late seventh or early eighth century. Jean Mabillon found its only manuscript at the monastery of Bobbio in northern Italy. It combines elements of a sacramentary, a lectionary and a ritual, setting Gallican prayers beside a form of the Roman canon. It also mentions Sigismund of Burgundy, which led some nineteenth-century scholars to name it after Besançon. Its origin is still disputed. It is an important witness to early medieval liturgy before the Carolingian reforms.

The Anaphora of the Apostles is an anonymous Eucharistic prayer and the ordinary anaphora of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, preserved in Ge'ez. It is closely based on the Eucharistic prayer of the Apostolic Tradition, traditionally attributed to Hippolytus, which reached Ethiopia through the collection known as the Church Ordinances. Its date is uncertain. It includes an invocation of the Holy Spirit on the offering, and scholars compare it with other Ethiopic anaphoras, such as the Anaphora of Our Lord, to trace how early liturgical prayer developed.

The Anaphora of Saint Athanasius is a eucharistic prayer in Ge'ez, one of the anaphoras used in the liturgy of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. It is attributed to Athanasius, the fourth-century patriarch of Alexandria, but the attribution is traditional, and its real author and date are unknown. It is appointed for the Christian Sabbath. The text opens with exhortations from the deacon and priest that call the clergy and people to reconciliation and to exclude grave sinners. It also shows the Ethiopian Church's special regard for the Sabbath.

The Anaphora of Saint John Chrysostom is a eucharistic prayer of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, preserved in Ge'ez and counted among the anaphoras of the Ethiopic liturgy. It bears the name of John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople (d. 407), but it is a different text from the Byzantine anaphora that carries his name, and the attribution is traditional. When and by whom it was written is unknown. It opens with a long hymn on God's eternal essence, with the refrain "was He in His essence" repeated before each act of creation.

The Anaphora of Saint Cyril is a eucharistic prayer, or "Thanksgiving", from the Ethiopian liturgical tradition. It survives in Ge'ez and is attributed to Cyril of Alexandria, but its real author is unknown and its date is uncertain. It should not be confused with the Coptic Anaphora of Saint Cyril, which is related to the Liturgy of Saint Mark. The prayer opens with praise of God's hidden, incomprehensible essence. It then describes the seraphim, cherubim and ranks of "watchers" singing the Sanctus, using imagery with roots in Isaiah and Enochic tradition.

The Anaphora of Saint Dioscorus is a eucharistic prayer of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. It is one of the anaphoras of the Ge'ez liturgy and was composed in Ge'ez. Tradition attributes it to Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria (444–451), who is honoured by the non-Chalcedonian churches. The real author is unknown and the date of composition is uncertain; it is probably much later than Dioscorus. It opens with a hymnic litany that praises God reigning in his kingdom before creation. Prayers on the Trinity and the Incarnation follow, set out as alternating parts for priest and deacon.

The Anaphora of Saint Epiphanius is a eucharistic prayer in Ge'ez. It is one of the fourteen anaphoras of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo liturgy. Tradition credits it to Epiphanius, the fourth-century bishop of Salamis, but the author is unknown. It was most likely composed later within the Ethiopian tradition, and its date is uncertain. The prayer opens with a long list of praises of God's greatness and incomprehensibility. It then moves to the sending of the Son as Saviour, with the deacon's responses set between the priest's prayers. It shows the rhetorical style typical of Ethiopian anaphoras.

The Anaphora of St. Gregory of Alexandria is an anonymous eucharistic prayer, or anaphora, used in the Ethiopian liturgical tradition, where it belongs to the Church's large collection of alternative anaphoras. Its attribution to a "Gregory of Alexandria" is traditional and does not match any securely identified author, and when it was written is uncertain. The text sets the deacon's calls against the priest's prayers of thanksgiving. It praises God's mercy and creation, then the incarnation of Christ, who came down without setting aside the glory of his Godhead and gave life through his death.

The Anaphora of Saint Gregory of Armenia is a eucharistic prayer from the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, preserved in Ge'ez and one of the anaphoras of the Ethiopian liturgy. Tradition attributes it to Gregory the Illuminator, the fourth-century apostle of Armenia, but this attribution is not considered historical. The actual date and place of composition are uncertain. The prayer begins with a long hymn of praise to God, who is exalted above angels, watchers and seraphim, and leads into the Sanctus. The text includes directions for the priest and the deacon.

The Anaphora of James (Jacob) of Serugh is a eucharistic prayer used in the Ge'ez liturgy of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. It is one of the church's many anaphoras and bears the name of Jacob of Serugh, the Syriac poet and bishop who died in 521. The attribution is traditional, and the prayer's actual date and origin are uncertain. Its exchanges between deacon and priest begin with intercessions for the departed and for the presiding patriarch and bishop. They then praise the authority and majesty of the Son, whom the angels worship.

The Anaphora of Saint John the Evangelist, also titled the Eucharistic Thanksgiving of Saint John the Son of Thunder, is one of the anaphoras, or eucharistic prayers, of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. It is preserved in Ge'ez and attributed to the apostle John, but its real author is unknown. When it was composed is also uncertain, and scholars disagree about how old the Ethiopian anaphoras are. Its opening addresses God in strongly apophatic language: God is without beginning, limit or end, hidden from all and known only to himself, yet he draws near through the coming of his Son.

The Anaphora of Our Lady Mary is a eucharistic prayer of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. It belongs to the collection of anaphoras used in the Ge'ez liturgy and survives in Ge'ez. Tradition attributes it to Abba Cyriacus (Heryaqos), bishop of Behnesa (Oxyrhynchus) in Egypt, but its date and authorship are uncertain. Unlike most anaphoras, much of the prayer is addressed to or praises the Virgin Mary as Mother of God, with lyrical Marian imagery. It is among the most widely used Ethiopian anaphoras and is a key witness to Ethiopian Marian devotion.

The Anaphora of the 318 Orthodox is a eucharistic prayer of the Ethiopian (Ge'ez) liturgy, one of the anaphoras used in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches. It is anonymous and traditionally attributed to the 318 fathers of the Council of Nicaea (325), but its actual date of composition is uncertain and probably much later than the attribution suggests. Like the other Ethiopic anaphoras, it includes an epiclesis asking that the Spirit descend and change the bread and cup into the Body and Blood of Christ.

The Anaphora of Our Lord Jesus Christ is a eucharistic prayer of the Ethiopian (Ge'ez) liturgical tradition and one of the anaphoras used in the Ethiopian Church. It is anonymous and its date is uncertain. Much of it is closely based on the eucharistic prayer of the Testamentum Domini, a church order attributed to Christ. Its epiclesis, the invocation of the Holy Spirit over the bread and cup, resembles those in the Ethiopian anaphoras of the 318 Fathers, of Dioscorus and of James of Serug.

1 Enoch, also called the Book of Enoch, is an ancient Jewish apocalyptic work attributed to the antediluvian patriarch Enoch. It brings together several sections written between about the third and first centuries BC, probably first in Aramaic and perhaps partly in Hebrew. It tells of the fall of the Watchers, the origin of the Nephilim and of evil, the coming judgement and Enoch's heavenly journeys. Aramaic fragments were found at Qumran, Greek portions survive, and the complete text exists only in Ge'ez. The Epistle of Jude quotes it, and the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Churches treat it as canonical.

1 Esdras, also called Greek Esdras or 3 Esdras (its Vulgate title), is an anonymous book of the Septuagint. It retells material found in 2 Chronicles 35–36, Ezra and part of Nehemiah: from Josiah's Passover, through the return from exile and the rebuilding of the Temple, to Ezra's reading of the Law. Its best-known addition is the contest of three guards at the court of Darius, which Zerubbabel wins. It is probably of the second century BC. Eastern churches accept it as canonical, but in the West it is counted among the apocrypha.

1 Meqabyan is the first of three anonymous Ge'ez books known as the Meqabyan, or Ethiopian Maccabees. They are canonical only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches. Despite the shared name, it is unrelated to the Greek books of Maccabees. It tells of Ṣirutsaydan, a proud idolatrous king, and of the sons of a man named Maccabeus who refuse to worship his idols and die as martyrs. The book praises faithfulness to God and condemns idolatry. When it was written is uncertain; scholars have suggested dates from late antiquity to the Middle Ages.

2 Kings is the second half of the Book of Kings in the Hebrew Bible. In the Septuagint and later Greek and Latin tradition it is called 4 Kingdoms. The anonymous work closes the Deuteronomistic history. It runs from Elijah's last days and Elisha's ministry through the fall of Samaria to Assyria and the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah. It ends with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and Jehoiachin's release in exile. Scholars generally date a first edition to the late seventh century BC and a final edition to the mid-sixth.

3 Meqabyan is one of the three books of Meqabyan, or Ethiopian Maccabees. These anonymous Ge'ez writings are canonical only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches. Despite the name, they are unrelated to the Greek books of Maccabees. The text opens with the attack of Meqabis, a Moabite, on Jerusalem and its people. It presents this disaster as God's punishment of Israel for its disobedience, and it urges repentance and faithfulness to God's law. The date of composition is uncertain, and the numbering of the three books is not the same in every tradition.

4 Baruch, also called the Paralipomena of Jeremiah ("things omitted from Jeremiah"), is an anonymous Jewish pseudepigraphon. It was probably written between the destruction of the Temple in 70 and the Bar Kokhba revolt, and its Christian ending was likely added later. It is usually thought to have been composed in Greek or a Semitic language and was later translated into Ge'ez. The book tells of Jeremiah and Baruch at the fall of Jerusalem, Abimelech's 66-year sleep, the return from Babylonian exile and Jeremiah's death. It belongs to the broader Ethiopian Orthodox biblical canon.

4 Ezra is a Jewish apocalypse written around 100 AD, after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem, by an anonymous author writing as Ezra (identified with Shealtiel) in Babylon. Its original Hebrew or Aramaic text is lost; it survives in Latin, Syriac, Ethiopic, Georgian, Armenian and other versions. Through seven visions, including dialogues with the angel Uriel, the eagle vision and the man from the sea, it wrestles with theodicy, sin and Israel's suffering. It forms chapters 3–14 of 2 Esdras and is canonical in the Ethiopian Church.

The Ethiopic Clement (Qalēmenṭos) is an anonymous pseudo-Clementine work in Ge'ez. It presents itself as teaching that the apostle Peter passed on to his disciple Clement of Rome. Its sayings deal with church order and Christian conduct: they condemn simony in baptism and ordination, and they urge forgiveness, works of mercy, just judgement, fasting and prayer, and care for orphans, widows, virgins and poor clergy. It probably goes back to earlier Clementine and church-order traditions, but when it was written is uncertain. It belongs to the broader New Testament canon of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches.

Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Torah and of the Christian Old Testament, is presented as Moses' farewell speeches to Israel on the plains of Moab before they enter the Promised Land. It reviews the wilderness wanderings, restates the law, and calls Israel to stay faithful to God. It ends with the Song and Blessing of Moses and his death. Tradition credited Moses with writing it, but most scholars date it to the 7th–5th centuries BC. It contains the Shema (6:4), which Jesus quoted as the greatest commandment.

Ecclesiastes (Hebrew Qoheleth, "the Preacher" or "Teacher") is a book of wisdom literature in the Ketuvim of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. Tradition attributes it to Solomon, but most scholars date it to roughly the fifth to second centuries BC, partly because of its late Hebrew and Persian loanwords. Its speaker reflects on how fleeting and "vain" human toil, wisdom and pleasure are "under the sun," since death comes to all. He recommends enjoying life's simple gifts from God, and the book closes by urging the reader to fear God and keep his commandments.

Exodus is the second book of the Bible and of the Pentateuch. Tradition ascribes it to Moses, but modern scholars think it took shape from earlier sources and oral traditions during and after the Babylonian exile, with final revision in the Persian period. It tells how the Israelites were enslaved in Egypt and freed under Moses. It goes on to describe the covenant and the giving of the Law at Mount Sinai, and the building of the Tabernacle. Passover and the crossing of the Red Sea became central images for Jewish and Christian interpreters alike.

The Book of Ezra is a book of the Hebrew Bible and Christian Old Testament, written in Hebrew and Aramaic and originally joined with Nehemiah as a single work. Its author is unknown; tradition credits Ezra himself. It tells how Cyrus allowed the exiles to return from Babylon in 538 BC and how the Temple in Jerusalem was rebuilt and dedicated in 515 BC. It then follows the scribe and priest Ezra's mission to reform the community, including his campaign against marriages with non-Jews.

Genesis is the first book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, and the opening book of the Torah, or Pentateuch. Tradition names Moses as its author. Most modern scholars instead see it as an anonymous composite work that took its final form during or after the Babylonian exile, perhaps in the fifth century BC. Its first part (chapters 1–11) tells of the creation, the fall, the flood and the early history of humanity. Its second part (chapters 12–50) follows the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. Church Fathers wrote many commentaries and homilies on it.

The Book of Isaiah is the first of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the first of the major prophets in the Christian Old Testament. It is attributed to Isaiah son of Amoz, an eighth-century BC prophet in Jerusalem. Most scholars think much of it was written later, during and after the Babylonian exile. Its oracles of judgment and restoration focus on Judah, Jerusalem and the nations. Christian writers read its prophecies of Immanuel and the Suffering Servant as foretelling Christ, and quoted it more often than almost any other book.

The Book of Judith is an anonymous Jewish narrative, probably composed in Hebrew around the second or first century BC. It survives mainly in the Greek Septuagint, and Jerome made a freer Latin version from an Aramaic text in the late fourth century. It tells how Judith, a devout widow of Bethulia, beheads the Assyrian general Holofernes and so saves her people. The Catholic and Orthodox churches accept it as deuterocanonical. It is not part of the Hebrew canon, and Protestants count it among the Apocrypha.

The Book of Job is an anonymous book of the Hebrew Bible. It belongs to the Ketuvim (Writings) and is the first of the Poetic Books of the Christian Old Testament. Its language points to composition in the Persian period, though the date is uncertain. A prose prologue and epilogue frame poetic dialogues between the righteous Job, who has lost his wealth, children and health, and his friends, followed by Elihu's speeches and God's reply from the whirlwind. The book's treatment of innocent suffering and divine justice made it a major subject of Jewish and Christian theology and exegesis.

The Book of Joel is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and one of the Twelve Minor Prophets. It names its author as "Joel the son of Pethuel", of whom nothing else is known. Its date is disputed. Many scholars place it in the Persian period, partly because it alludes so often to earlier prophetic texts. Starting from a devastating locust plague, it calls the people to repentance and announces the coming Day of the Lord. It also foretells the outpouring of God's Spirit on all people, a prophecy Peter quotes in his Pentecost sermon in Acts 2.

The Book of Jonah is an anonymous Hebrew narrative and one of the twelve Minor Prophets in the Jewish and Christian Old Testament. It tells of the prophet Jonah, son of Amittai, who flees God's command to preach against Nineveh. A great fish swallows him during a storm. After he is released he preaches, the city repents, and God spares it. Most scholars date the book to the postexilic period. Jesus' "sign of Jonah" led early Christian writers to read Jonah as a type of Christ's death and resurrection.

Joshua is the sixth book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It tells how Joshua son of Nun succeeded Moses and led the Israelites across the Jordan. It narrates their campaigns to conquer Canaan, the division of the land among the twelve tribes, and Joshua's closing call to remain faithful to the Law. Jewish tradition attributes the book to Joshua himself. Modern scholars treat it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, with an early form probably written in the late seventh century BC and completed during or after the Babylonian exile.

The Book of Jubilees is an anonymous Jewish work, probably composed in Hebrew in the second century BC. In it, an angel reveals to Moses on Mount Sinai the history of the world from Creation to the giving of the Law. Retelling Genesis and the opening of Exodus, it arranges events in "jubilees", periods of forty-nine years, and promotes a 364-day solar calendar. Hebrew fragments were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and early Christian writers knew the book. Only the Ge'ez version survives complete, and the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches count it as Scripture.

Judges is the seventh book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is anonymous: Jewish tradition attributed it to Samuel, while modern scholars see it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, with the main editing often dated to the 7th century BC and later. It covers the period between Joshua's conquest and the monarchy. The book follows a repeated cycle in which Israel is unfaithful, is oppressed, repents and is rescued by a leader. These leaders include Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson. Its closing chapters look ahead to the coming of kingship.

Lamentations is a book of the Hebrew Bible made up of five poems mourning the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians in 586 BC. Four are alphabetic acrostics. Tradition ascribes them to the prophet Jeremiah, and in Christian Bibles the book follows his. Most modern scholars reject this authorship but date the poems to shortly after the city's fall. The poems personify Zion as a bereaved widow and present the people's sin as the cause of divine judgment. Jews read the book on Tisha B'Av, and Christians read it during Holy Week.

The Lefafa Sedq ("Bandlet of Righteousness") is an anonymous Ethiopian funerary text in Ge'ez. It is a sequence of prayers that contain secret names of God and of Christ. According to tradition, Christ revealed it to the Virgin Mary to secure the salvation of believers. The text was copied onto a strip of parchment, often about the height of the dead person, and buried with the body. It was meant to protect the soul on its passage after death and gain it entry into heaven. Its date and origin are uncertain, and some scholars suggest Egyptian or Coptic influence.

Leviticus is the third book of the Torah (Pentateuch) and of the Old Testament, traditionally ascribed to Moses. Its anonymous text probably developed over a long period, and many scholars think it reached its present form in the Persian period, though this is disputed. Set at Mount Sinai, it consists mostly of divine instructions given to Moses for the Israelites and the Aaronic priests. These cover sacrifices, priestly ordination, purity laws, the Day of Atonement and the Holiness Code (chapters 17–26). Christian interpreters read its sacrifices and priesthood typologically.

Mysteries of Heaven and Earth is an anonymous apocryphal work that survives in Ge'ez, the classical language of Ethiopia. Its date and origin are uncertain. It is presented as mysteries that the apostle Peter revealed to his disciple Clement, which places it among the writings that circulated under Clement's name. The text gives an account of creation and a summary of biblical history down to the reign of King Jehoram. It also includes discourses on God's mercy toward humankind and on the role of Christ as Saviour.

Numbers is the fourth book of the Hebrew Bible and of the Pentateuch, traditionally attributed to Moses. Scholars think it has a long, complex history, and its final form probably comes from a Priestly editing in the early Persian period. It is named after the two censuses of Israel that it records. The book follows the Israelites from Sinai through their wanderings in the wilderness. It tells of their rebellions, the sending of the spies and the Balaam episode, and ends on the plains of Moab before Canaan.

The Book of Proverbs is a book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, and a classic example of biblical wisdom literature. Tradition ascribes it to King Solomon. Scholars instead see it as a "collection of collections" from different periods, with the final redaction often placed in the Persian or Hellenistic era. In short sayings and longer discourses it sets wise conduct against folly. It teaches that "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge" and personifies Wisdom as present at creation. Christian writers widely read Proverbs 8 in a Christological sense.

The Book of Ruth is a short anonymous Hebrew narrative in the Hebrew Bible. It is one of the Five Megillot in the Writings, while the Greek and Christian canons place it after Judges. The date is uncertain, but many scholars assign it to the Persian period. It tells how Ruth, a Moabite widow, stays loyal to her mother-in-law Naomi, goes with her to Bethlehem and marries their kinsman Boaz. Their son Obed became David's grandfather. Ruth appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, and the book is read in synagogues at Shavuot.

The Sinodos is an anonymous Ethiopian collection of church order and canon law, counted among the books of the broader Ethiopian Orthodox biblical canon. It brings together earlier Christian material dating roughly from the third to the seventh centuries, including the Apostolic Tradition, the Apostolic Canons, and canons of councils such as Nicaea, Ancyra, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea and Chalcedon. It also includes letters of Constantine, Athanasius and Cyril of Alexandria, along with liturgical and baptismal texts. The Ge'ez text was translated from Arabic, and it remains an important source for church discipline and early liturgy.

Sirach, also called Ecclesiasticus or the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach, is a Jewish wisdom book. Jesus ben Sira, a scribe in Jerusalem, wrote it in Hebrew around 196–175 BC. His grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt after 132 BC and added a prologue. The prologue is an early witness to the threefold division of the Hebrew scriptures. The book offers ethical teaching, praise of wisdom and a hymn to Israel's famous ancestors. Judaism excludes it from the Hebrew Bible, but it is in the Septuagint and was widely read in the early Church.

The Song of Songs, also called the Song of Solomon or Canticle of Canticles, is a book of Hebrew love poetry, one of the five megillot in the Ketuvim. Its superscription links it to Solomon, but its real author is unknown and its date is debated; many scholars place it in the Persian or Hellenistic period. In dialogues, dreams and rich imagery, a woman and her beloved express their desire. Jewish tradition reads it as an allegory of God and Israel. Christian commentators, from Origen onward, read it as an allegory of Christ and the Church or the soul.

The Ethiopian Synaxarion (Senkessar) is a liturgical collection of short commemorative notices of saints, martyrs, angels, prophets and church events. The notices are arranged day by day through the Ethiopian year, beginning with the month of Maskaram. It derives from the Arabic Synaxarion of the Coptic Church. Its preface attributes that work to Michael, bishop of Athribis and Malig, John, bishop of Burullus, and others, and dates it to the year 963 of the Martyrs (1246–47). It was probably translated into Ge'ez around 1400, later expanded with Ethiopian saints, and survives in more than one recension.

The Teaching of Mysteries (Ge'ez Tǝmhǝrtä ḫǝbuʾat, "Teaching of Hidden Things") is a short anonymous catechetical text in Ge'ez. Its opening says it is to be given to the faithful before the offering, the prosphora. It summarises the faith in Christ: his pre-existence and coming, and his suffering, death, burial and resurrection. It also tells of his descent to Sheol, his victory over death and the restoration of Adam's flesh and soul. It closes with a doxology. Its date is uncertain, probably between the fifth and eighth centuries. It may have been translated from Greek.

Tobit is an anonymous Jewish narrative from the Second Temple period, usually dated to the 3rd or early 2nd century BC and probably first written in Aramaic or Hebrew. It tells of the pious, blinded exile Tobit in Nineveh and his son Tobias, who travels guided by the angel Raphael. On the way Tobias frees Sarah from the demon Asmodeus and marries her, and Tobit's sight is restored. The short recension, preserved in Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus, is one of several ancient forms of this deuterocanonical book.

The Wisdom of Solomon, or Book of Wisdom, is a Jewish wisdom book written in Greek, probably by an Alexandrian author. Most scholars date it to the first century BC, though proposed dates vary. It speaks in the voice of Solomon and urges rulers to love righteousness. It praises wisdom as a divine spirit present with God from eternity, defends the immortality of the righteous, and retells the Exodus. It is part of the Septuagint and is counted as deuterocanonical by Catholic and Orthodox churches. Protestants class it among the Apocrypha. It shaped early Christian theology.

The Félire Óengusso is an Old Irish verse martyrology attributed to Óengus mac Óengobann, called the Culdee, a monk of the Céli Dé reform associated with Tallaght. It was composed around the early ninth century, though its exact date is debated. The work gives one quatrain for each day of the year, commemorating saints both universal and Irish. It is framed by a long prologue and epilogue that celebrate the martyrs' triumph over pagan kings. It is the earliest metrical martyrology in any European vernacular. Later scholars added Middle Irish prefaces and glosses to it.

The Divine Liturgy of Saint Basil the Great is a Eucharistic liturgy of the Byzantine Rite. Its central anaphora is traditionally attributed to Basil of Caesarea (d. 379). Many scholars accept that he revised or expanded an earlier Cappadocian prayer, while the surrounding service grew over later centuries. Its long anaphora sets out the history of salvation from creation to Christ. In Byzantine use it replaces the Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom about ten times a year, including the Sundays of Great Lent, Christmas Eve, Theophany Eve and Saint Basil's feast.

The Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom is the main eucharistic service of the Byzantine Rite, still celebrated on most days by Eastern Orthodox and Byzantine Catholic churches. It takes its name from its central anaphora, the eucharistic prayer, which is traditionally attributed to John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople (d. 407). His authorship is disputed. The full rite, with its litanies, antiphons, entrances and prayers, developed over centuries in Constantinople. It was translated early into other languages, including Georgian, and eventually replaced the Liturgy of Saint Basil as the usual Byzantine Eucharist.

Barlaam and Ioasaph is a Greek hagiographical romance about the Indian prince Ioasaph. His father, a king who persecutes Christians, shuts him away, but the hermit Barlaam reaches him and converts him through long instruction and parables. The story is a Christianized version of the legend of the Buddha, passed on through Arabic and Georgian versions. The Greek text was traditionally ascribed to John of Damascus, but it is now usually credited to Euthymius the Athonite, writing around the late tenth century. It spread widely in medieval Christian literature.

This is the first of three Greek homilies on the Dormition (Koimesis) of the Virgin Mary by John of Damascus, the monk and theologian of Mar Saba near Jerusalem who died around 749. It was probably composed in the second quarter of the eighth century. The sermon praises the Mother of God as the "city of God" that held the uncircumscribed Word. It celebrates her death, burial and glorification as a feast of joy. The three sermons are key witnesses to Byzantine teaching on Mary's end, which is why John is often called the "Doctor of the Assumption."

This is the second of three Greek homilies on the Dormition (Koimesis) of the Virgin Mary by John of Damascus, the monk and theologian of Mar Saba near Jerusalem. They were composed in the first half of the eighth century and probably delivered together for the feast. Addressed to assembled pastors, the sermon praises the Mother of God and describes her death, burial and bodily taking up into heaven. The three homilies are among the most important early witnesses to belief in Mary's Assumption, and John is often called the "Doctor of the Assumption" because of them.

This is the third of three Greek homilies on the Dormition (Koimesis) of the Virgin Mary by John of Damascus, the eighth-century monk and theologian of Mar Saba near Jerusalem. It is shorter than the first two and describes itself as a further tribute offered during the feast's night vigil. In it John praises the Mother of God and her passing from this world. Together the three sermons are key Byzantine witnesses to belief in her bodily assumption. They helped earn John the title "Doctor of the Assumption".

Three Greek treatises by John of Damascus, a monk of Mar Saba near Jerusalem, written in defence of icons after the Byzantine emperor Leo III began his iconoclast policy in the 720s. The exact dates are uncertain. John grounds the making and veneration of images in the Incarnation, since the invisible God became visible in Christ. He distinguishes worship due to God alone from the honour given to images and saints, and supports his case with collections of patristic testimonies. The treatises shaped the later Orthodox theology of icons that the Second Council of Nicaea (787) affirmed.

The Secret History, also called the Anecdota, is a Greek account of the reign of the Byzantine emperor Justinian I by the historian Procopius of Caesarea. It presents itself as a supplement to his History of the Wars, revealing what he could not safely publish. It is a fierce invective against Justinian, the empress Theodora, the general Belisarius and his wife Antonina. Its date is debated, with most scholars preferring 550–551 over 558–559. It circulated privately and is first mentioned in the tenth-century Suda.

The History of the Wars is a Greek historical narrative by Procopius of Caesarea, legal adviser and secretary to the general Belisarius, who witnessed many of the campaigns he describes. Written in the mid-sixth century, it covers the wars of Emperor Justinian I. Books I–II treat the conflicts with Sasanian Persia, Books III–IV the reconquest of Vandal Africa, and Books V–VIII the Gothic War in Italy. It is the principal source for the military and political history of Justinian's reign.

The Cathemerinon ("Daily Round") is a collection of twelve Latin lyric hymns by the Spanish Christian poet Aurelius Prudentius Clemens (348–after 405). It was probably published around 405 with his other poems. The first six hymns mark the hours of the Christian day, from cockcrow and morning to the lighting of lamps and sleep. The rest are for fasting, burial, Christmas, Epiphany and every hour. They use classical metres and draw on Ambrose's hymns. Excerpts entered the Latin liturgy, and parts survive as hymns such as "Of the Father's Love Begotten".

The Hudra ("Cycle") is the main choir book of the East Syriac liturgical tradition used by the Church of the East. It contains the proper hymns, anthems and prayers of the Divine Office for the Sundays, feasts and fasts of the liturgical year. Its core is traditionally linked to the reform of the Patriarch Ishoyahb III in the seventh century, following the use of the Upper Monastery at Mosul. Later poets added material to it over many centuries. This first volume opens with the ordinary weekday office, the Book of Before and After, and its rules for the alternating choirs.

The Liturgy of Addai and Mari is the main eucharistic liturgy of the East Syriac tradition. It is named after Addai and Mari, the missionaries traditionally credited with evangelising Edessa and Mesopotamia. Its anonymous core anaphora is usually dated to the third century or later, and the whole rite took shape over several centuries. It is one of the oldest eucharistic prayers still in use and is notable because its manuscripts lack an explicit narrative of institution. The Assyrian Church of the East, the Chaldean Catholic Church and the Syro-Malabar Church all still use it.

4 Ezra is a Jewish apocalypse written around 100 AD, after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem, by an anonymous author writing as Ezra (identified with Shealtiel) in Babylon. Its original Hebrew or Aramaic text is lost; it survives in Latin, Syriac, Ethiopic, Georgian, Armenian and other versions. Through seven visions, including dialogues with the angel Uriel, the eagle vision and the man from the sea, it wrestles with theodicy, sin and Israel's suffering. It forms chapters 3–14 of 2 Esdras and is canonical in the Ethiopian Church.

1 Chronicles is the first half of the Book of Chronicles, a Hebrew scriptural history that the Septuagint divided into two books and called Paralipomenon. Tradition ascribed it to Ezra. Modern scholars instead attribute it to an anonymous priestly author, "the Chronicler," writing in Jerusalem in the Persian or early Hellenistic period. It opens with genealogies from Adam to the exiles who returned from Babylon. It then narrates the death of Saul and the reign of David, stressing the ark, the Levites and the preparations for the Temple.

The First Epistle to the Corinthians is a letter of the New Testament written in Greek by the apostle Paul, with Sosthenes named as co-sender, to the church he had founded at Corinth. It was probably written from Ephesus around 53–57. Paul responds to reports of factions and to questions from the community about sexual morality, marriage, food offered to idols, conduct in worship, the Lord's Supper and spiritual gifts. It includes the celebrated hymn to love (chapter 13) and the earliest extended teaching on the resurrection (chapter 15).

The First Epistle of John is a New Testament writing in Greek, the first of the three Johannine epistles. It names no author. Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is disputed, and many scholars place it within the Johannine community around 85–100. It reads more like a homily than a letter. It teaches that God is light and God is love, and that believers must confess their sins and love one another. It also rejects those who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. Its theology of love and fellowship has strongly shaped Christian thought.

1 Kings is the first half of the Book of Kings in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint and Vulgate tradition calls it 3 Kingdoms (Regnorum III). The anonymous work belongs to the Deuteronomistic history. Scholars generally date a first edition to the late seventh century BC and a final edition to the mid-sixth. It tells of David's death and Solomon's accession and reign, including the building of the Jerusalem Temple. It then covers the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam and Jeroboam and the later kings of Israel and Judah, ending with Elijah's conflict with Ahab.

The First Epistle of Peter is a letter in the New Testament, one of the Catholic Epistles. Its author presents himself as the apostle Peter, writing from "Babylon", probably meaning Rome. Many scholars, however, think it came from a Roman Christian circle linked to Peter, sometime around 60–90. It is addressed to Christians scattered across Asia Minor who were suffering persecution. The letter urges them to keep hope, holiness and patient endurance, modelled on the sufferings of Christ. It also gives household instructions and contains a famous passage on Christ preaching to the "spirits in prison".

1 Samuel is the first half of the Book of Samuel in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint calls it 1 Kingdoms and the Vulgate 1 Kings. It is anonymous. Jewish tradition credits it to the prophet Samuel, with additions by Gad and Nathan. Modern scholars see it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, put together from older sources around the seventh to sixth centuries BC. It tells of Samuel's birth to Hannah and his career as a prophet, the fortunes of the Ark of the Covenant, Saul's anointing and rejection as Israel's first king, and David's rise.

The First Epistle to the Thessalonians is a letter of the New Testament sent by the apostle Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, to the Christian community he had founded at Thessalonica in Macedonia. It was probably written around 50–52, most likely from Corinth. Scholars widely accept it as authentic, and it is often regarded as the earliest surviving Christian writing. Paul gives thanks for the converts' faith under persecution and defends his own conduct among them. He urges them to live holy lives and addresses the fate of believers who have died before the Lord's return.

The First Epistle to Timothy is a New Testament letter written in Greek and addressed by the apostle Paul to his co-worker Timothy, who had been left at Ephesus. With 2 Timothy and Titus it forms the Pastoral Epistles. It warns against false teachers, gives directions on prayer and worship, and sets out qualifications for bishops and deacons and rules on widows and elders. Pauline authorship is disputed. Many scholars date it to the late first or early second century. It was important for later teaching on church order and ministry.

2 Chronicles is the second half of the Book of Chronicles in the Hebrew Bible, which was divided into two books in the Septuagint. Greek and Latin tradition calls it Paralipomenon. It is anonymous. Tradition credited it to Ezra, but scholars attribute it to an unknown "Chronicler" writing in the Persian or early Hellenistic period. It tells the story of Solomon's reign and the building of the Temple, then follows the kings of Judah to the Babylonian exile. It ends with the edict of Cyrus allowing the exiles to return.

The Second Epistle to the Corinthians is a New Testament letter written in Greek by the apostle Paul, with Timothy named as co-sender. It is addressed to the church at Corinth and the Christians of Achaia, and is usually dated about 55–57. Paul writes about comfort in suffering and defends his apostolic ministry. He also urges a collection for the church in Jerusalem and confronts rival "super-apostles." Many scholars think it combines parts of several letters. It was translated early into Syriac, Latin, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian and Georgian.

The Second Epistle of John is a short New Testament letter. Its author calls himself "the elder" and writes to "the elect lady and her children", which most readers take to mean a local church. Tradition ascribes it to the apostle John, but the authorship is disputed. It is usually dated to the late first century. The letter urges mutual love and obedience to the commandments. It warns against deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh and forbids welcoming them.

2 Kings is the second half of the Book of Kings in the Hebrew Bible. In the Septuagint and later Greek and Latin tradition it is called 4 Kingdoms. The anonymous work closes the Deuteronomistic history. It runs from Elijah's last days and Elisha's ministry through the fall of Samaria to Assyria and the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah. It ends with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and Jehoiachin's release in exile. Scholars generally date a first edition to the late seventh century BC and a final edition to the mid-sixth.

The Second Epistle of Peter is a short letter in the New Testament. Its author presents himself as the apostle Simon Peter, but most modern scholars consider it pseudonymous and date it to roughly 80–120, which may make it the latest New Testament book. It urges believers to grow in virtue and become "partakers of the divine nature," warns against false teachers, and defends the expectation of Christ's return. It overlaps closely with the Epistle of Jude, and its place in the canon was disputed in the early Church.

2 Samuel is the second half of the Book of Samuel in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint and Vulgate count it as the second Book of Kingdoms or Kings. It tells of David's reign, from his lament for Saul and Jonathan to his rule over Judah and Israel, his capture of Jerusalem, God's promise of a lasting dynasty, his sin with Bathsheba, and Absalom's revolt. Jewish tradition credits it to Samuel, Gad and Nathan. Modern scholars treat it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, compiled about 630–540 BC from older sources.

The Second Epistle to the Thessalonians is a short letter of the New Testament. It names Paul, Silvanus and Timothy as its senders and is addressed to the Christian community at Thessalonica in Macedonia. It encourages believers suffering persecution and promises God's just judgement when the Lord Jesus is revealed. It corrects the claim that the day of the Lord has already come, describing a "man of lawlessness" who must appear first. It also warns against idleness. Scholars disagree about whether Paul wrote it. Dates proposed range from about 50 to near the end of the first century.

The Second Epistle to Timothy is a New Testament letter. It is one of the three Pastoral Epistles and is presented as written by the apostle Paul to his co-worker Timothy. Many scholars think it was written by a later follower of Paul in the late first century, while others accept that Paul wrote it during his final imprisonment in Rome. It is framed as Paul's last charge: Timothy should endure hardship, guard sound teaching and resist false teachers. It contains the statement that all Scripture is inspired by God, and Paul's farewell, "I have fought the good fight."

The Third Epistle of John is the shortest book of the New Testament. It is a private letter from an author who calls himself "the elder" to a Christian named Gaius. Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is debated, and it is usually dated to the late first century. The elder praises Gaius for welcoming travelling missionaries and condemns Diotrephes for refusing to receive them and for seeking preeminence. He also recommends Demetrius. The letter sheds rare light on authority and hospitality in the early church. Some early churches questioned whether it belonged in the canon.

The Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament. It forms the second half of a two-volume work with the Gospel of Luke and is addressed, like that Gospel, to Theophilus. Tradition names Luke, a companion of Paul, as its author, though scholars disagree about this; it is usually dated around 80–90. Acts begins with Christ's ascension and Pentecost and describes the early Jerusalem church. It then follows the spread of the gospel to the Gentiles, mostly through Paul's missionary journeys, and ends with his imprisonment in Rome.

Amos is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is the third of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew order and the second in the Septuagint. It is attributed to Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah. He preached in the northern kingdom of Israel around 760–750 BC, under Jeroboam II and Uzziah. Its nine chapters announce oracles against the surrounding nations and then against Israel itself. They condemn oppression of the poor, empty worship and injustice. Scholars debate how much of the book's account of the prophet is historical.

The Epistle to the Colossians is a New Testament letter addressed to the Christian community at Colossae in Phrygia, Asia Minor. It names Paul and Timothy as senders, but many scholars doubt that Paul wrote it, and its date is uncertain. It is usually placed between about 58 and 80. The letter presents Christ as supreme over all creation and powers. It warns against a local "philosophy" involving ascetic and ritual practices and gives instructions for Christian households. Its close parallels with Ephesians have long attracted scholarly attention.

The Book of Daniel is a biblical apocalypse set during the Babylonian exile in the 6th century BC. Most scholars date its final form to about 167–163 BC, during the persecution under Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Its six court tales (chapters 1–6), written mostly in Aramaic, tell of Daniel and his companions at the Babylonian and Persian courts. Four visions follow (chapters 7–12), written mainly in Hebrew. The Greek versions, the Old Greek and Theodotion, add Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, and the Prayer of Azariah. Daniel strongly shaped Jewish and Christian apocalyptic thought.

Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Torah and of the Christian Old Testament, is presented as Moses' farewell speeches to Israel on the plains of Moab before they enter the Promised Land. It reviews the wilderness wanderings, restates the law, and calls Israel to stay faithful to God. It ends with the Song and Blessing of Moses and his death. Tradition credited Moses with writing it, but most scholars date it to the 7th–5th centuries BC. It contains the Shema (6:4), which Jesus quoted as the greatest commandment.
