Gregory describes perfection as endless progress in virtue toward the infinite God. His account of Moses entering the divine darkness on Sinai deeply influenced later Christian mystical theology.

The Homilies on the Song of Songs are fifteen sermons by Gregory of Nyssa, one of the Cappadocian Fathers, written late in his life, probably in the early 390s. They were dedicated to the deaconess Olympias of Constantinople, who had asked for them. The prologue defends allegorical reading against those who held to the literal sense alone. The homilies read the Song as the soul's endless ascent toward God, an idea later called epektasis. They are central to Gregory's mystical theology and shaped later Christian contemplative exegesis.

The Homilies on Ecclesiastes are eight sermons by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. They were written in the later fourth century, though the exact date is uncertain. The homilies interpret Ecclesiastes 1:1 to 3:13. Gregory reads the book as a guide that leads the soul away from attachment to passing, material things and toward contemplation of God. The fourth homily is especially well known. Commenting on the acquisition of slaves (Ecclesiastes 2:7), Gregory condemns slavery itself as an offence against human nature and against God. It is one of the earliest known outright condemnations of the practice.

The Explicatio apologetica in Hexaemeron, also called the Apology on the Hexaemeron, is a Greek treatise by Gregory of Nyssa. He addressed it to his brother Peter, later bishop of Sebaste, and probably wrote it around 379, soon after the death of their brother Basil of Caesarea. At Peter's request, Gregory defends and supplements Basil's Homilies on the Hexaemeron. He tries to resolve apparent contradictions in the Genesis account of the six days of creation. In doing so he argues that God created all things at once in potential, and that they then unfolded in an ordered sequence.

This short exegetical treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, dates from the late fourth century. Its exact date is uncertain. It explains 1 Corinthians 15:28, "then the Son himself will also be subjected." Arian and Eunomian opponents used this verse to argue that the Son is inferior to the Father. Gregory answers that the subjection refers to humanity, which forms Christ's body. When all evil is removed and every creature is united to God, God becomes "all in all." The work is an important witness to Gregory's teaching on universal restoration.

On the Inscriptions of the Psalms is a Greek exegetical treatise in two books by Gregory of Nyssa. It was written at the request of an unnamed "man of God", probably during his years as bishop, though the exact date is uncertain. The first book considers the aim of the whole Psalter, which Gregory identifies as blessedness. He reads the five divisions of the book as stages in the soul's ascent through virtue toward likeness to God. The second book interprets the psalm titles themselves. The work is an important example of Gregory's spiritual, Origenist-influenced approach to Scripture.

Ad Graecos ex communibus notionibus ("To the Greeks, from Common Notions") is a short Greek treatise on the Trinity by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It dates from the later fourth century, but its exact date is uncertain. Gregory argues from shared philosophical concepts that the word "God" names the divine essence, not the persons. Because Father, Son and Holy Spirit share one essence, Christians confess one God and not three. The treatise is closely related to his better-known Ad Ablabium (On Not Three Gods). Both defend Nicene doctrine against the charge of tritheism.

Against Arius and Sabellius is a short Greek theological treatise transmitted among the works of Gregory of Nyssa, though its authenticity is doubted and its real author is uncertain. It probably dates from the late fourth century. Starting from Psalm 45:1, "My heart has poured forth a good word," it attacks two opposite errors: the Arian view that the Son is a creature, and the Sabellian merging of Father and Son into a single "Son-Father." Against both it defends the Son's distinct hypostasis and full divinity as the narrow middle way of orthodoxy.

The Antirrheticus adversus Apollinarium is a Greek polemical treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It is generally dated to the later part of his career, probably the 380s, though the exact date is uncertain. In it Gregory refutes the Christology of Apollinarius of Laodicea, who taught that the divine Logos took the place of a human mind in Christ. Gregory argues that Christ assumed a complete human nature. The treatise quotes Apollinarius's Apodeixis at length, so it is also an important source for fragments of that otherwise lost work.

Contra fatum (Against Fate) is a short Greek treatise in the form of a letter by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. Its exact date is uncertain, but it falls within his active years in the late fourth century. Gregory writes at the request of an honoured correspondent and gives a brief account of a debate he held in Constantinople with a pagan philosopher. In it he argues against astrological determinism, the belief that the stars fix human lives. The work defends human free will and God's providence against the fatalism common in late antiquity.

On the Medium (De pythonissa) is a short Greek letter by Gregory of Nyssa, the fourth-century Cappadocian bishop, to a Bishop Theodosius who had sent him questions about Scripture. Its main subject is 1 Samuel 28, where the medium of Endor appears to call up the dead Samuel for King Saul. Gregory rejects the view of some earlier interpreters that the prophet really appeared. He argues instead that a demon took Samuel's likeness to deceive Saul. Its exact date is unknown, and it is a notable patristic example of interpreting this disputed passage.

Against Those Who Delay Baptism (Adversus eos qui baptismum differunt) is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. He preached it on a feast when baptism was given, sometime between about 370 and 395; the exact date is uncertain. It targets a common fourth-century habit: catechumens put off baptism until late in life or until they were dying. Gregory warns that death can come suddenly and urges his hearers to be baptized now. The sermon is an important witness to baptismal practice and pastoral preaching in the late fourth-century Greek Church.

De instituto Christiano, also called On the Christian Mode of Life, is a Greek ascetic treatise attributed to Gregory of Nyssa. It is addressed to a community of ascetics who asked about the goal of piety. It describes the soul's natural longing for God, its purification from the passions and the virtues of common monastic life. The text is closely parallel to the Great Letter of Pseudo-Macarius. Most scholars now think it is an adaptation of that letter, so Gregory's authorship and the date are disputed.

De mortuis ("On the Dead") is a Greek discourse by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. Its exact date is uncertain. It is addressed to those who grieve for the departed. Gregory argues that people mourn death bitterly out of irrational habit rather than reasoned judgement. He sets out what is truly good, what is distinctive about bodily life, and what is hoped for in the life to come. The work presents death as passing into a better, bodiless existence and develops his teaching on the soul, the body and resurrection.

De occursu Domini ("On the Meeting of the Lord, and on the Theotokos") is a Greek festal homily for the Presentation of Christ in the Temple, known in the East as the Hypapante or "Meeting". It has come down under the name of Gregory of Nyssa, but its authenticity is disputed and it is widely thought to be later than his time. Its date is therefore uncertain. The sermon opens with a rhetorical praise of the apostle Paul, then turns to the feast, Simeon's encounter with the infant Christ and the role of the Virgin Mary as Theotokos.

De pauperibus amandis I, also called On Good Works (De beneficentia), is the first of two Greek sermons on love for the poor by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop. It was preached during a fast, probably in Lent; its exact date is uncertain. Gregory moves from bodily fasting to a "bodiless" fast, abstaining from evil, and then urges his hearers to help the many destitute and homeless people of his day. It is an important witness to early Christian teaching on poverty and almsgiving.

De pauperibus amandis oratio II is the second of two Greek sermons "On the Love of the Poor" by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It was preached in the later fourth century, but its exact date is uncertain. The sermon is a commentary on Matthew 25:40, "Inasmuch as you did it to one of these." Gregory opens with a vivid picture of Christ's Last Judgment and goes on to urge compassion for the destitute sick, especially people suffering from leprosy. It is an important witness to early Christian teaching on charity and social care.

On Perfection is a short Greek ascetical treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. He addressed it to Olympius, a monk who had asked how one might become perfect through a life of virtue. Its exact date is uncertain. Gregory starts from the name "Christian" and argues that those who bear Christ's name should show his titles and attributes in their lives. Perfection is presented as a continual imitation of Christ, a theme central to Gregory's spiritual teaching.

De professione Christiana, also known as On What It Means to Call Oneself a Christian, is a short ascetic treatise in the form of a letter by Gregory of Nyssa, the fourth-century bishop and Cappadocian Father. It is addressed to Harmonius, a younger friend, and its exact date is uncertain. Gregory says the long letter makes up for the many he owes and stands in for their talks together. He argues that bearing Christ's name commits the believer to imitating the divine nature through a virtuous life.

De sancto Theodoro martyre is a panegyric sermon by Gregory of Nyssa, the fourth-century Cappadocian bishop and theologian. He delivered it at the shrine of the soldier-martyr Theodore, known as Theodore Tyro or "the Recruit," on the saint's feast before crowds of pilgrims gathered in winter. Gregory credits the martyr with turning back a "Scythian" invasion the year before. He then retells Theodore's confession and execution by fire and encourages devotion at his tomb. The exact year of delivery is disputed. The sermon is an important early witness to the cult of martyrs and the veneration of relics.

De vita S. Ephraem Syri is a Greek encomium, or panegyric, on Ephrem the Syrian, the fourth-century deacon, poet and theologian of Nisibis and Edessa who died in 373. It has come down under the name of Gregory of Nyssa, but its authenticity is widely doubted, and its date and real author are uncertain. Opening with Christ's parable of the lamp on the lampstand, the speaker argues that Ephrem's life should not stay hidden. He then praises Ephrem's asceticism, virtues and writings. The work shaped the legendary picture of Ephrem in the Greek-speaking world.

This is a collection of five Greek sermons for Easter that have come down under the name of Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian who died around 394. The orations celebrate Christ's resurrection and discuss the three days between his death and rising. They also present the paschal feast as fulfilling the blessings, laws, figures and prophecies of the Old Testament, and they hail the newly baptised as Abraham's promised offspring, shining like stars. Not all five orations are accepted as Gregory's own, and the authenticity of several of them is debated.

In diem natalem Christi is a Greek festal sermon on the Nativity of Christ by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian theologian and bishop. He preached it for the Christmas feast, probably in the 380s, although the exact date is uncertain. It opens with the psalm's call to "blow the trumpet" and presents the Incarnation as the true Feast of Tabernacles, in which Christ pitches a human tent and rebuilds humanity's dwelling that death had destroyed. The sermon also deals with the infants of Bethlehem killed by Herod. It is early evidence for the Nativity feast in the Greek East.

The Funeral Oration on the Empress Flacilla is a Greek funeral speech by Gregory of Nyssa. He gave it in Constantinople around 386 for Aelia Flaccilla, wife of the emperor Theodosius I, who died in Thrace. Gregory opens by reflecting on the silence the bishop of the city first imposed on the mourning church. He then praises the empress's piety, humility, charity to the poor and loyalty to Nicene orthodoxy, and offers consolation drawn from Christian hope. It is one of his occasional speeches tied to the imperial court, along with his oration for her young daughter Pulcheria.

The Oratio consolatoria in Pulcheriam is a Greek funeral oration by Gregory of Nyssa. He gave it in Constantinople around 385 for Pulcheria, the young daughter of Emperor Theodosius I and Empress Flaccilla, who had died in early childhood. Gregory compares the city's grief to an earthquake, and his speech is meant to comfort the imperial family and the people. He draws on classical rhetoric of consolation and on Christian teaching about the innocence of children who die young and the hope of resurrection. It belongs with his funeral oration for Flaccilla, who died soon afterwards.

This is the first of two Greek homilies by Gregory of Nyssa on Stephen, the first Christian martyr. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa in Cappadocia, preached it in the late fourth century on Stephen's feast, the day after the celebration of Christ's Nativity. The sermon links the two feasts: Christ put on humanity for us, and Stephen put off his life for Christ. Using athletic imagery, it shows Stephen as a champion who opened the way for the martyrs while heaven watched.

The second Encomium on Saint Stephen the Protomartyr is a Greek festal sermon by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, composed in the later fourth century. It is the companion to his first encomium on Stephen and was likewise preached for the saint's feast in the Christmas season. Gregory presents Stephen as the first fruit of the Church after Christ. He plays on his name (stephanos, "crown"), contrasts him with the crown of thorns, and praises his care for widows, his fullness of the Spirit and his witness unto death.

In suam ordinationem ("On his own ordination") is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It is usually dated to 381 and linked to the Council of Constantinople. The exact occasion is disputed, because Gregory had already been a bishop since 372. In the opening, the preacher modestly calls himself a poor, grey-haired guest at a "spiritual feast" of eloquent speakers and asks his hearers to support him with their prayers. The sermon is a source for Gregory's preaching during the Trinitarian controversies.

This Greek panegyrical sermon by Gregory of Nyssa, bishop and Cappadocian Father, was preached in the late fourth century in honour of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste. These Christian soldiers were remembered for dying of exposure on a frozen lake under the emperor Licinius. Its two parts are conventionally labelled Ia and Ib. Gregory begins by rejoicing at the crowded congregation and asking which of the day's readings to take up. He then turns to the martyrs, whose cult was particularly honoured in his family. The sermon is an important witness to their early veneration in Cappadocia and Pontus.

This is the second of Gregory of Nyssa's Greek homilies in honour of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste. These were Roman soldiers who, by tradition, were put to death by exposure on a frozen lake under Licinius in the early fourth century. Gregory gave the sermon the day after an earlier address, during their festival at the start of March. He contrasts the soldiers' new-year military exercises with the spiritual contest of Christ's forty soldiers and praises hearing stories of virtue as moral formation. It is an important witness to the early cult of these widely venerated martyrs.

The Life of Gregory the Wonderworker is a Greek panegyric by Gregory of Nyssa, written in the late fourth century and delivered as a speech at a festal gathering in honour of the saint. It praises Gregory Thaumaturgus, the third-century bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, and draws on local oral traditions about his conversion, his study under Origen, his miracles and his missionary work. It matters as an early example of Christian hagiography. It also contains the earliest known account of a vision of the Virgin Mary, in which a creed is revealed to Gregory.

Ad Stagirium a daemone vexatum is a consolatory treatise in three books by John Chrysostom. It is addressed to Stagirius, a young ascetic friend who had fallen into severe despondency and seizures that were believed to be the work of a demon. It is usually dated to Chrysostom's early years in Antioch, around 380, before he became a priest. Kept at home by illness, Chrysostom writes to encourage his friend. He reflects on divine providence, the purpose of suffering and the overcoming of despair, which makes the work an important early witness to his ascetic and pastoral thought.

This is a treatise in three books by John Chrysostom, written in Greek at Antioch, probably between about 376 and 386, before his ordination as priest. It defends monks and those who urged young men to take up the monastic life against hostility in the city. The first book answers the critics in general. The second addresses a pagan father whose son has become a monk, and the third a Christian father. The work argues that a monastic upbringing forms virtue better than worldly education, and it is an important early statement of Chrysostom's ascetic ideals.

Two Greek treatises by John Chrysostom on one theme. The first is addressed to clerics and ascetic men who kept consecrated virgins in their homes as "spiritual sisters" (subintroductae, Greek syneisaktoi). The second warns women vowed to virginity not to live with men. Chrysostom calls the arrangement a recent and strange invention. He rejects the reasons its defenders gave and argues that it caused scandal, temptation and damage to the reputation of virginity. The exact date of the treatises is uncertain. They are important evidence for the practice of spiritual marriage, called syneisaktism, in the late fourth-century Church.

On Compunction is a Greek ascetical treatise in two books by John Chrysostom. The first book is addressed to a monk named Demetrius, who had pressed the author for discourses on the subject. The second is addressed to Stelechius. The exact date is uncertain, but the work is usually placed in Chrysostom's years at Antioch. It describes compunction, the heartfelt sorrow for sin that frees the soul from worldly cares and lifts it toward God. It draws on Scripture, especially the example of David, and is an important early Greek source on penitence and tears in Christian spirituality.

De virginitate (On Virginity) is a Greek treatise by John Chrysostom, probably written in Antioch in the late 370s or early 380s, before he became a priest. It praises virginity as a higher calling than marriage while defending marriage as good. Chrysostom denies that heretical groups who condemn marriage as evil practise true virginity, and much of the work is an extended reading of Paul's teaching in 1 Corinthians 7. It is one of the main early Greek statements of the Christian ascetic ideal.

The Homilies on Repentance are a collection of nine Greek sermons attributed to John Chrysostom. Most are thought to have been preached at Antioch while he was a presbyter there, probably in the late 380s. However, the collection is composite, and the dating and authenticity of some pieces have been questioned. Drawing on biblical examples, the sermons describe the many roads to repentance, including confession of sins, forgiveness of others, prayer, almsgiving, tears and humility. They also urge hearers not to despair of God's mercy. The collection is an important witness to early Christian teaching on penance.

The Sermons on Genesis are a series of Greek sermons by John Chrysostom. He preached them at Antioch as a presbyter during Lent, usually dated to 386. They are separate from his longer series of sixty-seven Homilies on Genesis. Starting from the opening chapters of Genesis, they treat the creation of the world and of humankind, human dominion over creation, sin and its consequences. The first sermon opens the Lenten season by praising fasting and almsgiving as the "spiritual spring" of the soul.

The Commentary on the Twelve Minor Prophets is a Greek biblical commentary by Theodore of Mopsuestia (c. 350–428), the leading exegete of the Antiochene school. It is usually counted among his earlier writings, but its exact date is uncertain. It works through Hosea to Malachi and reads the prophecies mainly in their historical setting in Israel's past. Theodore avoids allegory and keeps messianic readings to a minimum. Most of his works were lost after his condemnation in 553, but this commentary survives complete in Greek. That makes it a key witness to Antiochene method.

On the Incarnation of the Only-begotten is a Greek theological dialogue by Cyril of Alexandria, usually dated to about 429–431, during the early Nestorian controversy. Two speakers discuss the incarnation of the Word. Its opening presents it as a sequel to the speakers' earlier discussion of the Son's divinity, probably Cyril's seven Dialogues on the Trinity. The dialogue argues that Christ is one Lord, the Word made flesh, against teachings that divide him into two. Cyril later reworked the text into his dialogue That Christ Is One. It is a key witness to his Christology before the Council of Ephesus.

Adversus anthropomorphitas ("Against the Anthropomorphites") is a Greek letter by Cyril of Alexandria, bishop of Alexandria from 412 to 444, addressed to Calosyrius, bishop of Arsinoe. Its exact date is unknown. Cyril had heard reports about monks of the mountain of Calamon in Egypt, and he rebukes some of them who argued that, because humanity was made in God's image, God must have a human form. Against this he holds that God is incorporeal, citing Christ's words "God is spirit." The letter is a witness to the anthropomorphite controversy among Egyptian monks in the late fourth and fifth centuries.

The Apologeticus pro XII capitibus contra Orientales is a Greek treatise by Cyril of Alexandria, written around 431. In it he defends his Twelve Chapters, or anathemas, against Nestorius from the objections of the Eastern bishops associated with Antioch, chiefly Andrew of Samosata. Cyril takes each anathema in turn, quotes the Eastern criticism and answers it, arguing for the single subject of the incarnate Word. It is one of several defences of the anathemas he produced during the controversy around the Council of Ephesus. Others were addressed to Theodoret of Cyrus and to the council itself.

This Greek commentary on the Song of Songs is by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It is usually dated to the 430s and is one of his earliest biblical commentaries. Theodoret wrote it at the request of a Bishop John and dedicated it to him. He reads the Song as a spiritual allegory of the love between Christ and the Church, or the soul, and rejects readings that treat it as a merely human love poem. The work is a notable example of Antiochene exegesis taking up allegorical interpretation.

The Commentary on the Visions of Daniel is a Greek biblical commentary by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was probably written in the 430s and is among his earliest exegetical works. Theodoret goes through the Book of Daniel, explaining its prophetic visions in the historical, restrained manner of the Antiochene school. He argues that Daniel should be counted among the prophets and reads the visions as foretelling the succession of empires and the coming of Christ. It is an important witness to early Christian interpretation of Daniel.

The Interpretation of Ezekiel is a Greek verse-by-verse commentary on the Book of Ezekiel by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It is usually dated to the late 430s or 440s and belongs to his series of commentaries on the Old Testament prophets. Its preface argues that the prophets seem obscure only to readers whose spiritual sight is clouded by unbelief. The commentary is a leading example of Antiochene exegesis. It reads the prophecies mainly against their historical setting and adds Christological interpretation where Theodoret thinks the text supports it.

This is a collection of Greek homilies and fragments attributed to Antipater, metropolitan bishop of Bostra in the Roman province of Arabia in the mid-fifth century. The homilies include a festal sermon on John the Baptist, which praises the forerunner who leapt in his mother's womb when the newly conceived Christ arrived at the Visitation. Other fragments survive mainly as quotations in later writers. They include material from Antipater's polemic against Origen, which made him one of Origen's leading critics. The collection shows Greek preaching and anti-Origenist controversy in the period after Chalcedon.

This collection gathers Greek theological writings from the sixth century that have been traditionally grouped under the name of Leontius of Byzantium. Some are also linked to Leontius of Jerusalem. The works defend the Christology of the Council of Chalcedon against Nestorians, Eutychians, Apollinarians and Severus of Antioch. They are notable for applying Aristotelian logical terms such as essence, nature, hypostasis and person to the doctrine of Christ. De sectis presents itself as notes from the lectures of Abba Theodore. Its authorship, like that of several other pieces here, is disputed.

This is a collection of homilies and fragmentary writings attributed to Eulogius, the Chalcedonian Greek Patriarch of Alexandria from about 580 to 607 or 608 and a correspondent of Pope Gregory the Great. Most of his writings, many of them aimed against the Monophysites and other dissenting groups, are lost or survive only in pieces. The collection includes a festal discourse for Palm Sunday that celebrates Christ's royal entry into Jerusalem in rhythmic, exultant rhetoric. The surviving pieces are rare evidence of Greek Chalcedonian preaching and theology in Alexandria on the eve of the Arab conquest.

The Scholia on the Books of Kingdoms and Chronicles is a Greek exegetical work attributed to Procopius of Gaza (c. 465–c. 528), the Christian rhetorician of the school of Gaza. It was probably written in the early sixth century. It comments on 1–4 Kingdoms (Samuel and Kings) and on Chronicles in short explanatory notes. These address questions such as who wrote the historical books, the genealogy of Samuel, and apparent contradictions in names and places. Like Procopius's other biblical commentaries, it reflects his practice of condensing and adapting earlier Greek exegesis.

This collection gathers Greek prose works by Sophronius, monk and Patriarch of Jerusalem (634–638). It opens with his homilies on feasts such as the Annunciation, which also set out Trinitarian and Christological teaching. The other pieces are treatises on the confession of sins and on the baptism of the apostles, and an encomium of the healing saints Cyrus and John. There is also an account of their miracles at their shrine in Menouthis near Alexandria. Finally, the Life of Saint Mary of Egypt is traditionally attributed to Sophronius, but scholars dispute that attribution.

This Greek liturgical poem is a triodion, a short canon of three odes rather than the full nine. It is attributed to Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem (died 638), though the attribution and date are uncertain. Written for the Lenten fast, it calls the soul to repentance, sobriety and tears. It asks Christ for enlightenment, turns from bodily pleasure to the "luxury" of fasting, and includes petitions to the Theotokos. Its troparia follow the model melodies of the biblical odes.

The Doctrinae diversae, often called the Instructions or Discourses, is a collection of spiritual teachings by Dorotheus of Gaza. He was a sixth-century monk and abbot who trained at the monastery of Seridus under Barsanuphius and John. Written in Greek for monks, the talks deal with humility, obedience, giving up one's own will, conscience, the fear of God and not judging others. An anonymous prologue defends the author's orthodoxy. It separates him from a namesake who followed Severus and cites Theodore the Studite in his support. The work became a standard guide to monastic life in both East and West.

De baptismo Christi sermo II is a Greek homily on the baptism of Christ, attributed to Gregory of Antioch, the sixth-century monk and abbot who was Patriarch of Antioch from about 570 to 593. The heading of the sermon calls its author a presbyter of Antioch. The preacher says he is continuing the sermon of the previous Sunday, which he had to break off for lack of time. That sermon dealt with Christ coming to John the Baptist. This one explains the Father's words from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

The Ordo et ritus confessionis is a Greek order of service for sacramental confession, attributed to John IV the Faster, patriarch of Constantinople from 582 to 595. Many scholars doubt the attribution and think the text may be considerably later. The priest stands the penitent before the altar and recites with him the Trisagion, penitential psalms and troparia. A prayer for forgiveness follows, recalling biblical penitents such as David, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Peter, the harlot and the tax collector. Penitential texts under John's name shaped Byzantine confessional practice.

This short Greek work records a disputation between Photinus, a Manichaean, and Paul the Persian, a Christian. It is usually dated to about 527–530 and placed in Constantinople under Justinian. Photinus argues that because good and evil are opposites, both must exist as substances. Paul answers this dualist case with philosophical argument. The work ends with a list of Manichaean "blasphemies" for formal rejection. Its authorship is uncertain: one manuscript credits the refutation to Zacharias, bishop of Mytilene. It is a useful witness to Christian polemic against Manichaeism in the sixth century.

This Greek record of a public debate between Paul the Persian, a Christian, and Photinus, a Manichaean teacher, survives in more than one session. It was held in Constantinople on the orders of the co-emperors Justin I and Justinian, in the presence of the prefect Theodore, and so is usually dated around 527. Written as question and answer, it begins with the origin and creation of souls, then turns to Manichaean dualism and Christian teaching on God and creation. Whether this Paul is the philosopher of the same name at Khosrow I's court is debated.

The Propositiones christianae adversus Manichaeos is a short Greek anti-Manichaean treatise attributed to Paul the Persian and usually dated to around 527–530. It uses philosophical argument against the Manichaean teaching that the world comes from an eternal evil matter. It asks whether things arise from matter by nature, by art or by choice, and argues that none of these can explain how many different and opposing natures could come from a single matter. Whether this author is the same Paul who wrote philosophical works at the Sasanian court remains uncertain.

This is a collection of Greek theological writings attributed to Anastasius I, Chalcedonian Patriarch of Antioch (561–571 and 593–599). It brings together fragments against the Arians, including quoted extracts from Arius and Aetius on the will and nature of the Son, along with a disputation against the Jews and various orations and sermons on orthodox faith. The authorship of several pieces is uncertain. Some are assigned to his namesake successor, Anastasius II, or to other writers, and the disputation is widely considered spurious.

The Pandects of Holy Scripture is a Greek compilation of moral teaching in 130 chapters by Antiochus, a monk of the lavra of Mar Saba near Jerusalem. He wrote it in the early seventh century, between the Persian conquest of Palestine in 614 and Heraclius's reconquest. Eustathius, abbot of Attaline near Ancyra, had asked for it after his monks were driven from their home. It gathers sayings from Scripture and earlier Christian writers. It opens with the martyrdom of forty-four Sabaite monks and ends with a list of heretics.

The Oratio de sacra synaxi is a Greek homily attributed to Anastasius of Sinai, priest and abbot of the monastery on Mount Sinai, and probably composed in the late seventh century. Its heading also announces themes of not judging others and not bearing grudges. Drawing heavily on the Psalms, it urges Christians to give unceasing attention to prayer, the reading of Scripture and attendance at the liturgical assembly, or synaxis. The homily is a witness to Byzantine pastoral teaching on prayer, the liturgy and Christian conduct.

The Ambigua ("Difficulties") is a major theological work by Maximus the Confessor, written in Greek around 628–634. It explains obscure or disputed passages in Gregory of Nazianzus and Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite. It is made up of two collections, a longer early set addressed to John, bishop of Cyzicus, and a later set addressed to Thomas. Through these explanations Maximus refutes Origenist ideas, sets out his teaching on the divine logoi in creation and discusses deification and Christ's two natures. John Scotus Eriugena translated it into Latin in the ninth century.

The Mystagogia is a Greek treatise by the monk Maximus the Confessor, usually dated to about 628–630. It interprets the church building and the rites of the Byzantine eucharistic liturgy (the synaxis) as symbols. Maximus says he is recording the teaching of an unnamed "great elder." He reads the church as an image of God, the cosmos, humanity and the soul. He then follows the stages of the liturgy, from the entrance to communion, as a path of ascent toward union with God. It is a foundational work of Byzantine liturgical commentary.

On Heresies (De haeresibus) is the second part of the Fount of Knowledge by John of Damascus, the Greek monk and theologian of Mar Saba. It was probably written in the decade or so before his death around 749. The work is a short catalogue of about one hundred heresies. It begins with four "mother" heresies: Barbarism, Scythism, Hellenism and Judaism. Much of it is drawn from the Panarion of Epiphanius of Salamis and from later compilations. Later entries cover more recent movements, and the chapter on the "Ishmaelites" is one of the earliest Christian discussions of Islam.

This is a group of Byzantine liturgical canons in Greek, attributed in the manuscripts to "John the Monk". They honour Saint Basil the Great, Saint John Chrysostom and the Apostle Peter. Each canon is a sequence of odes sung to model melodies (heirmoi), with Theotokia addressed to the Virgin. The canon on Basil has the acrostic "With songs I sing Basil the Great." It praises his angelic life, his purified mind and his miracles. The author's identity is uncertain. Liturgical tradition sometimes identifies him with John of Damascus. The canons probably date from between the eighth and tenth centuries.

This is the collected Greek homilies and liturgical poetry of Andrew of Crete (c. 650–712 or later), a monk of Jerusalem who later became archbishop of Gortyna in Crete. His sermons are on the feasts of Christ and the Virgin, including the Nativity and Dormition of the Theotokos, and on saints. The opening sermon presents Mary's Nativity as the threshold between law and grace. The hymns include canons and idiomela, chief among them the penitential Great Canon. It is still sung during Great Lent and is a landmark in the development of the canon as a hymn form.

The Opuscula are a collection of short Greek treatises and dialogues attributed to Theodore Abu Qurrah, the Melkite bishop of Harran (c. 750 – c. 825). They are usually dated to the late eighth or early ninth century. Many are written as disputations with Muslims ("Saracens"), Jews, Nestorians and Jacobites. They defend the Trinity, the Incarnation, the eternal Son and the Eucharist, deny that Muhammad's mission came from God, and set out philosophical terms. Some pieces are said to report the teaching of John of Damascus. Together they are important early evidence for Christian apologetic in the Islamic world.

The Isagoge in sacras Scripturas (Introduction to the Divine Scriptures) is a Greek handbook of biblical interpretation attributed to Hadrian (Adrian), an exegete of the Antiochene tradition. Little is known about him, and the work is usually dated to the fifth century. It sorts the figurative "idioms" of the Hebrew style into three kinds: those of sense, of wording and of arrangement. For example, it explains how Scripture speaks of God's actions through human limbs, senses and passions. Cassiodorus recommended it, and it is an important witness to Antiochene principles of reading Scripture.

The Catechesis chronica, or Chronological Catechesis, is an instruction in Greek addressed to the monks of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. It is attributed to Theodore the Studite (759–826), the monastery's abbot. Unlike his many other catecheses, it explains how the yearly cycle of feasts and fasts should be kept. It starts from the Mosaic festivals and grounds its teaching in the canons of the apostles and the Fathers. It was meant both to guide the faithful and to refute heretics. Its exact date is uncertain.

The Epistulae are the collected letters of Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. More than five hundred survive, written to monks, clergy, officials, emperors and many women, often during his several exiles. They give spiritual direction, encourage his scattered community, and defend his positions in the controversies of his time, especially his opposition to iconoclasm. The collection is a major source for Byzantine monasticism, church politics and the second period of iconoclasm.

The Orationes are a collection of Greek sermons by George of Nicomedia, a ninth-century Byzantine churchman. He was a cleric of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople and later became metropolitan of Nicomedia; he was a close associate of Patriarch Photios. The homilies were preached on church feasts and are mostly about the Virgin Mary, including her conception, nativity and presentation in the Temple, and her presence at the Cross. They are written in an elaborate rhetorical style. They are important evidence for Marian devotion and the development of feast-day preaching in middle Byzantine Constantinople.

The Life of Saint Stephen the Younger is a Greek hagiography written in the early ninth century, about 806–810, by Stephen the Deacon, a cleric of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. It tells the life, ascetic career, miracles and death of Stephen the Younger, a monk of Mount Auxentius near Chalcedon. He opposed the iconoclast policy of Emperor Constantine V and was killed in 765. The opening defends the honouring of saints through both images and written accounts. The work is a major source for the first period of Byzantine Iconoclasm and for iconophile polemic.

The Amphilochia is a Greek collection of questions and answers by Photius, patriarch of Constantinople. It is addressed to Amphilochius, metropolitan of Cyzicus, who had sent him some three hundred difficulties to resolve. Most of it is usually dated to Photius's exile after his first deposition in 867, the "time of trials" mentioned in its preface. The answers mostly deal with difficult passages of Scripture and points of theology, but some also take up philosophy, grammar and secular learning. Together with the Bibliotheca, it is a major witness to Photius's wide learning and to Byzantine scholarship in the ninth century.

Against the Manichaeans is a Greek polemical treatise in four books attributed to Photius, patriarch of Constantinople (858–867, 877–886). Its target is the Paulicians, a dualist movement that Byzantine writers saw as a revival of Manichaeism. The first book tells the history of the sect: its origins near Samosata, its leaders and how it spread. The remaining books refute its teachings with theological arguments. The text is an important source on the Paulicians. Scholars still debate its composition, how it relates to Peter of Sicily's history of the sect, and how much of it Photius actually wrote.

These are polemical treatises by Nicetas of Byzantium, a Byzantine philosopher and theologian of the ninth century, written at imperial request between about 842 and 886. The refutation answers a letter from an Armenian ruler that attacked Chalcedonian orthodoxy and the Fourth Ecumenical Council. It was composed in the name of the patriarch of Constantinople and defends the doctrine of Christ's two natures. The confutation of Muhammad's doctrines is a detailed critique of the Qur'an and one of the most substantial Byzantine anti-Islamic works.

The Chronographia is a Byzantine Greek chronicle that carries the name of Leo the Grammarian, about whom almost nothing else is known. A colophon dates the copy to 1013. The work is one version of the chronicle tradition linked with Symeon Logothete and depends closely on that text rather than being an independent composition. Its section on the "new emperors" begins with Leo V the Armenian in 813. It covers imperial reigns, iconoclasm and wars with the Bulgarians and Arabs, and runs to the mid-tenth century. It is a significant witness to ninth- and tenth-century Byzantine history.

The "Lives of the New Emperors" is an anonymous Byzantine Greek chronicle that continues the Chronicle of George the Monk (George Hamartolos). For this reason it is usually called Georgius Monachus Continuatus. It was probably written in the mid-tenth century and covers Byzantine history from the accession of Leo V the Armenian in 813 to about 948. It is closely related to the chronicle of Symeon the Logothete. The account is strongly hostile to the iconoclast emperors and presents Leo V's persecution of the Church and his exile of the patriarch Nikephoros as apostasy, comparing him to King Saul.

Theophanes Continuatus is the conventional name for an anonymous Byzantine Greek collection of histories that continues the chronicle of Theophanes the Confessor. It was compiled in the mid-tenth century under Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos, who commissioned it. The collection covers the emperors from Leo V the Armenian (813) to the reign of Romanos II. Its first four books run from Leo V to Michael III. The fifth book, the Vita Basilii, is a laudatory biography of Constantine's grandfather Basil I the Macedonian. It is often attributed to Constantine himself. The collection is a major source for ninth- and tenth-century Byzantium.

The Odes are a collection of biblical canticles, or songs of praise, attached to the Psalter in some Greek Bible manuscripts and in related Syriac and other traditions. The anonymous collection gathers Old Testament songs such as the two Songs of Moses (Exodus 15 and Deuteronomy 32), the prayers of Hannah, Habakkuk, Isaiah and Jonah, and the Song of the Three Young Men. New Testament canticles such as the Magnificat, Benedictus and Nunc dimittis are also included. It took shape for liturgical use, and its contents and order vary between traditions.

De fide et lege naturae ("On Faith and the Law of Nature") is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. Like many of his sermons, it survives in Greek among the spurious works credited to John Chrysostom. It opens by praising Scripture as inspired by the Holy Spirit, the single source of law, prophets and apostles. It then contrasts the poverty Adam brought on himself by losing his first godliness with the riches given through the incarnate Word.

De paenitentia et compunctione (On Repentance and Compunction) is a Greek homily by Severian of Gabala. He was a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the early fifth century, and this sermon probably dates from about 401 to 404. It comments on the day's readings: Paul's fear that he may mourn over the Corinthians who have not repented (2 Corinthians 12:21), and Christ's forgiveness of the paralytic. The preacher presents repentance as a healing remedy given by God's grace and urges his hearers to seek forgiveness.

This Greek homily on the Ascension of Christ and the opening of the Acts of the Apostles is attributed to Severian of Gabala. He was a Syrian bishop and a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404, and an opponent of John Chrysostom. The sermon opens by confessing that human speech cannot do justice to God's saving dispensations, citing David and Paul. It then moves on to the Lord's ascension and the beginning of Acts. Like most of Severian's Greek sermons, it was handed down under Chrysostom's name.

De spiritu sancto (On the Holy Spirit) is a Greek homily by Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. Like most of Severian's sermons, it was handed down in Greek among the works attributed to John Chrysostom. It was preached the day after an earlier sermon on the coming of the Spirit. Drawing on Scripture's names for the Holy Spirit, such as "Spirit of God" and "Spirit from God", it defends the Spirit's divinity and his undivided nature with the Father and the Son.

De Christo pastore et ove (On Christ the Shepherd and the Sheep) is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the early fifth century. It was delivered at a commemoration of martyrs and contrasts their suffering for Christ with Christ's suffering for all. Taking John 10:11, "I am the good shepherd," as its theme, it stresses that the Son laid down his life freely, as the Father's co-worker and not as a servant. In doing so it argues against heretics who denied the Son's equality with the Father.

In psalmum 96 is a Greek homily on Psalm 96 (97 in the Hebrew numbering), "The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice", attributed to Severian of Gabala. Severian was a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 401–404. The sermon opens by praising psalmody as the Holy Spirit's harp, which educates souls, calms the passions, rebukes heretics and builds up the Church. It then sets the preacher's interpretation apart from the scriptural teaching it explains, and expounds the psalm's proclamation of God's kingship.

In psalmum 95 is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 401–404. It comments on Psalm 95 in the Septuagint numbering (Psalm 96 in the Hebrew), which calls on all the earth to sing to the Lord. The preacher asks why God once confined Israel's worship to one land and did not let its divine songs be sung everywhere. His answer is that the unchanging God adapts his laws to human weakness. He compares this to a husband who shuts away a wife he suspects in order to guard her chastity.

The Homily on the Lawgiver (De legislatore) is a Greek sermon attributed to Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria, who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. Like most of Severian's Greek homilies, it survived among the spurious works of his opponent John Chrysostom. It opens by praising the word of God as the true food and wealth of the soul, drawing on the Beatitudes and the Psalms of David. It then takes up the theme of the divine law and its giver. Its exact date is uncertain, but it probably belongs to Severian's years in Constantinople.

This is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople around 400–404. It is dated roughly to 398–408. It takes as its theme the question the Jewish leaders put to Jesus in the temple: "By what authority are you doing these things?" (Matthew 21:23). The sermon opens by praising the fear of God and reverence for the divine law, which bring enlightenment. It then contrasts this humility with the arrogance of those who approached Christ "like tyrants" to challenge his authority.

This Greek homily by Severian of Gabala was probably preached in Constantinople, where he was a popular preacher between about 400 and 404. Its title means "How Adam received his soul." It was given at the end of the first week of a fast, on the weekday tied to Adam's creation. In it Severian resumes a discourse he had been unable to finish the day before. He explains Genesis 2:7 and contrasts God's personal shaping of humanity with his making of the other creatures. Like many of Severian's sermons, it survives in Greek among works attributed to John Chrysostom.

The Homily on the Serpent is a Greek sermon by Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. It follows a sermon given the day before, which had defended the glory of the Only-begotten Son against heretics. Severian now turns to Christ's prediction of his own cross. The title points to the bronze serpent that Moses lifted up in the wilderness, which Christ presented as a figure of his crucifixion. The homily shows Severian's Antiochene style of preaching and his concern with doctrinal controversy.

This Greek festal homily is attributed to Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It was delivered for the feast of the Dedication of the life-giving Cross. The preacher says the cross once brought victory over death at Golgotha and has now been shown to the whole world as a trophy over the devil. He stresses that the wonders at the crucifixion came from Christ, who suffered willingly in the flesh, and not from the wood. The homily is an early witness to devotion to the Cross.

In Genesim sermo 2 is a Greek homily on the early chapters of Genesis by Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It continues an earlier sermon, which taught that being made "in the image" of God means human lordship over creation and that the "likeness" means growth in virtue. This sermon explains how Adam, through sin, fell from that honour to become like the senseless beasts. Severian presents the story of Adam as moral instruction, a warning for his hearers to imitate virtue and avoid vice.

This is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It takes as its subject Genesis 24:2, where Abraham tells his servant, "Put your hand under my thigh," and makes him swear by God. Severian asks why the oath is taken by the thigh when Isaac had already been born. Drawing on Galatians 3:16, he explains it as pointing to Abraham's "seed," Christ. The sermon is a typical example of his Antiochene-style reading of the Old Testament as foretelling the Gospel. It also survives in an Armenian version.

In meretricem et pharisaeum ("On the Harlot and the Pharisee") is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the early fifth century. Like many of his sermons, it survives among works falsely ascribed to John Chrysostom. The homily is based on the Gospel story of the sinful woman who anointed Christ's feet in the house of a Pharisee. It stresses God's patience in giving sinners time to repent, and it presents the woman's tears and ointment as a model of repentance.

In filium prodigum is a Greek homily on the parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32), attributed to Severian of Gabala. Severian was a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. The preacher says it follows the previous day's sermon on repentance, which had passed over the Gospel reading. He presents repentance as the medicine of salvation and Christ as the physician of souls and bodies. He then explains the parable as a powerful image of repentance and of God's love for humankind.

This Greek homily is attributed to Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria, who was a popular preacher in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. It comments on John 7:15, where the Jews ask how Jesus knows letters without having studied. Severian answers that Christ, the divine Word, is the one spring of all wisdom, law and prophecy, and the source from which Moses, the prophets and the apostles drew. The Word was not made by letters; it was the Word that invented the art of writing. The homily is typical of Severian's Antiochene preaching and its polemic against the Jews.

In Chananaeam et Pharaonem is a Greek homily by Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople around 401–404. Severian begins by excusing an unruly crowd at an evening gathering, praising the listeners' eagerness instead. He then turns to the Canaanite woman's cry, "Son of David, have mercy on me", and sets the faith of this Gentile woman against the unbelief of Israel. As the title shows, the sermon also deals with Pharaoh. Like many of Severian's homilies, it reflects his Antiochene preaching style and his hostility towards the Jews.

This Greek homily by Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria, is on Paul's words in Romans 7:15, "For what I would, that I do not." He probably preached it in Constantinople, where he was a popular preacher between about 401 and 404. It opens by praising the congregation's zeal and rebuking those who had gone to the hippodrome the day before. Severian contrasts the chariot races with the "chariot of God," which scatters demons. Like most of Severian's Greek sermons, it has come down among the works attributed to John Chrysostom.

In incarnationem domini ("On the Incarnation of the Lord") is a Greek homily attributed to Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria. He was a popular preacher in Constantinople in the early 400s and later an opponent of John Chrysostom. The sermon is probably from about 401–404. It celebrates Christ's appearing as the rising of the "sun of righteousness," which makes earth into heaven and makes people heavenly. It also looks back to an earlier sermon on the prophetic voices heard at Christ's baptism. Like many of Severian's homilies, it shows his Antiochene preaching style.

In proditionem servatoris ("On the Betrayal of the Saviour") is a Greek homily attributed to Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria. Severian was a popular preacher in Constantinople, and the sermon probably dates from his time there, about 401–404. The preacher meant to continue a series of reflections on the cross but turns aside because of that day's Gospel reading, on the betrayal of Christ. He begins by arguing that God measures his revelation to the limited capacity of mortal hearers, as a mother feeds an infant milk rather than bread.

De fide ("On Faith") is a Greek homily attributed to Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria. He was a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 until 404, and the sermon is dated to roughly those years. It opens by comparing the Church's teacher to a physician who gives each sick soul the remedy it needs. Severian then follows an earlier speaker who had preached on the "threefold faith" and sets aside his planned commentary on the Gospel reading to speak about the faith instead. His aim is to equip listeners who are already sound in belief to heal others.

Contra Iudaeos in serpentem aeneum (Against the Jews, on the Bronze Serpent) is a Greek sermon by Severian of Gabala. He was a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople from around 400 to 404. The sermon is aimed at the Jews. It begins by saying that the word of God takes many names according to its effects. It then turns to Christ's parables of the vineyard, linking this sermon to one preached the day before. The title refers to the bronze serpent Moses lifted up in the wilderness, which Christians read as a type of the cross.

De sacrificiis Caini is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople. It probably dates from his time there, around 401 to 404. The homily follows earlier sermons on the creation of man and the fall in paradise, and continues the Genesis narrative with the story of Cain and Abel. It contrasts the outward offering of Cain with the sincere disposition of Abel, and shows how envy led to murder. It also presents Abel as the first martyr for righteousness and as a type of Christ.

The Homily on the Seals of the Books (De sigillis librorum) is a Greek sermon by Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. Like most of Severian's Greek homilies, it has come down among the spurious works attributed to his rival, John Chrysostom. It opens by praising the divine word as the soul's food and sets it against worldly, sophistic wisdom, citing Moses and Paul. It then turns to scriptural interpretation, explaining the sealed books of Scripture as mysteries opened by Christ.

A Greek sermon on the opening verse of the Gospel of John, "In the beginning was the Word", attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400. It continues a sermon given the previous day and calls the evangelist John a soaring eagle and a voice of thunder. Severian sets the Gospel's "was" against the heretics' claim that "there was when he was not", defending the eternal and passionless begetting of the Word against Arian teaching. Like most of Severian's Greek homilies, it has come down under the name of John Chrysostom.

This Greek homily for the feast of Pentecost is attributed to Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria, who preached in Constantinople between about 401 and 404. It treats Pentecost as one of the three great feasts and sets the giving of the Law to Moses beside the descent of the Holy Spirit on the apostles. Following Paul, it presents the Spirit as writing on hearts of flesh rather than on tablets of stone. Like many of Severian's sermons, it has come down among works ascribed to John Chrysostom.

"In pretiosam et vivificam crucem" ("On the Precious and Life-giving Cross") is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala. He was a Syrian bishop and popular preacher in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. Severian delivered the sermon after another speaker and opens by praising that preacher's treatment of the cross and of virginity. He then praises the cross as weak in word but great in power. Its effects, he says, appear in deeds: sinners are converted, paradise is opened, and the world turns to chastity. Severian also links the cross to its "root", the virgin birth.

The Homily on Peace is a Greek sermon by Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria and a popular preacher in Constantinople in the early fifth century. It is usually dated to about 401–404 and linked to Severian's brief reconciliation with John Chrysostom, after their quarrel had divided the city's church. It opens by echoing the angels' message to the shepherds and goes on to praise peace as the name of Christ and the glory of the Church, set against the turmoil of the heretics. Like most of Severian's homilies, its Greek text was handed down among the works of Chrysostom.

This Greek homily is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 401 and 404. Its subject is Christ's prayer in Gethsemane, "Father, let this cup pass from me" (Matthew 26:39). The opening praises the listeners' eagerness for an earlier sermon on almsgiving and hospitality. It compares God's word to rain on dry ground and the hearers to bees gathering from Scripture. Like many of Severian's sermons, it also survives in an Armenian translation.

The Homilia de lotione pedum is a Greek sermon on the washing of the feet, the episode in John 13 where Christ washes his disciples' feet. It is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. The sermon opens with a reflection on God's love for humankind as seen in creation. Drawing on the Psalms, it argues that God's mercy and justice belong together: justice moves the hearer to fear judgment, and mercy invites repentance. It then turns to Christ's humility as an expression of that love.

A Greek homily by Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the early fifth century. It was probably delivered between about 401 and 404. It opens with an image of snow whitening the earth, as Scripture whitens the soul. It then turns to the Gospel reading of the centurion whose faith Christ praised. Severian argues from the centurion's recognition of Christ's authority against heretics who make the Son subordinate to the Father, and he asserts that power belongs in common to the divine essence. As the title indicates, he also attacks Manichaean and Apollinarian errors.

This Greek homily by Severian of Gabala is thought to have been preached at Constantinople around 401–404, when he was a popular preacher in the city. The order of his sermon series called for a discussion of Noah, but Severian puts that subject off because the evening is short. He turns instead to Hosea's words, "Sow for righteousness, and harvest the fruit of life." He reads them as the giving back of the life Adam lost when he was barred from the tree of life and driven out of paradise. The title also lists the cherubim as a subject.

This Greek homily, attributed to Severian of Gabala, is a polemical sermon against Jews, pagans and heretics. It probably dates from Severian's preaching in Constantinople around 401–404, and, like most of his surviving homilies, it may have come down under the name of John Chrysostom. The sermon calls the heretics of its own day "new Jews." It says they are worse than those who crucified Christ's body because they deny his Godhead and his divine knowledge. Using texts from the Psalms, it argues for the Son's full divinity, a typical anti-Arian theme of Antiochene preaching at the time.

This is a Greek homily by Severian of Gabala on Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness." It was preached in Constantinople, probably between 401 and 404. Severian refers back to an earlier sermon on creation that a noisy crowd had interrupted. He asks his audience for silence, restates that God created matter itself out of nothing, and goes on to discuss what it means for humanity to be made in God's image. Like many of his sermons, it survives in Greek mainly among works attributed to John Chrysostom.

De caeco et Zacchaeo ("On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus") is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 401 and 404. It begins by praising the single source of all Scripture, the Holy Spirit. It then turns to the Gospel stories of the blind man healed near Jericho and of the tax collector Zacchaeus. Severian marvels that the blind man recognised Christ without having read the Law, the prophets or the Gospels. Like most of Severian's Greek sermons, it was handed down among works ascribed to John Chrysostom.

This Greek homily on 1 Corinthians 15:28, "When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected", is attributed to Severian of Gabala, who preached in Constantinople in the early 400s. It follows a sermon given the day before on the endless kingdom of Christ. The homily answers the objection that Paul's words imply the Son's subordination or that his reign will end, and defends his equal dignity with the Father. Like many of Severian's sermons, it has come down among the works attributed to John Chrysostom.

This Greek homily is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople from about 400 until 404. Its subject is the phrase "Brood of vipers," spoken by John the Baptist (Luke 3:7) and by Christ (Matthew 23:33). It opens by praising the Scriptures as springs of salvation from which hidden meanings must be laboriously "drawn" from the depths. Like most of Severian's Greek sermons, it survives among works wrongly attributed to John Chrysostom.

The Homily on Noah and the Ark is a Greek sermon attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It was delivered at the midpoint of the Lenten fast. Severian compares that midpoint to the height of a battle or of noon, and calls the Scriptures the fast's bright rays. He then turns to the story of Noah, presenting the deeds of the ancients as examples for his hearers to imitate. Like most of his sermons, it reflects the Antiochene tradition of preaching on Scripture.

This is a Greek sermon on Genesis by Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria, who was a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. Like most of his homilies, it survived among the works wrongly attributed to John Chrysostom. Starting from the "meadows of piety", it treats humanity as made in the image and likeness of God. Severian argues that virtue keeps that likeness intact, while vice drags people down to the level of the irrational animals. He also insists that the animals themselves are not evil, since God called all of creation "very good".

This Greek homily is the first in a series of sermons on the biblical figure Job, attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the early fifth century. Like many of Severian's sermons, it has come down mainly under the name of John Chrysostom, so its authorship has been debated. The preacher hails Job, whose story was read in church every year, as the "athlete of the whole world". He calls Job a champion often struck by the devil and vindicated by God, and says no human eloquence can praise him as he deserves.

In Iob sermo 2 is a Greek homily on the trials of Job, attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. The preacher begins by admitting that he is unequal to so great a subject, then explains the opening words of the Book of Job phrase by phrase, starting with "There was a man in the land of Ausitis." He argues that Scripture first stresses Job's ordinary human nature so that hearers will admire how his endurance and virtue went beyond the human condition.

This is the third in a series of Greek sermons on the Book of Job, attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. Like many of his homilies, it probably survives among the works of John Chrysostom. Preached in the evening as a continuation of the Job story, it holds up Job's endurance on the dunghill as a rebuke to a lazy congregation. It argues that only the blameless, righteous and God-fearing person is truly a "man," because he keeps the divine image intact.

This Greek homily is the fourth in a series of sermons on the biblical Job. It was handed down among the works of John Chrysostom and is now attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 401 and 404. The preacher returns to Job's story and argues that although Job lost all his possessions, he kept his virtue, which was the root of his good fortune. He holds up Job's endurance as a model, praising the courage of the soul while admitting that the body truly suffered.

De tribus pueris sermo is a Greek sermon on the three Hebrew youths of Daniel 3, attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. It retells how Nebuchadnezzar, portrayed as an arrogant tyrant who wished to be worshipped as a god, had the youths thrown into the fiery furnace. The sermon praises them as martyrs whose confession of faith the fire could not overcome. Like many of Severian's homilies, it has come down among the works attributed to John Chrysostom. Its exact date is uncertain.

De caeco nato ("On the Man Born Blind") is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the first years of the fifth century. It is probably from about 401–404. The sermon takes as its subject the Gospel account of Christ healing the man blind from birth (John 9). It begins with a reflection on the word of God as light that makes believers "sons of light," while ignorance and unbelief are darkness. Like many of Severian's sermons, it has come down among the writings attributed to John Chrysostom.

This Greek sermon in praise of the martyrs is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the early fifth century. It was probably delivered between about 401 and 404. Preached at a martyrs' festival, it teaches that honouring the martyrs honours Christ, to whom they bore witness. It sets the precious death of the righteous against the death of the ungodly, citing the Psalms. The martyrs are praised so that hearers will imitate their zeal and self-control.

This is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. It was delivered in the last week of the Lenten fast. Severian takes the psalm heading "To the end: do not destroy" as a call to bring a good beginning to a good end. He urges his hearers to finish the fast with eager longing rather than mere toil, because fasting frees the soul to contemplate divine things and curbs desire. The alternative title links the sermon's theme of the end to the Last Judgement.

In ascensionem Domini is a Greek homily for the feast of the Ascension, attributed to Severian of Gabala. Like many of his sermons, it has come down among the works once ascribed to John Chrysostom. It was probably preached while Severian was active in Constantinople, around 401–404, though the exact date is uncertain. The sermon celebrates the Ascension as the exaltation of human nature: Christ, the eternal Word, needs no elevation, but takes mortal humanity up above the angels and frees Adam from the ancient condemnation.

De cruce et latrone ("On the Cross and the Thief") is a Greek sermon for Good Friday. It has come down among the works of John Chrysostom but is attributed here to Severian of Gabala, who preached in Constantinople around 401–404. The authorship is not settled. The homily opens with a series of "Today…" acclamations celebrating the cross as the victory over death and the demons. It reads the darkness and earthquake at the crucifixion as signs, sets the Jews against the believers in polemical terms, and turns to the penitent thief's confession.

The Oratio de exaltatione Crucis is a Greek sermon on the cross attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. The homily opens by calling on the apostle Paul and building on his saying that "the word of the cross" is folly to those who are perishing but the power of God to the saved. It praises the cross as the power that silenced orators and philosophers, overthrew idols and oracles, drove out demons and destroyed death.

This Greek homily on the temptation of Christ in the desert is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. Commenting on the gospel account, the preacher stresses that Christ hid his divine rank and fought the devil "as in the person of humanity". He answered the tempter as a man, so that human nature itself might win the victory and the crown. The sermon shows the Antiochene concern with Christ's real humanity. Like most of Severian's homilies, it is probably dated to his years in Constantinople.

This is the first of six Greek homilies on the creation of the world by Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria. He preached them in Constantinople, probably between about 401 and 404. The opening sermon argues that every part of Scripture aims at the salvation of souls, and it presents the account of creation in Genesis as the foundation of the Law and the Prophets. Severian admits that earlier fathers already treated the subject but still adds his own reading. The homilies follow the literal Antiochene style of exegesis and survive in Greek among works wrongly attributed to John Chrysostom.

This is the second of six Greek homilies on the creation account of Genesis by Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria. He preached them in Constantinople, probably between about 401 and 404, while he was a popular preacher in the capital. The series came down to us among the works attributed to John Chrysostom. The sermon opens by comparing the word of God to a whetstone that cleans, sharpens and brightens the soul, then continues its line-by-line reading of the six days of creation. The series is an important example of Antiochene literal exegesis and of early Christian cosmology.

This Greek sermon is the third of six homilies on the creation account in Genesis by Severian of Gabala. He preached them in Constantinople, probably in the early 400s. Like most of Severian's sermons, the series survived among the writings attributed to his rival John Chrysostom. This homily recalls the work of the first two days and then turns to the third: the waters gathered together, dry land appearing and the earth producing plants. Severian combines a literal, Antiochene-style reading of creation with moral and Christological applications, urging his hearers to wonder at the works and worship their maker.

This is the fourth in a series of six Greek sermons on the creation account of Genesis by Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop and popular preacher in Constantinople. He delivered them around 401–404. Like most of his Greek works, the homilies survive among the writings attributed to John Chrysostom. The preacher first asks his hearers to pray for him, then resumes his account of the creation days in order. His exegesis is literal and follows the Antiochene tradition.

This is the fifth of six Greek homilies on the creation account of Genesis by Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the early 400s. Like most of his sermons, it survives among the works wrongly attributed to John Chrysostom. The homily turns to the creation of man. It opens by praising Scripture as God's greatest gift and defends the study of nature against hearers who wanted theology alone. It reflects the literal, Antiochene style of reading Genesis.

This Greek sermon is the last of six homilies on the creation account in Genesis by Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It goes back to the subject of paradise. It discusses Adam's dwelling there, the land outside it, and his expulsion, and it aims to answer believers' questions and refute unbelievers using Scripture alone. Like most of Severian's sermons, it survived in Greek among works wrongly attributed to John Chrysostom. It is a witness to Antiochene literal exegesis.

De incarnatione ("On the Incarnation") is a homily attributed to Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria, a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404 and an opponent of John Chrysostom. Severian preached in Greek, but this sermon survives in an ancient Armenian translation, like several of his homilies whose Greek text is lost. It opens with an extended contrast between light and darkness. Drawing on Psalm 43:3 ("Send out your light and your truth") and John 1:9, it presents Christ as the true light and the sun of righteousness who drives away the darkness of ignorance.

De dogmate baptismoque ("On Doctrine and Baptism") is a homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. It survives in an ancient Armenian translation and is one of the Severian sermons published from Armenian by J. B. Aucher in 1827. The preacher begins by recalling an earlier sermon on Christ's Ascension, which he says raised human nature to heaven. He then explains Paul's contrast between the earthy and the heavenly man (1 Corinthians 15:47–49) before moving to doctrine and baptism.

De apostolis ("On the Apostles") is a homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. Several of his sermons are lost in Greek and survive only in Armenian translation, and this text has come down in Armenian. It opens by recalling the previous day's sermon on the body and its "lamp", the eye. It then sets out a series of lamps: the evening lamp, the divine law and the gospel. It goes on to John the Baptist as a lamp who baptized Christ in obedience to God's command.

De pascha, deque catharis ("On the Pascha and on the Cathari") is a homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. It is among the sermons that survive in an ancient Armenian translation, and Severian would have preached it in Greek. The preacher begins by praising the presiding bishop, whom he calls the head of the fathers, and the earlier speakers. He then turns to the Paschal feast and argues against the Cathari, the rigorist Novatianist party. The homily shows how Severian preached in the capital.

This is a homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It was probably delivered in Greek but survives in an ancient Armenian translation. Its title refers to Daniel 7:10, "the books were opened." The opening, however, explains John 4:46 and following, where Jesus returns to Cana of Galilee. The preacher contrasts Christ's movement from place to place in the body with his divinity, which is present everywhere. He presents Christ as the single source of life, light and healing for both soul and body.

This festal homily in honour of the martyr Acacius is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It was presumably composed in Greek but survives in an Armenian translation. The sermon was preached the day after a feast of the apostles. It uses rich imagery of stars, crowns and lamps to celebrate the martyrs as a light and a rampart for the Church. It is one of several homilies by Severian that are preserved mainly or only outside Greek.

This is a homily on Christ's entry into Jerusalem riding a colt, attributed to Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It survives in an ancient Armenian translation. The sermon reads Zechariah's prophecy of the king coming on the colt of an ass as a sign that Christ defeats pride and the devil through meekness and humility, not through chariots and warhorses. It belongs to the group of Severian's sermons that were preserved in translation into other languages.

These Greek exegetical fragments on the letters of Paul are attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop and popular preacher at Constantinople around 400–404 who became an opponent of John Chrysostom.
