These sermons show how the cult of local martyrs was promoted through preaching in Antioch.

The Homilies on the Gospel of John are a series of eighty-eight sermons in Greek by John Chrysostom. He preached them at Antioch around 390 to 392, while he was still a priest there and before he became archbishop of Constantinople. Working through the Fourth Gospel passage by passage, they explain its literal meaning and defend the full divinity of the Son against Arian (Anomoean) teaching. Each sermon usually ends with moral exhortation. The series is among the most important patristic commentaries on John, and it circulated widely in translation, including into Old Georgian.

The Homilies on the Gospel of Matthew are a series of ninety sermons in Greek by John Chrysostom. He preached them at Antioch around 390, while he was still a priest there. This part contains Homilies I–XLIV. The series works through Matthew's Gospel passage by passage, explaining its literal and historical sense and ending each sermon with moral exhortation, often about almsgiving, care for the poor and Christian conduct. It is the oldest complete patristic commentary on Matthew to survive. It was widely read in both East and West and remains one of Chrysostom's most important exegetical works.

This is the second half of John Chrysostom's ninety homilies on the Gospel of Matthew. He preached them at Antioch around 390, while he was still a priest there. Homilies XLV–XC run from the parable discourse of Matthew 13 to the end of the Gospel. Each homily explains the passage verse by verse, then ends with moral exhortation, often on almsgiving, wealth and care for the poor. It is the earliest complete patristic commentary on Matthew to survive, and it was widely read in both East and West.

The Homilies on Philemon are three Greek sermons by John Chrysostom, later archbishop of Constantinople, that expound Paul's short letter to Philemon verse by verse. Scholars disagree about whether they were preached at Antioch or at Constantinople, so their date is uncertain. An opening argument tells the story of Onesimus, a slave who stole from his master Philemon, ran away, and was baptised by Paul in prison. The homilies then defend the letter's place in Scripture and draw moral lessons about forgiveness, care for slaves and Christian brotherhood.

The Homilies on Philippians are a series of fifteen sermons in Greek by John Chrysostom on Paul's Epistle to the Philippians. Like his other homilies on Paul, they work through the letter in order and pair close explanation of the text with moral exhortation. An introductory discourse on Philippi and Paul's imprisonment comes first. Scholars disagree about whether they were preached at Antioch or at Constantinople, so their date is uncertain. They are among the most important early Greek commentaries on the epistle, notably for their reading of the Christological hymn in chapter 2.

The Homilies on the Epistle to the Romans are a series of thirty-two Greek sermons by John Chrysostom. Most scholars date them to his years as a priest at Antioch (386–398), though some have argued for Constantinople. After an introductory "Argument" praising the Apostle Paul and urging constant reading of his letters, Chrysostom works through Romans verse by verse. He explains its teaching on sin, grace, faith and the law, and closes each homily with moral exhortation. The series is the most complete patristic Greek commentary on Romans to survive and was widely used in later Byzantine exegesis.

The Homilies on Second Corinthians are a series of thirty Greek sermons by John Chrysostom that work through Paul's Second Epistle to the Corinthians. They are usually dated to his years as a presbyter at Antioch (386–398), although the exact date and place are uncertain. Each homily explains a passage of the letter, including its themes of divine consolation in suffering, Paul's defence of his apostleship and the collection for Jerusalem, and then ends with moral exhortation. The series is one of the main patristic commentaries on this epistle.

The Homilies on Second Thessalonians are a series of five Greek sermons by John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), preacher at Antioch and later Archbishop of Constantinople. They expound Paul's Second Epistle to the Thessalonians verse by verse. Exactly when and where they were preached is uncertain. Chrysostom explains why Paul wrote again after his first letter and addresses the Thessalonians' confusion about the coming of Christ. He discusses the "man of sin" at length and takes the power restraining him to be the Roman Empire. Throughout, he joins this exegesis to moral exhortation, as in his other homilies on Paul's letters.

The Homilies on Second Timothy are a series of ten sermons in Greek by John Chrysostom. They expound Paul's Second Epistle to Timothy verse by verse. They were probably preached at Antioch in the late fourth century, but whether they belong to his time at Antioch or at Constantinople is uncertain. Chrysostom reads the letter as Paul's comfort to a young bishop weighed down by the cares of church leadership. He joins close exegesis with moral exhortation on endurance, faithful teaching and resistance to false doctrine. The series belongs to his larger body of commentary on the Pauline epistles.

The Three Homilies Concerning the Power of Demons (De diabolo tentatore) are a set of Greek sermons by John Chrysostom. They are generally thought to have been preached at Antioch during his years as a priest there. The first homily answers people who claimed that demons govern human affairs, or who were troubled by God's chastisements and by the wicked prospering while the just suffer. Across the series Chrysostom argues that the devil cannot force anyone to sin. The cause of evil lies in human free will and negligence, and God's providence guides all things for good.

This is a series of twenty-one Greek sermons that John Chrysostom preached at Antioch in 387, while he was still a presbyter. That year, crowds angered by a new imperial tax tore down statues of Emperor Theodosius I and his family, and the city feared severe punishment. Bishop Flavian travelled to Constantinople to ask the emperor for mercy. Meanwhile, through Lent, Chrysostom comforted his frightened congregation, urged repentance, and attacked vices such as swearing oaths. The homilies are a vivid record of a civic crisis and of his preaching.

The Homilies on Titus are a series of six Greek sermons by John Chrysostom on Paul's Epistle to Titus. They were preached in the late fourth century, but scholars disagree on whether they were given at Antioch or at Constantinople. Moving through the letter verse by verse, Chrysostom discusses Titus's role as Paul's trusted companion in charge of the church in Crete. He also covers the qualities required of bishops and elders, the refutation of false teachers, and Christian conduct in households and society. Like his other sermons on Paul's letters, they combine close reading of Scripture with moral exhortation.

This is a Greek sermon by John Chrysostom, probably preached at Antioch while he was a priest there (386–398). He opens by praising his congregation for crowding into church, which he calls a surgery for souls whose medicine is the word of Scripture. He then warns his hearers not to make public the sins of fellow Christians and not to call down curses on their enemies. Instead he urges them to correct others privately and to pray for those who wrong them.

This Greek sermon by John Chrysostom is generally dated to his years as a priest at Antioch (386–398). It explains Christ's prayer in Gethsemane, "Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me" (Matthew 26:39). Chrysostom answers Marcionites and Manichaeans, who denied that Christ truly took flesh, by arguing that the prayer shows his real human nature and natural fear of death. He also draws moral lessons: believers should not rush into danger, and they should put God's will before every other will. The sermon opens with a reference to an earlier homily against the greedy.

This sermon by John Chrysostom was originally composed in Greek and is usually dated to his years as a presbyter at Antioch (386–398). It refers back to a recent homily on the parable of the Pharisee and the publican. Chrysostom pictures virtue and vice as two chariots: pride overturned the Pharisee for all his fasting and tithes, while humility carried the sinful publican past him. The preacher warns against vainglory, the "mother of all evils." He then turns to explain Paul's words in Philippians 1:18, that Christ is proclaimed "whether in pretence or in truth."

This Greek sermon by John Chrysostom was probably preached at Antioch while he was a priest there (386–398). It follows an earlier homily on the paralytic healed at the pool of Bethesda (John 5). Chrysostom starts from that sick man's patience and hope in God, which he calls spiritual riches beyond the reach of thieves and death. He then turns to the paralytic let down through the roof (Mark 2; Luke 5) and contrasts the two healings. The homily is a typical example of his moral and exegetical preaching on the Gospel miracles.

This sermon was preached in Greek by John Chrysostom, probably while he was a priest at Antioch between 386 and 398. It opens by rebuking the many people who had again stayed away from church, despite his earlier appeals. He urges those who did attend to bring their absent brethren back. He then explains Paul's command in Romans 12:20, "If thine enemy hunger, feed him," and warns against holding grudges over injuries. The homily shows his concern with church attendance and with forgiveness of enemies.

The Instructions to Catechumens are baptismal sermons by John Chrysostom. He preached them at Antioch as a presbyter, probably around 387–390, to candidates preparing for baptism at Easter, who were called "those about to be illuminated." The first instruction explains why baptism is called a laver of regeneration rather than simply of remission of sins. It also warns against both swearing falsely and taking oaths at all. The second deals with renouncing Satan and condemns superstitious practices such as amulets and omens. Together they are important evidence for baptismal teaching and practice in late fourth-century Antioch.

The Letter to a Young Widow is a Greek consolatory treatise by John Chrysostom. It is usually dated to his early career at Antioch, around 380, before he became a priest, though dating varies. He addresses a young woman whose husband died after only a few years of marriage. He waits until her first grief has passed, then comforts her with Christian teaching on death, the resurrection and the passing nature of worldly honours. He also praises widowhood as an honourable state. With a companion treatise against second marriage, it is an important early example of Christian consolation literature.

The Letters to Olympias are a collection of seventeen Greek letters written by John Chrysostom, the deposed Archbishop of Constantinople, during his exile between 404 and 407, mostly from Cucusus in Armenia. They are addressed to the deaconess Olympias, a wealthy widow and close supporter who also suffered persecution for her loyalty to him. Chrysostom consoles her against despondency, reflects on suffering, patience and divine providence amid the turmoil in the Church, and reports on his own hardships. The letters are an important source for his final years and his spiritual teaching.

This moral treatise in Greek by John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople, is usually known by its Latin title Quod nemo laeditur nisi a seipso. He wrote it late in life, during his exile after 404. It argues that no one can truly be harmed by others, because the only real injury is damage to the virtue of one's own soul. Poverty, illness, slander, exile and death cannot hurt the person who keeps to virtue. Chrysostom illustrates this with biblical examples. The work is valued as a statement of Christian endurance shaped by his own persecution.

On the Priesthood is a treatise in six books by John Chrysostom, written in Greek, probably at Antioch. It is usually dated between about 386 and 391, though some scholars place it earlier. It takes the form of a dialogue between John and his close friend Basil. John had avoided ordination while letting Basil be ordained, and he defends that deception. He then sets out the dignity, responsibilities and dangers of the priestly office, including the care of souls and preaching. It became one of the most influential early Christian works on pastoral ministry.

The Oration to the Assembly of the Saints is a Greek speech attributed to the emperor Constantine the Great. Eusebius of Caesarea preserved it as an appendix to his Life of Constantine. The speech was given on Good Friday. Scholars disagree about its date and place, and they once doubted that Constantine wrote it, though many now accept it as his, probably translated from Latin. It attacks pagan polytheism and fatalism and defends divine providence and Christ's work. It is especially known for reading Virgil's Fourth Eclogue and an acrostic of the Erythraean Sibyl as prophecies of Christ.

These two short Greek letters by Cyril, Patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444, deal with church discipline. The exact date of each is uncertain. In the first, Cyril asks Domnus, a metropolitan, to call a synod to rehear the case of a deposed bishop named Peter. Peter said he had been denied a fair defence, stripped of his property and frightened into resigning. The second warns the bishops of Libya and Pentapolis against ordaining men who had been turned down by their own bishops or expelled from monasteries. The Eastern Church later counted both letters among its canonical writings.

The Catechetical Lectures are a series of eighteen Greek instructions by Cyril of Jerusalem, given during Lent around 350 to candidates preparing for baptism at Easter. They were delivered in Jerusalem, probably in Constantine's basilica at the Holy Sepulchre. The early lectures deal with repentance, baptism and faith. The rest explain the baptismal creed of Jerusalem one article at a time. They are one of the earliest surviving systematic courses of Christian instruction and an important witness to the creed, teaching and church life of fourth-century Jerusalem.

The Mystagogical Lectures are five Greek homilies given in Jerusalem to the newly baptized during Easter week. They follow and complete Cyril of Jerusalem's Catechetical Lectures. They explain the rites the neophytes have just received: the renunciation of Satan, baptism, anointing with chrism, the Eucharist and the eucharistic liturgy, including an early witness to the epiclesis. Their date is uncertain, and some scholars attribute them wholly or partly to Cyril's successor, John of Jerusalem. They are a key source for fourth-century sacramental theology and liturgical practice.

The Procatechesis is the introductory address to the Catechetical Lectures of Cyril of Jerusalem. It was delivered in Greek around 348–351, probably before or soon after Cyril became bishop. He spoke it to candidates preparing for baptism at Easter, the "ones to be enlightened." Citing the example of Simon Magus, Cyril urges them to come with a sincere purpose and not merely in body. He stresses regular attendance, exorcisms and secrecy about the teaching given. It opens the eighteen pre-baptismal lectures, a key witness to fourth-century catechesis.

Cyril of Alexandria wrote this synodal letter, his third letter to Nestorius, in 430 on behalf of an Alexandrian synod. It ends with twelve anathemas, propositions that condemn anyone who rejects the full unity of Christ. They insist that the Word is united to flesh "in hypostasis", that Christ is one and not two persons, and that Mary is Theotokos, the Mother of God. Nestorius replied with counter-anathemas, and the dispute between Alexandria and Antioch led to the Council of Ephesus in 431. The anathemas were read into the council's acts and remained central to later Christological debate.

Dionysius the Great, bishop of Alexandria from 248 to 264, wrote this Greek letter to Basilides, a bishop in the Libyan Pentapolis, answering his questions on church discipline. The exact date is unknown. Dionysius discusses when the fast before Easter should end, given that the Gospels do not fix the hour of the resurrection. He also considers whether menstruating women, married couples and men who have had a nocturnal emission may receive communion. His answers were later accepted as canons in Eastern church law, and Byzantine canonists such as Balsamon wrote commentaries on them.

This is a cycle of Syriac teaching hymns (madrāšê) for the feast of the Epiphany, traditionally attributed to Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), deacon of Nisibis and Edessa. Scholars have questioned whether all of them are his. Each hymn has a refrain. They celebrate Christ's baptism in the Jordan and the baptism of believers, and read Old Testament episodes as types of the sacrament: Elisha's washings, the sweetening of the waters at Marah, the guiding cloud and the crossing of the sea. They are an important witness to early Syriac baptismal theology and liturgical poetry.

The Hymns on the Nativity are a cycle of Syriac madrāšê, or teaching hymns, by Ephrem the Syrian. He was a deacon and poet who worked at Nisibis and later at Edessa, and he composed these hymns in the mid-fourth century. They celebrate the birth of Christ as the fulfilment of the prophets, kings and types of the Old Testament. They dwell on paradoxes such as the Creator becoming an infant and on the Virgin Mary's role. They are among the best-known works of early Syriac poetry and incarnational theology.

The Carmina Nisibena ("Nisibene Hymns") are a collection of Syriac madrāšê, or teaching hymns, by Ephrem the Syrian, written between about 350 and 373. About 77 of them survive. The early hymns deal with Nisibis, Ephrem's home city, and its sieges by the Persian king Shapur II. They pray for deliverance from the floodwaters turned against the city walls and praise its bishops. Other hymns concern Edessa and Harran. The later hymns dramatise Christ's descent into Sheol and his contest with Death and Satan. The collection is valuable both as poetry and as a historical source.

The Pearl is a set of seven Syriac teaching hymns (madrāšê) by Ephrem the Syrian, the fourth-century deacon and poet of Nisibis and Edessa. They belong to his larger cycle of Hymns on Faith. Ephrem turns a single pearl over in his hand and finds in it images of Christ, the Virgin, the Church, baptism and the Kingdom. He uses the pearl to argue that the Son cannot be fully understood and to warn against prying debate about the divine nature. The hymns are among the best-known examples of his symbolic theology.

A group of three sermons in Syriac attributed to Ephrem the Syrian, the fourth-century deacon and poet of Nisibis and Edessa. They were composed before his death in 373. The first, the Homily on Our Lord, is a long meditation in elevated prose on the Incarnation and the saving work of Christ. It describes his passage from the Godhead to the Virgin's womb, and from Sheol to the Kingdom, to bring humanity to life. The second homily deals with admonition and repentance. The third deals with the sign God gave to Hezekiah.

The Ecclesiastical History is a ten-book account of Christianity from the time of Christ to the early fourth century, written in Greek by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. He completed it in stages, with the final edition dating to around 324–326. It traces the succession of bishops in the major sees, Christian writers, heresies, the fate of the Jews and the persecutions, ending with Constantine's victory. Eusebius quotes many earlier documents that are otherwise lost, which makes the work the foundation of later church historiography. It was translated early into Latin, Syriac and Armenian.

Eusebius of Caesarea wrote this Greek letter to his church at Caesarea in 325, soon after the Council of Nicaea. In it he explains why he signed the council's creed. He quotes the baptismal creed of his own church, which he says he read before Emperor Constantine and which was approved. He then sets out the Nicene formula with its additions and explains how he understood terms such as "of the substance" and "consubstantial" (homoousios). Athanasius, Socrates and Theodoret preserved the letter, and it is a key eyewitness source for the council's debates.

The Life of Constantine is a Greek work in four books by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, written in honour of the emperor Constantine the Great. Eusebius composed it after Constantine's death in 337 and left it unfinished when he died in 339. It mixes panegyric and biography. It presents Constantine as a model Christian ruler and recounts his conversion, including the vision of the cross, his wars, his church building and his religious policy. It is one of the fullest sources for the religious history of his reign, and it quotes several imperial letters and documents.

The Martyrs of Palestine is a Greek account by Eusebius of Caesarea of the Christians who died in Palestine during the Great Persecution. It begins with Diocletian's edicts of 303 and continues to the persecution's end about 311. Eusebius lived in Caesarea at the time and witnessed many of the events, including the sufferings of his teacher Pamphilus. The work survives in two forms. This shorter recension is attached to Book VIII of some manuscripts of his Ecclesiastical History. A longer version survives mainly in Syriac. The work is an important eyewitness source for the last Roman persecution.

This Greek panegyric by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, was delivered in Constantinople in 336 to mark the thirtieth anniversary of Constantine the Great's reign. Eusebius presents the emperor as the earthly image of the divine Logos and his monarchy as a reflection of God's heavenly rule. It also praises Constantine's suppression of polytheism and his support for the Church. Its later chapters are generally thought to come from a separate speech on Christ's sepulchre. The work is an important early statement of Christian imperial ideology, which later shaped Byzantine political thought.

The Festal Index, or Chronicon Athanasianum, is an anonymous annotated list of the festal letters that Athanasius of Alexandria sent each year to the churches of Egypt and Libya to announce the date of Easter. It was compiled after his death in 373 and survives in Syriac. For each year from 328 onward, it records the Easter date, consuls, indiction, prefect of Egypt, and events such as Athanasius' exiles and returns. Scholars value it for the chronology of his career and for Roman Egypt's administration. The traditional numbering of the letters comes from it.

This Greek encyclical letter was issued by Gennadius I, patriarch of Constantinople from 458 to 471, together with a synod meeting in the capital. It is usually dated to about 459. Addressed to the metropolitans and to the pope of Rome, it condemns simony, the buying or selling of ordination. It argues that clergy must be ordained freely, as Christ ordained the apostles without payment, and it appeals to the Gospel and to the Council of Chalcedon's canon against simoniacal ordinations. The letter was later preserved among collections of Eastern canon law.

This Latin catalogue of Christian writers, usually called De viris illustribus, was written by Gennadius, a priest of Marseilles, in the later fifth century. Its exact date is uncertain. It continues Jerome's work of the same name, which ended in 392–393. In about ninety short notices it covers Greek, Latin and Syriac authors from the late fourth century to Gennadius's own time, describing their lives and listing their writings. Some notices were probably added by later hands. Many of the writers it records are otherwise poorly documented, so it is an important source for the literary history of the period.

A group of Greek letters by Gregory of Nazianzus to his close friend Basil of Caesarea, written between about 358 and Basil's death in 379. Some answer letters that are now lost. They trace the friendship that began when the two studied together at Athens. Topics include their shared plans for an ascetic life of "philosophy" in Pontus and Gregory's family duties. Later letters record the strain caused by Basil's appointment of Gregory as bishop of Sasima in 372. Together the letters are a vivid personal record of two leading Cappadocian Fathers.

This is a group of theological letters by Gregory of Nazianzus, written in Greek after he left the see of Constantinople in 381, probably between about 382 and 387. Two letters to the priest Cledonius (Epistles 101 and 102) and one to Nectarius, his successor as bishop of Constantinople (Epistle 202), attack the teaching of Apollinaris of Laodicea, who denied that Christ had a human mind. Gregory argues that Christ took on a complete human nature, summed up in his famous principle that "what has not been assumed has not been healed." The letters were influential in later Christological debate.

This is a group of theological letters by Gregory of Nazianzus, written in Greek after he left the see of Constantinople in 381, probably between about 382 and 387. Two letters to the priest Cledonius (Epistles 101 and 102) and one to Nectarius, his successor as bishop of Constantinople (Epistle 202), attack the teaching of Apollinaris of Laodicea, who denied that Christ had a human mind. Gregory argues that Christ took on a complete human nature, summed up in his famous principle that "what has not been assumed has not been healed." The letters were influential in later Christological debate.

Oration 1 is a short sermon Gregory of Nazianzus gave at Easter, usually dated to 362. It is the first of his collected orations. His father, the bishop of Nazianzus, had ordained him a priest against his will, and Gregory had withdrawn for a while to Pontus. Back for the feast, he presents the Resurrection as the start of his ministry. He asks for mutual forgiveness and defends his "tardiness" by pointing to Moses and Jeremiah. The sermon introduces themes he develops at length in Oration 2, his defence of his flight.

Oration 2 is a long apologetic discourse by Gregory of Nazianzus, written around 362–363 and probably never meant to be delivered aloud. In it Gregory explains why he fled to Pontus after his father, Gregory the Elder, ordained him priest at Nazianzus against his will. Defending his conduct leads him into a wider reflection on the priesthood. He describes the pastor as a physician of souls and stresses how hard and dangerous the work of spiritual direction is. The oration became a classic treatise on pastoral ministry and influenced John Chrysostom's On the Priesthood and Gregory the Great's Pastoral Rule.

Oration 3 is a short Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus, usually dated to around Easter 362. Gregory's father, the bishop of Nazianzus, had ordained him a priest against his will. Gregory then withdrew to the solitude he preferred, but he returned to take up his duties. In this oration he reproaches the people of Nazianzus: they had pressed him to come back, yet few came to hear him. He contrasts their eagerness to have him with their indifference to his teaching. The speech belongs with his first orations, which reflect his reluctant start in pastoral ministry.

Gregory of Nazianzus gave this funeral oration for his younger brother Caesarius, a physician, probably in 369. In it he recounts Caesarius's studies at Alexandria, his medical career at the court of Constantius, and how he resisted Julian's efforts to turn him from Christianity. He then covers Caesarius's later service as a treasury official in Bithynia and his early death. The speech joins the classical Greek funeral speech with Christian consolation and reflections on how short human life is. It is the main source for Caesarius's life, and Jerome placed it first among Gregory's orations.

Gregory of Nazianzus gave this Greek funeral oration for his sister Gorgonia. Its exact date is uncertain. It came after the death of their brother Caesarius in 369 and before their father's death in 374. It was probably delivered in the city where she had lived her married life with her husband Alypius, traditionally said to be Iconium. Gregory praises her modesty, generosity, prayer and self-discipline as a married woman. He also describes her healing from illness and her peaceful death. The speech is an important portrait of a Christian laywoman and a source for the life of Gregory's family.

Oration 12 is a short Greek discourse by Gregory of Nazianzus, delivered in 372 when he agreed to act as coadjutor to his aged father, Gregory the Elder, bishop of Nazianzus. Earlier that year Basil of Caesarea had consecrated him bishop of Sasima during his dispute with Anthimus of Tyana, but Gregory never took up that see. Here he gives himself to the Holy Spirit and accepts the new duties only provisionally, without being bound to the see. The oration documents his lasting reluctance about church office and his strong preference for a contemplative life.

Oration 16 is a sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus, usually dated to 373. He gave it at Nazianzus while serving as coadjutor to his father, Gregory the Elder. The town had suffered a cattle plague, then a drought, and finally a hailstorm that ruined the ripened crops. The aged bishop was too overwhelmed to preach, so his son spoke in his place, largely without preparation. He interprets the disasters as divine chastisement, calls the people to repentance and almsgiving, and asks why God allows such suffering. The text that survives may have been revised after delivery.

Oration 18 is a Greek funeral speech by Gregory of Nazianzus for his father, Gregory the Elder, bishop of Nazianzus. The elder Gregory died in 374, in about his hundredth year. Gregory delivered the speech that year in front of his mother, Nonna, and Basil of Caesarea. It tells how his father moved from the sect of the Hypsistarians to Christianity under Nonna's influence, and praises his work as bishop, his orthodoxy and his family life. The speech is one of the main sources of what is known about the Hypsistarians.

Oration 21 is a panegyric by Gregory of Nazianzus praising Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria who died in 373. Gregory delivered it at Constantinople, probably on an annual feast of the saint, in 379 or more likely 380. In it he portrays Athanasius as a model bishop and a steadfast defender of Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism. He recounts Athanasius' life, his exiles and his struggles with emperors and with church councils such as those of Seleucia and Constantinople. The oration is often considered a classic example of the Christian ecclesiastical panegyric.

Oration 27 is the first of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople in 380, while he led the small Nicene community there. It serves as an introduction to the series and is aimed at the Eunomians, radical Arians known for their skill in dialectic. Gregory does not yet discuss the Trinity itself. Instead he asks who may speak about God, when, before whom and how far, arguing that theology requires purity of life, quiet and restraint rather than clever debate.

Oration 28 is the second of the five Theological Orations by Gregory of Nazianzus. He preached them in Constantinople around 380, when he led the small Nicene community there against the Eunomians, who claimed that God's essence could be fully known. The first oration set out who may practise theology and under what conditions. This one argues that God's nature cannot be grasped by the human mind. Using the image of Moses on Sinai seeing only God's "back parts", Gregory shows that creation reveals that God exists, not what God is. The work is a classic statement of divine incomprehensibility.

The third of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople around 380 against the Eunomians and other Arian groups. After setting out the monarchy of the Father, Gregory defends the full divinity of the Son. He argues that the Son is eternally begotten without time or passion, and answers his opponents' arguments from the terms "begotten" and "unbegotten." The oration closes with a set of antitheses contrasting Christ's human lowliness with his divine glory. Oration 30 continues the argument with a fuller treatment of the disputed passages of Scripture.

Oration 30 is the fourth of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus delivered in Constantinople around 380 against the Eunomians and other Arians. It is his second discourse on the Son. Gregory answers, one by one, the scriptural texts his opponents used to make the Son subordinate, such as "The Lord created me" (Proverbs 8:22) and "the Father is greater than I." He assigns the exalted expressions to Christ's divinity and the lowly ones to his assumed humanity. The oration ends with a discussion of the titles of the Son.

Oration 31 is the last of the five Theological Orations that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople, probably in 380, against the Eunomians and the Pneumatomachi, who denied that the Holy Spirit is fully divine. Gregory openly calls the Spirit God and consubstantial with the Father and the Son. He separates the Spirit's procession from the Son's generation and answers the objection that Scripture is silent on the matter with a theory of progressive revelation. The oration was an important statement of Cappadocian Trinitarian theology shortly before the Council of Constantinople of 381.

Oration 33 is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus. He delivered it at Constantinople, probably around 380, while leading the small Nicene congregation there at a time when the Arians held the city's churches. Gregory replies to opponents who mocked his flock for its poverty and small numbers, and who measured the Church by its size. He defends his own conduct and character and argues that true faith is not judged by numbers. He closes by affirming the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity. The speech mixes personal apology with polemic against the Arians.

Oration 34 is a sermon Gregory of Nazianzus preached at Constantinople in 380, during his leadership of the city's small Nicene community at the Anastasia church. It welcomes Egyptian sailors, probably crews of the grain fleet, who passed the many Arian-held churches to worship with Gregory. They came shortly after Peter of Alexandria's envoys had tried to consecrate the intruder Maximus in Gregory's place. Gregory praises Egypt and its Christian heritage, seeks reconciliation with Alexandria, and restates the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity.

Oration 37 is a sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus, preached in Constantinople around 380 during his time as bishop there. It is his only surviving exegetical homily, a commentary on Matthew 19:1–12. Gregory starts from Christ's humility in becoming "all things to all men" and then turns to the Pharisees' question about divorce. He defends the permanence of marriage and condemns the unequal civil laws that punished women's adultery while excusing men's. He also praises virginity and celibacy as a higher calling, with brief remarks on Trinitarian doctrine.

Oration 38 is a festal sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus, preached in Constantinople around the end of 380, during his brief time leading the church there. Scholars disagree whether it was delivered on 25 December 380 or 6 January 381, since "Theophany" could mean either Christmas or Epiphany. It opens with the words "Christ is born, glorify Him" and reflects on the Incarnation, the creation and fall of humanity, and God becoming human for our salvation. It is one of the earliest witnesses to the Christmas feast in the East.

Oration 39, "On the Holy Lights", is a festal sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus. He preached it in Constantinople on the Feast of the Epiphany (Theophany), usually dated to 6 January 381, and Oration 40 on Baptism followed the next day. The feast was then known as the "Holy Lights" because baptism was called illumination. The sermon reflects on Christ's baptism in the Jordan, sets out a Trinitarian theology of God as light and lists five kinds of baptism: those of Moses, John and Jesus, baptism by martyrdom and baptism by tears.

Oration 40 is a Greek sermon on baptism by Gregory of Nazianzus. He preached it at Constantinople during the Epiphany festival, the day after Oration 39 on the Holy Lights. It is usually dated to January 381, though some scholars prefer 380. Gregory distinguishes three births: natural birth, birth by baptism and birth by resurrection. He describes baptism as illumination and explains its benefits, and he strongly urges his hearers not to put it off. The oration ends with a confession of Trinitarian faith. It is one of the most important early Christian treatises on the sacrament.

Oration 41 is a festal sermon for Pentecost by Gregory of Nazianzus. He delivered it at Constantinople while he led the Nicene community there, between 379 and 381. The exact year is uncertain, though the Benedictine editors favoured 381. Gregory first compares how Jews, pagans and Christians keep their feasts. He then reflects on the mystical meaning of the number seven. His main theme is the full divinity of the Holy Spirit, defended against the Macedonians. Here he uses arguments different from those of his Fifth Theological Oration (Oration 31) on the same subject.

Oration 42 is the farewell speech of Gregory of Nazianzus, given in Constantinople in 381 during the First Council of Constantinople. Gregory was archbishop of the city and had been presiding over the council. Opposition from some bishops, including challenges to whether his appointment was legitimate, led him to resign. Speaking before the assembled bishops and his own congregation, he defends his ministry with restraint and recalls how he rebuilt the city's small Nicene community. He restates his Trinitarian faith and takes a moving leave of his church. It is a key source on the council and on Gregory's life.

Oration 43 is the funeral oration of Gregory of Nazianzus for his close friend Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, who died in 379. Illness and his duties at Constantinople kept Gregory from the funeral. He most likely delivered the speech after returning to Cappadocia in 381 or 382, though the exact date and occasion are uncertain. The longest of his orations, it surveys Basil's family, their shared studies at Athens, his ascetic life, charity, resistance to the Arian emperor Valens and teaching. It joins classical encomium with Christian praise and is a key source for Basil's life.

Oration 45 is an Easter sermon in Greek by Gregory of Nazianzus. It is usually regarded as his last oration and is often dated to about 383, after he had retired to his estate at Arianzus near Nazianzus. It opens in biblical style with the watch of Habakkuk and the Angel of the Resurrection. Gregory then reads the ancient Passover allegorically, applying each of its details to Christ and the Christian life. Two passages repeat his Oration 38, on the Nativity, word for word. Byzantine readers knew the oration well and used it in the liturgy.

This short Greek poem by Gregory of Nazianzus belongs to his dogmatic poems (Carmina dogmatica). It was probably written during his retirement in Cappadocia in the 380s. It warns readers against "malignant writings" and lists the books of Scripture to be read. Gregory counts twenty-two Old Testament books, matching the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and leaves out Esther and the deuterocanonical books. His New Testament list names the four Gospels, Acts, fourteen Pauline and seven Catholic epistles, but not Revelation. The poem is an important witness to how the biblical canon developed in the fourth-century Greek East.

Against Eunomius is a long polemical treatise in Greek by Gregory of Nyssa, written around 380–383. It defends his late brother Basil of Caesarea against the Anomoean leader Eunomius of Cyzicus, whose "Apology for the Apology" had attacked Basil's earlier refutation. Gregory rejects the claim that "unbegotten" defines God's essence and that the Son is therefore unlike the Father. He argues for the Son's full divinity and for the infinity and incomprehensibility of God. The work was divided into differing numbers of books, and it is a major source for Cappadocian Trinitarian theology.

Against Eunomius is a long polemical treatise in Greek by Gregory of Nyssa, written around 380–383. It defends his late brother Basil of Caesarea against the Anomoean leader Eunomius of Cyzicus, whose "Apology for the Apology" had attacked Basil's earlier refutation. Gregory rejects the claim that "unbegotten" defines God's essence and that the Son is therefore unlike the Father. He argues for the Son's full divinity and for the infinity and incomprehensibility of God. The work was divided into differing numbers of books, and it is a major source for Cappadocian Trinitarian theology.

The Canonical Epistle to Letoius is a letter on penitential discipline by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, sent to Letoius, bishop of Melitene. It was written in the later fourth century, usually placed around 390. Gregory sorts sins by the parts of the soul they corrupt: reason, desire and anger. He then sets the length and stages of penance for apostasy, magic, fornication, adultery, murder, theft and grave-robbing. Its rulings were later received into Byzantine canon law and became part of the Orthodox canonical tradition.

This is a Greek funeral oration by Gregory of Nyssa for Meletius, bishop of Antioch. Meletius died in Constantinople in 381 while presiding over the Council of Constantinople, and Gregory gave the speech there before the assembled bishops. In it he counts Meletius among the apostles and mourns the loss of a father and leader at a time when heresy threatened the Church. Like other Christian funeral speeches of the period, it draws on the forms of classical rhetoric.

The Great Catechism, or Catechetical Oration, is a Greek theological treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, usually dated to about 383–387. It was written as a guide for those who teach the faith, not for catechumens. It argues from reason as well as Scripture to defend Christian teaching against pagans, Jews and heretics. It covers the Trinity, creation and the fall, the incarnation and redemption, including the well-known image of the divine bait and fishhook, and baptism and the Eucharist. After Origen's On First Principles, it is among the earliest attempts at a systematic account of Christian doctrine.

This is a short Greek letter by Gregory of Nyssa to his younger brother Peter, bishop of Sebasteia, printed with Peter's reply at the head of Gregory's treatise Against Eunomius. Gregory wrote it soon after the death of their brother Basil in 379. He explains that he answered only one of Eunomius' pamphlets, because he had the book for just seventeen days, and asks Peter whether he should publish his refutation. Peter answers by urging him to finish the defence of Nicene Trinitarian doctrine against Eunomius.

The Letters are the surviving correspondence of Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–c. 394), the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. Some thirty letters survive, written in Greek between roughly the 370s and his death. They include festal greetings, such as an Easter letter to Eusebius, and letters of friendship and church business. Others deal with his own troubles as a bishop, with doctrine, and with pilgrimage to Jerusalem. The collection sheds light on Gregory's character, his rhetorical training and church life in late fourth-century Asia Minor.

On "Not Three Gods" is a short Greek theological treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, written as a letter to a younger correspondent named Ablabius. Its exact date is uncertain. Ablabius had asked why, if Peter, James and John share one human nature and are called three men, Father, Son and Holy Spirit should not be called three gods. Gregory answers that "man" properly names a single nature. He adds that every divine action comes from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, and is therefore one. The work is a key statement of Cappadocian teaching on the Trinity.

On Infants' Early Deaths is a short theological treatise in Greek by Gregory of Nyssa, addressed to Hierius, a Cappadocian official. It was written late in Gregory's life, since he calls himself aged. It asks why God allows infants to die before they can do either good or evil, and what becomes of them afterwards. Gregory argues that such souls are neither punished nor rewarded like those who lived virtuously. Instead they share in the knowledge of God as far as their nature allows. The treatise is an important early Christian discussion of divine providence and of the fate of children who die young.

This Greek letter by Gregory of Nyssa, the fourth-century Cappadocian bishop, was written in the 380s, after his own journey to Jerusalem. Gregory replies to a correspondent who has asked whether monks and ascetics should visit the holy places. Measuring the practice against the Gospel, he argues that Christ never commanded pilgrimage. He warns of moral dangers on the road, especially for consecrated women, and notes the vices he found in Jerusalem. Spiritual change, he insists, does not depend on place. The letter is an important early critical voice in debates over Christian pilgrimage.

Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, preached this Greek homily for the Feast of Lights (Epiphany or Theophany). The feast commemorated Christ's baptism in the Jordan and was a customary day for baptisms. Its exact date is uncertain but falls within Gregory's episcopate in the later fourth century. He begins by welcoming the crowded congregation, then explains baptism as a new birth through water and the Spirit and finds figures of it in the Old Testament. The sermon is an important witness to fourth-century Eastern teaching on baptism and to how the Epiphany feast was kept.

On the Faith (to Simplicius) is a short dogmatic treatise in Greek by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It is addressed to a certain Simplicius and was written sometime between about 370 and 395. Gregory argues against the Arian claim that the Son "once was not" and is a creature. He draws on scriptural commands against worshipping any "new" or "strange" god to show that the Only-begotten is eternal and shares the Father's nature. It is a concise example of the Nicene teaching on the Trinity that Gregory defended against Arian and Eunomian opponents.

On the Holy Spirit, Against the Macedonians is a Greek polemical treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, one of the Cappadocian Fathers. He wrote it in the later fourth century, probably around the time of the debates linked with the Council of Constantinople (381), but the exact date is uncertain. It answers the Pneumatomachi, or followers of Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is fully divine. Gregory argues that the Spirit shares the same rank, nature and activity as the Father and the Son. The treatise is an important witness to the development of Nicene teaching on the Trinity.

This short Greek theological treatise in letter form is addressed to Eustathius, a physician whom the author praises for healing minds as well as bodies. It is usually attributed to Gregory of Nyssa, but it was also handed down among the letters of his brother Basil of Caesarea. It was probably written in the late 370s or early 380s. It defends the full divinity of the Holy Spirit against those who denied it. Its main argument is that Father, Son and Spirit share one operation, and therefore one nature. It is an important witness to Cappadocian Trinitarian theology.

On the Making of Man (De hominis opificio) is a Greek theological treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, written around 379, soon after the death of his brother Basil of Caesarea. Gregory sent it to his brother Peter as an Easter gift and meant it to complete Basil's homilies on the Hexaemeron, which had not dealt with the creation of humanity. It discusses humanity as made in the image of God, the relation of soul and body, the passions, and the resurrection. It is a foundational work of Christian anthropology. In the sixth century Dionysius Exiguus translated it into Latin.

On the Soul and the Resurrection is a philosophical dialogue in Greek by Gregory of Nyssa, written soon after the death of his sister Macrina in 379. It is set at her deathbed. Gregory, grieving for their brother Basil, questions her, and Macrina answers as his teacher, in a way consciously modelled on Plato's Phaedo. The dialogue argues that the soul is immaterial and survives death, and defends the resurrection of the body. It also explores the purification of souls and the final restoration of all things to God. It is a key source for Gregory's anthropology and eschatology.

On Virginity (De virginitate) is a Greek treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, generally regarded as one of his earliest works and dated to the 370s. It praises consecrated virginity as the gateway to a holier life. Gregory argues that freedom from the cares of marriage and worldly life allows undistracted contemplation of God and restores the soul toward its divine likeness. He begins by praising virginity, then contrasts it with the troubles of ordinary life and ends with an exhortation. The work is an important early statement of Cappadocian ascetic and mystical thought.

The Canonical Epistle is a Greek pastoral letter by Gregory Thaumaturgus, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus. He wrote it around 254–258, after Goths and Boradi had raided the region, and sent it to an unnamed fellow bishop. Its canons cover cases that arose from the invasions: captives who ate the barbarians' food, women who were raped, and Christians who looted property or helped the raiders. It is an important early witness to penitential discipline, and Eastern Christian canon law later adopted it. The final canon, which sets out grades of penitents, is often thought to be a later addition.

The Book of Pastoral Rule (Regula Pastoralis) is a Latin treatise on the duties of bishops and clergy, written by Pope Gregory I around 590, soon after his election. It is addressed to John, bishop of Ravenna, who had criticised Gregory for trying to avoid the papacy. Its four parts deal with who should take up spiritual rule, how the pastor should live, how he should teach people of differing character, and how he should stay humble. It became one of the most influential medieval guides to ministry, and King Alfred had it translated into Old English.

The Register of the Epistles is the collected official correspondence of Pope Gregory I (the Great), written during his pontificate from 590 to 604. It survives in fourteen books arranged by indiction year and contains around 850 letters in Latin. They deal with the management of the papal estates, church discipline, and relations with bishops, emperors, Frankish and Lombard rulers. They also cover the mission to the English and the dispute over the title "ecumenical patriarch." The collection is a major source for the history of the late sixth-century Church and of Italy.

The Register of the Epistles is the collected official correspondence of Pope Gregory I (the Great), written during his pontificate from 590 to 604. It survives in fourteen books arranged by indiction year and contains around 850 letters in Latin. They deal with the management of the papal estates, church discipline, and relations with bishops, emperors, Frankish and Lombard rulers. They also cover the mission to the English and the dispute over the title "ecumenical patriarch." The collection is a major source for the history of the late sixth-century Church and of Italy.

De Synodis ("On the Councils", also called "The Faith of the Easterns") is a Latin treatise by Hilary of Poitiers. He wrote it around 358–359, while exiled in Asia Minor during the Arian controversy. Hilary addressed it to the bishops of Gaul and Britain. In it he sets out and comments on the creeds of several Eastern councils, including those of Antioch, Sirmium and Ancyra. He argues that the term homoiousios ("of like substance") can be understood in an orthodox sense. The work sought to bring together Western Nicene bishops and the moderate Eastern Homoiousians against the more radical Arians.

The Tractatus super Psalmos is a Latin series of homilies on the Psalms by Hilary of Poitiers. It is generally dated to his last years, after he returned from exile in the East around 360. Only part survives, covering selected psalms, including Psalms 1, 53 and 130. Hilary drew heavily on Origen's exegesis. He reads the Psalms mainly as speaking of Christ, and he holds that interpretation begins by asking in whose person the psalmist speaks and whom he addresses. The work is among the earliest substantial Latin commentaries on the Psalter.

De Trinitate is a Latin theological treatise in twelve books by Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. He wrote most of it during his exile in Phrygia in the later 350s, and it was completed by about 360. Its first book opens with an autobiographical account of Hilary's search for truth, which led him to faith. The treatise argues against Arianism, defending the full divinity of the Son and his unity of nature with the Father from Scripture. It is the first major Latin work on the Trinity, and it brought Eastern theological debates to Western readers.

The Historia Acephala, or "headless history" because its opening is lost, is an anonymous Alexandrian chronicle of the career of Athanasius of Alexandria. It was composed in Greek, probably soon after his death in 373, but survives only in a Latin translation. It runs from his return to Alexandria in 346 through his later exiles and restorations to his death and succession. Events are dated precisely by Egyptian months and consular years. Together with the Festal Index, it is a key source for the chronology of Athanasius and the Arian controversy.

Jerome wrote this Latin polemical treatise in Rome around 383, while Damasus was bishop there. It answers Helvidius, a layman who claimed that the Gospels' references to the "brothers" and "sisters" of the Lord show that Mary had other children with Joseph, and who ranked marriage as equal to virginity. Jerome argues that Mary remained a virgin, that these "brothers" were the Lord's cousins, and that virginity is superior to marriage. Helvidius's own work is lost and is known only through this reply.

To Pammachius Against John of Jerusalem is a Latin polemical treatise by Jerome, written in the late 390s during the Origenist controversy. It is addressed to his Roman friend Pammachius. Jerome attacks John II, bishop of Jerusalem, for allegedly sheltering Origenist errors on the resurrection of the body, the soul and related doctrines. He also defends himself and Epiphanius of Salamis in the quarrel over Epiphanius' ordination of Jerome's brother Paulinian. The work is an important source for the controversy in Palestine and for church politics there at the time.

Against Jovinianus is a Latin polemical treatise in two books by Jerome, written in 393. It answers Jovinian, a Roman monk condemned at synods in Rome and Milan. Jovinian had taught that virgins are no better than wives, that abstinence is no better than eating with thanksgiving, that the baptized cannot sin, and that all sins and rewards are equal. Book I praises virginity over marriage, and Book II rejects the other claims. Many readers found its attack on marriage excessive, and Jerome defended it in letters to Pammachius. The treatise was later widely quoted in medieval writing against marriage.

The Dialogue Against the Pelagians is a Latin polemical work in three books by Jerome. He wrote it in Bethlehem late in life, around 415 to 417, and it was his last major controversial writing. It takes the form of a debate between Atticus, a Catholic, and Critobulus, who speaks for Pelagius. The work attacks the claim that a person can live without sin by free will alone and defends the necessity of divine grace, drawing heavily on Scripture. It was written while Pelagius was in Palestine, and it set Jerome beside Augustine in the Pelagian controversy.

Against Vigilantius (Contra Vigilantium) is a short polemical treatise by Jerome, written at Bethlehem in 406. Jerome says he dictated it in a single night. It answers a lost work by Vigilantius, a presbyter from Aquitaine who had once been Jerome's guest. Vigilantius had attacked the veneration of martyrs' relics, vigils at their tombs, clerical celibacy, monasticism and the sending of alms to Jerusalem. Jerome defends these practices in fierce, sarcastic terms, mocking his opponent as "Dormitantius" ("the sleepy one"). The treatise is an important witness to the cult of the saints in the early fifth century.

Jerome wrote this polemical Latin treatise at Bethlehem in about 401–402, during the Origenist controversy. Its first two books are addressed to Pammachius and Marcella. They answer Rufinus of Aquileia's Apology, which Jerome knew only from summaries sent to him and from passages his brother Paulinianus had memorized. A third book followed after Rufinus sent a letter in reply. Jerome defends his own orthodoxy and his translations, attacks Rufinus's Latin version of Origen's On First Principles and its preface, and denies any sympathy for Origen's errors. The work marks the bitter end of a long friendship.

The Dialogue Against the Luciferians is a Latin polemical dialogue by Jerome. It is one of his early works, usually dated around 379, though some scholars place it a few years later. In it, a follower of Lucifer of Cagliari debates an orthodox Christian. The Luciferians refused communion with bishops who had compromised with Arianism. Against them, Jerome argues that such bishops, especially those who signed the formula of Ariminum in 359, should be received back, and that baptism given by heretics is valid. The work includes his famous remark that the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.

This is the collected correspondence of Jerome (c. 342/347–420), arranged in chronological order. It also includes some letters written to him, among them letters from Augustine and Pope Damasus. The letters span roughly 370 to 420. They begin with an early letter to his friend Innocent from Jerome's time in Aquileia, and they follow him through Syria, Rome and Bethlehem. They deal with ascetic life, virginity, biblical interpretation, translation and theological controversy, including the Origenist dispute. Many are addressed to women of Roman ascetic circles. The letters are a major source for Jerome's life and for late fourth-century Christianity.

The Life of Saint Hilarion is a Latin hagiography written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 390. It tells the story of Hilarion, a fourth-century hermit from near Gaza who was a disciple of Antony of Egypt and is regarded as the founder of monastic life in Palestine. It follows his ascetic struggles, miracles and later wanderings, which took him to Egypt, Sicily, Dalmatia and finally Cyprus, where he died. Jerome wrote it to promote the ascetic ideal. Alongside his Lives of Paul and Malchus, it shaped Latin monastic hagiography.

The Life of Malchus, the Captive Monk is a short Latin hagiography written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 391. Jerome says he heard the story from Malchus himself, an aged monk living at Maronia in Syria. Malchus had left his monastery and was captured by Bedouin raiders. He was enslaved and forced to marry a fellow captive, but the two lived together chastely and finally escaped. The work celebrates chastity and monastic obedience, and it is the only record of Malchus.

The Life of Paul the First Hermit (Vita Sancti Pauli Eremitae) is a short Latin saint's life by Jerome. He wrote it around 375–376, probably while living as a hermit in the Syrian desert. Jerome argues that Paul of Thebes, not Antony, was the first Christian hermit. In his story, Paul flees the Decian persecution and lives for decades in an Egyptian desert cave, fed by a raven. Antony visits him and later buries him, and lions dig the grave. Jerome's first saint's life, it strongly shaped medieval monastic devotion, though scholars have questioned whether Paul really existed.

De viris illustribus (On Illustrious Men) is a Latin collection of short biographies and bibliographies of Christian writers. Jerome compiled it at Bethlehem in 392–393 and dedicated it to Nummius Aemilianus Dexter. It has a preface and 135 chapters, running from the apostles to Jerome himself. He modelled it on Suetonius's lives of pagan men of letters, presented it as a defence of Christian learning and took much of the early material from Eusebius. It was continued by Gennadius of Massilia and later by Isidore of Seville, and it is a key source for early Christian literary history.

Jerome wrote this preface to his Latin translation of the Book of Daniel from the Hebrew and Aramaic around 392 and addressed it to Paula and Eustochium. He explains that the churches read Theodotion's Greek version rather than the Septuagint, which he judged far from the original. He notes that parts of Daniel are written in Aramaic ("Chaldee") and recalls how hard he worked to learn that language. He also observes that the Jews counted Daniel among the Hagiographa rather than the Prophets, and that the Greek additions, such as Susanna, are absent from the Hebrew.

Jerome wrote this preface to his Latin translation of the Book of Job, made directly from the Hebrew around 392–393, while he was living in Bethlehem. He defends his work against critics who saw it as an attack on the Septuagint. He points out that Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion had already produced other Greek versions, and that Origen had marked the Old Testament with obeli and asterisks to show where the older Greek was defective. Jerome stresses that this was especially true of Job, where the Septuagint lacked many passages. The preface shows how he justified translating from the Hebrew.

The Prologus galeatus, or "Helmeted Preface," is Jerome's Latin preface to his translation from Hebrew of the books of Samuel and Kings, written about 391–392 and addressed to Paula and Eustochium. It was the first of his prefaces to his Hebrew-based translations. In it he sets out his method and lists the books of the Hebrew canon, which he counts as twenty-two to match the Hebrew alphabet. He classes Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, Tobit and the Shepherd of Hermas as outside the canon. This made it a key text in later debates over the Old Testament canon.

This short Latin preface was written by Jerome for his translation of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs from the Hebrew. It is addressed to the bishops Chromatius of Aquileia and Heliodorus of Altinum and is usually dated to the 390s. Jerome thanks them for paying for his secretaries and copyists, and says that, though weakened by illness, he finished the work in three days. The preface is best known for its view of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus: the Church may read them to build up the people, but not to establish doctrine.

This Latin dedicatory letter, known from its opening words as Novum opus, is the preface Jerome addressed to Pope Damasus I with his revised Latin text of the four Gospels. It is usually dated to about 383. Jerome explains that, at the pope's request, he corrected the widely differing Old Latin copies against Greek manuscripts. He expects to be attacked as a forger and defends the work. He also explains how to use the Eusebian Canons. The letter introduced the Vulgate Gospels and was copied at the start of many medieval Gospel books.

This is a collection of the Latin prefaces that Jerome (c. 347–420) wrote between about 380 and 415. They introduce his early translations, such as Eusebius's Chronicle, which he translated at Constantinople in 381–82. Others open his Old Testament versions, later part of the Vulgate, and his biblical commentaries. Addressed to friends and patrons, they explain how he went about translating, defend his return to the Hebrew text over the Septuagint and answer his critics. They are key evidence for his views on scholarship, the biblical canon and translation.

The Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith is a systematic summary of Christian doctrine by John of Damascus. He wrote it in the first half of the eighth century at or near Mar Saba as the third part of his Fountain of Knowledge. Its hundred chapters cover God and the Trinity, creation, angels, humanity, providence, the Incarnation and the two natures of Christ, sacraments, icons, Scripture and the resurrection. It largely draws on earlier Greek Fathers and became a standard reference in the East. A twelfth-century Latin translation influenced Western scholastic theology.

The Letters are the surviving correspondence of Leo the Great, bishop of Rome from 440 to 461. The collection includes some letters sent to Leo as well as his own. Writing to bishops, emperors, empresses and councils, Leo dealt with church discipline, Pelagian, Manichaean and Priscillianist errors, and the Eutychian controversy. The best known is Letter 28, the Tome to Flavian of Constantinople, which set out the two natures of Christ in one person and shaped the Council of Chalcedon. The letters are a major source for the growth of papal authority.

This is a collection of Latin sermons, also known as Tractatus, preached in Rome by Pope Leo I (Leo the Great) during his pontificate from 440 to 461. Most follow the liturgical year, with sermons for Christmas, Epiphany, Lent, the Passion, Easter, Ascension, Pentecost and the seasonal fasts. Others mark the anniversaries of his ordination, the feast of Peter and Paul, and collections for the poor. Written in polished, rhythmic prose, they set out Leo's teaching on the two natures of Christ and on the authority of Peter's see, and they shaped later Latin preaching and liturgy.

This is a collection of surviving fragments from the writings of Peter I, bishop of Alexandria from 300 until his martyrdom in 311, during the persecutions under Diocletian and his successors. It includes a letter warning the Alexandrian church against Meletius, who had ordained clergy in Peter's absence, the beginning of what became the Meletian schism. It also includes a passage on the Godhead and the Incarnation. Its best-known part is the Canons from his treatise on penitence, which set the terms for readmitting Christians who had lapsed under persecution. These canons were later received into Eastern church law.

The Epistolae Septem, or Doubtful Letters, are seven Latin letters handed down under the name of Sulpicius Severus, the late fourth- and early fifth-century Aquitanian writer and biographer of Martin of Tours. His authorship is doubted or rejected, and the real writer or writers and the date are uncertain. The letters are personal and spiritual. Some are addressed to a woman the writer calls his sister, encouraging ascetic Christian living, renunciation of the world and perseverance in the Lord's precepts. They show the devotional and ascetic correspondence circulating in the Latin West in late antiquity.

The Apology is a Latin defence in two books by Rufinus of Aquileia, written at Aquileia around 400–401 and addressed to his friend Apronianus. It answers Jerome's letter to Pammachius and the charges against Rufinus's translation of Origen's On First Principles and its preface. Rufinus defends his own orthodoxy and his method as a translator. He argues that Jerome had once admired and used Origen himself, and accuses him of inconsistency. Jerome replied with his Apology against Rufinus. The work is a key document of the first Origenist controversy and of the final break between the two former friends.

Rufinus of Aquileia wrote this short Latin apology around 400 and sent it to Anastasius I, bishop of Rome (399–401). Jerome's friends at Rome, among them Marcella and Pammachius, had accused Rufinus of spreading heresy through his Latin translation of Origen's On First Principles. Writing from Aquileia, Rufinus set out his own faith on the Trinity, the Incarnation, the resurrection of the body, judgement and the origin of the soul. He argued that a translator should not be held responsible for his author's opinions. The text is a key document of the first Origenist controversy.

Rufinus of Aquileia wrote this Latin exposition of the baptismal creed at the request of Laurentius, a bishop whose see is unknown. It dates from the early fifth century, probably around 400–404, though the exact date is uncertain. Rufinus goes through the creed of Aquileia article by article and notes where it differs from the Roman form, such as the clause on Christ's descent into hell. The work is an important witness to local Western creeds and their history. It also contains an early list of the canonical, ecclesiastical and apocryphal books of Scripture.

Rufinus of Aquileia wrote this short Latin treatise, usually called De adulteratione librorum Origenis, around 397. He addressed it to Macarius and attached it to his Latin translation of Pamphilus the Martyr's Apology for Origen. Rufinus argues that heretics had tampered with Origen's writings, and he cites cases where the works of other respected Church writers were also corrupted. The treatise was his reason for removing apparently unorthodox passages when he translated Origen's On First Principles. It became part of the bitter Origenist controversy between Rufinus and Jerome.

This is a collection of the prefaces and closing remarks that Rufinus of Aquileia attached to his Latin works and translations from Greek, written between his return to Italy in 397 and about 410. They introduce his commentary on Jacob's blessings of the twelve patriarchs, written at Paulinus of Nola's request, and his versions of Pamphilus's Apology for Origen, Origen's Peri Archon and other works, the pseudo-Clementine Recognitions, the Sentences of Sextus and Eusebius's Church History. The prefaces explain how Rufinus translated and defend his handling of Origen, a matter at the centre of his quarrel with Jerome.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in seven books by Socrates of Constantinople, also called Socrates Scholasticus. It was written in the 440s and continues Eusebius's history, covering events from 305 to 439: Constantine's conversion, the Arian controversy, the councils, and the affairs of the churches of the eastern empire. Socrates aimed for a plain style and drew on documents and on eyewitnesses. Sozomen used the work as a source. In the sixth century it was put into Latin as part of the Historia Tripartita, which carried it into the medieval West.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in nine books by Sozomen, a lawyer at Constantinople. He wrote it around the 440s and dedicated it to Emperor Theodosius II. It was meant to continue the work of Eusebius and covers events from the 320s to the 420s. The ninth book seems unfinished and stops short of the end date the author announced. Sozomen drew heavily on Socrates Scholasticus but added much material of his own, especially on monasticism, missions and the Church outside the empire. It is a key source for fourth- and early fifth-century Christianity.

The Dialogues are a Latin hagiographical work by Sulpicius Severus, the Aquitanian writer and biographer of Martin of Tours, composed in the early fifth century. Written as conversations between the author, his friend Postumianus, just back from the East, and Gallus, a Gaulish disciple of Martin, they first tell of the monks and hermits of Egypt and the East. They then turn to further miracles and deeds of Martin, presenting him as the equal of the famous Eastern ascetics. The work adds to Sulpicius's earlier Life of Martin and is an important source for early Western monasticism.

The three Latin letters of Sulpicius Severus (c. 363 – c. 425), a Christian writer from Aquitaine, add to his Life of Saint Martin of Tours. The first, to the priest Eusebius, answers a critic who asked why Martin, said to have worked miracles, had himself been put in danger by a fire. The second, to the deacon Aurelius, tells of a vision of Martin and mourns his death in 397. The third, to Bassula, the author's mother-in-law, describes Martin's last days and funeral. Together they form an important part of the early cult of Martin.

The Vita Sancti Martini is a Latin biography of Martin, bishop of Tours, written by the Aquitanian writer Sulpicius Severus, who knew him personally. It was completed around 396–397, apparently while Martin was still alive, and is introduced by a dedicatory letter to Desiderius. It covers Martin's military service, including the famous sharing of his cloak with a beggar, his monastic life, his work as bishop and his many miracles. It became one of the most influential models for later Western hagiography.

The Chronica, also called the Sacred History, is a Latin universal chronicle in two books by Sulpicius Severus, the Aquitanian writer best known for his Life of Saint Martin of Tours. Written in the early fifth century, it covers events from the creation of the world to the author's own time. It summarises the Old Testament and the life of Christ, then the persecutions, the Arian controversy and the Priscillianist affair, using secular historians to fix dates. Its brief, classical style earned Sulpicius the name "the Christian Sallust." Its accounts of fourth-century church conflicts are a valuable historical source.

The third Relatio is an official dispatch written in Latin in 384 by Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, prefect of Rome, to the Western emperor Valentinian II. Speaking for the pagan senators, he asked that the Altar of Victory, which Gratian had removed from the Senate House in 382, be restored. He also asked that the confiscated endowments of the Vestal Virgins and the priestly colleges be returned. Its well-known plea for religious tolerance drew rebuttals from Ambrose of Milan and later from Prudentius. The emperor refused the request.

This is a polemical Christological treatise by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, written around 430–431. It answers in turn each of the Twelve Anathemas that Cyril of Alexandria attached to his letter to Nestorius. Speaking from the Antiochene tradition, Theodoret argues that God the Word is immutable and was not changed into flesh but took flesh. He also insists that Christ's divine and human natures remain distinct. The work survives mainly through the quotations in Cyril's reply. Because it opposed Cyril, it was condemned posthumously as one of the Three Chapters at the Second Council of Constantinople in 553.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in five books by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was written around 449–450 and continues the history of Eusebius of Caesarea. It begins with the rise of Arianism under Constantine and ends in 429, with the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Theodoret writes from a firmly Nicene and Antiochene viewpoint and focuses on the struggle against Arianism. He quotes many letters, creeds and synodal documents in full. Along with the histories of Socrates Scholasticus and Sozomen, it is one of the main sources for fourth-century church history.

The Eranistes ("Beggar" or "Collector"), also called Polymorphus ("Multiform"), is a Greek theological treatise by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, written around 447–448. It consists of three dialogues between Orthodoxos and Eranistes. Eranistes speaks for the emerging Eutychian position, which Theodoret presents as pieced together from older heresies. The dialogues argue that the divine Word is immutable, that Christ's two natures remain unconfounded, and that the Godhead is impassible. A syllogistic summary follows. Each dialogue includes collections of patristic quotations, which make the work an important witness to Christological debate on the eve of the Council of Chalcedon.

The Letters of Theodoret of Cyrrhus (c. 393–c. 458), bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria from 423, form one of the largest surviving Greek letter collections of the fifth century. Over two hundred letters survive in several collections. They are addressed to bishops, monks, officials and friends, and cover consolation and friendship, the bishop's pleas for his poor diocese, and the Christological controversies that followed the Council of Ephesus (431). They also cover his deposition in 449 and his restoration at Chalcedon in 451. The letters are a major source for the church and society of the period.

This is a set of short disciplinary rulings in Greek by Theophilus, Patriarch of Alexandria from 385 to 412. It brings together a prosphonesis (address) on how to keep the Epiphany fast when the feast falls on a Sunday, a commonitory (memorandum) given to Ammon, letters to Agatho and Menas, and a ruling on the Cathari (Novatianists). Among the questions they answer are the treatment of clergy who had communicated with Arians, unworthy ordinations, fasting and the reception of returning schismatics. The Council in Trullo (692) accepted these rulings into the Byzantine collection of canons of the Fathers.

The Canonical Answers are a short collection of questions and answers on church discipline attributed to Timothy I, bishop of Alexandria (381–384), who took part in the Council of Constantinople in 381. Each brief answer settles a practical pastoral case: the baptism of catechumens who are sick or possessed, who may receive communion, ritual purity, marital continence and the duties of clergy. The Quinisext Council of 692 approved the collection, and it became part of the canon law of the Byzantine and Eastern Orthodox churches.

The Commonitory is a Latin treatise by Vincent of Lérins, a Gallic monk, written about 434, shortly after the Council of Ephesus. He wrote it under the pseudonym "Peregrinus." It offers a rule for telling Catholic truth from heresy: Scripture comes first, read in the sense held "everywhere, always, and by all," that is, by universality, antiquity and consent. Vincent also allows real development of doctrine, so long as it does not alter the faith. The second book was lost while he was still alive, and only his summary of it survives.

This passage is the closing section of the Commonitorium by Vincent of Lérins, a Gallic monk writing about 434, shortly after the Council of Ephesus. The work first had two books. The second was lost during Vincent's lifetime, and only this summary of it survives. The summary restates the work's method: Scripture is sufficient, but it must be interpreted by the Church's tradition, judged by universality, antiquity and consent. Ancient conciliar decisions come first, followed by the agreement of approved Fathers.

The Apocalypse of Moses is the Greek version of the Life of Adam and Eve. It is an anonymous apocryphal narrative presented as a revelation given to Moses through the archangel Michael. It tells of Adam and Eve after their expulsion from paradise, including Abel's murder, Adam's final illness, Eve's own account of the Fall, Adam's death and burial, and the promise of resurrection.
