The preacher praises the women for leaving the darkness of the world for chastity, abstinence and religious life. He then warns that the struggle against the devil lasts until death, and that lukewarm nuns who think a change of clothing is enough are mistaken. He urges daily good works and vigilance, citing Scripture throughout.

The Canons of Neocaesarea are the fifteen disciplinary rules of a regional synod held at Neocaesarea in Pontus, usually dated between about 314 and 320. That places it after the Council of Ancyra and before Nicaea. The canons deal with clerical discipline and penance. They depose a presbyter who marries after ordination, set rules on second marriages, catechumens and the minimum age for ordination, and limit each city to seven deacons. They became part of the Greek canonical collections. In the Latin West they circulated in versions such as the translation by Dionysius Exiguus in the early sixth century.

The Council of Gangra was a regional synod held at Gangra in Paphlagonia, Asia Minor, in the mid-fourth century. Its date is disputed, with estimates ranging from about 340 to the 360s. Its synodical letter, addressed to the bishops of Armenia, and its twenty canons condemn the followers of Eustathius of Sebaste for extreme asceticism. They had rejected marriage and married clergy, forbidden meat, encouraged slaves to leave their masters and held separate assemblies. The canons became part of the Greek canonical collections and circulated in Latin translations, including that of Dionysius Exiguus.

The Canons of Antioch are twenty-five disciplinary rules issued by a synod of eastern bishops at Antioch, usually identified with the Dedication Council of 341. Some scholars date them to an earlier Antiochene synod. They cover the Nicene date of Easter, the authority of metropolitans and provincial synods, clergy moving between dioceses, and the deposition and appeals of bishops. They entered the Greek canonical corpus and became widely authoritative. In the sixth century Dionysius Exiguus translated them into Latin for his collection of canons, which spread them through the West.

The Canons of Laodicea are the disciplinary decrees of a regional synod of bishops from Asia Minor held at Laodicea in Phrygia Pacatiana. Its exact date is uncertain, but it is usually placed between about 343 and 381, often around 363–364. Its sixty canons cover penance, liturgy, clerical conduct, the reception of heretics, and Christian practices that resembled Jewish ones. They also forbid reading non-canonical books in church, and a list of biblical books of disputed authenticity is attached. The canons entered the Greek canonical collections and Latin versions, including that of Dionysius Exiguus.

The creed and disciplinary canons of the Council of Constantinople, held in 381 under Emperor Theodosius I and later counted as the second ecumenical council. About 150 bishops reaffirmed the Nicene faith and condemned Arians, Macedonians (Pneumatomachi) and Apollinarians. They also issued the creed now known as the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed. The canons dealt with heresies and with church jurisdiction. One of them gave the bishop of Constantinople precedence of honour after Rome. In the sixth century Dionysius Exiguus translated the canons into Latin, and his collection spread them widely in the West.

This is a collection of documents from the Council of Ephesus of 431, the third ecumenical council. It was summoned by Emperor Theodosius II, and Cyril of Alexandria led its proceedings. The texts include extracts from the council's acts, Cyril's letters to Nestorius and the council's canons. The council condemned and deposed Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, and upheld the title Theotokos ("God-bearer") for Mary. One of its canons forbade drawing up any creed other than the Nicene. Later Latin canon-law collections passed on versions of these decrees.

This doctrinal letter by Dionysius, bishop of Rome from 259 to 268, survives only as a fragment quoted by Athanasius in his De Decretis. It was written after a Roman synod, in response to complaints about how Dionysius of Alexandria had argued against Sabellianism. The letter defends the divine monarchy, condemning both Sabellius's merging of Father and Son and teachings that split the Trinity into three separate gods. It also denies that the Son is a created being. It is an important witness to pre-Nicene Trinitarian theology.

Carmen de Deo, better known as De laudibus Dei ("In Praise of God"), is a Latin hexameter poem in three books by Blossius Aemilius Dracontius, a Christian poet and lawyer of Carthage. He wrote it under Vandal rule, probably while imprisoned by King Gunthamund (484–496). The first book is mostly an account of creation and circulated early on its own as the Hexameron. The poem celebrates God's mercy and providence and is a major work of late antique Christian poetry from Africa.

The Satisfactio is a Latin poem in elegiac couplets, 158 in most counts. Its author, the Carthaginian lawyer and poet Blossius Aemilius Dracontius, wrote it while imprisoned by a Vandal king, usually identified as Gunthamund (reigned 484–496). Dracontius had fallen from favour after praising a foreign ruler. The poem opens by praising God's eternal and unchanging power, then confesses this fault and asks the king for mercy and release. It borrows freely from his De laudibus Dei and is an important witness to Christian literary culture in Vandal Africa.

The Vita Sancti Maximi is a Latin hagiography of Maximus, abbot of Lérins and later bishop of Riez in fifth-century Provence. It was written in the late sixth century by Dynamius, a patrician of Provence. In a dedicatory letter to Bishop Urbicus of Riez, Dynamius explains that he had written an earlier Life some years before. Urbicus asked him to expand it with miracle accounts he had found in old documents gathered by Bishop Faustus, Maximus's successor. A later Life of Virgilius of Arles closely reworks this text.

These two short Latin letters were written by Dynamius, a patrician and governor of Provence in the later sixth century. He corresponded with Venantius Fortunatus and Pope Gregory the Great and also wrote a Life of Maximus of Riez. The first letter, to an unnamed friend, expresses joy at news of his safety. The second, to Bishop Villicus of Metz, praises the bishop's charity and humility. Both survive in the Austrasian Letters and show the ornate epistolary style of Merovingian Gaul.

The Vita Sancti Marii is a Latin saint's life of Marius (Maire), abbot of Bodon in the diocese of Sisteron in Provence. It is attributed to Dynamius the Patrician, a Provençal aristocrat of the late sixth century who also wrote a Life of Maximus of Riez. The work tells how Marius, a man of modest family from Orléans, became a monk there. With the consent of the Burgundian king Gundobad, the monks of Bodon chose him as their abbot. It praises his fasting, vigils and teaching, and records his prophecies and death.

This short Latin letter was sent by African bishops to the Gallic bishops Proculus and Cylinnius, probably between 418 and 426. It is signed by Aurelius of Carthage, Augustine of Hippo, Florentius and Secundinus, and appears among Augustine's correspondence as Letter 219. It concerns Leporius, a monk who had been censured in Gaul for Christological errors. He had denied that God became man, and his teaching implied a fourth person in the Trinity. After he was instructed in Africa, he recanted, and the bishops sent his written retraction (Libellus emendationis) with this letter, asking that he be received back.

The Relatio episcoporum ad Theodericum regem is a Latin report sent around 501–502 by the bishops of Italy, assembled in synod at Rome, to the Ostrogothic king Theoderic. It belongs to the Laurentian schism, when charges were brought against Pope Symmachus. The bishops tell the king that Symmachus refused to appear before their judgement. He complained that he had been violently attacked on his way to the synod, and he submitted himself to God and the king. The document is evidence for the dispute over whether a pope could be judged.

This Latin letter is presented as the work of Eastern bishops gathered at Antioch around 341, including Eusebius and Theognis, and is addressed to Pope Julius I. It protests that Rome received Athanasius and other bishops into communion after the East had condemned them, and that Rome disregarded the decisions of Eastern councils. It draws on the genuine dispute reported by Sozomen and Cassiodorus's Historia tripartita. Since Baronius, scholars have generally treated it as spurious: a Latin composition stitched together from fragments of other texts. It is usually associated with the forged papal decretal collections.

This Latin sermon was preached at Hippo by the presbyter Eraclius (Heraclius) in the presence of Augustine. Augustine publicly named him as his successor in 426. Eraclius opens by asking the congregation to support him with their prayers. He calls the task a burden laid on him by his "most blessed Father," since he must teach his fellow disciples while their master is present. He then praises Augustine as a teacher whose life matches his words, and urges his hearers to imitate his virtues as far as each is able. The text survives among Augustine's works.

This is a small group of Latin land charters attributed to Æthelberht, king of Kent (died 616), the first Anglo-Saxon king to accept Christianity. They record royal gifts to churches founded after Augustine's mission of 597. The first grants land east of Canterbury's walls to the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul, later St Augustine's Abbey. It is dated 605 and threatens anyone who violates the grant with excommunication. Modern scholars generally regard these charters as later fabrications or reworkings rather than authentic documents of Æthelberht's reign.

This is the opening provision of the law code issued by Æthelberht, King of Kent, after Augustine's mission arrived in 597. It was probably issued in the early seventh century, before the king died in 616. It sets compensation for theft of property belonging to God and the Church, a bishop, a priest, a deacon and other clergy, on a scale ranked by status. Bede reports that the code was written in English. It is the earliest law code in any Germanic language, and this text is a Latin rendering of it.

The Exhortatio ad monachos is a short Latin address to a community of monks, traditionally attributed to Eucherius of Lyon (c. 380–c. 449). Eucherius was a Gallic ascetic connected with the monastery of Lérins who later became bishop of Lyon, but his authorship of this piece is uncertain. The speaker says he can hardly teach monks who have already left the world and its riches. He praises them as the light of the world and as men living the life of angels on earth. He then urges them to keep up mercy, gentleness, obedience and charity, and above all humility.

This Latin work, in two books, abridges the monastic writings of John Cassian. It is traditionally attributed to Eucherius of Lyon (c. 380–c. 449), but that attribution is uncertain. Like Cassian's Institutes, it is addressed to Castor, bishop of Apt, who had asked for an account of the rules of the Egyptian and other Eastern monasteries for a monastery he had newly founded. The first book follows the Institutes and covers communal prayer, silence and discipline in the synaxis. The epitome shows how Cassian's teaching was condensed and passed on in Gaul and beyond.

This Latin letter of exhortation, also known as De contemptu mundi et saecularis philosophiae, was written by Eucherius of Lyon to his kinsman Valerianus, probably around 432, while Eucherius was living as an ascetic in the island monasteries of Lérins before becoming bishop of Lyon. Valerianus came from a family of high secular rank. Eucherius urges him to set aside worldly honours and philosophy and seek eternal life through Christian renunciation. The letter was admired for its polished style and became a well-known statement of Gallic monastic ideals.

This Latin profession of faith was submitted by the Catholic (Nicene) bishops of Vandal North Africa at the conference of Carthage in February 484. King Huneric had called the meeting to make them debate his Arian clergy. It is generally credited to Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, who led the Catholic side. The statement defends the Trinity, insisting on the full divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit and on the term homoousios. It survives in Victor of Vita's History of the Vandal Persecution. When the conference failed, Huneric began a harsh persecution and sent Eugenius into exile.

This short Latin pastoral letter was written by Eugenius, Catholic bishop of Carthage (480–505), to the faithful of his church. He wrote it when a royal edict of the Arian Vandal king Huneric summoned him to answer for his faith, around 484. Eugenius urges his flock to hold firmly to the Catholic faith that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Holy Spirit shares their divinity. He also warns them against accepting Arian rebaptism. Gregory of Tours preserves the letter in his History of the Franks.

This is a Latin panegyric, a formal speech of praise, addressed to the emperor Constantine in early fourth-century Gaul. It belongs to the Gallic speeches preserved in the Panegyrici Latini collection. Older editions attributed it to Eumenius, a rhetorician of Autun who served at the court of Constantius Chlorus. Modern scholars accept only the speech on restoring the schools of Autun as his, so the authorship of this oration is doubtful. Speeches of this kind are important evidence for imperial ideology, court rhetoric and the politics of Constantine's early reign.

This Latin panegyric thanks the emperor Constantine on behalf of the citizens of Autun (Augustodunum), whom the orator calls "Flavienses". It was delivered at Trier, probably in 311, during celebrations for Constantine's quinquennalia. Older editions attributed it to the rhetorician Eumenius, but modern scholars generally treat its author as anonymous. The speech recalls the Aedui's loyalty to Rome and the city's suffering under a seven-month siege. It then praises Constantine's visit to Autun, where he cancelled seven thousand tax assessments and five years of arrears. It survives in the Panegyrici Latini collection.

The Epistolae are a small collection of Latin letters attributed to Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli (d. 371), a leading Western opponent of Arianism. The first, addressed to Emperor Constantius II, accepts his summons to the synod of Milan in 355, the council that led to Eusebius's exile. The second, written from exile in the East, encourages the clergy and faithful of Vercelli, Novara, Ivrea and Tortona to remain firm in the Nicene faith. The letters are rare first-hand evidence for the Arian controversy in the West. Some items traditionally included are of disputed authenticity.

The Hexaemeron is a series of nine Greek homilies by Basil of Caesarea, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, on the six days of creation, working through Genesis 1:1–26. Basil preached them to his congregation in the 370s, possibly in 378. They pair a literal reading of the text with natural philosophy, describing the heavens, earth, plants and animals to show the Creator's wisdom. It was the first Christian work of its kind and shaped later hexaemeral writing, including Ambrose's Hexameron. Eustathius Afer translated it into Latin around 400.

These are Latin excerpts from sermons by Eutherius, bishop of Tyana in Cappadocia. He was a supporter of Nestorius who was deposed after the Council of Ephesus (431). The excerpts were translated from Greek by the anti-Nestorian Latin writer Marius Mercator, who set them in a hostile commentary presenting Eutherius as a subtler and more dangerous heretic than Nestorius or Theodoret. The passages attack statements by Cyril of Alexandria and other orthodox writers, especially Cyril's formula that Christ "suffered impassibly." They preserve part of the Antiochene case against Cyril's Christology.

This short Latin treatise in the form of a letter is attributed to Eutropius, bishop of Valencia in Visigothic Spain from about 589 until at least 610. It is addressed to a certain Peter, styled papa, a title then also used of bishops. It sets out the eight principal vices: gluttony, fornication, avarice, anger, sadness, acedia, vainglory and pride. It explains how each of the first six gives rise to the next, while vainglory and pride threaten even those who have overcome the others. It draws on the monastic teaching of Evagrius and John Cassian.

This Latin letter on the strict discipline of monks is by Eutropius, abbot of the Servitanum monastery and later bishop of Valencia (from 589, died about 610). Isidore of Seville records that it was addressed to Peter, bishop of Ercávica; "papa" was then still a title of honour for bishops. It draws on Moses, the Gospels and Paul to argue that a superior must be both gentle and severe, rightly correcting and even separating monks who refuse to repent. It is a rare witness to Visigothic monastic thought. Its exact date is uncertain.

This is a Latin critical notice on the decrees attributed to Pope Eutychian, bishop of Rome from about 275 to 283. It is not a work of Eutychian himself: it is an early modern commentary taken from the Benedictine scholar Pierre Coustant. It looks at two rulings that the Liber Pontificalis credits to him, the blessing of produce on the altar and the burial of martyrs in a dalmatic or purple colobium. It weighs Baronius's defence of these rulings against the Apostolic Canons. It also rejects two letters and ten decrees forged under his name in the Pseudo-Isidorian collection.

The Exhortatio ad Presbyteros is a Latin address to priests, attributed to Pope Eutychian (bishop of Rome 275–283). The attribution is spurious. The text mentions chess, the maniple and the chasuble, which points to a Carolingian or later medieval origin. It belongs to the tradition of the synodal admonition (Admonitio synodalis), which is also ascribed to other popes. The bishop reminds his priests that they will answer for their flocks. He then sets out rules for clerical life, the celebration of Mass, liturgical vestments, the care of the altar and sacred vessels, and pastoral duties.

The Altercatio Legis inter Simonem Iudaeum et Theophilum Christianum is a Latin dialogue, an anti-Jewish Christian polemic, written in the fifth century. It is attributed to Evagrius, sometimes called Evagrius Gallus, and is dedicated to a certain Valerius. Gennadius of Marseille mentions it. Presented as a debate the author witnessed, it has the Jew Simon and the Christian Theophilus argue over the Hebrew Scriptures. Theophilus uses prophetic texts to defend Christ's divinity, incarnation and crucifixion, and the dialogue ends with Simon's conversion. It belongs to the long tradition of Christian Adversus Iudaeos literature.

This is an ancient Latin version of the Sentences to Monks (Ad monachos), a collection of short sayings written in Greek by Evagrius Ponticus, a monk in Egypt, probably in the 380s or 390s. Gennadius of Marseille reports that Rufinus of Aquileia translated Evagrius's sentences into Latin. Like the Book of Proverbs, the sayings use paired, contrasting lines. They teach monks about faith, love, controlling the body, avoiding anger and grudges, and the ascent towards knowledge of God. The Latin version helped carry Evagrian ascetic teaching to Western monasticism.

This Latin treatise in twelve books was written by Facundus, bishop of Hermiana in the African province of Byzacena. It defends the "Three Chapters" against Emperor Justinian's condemnation: the person and writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, certain writings of Theodoret of Cyrus, and the letter of Ibas of Edessa. Facundus began it in Constantinople, addressing it to the emperor. He argued that condemning these writings undermined the Council of Chalcedon. Its completion date is uncertain, but it is the chief Western statement of opposition in the controversy.

This short Latin chronological summary covers eight years of the Three Chapters controversy, year by year from 546. It records Justinian's edict against the writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrus and Ibas of Edessa, and Pope Vigilius's arrival in Constantinople and his shifting position, including his Judicatum of 548. It also notes resistance from African, Illyrian and Dalmatian bishops. It is transmitted with the works of Facundus of Hermiane, but it refers to him in the third person. For that reason it is more likely an editor's compilation than his own work.

Contra Mocianum Scholasticum is a short Latin polemical treatise by Facundus, bishop of Hermiana in North Africa. He wrote it while in hiding from imperial persecution during the Three Chapters controversy. Its date is uncertain but falls after Pope Vigilius's Iudicatum of 548. Mocianus, a scholasticus, had condemned the African and other bishops who broke communion with Vigilius and those who supported the condemnation of the Three Chapters. He quoted Augustine's anti-Donatist writings against them. Facundus defends their separation as loyalty to the Council of Chalcedon. Baronius identified Mocianus with Mutianus, the Latin translator of Chrysostom's homilies on Hebrews.

The Epistola fidei catholicae in defensione trium capitulorum is a short Latin letter by Facundus, bishop of Hermiana in North Africa. It is distinct from his longer Pro defensione trium capitulorum in twelve books. It belongs to the later stage of the Three Chapters controversy. The letter refers to Chalcedon as held almost 120 years earlier, which places it around 570. Facundus argues that condemning Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret and Ibas undermines the Council of Chalcedon. He also maintains that those who condemned them, under imperial pressure, cannot be in communion with those who refused.

This Latin cento by the Roman aristocrat Faltonia Betitia Proba was probably composed in the mid-fourth century, after her conversion to Christianity. It is a poem made up entirely of lines and half-lines taken from Virgil and rearranged to retell episodes from the Old Testament and, above all, the life of Christ. It was widely copied and was later used in schools to teach Christian belief. A text attributed to Pope Gelasius I rejected it as apocryphal, and Jerome is often thought to have criticised it. Isidore of Seville, Petrarch and Boccaccio praised Proba's ingenuity.

De vita Christiana ("On the Christian Life") is a Latin treatise of moral exhortation from the early fifth century. It has come down among the works wrongly attributed to Augustine of Hippo. The author writes in a humble tone to a Christian woman, apparently a widow, and urges her toward holiness, righteousness and works of charity. Its outlook is close to Pelagian teaching. Scholars have attributed it to Pelagius himself or to Fastidius, a British bishop whom Gennadius names as the author of a work with this title. Its authorship remains disputed.

De vita Christiana ("On the Christian Life") is a Latin treatise of moral exhortation from the early fifth century. It has come down among the works wrongly attributed to Augustine of Hippo. The author writes in a humble tone to a Christian woman, apparently a widow, and urges her toward holiness, righteousness and works of charity. Its outlook is close to Pelagian teaching. Scholars have attributed it to Pelagius himself or to Fastidius, a British bishop whom Gennadius names as the author of a work with this title. Its authorship remains disputed.

This Latin petition is better known as the Libellus precum. Faustinus and Marcellinus, presbyters of the rigorist faction later called the Luciferians, addressed it to the emperors around 383–384, chiefly Theodosius I at Constantinople. They asked for recognition as the true church, or at least protection from persecution. The petition tells of the Arian conflicts under Constantius II, of bishops exiled for defending Athanasius, and of the disputed Roman succession after Liberius, and it is sharply hostile to Pope Damasus. Theodosius granted protection in a rescript, and the petition remains a key statement of Luciferian belief.

This Latin treatise on the Trinity was written by Faustinus, a presbyter of the Luciferian faction, which refused communion with Arians and with clergy who had compromised with them. Written in the early 380s, it is addressed to an empress who had asked how to answer the scriptural arguments Arians used against the Catholics. Its traditional title names Galla Placidia, but the empress was probably Flaccilla, wife of Theodosius I. Faustinus defends the full divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit with biblical testimony. The treatise is one of the few surviving Luciferian writings.

This short Latin profession of faith is by Faustinus, a Roman presbyter of the rigorist faction known as the Luciferians. It is usually identified with his Confessio fidei addressed to Emperor Theodosius I and dated to about 383–384. It defends the Nicene creed and confesses one substance of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It rejects the charges of Sabellianism and Apollinarianism and attacks those who speak of three substances in the Trinity, arguing that this amounts to three gods. Its title reflects its survival in a collection of Roman canons and decrees.

This short Latin sermon on the Lord's Passion is attributed to a homilist named Faustinus, generally dated to the later fifth century. Little is known of its author. The preacher argues that the Passion was foretold and prefigured from the beginning of the world, and that Christ can be proved to the Jews from their own Scriptures. He reads Old Testament types as figures of Christ, among them Eve formed from Adam's side, the murdered Abel and the ram caught in the thicket at Abraham's sacrifice. In places the sermon echoes Augustine's anti-Jewish polemic.

This is a Latin collection of letters and decrees attributed to an early bishop of Rome named Felix, here identified as Felix I (269–274). Material of this kind largely comes from the ninth-century Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals and is generally regarded as spurious. The collection opens with a letter in the name of Athanasius and the bishops of Egypt, Thebaid and Libya, addressed to "Pope Felix II". It asks the Roman see for help against Arian persecution and stresses Rome's authority as the "mother" church of appeal.

This short Latin fragment is attributed to Felix I, bishop of Rome from 269 to 274. It comes from a letter addressed to Maximus, bishop of Alexandria, and his clergy. The passage professes faith in the incarnation. It holds that Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, is the eternal Son and Word of God, not a man taken up by God as someone separate from him. Being perfect God, he also became perfect man. The fragment was later cited in fifth-century Christological debates, but modern scholars widely regard it as an Apollinarian forgery.

This is the collected correspondence and decrees of Pope Felix III, bishop of Rome from 483 to 492, written in Latin. Most of the letters deal with the crisis in the Eastern Church after the Emperor Zeno issued the Henotikon. They include letters to Emperor Zeno and to Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople, which urged them to defend the Chalcedonian faith and dealt with the disputed see of Alexandria. Felix's condemnation and deposition of Acacius in 484 began the Acacian schism between Rome and Constantinople, which lasted until 519. The collection is therefore a key source for that schism.

This is a collection of Latin letters and decrees attributed to Pope Felix IV, bishop of Rome from 526 to 530, who was raised to the see with the backing of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric. Its first letter is addressed to Caesarius of Arles. In it Felix supports the Gallic bishops' rule that laymen must not be ordained to the priesthood before a period of testing, citing Paul's warning to Timothy against laying hands on anyone hastily. The papal letter collections of this period also contain later forgeries, so not every piece is certainly by Felix.

The Letter to Eugippius on the Essence of the Trinity is a Latin theological letter by Fulgentius Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage, who died in 546/547. He wrote it to the presbyter Eugippius, probably the abbot of Lucullanum near Naples and biographer of Severinus. The letter answers a question recently put forward by an Arian count. It first sets out the teachings on which Arians and Catholics differ, then defends the Catholic doctrine of one God in three persons. It reflects the Trinitarian disputes of the North African Church after Vandal rule.

The Epistolae et Opuscula are the letters and short treatises of Fulgentius Ferrandus, a deacon of Carthage who died around 546/547 and was a pupil of Fulgentius of Ruspe. They are written in Latin. In the first letters Ferrandus asks Fulgentius about pastoral and doctrinal problems. One concerns the salvation of an Ethiopian catechumen who was baptized while unconscious and died without receiving the Eucharist. Other letters, such as one to the Roman deacon Anatolius, defend Chalcedonian Christology. They discuss the two natures in Christ and whether one of the Trinity can be said to have been born and to have suffered.

The Breviatio canonum is a Latin digest of church law compiled by Fulgentius Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage, in the first half of the sixth century, before his death around 546/547. It arranges brief summaries of conciliar canons by subject, starting with the ordination and duties of bishops and moving on to other clergy and church discipline. Each heading cites its sources: Greek councils such as Nicaea, Ancyra, Antioch, Laodicea and Sardica, along with many African synods. This makes it an early systematic canonical collection and an important witness to the conciliar legislation of the African Church.

The Regula ad monachos is a Latin monastic rule written by Ferreolus (Ferréol), bishop of Uzès in southern Gaul from about 553 to 581. He composed it for the monastery he founded, known as Ferreolacum. It opens by making obedience the foundation of monastic life and urges monks to revere their abbot, fearing him as a lord and loving him as a father. It is often cited for treating the copying of manuscripts as equal to manual labour, a sign of the value Gallic monasticism placed on books.

This Latin dedicatory letter is not by Filastrius. Cardinal Angelo Maria Querini addressed it to Pope Clement XII (reigned 1730–1740). Querini was librarian of the Apostolic See and bishop of Brescia. The letter introduces a volume that gathered for the first time the writings of four Brescian bishops: Philastrius, Gaudentius, Rampert and Adelmann. Querini links the project to his edition of Ephrem the Syrian and praises the see of Brescia. He also notes that Augustine pointed to Philastrius's catalogue of heresies, the Diversarum haereseon liber, when Quodvultdeus asked him to write such a treatise.

This letter was written around 256 by Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, to Cyprian of Carthage during the dispute over rebaptising heretics. It was probably composed in Greek and survives only in a Latin translation preserved among Cyprian's letters. Firmilian backs Cyprian's view that baptism given outside the Church is invalid. He cites an earlier synod at Iconium that rejected baptisms performed by the Cataphrygians (Montanists) and sharply criticises Pope Stephen I. The letter is an important witness to the third-century debates over baptism and Roman authority.

This is a short Latin letter from a court official named Florentius to Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari (Calaris) in Sardinia, who was then in exile for refusing to condemn Athanasius. It was written around 360. Florentius reports that a book bearing Lucifer's name had been presented to the Emperor Constantius II. On the emperor's orders, he asks Lucifer to confirm whether he sent it and to return the copy. The book was evidently one of Lucifer's polemical treatises against Constantius. The letter survives with Lucifer's works, together with his defiant reply.

This Latin letter was written around the mid-sixth century by Florianus, abbot of a "Romanum monasterium." Scholars disagree on where that monastery was: some place it at Romainmôtier in the Jura, others in northern Italy. He wrote to Nicetius, bishop of Trier. In ornate, biblically allusive prose, Florianus praises the bishop's monastic training and holiness and asks for his prayers. He names his own spiritual patrons, among them Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, who baptised him and whom he honours as a learned opponent of Nestorius and Eutyches. The letter is preserved in the Epistolae Austrasicae collection.

Psalmi et hymni is a collection of Latin religious poems by Florus of Lyon, the ninth-century deacon, theologian and poet who ran the scriptorium at Lyon and died around 860. It contains verse paraphrases of individual psalms, written in dactylic hexameters, along with hymns. Florus turns the biblical text into classicizing verse and gives it a Christian reading. In his version of Psalm 22 (Psalm 23 in Hebrew numbering), "The Lord is my shepherd", the speaker hopes to rise to the "starry temple of Christ." The poems are an example of Carolingian biblical poetry.

The Chronicle of Fredegar is a Latin universal chronicle, probably written in Burgundy in the 7th century. Its author is unknown, and the name Fredegar was only attached to it in the 16th century. It draws on the chronicles of Jerome, Hydatius, Isidore and Gregory of Tours, runs from the creation of the world to 642, and mentions a few events up to 658. Continuations written under the Carolingians carry the story to the death of Pepin the Short in 768. It is a key source for Merovingian history after 591, where Gregory's Histories end.

These are passages on Frankish history taken from the Latin Chronicle of Fredegar, a seventh-century compilation probably written in Burgundy. Its author is unknown, and the name Fredegar was first attached to it only in the sixteenth century. The fragments come from the chronicle's reworkings of earlier works such as Eusebius' Chronicle in Jerome's version. They include the legend that the Franks descended from the Trojans through Priam and an eponymous king Francio. The chronicle ends in 642, and Carolingian continuations carry it to 768. It is a key source for the Merovingian period after Gregory of Tours.

De fide ad Petrum is a Latin doctrinal treatise by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa. It was probably written in the 520s. Fulgentius addresses it to a certain Peter, who was about to travel to Jerusalem and wanted a concise rule of true faith to protect him from heresy. The work sets out teaching on the Trinity, creation, the Incarnation, grace and the sacraments, and ends with a series of rules to be firmly held. It circulated widely among the works of Augustine, and that attribution helped make it influential in medieval theology.

Ad Monimum Libri Tres is a Latin theological treatise in three books by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa. He wrote it in the early sixth century for his friend Monimus, who had sent him questions. The first book defends an Augustinian view of predestination and denies that God predestines anyone to sin. The later books treat questions about the eucharistic sacrifice and the sending of the Holy Spirit, and refute Arian readings of Scripture. The work is a key source for Fulgentius's anti-Arian and anti-Pelagian theology.

This Latin treatise by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa, defends Nicene Trinitarian doctrine against Arianism. It was written in the early sixth century, when Arian Vandal kings ruled North Africa. It takes the form of a list of objections, each followed by a reply. These are traditionally identified as the ten objections put by the Vandal king Thrasamund. Fulgentius argues that the names Father and Son mark a real distinction of persons and a true begetting, but not a difference of nature. The Son is coeternal with the Father and shares one substance with him.

Ad Trasimundum is a Latin theological treatise in three books by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa. He wrote it around 515 for the Arian Vandal king Thrasamund, who had brought him from exile in Sardinia to Carthage and demanded a written answer to his questions. The first book defends the union of Christ's divine and human natures in one person. The later books deal with the immensity of the Son's divinity and with his passion. The work is an important witness to Catholic–Arian controversy under Vandal rule.

The Epistolae are the collected Latin letters of Fulgentius of Ruspe, a North African bishop who wrote under the Arian Vandal kingdom in the early sixth century. They answer theological and pastoral questions from clergy, monks and lay people. The first letter addresses a husband whose wife had undergone penance during a grave illness: it discusses marital duty and vows of continence between spouses. Other letters deal with virginity, penance, the Trinity and the Incarnation, and grace in the tradition of Augustine. They show how Nicene belief and pastoral care were maintained in Vandal Africa.

This short Latin treatise on the Trinity was written by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa, in the early sixth century; its exact date is uncertain. It answers Felix, a notary who had asked how he should believe in the Trinity and how to defend the Catholic faith against the heretics he lived among. Fulgentius appeals to the faith preached by the apostolic sees of Rome, Antioch, Alexandria, Ephesus and Jerusalem. He sets out orthodox teaching on the one God in three persons against Arians, Donatists, Nestorians, Eutychians and Manichaeans.

Contra sermonem Fastidiosi Ariani is a Latin polemical treatise in one book by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa. He wrote it in the early sixth century, during the Arian Vandal kingdom, at the request of a Catholic named Victor. It answers a sermon by Fastidiosus, a former Catholic monk and priest who had become an Arian. Fastidiosus had mocked the "Homousians" for teaching an inseparable Trinity and the Son's equality with the Father. Fulgentius defends both doctrines and attacks the Arian claim that the Trinity can be divided.

De remissione peccatorum ("On the Forgiveness of Sins") is a Latin treatise in two books by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa. It is addressed to a layman named Euthymius, whose devotion to Scripture and to church attendance Fulgentius praises at the outset. Written in the early sixth century, it answers Euthymius's questions on the forgiveness of sins. Fulgentius teaches that sins are remitted only by God's grace within the Catholic Church and only in this present life. The work reflects his Augustinian theology of grace.

This is a Latin doctrinal letter by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa, written in the early sixth century to a layman named Scarila. A dispute over dinner at the house of a Catholic named Eventius had raised two questions. One was whether the Son alone, and not the Father, became incarnate. The other was whether God created lowly creatures such as flies and fleas. Fulgentius defends the incarnation of the Son alone within the undivided Trinity and argues that God made all creatures, however small.

De Veritate Praedestinationis et Gratiae Dei (On the Truth of Predestination and the Grace of God) is a Latin treatise in three books by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa, written in the early sixth century. It is addressed to the presbyter John and the deacon Venerius. In it Fulgentius defends an Augustinian view of grace against those who made salvation depend on human merit. He rejects the claim that God predestines people, including unbaptized infants, according to foreseen future deeds. Instead he insists that divine grace is unmerited and comes before any human merit.

De fide ad Petrum is a Latin doctrinal treatise by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa. It was probably written in the 520s. Fulgentius addresses it to a certain Peter, who was about to travel to Jerusalem and wanted a concise rule of true faith to protect him from heresy. The work sets out teaching on the Trinity, creation, the Incarnation, grace and the sacraments, and ends with a series of rules to be firmly held. It circulated widely among the works of Augustine, and that attribution helped make it influential in medieval theology.

This short Latin anti-Arian treatise is transmitted under the name of Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa during the Vandal period. Fulgentius's early biography records his dispute with an Arian bishop named Pinta, but the authenticity of the surviving text has been doubted. It answers an Arian booklet that called Catholics "Homousians" and assembled Old and New Testament passages against the term homoousios. The author defends the Church as one and unconquerable amid heresies. He explains the Greek word and appeals to the authority of the 318 fathers of Nicaea.

The Sermones genuini are the Latin sermons accepted as authentic works of Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa (died c. 527 or 533). The title separates them from the many doubtful or spurious homilies that circulated under his name. The first sermon, "On the Lord's Stewards", explains Christ's question about the faithful and prudent steward. It sets out the special duty of bishops to preach and the obedience that clergy and people both owe to God's commands. The sermons show the pastoral side of a leading Augustinian theologian of grace.

This is a pair of Latin sermons attributed to Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa (died c. 527 or 533). The title, "two sermons hitherto unpublished", marks them as later additions to his printed works. The first was preached for the feast of the Lord's Circumcision. Addressing his hearers as "brothers", the preacher reflects on the mystery of the Incarnation. He stresses that the eternal Son freely took on true flesh and true death out of mercy. This was an unearned grace given to the undeserving, which calls for humble thanksgiving and firm belief.

The Calendar of 354 is the civic calendar of the city of Rome and the central part of the Chronograph of 354. Furius Dionysius Filocalus produced the compilation in that year for a wealthy Roman Christian named Valentinus. Month by month, it lists public festivals, games and circus races, fixed meetings of the Senate, the birthdays of deified emperors, unlucky "Egyptian days" and the sun's entry into each zodiac sign. It names no Christian feasts, and it is an important witness to Roman public religion and civic life in the age of Constantius II.

This is the surviving collection of Latin sermons, or tractates, by Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia from 387 until his death around 410. Its core is a series of Easter homilies, preached during Easter week, that explain scriptural readings, especially the Exodus Passover and its fulfilment in Christ and the sacraments. Gaudentius wrote these down for Benivolus, a Christian who could not attend in person, and a prefatory letter addresses him. Further pieces deal with other biblical passages and occasions. The collection gives valuable evidence for preaching, exegesis and liturgy in northern Italy around 400.

This Latin hymn in Sapphic stanzas praises Filastrius (Philastrius), bishop of Brescia and author of a catalogue of heresies. It has traditionally been attributed to his successor, Gaudentius of Brescia (bishop c. 387–410), but its authorship and date are uncertain. The poem calls on the people of Brescia and the shores of Lake Garda to celebrate the city's seventh bishop, whose relics they keep. It recalls how he left his homeland, studied Scripture and preached against pagans, Jews and the Arians, among them Auxentius of Milan.

This is the collected Latin letters and decrees of Pope Gelasius I, bishop of Rome from 492 to 496. Many of them concern the Acacian Schism with Constantinople. Gelasius insists that no one can be received into communion with the apostolic see without condemning Acacius, along with Eutyches and other heretics. Other pieces deal with church discipline, clerical ordination and the rights of the Roman see. The collection includes the famous letter to Emperor Anastasius I, Duo sunt, which distinguishes priestly authority from royal power.

The Fragmenta are a group of short Latin excerpts from letters and decrees of Pope Gelasius I, who was bishop of Rome from 492 to 496. They survive only as pieces quoted in later collections, not as complete letters. Their subjects are practical church administration. One deals with which bishop should consecrate a newly built basilica: the right goes to the bishop whose see had baptized the local people. Another tells the defensor Dulcius that the deacon Anastasius has been ordained bishop of Lucera. Together they show Gelasius's attention to diocesan boundaries and church discipline.

De ecclesiasticis dogmatibus ("On Church Doctrines") is a short Latin summary of Christian belief, set out in numbered chapters. It is generally attributed to Gennadius, a priest of Marseilles who died around 496, and was written in the later fifth century. It begins with a confession of the Trinity, saying the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. It then condemns heresies and deals with the Incarnation, the soul, free will, grace and church practice. In the Middle Ages it was widely read, and copies passed it down under the names of Augustine and Isidore of Seville.

This Latin catalogue of Christian writers, usually called De viris illustribus, was written by Gennadius, a priest of Marseilles, in the later fifth century. Its exact date is uncertain. It continues Jerome's work of the same name, which ended in 392–393. In about ninety short notices it covers Greek, Latin and Syriac authors from the late fourth century to Gennadius's own time, describing their lives and listing their writings. Some notices were probably added by later hands. Many of the writers it records are otherwise poorly documented, so it is an important source for the literary history of the period.

This short Latin letter was written by Germanus, bishop of Paris (died 576), to Queen Brunhild, wife of the Austrasian king Sigebert I. It is usually dated to about 575, during the civil war among the Merovingian kings. Germanus calls himself a "sinner" and reports a popular rumour that Sigebert was set on ruining the region at the queen's urging. He says he does not believe it, but he begs her to give no grounds for such talk and to work for peace. The letter shows a Gallic bishop speaking up as a pastor in the politics of his day.

This Latin charter is a privilege of immunity issued in the name of Germanus (Germain), bishop of Paris, for the monastery of the Holy Cross and Saint Vincent in Paris, later known as Saint-Germain-des-Prés. It is dated 21 August 566. It recalls that King Childebert I founded the basilica, chose it as his burial place and endowed it by testament. It then frees the abbot and community from interference by future bishops of Paris. The document is an important witness to Merovingian monastic exemption, but its authenticity has been questioned.

De excidio Britanniae is a Latin sermon in the form of a letter by the British monk Gildas. It was written in the late fifth or sixth century; the exact date is disputed. It has three parts. The first tells British history from the Roman conquest to the author's own day and mentions Ambrosius Aurelianus and the victory at Mons Badonicus. The second condemns five contemporary kings, Maelgwn Gwynedd among them. The third attacks the British clergy. The work's history is not reliable, but it is the only major source for sub-Roman Britain written by a near-contemporary.

The Life of St Benedict is the second of the four books of the Dialogues by Pope Gregory the Great, written in Latin around 593–594. Like the rest of the work, it is a conversation between Gregory and his deacon Peter. It tells of Benedict of Nursia: his studies at Rome, his time as a hermit at Subiaco, the founding of Monte Cassino, his miracles and prophecies, his sister Scholastica and his death. Gregory names Benedict's disciples as his informants. The book is the fullest early source for Benedict's life and shaped later Western hagiography and monastic tradition.

This Latin inscription on a marble slab was set up in the portico of St Peter's Basilica in Rome during the pontificate of Gregory the Great (590–604). Addressed to the apostles Peter and Paul by Gregory as their "unworthy servant", it records how he recovered estates and olive groves, chiefly in the Appian patrimony, from those who held them. He assigned them permanently to supply oil for the basilica's lamps and bound his successors to keep the gift intact. It is valuable evidence of papal estate management and of Gregory's piety.

The Moralia in Job is Gregory the Great's long Latin commentary on the Book of Job, in thirty-five books. This part contains the dedicatory epistle, the preface and Books I–XVI. Gregory began the work as talks to his monks while serving as papal envoy in Constantinople, at the urging of Leander of Seville. He revised and finished it after becoming pope, around 595. It reads Job in literal, allegorical and moral senses, with the moral sense given most space. It became one of the most influential guides to moral and spiritual theology in the medieval West.

The Moralia in Job is Gregory the Great's long Latin commentary on the Book of Job, in thirty-five books. He began it as talks to his monks while serving as papal envoy at Constantinople around 579 and finished revising it in the 590s, after becoming pope. This second half covers Books XVII–XXXV. Reading Job historically, allegorically and morally, Gregory treats Job as a figure of Christ and the Church, and Job's friends as heretics. The work became a major source of moral and ascetic teaching in the medieval West.

The Homilies on Ezekiel are a set of twenty-two sermons by Pope Gregory I (the Great), preached to the people of Rome around 593, while the Lombards threatened the city. Book One has twelve homilies on the opening chapters of Ezekiel. Book Two has ten on the vision of the temple in chapter 40. About eight years later Gregory revised the notaries' transcripts and dedicated the collection to Bishop Marinianus. The homilies combine allegorical exegesis with teaching on prophecy, contemplation and the active life, and were widely read in the medieval West.

The Homilies on the Gospels are a collection of forty Latin sermons by Pope Gregory I (Gregory the Great), given at Mass in Rome early in his pontificate (590–604). Each homily explains the Gospel reading of a particular day. In his preface to Secundinus, bishop of Taormina, Gregory says that a notary read some of them aloud from his dictation and that he preached the others himself. He then revised them and arranged them in two books of twenty. Their plain moral and allegorical teaching made them widely read and much used in medieval preaching and liturgical homiliaries.

The Book of Pastoral Rule (Regula Pastoralis) is a Latin treatise on the duties of bishops and clergy, written by Pope Gregory I around 590, soon after his election. It is addressed to John, bishop of Ravenna, who had criticised Gregory for trying to avoid the papacy. Its four parts deal with who should take up spiritual rule, how the pastor should live, how he should teach people of differing character, and how he should stay humble. It became one of the most influential medieval guides to ministry, and King Alfred had it translated into Old English.

This is a collection of supplementary documents attached to the Register of letters of Gregory the Great, pope from 590 to 604. It opens with a profession of faith ascribed to Gregory. This creed is found at the head of the Register in most manuscripts and is also quoted by John the Deacon in his Life of Gregory. Tradition holds that Gregory pronounced it at his ordination. Other pieces follow, including the record of the deposition of the archdeacon Laurentius and the appointment of Honoratus in his place. Gregory's authorship of some of these items is uncertain.

The Dialogues are a Latin hagiographical collection in four books, traditionally attributed to Pope Gregory the Great and usually dated to about 593–594. Their authorship has been questioned by some modern scholars. Written as a conversation between Gregory and his deacon Peter, the first three books tell of the miracles and holy lives of Italian saints. The second book, on Benedict of Nursia, is the fullest early source for his life. The fourth book argues for the soul's survival and the afterlife. The work's wide influence led Eastern Christians to call Gregory "the Dialogist".

The Register of the Epistles is the collected official correspondence of Pope Gregory I (the Great), written during his pontificate from 590 to 604. It survives in fourteen books arranged by indiction year and contains around 850 letters in Latin. They deal with the management of the papal estates, church discipline, and relations with bishops, emperors, Frankish and Lombard rulers. They also cover the mission to the English and the dispute over the title "ecumenical patriarch." The collection is a major source for the history of the late sixth-century Church and of Italy.

This is a Latin allegorical commentary on the Song of Songs attributed to Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604). The preface explains that Scripture uses the language of bodily love so that the soul, grown cold after the loss of paradise, may be stirred to love God. Gregory's genuine exposition covers only the opening verses. The longer text printed under his name continues with material generally credited to the eleventh-century monk Robert of Tombelaine, so the authorship of the whole is mixed.

De fide orthodoxa contra Arianos is a Latin treatise defending the Nicene faith against the Arians. It is now attributed to Gregory, bishop of Elvira in Baetica (died c. 392). It was written probably soon after the Council of Rimini (359), and was long transmitted among the works of Ambrose and of Phoebadius of Agen. It opens with the Nicene Creed. In its prologue the author says this is a revised form of an earlier booklet. The work defends the Son's consubstantiality (homoousios) with the Father. It is an important witness to Western anti-Arian theology.

De fide orthodoxa contra Arianos is a Latin treatise defending the Nicene faith against the Arians. It is now attributed to Gregory, bishop of Elvira in Baetica (died c. 392). It was written probably soon after the Council of Rimini (359), and was long transmitted among the works of Ambrose and of Phoebadius of Agen. It opens with the Nicene Creed. In its prologue the author says this is a revised form of an earlier booklet. The work defends the Son's consubstantiality (homoousios) with the Father. It is an important witness to Western anti-Arian theology.

The History of the Franks is a Latin history in ten books, properly titled Decem Libri Historiarum. Gregory, bishop of Tours (c. 538–594), wrote it between about 573 and 594. It starts with the Creation and a short account of world and church history, then covers Gaul. Most of it describes the Merovingian kingdoms of the sixth century, many of whose events Gregory saw himself. It is often the only source for the period. Its lively and sometimes partisan stories have earned Gregory the title "father of French history."

The Life of the Fathers (Liber vitae patrum) is a Latin hagiographical collection by Gregory, bishop of Tours, written in the later decades of the sixth century. It forms part of his eight books of miracles. In twenty chapters it describes holy men, and one woman, of Gaul. They include abbots, hermits and bishops, among them members of Gregory's own family. In the prologue Gregory explains why he uses the singular "Life": the saints had different merits, but they shared one life. The work is an important source for Merovingian religious life.

These are the surviving fragments of a Latin commentary on the Psalms by Gregory of Tours (c. 538–594), the Gallo-Roman bishop and historian. At the end of his Histories, Gregory lists a book of commentary on the Psalter among his writings, but only small parts of it survive. The main fragment explains the psalm headings, such as "In finem", "Pro torcularibus" and "Pro octava". It reads them spiritually as references to Christ's passion and resurrection and to the Church. The fragments show that Gregory also wrote biblical exegesis.

This short Latin hagiographical account, attributed to Gregory of Tours (d. 594), opens with a dedicatory letter to Sulpicius, archbishop of Bourges. In it the writer says that Sulpicius asked him to record the life and death of the Seven Sleepers said to rest at the monastery of Marmoutier near Tours, and that he found an account in that monastery's archives. These Sleepers are a local Touraine legend, distinct from the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, about whom Gregory wrote a separate passio. The attribution to Gregory is doubtful, and the work is generally considered a later composition.

The Vita Sancti Aredii (Life of Saint Aredius) is a Latin hagiography of Aredius (Aridius, Yrieix), a sixth-century abbot in the Limousin who died in 591 and gave his name to Saint-Yrieix-la-Perche. It has traditionally been attributed to Gregory of Tours, who knew Aredius and mentions him in his Histories. Many scholars doubt the attribution, however, and it is uncertain who wrote it. Its prologue says the lives of the saints should be read at their yearly feasts to edify the faithful. It then tells of Aredius's birth, monastic life, miracles and death.

The Libri Miraculorum ("Books of Miracles") are a collection of Latin hagiographical writings by Gregory of Tours, bishop of Tours, written roughly between the 570s and his death in 594. They are usually counted as eight books: the Glory of the Martyrs, the Miracles of St Julian of Brioude, four books on the miracles of St Martin of Tours, the Life of the Fathers, and the Glory of the Confessors. The preface rejects pagan fables in favour of Christian edification. The books are a major source for the cult of saints, relics and religious life in Merovingian Gaul.

The Liber de gloria beatorum confessorum (Glory of the Confessors) is a Latin collection of miracle stories by Gregory of Tours, compiled during his time as bishop of Tours (573–594). It is the last of his eight books of miracles. In short chapters it records wonders linked to confessors, meaning saints who were not martyrs, together with their tombs and relics, mostly in Gaul. The preface opens with Gregory's famous apology for his rustic Latin. The book is a key source for saints' cults and religious life in Merovingian Gaul.

This is the prefatory letter that Gregory, bishop of Tours (d. 594), placed before his four books on the miracles of Saint Martin (De virtutibus sancti Martini). Addressed to the clergy and faithful of the church of Tours, it says that the miracles at Martin's tomb confirm those recorded in the earlier Life of the saint. Gregory explains that recurring dreams moved him to record them. He calls himself unlearned and wishes that Sulpicius Severus, Paulinus or Venantius Fortunatus could have done the task instead.

The Miracles of Saint Martin is a Latin hagiographical work in four books by Gregory of Tours, written over many years between his consecration as bishop of Tours in 573 and his death in 594. It belongs to his collection of miracle books. Gregory begins by naming earlier writers on Martin, notably Sulpicius Severus. He then records healings and other wonders worked at Martin's tomb and through his relics, including cures Gregory said he received himself. The work is an important source for the cult of saints in Merovingian Gaul.

The Prosa de Sancto Martino is a short Latin liturgical piece praising Martin of Tours, followed by a prayer. It survives in a manuscript from the abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris, alongside Gregory of Tours' books on Martin's miracles, which is why it is sometimes attributed to him. The early editor who printed it thought it was more likely taken from old missals. It celebrates Martin's Pannonian birth, his upbringing in Italy, his miracles and his destruction of idols, and asks for his intercession.

The Decretum de Ecclesia Toletana is a royal decree issued by Gundemar, Visigothic king of Hispania from 610 to 612, and addressed to the bishops of the province of Carthaginensis. It complains that some bishops of the province had disregarded canon law and ignored the authority of the metropolitan church. In response it rules that the bishop of Toledo, the royal city, holds primacy over all the churches of the province. It also forbids dividing the province between two metropolitans. The decree is an important witness to the rise of Toledo as the leading see of Visigothic Spain.

This is the collection of surviving Latin writings of Hadoindus (Hadoind), bishop of Le Mans in the seventh century under the Merovingian kings. Its main document is his testament. In it the bishop says that he dictated the will while sound in mind and body, to a deacon who wrote it down. It is dated to the fifth regnal year of King Clovis II, which scholars usually put at 642, and Hadoindus is thought to have died around 653. The testament is accepted as genuine. It is a valuable record of property, church institutions and legal practice in Merovingian Gaul.

This is the collected correspondence of Jerome (c. 342/347–420), arranged in chronological order. It also includes some letters written to him, among them letters from Augustine and Pope Damasus. The letters span roughly 370 to 420. They begin with an early letter to his friend Innocent from Jerome's time in Aquileia, and they follow him through Syria, Rome and Bethlehem. They deal with ascetic life, virginity, biblical interpretation, translation and theological controversy, including the Origenist dispute. Many are addressed to women of Roman ascetic circles. The letters are a major source for Jerome's life and for late fourth-century Christianity.

The Life of Paul the First Hermit (Vita Sancti Pauli Eremitae) is a short Latin saint's life by Jerome. He wrote it around 375–376, probably while living as a hermit in the Syrian desert. Jerome argues that Paul of Thebes, not Antony, was the first Christian hermit. In his story, Paul flees the Decian persecution and lives for decades in an Egyptian desert cave, fed by a raven. Antony visits him and later buries him, and lions dig the grave. Jerome's first saint's life, it strongly shaped medieval monastic devotion, though scholars have questioned whether Paul really existed.

This is Jerome's Latin translation of the treatise On the Holy Spirit by Didymus the Blind of Alexandria, with whom Jerome had studied. Pope Damasus urged him to begin it in Rome, and he finished it in Palestine around 387–390. He dedicated it to his brother Paulinianus. Didymus argues that the Spirit differs in nature from the angels and creatures and shares the divinity of Father and Son, and that the Spirit must be invoked in baptism. The Greek original is lost, so the treatise survives only through Jerome's version.

The Dialogue Against the Luciferians is a Latin polemical dialogue by Jerome. It is one of his early works, usually dated around 379, though some scholars place it a few years later. In it, a follower of Lucifer of Cagliari debates an orthodox Christian. The Luciferians refused communion with bishops who had compromised with Arianism. Against them, Jerome argues that such bishops, especially those who signed the formula of Ariminum in 359, should be received back, and that baptism given by heretics is valid. The work includes his famous remark that the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.

Jerome wrote this Latin polemical treatise in Rome around 383, while Damasus was bishop there. It answers Helvidius, a layman who claimed that the Gospels' references to the "brothers" and "sisters" of the Lord show that Mary had other children with Joseph, and who ranked marriage as equal to virginity. Jerome argues that Mary remained a virgin, that these "brothers" were the Lord's cousins, and that virginity is superior to marriage. Helvidius's own work is lost and is known only through this reply.

Against Jovinianus is a Latin polemical treatise in two books by Jerome, written in 393. It answers Jovinian, a Roman monk condemned at synods in Rome and Milan. Jovinian had taught that virgins are no better than wives, that abstinence is no better than eating with thanksgiving, that the baptized cannot sin, and that all sins and rewards are equal. Book I praises virginity over marriage, and Book II rejects the other claims. Many readers found its attack on marriage excessive, and Jerome defended it in letters to Pammachius. The treatise was later widely quoted in medieval writing against marriage.

Against Vigilantius (Contra Vigilantium) is a short polemical treatise by Jerome, written at Bethlehem in 406. Jerome says he dictated it in a single night. It answers a lost work by Vigilantius, a presbyter from Aquitaine who had once been Jerome's guest. Vigilantius had attacked the veneration of martyrs' relics, vigils at their tombs, clerical celibacy, monasticism and the sending of alms to Jerusalem. Jerome defends these practices in fierce, sarcastic terms, mocking his opponent as "Dormitantius" ("the sleepy one"). The treatise is an important witness to the cult of the saints in the early fifth century.

To Pammachius Against John of Jerusalem is a Latin polemical treatise by Jerome, written in the late 390s during the Origenist controversy. It is addressed to his Roman friend Pammachius. Jerome attacks John II, bishop of Jerusalem, for allegedly sheltering Origenist errors on the resurrection of the body, the soul and related doctrines. He also defends himself and Epiphanius of Salamis in the quarrel over Epiphanius' ordination of Jerome's brother Paulinian. The work is an important source for the controversy in Palestine and for church politics there at the time.

Jerome wrote this polemical Latin treatise at Bethlehem in about 401–402, during the Origenist controversy. Its first two books are addressed to Pammachius and Marcella. They answer Rufinus of Aquileia's Apology, which Jerome knew only from summaries sent to him and from passages his brother Paulinianus had memorized. A third book followed after Rufinus sent a letter in reply. Jerome defends his own orthodoxy and his translations, attacks Rufinus's Latin version of Origen's On First Principles and its preface, and denies any sympathy for Origen's errors. The work marks the bitter end of a long friendship.

The Dialogue Against the Pelagians is a Latin polemical work in three books by Jerome. He wrote it in Bethlehem late in life, around 415 to 417, and it was his last major controversial writing. It takes the form of a debate between Atticus, a Catholic, and Critobulus, who speaks for Pelagius. The work attacks the claim that a person can live without sin by free will alone and defends the necessity of divine grace, drawing heavily on Scripture. It was written while Pelagius was in Palestine, and it set Jerome beside Augustine in the Pelagian controversy.

The Life of Saint Hilarion is a Latin hagiography written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 390. It tells the story of Hilarion, a fourth-century hermit from near Gaza who was a disciple of Antony of Egypt and is regarded as the founder of monastic life in Palestine. It follows his ascetic struggles, miracles and later wanderings, which took him to Egypt, Sicily, Dalmatia and finally Cyprus, where he died. Jerome wrote it to promote the ascetic ideal. Alongside his Lives of Paul and Malchus, it shaped Latin monastic hagiography.

De viris illustribus (On Illustrious Men) is a Latin collection of short biographies and bibliographies of Christian writers. Jerome compiled it at Bethlehem in 392–393 and dedicated it to Nummius Aemilianus Dexter. It has a preface and 135 chapters, running from the apostles to Jerome himself. He modelled it on Suetonius's lives of pagan men of letters, presented it as a defence of Christian learning and took much of the early material from Eusebius. It was continued by Gennadius of Massilia and later by Isidore of Seville, and it is a key source for early Christian literary history.

The Liber de nominibus Hebraicis, also called Liber interpretationis Hebraicorum nominum, is a Latin glossary of the Hebrew proper names in Scripture. Jerome compiled it at Bethlehem around 390. Its preface says Jerome first meant to translate a Greek onomasticon credited to Philo and Origen. He found the copies so confused that he reworked the material instead, going through the biblical books in order and listing the names alphabetically with their meanings. Medieval writers used it widely for allegorical interpretation, and the title Stella Maris for Mary may come from a mistaken reading of one of its entries.

The Onomasticon, more fully On the Place Names in Holy Scripture, is a gazetteer of biblical place names in Palestine and Transjordan. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, compiled it and dedicated it to Paulinus. It is traditionally dated to before 324. The entries are arranged alphabetically and grouped by biblical book. Each gives a site's location and its name in Eusebius's own day. Jerome translated and revised it in Latin as the Liber de situ et nominibus locorum Hebraicorum. It is a key source for the historical geography of Roman Palestine and influenced the Madaba map and early pilgrim accounts.

The Excerpta de aliquot Palaestinae locis is a Latin gazetteer of passages taken from the writings of Jerome (c. 347–420) and arranged alphabetically by place name. It is a later compilation, not a treatise Jerome wrote himself. Its entries come mainly from his biblical commentaries and his Hebrew Questions on Genesis. They identify biblical sites such as Anathoth, Ar, Azotus and Beersheba, giving distances, their current names and Roman administrative details. They draw on Jerome's long residence at Bethlehem and are a useful witness to the geography of late antique Palestine.

The Hebrew Questions on Genesis is a Latin philological commentary by Jerome, written in Bethlehem in the early 390s. It works through selected passages of Genesis and compares the Hebrew text with the Septuagint and the other Greek versions. It explains Hebrew names, place-names and readings, often drawing on Jewish tradition. In the preface Jerome answers his critics, comparing himself with Terence, Virgil and Cicero. He planned it as the start of a larger series that he never finished. The work prepared the way for his translation of the Old Testament from the Hebrew.

The Commentarius in Ecclesiasten is Jerome's Latin commentary on the biblical book of Ecclesiastes, written at Bethlehem around 388 and dedicated to Paula and her daughter Eustochium. In the preface, Jerome says the work grew out of his reading of Ecclesiastes in Rome with Blesilla, Paula's daughter, to encourage her to reject worldly things. Her sudden death had interrupted the project. He gives his own Latin version made from the Hebrew, compares it with the Septuagint and other Greek versions, and draws on Jewish interpretation. The commentary combines literal and spiritual readings and shaped later Latin exegesis of the book.

The Life of Malchus, the Captive Monk is a short Latin hagiography written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 391. Jerome says he heard the story from Malchus himself, an aged monk living at Maronia in Syria. Malchus had left his monastery and was captured by Bedouin raiders. He was enslaved and forced to marry a fellow captive, but the two lived together chastely and finally escaped. The work celebrates chastity and monastic obedience, and it is the only record of Malchus.

Jerome's Latin translation of two homilies by Origen on the Song of Songs, made around 383 in Rome and dedicated to Pope Damasus. In the preface, Jerome says that Origen surpassed himself in his ten-volume commentary on the Song. He set that work aside as too great a task and translated these simpler sermons instead, offering "a taste, not a meal" of Origen's thought. The homilies read the Song as a wedding drama between Christ and the Church or the soul. The Greek original is lost, so this translation is the main witness to the text.

This is Jerome's Latin translation of the monastic rules of Pachomius, founder of communal monasticism in Upper Egypt, together with writings of his successors Theodore and Horsiesius. Jerome made it in 404, soon after the death of his companion Paula. The texts had been sent from Alexandria through the presbyter Silvanus. He worked from a Greek version of the Coptic originals, for Latin-speaking monks in Thebaid monasteries and at Metanoia near Canopus. His version is the main witness to the Pachomian Rule and shaped later Western monastic legislation.

The Instituta form part of the monastic rules of Pachomius (d. 348), founder of communal (cenobitic) monasticism in Upper Egypt. Jerome translated them into Latin at Bethlehem around 404, working from a Greek version of the Coptic originals. These short numbered regulations govern the daily life of the brethren: gathering for prayer and instruction, the duties of the monastery's officers, the care of books, tools and clothing, and correction for negligence. In Jerome's Latin, the Pachomian rules became a significant influence on Western monastic legislation.

The "Precepts and Judgements" is one section of the Rule of Pachomius, the founder of cenobitic monasticism in Upper Egypt. It survives in the Latin translation Jerome made at Bethlehem around 404 from a Greek version of the Coptic original. This section is a penal code for the monastic community. It lists offences such as slander, habitual anger, false accusation and leading simpler brothers astray, and sets graded penalties: repeated warnings, demotion in rank, separation with bread and water, and expulsion. Jerome's version was the main channel through which Pachomian legislation reached Western monasticism.

The Praecepta ac leges is the monastic rule of Pachomius (died 346), founder of communal (cenobitic) monasticism in Upper Egypt. It survives mainly in the Latin translation Jerome made at Bethlehem around 404 from a Greek version, because the Coptic original is largely lost. Its numbered precepts govern prayer gatherings, manual labour such as weaving palm leaves, and discipline and penance. They also set out the authority of each house's superior and his second. The rule shaped later Western monastic legislation.

The Monita S. Pachomii is a short Latin collection of spiritual admonitions for monks, attributed to Pachomius, the founder of communal monasticism in Egypt. It survives with the Latin versions of Pachomian writings that Jerome made in 404 from a Greek translation of Coptic originals. It urges its readers to honour God and stay of one mind in their calling. It also stresses obedience to God's law over one's own will and steadfast faith in times of trouble, citing Scripture throughout. Its exact origin and its place within the Pachomian material are uncertain.

This is a collection of short letters and sayings by Pachomius (d. 346), founder of communal monasticism in Upper Egypt, and his disciple and successor Theodore. They were written in Coptic and survive in a Latin version made by Jerome. He translated them from a Greek intermediary around 404, together with the Pachomian Rule. The letters are addressed to heads of other monasteries, such as Cornelius of Mochansis. They are famous for their obscure "spiritual alphabet", in which Greek letters serve as cryptic signs whose meaning was already unclear to the translator.

This Latin commentary on the Book of Isaiah, in eighteen books, was written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 408–410. He dedicated it to the ascetic Eustochium, fulfilling a promise made to her late mother Paula and her brother-in-law Pammachius. It follows his commentaries on the Twelve Prophets and Daniel. Jerome compares the Hebrew text with the Septuagint and other Greek versions and joins historical with spiritual interpretation. He presents Isaiah as evangelist as well as prophet. The prologue contains his famous saying that ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.

This is a Latin translation of nine homilies by Origen on the Book of Isaiah, traditionally credited to Jerome. When it was made is uncertain, and some scholars have questioned whether Jerome was the translator. Origen's Greek originals are almost entirely lost, so this version is a key witness to his preaching on the prophet. The first homily treats Isaiah's vision in the year King Uzziah died. Origen reads it morally: the sinful "king" ruling in each soul must die before a person can see the glory of God.

Jerome wrote this Latin commentary on the Book of Ezekiel in fourteen books at Bethlehem, roughly between 410 and 414. He dedicated it to the virgin Eustochium. Its preface describes how he had to break off the work at the news of the sack of Rome and the deaths of Pammachius and Marcella. The commentary sets out both the literal and the spiritual sense of the prophet, often comparing the Hebrew text with the Greek versions. Gregory the Great later drew heavily on it for his own homilies on Ezekiel.

This is a Latin commentary in two books on the prophet Micah, written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 392–393. It was one of the first in his series of commentaries on the Minor Prophets and, like others in that series, is dedicated to Paula and her daughter Eustochium. Jerome compares the Hebrew text with the Septuagint, explains Hebrew names (he reads Micah as "humility") and places, and sets a literal-historical reading alongside a spiritual one. In this he draws on Jewish learning and on earlier Greek exegetes, especially Origen.

This is Jerome's Latin commentary in one book on the Old Testament prophet Nahum. He wrote it at Bethlehem around 392–393 as one of the first in his series of commentaries on the twelve Minor Prophets, and he dedicated it to Paula and her daughter Eustochium. Jerome compares the Hebrew text with the Septuagint and with Aquila's version. He explains the prophecy against Nineveh historically, as comfort for Israel under Assyrian oppression. He also reads it figuratively, taking Nineveh, whose name he renders "beautiful", as a figure of the world.

This is a Latin commentary in two books on the prophet Habakkuk by Jerome. He wrote it in Bethlehem around 392–393, as part of his series of commentaries on the Minor Prophets, and dedicated it to Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia. Jerome begins by discussing the prophet's name, which he explains from the Hebrew as "embrace" or "wrestling", and the meaning of the Hebrew term massa ("burden"). He then works through the text verse by verse. He compares the Hebrew with the Septuagint, Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, and gives both historical and spiritual interpretations.

This Latin commentary on the Book of Zephaniah, ninth of the twelve Minor Prophets, is in one book.
