The letters show how bishops in late Roman Gaul kept in touch with one another.

This Latin letter was sent by Magnus Maximus, who seized power as Western Roman emperor in 383, to Pope Siricius around 385–386. Maximus promises to protect the Catholic faith. He undertakes that a synod will examine the case of Agricius, whom Siricius had complained was improperly ordained to the priesthood. He also restates his zeal for orthodoxy and sends the records of proceedings that had recently exposed the alleged crimes of "Manichaeans", meaning the Priscillianists. The letter is evidence for the imperial prosecution of Priscillian and his followers at Trier.

These are two Latin letters by Mappinius (Mapinius), bishop of Reims from about 535 to 550, preserved in the Epistulae Austrasicae collection. In the first, he congratulates Bishop Vilicus of Metz on his seventieth birthday and then asks about the price of pigs around Reims. In the second, he answers Bishop Nicetius of Trier and explains why he did not attend the Council of Toul (c. 549–550). King Theudebald had called the council after Nicetius excommunicated certain Franks for incestuous marriages. The second letter is a valuable source for that council.

The Chronicle of Marcellinus Comes is a Latin chronicle written at Constantinople by an Illyrian courtier. It continues the world chronicle of Eusebius as translated and extended by Jerome. Arranged year by year under indictions and consuls, it covers 379 to 518 and was later extended by the author to 534. An anonymous continuator carried it further. Its focus is the Eastern Empire, including emperors, church controversies, Constantinople and the Balkans. It is a valuable source for the fifth and early sixth centuries and is often cited for treating 476 as the end of the Western Roman Empire.

This letter was written to Pope Julius I by Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra, around 340–341. Marcellus had been deposed by his anti-Nicene opponents and wrote it at Rome, where he had waited more than a year for his accusers to appear. Composed in Greek and preserved by Epiphanius of Salamis, it lists the errors he attributes to the Arians and sets out his own profession of faith. That creed closely matches the Old Roman Creed, which makes the letter an important witness to the early history of the Apostles' Creed.

The Carmen de Sancto Benedicto is a short Latin poem in elegiac couplets praising Benedict of Nursia. It is attributed to Mark, a poet linked with Monte Cassino and traditionally described as Benedict's disciple. It probably dates from the later sixth century, though the date is uncertain. The poem tells how Benedict came to Monte Cassino, destroyed a pagan sanctuary of Jupiter and turned it into a temple of the living God. The poet also asks for Benedict's intercession. Paul the Deacon later quoted from it, and it is an early witness to Benedict's cult.

The Chronicle of Marius, bishop of Aventicum (Avenches) from 574, is a short Latin chronicle written in the late sixth century. It continues the chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine and covers the years 455 to 581. Its entries are brief and arranged by consular years. The chronicle records the fall of the Western emperors, the Burgundian settlement in Gaul, and Gothic, Frankish and Lombard affairs. It is a valuable contemporary source for Burgundy and the wider post-Roman West, especially for the region around Lake Geneva.

The Commonitorium super nomine Caelestii is a memorandum against the Pelagian Caelestius, written by the Latin layman Marius Mercator. He first wrote it in Greek at Constantinople. It was presented to the church there, to many clergy and to Emperor Theodosius II, and Mercator later translated it into Latin himself. The text dates it to the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, 429. It sets out the condemnations already passed on Pelagius and Caelestius. It helped get Caelestius and Julian of Eclanum expelled from Constantinople and condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431.

This Latin collection of passages from the writings of Nestorius, Archbishop of Constantinople, was presented to the bishops at the Council of Ephesus in 431 as evidence against his teaching. It survives in the acts of a session of the council, presided over by Cyril of Alexandria, and is preserved among the works of Marius Mercator, who is generally thought to have translated it from Greek. The excerpts record the Christological statements, especially his objections to the title Theotokos, for which Nestorius was condemned.

This is a Latin dossier of passages from the sermons and treatises of Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople. Marius Mercator translated it from Greek while he was living in Constantinople in the second quarter of the fifth century. The heading says that Cyril of Alexandria chose the chapters. In them Nestorius argues that the Nicene Creed speaks of "one Lord Jesus Christ", not of God the Word being born of the Virgin. Mercator compiled the collection against Nestorianism, and it keeps Nestorius's own words in Latin.

This is a Latin collection of short excerpts from the sermons of Nestorius, archbishop of Constantinople. It is traditionally attributed to Marius Mercator, a Latin writer active in Constantinople between about 429 and 448, during the Nestorian controversy. The third collection gathers passages that Cyril of Alexandria quoted and refuted in his five books Against Nestorius, most of them about whether Mary may be called Theotokos, Mother of God. Mercator's translations helped make the Greek dispute known to Latin readers, and they preserve fragments of Nestorius's otherwise largely lost preaching.

This is a Latin collection of extracts from the sermons and writings of Nestorius, transmitted among the works of Marius Mercator, a Latin writer active in Constantinople during the Nestorian controversy of the 430s and 440s. This fourth collection gathers passages of Nestorius quoted in the works of Cyril of Alexandria. These include Cyril's treatise On the Right Faith addressed to Emperor Theodosius II and his defence of his anathemas against the objections of the Eastern bishops. The extracts show Nestorius distinguishing the divine Word from the man he assumed. Such quotations preserve much of what survives of Nestorius's preaching.

This is a Latin anti-Nestorian dossier by Marius Mercator, a lay supporter of Augustine who was in Constantinople from 429 until about 448. He translated from Greek the twelve anathematisms that Cyril of Alexandria sent to Nestorius in 430, with the backing of Pope Celestine, and set beside each one Nestorius's counter-anathema. To these he added his own short refutations of Nestorius. The work is an important Latin witness to the texts of the Nestorian controversy around the Council of Ephesus (431).

The Liber subnotationum in verba Juliani is a Latin anti-Pelagian treatise by Marius Mercator, a lay supporter of Augustine. Older copies call it the Commonitorium adversus haeresim Pelagii et Caelestii vel etiam scripta Juliani. It was probably written while he lived in Constantinople, between 429 and about 448. Mercator quotes passages from Julian of Eclanum and answers each one with critical notes, defending the doctrine of original sin. The prologue traces the Pelagian error back to Syrian teachers, especially Theodore of Mopsuestia and Rufinus the Syrian.

This is a short Latin preface by Marius Mercator, the African-born lay writer who supported Augustine. It introduces his word-for-word Latin translation of excerpts from Theodore of Mopsuestia, former bishop in Cilicia. It was probably written during Mercator's years in Constantinople after 429. The preface presents Theodore's teaching on the Incarnation as alien to the Catholic faith and as the source of Nestorius's errors. It also aims to discredit the Pelagian Julian of Eclanum. Julian had sought out Theodore and praised him, but Mercator says Theodore's provincial synod later condemned him. The text links the Nestorian and Pelagian controversies.

This is a Latin polemical work by Marius Mercator, a lay supporter of Augustine. It contains his word-for-word translation of a Greek creed attributed to Theodore of Mopsuestia, followed by a refutation. It was probably written in Constantinople, some time after Theodore's death in 428. Mercator wanted to warn Latin readers against Theodore's teaching on the incarnation, which he blamed for misleading Nestorius. He also linked Theodore to Julian of Eclanum and the Pelagian party. The creed's attribution to Theodore was later disputed by Facundus of Hermiane.

This Latin dossier, compiled by Marius Mercator, documents the Nestorian controversy. Mercator translated it from Greek, probably soon after the Council of Ephesus (431), because his preface calls Nestorius "formerly" bishop of Constantinople. It contains thirteen sermons by Nestorius, one by Proclus, letters exchanged between Nestorius and Cyril of Alexandria, and passages Cyril excerpted from Nestorius's writings. Mercator explains that he translated word for word so that Latin readers could see the blasphemies for themselves and understand why the council deposed Nestorius. Some of this material survives only in this translation.

This is a short Latin anti-Manichaean treatise in the form of a letter addressed to Justinus, a Manichaean. It is traditionally attributed to the fourth-century rhetorician and convert Marius Victorinus, though many scholars doubt that he wrote it. Against the Manichaean teaching of two opposed first principles, it argues that all things, including human flesh, come from a single good Creator. It also defends the reality of Christ's flesh. Along the way it refers to Manichaean writings such as the Thesaurus and to apocryphal Acts of Andrew.

De Verbis Scripturae is a short Latin treatise on the words of Genesis about evening, morning and the first day. It is attributed to the fourth-century rhetorician and Christian convert Marius Victorinus, but his authorship is doubted. It replies to a friend who claimed that the whole world must share the same hour, so that day and night fall everywhere at once. The author argues that Scripture, read plainly and correctly, agrees with the fact that hours differ across the inhabited earth. He also criticises over-subtle philosophical disputation.

This Latin theological treatise by Marius Victorinus, the African rhetorician who converted to Christianity late in life, dates from around the late 350s. It answers a letter by Candidus, an Arian who argued that God, being unbegotten, cannot beget. Some think Candidus may be a literary figure Victorinus invented. Using Scripture and Neoplatonic metaphysics, Victorinus defends the eternal generation of the Son. He presents God as beyond being and the Son, the Word, as that being made manifest. It is one of the earliest Latin attempts to explain Nicene theology in philosophical terms.

Adversus Arium (Against Arius) is a Latin theological treatise in four books by Marius Victorinus, the African-born rhetorician and Neoplatonist who became a Christian late in life. It was written around the late 350s or early 360s. Continuing his exchange with Candidus, an Arian correspondent, it sets out the positions of Arius and Eusebius and defends the Nicene teaching that the Son is of the same substance (homoousios) as the Father. Victorinus draws heavily on Neoplatonic philosophy, and the work is among the earliest attempts in Latin to explain the Trinity in philosophical terms.

De homoousio recipiendo ("On Accepting the Homoousion") is a short Latin theological treatise by Marius Victorinus, the African-born rhetorician and Neoplatonist who converted to Christianity in Rome. It was written around 355–365, probably after his longer anti-Arian works. In brief, compact arguments it defends the Nicene term homoousios ("of one substance") against the Arians. It sets the Christian confession of one God, Father and Son, against pagan polytheism and Jewish denial of Christ. It also explains Greek ousia and hypostasis through the Latin substantia, drawing on Scripture.

The Hymns on the Trinity are three Latin hymns by Marius Victorinus, the African-born rhetorician and Neoplatonist who became a Christian in old age in Rome. They are usually dated to around 360, alongside his treatises against the Arians. In rhythmic, prayer-like prose verse, they call on the Father, Son and Holy Spirit and set out the unity of the three in Neoplatonic terms such as being, motion and rest. They are among the earliest Latin Christian hymns and are notable for combining speculative theology with devotion.

This Latin commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Galatians was written by Marius Victorinus, the African-born rhetorician and Neoplatonist who converted to Christianity in Rome around 355. It probably dates from the early 360s. It belongs to his commentaries on Paul's letters, which survive for Galatians, Philippians and Ephesians and are among the earliest Latin commentaries on Paul. Working verse by verse, Victorinus argues that the Galatians erred by adding Jewish observances to the gospel. He stresses that salvation comes through faith in Christ alone, not through works of the law.

This is a Latin commentary on Paul's Letter to the Philippians by Marius Victorinus, the African-born rhetorician and Neoplatonic philosopher who converted to Christianity at Rome around 355. It was written in the early 360s, after his anti-Arian theological treatises. Together with his commentaries on Galatians and Ephesians, it is among the earliest surviving Latin commentaries on the Pauline epistles. The work explains the letter verse by verse, with close attention to Paul's wording and argument. Its beginning is lost, and the surviving text opens at Philippians 1:15.

This is a Latin commentary on Paul's Letter to the Ephesians by Marius Victorinus, the African rhetorician and Neoplatonist philosopher who became a Christian in Rome around 355. It was probably written in the early 360s and is one of his commentaries on the Pauline letters, which are among the earliest surviving Latin commentaries on Paul. Victorinus divides the letter into teaching about Christ, who existed before the world, and moral precepts for Christian life. He reads it as a warning to the Ephesians against false apostles who were mixing Jewish observance with Christian teaching.

The Formula vitae honestae ("Rule for an Honourable Life") is a short Latin moral treatise by Martin of Braga, archbishop in Suebian Gallaecia. He dedicated it to King Miro, who reigned from 570 to 583, and meant it for the king's courtiers and counsellors. It sets out the four cardinal virtues of prudence, magnanimity, continence and justice as rules that lay people can follow by natural reason alone, without the precepts of Scripture. The treatise draws heavily on Seneca. In the Middle Ages it was widely copied, often under Seneca's name.

The Libellus de moribus is a short Latin collection of moral maxims in the Stoic tradition. It was handed down under the name of Martin of Braga, the sixth-century bishop and "Apostle to the Suevi", but it also circulated among the works of Seneca, and its authorship is uncertain. Its terse sentences treat sin as voluntary, the role of upbringing and habit, the control of tongue and appetite, friendship, avarice and readiness for death. Many echo Seneca and Publilius Syrus. It is an example of how classical ethical teaching was passed on to Christian readers.

Pro repellenda iactantia ("On Driving Out Vainglory") is a short Latin moral treatise by Martin of Braga (c. 518–580), the monk and later archbishop in the Suevic kingdom of Gallaecia. It was written in the third quarter of the sixth century. It first surveys vices such as anger, avarice, lust and gluttony, which each overcome only some people. It then argues that vainglory, the empty desire for human praise, is the one vice that attacks everyone, and describes how it wounds the soul. It belongs to a small group of Martin's ascetic writings on pride and humility.

De superbia ("On Pride") is a short Latin moral treatise by Martin of Braga (c. 518–580), the monastic founder, bishop of Dumium and later archbishop of Braga, known as the "Apostle to the Suevi". It was written in Suevic Gallaecia in the third quarter of the sixth century. Addressed to an unnamed "dearest" reader, it starts from David's prayer in Psalm 35, "Let not the foot of pride come against me." It explains vainglory, the delight in human praise, as the beginning of pride. It belongs with Martin's related writings against boasting and in praise of humility.

The Exhortatio humilitatis (Exhortation to Humility) is a short Latin moral treatise by Martin of Braga, the sixth-century bishop and missionary among the Suevi of Gallaecia. It was written between about 556 and 580, and some manuscripts wrongly attribute it to Isidore of Seville. It is addressed to someone who holds authority over others. In a deliberately plain style, it warns against flattery and pride and urges rulers to prefer useful truth to pleasing words. The treatise belongs to Martin's group of short moral writings influenced by Seneca.

De ira (On Anger) is a short Latin moral treatise by Martin of Braga (c. 518–580), the monastic founder and archbishop who worked among the Suevi of Gallaecia. It was written sometime between about 556 and 580 for his fellow bishop Vitimir, who had asked for a brief work on the passion of anger. The treatise depicts how anger shows in the body, sets out its harmful effects, and advises how to avoid or soften it. It draws heavily on Seneca's De ira and is one example of how Martin adapted classical Stoic ethics for Christian readers.

De Pascha is a short Latin treatise on the date of Easter, attributed to Martin of Braga (d. 580), bishop and monastic founder among the Sueves of Gallaecia. It answers people who asked why Christians follow a Jewish-style lunar reckoning instead of keeping a fixed anniversary such as 25 March. Some Gallic bishops had observed that date until recently. Drawing on Exodus 12, the work links Easter to the date of the world's creation. It explains that Easter must fall on a Sunday between the fourteenth and twenty-first day of the moon, and between 22 March and 21 April.

The work consists of two short Latin verse inscriptions by Martin of Braga, the sixth-century "Apostle to the Suevi" in Gallaecia. The first, written for a basilica, praises Martin of Tours as the patron whose miracles drew many peoples to Christ. It describes how the Suevi, moved by his merits, built the church in his honour, and it asks him to be patron of Gallaecia as he is of Gaul. The second, for a refectory, contrasts a humble monastic table with luxurious banquets and asks grace to supply what the meal lacks.

This short Latin verse epitaph is attributed to Martin of Braga (c. 518–580), and he probably wrote it for his own tomb. In a few hexameters the speaker recalls being born in Pannonia, crossing wide seas and being brought to Gallaecia by divine will. He addresses Martin of Tours, the confessor to whom the church is dedicated. He says that he set up its worship and rites, and that he rests there in Christ's peace, sharing his patron's name but not his merit. The poem gives a rare first-person outline of Martin's life.

This short Latin profession of faith in the Trinity is attributed to Martin of Tours, bishop of Tours from 371 until his death in 397. The attribution is doubtful, and the piece is usually regarded as of uncertain authorship. It affirms one divinity in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each dwelling in the others. It stresses that the divine mystery cannot be grasped by the human mind or expressed in words. It then quotes Psalm 115, "I believed, therefore I have spoken," and presents this simple confession as the foundation of the Church.

This is a collection of Latin homilies attributed to Maximus, the first known bishop of Turin, who preached in the first half of the fifth century. The homilies are grouped into four classes. The first covers the liturgical seasons, beginning with Advent and Christmas, and later classes treat saints' feasts and other subjects. These short, vivid sermons are an important witness to preaching, liturgy and the Christianization of northern Italy. Authorship of individual pieces has long been debated. Some were also handed down under the name of Ambrose, and modern scholarship regards several as not by Maximus.

This is a collection of Latin sermons attributed to Maximus, the first known bishop of Turin, who preached in the late fourth and early fifth centuries. In this traditional arrangement the sermons are grouped in three classes: sermons for the seasons and feasts of the liturgical year, beginning with Advent and Christmas; sermons on saints and martyrs; and sermons on various subjects. The short, vivid pieces were preached to the people of Turin. They are an important witness to early Christianity in northern Italy, though some sermons once credited to Maximus are now judged spurious.

This is a supplementary group of Latin sermons associated with Maximus, the first known bishop of Turin, who preached in northern Italy in the late fourth and early fifth centuries. It includes two Pentecost sermons, found late and printed as the seventh and eighth on that feast. Their source is an ancient manuscript from the monastery of Saint Dalmatius, and a Turin codex supports them. The group also lists the openings and endings of further sermons that manuscripts attribute to Maximus. Their style differs so sharply from his authentic preaching that they are generally considered spurious.

The Tractatus are Latin treatises on baptism traditionally attributed to Maximus, the first known bishop of Turin, who was active in the early fifth century. Their authenticity has been questioned. The first treatise is mystagogical preaching. It is addressed only to the newly baptized and the faithful after the catechumens have been dismissed. It explains the meaning of the rites they had already received in silence, beginning with the anointing of the ears with blessed oil. The treatises are evidence for baptismal practice and catechesis in late antique northern Italy.

The Expositiones de capitulis Evangeliorum is a series of short Latin expositions of selected Gospel passages, attributed to Maximus, first bishop of Turin, who was active in the early fifth century. Gennadius of Marseilles records that Maximus wrote wisely on chapters of the Gospels and of the Acts of the Apostles. Its editors linked the surviving text to that report because its themes resemble those of his sermons, it uses the Old Latin Bible, and it explains Scripture in both literal and mystical senses. The attribution is uncertain, and the work received little notice after antiquity.

Carmen de Christo is a short Latin poem of about thirty hexameters addressed to Christ. One manuscript attributes it to Flavius Merobaudes, the fifth-century rhetorician and court poet of Valentinian III and Aetius; another gives it to Claudian. The authorship is therefore disputed, although several scholars have defended Merobaudes. The poem praises the eternal Son, begotten before all ages, who took flesh from a virgin. It goes on to recall the Magi, Christ's descent among the dead, his resurrection and ascension, and the Trinity, "one and simple in threefold light."

The Sententia de Caeciliani causa is the final judgment given by Miltiades, bishop of Rome, at the Lateran synod held in October 313 in the house of the empress Fausta. The synod of nineteen Gallic and Italian bishops examined the dispute between Caecilian of Carthage and Donatus. Miltiades declared Caecilian innocent and kept him in communion. Donatus of Casae Nigrae was condemned for rebaptizing and for laying hands on lapsed bishops. Preserved by Optatus of Milevis and praised by Augustine, it marks an early stage of the Donatist controversy.

The Judicium de Donatistis is the Latin record of the verdict reached by the Roman synod that Pope Miltiades held at the Lateran in October 313. Emperor Constantine had called the synod to settle the disputed election of Caecilian as bishop of Carthage. The bishops cleared Caecilian and condemned Donatus of Casae Nigrae, although they took a moderate line towards the clergy who had followed him. The account survives mainly through Optatus and Augustine. The Donatists rejected the verdict and appealed to Constantine, who then summoned the Council of Arles in 314.

This short Latin critical study looks at the decrees attributed to Miltiades (Melchiades), bishop of Rome from 311 to 314. It is not by the pope himself but by a later editor. It sets aside two letters forged under his name in the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals. It then examines the Liber Pontificalis decree banning fasting on Sunday and Thursday. Citing Tertullian and the Apostolic Constitutions, it argues that this ascription is false and that the Sunday fast was banned earlier, partly in reaction to Manichaean practice.

The Epistolae are two Latin letters by Montanus, metropolitan bishop of Toledo, who presided over the Second Council of Toledo (527 or 531). The first, addressed to the clergy and faithful of the territory of Palencia, rebukes presbyters who had dared to consecrate chrism, a rite reserved to bishops, and claims metropolitan authority for Toledo. The second, to the monk Turibius, praises his efforts against Priscillianism. The letters are an important witness to church order and the rise of Toledo's primacy in Visigothic Spain.

A Latin panegyric delivered in 321 by Nazarius, a rhetorician whom Ausonius names as a teacher of rhetoric at Bordeaux. Nazarius gave the speech on 1 March, while Constantine was away. It marked the fifth anniversary of the Caesars Crispus and Constantine II and the fifteenth year of Constantine the Great's reign. The speech praises the young Caesars, including Crispus's victories over the Franks, and celebrates Constantine's achievements, above all his defeat of Maxentius. It survives among the Panegyrici Latini and is an important witness to Constantinian imperial ideology.

These are three letters by Nestorius, Archbishop of Constantinople (428–431). The Greek originals were lost, and the letters survive in a Latin translation by Marius Mercator, a lay polemicist who wrote against both Pelagianism and Nestorius. The first, to Pope Celestine I, probably dates from about 429. It asks about Pelagian bishops, including Julian of Eclanum, who had taken refuge in Constantinople, and defends Nestorius's objection to calling Mary Theotokos. These letters are important evidence of how the Nestorian controversy began, in the years before the Council of Ephesus in 431.

This is preaching against the Pelagian teaching of Pelagius and Caelestius, attributed to Nestorius, archbishop of Constantinople from 428 to 431. It was delivered while Caelestius and other exiled Pelagians were seeking support in the capital. The Greek original is lost. The text survives in the Latin translation of Marius Mercator, a lay opponent of both Pelagianism and Nestorius, who used it to set Nestorius's orthodox statements on original sin and grace against his Christology. The work sheds light on how the Pelagian and Nestorian controversies were linked in the years before the Council of Ephesus.

This is a small appendix of two medieval Latin documents from the cathedral chapter of Aquileia, one from the twelfth century and one from the thirteenth. They are not writings of Nicetas of Remesiana. They were printed with an early modern dissertation on Nicetas, at a time when he was often confused with Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia. The first document, dated 1183, records the dean and canons of Aquileia promising before the pope to defend the chapter's common life against the provost Gabriel. They accuse him of taking control of its administration in breach of earlier privileges.

De Ratione Fidei (On the Rule of Faith) is a short Latin treatise by Nicetas, bishop of Remesiana in Dacia (d. c. 414), written in the late fourth or early fifth century. It is generally thought to belong to his catechetical instructions for candidates preparing for baptism. Citing Paul's warnings against foolish questions, it criticizes those who try to measure God and argue about the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Against Arian teaching, it defends the full divinity of the Son and the unity of the Trinity. Its biblical quotations follow an Old Latin version that predates the Vulgate.

De Spiritus Sancti Potentia (On the Power of the Holy Spirit) is a short Latin treatise by Nicetas, bishop of Remesiana in Dacia (c. 335–414). It belongs to his series of instructional books for candidates preparing for baptism. Nicetas notes that the Nicene Creed simply said "We believe in the Holy Spirit." Against the Macedonians, who taught that the Spirit was a creature and a servant, he draws on Scripture to argue that the Spirit shares divine honour with the Father and the Son. It is a witness to late fourth-century pneumatology in the Latin West.

On the Various Names Fitting Our Lord Jesus Christ is a short Latin treatise by Nicetas, bishop of Remesiana in Dacia (c. 335–414). It cannot be dated precisely. It lists the titles given to Christ in Scripture, among them Word, Wisdom, Light, Power, Right Hand, Angel of Great Counsel, Lamb, Priest, Way, Truth, Life, Vine, Bread, Stone, Physician, Fountain, Judge and Door. It then explains briefly what each name reveals about the one Son of God and his saving work. It is often linked to Nicetas's instructional writings for candidates preparing for baptism.

The Explanatio Symboli is a short Latin catechetical treatise by Nicetas, bishop of Remesiana in Dacia (died c. 414), written for the competentes, catechumens preparing for baptism. It belonged to his larger series of instructional books for baptismal candidates. Starting from the renunciation of Satan and his works, it explains the baptismal creed article by article, from belief in God the Father almighty to the resurrection and eternal life. It is valued as evidence for the Balkan creed of its time, and it contains one of the earliest known uses of the phrase "communion of saints".

The Six Fragments are short Latin excerpts from the instructions for baptismal candidates (competentes) written by Nicetas, bishop of Remesiana in Dacia Mediterranea, in the late fourth or early fifth century. They are quoted as coming from his first book addressed to the competentes. They explain the catechumen's position as a "guest and neighbour" of the faithful and require a sincere renunciation of the devil before confession of faith. They also condemn idolatry, divination, the theatre, vice and vain adornment. These excerpts give evidence for how candidates were prepared for baptism in the Latin Balkans.

These are two Latin letters by Nicetius, bishop of Trier (died c. 566), written in the 560s. The first is addressed to Chlodosuinda, a Frankish princess married to the Lombard king Alboin. Nicetius praises her piety and urges her to win her husband from Arianism to Catholic belief in the Trinity, citing Scripture against the Arian teaching. The second, to Emperor Justinian, rebukes him for doctrinal error in his final years. Both letters show how a Frankish bishop dealt with rulers in matters of doctrine.

The Opuscula are two short Latin treatises, On the Vigils of the Servants of God (De vigiliis servorum Dei) and On the Value of Psalmody (De psalmodiae bono). They were once printed under the name of Nicetius, the sixth-century bishop of Trier. Modern scholars generally assign them to Niceta of Remesiana, who wrote around 400. The first treatise defends the practice of night vigils against critics and praises them as a time for prayer, hymns and readings. The second commends singing psalms and hymns in church worship.

This Latin letter was sent in 250 by the presbyters and deacons of Rome to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. It was written while the Roman see was vacant after the martyrdom of Pope Fabian, during the Decian persecution. Cyprian later says that Novatian drafted it, and it survives as Letter 30 in Cyprian's correspondence. The letter backs Cyprian's strict line on the lapsed, condemning the libellatici and harmful leniency. It says reconciliation must wait for peace and a new bishop.

De Trinitate is a Latin theological treatise by Novatian, a Roman presbyter who later led a rigorist schism and was considered an antipope. It is usually dated to about 240–250, before his break with Pope Cornelius in 251. In thirty-one chapters it follows the rule of faith, treating in turn God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Against the Monarchians and docetists, it argues that Christ is truly God and truly human and distinct from the Father. It draws heavily on Tertullian and is one of the earliest major works of Latin theology written in Rome.

On the Jewish Meats is a Latin pastoral letter by Novatian, the Roman presbyter and later rival bishop of Rome. He wrote it to his community while away from them, probably in the 250s. It follows two earlier letters against the Jews on circumcision and the Sabbath, which are now lost. Novatian argues that the Mosaic food laws taught moral lessons through symbols, and that in Christ all foods are clean. He still warns Christians against gluttony and against eating food offered to idols.

This short Latin sermon on humility, obedience and the overcoming of pride is ascribed to an author called Novatus Catholicus. His identity and date are uncertain, though he is usually placed in late antique Latin Christianity. The sermon speaks to a monastic community dressed in mourning garments and contrasts it with lay hearers. It teaches that the enemy within, the flesh warring against the spirit, is defeated only by humility and charity. Its model is Christ, who humbled himself out of love. Each brother is urged to count the others as his superiors.

The Commonitorium is a short Latin memorandum that the Spanish priest Paulus Orosius addressed to Augustine of Hippo, generally dated to about 414, soon after he arrived in Africa from the Iberian Peninsula. It sets out the errors then troubling the Spanish churches: the teachings of the Priscillianists and certain Origenist doctrines, such as the pre-existence of souls and the restoration of all things. Orosius asks Augustine to refute them. It is an important witness to Priscillianism, and it led Augustine to write his reply, Ad Orosium contra Priscillianistas et Origenistas.

The Commonitorium is a short Latin memorandum that the Spanish priest Paulus Orosius addressed to Augustine of Hippo, generally dated to about 414, soon after he arrived in Africa from the Iberian Peninsula. It sets out the errors then troubling the Spanish churches: the teachings of the Priscillianists and certain Origenist doctrines, such as the pre-existence of souls and the restoration of all things. Orosius asks Augustine to refute them. It is an important witness to Priscillianism, and it led Augustine to write his reply, Ad Orosium contra Priscillianistas et Origenistas.

The canons of the Council of Serdica (modern Sofia), held around 343, survive in Latin and Greek versions; which came first is disputed. Most of them take the form of proposals made by Ossius (Hosius), bishop of Corduba, who presided. The other bishops approved each one with "placet". The canons forbid bishops to move from one see to another, restrict their travel to other provinces and regulate how they deal with the imperial court. They are best known for allowing a deposed bishop to appeal to the bishop of Rome, which later shaped Western canon law.

Hosius (Ossius) of Corduba, the aged bishop who had probably presided at Nicaea and presided at Serdica, wrote this letter to Emperor Constantius II around 355–356. Recalling that he had confessed the faith under Maximian's persecution, he refuses to condemn Athanasius and urges the emperor to stop supporting the Arians and their allies Ursacius and Valens. He also warns him not to interfere in church affairs. The letter is a forthright statement of episcopal independence from imperial power and survives only in Athanasius' History of the Arians.

The Panegyricus Theodosio Augusto dictus is a Latin speech of praise by the Gallic rhetor Latinius Pacatus Drepanius. He delivered it before Emperor Theodosius I and the Senate in Rome in 389. The speech recounts Theodosius' origins in Hispania, his early career and his rise to the throne. Its main subject is his victory in 388 over the usurper Magnus Maximus, which it presents as a liberation of Gaul and the West. It is part of the collection known as the Panegyrici Latini. It is an important source for the history and court rhetoric of the late fourth century.

The Rule of Pachomius is a monastic legislation attributed to Pachomius (c. 287–348), the Egyptian founder of cenobitic monasticism at Tabennisi. It was written in Coptic and survives mainly through this Latin version, which Jerome made in 404 from a Greek translation. Jerome's preface is followed by precepts governing communal prayer, work, meals, clothing, obedience and discipline in the Pachomian monasteries. Early modern editors printed it as an appendix to the works of John Cassian, because Cassian describes the Tabennesiote monks. It shaped later Western monastic rules.

The Letters to Sympronian are three Latin letters by Pacian, bishop of Barcelona, written in the second half of the fourth century to Sympronian, a follower of the rigorist Novatianist movement. Pacian defends the name "Catholic" and the Church's power to forgive grave sins committed after baptism through penance and episcopal absolution, both of which the Novatianists denied. The first letter contains the famous phrase "Christian is my name, Catholic my surname." The letters are important evidence for the controversy over penance and for the church in Roman Hispania.

The Paraenesis, or Exhortation to Penance, is a short Latin treatise in the form of a sermon. It was written in the later fourth century by Pacian, bishop of Barcelona. It is addressed to his congregation and calls sinners to undergo the Church's public penance. It distinguishes the gravest sins, namely idolatry, murder and adultery, from lesser faults. It also rebukes those who hide their sins or avoid the humiliation of penance. The opening recalls his lost work the Cervus. The Paraenesis is an important witness to penitential discipline in the early Western Church.

The Sermo de Baptismo is a short Latin sermon by Pacian, bishop of Barcelona in the later fourth century. It was probably composed between about 360 and 390. It is addressed to the competentes, catechumens preparing for baptism, and explains how believers are reborn and renewed in the sacrament. Pacian describes humanity's subjection to sin and death through Adam and to evil powers before faith. He then sets out how Christ frees people from that bondage through faith and baptism. It is a valuable witness to baptismal teaching and catechesis in the early Spanish church.

De Spiritu Sancto is a Latin treatise in two books on the divinity of the Holy Spirit. It was long transmitted under the name of Paschasius, a Roman deacon who died around 512, but many scholars now attribute it to Faustus of Riez, the fifth-century bishop in southern Gaul. Taking the Creed as its starting point, it defends the Spirit's full deity and his equality within the Trinity, drawing on Scripture. It is also known for distinguishing belief "in" God from believing the Church, which it holds should be confessed without the preposition "in".

This short Latin letter was written by Paschasius, a deacon of the Roman church, to the priest Eugippius in the early sixth century, probably around 511. Eugippius had sent him his memoir of Severinus, the holy man who worked in the frontier provinces of Noricum and Pannonia, and asked him to rewrite it as a polished Life. Paschasius declined. He praised the simple, accurate account of a disciple who had witnessed what he described, and argued that the deeds of saints serve as models for the faithful. The letter is transmitted with Eugippius's Life of Severinus.

This Latin anthology of biblical exegesis was compiled by Paterius, a notary of Pope Gregory I who later became bishop of Brescia and died in 606. It is also known as the Liber testimoniorum. Paterius collected Gregory's explanations of passages from the Old and New Testaments, drawn mainly from the Moralia on Job, and arranged them in biblical order. As his preface explains, Gregory's commentary on Job had touched on nearly the whole of Scripture. The anthology was widely copied and helped spread Gregory's exegesis through the medieval West.

The Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus is a Latin open letter written by Patrick, the fifth-century British-born bishop in Ireland. Its exact date is uncertain. Soldiers of the British ruler Coroticus had killed some newly baptized Irish converts and carried others off as captives. They then mocked a priest Patrick sent to ask for the captives' release. Patrick denounces them as allies of the apostate Picts and Scots, cuts them off from Christian fellowship and calls for the captives' return. With the Confessio, it is one of only two writings generally accepted as Patrick's own.

The Synodus is a short Latin collection of church canons attributed to Saint Patrick and usually called the Second Synod of Saint Patrick. Each chapter answers a disciplinary question with scriptural citations. Topics include dealing with sinful brethren, refusing offerings from the wicked, penance after a fall, excommunication, suspected cases, church penalties and related matters of monastic and clerical life. Patrick's authorship is generally rejected. Scholars usually date the text to the seventh century or later, in Ireland, and value it as evidence for early Irish canon law and penitential practice.

This is a short Latin collection of church canons attributed to Saint Patrick, the fifth-century missionary bishop of Ireland. Its numbered rulings cover the church's authority to judge its own cases, respect for rulers, penance for clergy who sin and for adultery, deathbed repentance, and sending disputed questions "in this island" to the apostolic see. Scholars generally doubt that Patrick wrote it. It is usually seen as a later Irish compilation, and it is valuable evidence for early Irish church discipline and penitential practice.

The Synod of the Bishops Patrick, Auxilius and Iserninus, often called the First Synod of Saint Patrick, is a short collection of Latin canons for the church in Ireland. It opens as a letter from the three bishops to the priests, deacons and clergy. Its rulings cover church discipline: wandering clergy, Roman tonsure and dress, attendance at prayer, dealings with pagans, ransoming captives, and the conduct of monks and virgins. Scholars dispute whether it dates from Patrick's lifetime in the fifth century or was compiled later, perhaps in the sixth.

This is a short Latin collection of canons attributed to Saint Patrick, the fifth-century apostle of Ireland, though the attribution is doubtful and the canons probably come from later Irish church tradition. The canons cover the unity of the faithful, illustrated by the common life of the Jerusalem church and the fate of Ananias in Acts; the punishment of theft from churches holding the relics of martyrs and saints; and Paul's rules about true widows. Two more canons follow, on not putting away a wife. Their authorship is uncertain, and one is elsewhere assigned to an Irish synod.

The Proverbia Aliqua ("Some Proverbs") are a short Latin collection of sayings attributed to Saint Patrick, the fifth-century missionary bishop of Ireland. Most of the sayings address the judges of the Church. They warn them to fear God rather than men, to refuse gifts, to show no favouritism, not to judge in haste and not to lie, and they support each point with biblical quotations. Scholars doubt that Patrick wrote them. They are usually placed with the later Irish canonical tradition rather than with his genuine writings, the Confessio and the Letter to Coroticus.

The Charta S. Patricii is a short Latin charter written in the voice of Saint Patrick, the fifth-century apostle of Ireland. In it, Patrick says that after converting the Irish he returned to Britain and came to the island of Ynyswitrin (Glastonbury). There he found an ancient church of the Virgin Mary and a community of hermits descended from the disciples of Saints Phagan and Deruvian, and he lists their names. The charter is generally regarded as a medieval forgery from Glastonbury, not a genuine work of Patrick. It was meant to support the abbey's claims to great antiquity.

The Confessio is a Latin autobiographical work by Patrick, the fifth-century Romano-British bishop and missionary in Ireland. Its exact date is uncertain. Patrick tells how Irish raiders captured him at about sixteen, how he converted while a slave, how he escaped, and how he later returned to Ireland to preach. He wrote it partly to defend himself against accusations, and he gives thanks for God's grace throughout. It is one of only two writings generally accepted as Patrick's own, alongside the Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus, and it is the main evidence for his life.

The Liber exhortationis, also called De salutaribus documentis, is a Latin treatise of moral and spiritual instruction by Paulinus II, Patriarch of Aquileia, a leading scholar of the Carolingian court. He wrote it in the later 790s for Eric, Duke of Friuli, a layman. Addressed to a "dearest brother", it opens with love of God as the highest justice and happiness. It goes on to treat humanity's creation in the image of the Trinity, the virtues and vices, and penance. It draws heavily on earlier patristic writers and is an early example of Carolingian guidance for lay nobles.

This short Latin petition is addressed to Pope Zosimus by Paulinus, deacon of Milan and biographer of Ambrose. Paulinus had accused Caelestius, Pelagius's disciple, before a synod at Carthage in 411. When Zosimus reopened the case in 417, Paulinus sent this document, usually dated to late 417 or 418. In it he asks the pope to uphold Innocent I's condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius and recalls Zosimus's own demand that Caelestius condemn the charges against him. It is an important document of the Pelagian controversy in Rome.

De Benedictionibus Patriarcharum is a short Latin exegetical treatise attributed to Paulinus of Milan, the deacon, notary and biographer of Ambrose. It is usually dated to the early fifth century. It comments on Jacob's prophetic blessings of his twelve sons in Genesis 49. The author first sets out the literal and historical sense of each blessing, then turns to the spiritual or allegorical meaning wherever the letter alone cannot explain the text. He argues that neither sense should cancel out the other. The work was once transmitted among writings attributed to Jerome.

This is a short Latin letter by Paulinus of Périgueux, a Gallic poet, to Perpetuus, bishop of Tours. It is usually dated to the 460s or 470s. Paulinus thanks the bishop for encouraging him to write and says he has sent verses through a deacon, as Perpetuus asked, to be inscribed on the consecrated walls of the church at Tours. He also recalls how his grandson was healed by a document listing Saint Martin's miracles that Perpetuus had signed. The letter sheds light on the cult of Martin and on Paulinus's verse Life of Saint Martin.

This short Latin poem in hexameters is by Paulinus of Périgueux, the Gallic poet who wrote a six-book verse Life of Saint Martin in the later fifth century. In it Paulinus thanks Saint Martin for healing his young grandson and the grandson's bride, who had both fallen gravely ill. The cure followed the use of a written record of Martin's miracles sent by Perpetuus, bishop of Tours. The poem is evidence for the cult of Martin at Tours and for the healing power believed to reside in such writings.

The Vita S. Gregorii Magni is a Latin hagiographical life of Pope Gregory I (Gregory the Great, pope 590–604). It is attributed to Paul the Deacon, the Lombard monk and historian of Monte Cassino, and was written in the late eighth century. The work relies heavily on Bede's Ecclesiastical History. It describes Gregory's noble Roman family, his education, his turn to monastic life, and his career and virtues as pope. It is one of the earliest full Latin biographies of Gregory and came before John the Deacon's longer ninth-century Life.

The Lives of the Fathers of Mérida is a Latin hagiographical collection from Visigothic Spain, probably written in the 630s. Tradition attributes it to Paul, a deacon of Mérida, but the author may have been anonymous. Its model is Gregory the Great's Dialogues. It tells of miracles linked to the shrine of Saint Eulalia and of the city's sixth-century bishops, including Paul, Fidelis, Masona and Renovatus. It is a key source for Mérida's church, its wealth and charity, and the conflict between Arians and Catholics under King Leovigild.

The Regula ad monachos, usually called the Rule of Paul and Stephen (Regula Pauli et Stephani), is a short Latin monastic rule attributed to two abbots, Paul and Stephen. Nothing else is known about them. It is generally dated to the sixth century, roughly between 520 and 580, and was probably written in Italy. In a series of brief chapters it regulates the common life of a monastery: mutual charity between elders and juniors, discipline and attention in choral psalmody, sleep, meals, reading at table, kitchen service, and the care of shared property.

The Epistolae are the Latin letters of Pope Pelagius I, written during his pontificate (556–561). Justinian I had backed his election, and Pelagius had come to accept the emperor's condemnation of the Three Chapters. As a result, many Western churches would not recognise him, and he faced schism in Italy. Several letters are addressed to the general Narses, urging him to use secular power against bishops who disturbed church unity. Others deal with discipline, church property and his own orthodoxy. The collection is an important source for the papacy after the Gothic War.

The Epistolae et decreta are the collected Latin letters and decrees of Pope Pelagius II, bishop of Rome from 579 to 590. The collection opens with a letter to the deacon Gregory, the future Gregory the Great, then papal representative at Constantinople. In it Pelagius asks him to press the emperor for military help against the Lombards, who were threatening Rome. Other letters deal with the schism over the Three Chapters among the bishops of Istria and northern Italy. Some pieces traditionally ascribed to Pelagius, including items in the forged Pseudo-Isidorian decretals, are not authentic.

This is a Latin commentary on the letters of Paul that was long handed down under the name of Jerome and printed among his works. Its core is the brief exposition of the Pauline epistles that Pelagius wrote in Rome around 405–410, but it survives here in a reworked and interpolated form. A spurious preface addressed to Heliodorus presents it as the work of an aging Jerome. Its concise verse-by-verse notes stress moral effort and human freedom. Because it circulated under Jerome's name, Pelagius's exegesis was read widely in the medieval West.

The Testamentum is a Latin will attributed to Perpetuus, bishop of Tours from about 460 to 490. Speaking as a "sinner" and priest of the church of Tours, the testator wishes peace to his clergy and asks to be buried at the feet of Saint Martin. He frees slaves he bought and leaves estates, goods and money to his church, to the poor and to others. It is traditionally dated to the late fifth century, but its authenticity has been seriously questioned, and many scholars regard it as a later forgery.

The Sermones are the Latin sermons preached by Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna from about 433 until about 450. The surviving collection, put together by a later bishop of Ravenna, Felix, in the early eighth century, contains about 176 sermons. They are short, carefully crafted homilies, mostly explaining Gospel passages such as the parable of the prodigal son. Others deal with the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, the Incarnation, Lent and fasting. Their concise style and doctrinal clarity earned Peter his epithet "Chrysologus" ("golden-worded"), and he is known as the "Doctor of Homilies".

The Sermo de translatione S. Hilarii is a Latin festal sermon attributed to Peter Damian, the eleventh-century Italian reforming monk and cardinal. It was written to be preached on the feast of the translation of Hilary of Poitiers, that is, the moving of his relics. Most of the sermon tells how the saint appeared in a vision to Fridolin, abbot of Saint-Hilaire outside Poitiers. Hilary told him to seek funds from the Frankish king to rebuild the monastery and to prepare a fitting place for his body. Some sermons transmitted under Peter Damian's name are of doubtful authorship.

This Latin doctrinal letter was written around 519–520 by Peter the Deacon, John, Leontius, another John and other Scythian monks who had travelled to Rome on a matter of faith. They addressed it to the African bishops exiled in Sardinia, including Fulgentius of Ruspe. The monks set out their teaching on the incarnation, namely two natures united in the one person of Christ, and on grace, which they defended against Pelagian views. They asked the bishops to approve it. Fulgentius and his colleagues replied with a letter that agreed with them.

The Liber contra Arianos is a short Latin polemical treatise by Phoebadius, bishop of Agen in Gaul (died c. 392), a firm supporter of Nicene orthodoxy. It was written around 357–358 in response to the creed issued at Sirmium in 357, which banned the term "substance" (ousia) in speaking of the Father and the Son. Phoebadius argues that the creed's apparently simple language concealed Arian subordinationism. The work is one of the earliest Western responses to that creed, and Jerome mentions it.

The Libellus Fidei is a short Latin profession of faith from the late fourth century. It has been handed down under the name of Phoebadius, bishop of Agen, who died around 392 and defended Nicene orthodoxy, though the attribution is doubtful. In creedal form it confesses one God in Father, Son and Holy Spirit, while rejecting both belief in three gods and Sabellian confusion of the persons. It declares the Son "God from God, light from light", of one substance with the Father, and the Spirit coeternal with both. It is a witness to Western anti-Arian Trinitarian teaching.

This annotated Julian calendar, also called a laterculus or fasti, was compiled around 448–449 by Polemius Silvius, a writer active in southeastern Gaul. It goes through the year month by month, giving each month's name among the Hebrews, Egyptians and Athenians. It notes the Kalends, Nones and Ides, along with games, circus races, imperial birthdays, senate sessions and weather signs. Alongside these it records Christian feasts such as Epiphany and martyrs' days. The calendar is valuable evidence of how the traditional Roman festival cycle was combined with the Christian liturgical year in late antique Gaul.

This is a Latin letter to Emperor Justinian I by Pontianus, a sixth-century bishop in North Africa whose see is unknown. It was written around 544–545 during the Three Chapters controversy, in reply to the emperor's request that African bishops condemn Theodore of Mopsuestia, the writings of Theodoret and the letter of Ibas. Pontianus says he has never seen the condemned texts. He argues that men already dead should not be condemned, and he warns that their condemnation could revive Eutychianism and weaken the Council of Chalcedon. The letter is an early record of Western resistance to Justinian's policy.

The Life and Passion of Cyprian is a Latin hagiographical account of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, who was martyred in 258. It is attributed to Pontius, a deacon who served under Cyprian and accompanied him into exile. He wrote it shortly after Cyprian's death. It covers Cyprian's conversion, his time as bishop, his work during the plague at Carthage, his exile to Curubis and his execution under Valerian. It is often regarded as the earliest surviving Christian biography in Latin, and it praises its subject in a rhetorical style.

These are two Latin sermons by Potamius, the first recorded bishop of Lisbon, probably written in the mid-fourth century, though their exact date is uncertain. The first is about Christ raising Lazarus from the dead (John 11) and dwells vividly on the decay of the buried body. The second tells of the martyrdom of the prophet Isaiah, who according to tradition was sawn in two. Some manuscripts pass them down alongside the sermons of Zeno of Verona. Their elaborate, often obscure rhetorical style makes them among the earliest surviving Christian prose from the Iberian Peninsula.

This is a Latin commentary on the Pauline epistles that works through each letter verse by verse with short explanatory glosses. It has traditionally been attributed to Primasius, the sixth-century bishop of Hadrumetum in North Africa, but modern scholars generally reject this attribution. They regard the work as an anonymous reworking of Pelagius's commentary on Paul, linked to the circle of Cassiodorus, in which Pelagian views were purged. Its notes stress grace and predestination and argue against heretics such as the Manichaeans and Photinus.

This Latin commentary on the Book of Revelation, in five books, is by Primasius, bishop of Hadrumetum in North Africa, and was written in the mid-sixth century. It is dedicated to a man named Castorius. In the prologue Primasius says he drew on Augustine and also on the Donatist Ticonius, keeping what agreed with Catholic teaching and rejecting the rest. Because Ticonius's own commentary is lost, this work is one of the main sources for reconstructing it. It also shaped later Latin interpretation of Revelation.

This short Latin formula of abjuration was meant for people suspected of being Manichaeans. It is headed as chapters "of Saint Augustine" that such people had to read aloud in public and sign with their own hand. A series of anathemas condemns core Manichaean teachings, including two uncreated opposing principles, particles of God trapped in matter and freed through the meals of the Elect, and Adam's creation by the princes of darkness. It is attributed to a Prosper, a former Manichaean. Its date is uncertain, but it is commonly placed in the early sixth century.

De vocatione omnium gentium (On the Calling of All Nations) is a Latin theological treatise in two books, written around the mid-fifth century. It is usually attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine, though the attribution is not certain, and some manuscripts transmitted it among the works of Ambrose. It takes up the dispute between defenders of free will and preachers of grace, asking how God can will all people to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4) when grace is not given to all. Its moderate Augustinian answer made it an important text in later debates on grace and predestination.

This Latin letter from Prosper of Aquitaine to Augustine of Hippo survives as Letter 225 in Augustine's correspondence and was written around 428–429. Prosper reports that many monks and clergy in Marseille thought Augustine's anti-Pelagian teaching on grace, predestination and the calling of the elect was contrary to the Fathers and to Church tradition. He sets out their objections and asks Augustine to respond. Along with a similar letter from Hilary, it led Augustine to write On the Predestination of the Saints and On the Gift of Perseverance.

This Latin letter from Prosper of Aquitaine to Augustine of Hippo was written around 427–429 and survives among Augustine's correspondence as Letter 225. Prosper had already exchanged letters with Augustine through the deacon Leontius. Here he reports that many monks and clergy at Marseille judged Augustine's teaching on grace, predestination and the calling of the elect to be contrary to the Fathers, and that his On Rebuke and Grace had not settled the matter. Together with a similar letter from Hilary, it prompted Augustine's On the Predestination of the Saints and On the Gift of Perseverance.

This Latin anthology on grace, known as the Capitula Caelestini or Indiculus, collects rulings of Roman bishops, chiefly Innocent I and Zosimus, together with canons of African councils they approved. It was aimed at people who condemned Pelagius and Caelestius but rejected Augustine's teaching. In ten chapters it states that since Adam's fall no one can rise by free will without God's grace. It was transmitted with Pope Celestine I's letter of 431 to the Gallic bishops and is commonly, though not certainly, attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine. It became an authoritative statement of the Roman position.

Prosper of Aquitaine wrote this Latin polemical treatise, usually called Contra Collatorem, around 432–434, soon after Augustine's death. It answers John Cassian's thirteenth Conference, on God's protection, which Prosper saw as an attack on Augustine's teaching about grace. He takes twelve propositions from Cassian and argues that all but the first depart from catholic truth. He presents Augustine's critics as reviving Pelagian errors already condemned by the Church and the emperors. The work is a key document of the controversy later called "Semi-Pelagian" in southern Gaul.

The Expositio Psalmorum is a Latin commentary on Psalms 100 to 150 (Vulgate numbering) by Prosper of Aquitaine, the fifth-century lay theologian and disciple of Augustine of Hippo. Only this part of the work survives. It is largely a condensed reworking of Augustine's Enarrationes in Psalmos, going through the psalms verse by verse and drawing out their moral and doctrinal meaning. Its emphasis on divine grace, mercy and justice reflects Prosper's defence of Augustinian teaching. It is generally dated to the second quarter of the fifth century.

The Liber sententiarum is a Latin florilegium by Prosper of Aquitaine, the fifth-century lay theologian and disciple of Augustine of Hippo. It gathers several hundred short, numbered maxims taken from Augustine's writings, each under a brief heading. Many come from Augustine's Enarrationes in Psalmos, often by way of Prosper's own commentary on the Psalms. The maxims cover God, grace, sin, charity, virtue and the Christian life. Probably compiled toward the end of Prosper's life, around the 450s, it helped spread Augustine's teaching through the medieval West.

The Book of Epigrams from the Sayings of Saint Augustine is a Latin verse collection by Prosper of Aquitaine, a lay theologian and devoted disciple of Augustine of Hippo, written in the mid-fifth century. It opens with a verse preface. Each section then gives a short prose maxim drawn from Augustine's writings, followed by a poem in elegiac couplets that restates it, on topics such as true innocence and the right love of neighbour. The work helped spread Augustinian teaching on grace and the moral life in a form that was easy to memorise.

This is the Latin universal chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine (c. 390–c. 455), a lay disciple of Augustine. It is divided into two parts. The first runs from the creation of the world to the death of the emperor Valens in 378 and depends largely on Jerome's version of Eusebius's Chronicle. The second continues Jerome's chronicle, giving years by consuls counted from the Passion of Christ. Prosper issued successive versions, and the last ends in 455. The chronicle is a valuable source for fifth-century Western history, including the barbarian invasions and the Pelagian controversy.

This is a short anonymous Latin appendix found with the Chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine in some manuscripts. It goes beyond the end point of Prosper's own work, so it is a later addition rather than Prosper's writing. After listing three consulships that followed Valentinian III's death, it records the Vandal kings of Africa from Geiseric's capture of Carthage in 439. It gives the length of each reign and notes how the kings treated the Catholic Church. These events include Huneric's persecution and the exile of Bishop Eugenius of Carthage, and Gunthamund's later reopening of the churches.

This Latin letter by Prosper of Aquitaine, a lay theologian and disciple of Augustine of Hippo, is addressed to a friend named Rufinus and is often called the Letter to Rufinus. It was probably written in the late 420s. Prosper answers rumours spread against him by opponents in southern Gaul. He describes the Pelagian claim that God's grace is given according to human merit and defends Augustine's teaching that grace comes before any merit. The letter is an early document of the controversy later known as Semi-Pelagianism.

De vocatione omnium gentium (On the Calling of All Nations) is a Latin theological treatise in two books, written around the mid-fifth century. It is usually attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine, though the attribution is not certain, and some manuscripts transmitted it among the works of Ambrose. It takes up the dispute between defenders of free will and preachers of grace, asking how God can will all people to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4) when grace is not given to all. Its moderate Augustinian answer made it an important text in later debates on grace and predestination.

The Peri Achariston (Greek for "On the Ungrateful"), or De ingratis, is a Latin didactic poem in hexameters by Prosper of Aquitaine. It runs to about a thousand lines in four parts and is usually dated to around 429–430. The poem defends Augustine of Hippo's teaching on grace. It attacks the "ungrateful": those who deny that faith and the first movement of a good will are gifts of God. Its chief targets are the monks of southern Gaul later called Semi-Pelagians. It is one of the main literary documents of the controversy over grace in fifth-century Gaul.

The Epigrammata in obtrectatorem Augustini ("Epigrams against a detractor of Augustine") are short Latin poems in elegiac couplets by Prosper of Aquitaine, a lay disciple and defender of Augustine of Hippo. They were probably written around 430, perhaps while Augustine was still alive. They attack an unnamed writer who was reported to be criticising Augustine's books and preparing a work against them. Editors have traditionally identified this opponent as John Cassian. The poems belong to Prosper's polemic against the Gallic critics of Augustine's teaching on grace and free will.

This is a short set of Latin epigrams in elegiac couplets by Prosper of Aquitaine, the lay disciple and defender of Augustine of Hippo. They were written in the second quarter of the fifth century, probably during the controversies over grace that followed Augustine's death. The poems attack an unnamed writer who had criticised Augustine, picturing him as a small serpent that revives Pelagian teaching. They allude to the Britons, Pelagius's people, and to Campania, the home of Julian of Eclanum. The epigrams predict that the aged Augustine's teaching will defeat him.

The Epitaph of the Nestorian and Pelagian Heresies is a short Latin poem in elegiac couplets attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine. It was probably written soon after Nestorius was condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431. In it, Nestorianism speaks as both the daughter and the mother of Pelagianism. It claims that both heresies come from the same pride: trusting in human merit and free will instead of divine grace. The poem warns readers that anyone who treats God's gifts as owed to human beings shares their fate.

This short Latin treatise by Prosper of Aquitaine defends Augustine of Hippo's teaching on grace and predestination. It is usually dated to the early 430s, shortly after Augustine's death. Critics in Gaul had drawn up a list of brief "chapters" listing propositions they claimed to find in Augustine's books and condemned as dangerous, such as the idea that God predestines some people to sin or damnation. Prosper answers each charge in turn with a short, precise statement, arguing that the critics misread Augustine. It belongs to the controversy later called Semi-Pelagianism.

This Latin treatise by Prosper of Aquitaine defends Augustine of Hippo against sixteen objections that critics in Gaul circulated as summaries of Augustinian teaching on grace and predestination. One example is the claim that Christ did not suffer for the salvation of all people. Prosper takes each objection in turn and sets out what he considers the true doctrine, rejecting the distortions as slanders. The objections are traditionally linked to Vincent of Lérins, but that identification is uncertain. Written probably in the early 430s, the work is an important document of the so-called Semipelagian controversy.

The Responses on Behalf of Augustine to the Excerpts of the Genoese is a short Latin treatise by Prosper of Aquitaine. He probably wrote it soon after Augustine's death in 430. It is addressed to Camillus and Theodore, two priests of Genoa, who had sent Prosper passages from Augustine's On the Predestination of the Saints that puzzled them. Prosper takes each excerpt in turn and explains it, defending Augustine's teaching on grace, election and predestination. The work belongs to his wider defence of Augustine against critics in southern Gaul.

The Letter to the Holy Virgin Demetrias, or On Humility, is a Latin treatise in letter form, usually attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine and dated to the mid-fifth century. The attribution has been disputed, and some have assigned it to Pope Leo the Great. It is addressed to Demetrias, a consecrated virgin of the noble Anician family who also received letters from Jerome and Pelagius. It praises true humility as the foundation of Christian virtue, describes pride as its opposite, and urges Demetrias to guard against self-exaltation. Its stress on grace reflects Augustinian thought.

This short Latin liturgical text is attributed to Protadius, bishop of Besançon in the early seventh century. It contains the acclamations known as the Laudes regiae, which begin "Christus vincit, Christus regnat, Christus imperat". According to the old ordinary of the church of Besançon, they were sung at a pontifical Mass between the collect and the epistle. The acclamations pray for the pope, the bishop, the emperor and the queen, and call on local and military saints. Because it mentions an emperor and uses a form of the Laudes otherwise known from the Carolingian period, the attribution to Protadius is doubtful.

This Latin charter re-establishes the community of canons at the church of St Stephen the Protomartyr in Besançon. It has been attributed to the seventh-century bishop Protadius, but the text names its issuer as Hugh, archbishop of Besançon, and his predecessor Walter. This points to Hugh of Salins, who held the see from 1031 to 1066. Hugh endows the canons with churches and property for a common table. He praises the church's relics of Stephen and the head of St Agapitus, and orders daily services there.

The Catalogus Episcoporum Sanctae Bisunticensis Ecclesiae is a short Latin list of the bishops of Besançon in eastern Gaul. It is traditionally attributed to Protadius, bishop of the see in the early seventh century (c. 614–624). The list starts with the legendary first bishops, including Linus and Ferreolus, and marks most early names as saints. It also flags certain men as pseudo-bishops or intruders. Because it runs to Archbishop Hugh I in the eleventh century, later hands must have extended it. Its main value is as evidence for the episcopal succession of Besançon.

The Catalogus alter episcoporum Vesuntionensis Ecclesiae is a short Latin list of the early bishops of Besançon. It is traditionally attributed to Protadius, bishop of Besançon in the early seventh century. That attribution is doubtful, because the list names Protadius himself and his successor Donatus, and it appears to be later than another catalogue of the same see. It runs from Linus, the legendary founder, through Nicetius, a contemporary of Pope Gregory the Great. Brief notes record church foundations, burials, relics and martyrdoms, and the list leaves out bishops it judged unworthy.

Proterius, the Chalcedonian bishop of Alexandria, wrote this letter to Pope Leo I around 454 about when Easter should fall in the coming eighth indiction (455). Emperor Marcian had passed on Leo's doubts about the Alexandrian date. Proterius defends the hundred-year Easter cycle drawn up by his predecessor Theophilus, which put Easter on 24 April, and suggests that any error came from faulty manuscripts or copyists. He probably wrote in Greek, and the letter survives in a Latin version attributed to Dionysius Exiguus. It is an important source for fifth-century disputes over how to calculate Easter.

This is a group of Latin poems by the Spanish Christian poet Prudentius, written around 392–405. It opens with his verse Preface, in which the poet looks back on his life at about fifty-seven years old. The Cathemerinon is a set of twelve lyric hymns for the hours of the day and for feasts. The Apotheosis is a hexameter poem defending the Trinity and the divinity of Christ against heresies. The Hamartigenia, on the origin of sin, attacks Marcionite dualism. Together these poems helped shape Christian Latin poetry and hymnody.

The Psychomachia ("Battle of the Soul") is a Latin hexameter poem by Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, the Christian poet from Roman Spain. It was probably written around the turn of the fifth century, though its exact date is unknown. In roughly a thousand lines that borrow freely from Virgil's Aeneid, personified virtues such as Faith, Chastity, Patience and Humility fight and defeat their opposing vices in single combat. It is often called the first fully allegorical poem of the Christian West. It was widely copied and illustrated in the Middle Ages, and it shaped later allegorical literature and Romanesque sculpture.

The Dittochaeum, also known as the Tituli historiarum, is a Latin poem by the Christian poet Prudentius, probably written around the turn of the fifth century. It has forty-nine four-line stanzas in hexameters. Twenty-four describe scenes from the Old Testament, beginning with Adam and Eve, and twenty-five describe scenes from the New Testament. The stanzas may have been written as captions for a cycle of church paintings or mosaics. The meaning of the Greek title is uncertain; it is often explained as "double nourishment". Some early modern scholars doubted that Prudentius wrote it, but it is generally accepted as his.

Contra Symmachum ("Against Symmachus") is a Latin poem in two books by the Spanish Christian poet Prudentius, usually dated to the early fifth century. It is written in hexameters, and each book has a preface in another metre. It answers the pagan senator Symmachus, whose petition of 384 asked for the Altar of Victory to be restored to the Senate house. The first book attacks the pagan gods and their worship. The second rebuts Symmachus's arguments one by one, presenting Rome's empire as providentially preparing the world for Christ.

The Liber Peristephanon ("Book of Crowns") is a collection of fourteen Latin lyric poems by the Spanish Christian poet Prudentius, written around 400 and included in the edition of his poems he gathered about 405. The poems, in a range of classical metres, praise martyrs: Spanish martyrs such as Emeterius and Chelidonius, Eulalia of Mérida, Vincent and the eighteen martyrs of Saragossa, and others including Lawrence, Agnes, Hippolytus, Cyprian, Cassian and Romanus. Their vivid accounts of the martyrs' suffering, along with details about shrines and cult, made them important for later hagiography and devotion to the martyrs.

De Trinitate, also known as a treatise on the Apostles' Creed, is a Latin theological work that was once transmitted among the writings of Ambrose of Milan but is now regarded as spurious. Its author and date are unknown. It argues that God is an incorporeal, simple and incomprehensible nature, and that the Trinity is an inseparable, unconfused unity that existed before all creation. It draws on earlier Latin Trinitarian theology, including Hilary of Poitiers's formula "eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift," as taken up by Augustine.

De Dignitate Sacerdotali (On the Priestly Dignity) is a short Latin treatise once attributed to Ambrose of Milan but now regarded as spurious. Its author and date are uncertain, and it has sometimes been assigned to Gerbert of Aurillac (Pope Sylvester II). It is addressed to fellow clergy and opens with the parable of the talents. It argues that those entrusted with Christ's flock must preach and share the grace they have received. It goes on to exalt the dignity of bishops and priests and warns them about the grave responsibility of their office.

Ad virginem devotam ("To a Virgin Consecrated to God") is a short Latin exhortation to a woman vowed to virginity. It has come down among the works falsely attributed to Ambrose of Milan, and its real author and date are unknown. It opens with Psalm 44(45), "Hear, O daughter, and see; incline your ear," and reminds the virgin that she is the bride of Christ. Citing Peter, Paul, John and James, it warns her against friendships and talk with worldly people and against returning to the world she has renounced.

This anonymous Latin treatise was handed down among the works of Ambrose of Milan but is not considered genuinely his. Its author and date are unknown. It gives an allegorical reading of the Book of Numbers, and in particular of the forty-two stations where the Israelites camped between Egypt and Moses' death. Each stage of the journey is read as a step in the soul's spiritual progress. It begins by explaining that the census of fighting men aged twenty and over stands for spiritual maturity. Much of the treatise follows Origen's homilies on Numbers in Rufinus' Latin translation.

This is a collection of Latin sermons that were once attributed to Ambrose of Milan (d. 397) but are now regarded as spurious. They are by various unknown authors, many writing well after Ambrose's time. The sermons follow the liturgical year and cover feasts and seasons such as Advent, Lent and Easter, along with saints' days. The first sermon, for Advent, urges almsgiving, confession of sins and abstinence. Its references to Advent observance and penitential practice show that it comes from a later period than Ambrose.

This is a group of Latin letters that once circulated under the name of Ambrose of Milan (d. 397). Early modern editors judged them spurious and printed them apart from his genuine correspondence. The first is a passion of the Roman virgin martyr Agnes, framed as a festal letter from Ambrose to consecrated virgins. It tells of her refusal of the prefect's son, her miraculous preservation in a brothel and in fire, her death, and the healing of Constantina. Its authors and dates are uncertain, though the Agnes passion is generally placed after Ambrose's lifetime.

These are two Latin prayers that were long attributed to Ambrose of Milan but are now regarded as spurious. The first, opening "Summe sacerdos et vere pontifex," is a priest's private prayer of preparation before celebrating Mass.
