It asks Christ, the eternal high priest who offered himself on the cross, for the reverence, purity of heart and understanding needed to handle the eucharistic mystery worthily. Modern scholarship generally assigns it to the eleventh-century monk John of Fécamp. It became widely used and entered the preparatory prayers of the Roman Missal under Ambrose's name.

This short Latin treatise on penance once circulated among the works of Ambrose of Milan but is considered spurious. It is a separate work from his genuine two books De paenitentia. Its author and date are unknown. Written as an address to a "dearest brother", it urges the sinner to confess openly before God. It argues that nothing done in secret is hidden from God and that judging oneself first earns mercy before the divine judge. It also teaches that sincere confession is itself a form of justice, a point it supports with Ecclesiasticus.

De Spiritu Sancto libellus is a short Latin treatise on the Holy Spirit. It has come down among the works attributed to Ambrose of Milan but is considered spurious, and its real author and date are unknown. It opens with Romans 8:9–11 and argues from Paul's interchangeable phrases "Spirit of God" and "Spirit of Christ" that God, Christ and the Holy Spirit cannot be separated. From this it develops a defence of the unity of the Trinity and of the Spirit's divinity.

This short Latin exegetical treatise was transmitted among the works of Ambrose of Milan but is considered spurious. Its author and date are unknown. It deals with the apparent conflict between the genealogies of Christ in Matthew and Luke, starting from the principle that Scripture may contain differences but never contradictions. It explains that Matthew counts downward from Abraham through Solomon to show the Son of God becoming son of man. Luke counts upward through Nathan to Adam and God, showing that people become sons of God by adoption in baptism.

De dignitate conditionis humanae is a short Latin treatise on the creation of humanity. It was traditionally transmitted under the name of Ambrose of Milan but is not his work, and its true author and date are uncertain. Its starting point is Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man in our image and likeness." It argues that humanity's special dignity comes from being made by the counsel of the Trinity rather than by a simple command. It finds the divine image in the soul, whose unity and threefold powers reflect the one God and the Trinity.

The Exorcismus is a short Latin exorcism prayer traditionally transmitted among the works of Ambrose of Milan but generally regarded as spurious. Its author and date are unknown. The exorcist first asks Christ for forgiveness and for the confidence to confront the "cruel dragon." He then adjures every unclean spirit in Christ's name to "yield to God." He recalls biblical victories over evil: Job, Pharaoh drowned through Moses, Daniel's overthrow of Bel and the dragon, David's songs that drove the spirit from Saul, and the demons' fearful cry before Jesus.

De moribus Brachmanorum is a Latin adaptation of the Greek treatise On the Races of India and the Brahmans, which is attributed to Palladius of Helenopolis. It was handed down in manuscripts under the name of Ambrose of Milan, but differences of style have long made scholars doubt that he wrote it. The text is addressed to a certain Palladius. It describes India and the Ganges, which it identifies with the Phison of Paradise, and the ascetic life of the Brahmans. It belongs to the late antique tradition that held up the Indian sages as models of virtue.

The Philosophorum aliquot epistolae is a short Latin collection of letters attributed to early Greek sages and their contemporaries. They include Thales writing to Pherecydes and to Solon, and the Athenian tyrant Pisistratus writing to Solon. These letters are pseudepigraphic. Most of them survive in Diogenes Laertius's Lives of the Philosophers. This Latin version is credited to the humanist Gilbertus Cognatus (Gilbert Cousin) of Nozeroy. The work has no real connection with Ambrose; it was placed among the spurious writings transmitted under his name.

These are two short Latin letters that were transmitted among the works of Ambrose of Milan but are generally regarded as spurious. They concern a monk tormented by a demon that repeatedly fouled his clothing. The writer asks why God allowed this, suggesting either hidden inner corruption, such as unbelief or vainglory, or a trial meant to preserve humility, like Paul's thorn in the flesh. The first letter mentions Antony, Hilarion and Macarius. Its references to Germans and English argue against Ambrose's authorship. The date and author are unknown.

The Epistola de fide ad Hieronymum is a short Latin profession of faith addressed to the priest Jerome. It has come down under the name of Ambrose of Milan, but the attribution is spurious, and its real author and date are unknown. Citing Hebrews on the necessity of faith, it confesses one God in Father, Son and Holy Spirit and affirms that Christ is co-eternal and consubstantial with the Father. It then turns to the Incarnation, in which the Son took on human nature without any change to his own, and to original sin passed down from the first parents.

This is a group of Latin liturgical hymns traditionally ascribed to Ambrose, bishop of Milan (d. 397), but whose authorship is doubtful or unknown. They belong to the wider body of "Ambrosian" hymns, written in the iambic dimeter stanzas that Ambrose made popular and sung in the Western Office. One example is a Christmas hymn beginning "A solis ortus cardine / Et usque terrae limitem". Its section "Fit porta Christi pervia", based on the closed gate of Ezekiel 44, was later sung at Marian feasts. Sedulius borrowed its opening line for his alphabetical hymn.

These are two Latin letters falsely ascribed to Pope Anastasius I (399–401). The first is addressed to all the bishops of Germany and Burgundy. It rules that clergy must stand, not sit, while the Gospel is read, and it deals with receiving clerics from overseas and with Manichaeans discovered in Rome. Early modern editors already judged it spurious. The consular date it carries comes before Anastasius's pontificate, and much of the passage on the Manichaeans repeats a letter of Pope Leo the Great to the bishops of Italy. Who wrote the letters, and when, is unknown.

De Trinitate libri duodecim (The Twelve Books on the Trinity) is a Latin treatise on the Trinity, falsely attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria and probably written in the West in the late fourth or fifth century. Its authorship is disputed. It has been assigned to Vigilius of Thapsus, and some of its books to Eusebius of Vercelli. The work begins with a prayer to the one Godhead of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It defends the Nicene doctrine of the undivided divinity of the three persons against Arian and other heretical teachings.

The Rescriptum Athanasii ad Liberium papam is a short Latin letter presented as Athanasius of Alexandria's reply to Pope Liberius (352–366). It is generally regarded as spurious, part of a forged exchange between the two bishops, and its date and author are unknown. Under the heading "that God the Word assumed a perfect man for our salvation", it sets out a confession of faith. It affirms the one invisible God and his eternal Word, who created all things, appeared to the patriarchs, spoke through the prophets and finally took mortal flesh from the Virgin.

This Latin letter is presented as written by Athanasius of Alexandria and the bishops of Egypt, gathered in synod at Alexandria, to Pope Liberius (352–366). It praises the apostolic see as the guardian of the faith confirmed at Nicaea. It then complains of the persecution that the orthodox suffer from the Arians. Scholars generally regard it as a forgery. Parts of its wording closely match the letter of Victor of Carthage to Pope Theodore, which was read at the Lateran Synod of 649. That suggests it was written in the seventh century or later.

De vita eremitica ad sororem is a Latin rule of life for a female recluse. It survives among the spurious works of Augustine of Hippo. The text is in fact Aelred of Rievaulx's De institutione inclusarum, written about 1160 for his sister, or a version of it that was circulated under Augustine's name. Writing as her brother "in flesh and spirit," the author draws on the Fathers to explain why the solitary life arose. He warns that enclosing the body achieves nothing without inner discipline, and he sets out rules for the anchoress's daily life and devotion.

De benedictionibus Jacob patriarchae is a short anonymous Latin commentary on the blessings Jacob gives his twelve sons in Genesis 49. It has been handed down among the spurious works of Augustine and has also been linked with Jerome; its real author and date are unknown. Written as questions and answers, it says the blessings should be read both historically and allegorically. Historically, they refer to the division of the Promised Land among Jacob's descendants. Allegorically, they point to Christ and the Church in the last days.

This is the first class of the "supposititious sermons", a collection of Latin sermons once circulated under the name of Augustine of Hippo but judged spurious or doubtful by later editors. This class gathers sermons on passages of the Old and New Testaments. It opens with a homily on the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in Genesis, which was also once wrongly ascribed to Ambrose. The sermons are by various mostly anonymous authors of late antiquity and the early Middle Ages. A good number are the work of Caesarius of Arles, whose preaching drew heavily on Augustine.

This is the second class of the "supposititious sermons", Latin sermons once circulated under Augustine of Hippo's name. The Benedictine (Maurist) editors judged them spurious and grouped them in an appendix to Augustine's sermons. This class, "de tempore", is arranged by the liturgical year, beginning with Advent and Christmas. The opening sermon urges the faithful to prepare with a clean conscience to receive Christ's body and blood worthily at the Nativity. The sermons come from various later authors, chiefly Gallic preachers, and many are now credited to Caesarius of Arles.

This is the third class of the "supposititious sermons" that the Benedictine (Maurist) editors of Augustine placed in an appendix because they judged them not to be his. Its Latin sermons on the saints, by various anonymous and later authors, honour martyrs and other saints on their feast days. The section opens with a sermon on the deacon-martyr Vincent, earlier ascribed to Augustine or Leo the Great. Its author calls himself a Spaniard. The collection shows how preaching on the saints' cult circulated under Augustine's name.

This is the fourth class of the "supposititious" sermons. These are Latin sermons that circulated under the name of Augustine of Hippo but that his Benedictine (Maurist) editors judged spurious and placed in an appendix. This class gathers sermons "on various subjects" rather than on Scripture, the liturgical seasons or the saints. It opens with a sermon on the Trinity, which warns against curious speculation about God's nature. The sermons come from different, mostly unknown authors and periods. Scholars have since traced some of them to identifiable preachers such as Caesarius of Arles.

The Book of Twenty-One Sentences or Questions is a short Latin collection of theological and moral propositions. It was once transmitted among the works of Augustine of Hippo but is now regarded as spurious, and its author and date are unknown. The first sentence argues that no one who lives shamefully truly lives as he wishes or is happy, an idea that echoes Augustine. The second reads the Jewish Passover as a figure of Christ, the one true paschal lamb, sacrificed only once.

The Dialogue of Sixty-Five Questions is an anonymous Latin work in question-and-answer form, falsely attributed to Augustine of Hippo. It presents Orosius as the questioner and Augustine as the one who answers. In the preface the questioner asks for help with difficult passages in the Fathers and in Scripture. The questions then move from proofs of the Trinity, drawn from Genesis and the Gospels, to creation and other problems of biblical interpretation. The answers rely heavily on Augustine's genuine writings. The compiler and the date of composition are uncertain, but the work comes from after Augustine's lifetime.

De diligendo Deo ("On Loving God") is a short Latin devotional treatise that was long transmitted among the works of Augustine of Hippo but is not his. It was traditionally ascribed to Alcher, a twelfth-century Cistercian monk of Clairvaux. Many scholars now give it to an anonymous writer of the same period, who is also linked to the De spiritu et anima. The treatise presents charity, the twofold love of God and neighbour, as the "more excellent way" to heavenly life. It should not be confused with Bernard of Clairvaux's treatise of the same title.

De contritione cordis ("On Contrition of Heart") is a short Latin devotional treatise once credited to Augustine of Hippo. It is now counted among the Pseudo-Augustinian writings, and its real author and date are unknown. The work opens by recalling that death is certain but its hour uncertain, and that worldly pleasure is fleeting. It urges meditation on God's gifts of creation and redemption, and on one's own sins. Meditation leads to self-knowledge, and self-knowledge to compunction, devotion and prayer.

The Speculum ("Mirror") is a Latin devotional work that has come down under the name of Augustine of Hippo but is not by him. It is one of many medieval writings wrongly attributed to Augustine. It opens with a prayer to the Trinity ("Adesto mihi, verum lumen, Deus Pater omnipotens"), which closely follows the invocation that Alcuin placed after his treatise on the Trinity, so it can be no earlier than the Carolingian period. The text is a meditation in the first person, praising God's grace, faith and love. Its author and exact date are unknown.

De sobrietate et castitate ("On Sobriety and Chastity") is a Latin moral treatise once attributed to Augustine of Hippo but now regarded as spurious. Its real author and date are unknown. It warns anyone seeking a virtuous life against three vices: sloth, sleepiness and drunkenness. Drunkenness is called the "gulf of all vices". The work praises sobriety, discusses the proper use of wine and why priests are forbidden it, and condemns heavy drinking, including at funeral gatherings. It cites Scripture against the vice before turning to chastity.

The Psalterium is a Latin devotional prayer falsely attributed to Augustine of Hippo and grouped with the writings scholars assign to "Pseudo-Augustine". Its author and date are unknown. Addressed to "almighty God, King of eternal glory", it is a continuous penitential prayer built from phrases of the Psalms. It works through them in order, beginning with Psalm 1's blessed man who meditates on God's law day and night. The speaker asks for forgiveness, for protection from the ancient enemy, and for the grace to serve God with a pure heart.

The Cantici Magnificat Expositio is a short Latin commentary on the Magnificat, the song of Mary in Luke 1:46–55. It was handed down among the works of Augustine of Hippo but is not his, and its real author and date are unknown. The exposition begins with the Annunciation and Mary's visit to Elizabeth. It then reads the canticle verse by verse as an expression of the Virgin's humility and joy. One theme is that contemplating God's majesty brings forth chaste fear, while contemplating his goodness brings forth love.

De Visitatione Infirmorum ("On Visiting the Sick") is a Latin work of consolation and spiritual counsel that was once attributed to Augustine of Hippo but is now regarded as spurious. Its author and date are unknown. Its emphasis on confessing sins to a priest suggests it was written in the Middle Ages. The author speaks to his dying nephew, whom he has visited, weighing proper grief against excessive tears. He urges the nephew to confess and repent so that he may be ready for the journey to eternal life. The work belongs to the Christian literature of preparation for death.

De consolatione mortuorum ("On the Consolation for the Dead") is a Latin sermon collection, made up of two sermons, that was handed down among the works wrongly attributed to Augustine of Hippo. Its real author and date are unknown. Addressing grieving listeners as "brothers," the preacher calls his words a healing eye-salve for the mind and uses Paul's contrast between godly and worldly sorrow (2 Corinthians 7:10). He then argues that excessive mourning for the dead is pointless. He encourages Christian hope in the resurrection in place of despairing grief.

De rectitudine catholicae conversationis ("On the Right Conduct of Catholic Life") is an anonymous Latin pastoral treatise in the form of a sermon. It was long transmitted among the works of Augustine of Hippo but is not his. Its author and date are uncertain, though it belongs to the early medieval Gallic preaching tradition. It urges the faithful to remember their baptismal vows and the Last Judgement, avoid pagan rites, superstition and drunkenness, give alms and tithes, fast, pray, love their enemies and do penance without delay.

The Sermo de Symbolo is a Latin sermon on the Creed. It was once ascribed to Augustine of Hippo but is now counted among the spurious works circulating under his name, and its real author and date are unknown. Addressed to a congregation, it compares the Christian's profession of faith to the oath soldiers swear to earthly masters. It argues that faith must be held in the heart and also confessed aloud to keep the Church united. It then presents the Creed as the rule of faith handed down by the apostles in twelve articles, matching their number.

This anonymous Latin sermon for the Easter Vigil was handed down under the name of Augustine of Hippo. It also appears among the spurious works of Jerome, and its true author and date are unknown. Using Exodus 12, it reads the Passover lamb as Christ, slain for the salvation of all. It explains details of the rite allegorically: the lamb must be eaten in one house, meaning the one Church, along with the unleavened bread, the bitter herbs, the girded loins, the sandals and the staff.

This short Latin sermon on Psalm 41 (42), "As the hart longs for the fountains of waters", is addressed to the newly baptized. It has come down among works falsely attributed to Augustine and was also printed under Jerome's name. Its authorship and date are uncertain, though some modern scholars place it among Jerome's homilies on the Psalms. It reads the "sons of Core" as the sons of Calvary and compares the stag, which kills serpents and then thirsts for springs, to believers who renounce the devil in baptism and long for the Trinity.

This is an anonymous Latin sermon addressed to the newly baptized. It explains why priests anoint their ears and nostrils with holy oil, a rite related to the Ephphatha. The sermon describes the mysteries that are withheld from catechumens and interprets the anointing of the ears spiritually. It is one of a series of baptismal sermons that a manuscript from Fleury ascribes to Augustine of Hippo. Jacques Sirmond published it but judged that Augustine was not the author. Ivo of Chartres later cited the series under Augustine's name. Its date and real author are unknown.

Sermo de mysterio baptismatis is an anonymous Latin mystagogical sermon that was once transmitted under the name of Augustine of Hippo but is not his work. Its author and date are uncertain. The preacher speaks to the newly baptized and refers back to an earlier sermon on the anointing and the renunciation of the devil. This sermon explains what happened at the font: the grace given through consecrated water, the questions on faith in the Trinity and the resurrection, the meaning of the threefold immersion, and why baptism is never repeated.

This Latin sermon was handed down under the name of Augustine of Hippo, but it is not his work. Its real author and date are unknown. It is a mystagogical address to the newly baptized and continues an earlier talk on the rites before and during baptism. It explains the anointing of the head with chrism after baptism. Drawing on the Old Testament anointing of kings such as David and of the priest Aaron, it presents this anointing as giving believers an eternal royal and priestly dignity. As the title says, it then turns to the washing of feet.

This short Latin treatise on the creation of the first human is transmitted among the spurious works of Augustine. It comments on Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man in our image and likeness." It argues that humanity's dignity lies in being made by the counsel of the whole Trinity, not by a simple command, and so bears the Trinity's image. Manuscripts also attribute it to Ambrose, as De dignitate primi hominis, and to Alcuin. Its author and date are uncertain. Paulinus of Aquileia borrowed from it, and the later compilation De spiritu et anima includes the whole text.

The Sermo de vanitate saeculi ("Sermon on the Vanity of the World") is a short Latin sermon that was once attributed to Augustine of Hippo but is now counted among the pseudo-Augustinian writings. Almost all of it repeats sections 21–23 of the treatise De rectitudine catholicae conversationis, which is ascribed to Eligius of Noyon (7th century). Only about ten closing lines are added. The sermon urges its hearers to turn from sin, keep death and judgement in mind, and seek eternal joy in Christ rather than worldly prosperity.

The Sermo de contemptu mundi is an anonymous Latin sermon on contempt of the world. It was handed down among the spurious works of Augustine of Hippo and is labelled as being by an uncertain author. Its date and authorship are unknown. Speaking to "dearest brothers" who seek a heavenly inheritance, the preacher separates the special commandments binding on canons, clerics and monks from the common commandments binding on all Catholics. Drawing on the Gospels, he urges voluntary poverty, renunciation of family and property, and teaches that clerics should own nothing of their own.

The Sermo de bono disciplinae ("Sermon on the Good of Discipline") is a short Latin sermon that has come down among the spurious works of Augustine of Hippo. Melchior Goldast restored it to Valerian, bishop of Cimiez (Cemenelum) in the mid-fifth century, and manuscript fragments carrying his name support that attribution. The sermon defends discipline against people who call it tyranny or pride. It calls discipline the teacher of religion and true piety, which corrects in order to heal, citing Proverbs 3:11–12. It also argues that God set the whole created order under discipline.

The Sermo de obedientia et humilitate is a short Latin sermon, surviving as a fragment, that was handed down among the spurious works of Augustine of Hippo. Its author and date are unknown, though it is thought to be early. Addressed apparently to monks, it teaches that obedience to one's spiritual fathers is obedience to Christ. It uses the curse of Ham and the blessing of Shem as examples and cites Luke 10:16. It argues that without obedience, fasting, prayer and other ascetic practices lose all their value.

The Tractatus de charitate, also titled On the words of the Psalm "The earth has yielded its fruit", is a short Latin homiletic fragment once attributed to Augustine of Hippo. Its discoverer, Vignier, who found it in a manuscript at Dijon, judged it the work of an imitator of Augustine. Its author and date are unknown. Drawing on Psalm 84 and John 15, it teaches that charity is the fruit God asks of the soul he has blessed, and that love of the world is not true love.

The Tractatus de oratione et eleemosyna (Treatise on Prayer and Almsgiving) is a short Latin homiletic work transmitted under the name of Augustine of Hippo but generally regarded as spurious. Its author and date are unknown. Starting from Psalm 40 (41), "Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor", it teaches that alms should be given freely and in secret, before the poor have to ask, citing Matthew 6 and Sirach 29. It also urges that prayer should always accompany acts of mercy.

The Sermo de generalitate eleemosynarum ("Sermon on the Universality of Almsgiving") is a Latin sermon falsely attributed to Augustine of Hippo. Its real author and date are unknown. Preached to an audience addressed as "fathers", it argues that alms should be given to everyone, sinners included. It rejects the Manichaean refusal of food to sinners and corrects those who read Ecclesiasticus 12 as forbidding help to the wicked. Citing Galatians 6:10 and Christ's own example, it teaches that the just come first, but that sinners and enemies should be helped because they are human.

This short Latin treatise on the twelve precious stones forming the foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem in Revelation 21:19–20 has come down among works falsely ascribed to Augustine. Its real author and date are uncertain. One suggestion is Amatus, bishop and monk of Monte Cassino, since Peter the Deacon lists a treatise on the twelve stones among his writings. The text follows Bede's commentary on the Apocalypse closely. It describes each stone's colour and properties, then reads them allegorically as Christ, the saints and Christian virtues.

The Miscellaneae Sententiae ("Miscellaneous Sayings") is an anonymous Latin collection of short moral and spiritual maxims that was handed down among the spurious works attributed to Augustine of Hippo. Its author and date are unknown. It opens with a list of topics, such as simplicity and prudence, thieves and robbers, rulers, the stages of sin, Scripture, old age, friendship and the fleeting world. Each heading is followed by a brief reflection, often based on a biblical verse. The first explains Christ's command to be "simple as doves and wise as serpents".

The Altercatio Ecclesiae et Synagogae is an anonymous Latin dialogue that was long transmitted among the works falsely attributed to Augustine of Hippo. It is usually dated to the fifth century. It is framed as a lawsuit argued before judges: two women, Church and Synagogue, dispute who rightfully owns an inheritance. Each speaker cites the prophets, the law and other scriptural evidence, and Church claims that Synagogue has lost her rights. The text is a significant example of early Christian anti-Jewish polemic. Its legal framing also influenced the medieval imagery of Ecclesia and Synagoga.

The Commonitorium on how to deal with Manichaeans who convert is a short Latin text of instructions for the Church. It is traditionally attributed to Augustine of Hippo, but its authorship is doubtful and it is often classed as pseudo-Augustinian. It tells how a bishop should receive former Manichaeans who submit a written confession: they are given a dated letter, placed under the watch of Catholic neighbours, and only cautiously admitted to baptism or reconciliation. It ends with a set form of anathemas against Manichaean teaching, such as the belief in two opposing principles of good and evil.

De incarnatione Verbi ad Januarium is a Latin treatise in two books, addressed to a certain Januarius and falsely attributed to Augustine of Hippo. It is not an original composition. It is a compilation of extracts from Origen's Peri Archon (On First Principles), taken from Rufinus of Aquileia's Latin translation of that work. It opens with Origen's summary of the doctrines handed down by the apostles: the one God who created all things, the eternal birth of Christ from the Father, and his true incarnation, death and resurrection. Its compiler and date are unknown.

De Trinitate et Unitate Dei (On the Trinity and Unity of God) is a short Latin theological treatise that has come down among the works falsely attributed to Augustine of Hippo. Its real author and date are unknown. Arranged in brief chapters, it sets out orthodox Trinitarian doctrine mainly through scriptural proof-texts. It argues that the "beginning" of Genesis 1:1 refers to the Son, who is Son by nature rather than by adoption. It also teaches that the Holy Spirit is neither unbegotten nor begotten but proceeds from both the Father and the Son.

De Essentia Divinitatis (On the Essence of the Divinity) is a short Latin theological treatise that was handed down among the works of Augustine of Hippo but is not by him. Its real author and date are unknown. It begins by confessing the one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one in nature and three in persons. It then works through the divine attributes, among them invisibility, incorporeality, immensity, uncircumscribability and immutability. Each attribute is supported with proof texts from the Old and New Testaments.

De unitate sanctae Trinitatis dialogus is a short Latin theological dialogue once transmitted among the works of Augustine of Hippo, though not by him; its real author and date are uncertain. In it a questioner and a respondent go through the divinity of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The answers rest on biblical proof texts such as Romans 9:5 and John 20:22–23. It belongs to the anti-Arian literature of Late Antiquity, which defended the Trinity against those who denied that the Son and the Spirit are fully divine.

The Sermon on Rusticianus the Subdeacon is a Latin sermon attributed to Augustine of Hippo, though its authenticity is doubted and it is often classed as pseudo-Augustinian. It is known only from a seventeenth-century printing, and no manuscript of it is known to survive. Its full title says it concerns a subdeacon named Rusticianus whom the Donatists had rebaptized. The opening is a lament: the preacher grieves with his congregation for a beloved pastor, calls him a father, and hopes the people will give the same affection to his successor.

The Hypomnesticon (also called Hypognosticon) is an anonymous Latin treatise against the Pelagians and Caelestians, probably written in the second quarter of the fifth century. It was long transmitted under the name of Augustine of Hippo. That attribution is now rejected, and the real author remains unknown. In the form of a handbook, it states and refutes Pelagian teachings on original sin, free will, grace and predestination, defending the Augustinian position. Because it circulated as Augustine's work, it was widely read and cited in the medieval West.

This is a supplementary final chapter of the Soliloquia, a medieval Latin devotional work long circulated under the name of Augustine of Hippo but not written by him. The chapter survives in a manuscript that belonged to Count Faustino Avogadro of Brescia, where it follows the usual ending of the Soliloquies. Giovanni Crisostomo Trombelli first published it in the eighteenth century and left its authority an open question. Addressed to the soul, it urges a love for God that is single and undivided, preferred to every other attachment or consolation. Its author and date are unknown.

This is a small group of four anonymous Latin sermons that were handed down under the name of Augustine of Hippo but are not considered his. Their real author and date are unknown. The first sermon, given at a major feast, is on Colossians 3:1, "If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above." It describes baptism by triple immersion as restoring the image of the Trinity and undoing a threefold fall into sin through evil thought, fleshly delight and consent. It urges believers to die to the world and love their neighbour.

This short Latin sermon is attributed to Benedict of Nursia. It claims to be his farewell address to his monks when his disciple Maurus and companions set out for Gaul to found monasteries. The speaker tells the community not to grieve, since charity unites those whom distance separates. He urges the departing monks to persevere and promises to help them even more after his death. The attribution is spurious. The piece belongs to the legend of Maurus's mission, which is generally traced to the ninth-century Life of Maurus credited to Odo of Glanfeuil.

This short Latin letter is falsely attributed to Benedict of Nursia and addressed to Remigius, bishop of Reims. It is classed among Benedict's spurious writings, and its real author and date are unknown. The letter sits inside a miracle narrative. Benedict, calling himself a humble follower of the monastic life, praises Remigius's holiness and sends him a possessed girl so that he may free her by offering the Eucharist. When Remigius celebrates Mass, the demon admits that it is leaving because of Benedict's humility, not the bishop's command. The legend links two great saints of the sixth century.

This short Latin sermon, or consolatory address, on the death of Saint Placidus is written in the voice of Benedict of Nursia but is not considered authentic. Speaking as a father, the author says he rejoices rather than grieves that his beloved disciple Placidus has died a martyr and gone to Christ, calling the death an offering pleasing to God. It reflects the later legend that Placidus, the boy disciple of Benedict known from Gregory the Great's Dialogues, was martyred in Sicily. Its author and date are unknown.

This is a short Latin monastic customary that has been transmitted under the name of Benedict of Nursia, although he did not write it. From its opening words it is often called the "Qualiter". It is generally placed in the early medieval West, probably the Carolingian period, but its exact date and origin are uncertain. It sets out the daily conduct of monks: rising for the night office, private prayer, behaviour in choir, and decorum in the church, refectory and other shared spaces. It shows how the Benedictine way of life was put into practice.

This is a Latin geometry textbook in two books. It was attributed to Boethius (c. 480–524) but is now regarded as a later medieval compilation. Its opening addresses a certain Patricius and promises to explain Euclid's obscure teaching on geometrical figures. It confuses Euclid with Euclid of Megara. The work gives definitions of measure, point, line, surface, angle and figure, along with excerpts from Euclid's Elements that may come from Boethius's lost translation. These are combined with practical material from the Roman land surveyors. The work matters as a channel by which Euclidean geometry reached the early medieval West.

The Liber de geometria is a Latin treatise on geometry that has come down among the works of Boethius but is not by him. It was compiled in the early Middle Ages, and scholars disagree about its date and origin. It opens by defining geometry as the "measurement of the earth" and tells how the art began in Egypt with the flooding of the Nile, citing Varro and Seneca. It then describes the uses of geometry for craftsmen, physicians and philosophers. The treatise is a key witness to how Roman land-surveying (agrimensorial) and Euclidean material survived in early medieval schools.

Brevis fidei Christianae complexio, also known as De fide catholica, is a short Latin summary of Christian doctrine. It is transmitted as the fourth of the theological tractates (Opuscula sacra) ascribed to Boethius in the early sixth century. Its authenticity has long been disputed, though many modern scholars accept it as his work. It sets out the Trinity, with the Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, and rejects Arius and the Sabellians. It goes on to trace sacred history from creation through the Incarnation to the Church and the final resurrection.

This Latin letter is attributed to Pope Boniface II (530–532) and addressed to a bishop Eulalius of Alexandria. It is generally held to be spurious. The letter opens by defending the authority of the Roman see, which it traces to the apostle Peter. To support a hierarchy of ranks in the Church, it points to the different orders of angels. It then announces that the Church of Carthage has returned to communion with Rome. Parts of the wording closely follow a letter of Pope Hormisdas about the reconciliation of Constantinople. The date and circumstances of the forgery are uncertain.

This is a small group of Latin letters ascribed to Pope Boniface I (418–422) whose authorship is doubtful or wrong. One, to Justus, bishop of Canterbury, sends him the pallium and permits him to consecrate bishops. It actually belongs to Pope Boniface V (619–625), as Bede's account shows. Another, to Bishop Faustinus and the presbyters Philip and Asellus, the legates Pope Zosimus sent to the African synod, celebrates restored harmony between them. It was first printed by Mansi from an old Freising manuscript, and it relates to the Roman–African dispute over appeals to Rome.

The Epistola ad quosdam Germanos is a short Latin letter of monastic exhortation once transmitted under the name of Caesarius of Arles (died 542), though its authorship is doubtful. The writer cannot visit his "venerable sons" often, so he sends them this little admonition in place of his presence. He urges them to keep peace and chastity, to thank God for drawing them from the world into religious life, and to arm themselves spiritually against the devil's many snares.

The Epistola ad Felicem episcopum is a forged papal letter attributed to Pope Caius, bishop of Rome in the late third century, and addressed to a bishop Felix. It belongs to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, which were compiled in the Frankish realm around 847–852. Like other letters in that collection, it is pieced together from earlier genuine material, including a letter of Pope Vigilius. Its chapters say that pagans and heretics may not accuse Christians and that bishops may not be tried before secular judges. They also cover accusations against clergy, the Incarnation, Christ as sole mediator, and the ecclesiastical orders.

The Expositio in Cantica canticorum is a short Latin commentary on the Song of Songs, long transmitted under the name of Cassiodorus. Early editors already doubted that attribution, and the real author and date are unknown. The commentary reads Solomon's book as an epithalamium, or wedding song, for Christ and the Church. It explains the verses allegorically as exchanges between speakers. The opening words, for example, are given to the Synagogue longing for Christ's coming, and the Gospel's sweetness is set against the severity of the Law.

This short Latin grammatical treatise on speech (oratio) and the eight parts of speech has come down under the name of Cassiodorus, but it is considered spurious, and its real author and date are unknown. It opens by deriving oratio from "oris ratio," the reason of the mouth. It then treats the noun and verb as the principal parts and contrasts the classifications used by Aristotelians, Stoics, Greeks and Latins. It also explains which parts are inflected by case, tense or person, drawing examples from Virgil. It belongs to the tradition of late antique and early medieval school grammar.

De schematibus et tropis is an anonymous Latin treatise on the figures of speech (schemata) and tropes found in Scripture. It was once attributed to Cassiodorus, but its author is unknown, and so is its exact date. It opens by quoting Cassiodorus's preface to his commentary on the Psalms and Augustine's De doctrina christiana. With these it argues that the figures of rhetoric were first used in the divine Scriptures, and that pagan grammarians and rhetoricians only borrowed them later. The treatise belongs to the early medieval tradition of studying the Bible through grammar and rhetoric.

This Latin appendix is a modern editorial survey, not a patristic work. It lists the lost writings of Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia (died c. 407), and the writings falsely attributed to him. It argues that his tractates on the Gospel of Matthew originally began at the opening of the Gospel and probably went further than the surviving portion, which ends at Matthew 6:24. Among the lost writings it names the sections on Matthew 1–3 and 3:17–4, and several letters Chromatius is known to have sent to Ambrose, Jerome, John Chrysostom and the emperors Honorius and Arcadius.

This is a small group of Latin Christian poems of doubtful authorship, transmitted under the name of Claudianus Mamertus, the fifth-century priest of Vienne in Gaul. Earlier editors printed them among his works, taking them from an eighteenth-century Pesaro anthology of Christian poets. The first piece, a hexameter poem "against vain poets", urges a gifted poet to give up mythological subjects, such as the judgment of Paris and the war of the giants. Instead he should write about sacred themes, the origins of the world and the miracles of God. The true author or authors are uncertain.

Three Latin documents falsely attributed to or about the emperor Constantine the Great (d. 337), traditionally printed together as an appendix to his writings. The first is a letter falsely ascribed to Pope Miltiades that praises Constantine's generosity to the early Church; it is transmitted with the ninth-century Pseudo-Isidorean decretals. The second is the Constitutum Constantini, or Donation of Constantine, probably forged in the eighth century, which claims that the emperor granted authority over Rome and the West to Pope Sylvester. The third is a spurious treaty of alliance with the Armenian king Tiridates, written much later.

De Rebaptismate is an anonymous Latin treatise from the mid-third century. It was probably written around 256, during the controversy over baptism between Cyprian of Carthage and Pope Stephen I of Rome. Opposing Cyprian's position, the author argues that people baptized by heretics in the name of Jesus Christ should not be baptized again when they return to the Church. Instead, the bishop's laying on of hands, which confers the Holy Spirit, is enough. The work was handed down among Cyprian's writings, and its author's identity and place of origin remain unknown.

Ad Novatianum is an anonymous Latin treatise written in the mid-third century, probably in the 250s, by a bishop opposing the Roman schismatic Novatian. It has come down among the works attributed to Cyprian of Carthage, but it is not his. Its author is unknown, and scholars have proposed several candidates, including a Roman bishop. The treatise argues that Christians who lapsed during persecution should not be refused hope of pardon and readmission through penance. It attacks Novatian's rigorism as cruel and schismatic. It is an early witness to the third-century controversy over penance and the lapsed.

De duodecim abusivis saeculi ("On the Twelve Abuses of the World") is an anonymous Latin moral treatise, generally thought to have been written in Ireland in the seventh century. In the Middle Ages it circulated under the names of Cyprian of Carthage and Augustine. It lists twelve kinds of disorder, among them the wise man without works, the old man without religion, the unjust king and the negligent bishop, and gives a short chapter to each. Its account of the just and unjust king had a wide influence on later medieval ideas of Christian kingship.

De duodecim abusivis saeculi ("On the Twelve Abuses of the World") is an anonymous Latin moral treatise, generally thought to have been written in Ireland in the seventh century. In the Middle Ages it circulated under the names of Cyprian of Carthage and Augustine. It lists twelve kinds of disorder, among them the wise man without works, the old man without religion, the unjust king and the negligent bishop, and gives a short chapter to each. Its account of the just and unjust king had a wide influence on later medieval ideas of Christian kingship.

Oratio II is an anonymous Latin prayer handed down among the works falsely attributed to Cyprian of Carthage. One title presents it as the prayer that Cyprian of Antioch spoke on the day of his martyrdom. Its author and date are unknown. The speaker addresses God as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and of the prophets, apostles and martyrs. He confesses his sins and asks to be saved from death, recalling biblical examples such as Israel's escape from Egypt, Jonah, the penitent Ninevites and David.

De montibus Sina et Sion is an anonymous Latin treatise against the Jews. It was passed down among the works of Cyprian of Carthage but is not by him, and it is usually placed in third-century North Africa, though its date is uncertain. It contrasts Mount Sinai, where the Mosaic law was given, with Mount Sion, from which the new law goes forth. Using etymology and figurative readings of Scripture, it treats Sinai as earthly and Sion as heavenly and spiritual, fulfilled in Christ. It matters for its early Latin biblical quotations, its popular Latin style and its archaic Christology.

The Coena Cypriani ("Cyprian's Supper") is an anonymous Latin prose work, probably written in the fifth century and falsely attributed to Cyprian of Carthage. It is a comic tale of a wedding feast held by a king named Joel at Cana. Figures from both Testaments attend, and each one sits, eats, drinks, brings a gift or acts in a way that wittily recalls a detail of their biblical story. It may have served as a memory aid or as entertainment. It was very popular in the Middle Ages, and Hrabanus Maurus and John the Deacon both produced reworkings of it.

De revelatione capitis B. Joannis Baptistae is an anonymous Latin hagiographical account of the relics of John the Baptist, falsely attributed to Cyprian of Carthage. Drawing on Josephus and Rufinus's church history, it tells of John's beheading at Machaerus and his burial at Sebaste in Samaria. Pagans later desecrated and burned his bones, and monks rescued what remained and sent it through Philip of Jerusalem to Athanasius of Alexandria. Because it mentions Bishop Theophilus and Emperor Theodosius, it must postdate the late fourth century. Its exact date and author are unknown.

The Carmen de resurrectione mortuorum ad Felicem is an anonymous Latin poem in dactylic hexameters on the resurrection of the dead. It is addressed to a certain Felix. An early manuscript from Corbie attributes it to Cyprian, but its rough style and frequent breaches of metre rule out Cyprian of Carthage. Its date and author are disputed. The poem defends bodily resurrection against philosophers who denied it, describes the Last Judgement and the punishment of idolaters and persecutors, and shows traces of millenarian ideas.

Ad Vigilium episcopum de Iudaica incredulitate ("To Bishop Vigilius, on Jewish Unbelief") is a short Latin letter that came down among the spurious works of Cyprian of Carthage. In it a certain Celsus introduces his Latin translation of the Altercatio Iasonis et Papisci, a lost Greek dialogue in which a Jewish Christian argues with a Jew. The letter condemns Jewish refusal to accept Christ and presents the dialogue as a means of persuasion. The author and date are uncertain. Its chief value is as evidence for the lost dialogue.

This is a collection of Latin letters and decrees falsely attributed to Pope Damasus I (366–384). It includes letters addressed to Stephen and the bishops of Mauretania, to Prosper and the bishops of Numidia, to Aurelius of Carthage and to the bishops of Italy, along with a supposed exchange with Jerome. Most of these pieces come from the ninth-century Pseudo-Isidorian forgeries ascribed to "Isidore Mercator". Early modern scholars such as Philippe Labbe and Pierre Coustant showed that they were spurious. The texts still matter for the history of papal authority and canon law.

These are two short Latin poems in hexameters that were once attributed to Pope Damasus I (366–384) but are regarded as not by him. Their authorship and date are uncertain. The first is a verse epitaph for the presbyter Sisinnus, praising him as a worthy priest who was loyal to the Church and kept away from the imperial court. The second warns a fellow Christian. It opens by reworking the first line of Virgil's first Eclogue ("Tityre, tu…") and urges the reader to study Holy Scripture instead of vain fables, setting eternal life against endless punishment.

The Sermones are a small group of Latin sermons attributed to Eleutherius, traditionally bishop of Tournai in the early sixth century. Scholars generally regard the attribution as spurious, and the texts are thought to be later compositions, though their exact date and authorship are uncertain. The collection opens with a sermon or "confession" on the Holy Trinity. It sets out the unity of substance and the distinction of persons, and teaches that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both the Father and the Son. Its other pieces are short pastoral and doctrinal addresses.

These are Latin liturgical hymns for the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul. The first begins "Decora lux aeternitatis" and the second "Beate Pastor Petre." Tradition credited them to Elpis, said to have been the wife of Boethius, but that attribution is doubtful, so the author is called Pseudo-Elpis. The hymns praise Peter as keeper of heaven's gate and Paul as teacher of the nations. They honour Rome as the city made holy by the two apostles' martyrdom, and each ends with a doxology to the Trinity.

The Homiliae quaedam are a group of Latin homilies that were handed down under the name of Eucherius, bishop of Lyon (d. c. 449). Modern scholars do not accept that he wrote them, and their actual authors and dates are uncertain. They are generally placed in southern Gaul in the fifth or sixth century, where monastic preaching flourished. The first homily is addressed to monks. It urges them to make spiritual progress while there is still light, and gives a vivid picture of the soul at death, separated from its body and led away to judgement.

This short Latin letter is attributed to Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, but its authenticity is doubted and its real author and date are uncertain. The writer asks the priest Philo to visit the monastery of Île Barbe (Insula Barbara) near Lyon. There he is to encourage Abbot Maximus, who is said to be thinking of leaving because many donors, out of fear of foreign peoples, had stopped their offerings. The bishop promises support and plans to spend Lent there to finish a work already begun. He also orders grain, wine, cheese and oil to be sent to the community.

De sancta Trinitate confessio is a short Latin profession of faith on the Trinity. It has come down under the name of Eusebius of Vercelli, the fourth-century bishop and opponent of Arianism, but it is not considered his work. Its real author and date are unknown. In numbered sections it confesses one undivided Trinity of one substance, nature and majesty. The Father is presented as the unbegotten source of the whole Godhead. The Son is eternally born of the Father's substance and is not made. The text explains the Nicene term homoousios by breaking the Greek word into its parts.

These are forged Latin letters attributed to Pope Eusebius, who was bishop of Rome briefly around 309–310. They belong to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, a collection of false papal decrees compiled in Francia around 847–852. The first letter is addressed to the bishops of Gaul. It forbids lay people and their dependants to bring accusations against clergy, limits who may act as accuser in church courts, and says converted heretics should be received by the laying on of hands. Like the rest of the collection, the letters aimed to protect bishops and strengthen Roman authority.

The Decreta Eutychiani papae is a short series of Latin canons falsely attributed to Pope Eutychian, bishop of Rome in the late third century, and printed in Philippe Labbe's collection of church councils. The canons forbid obeying a bishop or abbot who orders Masses for heretics. They also bar abbesses from veiling virgins or widows and impose severe penance and exclusion for perjury. Their language and concerns belong to a much later period, probably early medieval, and some were later taken into canonical collections such as Ivo of Chartres's.

These Latin letters and decrees are falsely attributed to Eutychian, bishop of Rome from about 275 to 283. They belong to the forged papal decretals known as the Pseudo-Isidorian collection, compiled in Francia in the mid-ninth century. The first letter is addressed to a bishop John and the bishops of Baetica in Spain. It sets out the doctrine of the Incarnation, teaching that Christ is true God and true man, with each nature keeping its own properties. It is made up largely of borrowed phrases from later authors such as Leo the Great and Hilary of Poitiers.

This is a group of four Latin letters attributed to Pope Felix I, bishop of Rome around 269–274, but now recognised as spurious. Letters of this kind belong to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, forgeries produced in the Frankish realm in the mid-ninth century. The first letter is addressed to a bishop Paternus. It deals with ecclesiastical trials, the accusation and defence of clergy, and procedures against accused bishops. Like other Pseudo-Isidorian texts, it borrows freely from later writers, including Leo the Great and Gregory the Great.

The Liber de praedestinatione et gratia is an anonymous Latin treatise on predestination and grace. It has been handed down among the doubtful or spurious works of Fulgentius of Ruspe, but its author and exact date are unknown. It probably belongs to the late patristic debates on grace that followed Augustine. The work starts from Pauline texts that seem to conflict, such as "he has mercy on whom he wills" (Romans 9:18) and God "wills all men to be saved" (1 Timothy 2:4). It tries to reconcile them in a way that keeps God both just and all-powerful.

The Sermones octoginta are a collection of eighty Latin sermons that were once attributed to Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa (died c. 533). Their author is unknown, and the attribution to Fulgentius is now considered false. The sermons are pastoral addresses to a congregation that explain passages of the Gospels and other Scripture. The first sermon begins by asking listeners to hear the word of God attentively whoever preaches it, and it urges moderation and sobriety when interpreting the Gospel.

The Canones Gelasio ascripti are a gathering of Latin decrees and canonical fragments that circulated under the name of Pope Gelasius I (492–496). An early modern editor compiled them mainly from the medieval canon-law collections of Burchard of Worms, Ivo of Chartres and Gratian. The editor stated that he did not consider all of them genuine. The excerpts deal with church discipline and sacramental practice. One, addressed to the bishops Majoricus and John, forbids receiving the body of Christ without the cup. Together they show how widely canonists cited Gelasius's authority.

The Expositio brevis antiquae liturgiae Gallicanae is a short Latin commentary in two letters that explains the order of the Gallican Mass. It names Germanus, bishop of Paris (d. 576), as its author, but it is generally thought to be a later work, usually dated to around 700 or the eighth century. It goes through the Mass step by step, from the opening antiphon, the call for silence and the Aius (the Trisagion, sung in Greek), and gives each element an allegorical meaning. It is one of the most important witnesses to the Gallican liturgy before Roman practice replaced it.

This is a collection of Latin hymns for the Divine Office that medieval tradition attributed to Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604). The hymns are arranged by day and canonical hour, beginning with the Sunday night office, Lauds and Vespers. They include well-known pieces such as "Primo dierum omnium," "Nocte surgentes," "Ecce iam noctis" and "Lucis Creator optime." Most are written in Ambrosian-style iambic dimeters, while some use Sapphic stanzas. Scholars generally regard Gregory's authorship as doubtful, and the hymns' actual origins and dates are uncertain. Many of them nonetheless held a lasting place in the Western breviary.

The Concordia quorumdam testimoniorum S. Scripturae ("Harmony of Certain Testimonies of Holy Scripture") is a short Latin treatise once transmitted under the name of Pope Gregory the Great but now considered spurious. Its author and date are unknown. It takes passages of Scripture that seem to contradict each other and reconciles them through a series of questions and answers. The first case sets Paul's calling himself a "servant" of Christ beside Christ's words "I will not call you servants, but friends." The answer distinguishes a servitude of fear from a servitude of love.

This is a group of Latin hagiographical writings handed down under the name of Gregory of Tours, the sixth-century bishop and historian of Merovingian Gaul, but of doubtful or disputed authorship. The main piece is a book of the miracles of the apostle Andrew. Its preface says it is a shortened version of an older Acts of Andrew, which some had rejected as apocryphal because it was too wordy. The book tells of Andrew's preaching in Achaia, his martyrdom, and the oil said to flow from his tomb. Such texts show how apocryphal apostolic legends were reworked for Latin readers.

De excidio Hierosolymitano is an anonymous Christian Latin history in five books, usually dated to around 370. It is a free adaptation of the Jewish War of Flavius Josephus and covers events from the Maccabees to the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple by Titus in AD 70. The author treats the city's fall as divine punishment of the Jews. The work was once ascribed to Ambrose of Milan, but this remains uncertain. The name "Hegesippus" probably comes from a corruption of "Iosippus", a form of Josephus's name. The book was widely read in the Middle Ages.

This is a short Latin summary, or recapitulation, of the Roman siege and destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. It is connected with De excidio Hierosolymitano, the fourth-century Christian Latin adaptation of Josephus's Jewish War whose anonymous author is known as Pseudo-Hegesippus. Its author and date are uncertain. It dates the catastrophe to the forty-second year after Christ's Passion and the first year of Vespasian's reign. In rhetorical laments, it calls on Moses, Aaron and Joshua to witness God's people perishing by their own hands through civil strife, famine and slaughter.

De vitis apostolorum is a short Latin catalogue of the apostles and early disciples, wrongly attributed to Jerome. Erasmus found it inserted into a manuscript of the Greek version of Jerome's De viris illustribus, which circulated under the name of Sophronius. For each figure, including Andrew, James son of Zebedee, Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, Simon the Canaanite and Matthias, it briefly records the regions where he preached and where he died or was buried. Its date and author are unknown.

The Epistola ad Desiderium de duodecim doctoribus is a short Latin letter that briefly describes twelve Church writers, presented as "luminaries" shining across the world. It was long transmitted under the name of Jerome, and also under Bede's as De luminaribus ecclesiae, but its author and date are unknown. Erasmus and later critics rejected it as spurious, pointing to its clumsy style, its chronological errors and its odd judgments of the writers it discusses. It also mentions heretics such as Pelagius and Jovinian, whose writings it censures.

This short Latin letter is addressed to a "brother Desiderius" and falsely attributed to Jerome. Its author and date are unknown. The writer says he will describe, briefly and kindly, the church writers who shed light on the obscurities of Scripture. He compares them to lights shining in the firmament. He then offers short, image-filled sketches of individual authors, beginning with Augustine as an eagle soaring over mountain peaks, Hilary as a lamp of the churches and Origen as a lofty but wandering thinker. It belongs to the many spurious works that circulated under Jerome's name.

The Liber nominum locorum ex Actis is a short Latin gazetteer of the places named in the Acts of the Apostles. It was transmitted among the works of Jerome but is not by him, and its author and date are uncertain. The entries are arranged alphabetically, from Acheldema, Asia, Egypt, Arabia and Ethiopia onward. Each gives the biblical reference with a brief geographical or historical description. The material draws on earlier Latin geographical writing and on Jerome's own work on biblical place-names. Like other early medieval aids to reading Scripture, it was meant to help readers understand the biblical text.

The Hebraici alphabeti interpretatio is a short anonymous Latin glossary that gives the meanings of the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet. For example, aleph is glossed as "thousand" or "teaching" and beth as "house". It has come down among the spurious works of Jerome, and most of its glosses are taken from his writings. Its date and author are unknown. A brief list of ten Hebrew names of God, such as Sabaoth, Adonai and El, follows it and is attributed to a certain Symeon the Jew. Works like this show how medieval Latin readers learned about Hebrew.

De Deo et nominibus ejus ("On God and His Names") is a short Latin treatise wrongly attributed to Jerome. Its author and date are unknown. It opens by praising Jerome as the first to translate the interpretation of Hebrew names into Latin. It then explains the ten Hebrew names of God, including El, Elohim, Sabaoth, Elyon and Ehyeh, and gives their Latin meanings and etymologies with a Trinitarian reading. Its wording closely follows the opening of Book VII of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies.

De benedictionibus Jacob patriarchae is a short anonymous Latin commentary on the blessings Jacob gives his twelve sons in Genesis 49. It has been handed down among the spurious works of Augustine and has also been linked with Jerome; its real author and date are unknown. Written as questions and answers, it says the blessings should be read both historically and allegorically. Historically, they refer to the division of the Promised Land among Jacob's descendants. Allegorically, they point to Christ and the Church in the last days.

This is an anonymous Latin commentary on the blessings Jacob gave his twelve sons in Genesis 49. It has come down under the name of Jerome but is not his work, and its date and real author are uncertain. The author says the patriarch's prophecy can't be read purely literally, but its historical meaning shouldn't be lost in allegory either. So he first sets out the literal sense as a foundation. He then turns to the spiritual meaning where the letter falls short, taking each son in turn, beginning with Reuben.

The Decem tentationes populi Israel in deserto ("The Ten Temptations of the People of Israel in the Desert") is a short Latin exegetical tract once wrongly attributed to Jerome. Its real author and date are unknown. It takes the place names of Deuteronomy 1:1 as Moses' brief and veiled rebuke of Israel, and links each one to a separate occasion in Exodus and Numbers when the people tested God in the wilderness. The ten are counted to match Numbers 14:22, where God says Israel has tempted him "ten times."

This is a brief Latin summary, falsely attributed to Jerome, that lists the ten times Israel tempted God in the wilderness, alluding to Numbers 14:22. In order it names the Red Sea, the golden calf, the complaints about food and the fiery serpents, the waters of contradiction before and after Miriam's death, the rotting manna, the quails, Korah's rebellion and the spies. It works as a recapitulation of a longer treatise on the same subject. Its author and date are unknown.

The Commentarius in canticum Debborae is a short Latin commentary on the Song of Deborah in Judges 5. It was once attributed to Jerome and printed among his works, but it is now considered pseudonymous; its real author and date are uncertain. It goes through the song verse by verse, mixing historical and etymological explanation with allegory. For example, it identifies Barak as Deborah's husband Lapidoth by playing on the meanings "lightning" and "flash", and it reads the shaking earth as the theophany at Sinai. Some of its explanations parallel traditions found in Jewish exegesis.

The Quaestiones Hebraicae in libros Regum et Paralipomenon is an anonymous Latin commentary on the books of Samuel–Kings and Chronicles. It was long passed down among the works of Jerome, but it is not his, and its author and date are uncertain. It is generally placed in the early medieval or Carolingian period. Working verse by verse, it explains Hebrew names and draws on Jewish traditions and interpretations, for example on Elkanah's descent. Rabanus Maurus used it in his commentary on Kings, which makes it a witness to Jewish learning reaching Latin biblical scholarship.

The Excerpta ex commentario in Job is a short Latin commentary on the Book of Job. It was once attributed to Jerome but is now classed as pseudonymous, and its author and date are unknown. It opens by explaining that Scripture is read historically, allegorically and morally, and that some verses of Job cannot be taken literally. Its methods and images, including Scripture as a river where the simple can wade and an elephant can swim, closely follow Gregory the Great's Moralia in Job.

This is a short Latin commentary on Isaiah, a "little abridgement" on a few chapters, traditionally attributed to Jerome but not his work. Its author and date are unknown. A prologue presents the prophets as spiritual physicians treating the wounds of the soul. The twelve minor prophets set out in brief the same pattern that the major prophets develop at length: humanity, sick through its own fault, is healed after death by Christ, the true physician. The commentary then glosses selected verses in both their historical and their tropological sense.

In Lamentationes Jeremiae is an anonymous Latin commentary on the Lamentations of Jeremiah. It was handed down among the works of Jerome but is not by him, and its author and date are unknown; it is generally placed in the early Middle Ages. The commentary works through the alphabetic acrostic of the Hebrew poem and reads each letter for its symbolic meaning; aleph, for example, is taken to mean "doctrine". It explains the laments in three senses: historically, of Israel in captivity; spiritually, of the Church as the city of God; and morally, of each individual soul.

Commentarii in librum Job is an anonymous Latin commentary on the Book of Job, handed down among the works of Jerome but not by him. Scholars usually connect it with the Job commentary of Philip the Presbyter, a fifth-century disciple of Jerome, of which it appears to be a reworking. Its date and exact authorship remain uncertain. The commentary reads Job allegorically. Job is a figure of Christ, his three friends stand for heretics who blaspheme Christ under his name, and Elihu represents philosophers outside the faith who lie in wait for the Church.

The Breviarium in Psalmos is a Latin commentary on the whole Psalter, long transmitted among the works of Jerome but now regarded as spurious. Its preface borrows from Jerome's genuine Commentarioli in Psalmos, which presents the notes as brief remarks supplementing Origen's Enchiridion on the Psalms. Its true author and date are uncertain, and it is generally considered a later compilation, probably early medieval. Psalm by psalm, it offers short explanations of titles and verses, reading all the psalms as referring to Christ.

A Latin commentary on the Psalms handed down under the name of Jerome but generally treated as pseudonymous. Its date and author are uncertain. It works through the Psalter psalm by psalm. It opens with a comparison, taken ultimately from Origen, of the Psalter to a great house: the Holy Spirit is the key to its main door, but each psalm is a room with its own key. The comment on Psalm 1 rejects reading the "blessed man" as Christ. The work shows how Jerome's name and Origen's methods of exegesis shaped Latin interpretation of the Psalms.

This is a short Latin preface to the seven Catholic Epistles that circulated in Vulgate Bibles under the name of Jerome. Its style and wording show it is not his, but it was written by the mid-sixth century, since it appears in the Codex Fuldensis. It argues that the Latin codices should follow the Greek order of the letters: James, Peter, John and Jude. It is best known for accusing unfaithful translators of leaving out the witness of Father, Word and Spirit in 1 John. This makes it early evidence in the debate over the Comma Johanneum.

This is a collection of Latin letters and short treatises that were handed down under the name of Jerome (d. 420) but are not his work. Early modern editors of Jerome set them apart as spurious. Their authors, dates and origins vary, and many are unknown. The collection opens with the Letter to Demetrias, which Bede had already rejected as Jerome's. Augustine's testimony shows that Pelagius wrote it around 413. Such misattributions helped circulate writings that might otherwise have been lost, including some by authors whose teaching was condemned.

The Gospel of the Nativity of Mary (Libellus de Nativitate Sanctae Mariae) is an anonymous Latin apocryphal narrative, probably written in France in the tenth century, though possibly the late ninth. It reworks the first chapters of the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew together with material from Matthew and Luke. It tells of Mary's parents Joachim and Anna, her birth, her upbringing in the Temple, and events up to the Annunciation. It long circulated under Jerome's name and was widely used in the medieval West, including in the Golden Legend.

The Liber comitis, or Comes, is a Latin lectionary that sets out the readings from the epistles, the prophets and the Gospels for Mass through the liturgical year, starting with the vigil of Christmas. Medieval tradition attributed it to Jerome, but that attribution is spurious. Its prologue says that this form of the book was expanded by Theotinchus, a priest, at the request of Hechiardus, count of Amiens. It probably dates from the early medieval Frankish period, though the exact date is uncertain. It is important evidence for the history of the Latin liturgy and of systems of biblical readings.

The Expositio quatuor Evangeliorum is a Latin commentary on the four Gospels that was handed down under the name of Jerome, though he did not write it. Modern scholarship generally regards it as an early medieval work, probably Hiberno-Latin, from around the seventh or eighth century. Its author and exact date are unknown. The commentary uses allegory and numerical symbolism heavily. It links the four evangelists to the four elements, the four rivers of Paradise and the four cardinal virtues. It also offers brief glosses on passages of the Gospels.

This Latin commentary on the Gospel of Mark was transmitted among the works of Jerome but is not by him. It is usually dated to the first half of the seventh century and is often thought to be the work of an Irish author; Cummian has been suggested, though this is uncertain. The preface says that earlier interpreters had largely passed over Mark because his Gospel overlaps so much with Matthew's. The commentary combines historical and mystical readings, and it is among the earliest surviving Latin commentaries on Mark.

This short Latin preface to the Gospel of Luke belongs to the so-called Monarchian Prologues. These prefaces to the four Gospels circulated in Vulgate manuscripts and were long falsely attributed to Jerome. It presents Luke as a Syrian of Antioch, a physician and companion of Paul, who never married and died in Bithynia at seventy-four. It says he wrote his Gospel in Achaia after Matthew and Mark, and it explains his genealogy and his authorship of Acts. Its date and origin are disputed; many scholars place it in the fourth century.

Ad monachos ("To the Monks") is a short Latin work of moral and ascetic advice. It has come down among the writings attributed to Jerome but is not by him, and its author and date are unknown. Written as a series of brief, pointed maxims, it urges monks to aim for perfect virtue rather than mediocrity. It recommends giving up possessions, remembering death, eating simple food, praying often and keeping vigils, and staying away from flatterers, banquets and worldly company. Several of its phrases echo Jerome's own letters.

The Canones poenitentiales is a short Latin penitential, a handbook that sets out the penance due for particular sins. It was transmitted under the name of Jerome, but the attribution is false; it belongs to the penitential literature of the early medieval West, and its exact date and origin are uncertain. It sets penances graded by the sinner's rank, whether bishop, priest, deacon, monk or layman. Offences covered include drunkenness and vomiting, homicide and complicity in murder. Typical penalties are fasting on bread and water, deposition from office and pilgrimage.

This Latin letter serves as the preface to the Comes, or Liber comitis, a lectionary listing the Scripture readings for the feasts of the church year. It is addressed to a "venerable brother" Constantius and claims Jerome as its author, but the attribution is spurious and its date is uncertain. The writer explains that the book, commonly called the Comes, gathers suitable readings from the prophets, the apostles and the Gospels, arranged in order beginning with the Nativity vigil. The letter is an early witness to how the Latin liturgical lectionary was organised.

This short Latin sermon, or narrative, tells of a miracle performed by Genesius, martyr of Arles. Manuscripts attribute it to Hilary of Arles (d. 449), but the attribution is doubtful, and its author and date are uncertain. On the saint's feast day, crowds of pilgrims crossed the Rhône to the place of his martyrdom and his tomb. The pontoon bridge collapsed beneath them, and the narrator, who claims to have watched it happen, credits their rescue to the martyr. The text is evidence for the cult of Genesius in late antique Arles.

The Versus in natali Machabaeorum martyrum is an anonymous Latin poem in hexameters for the feast of the Maccabean martyrs. It has been handed down among works attributed to Hilary of Arles, but the attribution is not accepted, and its author and date are uncertain. It retells the story in 2 Maccabees 7. King Antiochus tries to make a mother and her seven sons give up their ancestral law with promises and then torture. The mother refuses and puts her hope in God's promise of eternal life.

The Metrum in Genesim ad Leonem papam is a short Latin poem retelling the opening chapters of Genesis. Manuscripts attribute it to a Hilary, but its true author is unknown. It has been linked to Hilary of Arles and to Hilary of Poitiers, and it is usually placed in 5th-century Gaul. The poem opens with elegiac couplets addressed to a Pope Leo, who had asked for the work. Hexameters follow, praising the eternal, self-originating Creator and describing how the world was shaped out of formless chaos. It belongs to the late antique tradition of biblical epic.

The Epistola seu libellus is a short Latin instructional treatise. It has come down under the name of Hilary, but its authorship is doubtful and its date uncertain. It sets out the order in which converts should be taught the faith. Jews, who already know the Law and the Prophets, need chiefly to believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God and to be baptised in his name. Gentiles must first give up idols, then learn belief in one God the Creator and the divine inspiration of Scripture. This makes it a witness to early catechetical method.

The Liber de Patris et Filii unitate is a short Latin treatise on the unity of the Father and the Son. It was falsely attributed to Hilary of Poitiers and first printed by Froben in 1535. It is not an original work. An unknown compiler assembled it mainly from books two and nine of Hilary's De Trinitate. It closes with an appendix on the names of Christ, taken from the De fide orthodoxa, which is usually credited to Gregory of Elvira. Its date and author are unknown.

De essentia Patris et Filii contra haereticos ("On the Essence of the Father and the Son, against the Heretics") is a short anonymous Latin treatise once attributed to Hilary of Poitiers. It is a cento, a patchwork of passages taken from books seven and eight of Hilary's De Trinitate. These passages defend the unity of nature between the Father and the Son against Arian teaching. Its compiler and date are unknown. The work was published from a manuscript of the Abbey of Saint-Victor, and Jacques Gillot was the first to recognise that it was assembled from Hilary's genuine writings.

Ad caeli clara non sum dignus sidera is an anonymous Latin penitential hymn once attributed to Hilary of Poitiers. Its date is unknown. Some identified it with the evening hymn that Hilary's letter to his daughter Abra mentions. Opening with the stars, it is a general confession of sins such as lust, pride, envy and vainglory, and it asks pardon through Christ's mercy. It condemns Arius, Sabellius and Simon Magus. Critics reject Hilary's authorship because of its unpolished rhythmic verse, counted by syllables, and its masculine speaker.

This is a small group of spurious letters falsely attributed to Pope Innocent I (401–417), all concerned with the exile and death of John Chrysostom. The best known has Innocent excommunicating the emperor Arcadius and the empress Eudoxia, deposing Arsacius and anathematizing Theophilus of Alexandria. Other pieces purport to be exchanges with the imperial court. Most survive only in Greek, in the Byzantine historians Nicephorus Callistus and Michael Glycas. They are judged forgeries mainly because they present Eudoxia as still alive after Chrysostom's death, although she died in 404, three years before him.

This Latin letter is forged in the name of Pope John III (561–574) and addressed to the bishops of Germany and Gaul. It belongs to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, the collection of forged papal and conciliar texts produced in the Frankish realm around the mid-ninth century. The letter condemns chorbishops who confirm by the laying on of hands and perform other acts reserved to bishops. It also claims that Peter himself handed the apostolic see to Clement I, and it describes the duties of those who shepherd Christ's flock.

This is a very short Latin letter that claims to be from Pope John III (561–574) to Edaldus, archbishop of Vienne. It is generally regarded as spurious, and Philippe Labbe pointed out that its consular dating is false. The letter says that the order of the Mass differs between churches such as Alexandria, Jerusalem, Ephesus and Rome, and tells Vienne to follow Roman custom. It also sends the pallium through a priest named Felix, together with hair of Saint Paul, whose disciple was said to have founded the church of Vienne. It was first printed in the Bibliotheca Floriacensis.

This is a small collection of Latin verses linked to Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636). The main group is a series of short verse inscriptions said to have been read in his episcopal library at Seville. They describe its holdings of sacred and secular books, including the Old and New Testaments. They also present epigrams on individual authors such as Origen, Hilary of Poitiers and Ambrose.
