Other poems attributed to Isidore accompany them. The verses do not follow strict rules of metre or classical Latin. Whether Isidore wrote them is debated.

The Expositio in Canticum canticorum is a short anonymous Latin commentary on the Song of Songs. It was once attributed to Isidore of Seville and was later printed among the spurious works linked to him. Its author and date are unknown. The commentary works verse by verse and reads the Song allegorically as a dialogue between Christ and the Church. It contrasts the sweetness of the Gospel with the severity of the Law, and it links the anointing to baptism and the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

The Conflict of Vices and Virtues is a Latin moral treatise by Ambrose Autpert, the Frankish Benedictine abbot of San Vincenzo al Volturno, written between about 760 and his death in 784. In the Middle Ages it circulated under the names of Augustine and Isidore of Seville. Taking up Paul's saying that all who live godly lives will suffer persecution, it argues that in peaceful times Christians are persecuted from within by the vices. It then pairs each vice with the virtue that opposes it. The treatise was widely copied and read as a guide to the spiritual life.

Expositio in missa is a short anonymous Latin commentary on the words of the Mass. It has been passed down under the name of Isidore of Seville (d. 636), but the attribution is spurious, and its real author and date are unknown. It is generally placed among the early medieval Latin explanations of the liturgy. Going through the rite phrase by phrase, it explains the dialogue and formulas, among them "Dominus vobiscum", "Oremus", the Trinitarian ending of prayers, "Amen" and "Sursum corda". It teaches the meaning of each response and draws out the doctrine of the Trinity's equality and eternity.

The Sententiarum liber quartus is an anonymous Latin compilation that was handed down as a fourth book to the three books of Sentences by Isidore of Seville. Isidore did not write it, and its date and author are unknown. Its opening chapters deal with church leaders: how they should live, keep their thoughts pure and set an example to their flock. The text reworks material from Gregory the Great's Pastoral Rule and from Taio of Zaragoza's Sentences. It shows how Gregorian ideas about pastoral leadership spread through collections of maxims ascribed to Isidore.

The Exhortatio humilitatis (Exhortation to Humility) is a short Latin moral treatise by Martin of Braga, the sixth-century bishop and missionary among the Suevi of Gallaecia. It was written between about 556 and 580, and some manuscripts wrongly attribute it to Isidore of Seville. It is addressed to someone who holds authority over others. In a deliberately plain style, it warns against flattery and pride and urges rulers to prefer useful truth to pleasing words. The treatise belongs to Martin's group of short moral writings influenced by Seneca.

The Testimonia divinae Scripturae et Patrum is an anonymous Latin florilegium, a collection of quotations arranged by topic, that has come down among the spurious works attributed to Isidore of Seville. Its author and date are unknown. Short chapters gather proof-texts from the Prophets, Proverbs, the Gospels and the Epistles on subjects such as the oneness of God, the distinction of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and turning from the world. It is notable for quoting the Johannine Comma (1 John 5:7–8) as a witness to the Trinity.

This is a small collection of Latin sermons that circulated under the name of Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636) but are not considered authentic. Their real authors and dates are unknown. The first sermon, headed "Ad carnes tollendas", is for the start of Lent. It urges the faithful to keep the fast on every day except Sundays and sets out how the sick, who are excused, should eat in private without tempting the healthy to break the fast. The collection shows the kind of practical pastoral preaching on church discipline that was attached to Isidore's name.

De ecclesiasticis dogmatibus ("On Church Doctrines") is a short Latin summary of Christian belief, set out in numbered chapters. It is generally attributed to Gennadius, a priest of Marseilles who died around 496, and was written in the later fifth century. It begins with a confession of the Trinity, saying the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. It then condemns heresies and deals with the Incarnation, the soul, free will, grace and church practice. In the Middle Ages it was widely read, and copies passed it down under the names of Augustine and Isidore of Seville.

This short Latin treatise on the distinction between the active and contemplative lives was handed down among the works of Isidore of Seville but is considered spurious. Its author and date are unknown. In numbered sentences, it relates the active life to love of neighbour and the contemplative life to love of God, and holds that each needs the other. It links marriage to the active life and virginity and continence to the contemplative, drawing on Paul, the Gospels and Isaiah.

Norma vivendi ("Rule of Living") is a short Latin moral exhortation that has come down among the writings falsely attributed to Isidore of Seville, and is printed among the spurious works in editions of his writings. Its author and date are unknown. It speaks to a "son" in short, balanced, rhythmic sentences that resemble Isidore's Synonyma. It urges him to avoid sin and to bear insults and hardship with patience and meekness. He should bless those who curse him, overcome malice with kindness and make amends with any brother he has wronged.

The Exhortatio poenitendi cum consolatione et misericordia Dei is an anonymous Latin poem in rhythmic verse, addressed to a soul that fears the coming judgement. It has been handed down among the spurious works of Isidore of Seville. Its author and date are uncertain. The poem urges the troubled soul to stop mourning lost worldly goods and honours and to weep instead for its sins. It presents suffering as God's chastisement and calls for confession and amendment of life. It ends with comfort in God's mercy. In theme and style it recalls Isidore's Synonyma.

The Lamentum poenitentiae ("Lament of Penitence") is a Latin rhythmic poem of penitence. It has been transmitted among works wrongly attributed to Isidore of Seville, and its true author and date are unknown. In six-line stanzas of alternating eight- and seven-syllable lines, a sinner speaks to Christ. He confesses his guilt, laments his long afflictions and pleads for mercy rather than strict justice. The language echoes the Psalms and Lamentations. Its opening stanzas all begin with the letter A, which suggests an alphabetical arrangement. The poem is an example of early medieval Latin devotional verse on repentance.

The Oratio pro correptione vitae ("Prayer for the amendment of life") is a Latin penitential prayer transmitted under the name of Isidore of Seville. It is generally regarded as spurious, and its real author and date are unknown. The speaker addresses God as the "Father of mercies" and confesses that a sinner's recognition of sin, repentance and conversion are entirely God's gift, citing Jeremiah 10:23, Romans 9:16 and Exodus 33:19. The prayer then asks for mercy, deliverance from sin and help in reforming one's life. It belongs to the early medieval tradition of private devotional prayers of confession.

The Oratio contra insidias diaboli ("Prayer against the snares of the devil") is a short Latin devotional prayer transmitted among the spurious works attributed to Isidore of Seville. It is not regarded as his, and its real author and date are unknown. The speaker addresses Christ as teacher, creator, redeemer and judge, and as the strongest warrior and ever-victorious conqueror. He confesses his sins and frailty, then asks for forgiveness and protection against the devil, the "roaring lion". He also prays to be brought to the contemplation of God, where he can no longer go astray.

The Liber de ortu et obitu patrum is an anonymous Latin collection of short biographical notices on biblical figures. It was falsely attributed to Isidore of Seville and is distinct from his genuine work of the same name. It begins with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. For each figure it records family, birthplace, chief deeds, age at death and burial place, and it often reads them as types of Christ. Its date and origin are uncertain. Scholars have commonly linked it to early medieval Irish learning, which makes it evidence for how Isidore's handbooks were imitated and expanded.

The Liber de numeris is an anonymous Latin treatise on the mystical and allegorical meaning of numbers. It was once attributed to Isidore of Seville, but is now generally regarded as a later Hiberno-Latin work, probably from the eighth century. Taking the numbers from one to twenty-four in turn, it lists the things in Scripture, the faith and creation that each number signifies, beginning with the oneness of God. It illustrates early medieval Irish exegesis and its liking for enumeration and number symbolism.

The Glossae in sacram Scripturam are an anonymous Latin collection of short glosses on the Bible, transmitted under the name of Isidore of Seville but not regarded as his work. Their date and author are unknown. Taking the biblical books in order, beginning with Genesis, the glosses explain individual words and phrases. They give brief synonyms for rare terms, explain proper names and add short allegorical or moral comments. The collection shows the glossary tradition that early medieval readers used to study the Latin Bible.

The Differentiarum sive de proprietate sermonum liber ("Book of Differences, or On the Proper Use of Words") is a short Latin glossary of synonyms that was once attributed to Isidore of Seville but is now regarded as spurious. Its author and date are unknown. Each numbered entry follows the formula "inter X et Y hoc interest" to tell apart words with similar meanings, such as polliceri and promittere, flumen and fluvius, or innocens and innoxius. It belongs to the late antique and early medieval tradition of differentiae, the same genre as Isidore's genuine Differentiae.

The Letter to Dionysius is a short Christological letter that circulated under the name of Pope Julius I of Rome. It is now generally regarded as a forgery by followers of Apollinaris of Laodicea, written in the later fourth century. It attacks those who speak of "two natures" in Christ and links them with the followers of Paul of Samosata. Against them it argues that the incarnate Word is a single nature. Its false papal authority later gave "one nature" language weight in the fifth-century Christological controversies.

These are letters circulated under the name of Pope Julius I (d. 352). They are generally thought to be the work of Apollinaris of Laodicea or his followers in the later fourth century. Among them is a letter to a bishop Dionysius. It accuses those who speak of "two natures" in Christ of repeating Paul of Samosata's division of Christ, and it insists on one nature and one person of the incarnate Word. Because they carried a pope's authority, these forgeries influenced Cyril of Alexandria, Eutyches and later Miaphysite theology. One letter survives in an old Latin version.

The Triumphus Christi heroicus is a short anonymous Latin poem in dactylic hexameters about Christ's descent into hell after the crucifixion. It was once attributed to the fourth-century Spanish poet Juvencus, but the attribution is spurious, and its real author and date are unknown. The poem describes creation mourning at the Passion. Pluto, prince of the underworld, then calls his followers to arms. Christ breaks through the darkness in shining light, and the gates fall before him. In the manner of Virgil, it mixes classical mythological imagery with biblical language, especially Psalm 24 (23): "Lift up your gates."

This is a group of Latin sermons and tracts that have been handed down under the name of Pope Leo I (the Great, d. 461) but are not accepted as his work. Their authors and dates are unknown. One of them is a treatise against the errors of Eutyches. Some manuscripts give it the title of Leo's letter to Flavian of Constantinople, the Tome, and Gerardus Vossius first printed it in 1604. Such pieces show how Leo's reputation as a teacher of Christological orthodoxy drew other writings under his name.

This is a supplementary section printed with the letters of Pope Leo the Great (d. 461). It belongs to the eighteenth-century critical tradition of Leo's works and was later reprinted in Migne's Patrologia Latina. It is ascribed to "Pseudo-Leo", which suggests that it gathers documents wrongly or doubtfully attributed to Leo. Its editorial preface compares the manuscript evidence with the rival Roman edition printed by Giuseppe Collini and points out errors in how that edition cites Vatican manuscripts. The section matters for separating Leo's genuine correspondence from spurious material.

This is a collection of Latin letters and canons falsely attributed to Pope Leo I (440–461), traditionally printed as an appendix to his genuine correspondence. The opening letter is addressed to the bishops of Germany and Gaul. It claims to report a Roman synod and forbids chorepiscopi, whom it treats as equal to presbyters, to consecrate altars and churches, citing Moses and Aaron as types of the high priesthood. Scholars generally regard such pieces as later forgeries. The letter on chorepiscopi is usually linked to the ninth-century Carolingian campaign against chorepiscopi associated with the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals.

De professione fidei, also called Fides S. Luciferi, is a short Latin profession of faith that bears the name of Lucifer, the fourth-century bishop of Cagliari known for his strong opposition to Arianism. It survives in an early medieval codex of the Ambrosian Library in Milan, where it stands among other credal texts attributed to Ambrose, Athanasius and the Council of Nicaea. Bernard de Montfaucon first drew attention to it. Whether Lucifer actually wrote it is doubtful, and it is usually counted among the works falsely attributed to him. Its date and real author are unknown.

This forged papal letter claims to be from Pope Lucius I (253–254) to the bishops of Gaul and Spain. It belongs to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, which were compiled in the Frankish kingdom around 847–852. The letter rules that a bishop must always keep two presbyters and three deacons with him as witnesses. It also covers accusations against bishops and their right of appeal, and says a metropolitan and his suffragan bishops should act together. Finally, it condemns as sacrilegious thieves anyone who seizes church property or the offerings of the faithful.

This short series of Latin canons on clerical discipline was taken from Gratian's Decretum (c. 1140), which attributed them to Pope Lucius I (253–254). The attribution is spurious. Some passages actually come from the apocryphal second letter of Clement to James and from early medieval penitentials, which were passed down partly through the Pseudo-Isidorian forgeries. The decrees require clerics to remain continent after ordination and forbid them to visit women alone or live with them. Anyone who breaks these rules is to be deposed or kept from the altar.

This Latin letter claims to be from Pope Marcellinus (296–304) to a bishop named Salomon. In fact it is a forgery, one of the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals compiled in Francia around 847–852. It answers people who held that the Father is greater than the Son. They argued that sacrifice is offered to the Father alone, cited Psalm 82, and pointed to Christ's cry on the cross. Like other Pseudo-Isidorian pieces, it is pieced together from older texts, including a letter of Leo the Great and the anti-Arian treatise Contra Varimadum.

This Latin letter is attributed to Pope Marcellinus (296–304) and addressed to the bishops of the East. It is in fact a forgery from the Pseudo-Isidorian False Decretals, compiled in Francia around 847–852. Its chapters say that disputes among Christians should be settled by church courts and that a superior may not be judged by an inferior. They also forbid clerics to take anyone to secular courts without their bishop's permission and forbid laymen to accuse clerics. Like the rest of the collection, it was meant to protect bishops and strengthen papal authority.

These Latin letters are falsely attributed to Pope Marcellus I, bishop of Rome in the early fourth century. They belong to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, a collection of forged papal letters compiled in the Carolingian Frankish realm around 847–852. The first letter is addressed to the bishops of the province of Antioch. It argues for the primacy and authority of the Roman Church, holding that Peter's see moved from Antioch to Rome. Like the rest of the collection, the letters stitch together passages from genuine earlier sources. They were later used to support papal and episcopal claims in medieval canon law.

This short set of Latin letters is falsely attributed to, or addressed to, Pope Mark, who was bishop of Rome in 336. It opens with a supposed letter from Athanasius and the bishops of Egypt. They complain that Arians have burned their books, including the acts of the Council of Nicaea, and ask Rome to send copies of the Nicene canons. The letters belong to the Pseudo-Isidorian forgeries of the ninth century, whose compiler called himself Isidore Mercator. Since the early modern period, scholars have regarded them as forgeries.

This is a collection of Latin sermons handed down in manuscripts under the name of Maximus, bishop of Turin in the early fifth century, but judged doubtful or spurious by modern scholars. As with his genuine works, they are grouped as sermons for the seasons of the Church year, feasts of saints and other occasions. Their authors and dates are mostly unknown. Some reuse passages from Maximus's authentic homilies. The first, for Advent, tells the faithful to prepare for Christmas by doing good works, avoiding drunkenness, anger and hatred, and receiving the Eucharist worthily.

The Homiliae dubiae are a small group of Latin sermons attributed to Maximus, bishop of Turin in the fifth century, but generally judged to be by another author because their style differs from his genuine preaching. Their author and date are unknown. The first homily is for the third Sunday of Advent. It explains Matthew 11, where the imprisoned John the Baptist sends disciples to ask Christ, "Are you the one who is to come?", and reads the passage both literally and allegorically.

The Epistolae dubiae are two Latin letters of uncertain authorship. They were once transmitted among the works of Jerome and printed under his name. Later editors placed them among the spurious writings of Maximus of Turin, but their author is still unknown. The first letter consoles a sick friend and praises the strength of his mind amid bodily suffering. Erasmus thought its style resembled Tertullian's. Because the writer describes himself as busy with church affairs, some scholars think he was a bishop.

This Latin letter is falsely attributed to Pope Miltiades (Melchiades), bishop of Rome from 311 to 314. It belongs to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, a collection of forged papal decrees compiled in the Frankish kingdom around 847–852. Addressed to the bishops of Spain, it urges them to avoid accusations and quarrels and insists that major cases involving bishops may be appealed to the apostolic see. It also asks whether episcopal laying on of hands or baptism is the greater sacrament, and deals with fasting on Sundays and Thursdays.

De tribus habitaculis (On the Three Dwellings) is a short Latin treatise on the last things, handed down under the name of Saint Patrick. Modern scholarship generally assigns it to Patrick, bishop of Dublin (died 1084). It describes three dwellings under God's hand: the kingdom of heaven above, hell below, and the present world between them, where good and evil are mixed. From this world people pass to one of the other two. The work sets the joys of heaven against the torments of hell to urge readers toward a virtuous life, and it circulated widely in medieval manuscripts.

The Carmen adversus gentes is a short Latin didactic poem in hexameters. It has come down among the works of Paulinus of Nola, but his authorship is rejected, and the speaker names himself Antonius. Nothing else is known of him. It was probably written in the late fourth or early fifth century. The poet says he examined every sect and found nothing better than faith in Christ. He then criticises the Israelites' idolatry after the Exodus and pagan worship of statues and animal sacrifice. He sets these against Christian belief in the one creator God.

This is a group of seven Latin sermons that circulated under the name of Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna (died c. 450). Earlier editors judged them not to be his, so they were printed apart from his authentic sermon collection. Who wrote them and when remain uncertain. The first sermon explains the Lord's Prayer to people who have just been taught the creed. It moves clause by clause, starting from "Our Father who art in heaven." Its style and themes closely resemble Chrysologus's own catechetical preaching.

The Confessio is a Latin penitential prayer once attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine, the fifth-century defender of Augustine's teaching on grace. Most scholars no longer accept that he wrote it, and its real author and date are unknown. It is addressed to God in the first person. The speaker gives thanks for being baptised in infancy, before he understood the slavery of sin. Then, drawing on the parable of the prodigal son, he confesses that he left his Father's house for a life of vice and asks for mercy and restoration.

The Poema conjugis ad uxorem is a short Latin poem in which a husband urges his wife to devote the rest of their brief lives wholly to God. It was traditionally printed among the works of Prosper of Aquitaine, but his authorship is uncertain, and the poem has also been linked with Paulinus of Nola. It probably dates from early fifth-century Gaul. It opens in short anacreontic lines and continues in elegiac couplets. The poem contrasts the collapse of wealth and power amid war, plague and famine with lasting rest gained through brief labour in Christian life.

The Carmen de providentia divina is an anonymous Latin poem written in Gaul around 415–420. It has traditionally been attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine, but his authorship is disputed. It opens in elegiac couplets and then moves into hexameters. Its occasion is the decade of devastation brought on Gaul by Vandal and Gothic invaders. Answering those who asked why so many towns and peoples had perished, the poet defends God's providence and justice. He presents the disasters as calls to repentance and weighs human free will against divine grace.

The Libellus de fide, or Twelve Anathemas, is a short Latin profession of faith once credited to Rufinus of Aquileia but now regarded as pseudonymous. Its author and date are uncertain, though it probably belongs to the late fourth- or early fifth-century Origenist controversies. The speakers say they came as pilgrims to Jerusalem and Bethlehem and found their orthodoxy questioned. They then condemn a series of errors: denying eternal punishment, claiming that saints can be perfect without God's help, and teaching that souls existed before bodies. They also reject Arian, Photinian and other Trinitarian and Christological heresies.

The Constitutum Silvestri is a Latin text falsely attributed to Pope Silvester I. It claims to record the canons of a Roman synod that Silvester held after baptising Emperor Constantine and healing him of leprosy. It is one of the so-called Symmachian forgeries, written in Rome in the early sixth century during the Laurentian schism. Its twenty chapters regulate clerical grades, church revenues, clerical marriage and the immunity of clergy from lay courts. They end with the principle that the first see is judged by no one. The text was later taken into the Pseudo-Isidorian collection.

These are Latin letters attributed to Pope Sixtus II, who was martyred at Rome in 258. They are not authentic and are generally placed among the ninth-century forgeries of the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals. The first, addressed to a bishop Gratus, argues that accused or condemned bishops may appeal to the apostolic see, whose authority is needed to settle their cases. It also defends the eternal generation of the Son against Sabellian and related heresies. Much of the letter is pieced together from passages in Leo the Great's letters and the anti-Arian treatise Contra Varimadum.

These decretal letters are falsely attributed to Pope Stephen I (254–257) and belong to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals. That large collection of forged and altered papal and conciliar documents was compiled in Francia around 847–852. The letter to Bishop Hilarius sets out who counts as infamous and therefore may not be ordained or bring accusations. It also requires reverence toward superiors and the consecration of ministers' vestments. Like the rest of the collection, it draws on genuine sources, including letters of Leo the Great. It was written to protect bishops against accusers and lay interference.

This is a Latin sermon for the feast of Cyprian, the third-century bishop and martyr of Carthage. It has been transmitted with the works of Victor of Vita, but his authorship is doubtful, so it is attributed to Pseudo-Victor. The preacher grieves that Cyprian's own see has been lost to "barbarians" and heretics, with the people torn apart, the clergy scattered and the altar profaned. He says the martyr suffers again in his members, yet he urges hope in Christ. The sermon most likely reflects North Africa under the Vandals.

De physicis liber is a short Latin theological treatise that has come down under the name of Victorinus. Its author is uncertain, and it is usually treated as spurious, hence the label Pseudo-Victorinus. It survives in late medieval Vatican manuscripts together with other writings attributed to Victorinus, and Angelo Mai first printed it in the nineteenth century. Its date is unknown, though it is usually placed in late antiquity. The treatise argues from the natural order and the account of creation about God's work, humanity's fall and redemption through Christ.

A short Latin letter attributed to Pope Zosimus (417–418) and addressed to Simplicius, bishop of Vienne, whom it calls "archbishop." It refers to Simplicius's case at the Synod of Turin. It allows him to claim the nearby cities of his province until the matter is examined more fully, and it reports that Lazarus has been condemned. It is generally regarded as spurious. The title "archbishop" is anachronistic, and the letter contradicts Zosimus's authentic letters of 417 and 418, which gave metropolitan rights over the Viennensis and both Narbonensis provinces to the bishop of Arles.

This short Latin prose letter is addressed to the emperor Constantine I by the poet Publilius Optatianus Porfyrius. It was written during Constantine's reign, but its exact date is uncertain. Optatian thanks the emperor for graciously accepting a poem he had composed under the tight formal constraints of his figured verse. He compares himself modestly with Virgil, whom Maecenas honoured, and praises Constantine as both a victorious ruler and a patron of the Muses. The letter is preserved alongside Optatian's poems. It sheds light on literary patronage and imperial praise at the court of the first Christian emperor.

This is a collection of Latin poems in praise of the emperor Constantine I by Publilius Optatianus Porfyrius, a fourth-century poet who is probably the same man as the city prefect of 329 and 333. He wrote them while in exile, probably in the 320s, and the panegyric is said to have won his recall. The poems show great technical skill. They include acrostics, figure poems and grid poems in which coloured letters form further verses, patterns and Christian monograms. They are early and important witnesses to Latin visual poetry.

The Chronologia sive Libellus de mundi duratione, also called De cursu temporum, is a Latin treatise on salvation history. Quintus Julius Hilarianus, a chronographer in Roman Africa, wrote it in 397. Working from biblical chronology, it argues against those who held that the world's beginning and end cannot be known. It dates the Second Coming to 498, when the world would be 6,000 years old, followed by Christ's thousand-year reign and a final battle. It is one of the last open defences of a millenarian view that was soon judged heretical.

The Expositum de die Paschae et mensis, also called De ratione Paschae et mensis, is a Latin computistical treatise by the Roman African chronographer Quintus Julius Hilarianus, completed on 5 March 397. Written at the request of fellow "servants of God", it starts from Exodus 12 and explains how the first month and the Easter full moon are fixed. It defends the lunar limits used in the church's paschal reckoning. Some have read it as a sermon, but this is uncertain. The Carthaginian Computus of 455 drew on it.

This Latin catechetical sermon is addressed to candidates for baptism who have received and memorised the Creed (symbolum). It is one of three sermons De symbolo that were once transmitted among the works of Augustine and are now generally attributed to Quodvultdeus. He was a deacon and later bishop of Carthage in the fifth century. The sermon first explains the renunciation of the devil and his "pomps": the desires of the flesh, the lure of public spectacles and worldly pride. It then condemns idol worship and goes through the articles of the Creed, stressing that faith comes before understanding.

This Latin catechetical sermon explains the Creed to catechumens preparing for baptism. It was long printed among the works of Augustine of Hippo but is now generally attributed to Quodvultdeus, the fifth-century bishop of Carthage. It describes the rites before baptism, such as exorcisms, prayers and the renunciation, as nourishment given by Mother Church to the children she carries in her womb. Using the woman and dragon of Revelation 12, it presents the Creed as protection against the devil and then explains its clauses one by one.

De cataclysmo ("On the Flood") is a Latin catechetical sermon addressed to candidates preparing for baptism. It was long transmitted among the sermons of Augustine but is now generally attributed to Quodvultdeus, bishop of Carthage. It was probably preached at Carthage in the 430s, before the Vandal conquest of 439. The preacher warns that baptism does not end the Christian's struggle. He calls the newly baptized ship a vessel that needs Christ as its pilot on the sea of the world, and a soldier fighting the vices. Citing Cyprian, he presents the Flood as a figure of baptism.

Sermo de tempore barbarico ("Sermon on the Time of the Barbarians") is a Latin sermon long transmitted among the spurious works of Augustine of Hippo. It is now generally attributed to Quodvultdeus, deacon and later bishop of Carthage. It was preached in North Africa in the second quarter of the fifth century, as the Vandals invaded. The preacher presents the calamities as God's scourge for sin and urges his hearers to repent. He also rebukes those who fear human power and worldly loss more than God. The sermon is valuable evidence of how African Christians responded to the Vandal conquest.

A Latin sermon on the Creed addressed to competentes, candidates preparing for baptism at Carthage. It is one of a group of sermons De symbolo long transmitted among the works of Augustine and now generally attributed to Quodvultdeus, deacon and later bishop of Carthage, in the fifth century. It explains the rites of the preceding night, including the scrutiny held before the assembled church and the renunciation of the devil and his pomps, then expounds the Creed. It is an important witness to North African baptismal catechesis.

Adversus quinque haereses ("Against Five Heresies") is a Latin sermon-treatise. It was long transmitted among the works of Augustine of Hippo but is now generally attributed to Quodvultdeus, Augustine's correspondent and later bishop of Carthage, and dated to the second quarter of the fifth century. The preacher keeps an earlier promise to his hearers and answers five groups of opponents in turn: pagans, Jews, Manichaeans, Sabellians and Arians. He defends the Trinity and the true divinity and humanity of Christ, and illustrates his case with scriptural types such as David's victory over Goliath.

This Latin sermon on the Creed was long transmitted among the works of Augustine of Hippo but is now generally attributed to Quodvultdeus, bishop of Carthage. He wrote it in the fifth century, amid the troubles of Vandal-era North Africa. It was preached after a night vigil to people preparing for baptism. The sermon explains the faith of the Creed and defends it against Jews, pagans and Arians. It is best known for its procession of witnesses to Christ, which include Old Testament prophets, Virgil and the Sibyl. This passage inspired the medieval liturgical drama known as the Ordo prophetarum.

De quattuor virtutibus caritatis (On the Four Virtues of Charity) is a short Latin sermon. It was long transmitted among the works of Augustine and is now generally attributed to Quodvultdeus, bishop of Carthage in the fifth century. It explains Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 13:7 that charity "bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things." Each of these virtues is shown in a biblical example: endurance in Noah, faith in Abraham, hope in the people of Israel, and patient bearing in Christ, who is himself true charity.

The Book of the Promises and Predictions of God is a Latin treatise of biblical interpretation. It was once transmitted among the works of Prosper of Aquitaine but is now generally attributed to Quodvultdeus, the exiled bishop of Carthage, and dated to about 445–453. In 153 chapters it gathers divine promises and prophecies from Scripture. It arranges them by period: before the Law, under the Law and under grace, followed by the "half of time" and the glory of the saints. Its argument is that so many fulfilled promises guarantee those still to come.

The so-called Testament of Radegund (c. 520–587), the Thuringian princess and former Frankish queen, is a Latin letter addressed to the bishops of Gaul. It is preserved by Gregory of Tours in his Histories (book IX). In it Radegund recounts founding the convent of nuns at Poitiers under King Chlothar I, which she endowed and placed under the Rule of Caesarius of Arles. She asks the bishops to protect the community's property and independence. Its date is disputed: it is often linked to the Council of Tours (567), though some place it near her death.

This Latin royal edict was issued by the Visigothic king Reccared I to confirm the decrees of the Third Council of Toledo. The council met in 589, the fourth year of his reign, and marked the Visigoths' formal turn from Arianism to Catholic Christianity. The edict gives the canons the force of civil law throughout the kingdom. It sums up their provisions, including the observance of earlier canons and the recitation of the Creed by the people in church. It also sets penalties for disobedience: excommunication for clergy, and confiscation of property or exile for laypeople, depending on their rank.

De benedictionibus patriarcharum (On the Blessings of the Patriarchs) is a short Latin exegetical treatise in two books by Rufinus of Aquileia. It was written late in his life, around 408, in reply to questions from his friend Paulinus of Nola. It explains the blessings Jacob gave his twelve sons in Genesis 49, reading them on several levels: historical, mystical or Christological, and moral. The first book deals with the blessing of Judah, and the second with the remaining sons. It is one of the few original works by Rufinus, who is known mainly as a translator.

Rufinus of Aquileia wrote this Latin exposition of the baptismal creed at the request of Laurentius, a bishop whose see is unknown. It dates from the early fifth century, probably around 400–404, though the exact date is uncertain. Rufinus goes through the creed of Aquileia article by article and notes where it differs from the Roman form, such as the clause on Christ's descent into hell. The work is an important witness to local Western creeds and their history. It also contains an early list of the canonical, ecclesiastical and apocryphal books of Scripture.

The Historia monachorum in Aegypto is the Latin version, made by Rufinus of Aquileia around the beginning of the fifth century, of an anonymous Greek account of a journey through Egypt in about 394–395. The travellers were a group of monks from the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem. The book describes the desert fathers they met, with their asceticism, miracles and teaching, and is meant to edify its readers. Rufinus adapted the Greek original freely. His version was widely read in the Latin West and became part of the collection known as the Vitae Patrum.

This is the Latin version of Eusebius of Caesarea's Ecclesiastical History, made by Rufinus of Aquileia around 402–403. Bishop Chromatius of Aquileia asked for it as a consolation while Alaric's Goths were invading Italy. Rufinus freely abridged and adapted Eusebius's ten books into nine. He then added two books of his own that carry the story from the Council of Nicaea to the death of Theodosius I in 395. The work brought Eusebius to Latin readers, and its continuation became an important source for fourth-century church history.

The Apology is a Latin defence in two books by Rufinus of Aquileia, written at Aquileia around 400–401 and addressed to his friend Apronianus. It answers Jerome's letter to Pammachius and the charges against Rufinus's translation of Origen's On First Principles and its preface. Rufinus defends his own orthodoxy and his method as a translator. He argues that Jerome had once admired and used Origen himself, and accuses him of inconsistency. Jerome replied with his Apology against Rufinus. The work is a key document of the first Origenist controversy and of the final break between the two former friends.

Rufinus of Aquileia wrote this short Latin apology around 400 and sent it to Anastasius I, bishop of Rome (399–401). Jerome's friends at Rome, among them Marcella and Pammachius, had accused Rufinus of spreading heresy through his Latin translation of Origen's On First Principles. Writing from Aquileia, Rufinus set out his own faith on the Trinity, the Incarnation, the resurrection of the body, judgement and the origin of the soul. He argued that a translator should not be held responsible for his author's opinions. The text is a key document of the first Origenist controversy.

The Liber de fide (Book of Faith) is a Latin theological treatise from around 400, usually attributed to Rufinus the Syrian. He was a priest linked with Pelagian circles. The only surviving manuscript calls the author a priest from the province of Palestine. The book begins with a statement of faith in the Trinity and the incarnation. It then argues against Arianism and Origenism and rejects the doctrine of original sin. It was long wrongly credited to Rufinus of Aquileia. Scholars value it as one of the earliest witnesses to the ideas behind the Pelagian controversy.

The Fides Rufini is a short Latin profession of faith with anathemas. Its author, a Rufinus, says he came to Jerusalem and Bethlehem to venerate the holy places. It is usually assigned to Rufinus the Syrian, although which of several contemporaries named Rufinus wrote it is uncertain. It seems to date from around 399–411, before Pelagius and Nestorius were condemned. It was written while controversy over Origen's De principiis was at its height. It survives in manuscripts after Pope Anastasius I's letter on Origenism.

The Contra Acephalos Disputatio is a Latin theological dialogue by Rusticus, a Roman deacon and nephew of Pope Vigilius. He opposed the condemnation of the Three Chapters and spent his later years in exile in the East. Written in the mid-sixth century, probably in Constantinople, the work defends the Chalcedonian teaching that Christ has two natures. It argues against the "Acephali", anti-Chalcedonian Miaphysites. The preface laments the theological turmoil and moral decline of the author's day. It is a significant Western witness to the sixth-century Christological debates.

The Carmen de Christi Jesu beneficiis is a Latin hexameter poem by Rusticius Helpidius, a Christian poet of the late fifth or early sixth century. Some scholars identify him with Helpidius, the deacon and physician at the court of Theodoric in Ravenna, but this is uncertain. The poem praises the saving works of Christ. It is transmitted with his Tristicha, twenty-four three-line epigrams that pair Old and New Testament scenes, such as Eve's temptation and the Annunciation, or Joseph's sale and Judas's betrayal. These epigrams were probably written as captions for pictures and show early typological reading of Scripture.

The In Parabolas Salomonis Expositio Mystica is a Latin commentary on the Book of Proverbs attributed to Salonius, bishop of Geneva in the mid-fifth century and son of Eucherius of Lyon. It takes the form of a question-and-answer dialogue between Salonius and his brother Veranus. It reads Proverbs allegorically rather than literally: Solomon, the "peaceful" and "beloved", stands for Christ, and his peaceful reign stands for the eternal kingdom of Christ and the Church. A similar mystical exposition of Ecclesiastes is also attributed to Salonius, and some scholars have questioned whether he wrote either work.

The In Ecclesiasten Expositio Mystica is a Latin commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes attributed to Salonius, bishop of Geneva from 440. It probably dates from the mid-fifth century. It takes the form of questions and answers between Salonius and his brother Veranus, later bishop of Vence, both sons of Eucherius of Lyon. The work reads Solomon allegorically as a figure of Christ, the true peacemaker and preacher, and interprets the book's teaching on worldly vanity spiritually. It forms a pair with Salonius's similar exposition of Proverbs.

A Latin treatise in four books, usually called Ad Ecclesiam ("To the Church"), by Salvian of Marseilles, written in fifth-century Gaul. Salvian issued it under the pseudonym "Timothy, least of the servants of God" and explained why he hid his name in a letter to Bishop Salonius. Gennadius lists it as four books "Against Avarice." The work attacks greed among Christians and urges believers, especially clergy and those vowed to religious life, to leave their wealth to the Church and the poor rather than to heirs. It is an important source for early Christian attitudes to wealth and inheritance.

"Audite omnes amantes Deum" is an abecedarian Latin hymn in praise of Saint Patrick: each stanza begins with the next letter of the alphabet. Tradition attributes it to Secundinus (Sechnall), a fifth-century bishop said to be Patrick's disciple, and holds that he wrote it while Patrick was still alive. Both the attribution and the date are disputed. The hymn praises Patrick's holiness, his apostolic mission to the Irish and his faithful preaching. It survives in the Antiphonary of Bangor and is counted among the earliest Hiberno-Latin poems.

This short Latin sermon for the feast of the Epiphany is attributed to Sedatus, a bishop of Béziers in Visigothic Gaul in the late sixth century who took part in the Third Council of Toledo in 589. It explains the feast as honouring three manifestations of Christ's divinity: the star that announced his birth, the changing of water into wine at Cana, and his baptism in the Jordan, which blessed the waters for baptism. It reads the six water jars at Cana as the six ages of the world, and their measures as signs of faith in the Trinity.

The Epigramma is a short Latin poem of four lines in two elegiac couplets, attributed to Sedulius, the Christian poet of the first half of the fifth century best known for the Carmen Paschale. It is a closing prayer asking Christ to keep in the poet's heart the teachings of eternal life he has written, and to lead him to the joys of heaven. It is noted for its wordplay on forms of the pronoun "you" (te, tua, tete, tibi). Manuscripts place it among Sedulius's other poems. One adds further lines, generally judged to be a later scribe's addition.

The Epistola de Judaeis is a Latin circular letter written about 417–418 by Severus, bishop of Minorca, to bishops, clergy and Christians throughout the world. It describes how relics of the protomartyr Stephen arrived on the island and how, in early 418, tensions led to the burning of the synagogue and the conversion of about 540 Jews within eight days. Its authenticity was once questioned but is now widely accepted. The letter is an important source for Jewish–Christian relations and the cult of relics in late antiquity.

The Epistola de Judaeis is a Latin circular letter written about 417–418 by Severus, bishop of Minorca, to bishops, clergy and Christians throughout the world. It describes how relics of the protomartyr Stephen arrived on the island and how, in early 418, tensions led to the burning of the synagogue and the conversion of about 540 Jews within eight days. Its authenticity was once questioned but is now widely accepted. The letter is an important source for Jewish–Christian relations and the cult of relics in late antiquity.

This Latin bucolic poem, also known as De mortibus boum ("On the Deaths of Cattle"), is by Severus Sanctus Endelechius, a rhetorician and poet of the late fourth century. It was probably written around 395–400. Written as a dialogue between herdsmen, it tells of a cattle plague, often identified as rinderpest, that had spread from Pannonia, Illyricum and Belgica. One herdsman, Tityrus, tells how the sign of the cross saved his herd, and the grieving Buculus decides to accept Christ. The poem is a notable early adaptation of Virgilian pastoral to Christian apologetic.

The Letters of Sidonius Apollinaris, the Gallo-Roman aristocrat who became bishop of Clermont, are a collection of about 147 letters in nine books. He revised them and published them in stages, probably during the 470s and early 480s. The opening letter, addressed to his friend Constantius, places the collection in the tradition of Pliny and Symmachus. Written in an ornate, allusive Latin, the letters describe aristocratic life, the Church and politics in Gaul as Roman rule gave way to the Visigoths and Burgundians. They are a major source for the fifth-century West.

The Carmina are the collected Latin poems of Sidonius Apollinaris, a Gallo-Roman aristocrat who later became bishop of Clermont. Most were written before he became bishop in 469, and the collection runs to twenty-four poems. The best known are three verse panegyrics, each with a preface, on the emperors Avitus, Majorian and Anthemius. The rest include wedding poems, descriptions of villas, occasional verse and a closing send-off to the book itself. Their classical style and dense mythological allusion make them important evidence for late Roman culture and politics in the West.

The Coronis Sidoniana is a Latin philological excursus attached as a closing "coronis", or finishing flourish, to an early modern scholarly commentary on Sidonius Apollinaris. Sidonius did not write it, though it is indexed under his name. It starts from his verses on Avitus walking to Toulouse between the Visigothic king Theodoric II and his brother Frederic. From there it discusses Roman ideas of precedence: which place counted as "inner" or "outer", the honour of the middle position, guarding someone's flank, and whether the right or the left side ranked higher.

This is a small collection of letters and fragments attributed to Silvester I, bishop of Rome from 314 to 335, a pope about whose life and writings very little is reliably known. It includes a Greek fragment from an otherwise unknown work against the Jews. That fragment uses two analogies, wool dyed purple and a sunbeam in a tree being cut, to argue that the divine Word was united to the suffering flesh at the crucifixion without itself suffering. The authenticity of much of the material is doubtful.

This is a group of short Latin texts attributed to Pope Silvester I, bishop of Rome from 314 to 335, whose authorship is doubtful or spurious. It consists of canons, decrees and letters taken from later canonical and conciliar collections. One canon forbids marriage with a spiritual kinswoman from baptism or chrismation. A decree sets out stages of warning and suspension before excommunication. Part of the material is known to be misattributed: a letter of Pope Zosimus, for example, circulated under Silvester's name. Such pieces show how later canon law gathered authority around early popes.

The Epistolae are the surviving Latin letters of Simplicius, bishop of Rome from 468 to 483. They deal with church discipline in the West and with the doctrinal conflicts in the East. In them Simplicius makes Zeno, bishop of Seville, papal vicar for the churches of Spain. He also rebukes John of Ravenna for forcibly ordaining Gregory as bishop of Modena. Other letters, to the emperor Zeno and to Acacius of Constantinople, defend the Council of Chalcedon against its Miaphysite opponents in Alexandria and Antioch. They are an important source for the background to the Acacian schism.

This Latin letter, known as the Directa decretal, was written by Pope Siricius, bishop of Rome, in 385. It answers questions sent to his predecessor Damasus by Himerius, bishop of Tarragona in Spain. Its rulings deal with church discipline. They say that converted Arians should not be rebaptized, limit baptism to Easter and Pentecost, and cover penitents, apostates, monks and virgins. They also require clergy to stay continent and set rules for ordination. It is the oldest papal decretal preserved complete, and it was copied widely into early collections of canon law.

This is a short Latin letter from Pope Siricius, bishop of Rome from 384 to 399, to Anysius, bishop of Thessalonica. It orders that no bishop be ordained in Illyricum without Anysius's consent. It also repeats an instruction from an earlier letter, carried by the bishop Candidianus, because Siricius did not know whether that letter had arrived. The exact date is uncertain, but it is usually placed around 386. Later popes, including Innocent I and Leo I, appealed to it. It is an early witness to the papal vicariate of Thessalonica, through which Rome exercised oversight in Illyricum.

This Latin synodal letter from Pope Siricius, bishop of Rome from 384 to 399, sets out the decisions of a Roman synod held at the relics of Saint Peter, usually dated 386. It was first addressed to the bishops of that synod and later sent to other provinces, including Africa. It survives through the acts of the Council of Telepte. Its canons regulate the ordination of bishops, forbid clerics to marry widows, bar former soldiers from the clergy, and govern the reception of returning Novatianists and Donatists. It also requires priests and deacons to remain continent.

This Latin letter was written by Pope Siricius, bishop of Rome from 384 to 399, to orthodox bishops in various provinces. Its exact date is uncertain. Siricius writes as one responsible for the care of all the churches. He protests against new customs in ordination that break the canons handed down from earlier generations. He sets three rules: no unworthy man may be made a bishop, the priesthood must not be given to men who are not known, and neophytes or laymen must not be ordained directly. It belongs to the earliest group of papal decretals concerned with church discipline.

This is a Latin letter by Pope Siricius, bishop of Rome from 384 to 399, sent to various bishops in the early 390s. It reports that a Roman synod had condemned the monk Jovinian and his named associates and excluded them from the communion of the Church. Jovinian denied that virginity and fasting were more meritorious than marriage and ordinary eating. Siricius presents his teaching as diabolical and warns other bishops against these men. A synod at Milan under Ambrose wrote back in support, and the letter is an important document of the controversy over Jovinian.

This Latin letter, attributed to Pope Siricius (bishop of Rome 384–399), is addressed to Anysius of Thessalonica and the other bishops of Illyricum. It is also transmitted among the letters of Ambrose of Milan, and its authorship is disputed. The bishops had asked for a ruling on Bonosus, a bishop accused of teaching that Mary bore other children. The letter declines to give a verdict, because the Council of Capua had assigned the case to them as judges. It nonetheless condemns Bonosus's view and affirms Mary's perpetual virginity.

The Canons of a Roman Synod to the Bishops of Gaul is a Latin letter of the late fourth century, sent by a Roman synod to answer questions from Gallic bishops. It is traditionally numbered among the letters of Pope Siricius (384–399), but its authorship is disputed, and some scholars attribute it to his predecessor Damasus. Its canons cover consecrated virgins, clerical chastity and continence, baptism, marriage to a deceased wife's sister or an uncle's widow, the ordination of clergy and the limits of episcopal jurisdiction. Along with Siricius's decretals, it is an early witness to Roman canonical rulings.

These Latin letters were written by Sisebut, king of the Visigoths in Hispania from 612 to 621, and survive among the Visigothic royal and ecclesiastical correspondence. The collection opens with a letter to Caecilius, bishop of Mentesa, who had shut himself away in a monastery. In it the king rebukes him with Gospel images of the good shepherd and the talents for abandoning his flock. Other letters deal with church and political affairs. They show the learned, rhetorical Latin of Sisebut's court, which was shaped by Isidore of Seville.

The Vita et Passio Sancti Desiderii is a Latin hagiography written by Sisebut, king of the Visigoths from 612 to 621, and probably composed during his reign. It tells the life and martyrdom of Desiderius (Didier), bishop of Vienne in Gaul. It describes his Roman noble birth, his education and virtues, his opposition to the Frankish court, and his violent death in the early seventh century, blamed on Queen Brunhild and King Theuderic II. Its strong hostility to Brunhild makes it an important witness to Visigothic royal literary culture and its view of Frankish politics.

This Latin collection gathers the letters and decrees of Sixtus III (Xystus), bishop of Rome from 432 to 440. Among the most important are two letters written soon after his ordination in 432. They survive only in Greek translation, though they were probably composed in Latin. In them Sixtus answers the envoys whom Cyril of Alexandria and other Eastern bishops had sent to his predecessor Celestine to restore peace in the East after the Nestorian controversy. Some decretals transmitted under his name are regarded as spurious.

The Statuta is a short Latin collection of diocesan regulations attributed to Sonnatius, bishop of Reims in the early seventh century (c. 613–631). Its numbered clauses tell clergy to hold the faith according to Roman tradition and to instruct their people. They are to give the sacraments, including baptism and confirmation, carefully and without charging fees. Parishioners must attend Mass on Sundays and feast days, and Lenten confessions are reserved to their own pastor. Its authenticity is doubtful, because features such as calling parish priests "pastors" suggest a later date.

This short Latin letter was written by an abbot named Stephen to Aunarius, bishop of Auxerre, who held the see from about 572 to 605. Aunarius had asked him to write about the lives and deeds of two earlier bishops of Auxerre, Germanus and Amator. Using the elaborate language of modesty typical of late antique Gaul, Stephen protests that his skill is too limited for the task. He nevertheless agrees to obey and asks the bishop to forgive any clumsiness in his style. The letter shows how hagiography of local saints was commissioned in Merovingian Gaul.

The Epistolae Tres are three short Latin letters by Sulpicius II "the Pious", bishop of Bourges from 624 until his death in the 640s. They were written to fellow Gallic bishops, including Desiderius of Cahors and Verus of Rodez, both in the ecclesiastical province of Bourges. In an elaborate rhetorical style, the letters exchange greetings and express friendship, and they touch on church business between the sees. They are a small but useful witness to Merovingian episcopal correspondence and the Latin epistolary culture of seventh-century Gaul.

The Epistolae et decreta are the Latin letters and decrees of Pope Symmachus, bishop of Rome from 498 to 514. His time in office was troubled by the Laurentian schism. The collection gathers official correspondence with bishops and lay officials. One letter, dated 499, deals with the dispute between the sees of Arles and Vienne. Another concerns the election of a bishop of Aquileia. Together these documents show how the Roman see used appeals, adjudication and church discipline in Italy and Gaul at the start of the sixth century.

The third Relatio of Quintus Aurelius Symmachus is an official petition sent in 384, while he was prefect of Rome. It was addressed to the emperors Valentinian II, Theodosius I and Arcadius, though it was really meant for Valentinian. Speaking for the Senate, Symmachus asked for the Altar of Victory to be restored to the senate house and for the funds of the Vestals and priesthoods to be returned. He appealed to ancestral custom and religious tolerance. Ambrose of Milan wrote letters rebutting it, and the request was refused.

The Aenigmata is a collection of one hundred Latin verse riddles by Symphosius, an otherwise unknown poet usually dated to the late antique period, probably the fourth or fifth century. Each riddle has three hexameter lines and is transmitted with its solution. A verse preface presents the collection as improvised during the feast of the Saturnalia. The subjects are everyday objects, animals and natural things, such as the stylus, the reed pen, the key and the chain. The collection became the model for medieval Latin riddle-writing, especially Aldhelm and other Anglo-Saxon riddlers.

The Epistolae are the surviving Latin letters of Taio (Taius), bishop of Zaragoza in Visigothic Spain, who succeeded his teacher Braulio in 651. Among them is a letter addressed to Eugenius, bishop of Toledo. Written in an ornate style, it uses the image of a flowering paradise to praise the writings of an eminent teacher, which are almost certainly those of Gregory the Great. Taio also wrote to Quiricus of Barcelona. These letters accompanied his compilations of Gregory's works and show how Gregorian learning reached seventh-century Hispania and was valued there.

The Sententiarum libri quinque (Five Books of Sentences) is a Latin theological anthology compiled by Taio (Taius), bishop of Zaragoza in Visigothic Spain. Taio began it in about 653 at the request of Bishop Quiricus of Barcelona, to whom it is dedicated. It arranges extracts, chiefly from Gregory the Great, under thematic headings covering doctrine and the Christian life. Its preface vividly describes the disruption caused by Froia's revolt against King Recceswinth and the Basque invasion that followed. It is an early example of a systematic collection of sentences.

De Visione Taionis Episcopi is a short Latin legend about Taio, bishop of Zaragoza in the mid-seventh century. Although it is catalogued under Taio's name, it is an anonymous account, not his own writing, and its date is uncertain. It tells how King Chindasuinth sent Taio to Rome to obtain the missing books of Gregory the Great's Moralia on Job. The papal archive could not find them until an angel showed Taio where they were during a night vigil at Saint Peter's. The story became part of Spanish tradition about how Gregory's works reached Visigothic Spain.

The Letter to King Reccared is a short Latin letter by Tarra, a monk of the Caulianan monastery near Mérida in Visigothic Spain, addressed to Reccared I (reigned 586–601). Tarra says he had been driven from his community after being falsely accused of sexual misconduct, and that the king had ordered him to speak. He protests his innocence, citing Scripture throughout and writing in an elaborate, rhetorical style. The letter is a rare first-person witness to monastic discipline and to monks appealing to the king in the time of Reccared.

This is a Latin royal letter (praeceptio) from Theodoric the Great, Ostrogothic king of Italy, carried by the bishops Germanus and Carosus. It is addressed to the bishops Laurentius, Marcellinus and Peter and to the other bishops staying in Rome. It belongs to the Laurentian schism over the disputed papacy of Symmachus, around 501. Theodoric regrets the disorder that broke up the synod and orders the same bishops to meet again on 1 September. He refuses to move the council to Ravenna and offers to come to Rome himself if needed.

This is a royal mandate in Latin from Theodoric the Great, the Ostrogothic king of Italy, addressed to the bishops gathered in Rome in 501 during the Laurentian schism. Pope Symmachus had been accused of crimes by his opponents. At the request of the Senate and clergy, Theodoric had called bishops from several provinces to judge the case. In this second letter he complains about their delays and divisions, warns that discord is "the mother of confusion", and urges them to reach a united verdict quickly. It is an important source for royal involvement in papal disputes under Gothic rule.

The Praeceptio Tertia is a short Latin royal mandate issued by Theodoric the Great, the Arian Ostrogothic king of Italy, to the Catholic bishops summoned to a synod in Rome. It belongs to the Laurentian schism, the disputed papal succession between Symmachus and Laurentius, and is usually dated to around 501. Theodoric declares that he will not judge church matters himself. He leaves the bishops free to decide the case as they see fit, provided that their judgement restores peace and concord to the Senate and people of Rome.

This Latin instruction is issued in the name of Theodoric the Great, Ostrogothic king of Italy (493–526), and addressed to a synod of bishops through a royal official, the Anagnosticus. It belongs to the dispute over Pope Symmachus during the Laurentian schism of about 501. The king declines to judge a church matter himself. He urges the bishops to hear the case as the Gospel and the Apostle direct, without fear or favour, and to restore peace to the senate, clergy and people of Rome. The text also recalls an anecdote about Aspar.

The Praeceptio Quarta is a short Latin edict issued by Theodoric the Great, Ostrogothic king of Italy, to the Senate of Rome. It is dated at Ravenna on 11 March 507, in the consulship of Venantius. Responding to a senatorial petition, and confirming what an earlier synod had decreed, it forbids any bishop to sell or give away church property. Clergy may grant only the use of its revenues. Anything alienated beyond that must be reclaimed, with its income, by the bishop. The edict shows the Arian king's involvement in the property affairs of the Catholic Church in Italy.

This is a series of Latin extracts from the lost Greek work in five books, the Pentalogos, that Theodoret of Cyrrhus wrote against Cyril of Alexandria and the Council of Ephesus (431), which had condemned Nestorius. The Latin translation is credited to Marius Mercator, a strong opponent of Nestorianism, who added hostile headings. The passages defend the Antiochene distinction between Christ's divine and human natures and reject any mixture or confusion of them. Little of the original work survives apart from fragments such as these.

These Latin fragments come from a lost Greek treatise by Theodore of Mopsuestia (c. 350–428), bishop of Mopsuestia and leading exegete of the Antiochene school. The treatise attacked the doctrine of original sin and was apparently aimed at Jerome, called "Aram" or "Hiramus." The excerpts survive because Marius Mercator translated them into Latin and quoted them in his polemic against Pelagianism and Nestorianism. Theodore argues that Adam was created mortal by nature, and that death was not a penalty brought on by his transgression. The fragments are important evidence for how Antiochene theology related to the Pelagian controversy.

These are Latin excerpts from a lost Greek treatise by Theodore of Mopsuestia (bishop 392–428) attacking the doctrine of original sin. They survive in a translation by Marius Mercator, a Latin lay writer active in Constantinople who opposed Pelagianism and Nestorianism. In them Theodore argues that Adam was created mortal by nature and that the threat "you shall die" meant only that he would deserve death. The heading names Augustine as the target, but who the treatise was aimed at is uncertain. Mercator's translation preserves Theodore's arguments, which later opponents cited in condemning his teaching.

This is a compilation of imperial laws issued under Theodosius I, Roman emperor from 379 to 395. Most were issued jointly with his co-emperors Gratian, Valentinian II and Arcadius. The laws are excerpted from the Theodosian Code, which was compiled later under Theodosius II, and are arranged by the Code's books and titles. The constitutions mainly concern religion and the Church, though they also cover related administrative matters such as the duties of officials. They document the legislation by which Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the established faith and restricted heretics and pagan cults.

This Latin letter was written around 519–520 by Trifolius, a priest, to the Roman senator Faustus, who had asked for his judgment. Its subject is the Scythian monks who had come from Constantinople, led by John, and who taught that "one of the Trinity suffered" in the flesh. Trifolius argues that this formula is not found in the four ecumenical councils or in the letters they approved. He links it to Arian and Apollinarian error. The letter is a Western witness to the early stage of the Theopaschite controversy under Pope Hormisdas.

This is a short Latin letter from the sixth century, written by a Gallic bishop to Eumerius, bishop of Nantes. Eumerius had asked what to do about a boy who did not know whether he had been baptized. The reply follows the ruling of Pope Leo I in his letter to Rusticus: anyone who cannot remember being baptized, and whose baptism no witness can confirm, should be baptized without delay. The manuscripts give the writer's name in a corrupt form. Jacques Sirmond identified him, by conjecture, as Troianus, bishop of Saintes.

The Book of Rules (Liber Regularum), often called De septem regulis, is a Latin treatise on interpreting Scripture by the Donatist theologian Tyconius of North Africa. It was probably written around 380. It sets out seven "mystical rules" as keys to the hidden sense of prophecy: the Lord and his body, the twofold body of the Lord, promises and law, species and genus, times, recapitulation, and the devil and his body. It is the earliest surviving Latin handbook of biblical hermeneutics. Augustine summarized and commended it in De doctrina christiana, and through him it shaped medieval exegesis.

This short Latin letter by Uranius, a presbyter of Nola, describes the death of Paulinus of Nola in 431. He wrote it to Pacatus, a man of high rank who was planning a verse life of Paulinus and had asked for reliable material. Uranius recalls that Paulinus was born at Bordeaux and died in Campania beside the shrine of the confessor Felix. He describes the bishop's last days, including a visit from the bishops Symmachus and Acindynus, as evidence of a holy life. The letter is a key eyewitness source for Paulinus's death and early cult.

This is a short Latin letter to Pope Julius I. Valens of Mursa wrote it in his own hand at Rome, and Ursacius of Singidunum signed it. It is usually dated around 347, though ancient writers link it to a synod at Jerusalem, so the exact date is uncertain. The two Illyrian bishops admit that their charges against Athanasius were false, condemn Arius and his teaching, and ask for communion with Julius. The letter survives in Hilary of Poitiers' historical fragments, and Athanasius quotes it in Greek. Both bishops later withdrew this retraction.

This is a short imperial rescript in Latin, issued in the name of the Western emperor Valentinian II to Pinianus, prefect of the city of Rome. It is usually dated to early 385. In it the emperor approves the election of Siricius as bishop of Rome after the death of Damasus in December 384. Siricius had been chosen over a rival candidate, Ursinus. The letter is preserved in the Collectio Avellana and shows how the imperial court took part in confirming disputed episcopal successions in Rome.

Valentinus, abbot of the monastery at Hadrumetum in North Africa, wrote this Latin letter to Augustine of Hippo around 426–427. It is preserved among Augustine's correspondence as Letter 216. It answers Augustine's treatise On Grace and Free Will, which he wrote after some of Valentinus's monks were troubled by his teaching on grace. Valentinus thanks Augustine respectfully and explains how the dispute began, starting with the visit of the monk Florus to Uzalis. The letter is an early witness to the debates among monks that later became known as the Semi-Pelagian controversy.

This is a Latin dedicatory letter by the Jesuit scholar Jacques Sirmond to Cardinal Francesco Barberini. It accompanies an edition of the homilies of Valerian, bishop of Cimiez in the fifth century, and is not a work by Valerian himself. Sirmond defends Valerian's reputation against an accuser who objected to calling him "Saint" and suspected him of Semipelagianism. He recalls that the Holy Office had earlier approved Valerian's defence, cites the vindication published at Lyon by Théophile Raynaud, and asks the cardinal to see that the earlier favourable ruling stands.

The Homiliae XX are a collection of twenty Latin sermons by Valerian, bishop of Cemenelum (Cimiez, near modern Nice) in southern Gaul. He took part in Gallic councils of the 430s and 440s, and the sermons date from about the middle of the fifth century. They are practical moral and ascetic addresses rather than scriptural commentary. The first praises discipline as the order God built into creation and the teacher of true religion. Others deal with Christian conduct, the virtues and the dangers of vice. The collection shows how pastors preached in fifth-century Provence.

The Epistola ad monachos is a Latin letter of spiritual exhortation addressed to a community of monks by Valerian, bishop of Cemenelum (Cimiez, near Nice) in the mid-fifth century. Writing while absent in body but present in spirit, Valerian follows the example of Paul. He goes through the Pauline epistles in order, from Romans to Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians and onward, and draws from each a monastic virtue: faith, charity, freedom from the world, unity of doctrine and blamelessness. It survives alongside his collection of homilies and is a witness to early monasticism in southern Gaul.

This is a collection of selected testimonies about Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona in the fourth century. The passages come from various later writers and were gathered by an editor to go with editions of Zeno's sermons. It opens with Ambrose of Milan's letter to Syagrius, bishop of Verona, which mentions Zeno "of holy memory". Next comes Gregory the Great's account in his Dialogues (III.19) of the Adige flood, when the water would not enter Zeno's church in Verona. The collection documents Zeno's early reputation and cult.

This is a collection of Latin documents on the history of the Donatist schism in Roman North Africa, assembled by later scholars rather than written as a single work. It covers the years from Emperor Julian's rescript of 362, which restored the Donatist bishops, to the Conference of Carthage in 411. The items include imperial laws against rebaptism from the Theodosian Code and passages preserved by Augustine. Together they show how imperial policy toward the Donatists changed over the half-century before the conference.

This is the official stenographic record, in Latin, of the conference held at Carthage in 411 between Catholic and Donatist bishops of North Africa, convened by order of Emperor Honorius. The imperial commissioner Marcellinus presided over three sessions. Each side chose seven spokesmen: Aurelius, Augustine and Alypius for the Catholics, and Primian, Petilian and Emeritus for the Donatists. Marcellinus ruled for the Catholics. The acts survive incomplete, and Augustine's summary of the conference supplies much of the lost third session. They are a key source for the Donatist controversy.

This is a collection of Roman imperial laws issued against the Donatists, the schismatic North African church that broke with the Catholic communion in the early fourth century. Most of the laws come from the Theodosian Code, chiefly its title on heretics, and were issued by emperors such as Honorius and Theodosius II in the late fourth and early fifth centuries. One example, issued in 412 after the Conference of Carthage, fined Donatist clergy and laity who would not return to the Catholic Church. The collection documents how the state enforced religious unity in Roman Africa during Augustine's lifetime.

This is an anthology of short excerpts from various ancient Latin writers about the Donatists, the schismatic church of Roman North Africa. It was assembled by early modern editors, not written as a single work. The numbered passages include a ruling of Pope Leo I to the bishops of Mauretania Caesariensis, a remark by the Arian Fastidiosus preserved in Fulgentius, a sermon of Peter Chrysologus and Cassiodorus's commentary on the Psalms. Imperial legislation with Jacques Godefroy's commentary accompanies the excerpts. Together the extracts show how later writers, from the fourth to the sixth century, remembered and judged the schism.

This is a modern collection of fourth-century documents on the Arian controversy, gathered from earlier conciliar compilations such as Labbe's. It brings together letters and decrees by emperors, bishops and synods, mostly from about 340 to 400, some in both Greek and Latin. It opens with Constantius II's letter inviting Athanasius of Alexandria to come back from exile and promising him his see. The collection gives primary evidence for the church politics and imperial involvement in the disputes over Nicene orthodoxy. Its pieces come from many different authors.

The Elogia Symmachiana is an anonymous Latin collection of ancient testimonies praising the Symmachi, chiefly the late fourth-century Roman senator and orator Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, and it typically accompanies editions of his letters and speeches. It gathers excerpts from several writers. Macrobius ranks Symmachus's rich, florid style with that of Pliny the Younger. Prudentius, in his poem Contra Symmachum, admires his eloquence while attacking his defence of paganism. Ammianus Marcellinus praises a Symmachus's learning and his term as prefect of Rome. Together the passages show how pagan and Christian contemporaries regarded Symmachus.

This is a collection of ancient, medieval and Renaissance testimonia about Publilius Optatianus Porfyrius, the Latin poet of Constantine the Great's reign, made by an anonymous editor. It gathers Jerome's Chronicle notice that Porfyrius was freed from exile after sending Constantine a remarkable volume of verse. It also includes epigrams quoted by Fulgentius and Bede's mention of his metres in De arte metrica. Hrabanus Maurus acknowledges him as the model for his own figured poems in praise of the Cross. Later humanist witnesses include Cuspinianus and Giraldi. Together they trace how Porfyrius's pattern poetry was received.

This is a collection of Latin letters from about 254–257 connected with Stephen I, bishop of Rome. Its central pieces are letters of Cyprian of Carthage. In one, Cyprian urges Stephen to write to the bishops of Gaul so that Marcianus of Arles, a follower of Novatian, can be deposed and replaced. The collection also bears on the dispute between Stephen and the African and Eastern churches over whether those baptized by heretics must be rebaptized. That controversy shaped later Western teaching on the sacraments, and Augustine took it up again against the Donatists.

This is a collection of the surviving rulings of Pope Stephen I (254–257) in the controversy over baptism by heretics, dated about 255 to 257. Stephen's own letters to the African and Eastern bishops are lost. His statements were therefore gathered later from quotations in the letters of Cyprian of Carthage and Firmilian of Caesarea, who opposed him. The best-known ruling is "nihil innovetur nisi quod traditum est": converts from heresy were to be received by the laying on of hands for penance, not rebaptized.

These are short Latin letters preserved among the correspondence of Cyprian of Carthage (Letters 21–24 in modern numbering). They were written by confessors and clergy during the Decian persecution of about 250. Celerinus, a Roman confessor, asks the Carthaginian confessor Lucianus to obtain peace for his lapsed sisters. Lucianus replies that he grants peace in the name of the martyr Paulus. Further letters come from the confessors collectively and from Bishop Caldonius. Together they document the dispute over martyrs' letters of peace and the reconciliation of the lapsed.

This is a collection of ancient Latin documents and excerpts on the history of the Donatist schism in Roman North Africa, from the Diocletianic persecution of 303 to the early fifth century. It was assembled by modern editors, not composed as a single work. It opens with Optatus of Milevis's account of the schism's origin, which names bishops accused of having been traditores, those who handed over the Scriptures during the persecution. Other material includes records of hearings, imperial letters and conciliar acts. The collection is a basic source for the conflict between Catholics and Donatists.

This is a compilation of ancient and early medieval passages about Sidonius Apollinaris (c. 430–c. 485), the Gallo-Roman aristocrat, poet and letter-writer who became bishop of Clermont. Writings by several authors are gathered here as prefatory material to his works. They include the dedication of Claudianus Mamertus's On the State of the Soul, which praises Sidonius as a restorer of the old eloquence, and chapter 92 of Gennadius of Marseille's On Illustrious Men. Gennadius commends Sidonius's learning, his verse and prose, and his Catholic steadfastness under barbarian rule.
