This is an anonymous compilation of testimonia, meaning short statements by later authors, about Gennadius of Marseille and his catalogue of Christian writers, De viris illustribus, which continued Jerome's work of the same name. It gathers comments by Cassiodorus, who kept the two catalogues together in one volume, and by Isidore of Seville. It also includes the Counter-Reformation cardinal Robert Bellarmine, who dated Gennadius to about 490 under Pope Gelasius. Bellarmine also suspected Gennadius of Semipelagian sympathies because he praised Cassian and Faustus while criticising Prosper of Aquitaine.

This is an anonymous Latin account of a debate between Catholic bishops and Arian clergy. It is said to have taken place around 499 to 501 before Gundobad, the Arian king of the Burgundians, at Sarbiniacum. The text names Avitus of Vienne as chief spokesman, with Aeonius of Arles and others, and links the meeting to the feast of Saint Justus and to Remigius of Reims. Although it was long treated as a genuine record, modern scholars widely regard it as a seventeenth-century forgery.

This is a small collection of letters about Sixtus II, bishop of Rome in 257–258, gathered from various authors. Its main part is fragments of letters from Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, to Sixtus. Dionysius wrote them in Greek, and they survive through Eusebius's Church History. They deal with the dispute over rebaptising converts from heresy, which had set Sixtus's predecessor Stephen against the churches of Asia Minor and Africa. They also mention Dionysius's correspondence about Sabellianism. The letters are important evidence for the baptismal controversy of the mid-third century.

This appendix gathers letters spuriously attributed to Pope Felix IV (526–530). Its first item, an encyclical to all bishops, is marked in its own heading as inauthentic. It urges bishops to keep to apostolic order and to stay united with their head. It also rules that Mass should be celebrated only in consecrated places, except in grave necessity, and explains what to do when it is uncertain whether a church has been consecrated. Drawing heavily on letters of Leo the Great, such forgeries belong to the ninth-century Pseudo-Isidorian decretals rather than to Felix's pontificate.

This is a Latin collection of doctrinal fragments drawn from the writings of Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in North Africa (died c. 533). It was put together by an anonymous compiler, probably not long after his death. The opening excerpts defend the full equality of the Son and the Holy Spirit with the Father against Arian arguments. They show that Scripture gives all three the same divine names, such as "Most High", and the same works. Material of this kind seems to come from Fulgentius's lost anti-Arian works, and the collection preserves passages that would otherwise be lost.

This is a miscellany of Latin documents relating to Saint Benedict of Nursia (died c. 547) and his monastery of Monte Cassino, gathered as a supplement to his works. The pieces come from different authors and dates, from the sixth century to the late eleventh. Among them is a sermon on Benedict's sister Saint Scholastica, attributed to Alberic the deacon, a monk of Monte Cassino in the eleventh century. Drawing on Gregory the Great's Dialogues, it describes her religious life near Monte Cassino and her yearly meetings with her brother.

This anonymous Latin compilation of papal decrees was added as a supplement to the collection of decretals of the Roman bishops made by Dionysius Exiguus in the early sixth century. It probably dates from the sixth century. It opens with a list of the popes whose rulings it contains. Its first document is the record of a Roman synod held under Pope Hilarus in 465, which issued rules on ordinations based on Scripture and the canons of Nicaea. The collection is a witness to how early papal legislation was gathered and passed on within the Latin canonical tradition.

This is a collection of Latin sermons, admonitions and other short pieces gathered as an appendix to the works of Caesarius, bishop of Arles from 502 to 542. Their attribution to him is doubtful or uncertain. Several are probably by other authors, and some reuse earlier writers. The opening piece, an exhortation to keep true charity, openly includes passages from a homily of Augustine on charity. It contrasts charity, the root of all good, with cupidity, the root of all evil. These texts show how sixth-century Gallic preachers reworked earlier material, especially Augustine's, for pastoral preaching.

This is a small group of Latin documents from the early sixth century connected with Caesarius, bishop of Arles (c. 502–542). Its first piece is a letter from Pope Hormisdas (514–523) to Caesarius. The pope praises his zeal for building up the Church of Arles and approves his request about the convent for consecrated virgins he had recently founded there. Under this ruling, later bishops of Arles would have no power over the convent, so the nuns could serve God undisturbed. The documents shed light on early Gallic monasticism for women and on ties between Arles and Rome.

This is an editorial appendix to the works of Gregory of Tours, the sixth-century bishop and historian. It gathers ancient documents by several authors that Gregory praises or that help explain his writings. They include a verse epitaph by Pope Damasus for the Roman martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria and an apse inscription recording Pope Honorius's rebuilding of the basilica of Saint Pancras. There is also a testament attributed to Perpetuus, a fifth-century bishop of Tours, although its authenticity has been questioned. Together these texts show the liturgical, hagiographical and ecclesiastical background to Gregory's works.

This is a group of anonymous Latin liturgical books of the Gallican rite, used in Merovingian Gaul before Roman usage replaced it under the Carolingians. Jean Mabillon brought them together in his study De liturgia Gallicana libri tres (1685). The group includes the Lectionary of Luxeuil, with readings for the year; the Missale Gothicum, a sacramentary of about 700, probably from Burgundy; the Missale Francorum; and the Missale Gallicanum vetus. Their exact dates and origins are debated, but they are central evidence for early Western liturgy outside Rome.

This is a collection of Latin liturgical texts gathered as supporting evidence ("probationes") in an appendix to Jean Mabillon's study of the ancient Gallican liturgy, De liturgia Gallicana (1685). It is the work of many hands rather than one author. It sets out formularies for comparison with the Gallican rite. These include Mass texts taken from the Mozarabic (Old Spanish) Missal, beginning with the First Sunday of Advent. The prayers, chants and readings show the close relationship between the non-Roman Western liturgies of Gaul and Spain.

This is a collective letter, or decree, addressed to Queen Radegund by seven Gallic bishops: Euphronius of Tours, Praetextatus of Rouen, Germanus of Paris, Felix of Nantes, Domitianus of Angers, Victorius of Rennes and Domnolus of Le Mans. It was written around 567, while Euphronius still lived. Answering Radegund's request, the bishops approve her convent at Poitiers, later called Holy Cross, and its way of life. They also threaten excommunication for any nun who leaves the enclosure to marry. Gregory of Tours preserves the letter in his Histories (IX.39), and it is an important witness to early Frankish women's monasticism.

The Vitae Patrum is a large Latin collection of lives, sayings and histories of the Desert Fathers and Mothers of Egypt, Palestine and Syria, arranged in ten books. It brings together anonymous and attributed texts mostly written between the fourth and seventh centuries. They include Jerome's lives of Paul of Thebes, Hilarion and Malchus, Rufinus's Historia monachorum, Latin versions of Palladius's Lausiac History, and the Verba seniorum translated by Pelagius and John. The collection was widely read in the medieval West and shaped Latin ideals of monastic and ascetic life.

This is a small collection of Latin charters and related documents about the Irish monk Columbanus (d. 615) and his monastery at Bobbio in northern Italy. It opens with a diploma issued at Milan in the name of the Lombard king Agilulf, granting Columbanus and his companions land for four miles around the basilica of Saint Peter at Bobbio. A charter follows in which Columbanus is said to place the monastery under the apostolic see. The authenticity and dating of some pieces are disputed. Together they document the early endowment and privileges of Bobbio.

This is a collection of Latin charters and related legal documents from the Merovingian period, roughly the reign of the Frankish king Chlothar II (584–629). The texts are anonymous and record grants and transfers of property, often to churches and monasteries. The first, dated 625, is a deed in which Lonegisilus, a priest and monk from Alamannia, gives a small monastery he founded at the village of Busiacum to Hadoindus, bishop of Le Mans, and his church. Charters like these are valuable evidence for Merovingian religious life, land tenure and the use of documents in the early seventh century.

This appendix gathers various Latin documents about Pope Honorius I (625–638) and the Monothelete controversy. It opens with an excerpt from Maximus the Confessor's letter to the presbyter Marinus. There Maximus defends Honorius's letter to Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople. He argues that when Honorius spoke of "one will" in Christ, he was not denying Christ's human will. He meant only that no sinful fleshly will came before the Incarnation, and he supports this reading with a passage attributed to Athanasius. The collection is evidence for the long debate over Honorius's orthodoxy, which ended in his condemnation in 681.

This is a collection of early Latin documents on the origins and history of the Donatist schism in Roman North Africa. Early modern editors assembled it from various authors and arranged it in chronological order. It opens in AD 303 with Optatus of Milevis's account, addressed to the Donatist bishop Parmenian, of the traditores: bishops who handed over the Scriptures during the Diocletianic persecution. It then turns to the meeting of bishops at Cirta. The texts it brings together are basic evidence for how the schism began and for the earliest stages of the dispute.

This is a Latin anthology of ancient testimonies about Hilary of Poitiers, the fourth-century bishop and opponent of Arianism. Editors of Hilary's works compiled it from earlier writers, chiefly Jerome. Its excerpts come from Jerome's letters and his Apology against Rufinus. They mention Hilary's commentary on the Psalms, his book On the Synods and his translations of Origen. They also praise his orthodoxy and eloquence, and note his elaborate "Gallic" style, which Jerome thought hard for simpler readers. The collection shows how Hilary was regarded in late antiquity.

This is a Latin epitaph in elegiac couplets by Venantius Fortunatus, preserved as poem 5 of the fourth book of his Carmina and written in the later sixth century. It honours two bishops of Limoges named Ruricius, a grandfather and grandson who were buried in the same tomb. The poem claims kinship with the Roman Anicii and says the bishops founded churches dedicated to Augustine and to Peter. It praises their almsgiving and describes holiness as a triumph over death. It is typical of the funerary verse Fortunatus wrote for Gallic bishops.

The Life of Germanus, Bishop of Paris, is a Latin prose saint's life by the poet Venantius Fortunatus, written in the late sixth century, after Germanus died in 576. It tells how Germanus, born in the territory of Autun, survived dangers in childhood, received his training from a kinsman, Scopilio, and later served as bishop of Paris. Most of the work recounts his miracles of healing and deliverance. It is a key source for the saint's cult and for religious life in Merovingian Gaul.

This Latin saint's life of Radegund (c. 520–587) was written by Venantius Fortunatus, the poet who was her close friend and later bishop of Poitiers. He wrote it soon after her death in 587. It tells of her royal Thuringian birth and her capture by the Franks, followed by her marriage to King Chlothar I. It then describes how she left him to take religious vows and founded the Abbey of the Holy Cross at Poitiers. The life stresses her severe asceticism, her charity and her miracles. A second book, written by the nun Baudonivia, later added to it.

This Latin poem by Venantius Fortunatus is addressed to Felix, bishop of Nantes. It was written in the second half of the sixth century, while Fortunatus lived in Merovingian Gaul. It opens with a long description of nature reviving in spring: sun, stars, flowers, crops, vines, trees and bees. This renewal of the world is then celebrated as a sign of Christ's resurrection and triumph over hell. Lines from the poem were later taken into the liturgy as the processional hymn "Salve festa dies", which was sung widely in medieval Easter celebrations.

This is a pair of short Latin poems in elegiac couplets by Venantius Fortunatus, found in the third book of his Carmina. Both are addressed to Bertichramnus (Bertram), bishop of Bordeaux, and were written in Merovingian Gaul in the later sixth century. The first thanks the bishop for taking the poet up into his carriage, comparing him to a swallow caring for its young. The second praises the bishop's own verses but gently points out borrowings from older poets and faults in the metre. Together they show the literary friendships among Gallic clergy.

The Vita S. Hilarii is a Latin hagiography in two books about Hilary of Poitiers, the fourth-century bishop and opponent of Arianism. It is attributed to Venantius Fortunatus and was written in the later sixth century. Both books are addressed to Pascentius, bishop of Poitiers. The first recounts Hilary's life and episcopate. The second, which in many manuscripts survives separately or is missing, records miracles linked to him, including some after his death. Early editors questioned whether both books have the same author. The work is a key witness to the cult of Hilary in Merovingian Gaul.

This short Latin address on clerical continence is attributed to Veranus, bishop of Cavaillon in Provence, who died about 590. Its heading says it was spoken at an unnamed synod of his time, probably in the later sixth century. Veranus argues that clergy who serve at the altar should not live as husbands. He cites the priest who gave David the showbread only after his men had kept away from women, and Paul's call to self-examination. He urges bishops to recruit worthy clergy from nearby monasteries, since a few good men are better than a careless crowd.

These two short Latin letters were written in the first half of the seventh century by Verus, bishop of Rodez in Merovingian Gaul, to Desiderius, later bishop of Cahors. In the first, addressed to Desiderius as bishop, Verus answers his instruction about a synodal decision that "lord Sulpicius" had apparently changed, and asks for his prayers. The second, addressed to Desiderius as a powerful layman, asks for his patronage on behalf of Verus's nephews. The letters show the network of correspondence and patronage among Gallic bishops and nobles of the time.

This short Latin fragment comes from a lost treatise on the date of Easter by Victor, bishop of Capua (died 554). It survives because Bede quotes it in his De temporum ratione. Victor wrote when the Easter date for the thirteenth indiction, dated after the consulship of Basilius, was in dispute. Some followed the paschal cycle of Victorius of Aquitaine, but Victor held that Easter should be kept on 24 April. He set out to show the errors of Victorius's tables. The fragment is evidence for sixth-century Western arguments over how to calculate Easter.

This is a Latin gospel harmony that weaves the four Gospels into one continuous narrative of Christ's life. It opens with Luke's prologue, followed by the prologue of John. Victor, bishop of Capua (d. 554), found an anonymous harmony and issued it in the mid-sixth century with Vulgate wording. In his preface he asked whether it came from Tatian's Diatessaron or from Ammonius of Alexandria, and he leaned towards Tatian. Modern scholars place it in the Diatessaron tradition. It is the oldest complete witness to that harmony's order of material and influenced later Western gospel harmonies.

This is a set of short Latin exegetical fragments on the Gospels, preserved under the name of Victor, bishop of Capua (541–554). They were drawn from a catena on the four Gospels. Victor introduces them as excerpts from the "Responsiones capitulorum" of Polycarp of Smyrna, disciple of John the Evangelist. The fragments explain individual Gospel passages: Genesis 2:24 as quoted in Matthew, the "cup" of martyrdom offered to James and John, and why the evangelists open their Gospels differently. Their attribution to Polycarp is generally regarded as doubtful.

This Latin letter was written around 646 by Victor, bishop of Carthage, to Pope Theodore I. It appears to be a synodical letter, the kind of letter a newly consecrated bishop sent to announce his consecration and show that he was in communion with Rome. It opens with lavish praise of the pope's holiness and apostolic teaching, supported by quotations from Paul and the Psalms. The letter shows how close the African church and the Roman see were in the mid-seventh century, during the controversy over Monothelitism and shortly before the Arab conquest of North Africa.

This Latin chronicle was written by Victor, bishop of Tunnuna in North Africa, in the 560s, during his imprisonment and exile for opposing Justinian I's condemnation of the Three Chapters. It picks up where the chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine ends and records events year by year, dated by consuls, from 444 to the mid-560s. It focuses on church affairs, especially the Eutychian and Monophysite controversies, the Council of Chalcedon and the Three Chapters dispute, and also covers Vandal Africa. John of Biclaro later continued it.

De laude sanctorum ("In Praise of the Saints") is a Latin sermon by Victricius, bishop of Rouen, usually dated to about 396. He preached it when relics of martyrs, many of them sent from Italy by Ambrose of Milan, arrived in Rouen. Victricius explains that he met the relics late because he had been in Britain, settling a dispute among bishops there. The sermon defends the cult of relics, arguing that each fragment holds the martyr's whole power. It is an early Western theological treatment of relics.

The Regula Orientalis ("Eastern Rule") is a short Latin monastic rule attributed to an otherwise unknown Vigilius the Deacon. It is usually dated to the fifth century, probably in Gaul. Its name reflects its heavy borrowing from the Pachomian rules of Egypt, which were known in the West through Jerome's Latin translation. It describes the qualities required of the abbot and the duties of two senior monks who share in governing the community. It also regulates discipline, work and daily life. It is an early witness to how Eastern cenobitic traditions were adapted for Western monasteries.

This is a collection of Latin letters and decrees of Pope Vigilius, bishop of Rome from 537 to 555. It begins with a letter, headed as written while he was still regarded as an irregular pope, answering a distant bishop's questions on church discipline. Among the questions are the treatment of Priscillianists and other points of practice. Later documents deal with the Three Chapters controversy, Vigilius's long detention in Constantinople, and his dealings with Emperor Justinian I. Together they are a major source for papal–imperial relations and for the period of the Second Council of Constantinople (553).

This Latin papal decree is usually identified with the second Constitutum of Pope Vigilius, issued in Constantinople in February 554. In it Vigilius reversed his earlier resistance and accepted the condemnation of the Three Chapters by the Second Council of Constantinople (553). The Three Chapters were the person and writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, certain writings of Theodoret of Cyrrhus, and the letter of Ibas of Edessa. The decree reaffirms the Chalcedonian definition of faith and argues that condemning these texts does not detract from Chalcedon's authority. Its acceptance provoked prolonged schisms in the Western Church.

This Latin treatise on the unity of the Trinity is written against Felicianus, an Arian. It has come down among the works of Augustine but is usually attributed to Vigilius of Thapsus, the North African bishop who wrote against Arianism under Vandal rule in the late fifth century. Answering a request from a "beloved son", the author retells a recent debate with Felicianus as a dialogue, marking the speakers by their initials. He defends the full divinity of the Son against Arian objections.

Contra Varimadum Arianum is a Latin anti-Arian treatise in three books, traditionally attributed to Vigilius of Thapsus but now generally treated as the work of an anonymous author ("Pseudo-Vigilius"). Its date is uncertain, though it is usually placed in the late fifth century. In the preface the author says he once answered the propositions of Varimadus, an Arian deacon, while at Naples. He now refutes Arian objections point by point with scriptural testimonies, defending the unity of the Trinity. The work is an important example of North African biblical florilegia.

This is a Latin anti-Arian work in two books, transmitted among the writings of Vigilius, the late fifth-century bishop of Thapsus in North Africa. The attribution is uncertain. The first book preserves the minutes of the Council of Aquileia, held on 3 September 381. There Ambrose of Milan and other western bishops questioned and condemned the Homoian bishops Palladius and Secundianus. The record is an important source for the Arian controversy in the West and for Ambrose's role in church politics. The second book continues the polemic against Palladius.

Contra Eutychetem (Against Eutyches) is a Latin theological treatise in five books by Vigilius, bishop of Thapsus in North Africa. It was probably written in the later 480s, after the Vandal king Huneric's persecution of 484 had driven its author into exile. Vigilius describes the conflict over Christ's natures dividing many Eastern churches. He attacks the teaching of Eutyches while also rejecting that of Nestorius, and he defends the Christology of the Council of Chalcedon and Pope Leo's Tome. It is a major Western witness to the post-Chalcedonian debates.

The Contra Arianos dialogus is a Latin theological dialogue by Vigilius, bishop of Thapsus in North Africa. He probably wrote it in the late fifth century, when Arian Vandal kings ruled the region and persecuted Catholics. The work stages an imagined debate between Athanasius and Arius, with Probus acting as judge. It opens with an account of the Council of Nicaea, the exile and recall of Arius, and the death of Constantine. It defends Nicene Trinitarian doctrine, and its literary form makes it a notable example of anti-Arian polemic in Latin.

A Latin theological dialogue by Vigilius, bishop of Thapsus in North Africa, probably written in the 480s, during or shortly after the Vandal persecution of Catholics under the Arian king Huneric. Athanasius is shown debating Arius, Sabellius and Photinus, with a judge named Probus weighing their arguments. Each heretic states his own doctrine, and Athanasius answers him in turn. Vigilius chose the dialogue form to refute many errors briefly. The work circulated under Athanasius' name, and it is an important witness to anti-Arian Trinitarian argument in Vandal Africa.

This Latin treatise on the unity of the Trinity is written against Felicianus, an Arian. It has come down among the works of Augustine but is usually attributed to Vigilius of Thapsus, the North African bishop who wrote against Arianism under Vandal rule in the late fifth century. Answering a request from a "beloved son", the author retells a recent debate with Felicianus as a dialogue, marking the speakers by their initials. He defends the full divinity of the Son against Arian objections.

These two Latin letters by Vigilius, bishop of Trent, were written shortly after 397. One is addressed to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, and the other to John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople. They describe the martyrdom of three clerics, Sisinnius, Martyrius and Alexander, who were missionaries from Cappadocia. Pagan inhabitants of the Anaunia valley (Val di Non) killed them after they founded a church there. The letters are early eyewitness accounts of the Christianisation of the Alpine regions, and they helped spread the cult of these martyrs.

The Commonitory is a Latin treatise by Vincent of Lérins, a Gallic monk, written about 434, shortly after the Council of Ephesus. He wrote it under the pseudonym "Peregrinus." It offers a rule for telling Catholic truth from heresy: Scripture comes first, read in the sense held "everywhere, always, and by all," that is, by universality, antiquity and consent. Vincent also allows real development of doctrine, so long as it does not alter the faith. The second book was lost while he was still alive, and only his summary of it survives.

This passage is the closing section of the Commonitorium by Vincent of Lérins, a Gallic monk writing about 434, shortly after the Council of Ephesus. The work first had two books. The second was lost during Vincent's lifetime, and only this summary of it survives. The summary restates the work's method: Scripture is sufficient, but it must be interpreted by the Church's tradition, judged by universality, antiquity and consent. Ancient conciliar decisions come first, followed by the agreement of approved Fathers.

The Epistolae are the small surviving Latin correspondence of Viventiolus, bishop of Lyon from about 514 to 523. The first letter, to Avitus of Vienne, survives among Avitus's works. The second is a circular letter summoning the bishops, clergy, notables and landowners of his province to the Council of Epaon, held in September 517. It lets lay people attend and invites open charges against clergy of bad conduct, provided accusers can prove them. The letter is useful evidence for church discipline in Burgundian Gaul.

This is a Latin hagiographical dossier by Warnaharius, a cleric of Langres, written in the early seventh century. It was composed at the request of Ceraunius, bishop of Paris, who was collecting acts of the martyrs. In a dedicatory letter, Warnaharius compares that project to the work of Eusebius. The text tells of the martyrdom of the twin (traditionally triplet) brothers Speusippus, Eleusippus and Meleusippus in the suburbs of Langres, and mentions the arrival of Saint Benignus. It also treats Desiderius, a martyred bishop of Langres.

The Vita Sancti Desiderii is a Latin hagiographical account of Desiderius (Didier), bishop of Langres, who was venerated as a martyr. It is attributed to Warnaharius, a cleric of Langres, and probably dates from the early seventh century. The text describes barbarians it calls Vandals, led by a king named Crocus, invading and plundering Gaul. It tells how Desiderius and his companions were killed during this invasion. The date of the events is uncertain. The work preserves the Langres tradition about its martyr-bishop and his feast.

The Tractatus are a collection of Latin sermons attributed to Zeno, bishop of Verona in the later fourth century. They were probably preached between about 362 and 380 and survive in two books of roughly ninety pieces. Some are full homilies and others only short outlines. Many are addressed to catechumens and the newly baptized at Easter. Others treat faith, the Trinity against the Arians, virtues and biblical figures. Their polished rhetorical style draws on Tertullian and Cyprian. They are the earliest surviving collection of Latin sermons from northern Italy.

The Letters and Decrees (Epistolae et decreta) are the surviving Latin letters and rulings of Pope Zosimus, bishop of Rome from 417 to 418. Several back Patroclus of Arles, granting his see metropolitan rights in southern Gaul over rivals such as Vienne. Others concern the Pelagian controversy. Zosimus at first favoured Pelagius and Caelestius, but in 418 he condemned them in his Epistula tractoria, which survives only in fragments. The letters are a key source for papal claims to authority over Gaul and Africa in the early fifth century.

This Latin collection gathers short canonical rulings taken from the letters of Pope Zosimus, bishop of Rome from 417 to 418. The excerpts survive in later canon-law collections, including Gratian's Decretum. They state that even the apostolic see cannot grant or change anything against the statutes of the Fathers. They also summarize rules from his letter to Bishop Hesychius of Salona on clerical discipline. These rules require bishops to be learned in Scripture, set fixed periods of service in each grade from lector to priest, and exclude men who had married twice, and former public penitents, from the clergy.

A letter in Greek from the church of Rome to the church of Corinth. It names no author, but it is traditionally attributed to Clement, bishop of Rome, and most scholars accept this. It is usually dated to about AD 96, although some scholars place it before 70. Members of the Corinthian congregation had deposed their presbyters, and the letter urges them to repent and to restore these leaders, who had been appointed in succession from the Apostles. One of the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament, it was read aloud in churches and copied into some biblical codices.

The so-called Second Epistle of Clement is an early Christian sermon in Greek, usually dated to the mid-second century. Its author is unknown. Tradition attributed it to Clement of Rome, but scholars generally reject that attribution. The text begins by urging its hearers to think of Jesus Christ "as of God," the judge of the living and the dead. It then calls for repentance, self-control and steadfast faith in view of the coming judgment. Often counted as the oldest surviving Christian homily, it appears alongside 1 Clement in Codex Alexandrinus and is grouped among the Apostolic Fathers.

The Apostolic Constitutions is a Greek church order in eight books. It claims to give the apostles' own instructions, handed on through Clement of Rome. It was actually compiled around 375–380, probably in Syria, perhaps at Antioch. The compiler is unknown but is often identified with the interpolator of the Pseudo-Ignatian letters. The work reworks earlier sources, chiefly the Didascalia Apostolorum and the Didache. It covers Christian morals, clergy, liturgy and church discipline. Book 8 includes a complete eucharistic liturgy and the Apostolic Canons, which makes the collection valuable for the history of early Christian worship.

This is a set of miscellaneous material collected with the writings of Clement of Rome, the late first-century bishop of Rome. It includes introductory matter, notes and short pieces not catalogued separately. Much of it consists of ancient testimonies about Clement. These include Irenaeus's account of Clement as a hearer of the apostles who sent the Roman church's letter to Corinth, and passages in which Clement of Alexandria quotes that letter. Because the pieces have different authors and dates, no single attribution or date applies to the whole.

This is a small collection of Greek sayings attributed to two apostles and preserved only as quotations in later writers. The Matthias fragments come mainly from Clement of Alexandria, who cites a work known as the Traditions of Matthias. One teaches that one should fight the flesh and make use of it without giving in to unrestrained pleasure, while strengthening the soul through faith and knowledge. The saying of Bartholomew, that theology is both abundant and very small and the Gospel broad yet concise, is quoted by Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite. Their origin and date are uncertain.

The Epistle of Barnabas is an early Christian treatise in Greek, usually dated between about 70 and 135. Some early Church Fathers, including Clement of Alexandria, attributed it to the apostle Barnabas, but most modern scholars think an unknown teacher wrote it. It reads the Jewish Scriptures allegorically and argues that their laws on sacrifice, circumcision, food and the Sabbath point to Christ and belong to Christians. It ends with a "Two Ways" teaching on moral life. It is counted among the Apostolic Fathers, and the complete text survives in Codex Sinaiticus.

An anonymous Greek collection of church rules, whose title means "Order of Ecclesiastical Canons". It was probably compiled between the fourth and sixth centuries, though its date is uncertain. Sections are attributed to apostles, including Paul. The text closely parallels the eighth book of the Apostolic Constitutions. It sets out who may be admitted as a catechumen and on what terms. It covers slaves and their masters, married and unmarried people, the possessed, pimps, charioteers, gladiators and other performers, soldiers, magicians and diviners, and concubines. It also rules on how many days slaves should work and when they should rest.

The Epitome of the Deeds of Saint Peter is a Byzantine Greek abridgment of the Pseudo-Clementine Homilies, an early Christian romance falsely attributed to Clement of Rome. It begins with Clement's letter to James, bishop of Jerusalem. Clement then tells of his youthful anxieties about death, immortality and the origin of the world, his conversion, and his travels with the apostle Peter. It condenses Peter's discourses and the recognition of Clement's family. Its date is uncertain, and it exists in more than one recension, including one associated with Symeon Metaphrastes. It helped spread the Clementine legend in later Byzantine tradition.

The Clementine Homilies are a Greek Christian romance in twenty books, falsely attributed to Clement of Rome and probably composed in the fourth century. Narrated by Clement, they tell of his conversion, his travels with the apostle Peter, Peter's discourses and debates with Simon Magus, and the reunion of Clement's family. Letters of Peter and of Clement to James of Jerusalem stand before the work. With the Recognitions, it is one of two surviving versions of the Pseudo-Clementine romance and is valued as evidence for Jewish-Christian thought.

This anonymous Greek apocryphal passion of the apostle Andrew is framed as an encyclical letter from the presbyters and deacons of Achaia to churches everywhere. It tells how Andrew confronted the proconsul Aegeates at Patras, defended the Christian faith, and was crucified there. The work opens with a developed Trinitarian confession, and its date is uncertain, probably between the fifth and sixth centuries. It draws on the earlier Acts of Andrew and became an important source for the later tradition of Andrew's martyrdom.

This Greek hagiographical discourse is attributed to Ephraim, archbishop of Cherson in the Crimea, a figure about whom little is known. Its date is uncertain. It opens by praising Clement of Rome, the successor of Peter, and tells of a miracle at his tomb in the sea near Cherson, where tradition said he was martyred. Each year on his feast the sea drew back and pilgrims could visit the tomb. In the best-known episode, a child left behind there was found alive the following year. The text is an important witness to the cult of Clement in the Crimea.

The Epistle to Diognetus is an anonymous Greek apology for Christianity, addressed to an otherwise unknown enquirer named Diognetus. It survived among the works of Justin Martyr, but he is not thought to be its author. Estimates of its date range from about AD 130 to the later second century. The writer rejects Greek idolatry and Jewish worship and explains God's plan of salvation through his Son. The epistle is best known for its description of Christians as living in the world like the soul in the body. Its closing chapters may have been added later.

The Shepherd of Hermas is an early Christian apocalyptic and moral work written in Greek at Rome, probably in the first half of the second century. The Muratorian fragment attributes it to Hermas, brother of Bishop Pius of Rome. It is divided into Visions, Mandates and Similitudes, and in it an angel in the form of a shepherd teaches about repentance after baptism, simplicity and Christian conduct. Some early Christians treated it as scripture, and it is included in Codex Sinaiticus. It is counted among the Apostolic Fathers.

The Martyrium S. Clementis is an anonymous Greek hagiographical account of the martyrdom of Clement of Rome, here described as the third leader of the Roman church after the apostle Peter. Its date is uncertain, probably between the fifth and eighth centuries. It praises Clement's teaching, which won the goodwill of Jews, Greeks and Christians alike. It then tells the legend of his exile under Trajan to the quarries of the Crimea, his miracles there, and his death by drowning with an anchor. This legend was a main source for Clement's later cult in East and West.

This is a miscellaneous group of Greek texts from the second volume of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, a volume given over mainly to the Apostolic Fathers, including the Shepherd of Hermas. It gathers prefatory matter, editorial notes and short pieces that are not catalogued as separate works. The opening passage collects ancient testimonies to the Shepherd, in the style of Clement of Alexandria. It quotes Hermas on false prophets, double-mindedness, the righteous dead, the virtues as daughters of faith, the fear of the Lord, and repentance. The material is anonymous and varies in date.

The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs is a pseudepigraphal work presenting the deathbed speeches of Jacob's twelve sons to their descendants. Each patriarch reflects on his own life, warns against a particular vice or praises a virtue, and foretells the future of Israel. It survives in Greek and took its final form around the second century AD. Scholars still disagree about its origins. Some see it as a Jewish work later expanded by Christians, while others think it was composed by Christians drawing on older Semitic material.

The Celestial Hierarchy is a Greek treatise in the Corpus Dionysiacum. It is addressed to "Timothy" by an author writing as Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul's Athenian convert. In fact it was written by an anonymous Christian Neoplatonist, probably in Syria, around 485–530. The treatise reads the symbolic images of angels in Scripture and arranges the heavenly beings into nine orders grouped in three triads. Through these orders, divine light passes down to purify, illuminate and perfect. It became the basis of medieval angelology in both East and West.

The Divine Names is a Greek theological treatise in thirteen chapters belonging to the Corpus Areopagiticum. It was written in the late fifth or early sixth century by an anonymous author who presents himself as Dionysius the Areopagite, the Athenian convert of Paul. Addressed to Timothy, it interprets the names Scripture gives to God, such as Good, Light, Beauty, Love, Being, Life and Wisdom. It holds that God is beyond every name and includes an influential account of evil as privation. Drawing on Proclus, the work shaped later Byzantine and medieval Latin theology.

The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy is a Greek treatise in the Corpus Dionysiacum. Its author wrote under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul's Athenian convert, but was probably a Syrian monk of the late fifth or early sixth century. Addressed to "Timothy", it pairs with the Celestial Hierarchy. It interprets the Church's rites as sacred symbols: baptism, the Eucharistic synaxis, the consecration of myron, ordination, monastic tonsure and funeral rites. It also describes the ordered ranks of clergy, monks and laity through which divine light leads believers toward deification. The treatise deeply influenced Byzantine liturgical commentary and medieval Western theology.

The Mystical Theology is a short Greek treatise in five chapters belonging to the Corpus Dionysiacum. Its anonymous author wrote under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul's Athenian convert, probably in Syria around 485–530. Addressed to Timothy, it opens with a prayer to the Trinity. It then describes the soul's ascent beyond sense and intellect into the "divine darkness," where God is known by unknowing. By contrasting affirmative with negative theology, it became a founding text of Christian apophatic mysticism in both East and West.

The Letters are a collection of ten short Greek epistles that form part of the Corpus Areopagiticum. They were written in the late fifth or early sixth century by an anonymous author, probably in Syria, who presented himself as Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul's Athenian convert. Their addressees are figures from the apostolic age, among them the monk Gaius, Bishop Polycarp, Titus and John the Evangelist on Patmos. The letters return to the corpus's main themes: God's unknowability beyond being, the "divine darkness", the interpretation of scriptural symbols and the right ordering of the church hierarchy.

This is a collection of supplementary material from the third volume of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, which contains the writings attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite. It brings together front matter, editorial notes and shorter pieces that are not catalogued separately. Among them is a Greek note recording that Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos sent a manuscript of the Dionysian corpus to the abbey of Saint-Denis near Paris in 1408, delivered by his envoy Manuel Chrysoloras. Another is a prologue attributed to Maximus the Confessor or to John of Scythopolis. There are also excerpts and variant readings from the Celestial and Ecclesiastical Hierarchies.

This anonymous Greek hagiographical narrative tells of the martyrdom of Dionysius the Areopagite, the Athenian converted by Paul. Its heading credits it to Methodius, "or, as others say, Metrodorus." It opens with Peter's preaching in Rome under Nero and goes on to follow the later legend that made the Areopagite the same person as Denis, the martyred first bishop of Paris. The date is uncertain, probably between the seventh and tenth centuries. The text shows how Western traditions about Saint-Denis reached the Greek world.

The Life and Conduct of Saint Dionysius is a Greek hagiographical text by Symeon Metaphrastes. It was written in the late tenth century as part of his great menologion, a collection of reworked saints' lives. It tells the story of Dionysius the Areopagite, the Athenian convert of the apostle Paul mentioned in Acts 17:34, whom tradition honoured as the first bishop of Athens. The narrative begins with the Incarnation and Paul's missionary journeys, then turns to Dionysius's noble birth, learning, conversion, ministry and martyrdom. It brings together the legends that had grown up around this figure.

This Greek encomium praises Dionysius the Areopagite, the Athenian converted by Paul in Acts 17. It is attributed to Michael Syncellus (c. 760–846), a priest of Jerusalem and later synkellos of the patriarchate of Constantinople, who was imprisoned for opposing iconoclasm. It was probably written in the first half of the ninth century. The speech presents Dionysius as the author of the Areopagitic writings, including the Divine Names and the Celestial and Ecclesiastical Hierarchies, and calls him a companion of the apostles, a hierarch and a martyr. It shows how highly the Byzantines revered the Areopagite and his writings.

This is miscellaneous material from the fourth volume of Migne's Patrologia Graeca: prefaces, editorial notes and shorter pieces that are not indexed as separate works. The volume deals with the writings attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite. It contains Byzantine commentary on them, including scholia ascribed to Maximus the Confessor and to a patriarch Germanus, and later paraphrase. It also includes hagiographical material that identifies Dionysius, Paul's Athenian convert, with the martyr-bishop of Paris. The pieces are by various authors, mostly anonymous, and date from roughly the late fifth century to about 1300.

These Greek marginal notes comment on the Corpus Areopagiticum, the writings attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite: the Celestial Hierarchy, Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, Divine Names and Mystical Theology. They open with a prologue on Dionysius as the Athenian convert of Paul in Acts 17:34. Long transmitted under the name of Maximus the Confessor, most of the scholia are now credited to John of Scythopolis, writing around 530. Later additions, some perhaps by Maximus, were mixed in. The scholia were very influential in establishing the orthodox reading and authority of the Dionysian corpus.

These Greek marginal notes explain the letters of the Corpus Areopagiticum, the writings that claim to be by Dionysius the Areopagite. They belong to the larger body of scholia on the whole corpus. That body was long credited to Maximus the Confessor, but much of it is now assigned to John of Scythopolis (c. 530s–540s), with later additions. The notes identify people named in the letters and explain hard passages. On divine "unknowing", they say it means knowledge that goes beyond all knowing, not a lack of knowledge. The scholia shaped how later readers understood Dionysius.

This is the entry on Dionysius the Areopagite from the Suda, the Byzantine Greek encyclopedic lexicon compiled in the late tenth century. It presents Dionysius as a highly learned Athenian, steeped in Greek philosophy, who was converted by Paul's preaching in Athens and appointed by him bishop of the city. It tells how, in the reign of Tiberius, he and the sophist Apollophanes were at Heliopolis in Egypt and saw the unnatural solar eclipse at Christ's Passion. It draws on the Dionysian letter to Polycarp, and so shows how Byzantine tradition accepted the Areopagitic writings as genuine.

This anonymous Greek hagiographical and liturgical compilation honours Dionysius the Areopagite, the Athenian converted by the Apostle Paul (Acts 17:34). It is drawn from the Menaia, the Byzantine service books, for his feast on 3 October. It brings together hymns praising him as Paul's disciple, a martyr and the theologian of the heavenly and ecclesiastical hierarchies and the divine names. These are the works attributed to him in the Dionysian corpus. One canon is ascribed to Andrew of Jerusalem, or by others to Andrew of Byzantium. Its date is uncertain, perhaps between the ninth and tenth centuries.

This is the surviving notice of a lost Greek refutation of the Alexandrian Gnostic teacher Basilides, written by Agrippa Castor in the reign of Hadrian, around 135. The work itself is lost and is known only from Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History (4.7). Eusebius reports that Agrippa described Basilides' twenty-four books on the Gospel, his invented prophets Barcabbas and Barcoph, and his use of barbarous names. Agrippa also charged that Basilides allowed eating food offered to idols, permitted denying the faith under persecution, and imposed a Pythagorean five-year silence. It is among the earliest recorded Christian writings against heresy.

The Disputation (or Dialogue) of Jason and Papiscus is a lost Greek dialogue from the second century, probably written around 140. In it Jason, a Hebrew Christian, debates Papiscus, an Alexandrian Jew, and shows from the Hebrew Scriptures that Jesus is the Messiah. At the end Papiscus is convinced and asks to be baptized. Celsus mocked the work, while Origen defended it. Only brief quotations survive, mainly in Jerome. Maximus the Confessor attributed it to Aristo of Pella, but scholars disagree about that attribution. It is among the earliest known Christian dialogues with Judaism.

These are the surviving Greek fragments of the writings of Claudius Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia and apologist, written around 165–180. His works, which included an Apology addressed to the emperor Marcus Aurelius, treatises against the pagans and the Jews, and writings against Montanism, are otherwise lost. Eusebius preserves his account of the "Thundering Legion," in which a rainstorm that saved the Roman army is presented as an answer to Christian prayer. Passages on the Passover, preserved in the Chronicon Paschale, bear on the second-century Quartodeciman controversy.

These are surviving fragments of the Hypomnemata (Memoirs or Commentaries) in five books by Hegesippus, a second-century Christian writer who may have been a Jewish convert. He wrote around 165 to 185 after visiting Corinth and Rome. The work defended orthodox teaching against Gnostic and other heresies by tracing the succession of bishops. It is known almost only through quotations in Eusebius. The fragments include a famous account of the martyrdom of James the Just, together with traditions about the relatives of Jesus and the early Jerusalem church.

The Epistle to Polycarp is one of the seven letters Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote in the early second century while under guard on his way to martyrdom in Rome. It is his only letter to an individual. Ignatius writes to Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, urging him to preserve unity, pray without ceasing, endure hardship like an athlete and care for every member of his flock. He also gives counsel on widows, slaves and marriage. The letter survives in a shorter, authentic recension and a longer, later interpolated recension.

This is a group of Greek letters falsely attributed to Ignatius of Antioch, the early second-century bishop. They are addressed to the Tarsians, the Antiochians, the deacon Hero and the Philippians, and they include an exchange with Mary of Cassobola, called Mary at Neapolis. They were composed in the later fourth century, probably in Syria, alongside the interpolated long recension of the genuine letters. The compiler is often identified with the author of the Apostolic Constitutions. The letters attack docetism and promote church order, and their Christology has been called subordinationist.

The Martyrdom of Ignatius is an anonymous Greek hagiographical account of the death of Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, whom it calls a disciple of John the apostle. It tells how Trajan, in the ninth year of his reign, condemned Ignatius at Antioch. He was taken to Rome, meeting Polycarp at Smyrna on the way, and was thrown to wild beasts in the amphitheatre. The narrative claims to be by companions who saw these events. Most scholars, however, date it well after the second century, perhaps to the fourth or fifth. It shaped later tradition about Ignatius's martyrdom.

The Martyrdom of Polycarp is a Greek letter from the church of Smyrna to the church at Philomelium and to all churches. It describes the arrest, trial and execution of Polycarp, the aged bishop of Smyrna, usually dated to around 155–160, though some scholars place it later. It is the earliest surviving Christian account of a martyrdom outside the New Testament. It presents Polycarp's death as an imitation of Christ's passion and gives early evidence of honouring martyrs' relics and anniversaries. It is traditionally grouped with the Apostolic Fathers.

This Greek fragment argues that matter is created and is not the cause of evil. It rejects the idea that two uncreated substances, God and matter, could exist side by side. Eusebius quoted it in his Preparation for the Gospel under the name of Maximus, traditionally identified as a late second-century bishop of Jerusalem. The same passage also appears in the Dialogue of Adamantius against the Marcionites. Most scholars, however, think it actually comes from On Free Will by Methodius of Olympus (died c. 311). The work is an early Christian contribution to the debate over the origin of evil.

This is a collection of short passages from the lost writings of Melito, bishop of Sardis in Asia Minor in the later second century. They survive as quotations in later authors such as Eusebius and Anastasius of Sinai, in catenae and in Syriac translations. They include passages from his Apology addressed to Marcus Aurelius, from the Extracts to Onesimus with its early list of Old Testament books, and from works on soul and body, the cross and faith. The authenticity of some pieces is disputed. Together they show Melito's paradoxical rhetoric about the incarnation and the passion of Christ.

This is a miscellaneous collection of material from volume 5 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the volume devoted mainly to Apostolic Fathers and other second-century Christian writers, including Ignatius of Antioch and Polycarp of Smyrna. It contains front matter, editorial notes, testimonia and short pieces not listed as separate works. The opening passage is Eusebius's account of Ignatius, who was taken under guard through Asia to martyrdom in Rome and wrote letters to the churches on the way, from Smyrna and Troas. The pieces date from different periods and have different authors.

These are short Greek passages attributed to Pantaenus, the second-century Christian teacher at Alexandria. He was remembered as Clement of Alexandria's master and as a missionary to "India." Pantaenus is not known to have left any complete writings, so only these scattered sayings survive, quoted by later authors. One comments on Psalm 19:4, "In the sun hath He set His tent," and on how the prophets use verb tenses. Another concerns how God knows created things. They are a rare direct glimpse of the earliest Alexandrian Christian teaching.

The surviving fragments of the Exposition of the Sayings of the Lord, a Greek work in five books by Papias, bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia. It was written in the early second century, with dates proposed from about 100 to 140. The work itself is lost. Its excerpts survive as quotations in later writers, chiefly Irenaeus and Eusebius. Papias collected oral traditions from the "elders" who had known the apostles. The fragments matter most for their early and much-debated statements about how the Gospels of Mark and Matthew came to be written.

The Epistle to the Philippians is a Greek letter by Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, and his presbyters, written to the church at Philippi in the first half of the second century. Many scholars think it combines two letters written at different times. It urges faith, righteousness and good conduct, warns against greed and docetic error, and draws heavily on New Testament writings. It also mentions the letters of Ignatius of Antioch. Irenaeus praised it, and it is Polycarp's only surviving writing and one of the Apostolic Fathers.

Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, wrote this Greek letter to Pope Victor of Rome in the 190s during the Quartodecimans controversy. Writing for a synod of Asian bishops, he defends their custom of keeping Pascha on the fourteenth day of the lunar month. He appeals to the tradition of the apostles Philip and John, Polycarp, Melito and others buried in Asia. He also says seven of his relatives had been bishops before him. The letter survives only in fragments quoted by Eusebius. A later Latin Acts of Timothy has also been attributed to Polycrates.

The Apology of Quadratus is the earliest known Christian apology. Quadratus wrote it in Greek and addressed it to the Emperor Hadrian, probably around 124–125, when Hadrian visited Athens. Only one short passage survives, quoted by Eusebius in his Ecclesiastical History. In it Quadratus argues that the Saviour's miracles were real and lasting: people Christ had healed or raised from the dead stayed alive long after his time on earth, and some survived into the author's own day. It is uncertain whether this apologist was the same person as Quadratus, bishop of Athens.

Rhodon was a Greek Christian writer of the late second century, active around 180–200. Only small fragments of his work survive, all preserved by Eusebius in his Ecclesiastical History. Rhodon was a pupil of Tatian in Rome. The main passage comes from a treatise against the followers of Marcion, addressed to Callistion. It describes divisions among them: Apelles taught a single first principle, while Potitus and Basilicus held two. It also recounts Rhodon's conversation with the aged Apelles. Rhodon also said he meant to answer Tatian's "Problems". Jerome attributed an anti-Montanist work to him, but that ascription is doubtful.

Two Greek fragments by Serapion, bishop of Antioch from about 190 to 211, survive because Eusebius quoted them in his Ecclesiastical History. The first comes from a letter to Caricus and Pontius. It condemns the "New Prophecy", or Montanism, and sends along letters by Claudius Apollinaris of Hierapolis. The second comes from a treatise on the Gospel of Peter, written for the church at Rhosus. Serapion had first allowed that gospel to be read there. After examining a copy from Docetist circles, he rejected it. The fragments are important early evidence for how Christians judged which writings were authentic.

This short Greek fragment comes from the synodal letter of a council held at Caesarea in Palestine in the 190s, during the controversy over the date of Easter. Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea, presided, with Narcissus of Jerusalem, Cassius of Tyre and Clarus of Ptolemais. The letter backed keeping the Paschal feast on Sunday, against the Quartodeciman custom of Asia Minor. The surviving passage, preserved by Eusebius in his Church History (5.25), asks that copies be circulated among the churches. It also notes that Alexandria keeps the feast on the same day, and that the two churches exchange Paschal letters.

The First Apology is a Greek defence of Christianity written by Justin Martyr, a philosopher from Flavia Neapolis in Palestine. It was addressed to the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius and his adopted sons, and is usually dated to about 150–155. Justin argues that Christians should not be punished for the name alone. He defends their morals, presents Christ as the incarnate Logos and appeals to the fulfilment of prophecy. The work contains some of the earliest descriptions of Christian baptism and the Eucharist, and it is a founding text of Christian apologetics.

The Second Apology is a short Greek defence of Christianity by Justin Martyr. It was probably written in Rome in the 150s and is traditionally said to be addressed to the Roman Senate. It was prompted by the execution of the Christians Ptolemaeus and Lucius under the city prefect Lollius Urbicus. Justin protests that Christians are condemned for the name alone and blames such persecution on demons. He also develops his teaching on the "seminal Logos" present in philosophers such as Socrates. Scholars still debate whether it was a separate work or a supplement to the First Apology.

On the Resurrection of the Dead is a philosophical treatise in Greek defending the Christian belief in bodily resurrection. It is traditionally attributed to Athenagoras of Athens, a late second-century apologist, though some modern scholars have questioned his authorship. The work separates arguments "for" the truth, which answer objections such as the impossibility of reassembling dispersed bodies, from arguments "about" the truth. These draw on God's purpose in creation, human nature as a unity of soul and body, and divine judgment. It is one of the earliest systematic Christian treatments of the subject.

The Legatio pro Christianis ("Plea for the Christians") is a Greek apology by the Athenian Christian philosopher Athenagoras, written about 176–180. It is addressed to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus. It answers three common charges against Christians: atheism, cannibalistic feasts and incest. Drawing on Greek poets and philosophers, Athenagoras argues for one God, mocks the myths and cults of the pagan gods, and describes Christian moral life. The work matters as an early statement of the unity and distinction of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

The Hortatory Address to the Greeks is an anonymous Greek Christian protreptic in thirty-eight chapters. It was long attributed to Justin Martyr, but it is now generally regarded as the work of a later writer. Its date is disputed and is usually placed in the third century or later. The author argues that Greek poets and philosophers contradict one another and are of little use as guides to religion. He holds that whatever truth they reached was borrowed from Moses and the prophets, who were older, and he urges his Greek readers to accept the true religion.

On the Sole Government of God (De monarchia) is a short Greek apologetic treatise attributed to Justin Martyr but generally regarded as the work of an unknown later author, probably of the third century. It argues that there is one true God and that idolatry arose through forgetfulness and custom. It makes its case almost entirely through quotations from Greek poets and philosophers, some of them spurious, including a Pseudo-Orphic poem. Eusebius mentions a work by Justin under this title, but whether it is the same text is doubtful.

The Dialogue with Trypho is a Greek apologetic work by Justin Martyr, generally dated to about 155–160. It presents a debate over two days between Justin and Trypho, a Jew who fled the recent war in Judaea. Eusebius places the conversation at Ephesus. The work opens with Justin's account of how he moved from philosophy to Christianity. It then argues from the Hebrew Scriptures that Christ has replaced the Mosaic Law, that prophecy is fulfilled in Jesus, and that Christians are the new Israel. It is the earliest surviving full-length Christian work addressed against Judaism.

On the Resurrection is a Greek treatise from the second century that survives only in fragments. It is traditionally attributed to Justin Martyr and would date from around the middle of that century, but its authenticity is disputed. The surviving excerpts were preserved mainly in the Sacra Parallela, a Byzantine anthology associated with John of Damascus. The work defends the bodily resurrection against those who held that only the soul is saved. It argues that the flesh, created by God and taken on by Christ, will share in salvation, and it points to Christ's own risen body as proof.

The Irrisio gentilium philosophorum (Greek Diasyrmos tōn exō philosophōn, "Mockery of the Pagan Philosophers") is a short Greek satire attributed to Hermias, an otherwise unknown Christian apologist. Its date is disputed; proposals run from the late second century to the sixth. It begins with Paul's saying that the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God and traces philosophy back to the fall of the angels. It then mocks the conflicting opinions of Greek thinkers on the soul and on the first principles of the universe, drawing mostly on doxographical summaries and anecdotes.

The Martyrdom of Justin and his companions, also called the Acts of Justin, is an anonymous Greek account of the trial and execution of the Christian philosopher Justin Martyr and several fellow believers at Rome. They were tried before the urban prefect Junius Rusticus, who held office around 162–168. The text is largely a record of questions and answers in which Justin states his faith and refuses to sacrifice. It survives in several recensions and is valued as one of the earliest and most sober martyr acts.

The Discourse to the Greeks (Oratio ad Graecos) is a short Christian apologetic treatise in Greek. It was handed down under the name of Justin Martyr, but scholars do not accept it as his work. It is usually dated to the first half of the third century. In five chapters the anonymous author explains why he turned away from Greek religion. He attacks the immorality of the Homeric heroes and of the gods in the poets. He then urges his fellow Greeks to follow him in turning to Christianity. A Syriac version was made before the seventh century.

This heading gathers the miscellaneous material in volume 6 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca that is not indexed as a separate work: front matter, editorial notes, appendices and shorter pieces. The volume is mainly given to the Greek apologists of the second century, including Justin Martyr, Tatian, Athenagoras, Theophilus of Antioch and Hermias. The material is mixed and has no single author or date. It includes non-Christian texts printed for comparison, such as the Doric treatise "On the Nature of the World and the Soul", attributed to Timaeus of Locri, which summarises Plato's cosmology in the Timaeus.

This is a group of Greek writings that came down under the name of the second-century apologist Justin Martyr but are not his work. Scholars generally date them to the fifth century or thereabouts. The group includes the Exposition of the Right Faith, a treatise on the Trinity and the Incarnation; the Questions and Answers to the Orthodox; the paired Questions of Christians to pagans and of pagans to Christians; and a Refutation of certain Aristotelian doctrines. Several have been plausibly but uncertainly attributed to Theodoret of Cyrrhus or his circle.

The Oratio ad Graecos (Address to the Greeks) is a Greek apologetic treatise by Tatian, the Syrian pupil of Justin Martyr. It was probably written around 165–175, though its exact date is disputed. Tatian fiercely attacks Greek culture. He argues that the Greeks took their arts and learning from "barbarians" and he ridicules their philosophy, mythology, religion and theatre. Against this he sets Christianity, a "barbarian philosophy." He also discusses the Logos, creation, demons and the resurrection and describes his own conversion. His argument that Moses was older than Homer influenced later Christian writers.

To Autolycus is a Greek apology in three books by Theophilus, bishop of Antioch, addressed to a learned pagan friend and written shortly after 180. It is his only surviving work. Theophilus defends the Christian name, attacks idolatry and Greek myths and philosophy, and explains the Genesis account of creation. He also builds a world chronology to show that Moses and the prophets are older than Greek writers. The work is notable as the earliest known Christian use of the word "triad" (trias) for God, his Word and his Wisdom.

Against Heresies, originally titled Refutation and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So-called, is a five-book treatise by Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, written in Greek around 180. It sets out and refutes the teachings of various Gnostic groups, especially the Valentinians. Against them it defends the one God who created the world, the unity of Scripture, and apostolic tradition handed down through the succession of bishops. Only fragments of the Greek survive, but there is a complete early Latin translation. It is a key witness to second-century theology and to the fourfold Gospel.

This is a collection of Greek passages attributed to Irenaeus of Lyon (late second century), drawn from works that are otherwise lost. Most survive as quotations in later writers such as Eusebius of Caesarea, and in catenae and florilegia. They include his letter to Florinus, which recalls Irenaeus' boyhood memories of Polycarp in Asia, and the scribal adjuration from his treatise On the Ogdoad. Other pieces come from his letters on the Easter controversy and from scriptural comments. A few fragments are of doubtful authenticity. Together they extend what is known of Irenaeus beyond Against Heresies.

The Letter to Flora is a Greek epistle by Ptolemy, a Valentinian Gnostic teacher and disciple of Valentinus, probably written in the mid-second century. Ptolemy addresses Flora, a Christian woman, about the Law of Moses. He rejects two views: that it came from the perfect God and Father, and that it came from the devil. Instead he divides the Law into parts and attributes the main portion to an intermediate, just creator-god. The letter survives complete only because Epiphanius quoted it in his Panarion. It remains one of the few undisputed Gnostic writings known before the Nag Hammadi discoveries.

This is a miscellany of front matter, editorial notes and shorter unindexed pieces from the volume of Migne's Patrologia Graeca devoted to Clement of Alexandria, the Greek Christian teacher active around 190 to 215. It includes historical notices on Clement's life and writings, with testimonies from later authors such as Eusebius and Jerome. It also covers his lost works, such as the treatise On the Pascha and the discourses on fasting. Other material relates to the Stromata, the Excerpts from Theodotus and the Prophetic Eclogues. The collection is anonymous and composite, not a single work.

The Paedagogus ("The Instructor" or "Tutor") is a Greek treatise in three books by Clement of Alexandria, written around the end of the second century. It is the second part of a trilogy, following the Protrepticus (Exhortation to the Greeks) and preceding the Stromata. Here the divine Logos is presented as the tutor of believers, who are treated as God's children. Book one sets out the religious basis of Christian morality. Books two and three give practical rules on food, drink, dress, marriage and daily conduct. These rules draw heavily on Stoic ethics, especially Musonius Rufus.

The Protrepticus, or Exhortation to the Greeks, is an apologetic treatise written in Greek by Clement of Alexandria, probably near the end of the second century. It is usually seen as the first part of a trilogy with the Paedagogus and the Stromata. It exposes and ridicules the myths, mysteries and idol worship of Greek religion, and urges pagan readers to turn to the divine Logos, Christ, the "new song." Its many quotations from classical poetry and philosophy make it a key witness to early Christian engagement with Hellenistic culture.

The Stromata, or "Miscellanies" (literally "patchwork carpets"), is a Greek work by Clement of Alexandria, written around the end of the second century or early in the third. Its eight books are deliberately unsystematic and treat the relation of Christian faith to Greek philosophy, which Clement saw as a preparation for the Gospel. They also describe the true Christian "gnostic" and attack heretical Gnostic teaching, with discussions of marriage and martyrdom. It follows the Protrepticus and Paedagogus, and it is a key witness to early Alexandrian theology and to many lost classical texts.

The Eclogae propheticae (Prophetic Extracts) is a collection of short exegetical and theological notes in Greek by Clement of Alexandria, written in the late second or early third century. It survives alongside the Excerpta ex Theodoto, after the eighth book of the Stromata. The notes are loosely connected. They comment on scriptural passages, especially from the prophets, and on topics such as creation, baptism, angels and spiritual powers. They cite texts like Enoch and the Apocalypse of Peter. Their exact purpose is uncertain, and they may be preparatory notes.

The Excerpts of Theodotus are a collection of notes by Clement of Alexandria, probably made around 200. They quote and summarise the teaching of Theodotus, a Valentinian Gnostic of the Eastern school, and of other Valentinians. Clement often adds his own critical comments. The notes cover the Pleroma, the Saviour, the origin of the world, the classes of humanity and baptism. They are among the most important first-hand evidence for Valentinian thought. They survive alongside Clement's Prophetic Eclogues, a related set of notes on Scripture, and some translations have printed the two together under one title.

These are surviving fragments of lost writings by Clement of Alexandria, the Greek theologian who taught at Alexandria around 190–215. The main group comes from his Hypotyposes ("Outlines"), a set of brief commentaries on Scripture. It includes the Adumbrations, notes on 1 Peter, Jude and 1 and 2 John that survive in a Latin version made under Cassiodorus. Other pieces are preserved in Greek catenae and florilegia. Short as they are, the fragments show how Clement read Scripture and give evidence for his views on the soul, resurrection and knowledge (gnosis).

This is a set of miscellaneous material from the volume of Migne's Patrologia Graeca given to the writings of Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–c. 215), the Greek Christian teacher active in Alexandria. It includes editorial front matter, notes and shorter pieces not catalogued separately. Among them are fragments attributed to Clement, such as a passage said to come from an eighth book of the Stromata, and texts connected with the later books of the Stromata. These books discuss faith and knowledge and describe the true Christian "gnostic".

A Greek treatise or homily by Clement of Alexandria, written around the turn of the third century, though its exact date is uncertain. It interprets the Gospel episode of the rich young man in Mark 10:17–31. Clement argues that wealth does not of itself exclude anyone from salvation. What matters is the soul's freedom from greed and passion, and the right use of riches, especially in almsgiving. The work ends with the story of the apostle John and the young robber, which Eusebius later preserved. It is an important early Christian statement on wealth.

The "old scholia" are anonymous Greek marginal notes on two works by Clement of Alexandria: the Protrepticus (Exhortation to the Greeks) and the Paedagogus (The Instructor). They probably date from around the ninth or tenth century and survive alongside Clement's text in Byzantine manuscripts. Some of them have been linked to the circle of Arethas of Caesarea, though their authorship is uncertain. The notes explain difficult words, mythological and literary allusions, and points of doctrine. They show how Byzantine scholars read Clement, and they help modern editors with his text.

The Stromata, or "Miscellanies" (literally "patchwork carpets"), is a Greek work by Clement of Alexandria, written around the end of the second century or early in the third. Its eight books are deliberately unsystematic and treat the relation of Christian faith to Greek philosophy, which Clement saw as a preparation for the Gospel. They also describe the true Christian "gnostic" and attack heretical Gnostic teaching, with discussions of marriage and martyrdom. It follows the Protrepticus and Paedagogus, and it is a key witness to early Alexandrian theology and to many lost classical texts.

The Acta Archelai is a fourth-century anti-Manichaean polemic, traditionally attributed to an otherwise unknown Hegemonius, although the attribution is uncertain. It was written in Greek and survives mainly in an early Latin translation, while long Greek passages are preserved in the Panarion of Epiphanius. It gives a fictional account of debates between Mani and Archelaus, bishop of Carchar in Roman Mesopotamia. It also contains a summary of Manichaean cosmogony and a hostile life of Mani. It is the oldest major anti-Manichaean text and shaped later polemic in Late Antiquity and the Middle Ages.

Against Beron and Helix is a Greek theological treatise on the divine nature and the Incarnation, written against two otherwise unknown heretics. It survives only in fragments and was once attributed to Hippolytus of Rome. Modern scholars regard it as pseudonymous and much later, perhaps from the seventh century or after. The fragments argue that the infinite God cannot change. They also hold that the Word became truly man without any conversion of his divinity, with each nature keeping its own properties and activity.

Against Plato, on the Cause of the Universe, also known as the Discourse to the Greeks concerning Hades, is a short Greek treatise generally attributed to Hippolytus of Rome (early third century). The surviving fragment describes Hades as an underground place where the souls of the righteous and the unrighteous are held apart until the final judgment. It covers the lake of unquenchable fire, the bosom of Abraham and the coming resurrection of the body. From at least the ninth century the work was wrongly attributed to Josephus, and it still appears among his writings in many English editions.

The Expository Treatise Against the Jews (Demonstratio adversus Judaeos) is a short Greek polemical text attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, who died around 235. Some scholars question the attribution, and the date is uncertain. It survives only in part. Addressing an imagined Jewish listener, it reads Psalm 69 as David's prophecy of Christ's passion, including the vinegar and gall given to him. It argues that the sufferings of the Jewish people came from their rejection of Jesus. It is an early example of the Christian Adversus Judaeos tradition, in which writers argued against Judaism from Old Testament prophecy.

These fragments come from letters by Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, who died in prison during the Decian persecution around 250–251. They survive as quotations in Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History. One letter, written while Alexander was imprisoned, congratulates the church of Antioch on the appointment of Asclepiades as bishop and was carried by the presbyter Clement, generally identified as Clement of Alexandria. Another, to the Antinoites, mentions that the aged Narcissus, then 110 years old, shared the see of Jerusalem with him. A third recalls his friendship with Origen. The fragments are valuable evidence for church life in the early third century.

The Institutes of Arithmetic were written in Greek by Anatolius of Laodicea, a third-century scholar from Alexandria who became bishop of Laodicea in Syria and died around 283. Eusebius records that Anatolius wrote ten books of arithmetical introductions, but only fragments survive. They are preserved in later Greek mathematical writings. The fragments ask what mathematics is and trace its origins to the Chaldaeans and Egyptians. They draw on Aristotelian and Pythagorean ideas about its name, its branches and its place within philosophy. They are rare evidence of a Christian bishop working in the sciences of his day.

The Paschal Canon is a treatise on calculating the date of Easter by Anatolius, a noted mathematician and bishop of Laodicea in Syria, who died around 283. Eusebius preserves a Greek excerpt in his Ecclesiastical History. A fuller text survives in Latin, but whether it is authentic has been debated. The work criticizes earlier Easter tables, including Hippolytus's sixteen-year cycle, for following only the moon. It argues that lunar and solar reckoning must be combined. It is an early witness to the nineteen-year Easter cycle.

This anti-Montanist treatise in Greek, written about 190–195 by an unknown presbyter, survives only in fragments quoted by Eusebius in his Ecclesiastical History (5.16–17). It is addressed to Avircius Marcellus, often identified with Abercius of Hierapolis. The author says he debated the "new prophecy" for several days at Ancyra in Galatia. He then describes how Montanus began prophesying at Ardabau in Phrygian Mysia and attacks the ecstatic prophecy of Maximilla and Priscilla. It was once wrongly attributed to Asterius Urbanus, who is in fact named within the work. It is one of the earliest sources for the history of Montanism.

These Greek fragments are ascribed to Gaius (Caius), a learned Roman churchman of the early third century.
