Most of them come from his Dialogue against Proclus, a Montanist, written at Rome under Bishop Zephyrinus and preserved only in quotations by Eusebius. They point to the "trophies" of Peter and Paul on the Vatican and the Ostian Way, attack Cerinthus's earthly millenarianism, and count only thirteen Pauline epistles, leaving out Hebrews. Excerpts from the "Little Labyrinth", a work against the adoptionism of Artemon, are also attributed to him, though its authorship is disputed.

The Twelve Topics on the Faith is a short Greek doctrinal treatise attributed to Gregory Thaumaturgus, the third-century bishop of Neocaesarea. Its authenticity is generally rejected, and it is usually dated to between the later fourth and the fifth century. It sets out twelve anathemas on the person of Christ, each followed by an explanation. They condemn claims that Christ's body was uncreated or of the same substance as his divinity. Its insistence on both his full divinity and his real humanity reflects the Christological controversies that followed Apollinarianism.

Against the Heresy of One Noetus (Contra Noetum) is a Greek theological treatise attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, generally dated to the early third century. It refutes Noetus of Smyrna, who taught that Christ was the Father himself, so that the Father was born, suffered and died. This view was later called modalism or patripassianism. After recounting Noetus's examination by the presbyters, the author argues from Scripture for the distinction of Father and Son within the one God. It is an important early witness to Logos theology, though its authorship and original form are debated.

This pair of short Greek lists is falsely attributed to Hippolytus of Rome. The first, on the Twelve Apostles, says briefly where each apostle preached, how he died and where he was buried. The second names the Seventy disciples of Luke 10 and usually gives each one's episcopal see. The date and author are unknown, and the lists are generally placed somewhere between the seventh and ninth centuries. They are close to the similar lists ascribed to Pseudo-Dorotheus. They show how Byzantine tradition told the story of the apostles' missions and the founding of churches by apostles.

The Treatise on Christ and Antichrist is a Greek treatise on the end times by Hippolytus of Rome, usually dated to the early third century, around 200. It is addressed to a "beloved brother Theophilus" and draws largely on Scripture, especially Daniel, Isaiah, the Gospels, 2 Thessalonians and Revelation. It contrasts Christ with the Antichrist, who is expected to come from the tribe of Dan, and reads the four kingdoms of Daniel as a sequence ending in Rome. It is among the earliest surviving Christian works devoted entirely to the Antichrist.

The Discourse on the End of the World is a Greek eschatological sermon that names Hippolytus of Rome, bishop and martyr, as its author. It is generally regarded as spurious and much later than him; its date is uncertain, but it is often placed between the seventh and ninth centuries. Drawing heavily on Hippolytus's genuine treatise On Christ and Antichrist, it uses the prophets and Revelation to describe the signs of the last times, the rise and deceptions of Antichrist, the second coming of Christ and the final judgment, and it urges repentance.

This collection gathers the surviving letters and fragments of Dionysius the Great, bishop of Alexandria from 248 to 264. Most of his extensive correspondence survives only in excerpts, many preserved by Eusebius. The only complete letter is the canonical letter to Basilides, a bishop in the Pentapolis. It deals with when the Paschal fast should end and with questions of ritual purity, and it later entered Eastern collections of canon law. The fragments include his treatise On Promises, which argued against the millenarian teaching of the Egyptian bishop Nepos.

These Greek fragments of biblical commentary are attributed to Dionysius the Great, bishop of Alexandria from 248 to 264. They survive mainly in later exegetical chains (catenae), and some of the attributions are uncertain. The first group comments verse by verse on the opening of Ecclesiastes. It reads Solomon's reflections on labour and wisdom morally and spiritually, urging effort toward a goal "beyond the sun." The second group deals with passages in Luke's Gospel. Together they give a rare glimpse of Dionysius as an interpreter of Scripture, since most of his surviving work is correspondence.

This is a collection of biblical commentaries and fragments attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, written in Greek in the early third century. It includes comments on the Hexaemeron and Genesis, and on other books down to Daniel and Susanna, Matthew and the Apocalypse. Much survives only in catenae and later quotations, and the attribution of some pieces is uncertain. The Commentary on Daniel, the most complete part, is among the earliest surviving Christian commentaries on a book of Scripture. It is important evidence for early Christian exegesis and for early ideas about the end times.

The Discourse on the Holy Theophany is a Greek homily for the feast of the Theophany (Epiphany), which celebrates Christ's baptism in the Jordan. It has come down under the name of Hippolytus of Rome, but its authenticity is widely doubted and its date is uncertain, probably between the fourth and sixth centuries. The sermon begins by praising the goodness of creation and the life-giving power of water. It then reflects on Christ's baptism by John and the descent of the Spirit, and ends by urging its hearers to seek rebirth through baptism.

This collection gathers the surviving Greek writings of Sextus Julius Africanus, a Christian scholar of the early third century. His letter to Origen questions whether the story of Susanna belongs to the original Book of Daniel. His letter to Aristides reconciles the differing genealogies of Christ in Matthew and Luke. The Chronographiae, known only from fragments, was a five-book world chronicle from Creation to about 221 and shaped later Christian historiography, including that of Eusebius. The Passion of Symphorosa, a martyr account, is attributed to him only doubtfully.

The Kata meros pistis, or Sectional Confession of Faith, is a Greek doctrinal statement handed down under the name of Gregory Thaumaturgus, the third-century bishop of Neocaesarea. Most scholars regard it as a fourth-century work, and since Hans Lietzmann's study it has usually been assigned to Apollinaris of Laodicea or his circle. Written as a series of condemnations, it rejects those who say the Son was made from nothing or became divine by grace, and those who call the Spirit a created being. It sets out the Trinity as one Godhead and explains how Christ became incarnate.

This encyclical letter was issued by the Synod of Antioch around 268–269. That synod condemned and deposed Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, for his teaching about Christ and for his conduct. The letter was drafted by Malchion, a presbyter and teacher of rhetoric at Antioch, who had exposed Paul's views in a public disputation. It is addressed to Dionysius of Rome, Maximus of Alexandria and the whole Church. Eusebius preserves extensive extracts in his Ecclesiastical History, and fragments of the acts of the disputation survive in later writers.

The Narrative of Events Happening in Persia on the Birth of Christ is a legendary Greek account attributed to Sextus Julius Africanus, the third-century Christian chronographer. Scholars have long rejected that attribution, and the work probably dates from between the fifth and seventh centuries. It describes miraculous signs at a Persian temple announcing Christ's birth, followed by the Magi's journey to Bethlehem and their report on their return. It is an example of the apocryphal tradition that grew up around the Nativity and the Magi.

This is not a single work. It gathers the miscellaneous material in volume 10 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca: editorial front matter, prefaces, notes and short pieces not listed as separate works. The volume deals with Greek Christian writers of the third century. The surviving passages include scholarly discussion of the Roman presbyter Gaius and the anti-heretical treatise known as the Little Labyrinth. There are also fragments of the anonymous anti-Montanist writer, which mention Maximilla. The Greek texts come with Latin commentary.

This short Greek text summarises the Acts of the Apostles chapter by chapter. It belongs to the Euthalian apparatus, the body of prologues, chapter lists and reading aids attached to the Acts and Epistles in many New Testament manuscripts. It has sometimes been attributed to Pamphilus of Caesarea, but the attribution is doubtful, and the date of the apparatus is disputed. Its author follows Luke's narrative, marks whole chapters with letters of the alphabet and marks their subdivisions with asterisks. The work shows how early Christian scholars divided the biblical text and made it easier to consult.

This short Greek exegetical fragment comes from a lost commentary on Paul's First Epistle to the Corinthians by Pierius, an Alexandrian priest and teacher of the late third century who was known as "Origen the Younger." It survives because Jerome quoted it. Jerome places Pierius alongside Origen, Dionysius, Eusebius, Didymus and Apollinaris as major interpreters of the epistle. Commenting on 1 Corinthians 7:7, "For I would that all men were even as I myself," Pierius says that Paul here openly preaches celibacy. The fragment is a small surviving witness to early Alexandrian biblical interpretation.

This is a collection of Greek writings that have come down under the name of Gregory Thaumaturgus, the third-century bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, but whose authenticity is doubtful or rejected. It includes a fragment on the Trinity, a treatise on the soul addressed to Tatian, homilies, a discourse on all the saints and a comment on a passage of Matthew. Their dates and authors are uncertain. Some pieces probably belong to later centuries, as their developed Trinitarian and Christological language suggests.

The Canonical Epistle is a Greek pastoral letter by Gregory Thaumaturgus, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus. He wrote it around 254–258, after Goths and Boradi had raided the region, and sent it to an unnamed fellow bishop. Its canons cover cases that arose from the invasions: captives who ate the barbarians' food, women who were raped, and Christians who looted property or helped the raiders. It is an important early witness to penitential discipline, and Eastern Christian canon law later adopted it. The final canon, which sets out grades of penitents, is often thought to be a later addition.

The Declaration of Faith (Expositio fidei) is a short Trinitarian creed attributed to Gregory Thaumaturgus, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, and usually dated to the 260s. It confesses one God the Father, one Lord the Son, and one Holy Spirit, forming a perfect Trinity in which nothing is created or subordinate. Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Gregory Thaumaturgus says it was revealed to him in a vision of the Virgin Mary and John the Evangelist. It is valued as an early statement of Trinitarian doctrine from before Nicaea.

The Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes is a Greek paraphrase of the biblical book of Ecclesiastes, traditionally attributed to Gregory Thaumaturgus, the third-century bishop of Neocaesarea and pupil of Origen. It was probably written in the mid-third century. The work goes through the biblical text chapter by chapter and restates Solomon's words in fuller, more literary Greek. It brings out a Christian moral reading, presenting the vanity of earthly pursuits as a reason to turn toward heavenly things. It is one of the earliest surviving Christian treatments of the book.

This Greek farewell speech is attributed to Gregory Thaumaturgus, who delivered it around 238 to 240 when he left Origen's school at Caesarea in Palestine. Gregory tells how he turned from studying Roman law to studying under Origen. He then describes Origen's method of teaching, which moved through logic, natural science, geometry, astronomy and ethics, included wide reading among the philosophers, and ended with the study of Scripture. It is a rare first-hand witness to Christian education in the third century and to Origen as a teacher.

The Hypotyposes, or Outlines, was a theological treatise in seven books by Theognostus of Alexandria. He was a late third-century teacher in the Origenist tradition, said to have led the Alexandrian school. The work itself is lost. It is known from Photius's summary and from a few short fragments, chiefly quoted by Athanasius. These passages teach that the Son comes from the Father's substance, as a ray from the sun, without dividing it. They also comment on the sin against the Holy Spirit. Photius criticised parts of its teaching about the Son.

A short Greek letter by the Christian chronographer Sextus Julius Africanus to Origen, probably written around 240. Africanus argues that the story of Susanna, found in the Greek Book of Daniel, is a later forgery. He points to puns that only work in Greek, such as the play on the Greek words for "holm-tree" and "saw asunder", to its absence from the Hebrew text, and to its implausible narrative details. Origen's long reply defending the story survives. Together the two letters are an important early example of Christian textual and canonical criticism.

Against Celsus is an apologetic treatise in eight books by Origen of Alexandria, written around 248 at the request of his patron Ambrose. It refutes The True Word, an attack on Christianity by the second-century pagan philosopher Celsus. Origen answers him point by point, defending faith, the identity of Jesus, allegorical reading of Scripture and Christianity's relation to Greek religion. It survives complete in Greek and is among the most important works of early Christian apologetics. It also preserves most of what is known of Celsus's lost work.

On Prayer (Peri euchēs) is a Greek treatise by Origen of Alexandria, usually dated around 233–234 and addressed to his patron Ambrose and to Tatiana. It is the earliest surviving systematic Christian study of prayer. Origen asks why prayer is worthwhile if God already knows all things, explains the kinds of prayer named in 1 Timothy 2:1, and argues that prayer in the strict sense should be offered to the Father through the Son. He gives a long commentary on the Lord's Prayer and ends with advice on posture, place and times for prayer.

On First Principles (Greek Peri Archon, Latin De Principiis) is a theological treatise in four books by Origen of Alexandria. He wrote it at Alexandria around 220–230, and it is regarded as the first systematic exposition of Christian theology. It covers God, the Trinity, rational beings, the world, free will, and how to interpret Scripture. Only fragments of the Greek original survive, mainly in the Philocalia. The full text comes down in Rufinus's Latin translation of 397, which softened passages thought unorthodox. Its teachings fuelled the later Origenist controversies.

Origen of Alexandria wrote On the Resurrection (De resurrectione), a Greek treatise in two books, at Alexandria before he moved to Caesarea around 231. The work is lost and survives only in fragments and reports by later writers. Methodius of Olympus attacked its ideas, and Pamphilus and Jerome also cite it. Origen held that the risen body keeps the individual's identity while being changed into a spiritual body free of its earthly qualities. This spiritualizing view later became one of the main charges in the controversies over Origenism.

This Greek letter is Origen's reply to the Christian chronographer Julius Africanus, written from Nicomedia, probably around 240. Africanus had objected that the story of Susanna in the Book of Daniel was a late forgery. He pointed to Greek wordplays that could not have existed in a Hebrew original and to features he found implausible. Origen defends the story's place in the Church's Scriptures and discusses differences between the Hebrew and Greek texts of the Bible. The letter is one of Origen's few complete surviving letters and an important early witness to debates over the biblical canon and textual criticism.

The Letter to Gregory is a short Greek letter by Origen, probably written in the 230s or 240s. It is traditionally addressed to his pupil Gregory Thaumaturgus, though some scholars question whether this is the same Gregory. Origen urges the gifted young man, who could have become a lawyer or philosopher, to turn his talents to Christianity. He should take from Greek philosophy and the liberal arts whatever helps in understanding Scripture, just as the Israelites "spoiled the Egyptians" (Exodus). The letter survives in the Philocalia and is an early statement of how Christians might use classical learning.

The Exhortation to Martyrdom is a Greek treatise by Origen of Alexandria, generally dated to about 235, during the persecution under the emperor Maximinus Thrax. It is addressed to his patron Ambrose and to Protoctetus, a presbyter of Caesarea, who were both facing arrest. Drawing heavily on Scripture, Origen urges them to stand firm, to reject idolatry and apostasy, and to see suffering for Christ as a contest that leads to glory. It is one of the most important early Christian writings on the meaning of martyrdom.

This is a miscellaneous collection of material from the volume of Migne's Patrologia Graeca devoted to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 254), rather than a single work. It holds prefaces, editorial notes and shorter pieces not indexed separately. They include ancient testimonies about Origen, such as Eusebius's account of the chains and tortures he suffered in the Decian persecution, and notices of his correspondence. Among these is Julius Africanus's letter questioning the authenticity of the Susanna story in Daniel, which Origen answered. Most items are anonymous or of mixed authorship.

This is a collection of surviving fragments of Origen's lost Greek commentary on the Book of Genesis. He began the work in Alexandria and finished it after moving to Caesarea, in the 220s–230s. The full commentary is lost. Pieces survive mainly as quotations in later writers, including Eusebius of Caesarea and the anthology known as the Philocalia. The fragments argue that God has always been Father of the Son. They also reject the Platonic idea that matter is uncreated, and they discuss fate and astrology. They are important evidence for Origen's early thinking about creation.

This is a miscellany of material from the twelfth volume of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, which is devoted to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 254). It gathers front matter, editorial notes and shorter pieces not listed as separate works. Much of it consists of Greek exegetical fragments on books of the Old Testament, many preserved in catenae, together with later testimonies to Origen's interpretations. One example is his reading of Adam and Eve as figures of Christ and the Church. The pieces vary in authorship and authenticity.

Selecta in Deuteronomium ("Selections on Deuteronomy") is a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Deuteronomy attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). The notes survive as fragments rather than as a continuous commentary, mostly drawn from later catenae, and the authorship of some passages is uncertain. They comment briefly on individual verses. Topics include Moses as the prophetic voice of God, Joshua as his successor, the inheritance of Reuben and Gad, and how the divine "voice" at Sinai should be understood without suggesting that God has a bodily nature.

The Selecta in Exodum are Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Exodus attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive only in fragments, mostly preserved in later catenae (chains of excerpts from biblical commentators), and their exact relation to Origen's lost commentaries is uncertain. They comment on selected verses. A notable passage deals with the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, where Origen distinguishes between a heart described as "hardened", "strengthened" or "made heavy". This question of divine action and human free will recurs elsewhere in his writings.

Selecta in Genesim is a collection of Greek fragments of Origen of Alexandria's (c. 185–c. 253) exegetical writings on Genesis. Most survive in later catenae, the chains of excerpts that Byzantine compilers made from earlier commentators. Origen's own Commentary on Genesis, written in Alexandria, is largely lost. The collection opens with a passage from its third tome, preserved by Eusebius, on where the apostles went to preach. The other excerpts discuss particular verses: grammar, punctuation, the blessing to increase and multiply, and the creation of humanity in God's image. They are an important witness to Origen's lost interpretation of Genesis.

The Selecta in Jesum Nave are short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Joshua attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts, mainly through catenae, and so their exact wording and authenticity are not always certain. The notes comment on individual verses and mix literal remarks with allegorical readings. Rahab, for example, is presented as a figure of the Church gathered from the nations, and her lowering of the spies through the window is compared to Paul's escape from Damascus.

The Selecta in Job is a collection of short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Job attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like other Origenian "selecta", the comments survive as fragments rather than a continuous commentary. They are mostly preserved in later catenae, so some attributions are uncertain. The notes explain individual verses, often morally or allegorically. For example, they read Satan's attacks on Job's household as possible only through drunkenness, and they treat harsh words from Job's friends as a heavy burden on the soul.

Selecta in Judices ("Selections on Judges") is a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Judges attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as fragments, mainly in exegetical catenae, so how much of the material is genuinely Origen's is uncertain. The notes take up individual verses. They discuss whether the Spirit was behind Jephthah's rash vow, the "shibboleth" password test, Samson's Nazirite hair, the ephod and teraphim, and the defeat of Benjamin. They also add to what survives of Origen's Homilies on Judges, which are preserved in Latin.

Selecta in Leviticum ("Selections on Leviticus") is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Leviticus attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like other fragments of his biblical commentary, they survive mainly as excerpts in later catenae, so how much of the wording is Origen's own is uncertain. The comments explain the book's title and defend its laws on priesthood and sacrifice against critics who thought them unworthy of the Creator. Drawing on Paul's statement that "the law is spiritual," they read the ritual prescriptions as hidden teaching worthy of God.

The Selecta in Numeros ("Selections on Numbers") is a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Numbers attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). The notes survive as fragments, mainly through the catenae, the medieval chains of patristic commentary, and their authenticity is not always certain. They comment on individual verses, including the meaning of the word "manna", the prophesying of the seventy elders, Miriam's exclusion from the camp and the sending of the spies. They also read Joshua, son of Nun, as a type of Christ. The notes add to Origen's better-known Homilies on Numbers.

The Selecta in Psalmos are a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Psalms attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive mainly as excerpts in later catenae, and their authenticity is doubtful in part because some passages may come from other writers, such as Evagrius Ponticus. The opening gathers philosophical definitions of "end" from Aristotle and Stoic sources to explain psalm titles. Even so, the fragments remain an important witness to Origen's lost commentaries and homilies on the Psalter.

The Selecta in libros Regnorum are short Greek exegetical notes on the Books of Kingdoms (1–2 Samuel and 1–2 Kings), attributed to Origen of Alexandria, who died around 253. They survive as fragments, mostly preserved in catenae, and their authenticity is uncertain in places. The notes explain how biblical language about God's anger and repentance should be read without ascribing passions to God, for example in God's regret over Saul. They also discuss Saul's sparing of Agag and give typological readings of David that point to Christ.

This is Origen of Alexandria's verse-by-verse exegesis of the Gospel of Matthew, written in Greek at Caesarea late in his life, around 246–248. It originally ran to twenty-five books. Only books 10 to 17 survive in Greek, covering roughly Matthew 13:36 to 22:33. An anonymous early Latin translation preserves much of the rest, and a few fragments survive in other writers, including Origen's account of the order of the four Gospels. The commentary combines literal and allegorical interpretation and is a major witness to early Christian biblical scholarship.

These Greek exegetical fragments on the Song of Songs are attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) and survive through the catena, or chain commentary, compiled by Procopius of Gaza in the early sixth century. They are usually linked with Origen's commentary on the Song from the 240s. That commentary is otherwise known chiefly from Rufinus's partial Latin translation. The fragments read the bride and bridegroom allegorically as the soul seeking the divine Word. They help recover Origen's lost Greek, although the attribution of individual excerpts is not always certain.

The Fragmenta in Lucam are Greek exegetical fragments on the Gospel of Luke attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive mostly in later catenae, the anthologies of commentary that Byzantine compilers arranged verse by verse. Origen's Greek homilies and his commentary on Luke are otherwise lost, although thirty-nine homilies survive in Jerome's Latin translation. Some passages transmitted under his name may come from other writers. The fragments discuss the infancy narratives, including the naming of John the Baptist and Elizabeth's greeting to Mary.

The Fragmenta in Proverbia are Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Proverbs attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253). Most were preserved in later excerpt collections. Origen's full exposition of Proverbs is lost, and the authenticity of some fragments is uncertain. The surviving notes read the book christologically. Solomon, "son of David" and peaceable king, is taken as a figure of the Saviour. Wisdom is identified with Christ, "the power of God and the wisdom of God," through the imagery of Wisdom 7. The fragments help show how Origen interpreted the Bible's wisdom literature.

This work contains Origen of Alexandria's exegesis of the prophet Ezekiel, probably written in the early 240s. Origen preached homilies on Ezekiel, fourteen of which survive mainly in Jerome's Latin translation. He also wrote a long commentary on the book, which is now largely lost. This text begins with a Greek fragment from its twentieth tome on Ezekiel 34. There Origen reads the good pasture and clear water allegorically as the whole of Scripture. He criticizes those who reject the Old Testament or attribute parts of it to a lesser power.

Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) preached this series of sermons on the Book of Jeremiah at Caesarea in Palestine, probably in the 240s. Twenty homilies survive in Greek, which is unusual because most of Origen's preaching is known only through Latin translations. Jerome translated some of them into Latin. Working through the biblical text passage by passage, Origen reads the prophet's warnings as signs of God's patience and his call to repentance, and he moves from the literal history to spiritual and moral interpretation. The homilies are important evidence for early Christian preaching and for Origen's exegetical method.

The Homilies on Luke are a series of sermons by Origen of Alexandria on the Gospel of Luke, probably preached at Caesarea in Palestine during the 230s, though the exact date is disputed. Thirty-nine homilies survive complete only in Jerome's Latin translation of about 390. Most of them cover the infancy narratives and the opening chapters of the Gospel. Greek fragments survive in the catenae, or chains of commentary. The homilies are among the earliest Christian commentary on Luke and show Origen's pastoral and allegorical approach to the Bible.

Origen of Alexandria wrote several works on the Song of Songs, and this title gathers what survives of them. The main work was a commentary in ten books, begun in Athens and completed at Caesarea around 240–245. Only part of it survives, in Rufinus's Latin translation. Jerome translated two homilies into Latin, and a few Greek fragments remain, including some from an early "little tome" written in Origen's youth. Origen read the Song as a picture of the love between Christ and the Church, or between the Word and the soul. This reading shaped later Christian mystical interpretation.

This is a Greek fragment from Origen's lost commentary on the prophet Hosea, probably written at Caesarea in the 240s as part of his exegesis of the Twelve Minor Prophets. The surviving passage deals with Hosea 12:4, where the text shifts from plural to singular. Origen argues that such apparent grammatical errors in Scripture must not be "corrected" by copyists, because careful readers can still follow the sense. He supports this with a similar case from Genesis 2. The extract survives in the Philocalia, an anthology of Origen's writings.

This is a miscellaneous group of Greek material from the volume of the Patrologia Graeca given over to writings of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 254). It includes passages from his exegetical works, among them the Commentary on Matthew, along with prefatory matter, textual notes, lists of variant readings and short pieces not catalogued separately. The opening passage discusses the Transfiguration and why Jesus told the disciples not to speak of it until after his Passion.

The Selecta in Ezechielem are Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Ezekiel attributed to Origen of Alexandria. They survive as fragments, chiefly in the catenae, the medieval chains of patristic comment on Scripture. They are usually linked to his work on Ezekiel of the 240s, though the date is uncertain and not every fragment can be securely assigned to him. The notes move between literal explanation and spiritual reading. They present the prophet as a type of Christ, comparing his vision by the river Chebar in his thirtieth year with Christ's baptism in the Jordan.

This is a collection of short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Jeremiah, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts in the Byzantine catenae on the prophets, the chains of patristic comment arranged verse by verse. Some may come from Origen's lost homilies or notes on Jeremiah, though catena attributions are not always reliable. The fragments show his usual allegorical and moral reading, applying the prophet's images to sin, temptation and the soul's struggle, and they add to the Greek homilies on Jeremiah that survive in full.

The Selecta in Threnos are Greek fragments of Origen of Alexandria's exegesis of the Book of Lamentations, which survive mainly in later catenae (chains of excerpts from commentators). Eusebius records that Origen wrote a commentary on Lamentations in several books, apparently during his years in Alexandria, but its exact date is uncertain. The fragments treat Jeremiah's laments over Jerusalem and its exiled people, note the Hebrew alphabetic structure of the poems, and pair historical explanation with allegory. Babylon, for example, is read as the confusion of the soul. They should not be confused with the apocryphal Penitence of Origen.

This is a large Greek exegetical work by Origen of Alexandria, written for his patron Ambrose. He began it in Alexandria around the early 230s and continued it after moving to Caesarea. It originally ran to at least 32 books, but only a few survive, among them books 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 19, 20, 28 and 32. Origen reads the Fourth Gospel at both a literal and a spiritual level. He often argues against the Gnostic commentary of Heracleon, which makes this one of the earliest surviving Christian commentaries on John.

This is a collection of Greek fragments attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253), centred on his Commentary on Romans. The full commentary survives only in Rufinus's abridged Latin translation, so the Greek fragments are an important witness to its original wording. The collection also gathers other passages. These include Origen's remarks on the Epistle to the Hebrews, preserved by Eusebius, which judge its thought Pauline but its style the work of another hand. There are also extracts on interpreting Scripture from book IV of On First Principles, transmitted through the Philocalia.

This is a surviving Greek fragment of the homilies on the Acts of the Apostles by Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253). Most of his homilies are lost, and this series survives only in excerpts. The fragment comments on Peter's speech about Judas in Acts 1, which quotes the Psalms. It argues that the Holy Spirit is always the true speaker in prophecy, even when the words are put in the mouth of God, Christ, the prophet or the people. This makes it an important witness to Origen's views on scriptural inspiration and interpretation.

This is a miscellany of front matter, editorial notes and smaller unindexed pieces from volume 14 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, a volume given over to the writings of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–254). The material is in Greek and centres on his exegesis. It includes excerpts from his Commentary on John. One is the opening of Book 1, where Origen calls the Gospels the firstfruits of all the Scriptures. Another is the preface to Book 6, which recalls his forced departure from Alexandria and the hostility he faced there.

The Hexapla was Origen's great comparative edition of the Old Testament, compiled probably at Caesarea in the second quarter of the third century. It set out in parallel columns the Hebrew text, a Greek transliteration, and the Greek versions of Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint and Theodotion. Origen marked the Septuagint with critical signs such as the obelus and the asterisk. The work itself is lost. This collection gathers what survives of it for the books from Genesis to Kingdoms, drawn from manuscript margins, catenae, patristic citations and the Syro-Hexapla.

This section gathers the surviving fragments of Origen's Hexapla for the books from Chronicles (Paralipomena) to the Psalms. Origen compiled the Hexapla, a vast critical edition of the Old Testament, in the first half of the third century, largely at Caesarea. It set out the Hebrew text, a Greek transliteration, and the Greek versions of Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint and Theodotion in parallel columns. The complete work is lost. Its readings survive mainly through marginal notes in manuscripts, catena excerpts and quotations by later writers, and they remain important evidence for the history of the Greek Bible.

These are the surviving fragments of the Hexapla for Proverbs through Lamentations. The Hexapla was Origen's multi-column edition of the Old Testament, compiled at Caesarea in the first half of the third century. It set the Hebrew text and a Greek transliteration beside the Greek versions of Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint and Theodotion. The complete work is lost. Its readings survive mainly through marginal notes in manuscripts, citations by Church Fathers and the Syro-Hexapla. They remain important evidence for the history of the Greek Old Testament.

This collection gathers the surviving fragments of the Hexapla for the books from Ezekiel to the Minor Prophets. Origen compiled the Hexapla, largely at Caesarea, in roughly the 230s and 240s. It set out the Old Testament in parallel columns: the Hebrew text, a Greek transliteration, and the Greek versions of Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint and Theodotion. Some books also had further anonymous versions. The complete work is lost. Its readings survive through marginal notes in Septuagint manuscripts, Origen's critical signs, the Syriac translation and quotations in Church writers. They remain important evidence for the history of the Greek Bible.

This is miscellaneous material from the third part of volume 16 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, including front matter, editorial notes and short unindexed pieces. The volume reprints surviving fragments of the Hexapla, the multi-column edition of the Old Testament that Origen compiled in the first half of the third century. The passages set out the readings of Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, the Septuagint and other versions side by side, here for verses from the Minor Prophets such as Zechariah. Latin editorial annotations accompany them, recording manuscript readings and citing Jerome.

The Refutation of All Heresies, also called the Elenchus or Philosophumena, is a long Greek polemical treatise from the early third century. It is traditionally attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, but some scholars assign it to an unknown "Pseudo-Hippolytus", and it was once credited to Origen. The work argues that Christian heresies come from Greek philosophy, the mysteries and astrology. It surveys pagan thought and then describes some thirty-three Gnostic and other systems, which makes it a major source for early Christian heterodoxy. Books II and III are lost. Books IV–X were rediscovered at Mount Athos in 1842.

This is a Greek collection of exegetical fragments, selections (eklogai) and scholia on books of the Bible, put together to supplement the main body of Origen's biblical commentary. Origen was the Alexandrian theologian who died around 253. Most of his exegetical works survive only in part, and much of what remains comes from excerpts preserved in later catenae. Not every piece is certainly his. The collection opens with notes on Genesis, which discuss why God sent the Flood and why Noah took seven of every clean animal into the ark.

This is a collection of miscellaneous material from volume 17 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, which completes that series' edition of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 254). It includes editorial prefaces, notes and short pieces that are not catalogued as separate works. The opening section discusses the Apology for Origen that Pamphilus of Caesarea wrote with Eusebius while imprisoned during the persecution. It cites Photius and other Greek witnesses on the work's composition and on how it defended Origen's teaching on the Trinity. The material is mixed, with no single author or date.

This is a small group of Greek letters by Alexander, bishop of Alexandria (died 328), written during the early Arian controversy, roughly between 318 and 325. They include a long letter to a bishop named Alexander, traditionally styled "of Constantinople" (the identification is uncertain), and an encyclical to bishops everywhere. Both denounce the teaching of the presbyter Arius and his associates and announce their excommunication. These letters are among the earliest surviving documents of the dispute that led to the Council of Nicaea.

This is a short Greek treatise in twenty-six chapters against the teachings of Mani. It was written by Alexander of Lycopolis, a philosopher in Egypt in the late third century. Photius called him a bishop of Lycopolis, but since Tillemont most scholars have taken him to be a pagan Platonist. Alexander says he learned Mani's doctrine from people who knew Mani. He uses philosophical reasoning to argue that Manichaean dualism is irrational and incoherent. The work is one of the earliest and most valuable witnesses to Manichaeism in the Roman Empire.

The Expositio fidei ad Athanasium is a Greek profession of faith presented around 371–372 to Athanasius of Alexandria by Eugenius, a deacon of Ancyra. He acted for the community that had remained loyal to Marcellus of Ancyra. At the time, Basil of Caesarea and others were pressing Athanasius to condemn Marcellus, whose teaching on the Word they judged Sabellian. The statement sought to prove the group's orthodoxy and win recognition of their communion. To do so, it affirmed the Trinity and rejected both Arian and Sabellian errors. It is an important witness to the later history of the Marcellan party.

This Greek collection gathers the surviving writings of Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, a firm supporter of the Council of Nicaea who was deposed around 330. Its main piece, the treatise On the Belly-Myther (De engastrimytho), is addressed to Eutropius. It attacks Origen's reading of 1 Samuel 28, which held that the medium of Endor really raised Samuel's soul. Eustathius argues that the apparition was a demonic deception and criticises Origen's allegorical method. The collection also contains an address to Emperor Constantine, whose attribution is uncertain, and fragments of anti-Arian works preserved by later authors.

These are short Greek fragments of two lost works by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. The first set comes from his books against Porphyry, the Neoplatonist critic of Christianity. They teach that the truly beautiful is whatever God judges beautiful, even if people mock it. They also hold that repentance wipes out sin when it is not put off, that evil is unlikeness to God, and that good is becoming like him. A fragment from a sermon on the martyrs praises martyrdom as a witness first given by Christ himself.

The Banquet of the Ten Virgins is a Greek dialogue by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. Its title and form deliberately echo Plato's Symposium. Gregorion tells Euboulios about a banquet held by Arete (Virtue) in a garden, where ten virgins give speeches in turn praising chastity and virginity. They draw heavily on allegorical readings of Scripture. Thekla gives the fullest speech, and the work ends with her hymn to Christ the Bridegroom. It is Methodius's only work to survive complete in Greek and an important early Christian treatise on virginity.

On Things Created (De creatis) is a Greek theological treatise by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. The full work is lost. It survives only in a summary of excerpts made by the ninth-century patriarch Photius in codex 235 of his Bibliotheca. The surviving passages argue against Origen and his followers. They criticize his allegorical reading of texts such as "cast not your pearls before swine" and dispute his view that the created world is coeternal with God. The work is an important witness to early opposition to Origen.

This is a collection of Greek fragments attributed to Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. The main excerpts come from a homily on the Cross and the Passion of Christ. It answers people who asked what good the incarnation of the Son of God did, and why he suffered on a cross rather than by some other punishment. Methodius argues that Christ took flesh to overthrow the tyranny of the demons and free human souls from slavery. Other short fragments are gathered with it. Their authenticity and date are not certain.

De resurrectione (On the Resurrection), also called Aglaophon after the physician in whose house it is set, is a dialogue by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop who died around 311. It argues against Origen's teaching that the risen body will not be the same flesh. It holds that the "garments of skin" of Genesis are not human bodies, and that God is not the cause of evil. The full Greek text is lost. It survives in excerpts quoted by Epiphanius and Photius, and in an Old Slavonic version.

The Sermon on Simeon and Anna is a Greek festal homily for the Hypapante, the feast of the Presentation of Christ in the Temple. It is attributed to Methodius, bishop of Patara (Methodius of Olympus), and opens by recalling his Symposium on virginity. Scholars generally treat it as spurious and date it between the fifth and seventh centuries. The sermon praises the Virgin Mary as the living ark carrying Christ, then turns to the meeting with the aged Simeon and the prophetess Anna. It is an early witness to the feast's preaching and to Marian devotion.

The Oratio in ramos palmarum is a Greek homily for Palm Sunday. It has come down under the name of Methodius of Olympus, but it is not his work and its real author is unknown. It is usually dated loosely between the fifth and seventh centuries. The preacher compares the Gospel miracles to the links of a golden chain and calls the faithful to welcome Christ's entry into Jerusalem joyfully, singing "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord".

Concerning Free-Will, also known as De autexusio, is a Greek theological dialogue by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. It is a debate between an orthodox speaker, Orthodoxus, and a follower of Valentinian Gnosticism. The work argues against the view that matter is eternal and is the source of evil. Instead, it traces evil to the misuse of the free will that God gave to created beings. It is an important early Christian treatment of the origin of evil and of human moral freedom.

This is a collection of the supplementary material in volume 18 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, which gathers Greek Christian writers of the late third and early fourth centuries. It includes the editors' prefaces, notes, ancient testimonies and shorter unindexed pieces. Much of it concerns Methodius of Olympus, bishop and martyr. The ancient notices list his works: the Symposium of the Ten Virgins, On the Resurrection against Origen, On Free Will, writings against Porphyry, and commentaries on Genesis and the Song of Songs. They also record varying traditions about his martyrdom.

This is a collection of the surviving writings of Peter I, bishop of Alexandria from 300 until his martyrdom in 311. The Canonical Epistle, also called On Penance, dates from around 306, the "fourth Easter" of the Diocletianic persecution. Its canons set penances for Christians who lapsed under persecution, graded by circumstance, and entered Byzantine canon law, where Balsamon and others commented on them. The letter to the Alexandrian church warns against Melitius of Lycopolis, whose ordinations caused the Melitian schism. Theological and other fragments complete the collection.

This anonymous Greek commentary on the six days of creation in Genesis was probably written in the late fourth or fifth century. The manuscripts attribute it to Eustathius of Antioch, but he cannot be the author: he was deposed around 330, and the work draws on Basil the Great's Hexaemeron homilies of about 370. Besides discussing creation, it collects chronological and historical material taken from earlier Christian writers, running down to Alexander the Great, so it is sometimes called the Liber chronicorum. It preserves extracts from the lost writings of Alexander Polyhistor and is an early witness to the Physiologus.

These Greek fragments come from a commentary on the Book of Isaiah by Theodore, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace from about 330 until he was deposed in 347. He died around 355 and was an ally of Eusebius against the Athanasians. The surviving passages mostly come down through exegetical catenae. They explain the prophet's words verse by verse, sometimes as moral teaching and sometimes as pointing to Christ. One example reads the "seed" left to Israel as the apostles. The fragments are rare evidence for biblical interpretation among the anti-Nicene party.

Contra Manichaeos is a polemical treatise in four books by Titus, bishop of Bostra in the Roman province of Arabia. He wrote it in Greek in the 360s, after the death of the emperor Julian. Titus rejects Mani's teaching that evil is an uncreated principle eternally opposed to God. The first books use reason to defend divine providence and human free will. The later books defend the Scriptures, including the Old Testament, against Manichaean criticism. Only part of the Greek original survives, but an early Syriac translation preserves the whole work. It is an important source for fourth-century Manichaeism.

The Oratio in ramos palmarum is a Greek homily for Palm Sunday, transmitted under the name of Titus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia (died c. 378). Whether Titus really wrote it is uncertain. The preacher opens with an image: as the abyss feeds springs and rivers that water the earth, Christ's love gives the Church its feasts, and inspired teachers carry their grace to the faithful. He then asks why both people and angels hailed Christ as king on his entry into Jerusalem. He points to the raising of Lazarus as the immediate cause.

The first book of the Chronicle by Eusebius of Caesarea was probably compiled in the early fourth century. Sometimes called the Chronographia, it sets out the chronologies of the Chaldeans, Assyrians, Hebrews, Egyptians, Greeks and Romans through extracts from earlier historians. Eusebius uses these to place the biblical patriarchs and prophets, especially Moses, alongside the history of other nations, and he warns that exact chronology cannot be achieved. It prepared the way for the dated tables of book 2. The Greek original is lost except for quotations in later writers, but the book survives largely in an Armenian translation.

This is a gathering of miscellaneous material from volume 19 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the first of the volumes devoted to Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339/340). It is not a single work. It brings together front matter, editorial prolegomena and notes, and short pieces not indexed separately. Much of it is an early modern survey of Eusebius's writings, quoting their Greek titles and openings. Among them are the General Elementary Introduction, the Martyrs of Palestine, the reply to Hierocles, the Ecclesiastical Theology against Marcellus, and the Gospel Questions addressed to Marinus.

This is a collection of Greek astronomical and chronological writings that the Jesuit scholar Denis Pétau (Petavius) gathered under the title Uranologion. The texts span many centuries, from the Hellenistic period to Byzantium. They include Suda notices on Hipparchus and on Achilles Tatius, Geminus's Introduction to the Phenomena, Hipparchus's commentary on Aratus, and Achilles' introduction to Aratus. It also contains later Byzantine computistic treatises on reckoning the calendar and the date of Easter. The collection preserves important evidence for ancient astronomy and for Christian methods of calculating time.

This Greek panegyric by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, was delivered in Constantinople in 336 to mark the thirtieth anniversary of Constantine the Great's reign. Eusebius presents the emperor as the earthly image of the divine Logos and his monarchy as a reflection of God's heavenly rule. It also praises Constantine's suppression of polytheism and his support for the Church. Its later chapters are generally thought to come from a separate speech on Christ's sepulchre. The work is an important early statement of Christian imperial ideology, which later shaped Byzantine political thought.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek account in ten books of Christianity from its beginnings to the early fourth century. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, wrote it and revised it in several stages, finishing around 324–325. It traces the succession of bishops in the major sees and covers Christian writers, heresies, the fate of the Jews, persecutions and martyrdoms, ending with the Great Persecution and Constantine's victory. Because it quotes many earlier documents that are otherwise lost, it is a key source for early Christianity. An early Syriac translation also survives.

The Oration to the Assembly of the Saints is a Greek speech attributed to the emperor Constantine the Great. Eusebius of Caesarea preserved it as an appendix to his Life of Constantine. The speech was given on Good Friday. Scholars disagree about its date and place, and they once doubted that Constantine wrote it, though many now accept it as his, probably translated from Latin. It attacks pagan polytheism and fatalism and defends divine providence and Christ's work. It is especially known for reading Virgil's Fourth Eclogue and an acrostic of the Erythraean Sibyl as prophecies of Christ.

The Life of Constantine is a Greek work in four books by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, written in honour of the emperor Constantine the Great. Eusebius composed it after Constantine's death in 337 and left it unfinished when he died in 339. It mixes panegyric and biography. It presents Constantine as a model Christian ruler and recounts his conversion, including the vision of the cross, his wars, his church building and his religious policy. It is one of the fullest sources for the religious history of his reign, and it quotes several imperial letters and documents.

This is a set of miscellaneous material from volume 21 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, a volume given over to the Praeparatio Evangelica of Eusebius of Caesarea (early fourth century). It brings together editorial front matter, explanatory notes and short unindexed pieces rather than a single work. The notes comment on Greek passages quoted or discussed by Eusebius. They cover allegorical readings of myth, Democritus on images, Stoic views of fate held by Chrysippus, and the worship of the elements and heavenly bodies.

The Preparation for the Gospel is a Greek work of Christian apologetics in fifteen books by Eusebius of Caesarea. He began it around 313 and dedicated it to Bishop Theodotus of Laodicea. It argues that Christians were right to give up pagan religion and philosophy for the Hebrew Scriptures. It surveys Phoenician, Egyptian and Greek theology and claims that Greek philosophers owed a debt to the Hebrews. It was written as a companion to the Demonstration of the Gospel, and it is valued for preserving many passages from authors whose works are otherwise lost.

Against Hierocles is a short Greek polemical treatise traditionally attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea, although some scholars have questioned this attribution. It probably dates from the early fourth century, around the time of the Great Persecution. It answers the Lover of Truth (Philalethes), an anti-Christian work generally identified with the Roman official Sossianus Hierocles, which compared Apollonius of Tyana with Jesus. The treatise leaves Hierocles' other arguments to Origen's reply to Celsus. Instead, it attacks Philostratus' Life of Apollonius, the account on which the comparison relied, and argues that its miracle stories are unreliable.

The Proof of the Gospel (Demonstratio evangelica) is an apologetic treatise in Greek by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, probably written in the 310s. It is dedicated to Theodotus, bishop of Laodicea, and follows his fifteen-book Preparation for the Gospel. Eusebius uses the Hebrew prophecies to argue that Christ and the Church fulfil the Scriptures, and explains why Christians follow the faith of the patriarchs rather than the Mosaic Law. Of the original twenty books, only the first ten survive, along with a fragment of the fifteenth. It is a major source for early Christian interpretation of prophecy.

The General Elementary Introduction is a Greek work in ten books by Eusebius of Caesarea. Its date is disputed: it may come from before the Great Persecution of 303 or from somewhat later. Only books six to nine survive, known as the Prophetic Extracts (Eclogae propheticae). They gather Old Testament prophecies about Christ, arranged by scriptural book and given brief commentary. They follow earlier books that argued for the faith without relying on Scripture. The work is an early source for Eusebius's exegesis and apologetic method.

This is a group of shorter Greek writings attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339). The General Elementary Introduction was an introductory work in ten books. Only books 6–9 survive, known as the Prophetic Eclogues: selections of Old Testament prophecies about Christ, each with a short commentary. The work probably dates from the early fourth century. On the Lives of the Prophets is a brief account of the prophets, and its attribution is doubtful. The Ten Canons are Eusebius's tables of parallel passages in the four Gospels, which were widely copied in later Gospel manuscripts.

The Gospel Questions and Solutions, also called On Discrepancies between the Gospels, is a Greek exegetical work by Eusebius of Caesarea in question-and-answer form. Its exact date is uncertain. The questions to Stephanus deal with the infancy narratives and the genealogies of Christ, for example why the evangelists trace Joseph's line rather than Mary's. Those to Marinus deal with apparent contradictions in the resurrection accounts. The full work is lost. It survives in a Greek abridgement and in fragments in catenae and other languages, and it shaped later Christian work on harmonizing the Gospels.

The Commentary on the Psalms is a large Greek exegetical work by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, generally dated to his last years, probably after the Council of Nicaea and before his death in 339. Only part of it survives as continuous text. Much of the rest is preserved in fragments in the catenae, whose attribution is not always certain. Eusebius discusses the titles and musical terms of the Psalms. He combines historical and textual scholarship, drawing on the Hexapla, with Christological and allegorical interpretation. The commentary influenced later Greek and Latin exegesis of the Psalter.

This is a set of miscellaneous material from volume 23 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca. The volume is mainly given over to the writings of Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), above all his Commentary on the Psalms. The set brings together front matter, editorial notes and shorter unindexed pieces. Much of it is Greek exegesis of the Psalms, some of it attributed to Eusebius, set among Latin editorial remarks. It also includes later critical comments on Eusebius's interpretation and style. It is not a single work. Authorship and date vary from piece to piece.

The Commentary on Isaiah is a Greek exegetical work by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. He wrote it late in life, probably after the Council of Nicaea in 325 and before his death in 339. It works through the Book of Isaiah, and its preface sets out a method that separates passages to be read literally from those that speak through symbols. Eusebius combines historical explanation with figurative and Christological reading. The commentary is an important witness to Christian biblical scholarship at Caesarea after Origen.

This is a set of Greek exegetical fragments attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339). It adds further material to his Commentary on the Psalms, which probably dates from his later years, and includes scattered comments on the Book of Proverbs. Most of these passages survive only as excerpts in catenae, the chains of patristic comment on Scripture, so some attributions are uncertain. The notes on the Songs of Ascents read them as stages in the soul's climb back to God through affliction. They also explain Hebrew names through their meanings and follow the allegorical method of Origen.

Contra Marcellum ("Against Marcellus") is a Greek polemical treatise in two books by Eusebius of Caesarea, written about 336–338. It followed the deposition of Marcellus of Ancyra at a synod in Constantinople in 336. Eusebius attacks Marcellus's only treatise, which had criticised Asterius and other eastern bishops, both living and dead. He charges Marcellus with Sabellian views that denied the distinct existence of the Son. Eusebius soon followed it with his Ecclesiastical Theology. The work matters because it quotes Marcellus at length, and these quotations preserve much of his otherwise lost writing.

De ecclesiastica theologia (On Ecclesiastical Theology) is a Greek polemical treatise in three books by Eusebius of Caesarea, written in the last years of his life, around 337–339. It is dedicated to Flacillus, bishop of Antioch. It follows Eusebius's two books Against Marcellus, which mostly quoted Marcellus of Ancyra's own words. This work goes further and refutes them. Eusebius rejects Marcellus's teaching that the Word has no distinct existence from God and defends the Son as a real, distinct being. The treatise is an important source for the fragments of Marcellus and for the Trinitarian debates after Nicaea.

The Theophania, or "Divine Manifestation", is an apologetic treatise in five books by Eusebius of Caesarea. It was probably written in the later years of his life, though its exact date is disputed. The Greek original survives only in fragments, but a complete early Syriac translation is extant. The work argues against atheism and polytheism and presents the divine Word as creator and governor of the world. It then treats the incarnation, Christ's teaching and miracles, and the fulfilment of prophecy. Much of its material overlaps with Eusebius's Demonstratio Evangelica and his oration in praise of Constantine.

This Greek letter was written by Athanasius of Alexandria around 354–355 to Dracontius, the head of a monastic community. Dracontius had been chosen unanimously as a bishop in the region of Alexandria but fled to avoid ordination, partly because the Church was under pressure at the time. Athanasius rebukes him and argues that his flight would harm the faithful and the pagans who had promised to convert. He gives examples of monks who became bishops to show that the monastic life is compatible with pastoral office. The letter is an important source for relations between Egyptian monasticism and the episcopate.

The Circular to the Bishops of Egypt and Libya is a Greek encyclical letter by Athanasius of Alexandria, written around 356–357 at the start of his third exile under Emperor Constantius II. Opening with Christ's warning against false prophets, it urges the bishops of Egypt and Libya not to accept creeds proposed by Arian opponents in place of the Nicene faith. It sets out and refutes the teachings of Arius and his followers. The letter shows how Athanasius tried to keep the Egyptian episcopate united behind Nicaea during the Arian controversy.

The First Letter to Monks is a short Greek letter by Athanasius of Alexandria. He wrote it during his third exile, around 357–359, to monks "in every place" who had asked him for an account of what he and the Church had suffered under the Arians. It accompanied an anti-Arian writing, usually taken to be his History of the Arians. In the letter Athanasius describes how hard he found it to write about the divinity of the Word, since that mystery is beyond human understanding. The letter shows how closely he worked with the monastic movement against Arianism.

The Apology to the Emperor Constantius is a Greek defence written by Athanasius of Alexandria and usually dated to 356–357, during his third exile. Addressed to Constantius II, it answers political charges brought against him: that he had turned the emperor's brother Constans against him, corresponded with the usurper Magnentius, used a new church in Alexandria before it was dedicated, and disobeyed an imperial summons. It also describes the armed attack on his church in 356 and his flight. The work is an important source for the Arian controversy and for relations between church and empire.

The Defence Against the Arians, also called the Second Apology, is a Greek apologetic work by Athanasius of Alexandria. It is generally dated to the 350s, though its exact date and stages of composition are debated. In it Athanasius answers the charges his opponents brought against him, including those upheld at the Council of Tyre in 335. He points to his acquittal by Egyptian bishops, at Rome and at the Council of Serdica. The work matters chiefly because it reproduces many original documents, such as synodal and imperial letters, which make it a key source for the Arian controversy.

The Defence of His Flight is an apologetic treatise by Athanasius of Alexandria, written in Greek around 357, during his third exile. In February 356 soldiers broke into the church of Theonas in Alexandria and Athanasius escaped. Leontius of Antioch, Narcissus of Neronias, George of Laodicea and other Arian bishops then accused him of cowardice. He answers with examples from Scripture, including patriarchs, prophets, apostles and Christ himself, to argue that fleeing persecution is lawful. His account of the attack makes the work an important source for the history of the Arian controversy.

Against the Heathen (Contra Gentes) is a Greek apologetic treatise by Athanasius of Alexandria, addressed to a certain Macarius. It forms the first half of a two-part work completed by On the Incarnation. Its date is disputed: some scholars place it before the Arian controversy, around 318, and others in the 330s. Athanasius answers pagan mockery of the Cross by attacking idolatry and the worship of nature. He argues that the soul, being rational and immortal, and the order of creation both lead to knowledge of the one God through his Word.

De Decretis is a Greek treatise in the form of a letter by Athanasius of Alexandria, usually dated to the 350s. It is written to an unnamed correspondent who had argued with supporters of Arius, including friends of Eusebius. Athanasius answers the Arian objection that the Council of Nicaea (325) used unscriptural terms, "of the essence" and "one in essence" (homoousios). He argues that these words express the meaning of Scripture about the Son's true divinity. The work is a major early defence of the Nicene formula. It also preserves documents connected with the council.

On the Incarnation of the Word is a Greek theological treatise by Athanasius of Alexandria. It is the second part of a double work that opens with Against the Pagans, and both are addressed to a certain Macarius. Its date is disputed: some place it before the Arian controversy, around 318, while others place it in the 330s. It explains why the divine Word, through whom the world was made, took a human body to restore humanity from corruption and death. It also answers Jewish and pagan objections and remains a classic of Christian thought on the incarnation.

This short Greek letter by Athanasius of Alexandria was written about 357–359 to Serapion, bishop of Thmuis, during Athanasius's third exile. Serapion had asked about Athanasius's own experiences, the Arian heresy and the death of Arius. Athanasius refers him to a work he had already sent to the monks, then turns to the disputed question of whether Arius died in communion with the Church. He describes Arius's sudden death in Constantinople around 336, on the eve of his planned readmission, and presents it as a divine judgement. The account became an important source for later tradition about Arius's end.

On the Opinion of Dionysius is a Greek letter by Athanasius of Alexandria, usually dated to the 350s. It answers Arian claims that Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria in the third century, had shared their view that the Son of God is a creature. Athanasius argues that the disputed phrases came from letters against Sabellianism and referred to Christ's human nature. He quotes Dionysius's later Refutation and Defence to show that Dionysius held the Son to be eternal and of one being with the Father. The letter preserves important fragments of Dionysius's writings.

The Encyclical Letter is a circular letter that Athanasius of Alexandria sent to bishops everywhere in 339. He wrote it soon after the imperial authorities forced him out of his see and installed Gregory of Cappadocia as bishop of Alexandria in his place. Athanasius describes the violence done to churches, clergy and virgins during the takeover. He compares the outrage to the Levite's appeal to the tribes of Israel in Judges and asks his fellow bishops to treat the injury as their own. The letter is an important source for the Arian controversy and for Athanasius's second exile.

The Expositio fidei (Statement of Faith) is a short Greek creed-like confession that has come down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria. Its authenticity is disputed, and some scholars attribute it to another fourth-century author. It affirms one unbegotten Father and an only-begotten Son who is eternally begotten and equal in honour. It denies that the Word is merely an uttered or mental word, or an emanation. It then turns to the Incarnation from the Virgin Mary and the Holy Spirit. It is a witness to the anti-Arian Trinitarian debates.

The History of the Arians is a polemical Greek history by Athanasius of Alexandria. It was addressed to monks and written around 357–358, during his third exile. The text begins abruptly. It tells how the Arian party had Arius and his followers readmitted to communion, used imperial authority to exile bishops opposed to them, and persecuted Nicene Christians under Constantius II, including violence in Alexandria. The work is notable for its fierce attack on Constantius himself, whom Athanasius calls a forerunner of Antichrist. It is an important if partisan source for the Arian controversy.

This is a short exegetical and polemical treatise by Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373) on the saying "All things were delivered to me by my Father" (Luke 10:22; Matthew 11:27). Its exact date is uncertain. Followers of Arius and Eusebius used the verse to argue that the Son once lacked lordship over creation and so was not truly from the Father. Athanasius answers that the words concern the Incarnation, not the eternal Word: the Son received all things as man in order to restore fallen humanity. The treatise is a concise example of his anti-Arian reading of Scripture.

This is a miscellaneous collection of material from the volume of the Patrologia Graeca (vol. 25) that opens the works of Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373). It is not a single work but gathers prefatory matter, editorial notes and shorter pieces that are not catalogued separately. It includes Greek fragments and testimonia on Christology and the Trinity, some attributed to Athanasius, and excerpts of Psalm commentary. Most of these are quoted within Latin editorial apparatus. Their authorship and dates vary, and many attributions are uncertain.

Athanasius of Alexandria wrote this Greek letter late in his life, probably around 370–372. It is addressed to Adelphius, a bishop and confessor who had been exiled for the Nicene faith. Athanasius answers Arian opponents who said that worshipping the incarnate Christ meant worshipping a creature. He argues that the Word's flesh is not worshipped as something separate from him. Instead, the Word, who became flesh, is worshipped together with his body. The letter is an important statement of Athanasius's teaching on the Incarnation and on the worship of Christ.

The Letter to the Bishops of Africa is a Greek synodal letter issued by about ninety bishops of Egypt and Libya under Athanasius of Alexandria, who wrote it, probably between about 367 and 372. It warns the African churches against attempts to set the Council of Ariminum (359) above the Council of Nicaea. The letter defends the Nicene creed and the term homoousios, and cites the condemnation of Auxentius, Ursacius and Valens by Pope Damasus and Western synods. It is one of Athanasius's last anti-Arian writings.

The Letter to Amun is a short Greek pastoral letter by Athanasius of Alexandria, patriarch from 328 to 373. It is addressed to Amun, a monk, and its exact date is uncertain. Athanasius answers monks troubled by scruples about involuntary nocturnal emissions. He argues that everything God made is good and that natural bodily processes are not sinful. Such worries, he says, are a trick of the devil to distract ascetics from their discipline. He also says that marriage is honourable, though virginity is the higher calling. The letter was later received among the canonical epistles of Eastern church law.

The Letter to Epictetus is a Greek letter by Athanasius of Alexandria to Epictetus, bishop of Corinth, written around 370–372. It holds up the Creed of Nicaea as sufficient against heresy. It then rebuts errors about the Incarnation reported from Corinth: that Christ's body was consubstantial with the Godhead or came from heaven, that the Word changed into flesh, or that Christ had no true human body from Mary. The letter became an important text in later Christological debate. It was read at the Council of Ephesus in 431 and cited widely afterwards.

This is a short doctrinal letter by Athanasius of Alexandria to the Emperor Jovian, written between 363 and 364. It comes with Jovian's own brief letter, which praises Athanasius's steadfastness and recalls him from the exile imposed under Julian. Jovian had asked to learn the true faith. In reply, Athanasius sets out the Nicene Creed as the faith of the whole Church and defends the full divinity of the Son against Arian teaching. The exchange shows the brief return of imperial favour to the Nicene party after Julian's death.

The Epistulae II ad Luciferum are two short letters attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria and addressed to Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia. They are usually dated to around 360, when both men had been exiled for opposing Arianism under the emperor Constantius II. Athanasius praises Lucifer's firmness in defending the faith of the Council of Nicaea and commends the polemical treatises Lucifer had sent him. The letters show the close ties between the leading Nicene opponents of imperial church policy in the East and the West.

Athanasius of Alexandria wrote this short Greek letter about 371, near the end of his life. It replies to Maximus, a Christian philosopher whom some scholars identify with Maximus the Cynic, later a claimant to the see of Constantinople, though this is uncertain. Athanasius answers opponents who had questioned how Christ is understood. He insists that the crucified one is truly God and Lord of glory, the Word made flesh, and not a mere man on whom the Word came, as it once came on the prophets. The letter witnesses to his late thinking about the person of Christ.

This is a short pastoral letter by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria (d. 373), written in Greek to the monks and solitaries of Egypt. It is known in English as the Second Letter to Monks. Athanasius warns the monks that supporters of Arius were visiting monasteries to mislead the simple. He tells them to avoid open Arians, and also those who deny holding Arian views yet worship with Arians, because such communion causes scandal and suggests the matter is unimportant. Its exact date is uncertain. The letter shows how Athanasius sought the support of Egyptian monasticism in the Arian controversy.

Two short Greek letters from Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, to Orsisius (Horsiesi), abbot of the Pachomian monastic communities in Upper Egypt, and the brethren with him. They survive within the narrative of the Life of Pachomius. The first was sent with Theodore, Pachomius's disciple, after Theodore had visited the bishop, and praises him warmly. The second consoles the monks on Theodore's death, about 368. The letters show Athanasius's close ties with Egyptian monasticism and his support for the Pachomian leadership.

This short Greek letter was written by Athanasius of Alexandria to Rufinianus, a fellow bishop, probably soon after the Council of Alexandria of 362. Rufinianus had asked how to treat clergy who had joined Arian communion under pressure rather than from conviction. Athanasius explains that synods in Alexandria, Greece, Spain and Gaul had reached the same decision. Leaders of the heresy were to be pardoned if they repented, but could not keep their clerical rank. Those who had only given way to violence could keep their rank. The letter was later included among the canonical epistles of Eastern church law.

The Letters to Serapion are a group of Greek doctrinal letters by Athanasius of Alexandria to Serapion, bishop of Thmuis in Egypt. He wrote them around 358–361 while hiding in the desert during his third exile. They answer people who had left the Arians over the Son's divinity but held that the Holy Spirit was a creature, one of the ministering angels. Athanasius argues from Scripture that the Spirit is fully divine and belongs to the Trinity. The letters are among the earliest sustained defences of the Spirit's divinity and came before the later debates of the 370s and 380s.

This Greek treatise in two books attacks the Christology of Apollinarius of Laodicea. It has come down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria, but it is generally judged inauthentic and was probably written in the last quarter of the fourth century by an unknown anti-Apollinarian author. It is addressed to a correspondent who had asked about the faith. The work defends the completeness of Christ's humanity, including a human soul and mind, against the view that the divine Word took their place. It is an important witness to the Christological controversies after Nicaea.

The Opusculum de azymis ("On Unleavened Bread") is a short Greek treatise transmitted under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria but not by him. It discusses the Jewish Passover, which it describes as kept with three elements, three virtues and three witnesses. Drawing on the Gospel of John, it argues that Christ did not eat the legal Passover before his Passion, and that no church of the apostolic age offered unleavened bread. Its date is uncertain. Its subject belongs to the Greek–Latin dispute over the use of azymes in the Eucharist, which became acute in the eleventh century.

De incarnatione Verbi Dei et contra Arianos is a Greek theological treatise against Arianism. It has come down among the works of Athanasius of Alexandria, but he is generally not thought to be its author. Some scholars have attributed it to Marcellus of Ancyra or his circle, and its date is uncertain, though it belongs to the fourth-century Arian controversy. The treatise takes up scriptural texts that Arians used to call the Son a creature or unlike the Father. It argues that such passages refer to Christ's incarnation, his voluntary poverty and his sufferings, not to his divine nature.

Athanasius of Alexandria wrote this Greek treatise in 359, while in exile, and added to it over the following years. It reports on the twin councils that Emperor Constantius II called that year, at Ariminum in Italy for the Western bishops and at Seleucia in Isauria for the Eastern bishops. The work collects and criticises the series of Arian creeds drawn up after Nicaea, defending the term homoousios. It also reaches out to the Homoiousians, and it remains a valuable record of the creeds of the period.

The Festal Letters are a series of pastoral letters that Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, wrote between 329 and 373.
