Following Alexandrian custom, he sent one each year to the churches of Egypt to announce the dates of Lent and Easter. The letters also give moral and spiritual exhortation and comment on doctrinal and church affairs. Many are lost. The rest survive mainly in Syriac and Coptic translations and in Greek fragments. The Thirty-ninth Letter, of 367, is especially important because it lists the twenty-seven books of the New Testament as now accepted.

Fragmenta et sermones is a modern editorial collection of short Greek pieces handed down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373). It brings together excerpts preserved in catenae, florilegia and later writers with sermons of varied authenticity. Many items carry the heading "of the great Athanasius" but may be spurious or later narratives about him. Among the subjects are the condemnation of Paul of Samosata, who denied the Son's pre-existence, and episodes from Athanasius's struggles with the Arians under Constantius II.

Fragmenta varia ("Various Fragments") is a modern editorial grouping of short Greek passages attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373), the bishop known for opposing Arianism. The pieces survive mainly through later quotation and compilation, and some may not be by Athanasius. One passage explains Hebrews 6:1 and compares repentance and faith in the resurrection and judgement to a building's foundation or the letters of the alphabet. Christian life, it says, must build on them toward perfection rather than keep returning to first principles.

This is a short Greek text attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria and linked to Bishop Ammon. It recalls how Athanasius fled up the Nile in 362–363, after the emperor Julian ordered him out of Alexandria. He was sheltered by Pachomian monks, among them Theodore of Tabennesi, who reportedly foresaw the emperor's death. The text as transmitted also contains Athanasius's letter of consolation to Horsiesius on Theodore's death in 368, urging the monks to imitate Theodore's life rather than mourn him. It is an important witness to Athanasius's close ties with early Egyptian coenobitic monasticism.

The second of the Orations against the Arians is a Greek theological treatise by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. Its date is debated, though it is often placed in the late 330s or 340s. It continues his defence of the Nicene faith by examining scriptural texts that his opponents used to argue that the Son of God is a creature. These include Hebrews 3:2, "faithful to him that made him", and Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created me a beginning of his ways". Athanasius reads such passages as referring to the Son's incarnation rather than to his eternal being.

The third of the Greek Orations (Discourses) against the Arians by Athanasius of Alexandria, generally dated to around 340, though the exact date is debated. Its authenticity was questioned in modern scholarship but is widely accepted. Continuing the earlier discourses, it explains texts used by Arian opponents such as Asterius the Sophist, starting with John 14:10, "I in the Father and the Father in me." It argues for the mutual indwelling of Father and Son, who share one essence. It then attributes the Gospel accounts of Christ's ignorance, growth and suffering to the humanity the Word took on.

The Fourth Discourse Against the Arians is a Greek theological treatise that has come down with the three Orations Against the Arians of Athanasius of Alexandria (4th century). Most scholars doubt that Athanasius wrote it, and its true author and date are uncertain. It is a series of short arguments rather than a continuous discourse. Using Scripture, it argues that the Word is substantial and is the Father's own Son, and so preserves the single "Monarchy" of the Godhead. It attacks Arian teaching, and also views that separate the Word from the Son or merge Father and Son into one.

The First Discourse Against the Arians is the opening book of Athanasius of Alexandria's Greek polemical treatise against Arianism. Its date is disputed: scholars place it either around 339–346, during his exile in Rome, or in the later 350s. Athanasius argues that the Arians are sectaries named after their founder rather than Christians. He attacks the teaching of Arius's Thalia and defends the eternity of the Son and his unity of essence with the Father. He also begins interpreting disputed biblical texts such as Philippians 2:9–10 and Hebrews 1:4. It is a central text of Nicene theology.

This is a collection of supplementary material from volume 26 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, which is devoted to writings of Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373). It contains front matter, editorial notices, notes and shorter pieces that are not indexed as separate works. The opening notice deals with the so-called fourth Oration against the Arians. It cites Severus of Antioch and Theodore of Pharan as witnesses that the oration was counted among Athanasius' works. It also quotes an older Byzantine verdict praising the clarity and force of Athanasius' books against Arius.

The Sermo maior de fide is the later title, now considered mistaken, of a Greek letter said to have been addressed by Athanasius of Alexandria to the church of Antioch. Most scholars regard it as Pseudo-Athanasian, though some argue that Athanasius wrote it, and its date is uncertain. Written against the Arians, especially the Anomoeans, it discusses the incarnation of the Word, the resurrection and Christ's humanity, using Athanasius's phrase "the dominical man". Only excerpts survive in Greek, mostly in catenae, along with Latin and Syriac quotations. A nearly complete Armenian translation also survives.

The Tomus ad Antiochenos is a synodal letter issued by Athanasius of Alexandria and the council he held at Alexandria in 362, after Julian allowed exiled bishops to return. It is addressed to bishops including Eusebius of Vercelli, Lucifer of Cagliari and Asterius of Petra. It aimed to heal the schism at Antioch and set lenient terms for receiving former Arians who accepted the Nicene faith. It also accepted both "one hypostasis" and "three hypostases" as orthodox when properly understood, an important step toward settling Trinitarian terminology.

The Life of Antony is a Greek hagiographical biography of the Egyptian hermit Antony the Great. It was written by Athanasius of Alexandria soon after Antony's death in 356, probably before 362. The work follows Antony from his youth through his withdrawal into the desert, his battles with demons, his long address to monks and his final years on the "inner mountain." It was quickly translated into Latin and other languages. It became the model for later saints' lives and did much to spread the ideal of Christian monasticism in both East and West.

The Letter to Marcellinus on the Interpretation of the Psalms is a Greek letter by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria (d. 373). Its exact date is uncertain. Athanasius writes to Marcellinus, who is recovering from illness, and passes on the teaching of a learned old man about the Psalter. The letter presents the Psalms as a summary of all Scripture and as a mirror in which readers see their own souls. It also explains which psalms suit different spiritual situations and why psalms are sung. The work strongly shaped how Christians later used the Psalms in prayer.

De titulis Psalmorum is a Greek commentary on the Psalms that has come down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria. Its authenticity is doubted, and some scholars attribute it to Hesychius of Jerusalem. The date is uncertain. It offers short explanatory glosses verse by verse and reads the Psalms christologically and sacramentally. On Psalm 1, for example, it applies the blessed man to Joseph of Arimathea and takes the tree planted by the waters as the cross beside the baptismal font.

The Expositiones in Psalmos is a Greek commentary on the Psalms traditionally attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373). It gives short notes on individual verses and reads the Psalter as Christological prophecy. Psalm 1 is taken as David dedicating his prophecy to Christ, and the "counsel of the ungodly" is linked to those who opposed the Saviour. Much of the commentary survives through excerpts in exegetical catenae, so its exact form and how much of it is by Athanasius remain debated. It differs from his Letter to Marcellinus on the Psalms.

This is a Greek collection of short exegetical fragments attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria (died 373). Later writers and catena compilers quoted them under his name, so many cannot be securely authenticated. Most deal with the Psalms and give them a Christological reading. The Lord seated at God's right hand and the ark of sanctification are read as Christ's ascension in his holy flesh, which he never lays aside. Other passages discuss the cherubim and the "hand" of God. A preface to the Psalter, preserved in a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library in Milan, accompanies the fragments.

This is a collection of short Greek exegetical fragments attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria (d. 373), on Job, the Song of Songs, Matthew, Luke and 1 Corinthians. They survive mainly as excerpts in later catenae, and the authenticity of individual pieces is often uncertain. Several are shaped by the Arian controversy. In one, the verse "seven sons were born to him" from Job leads into an argument that scriptural words such as "made" or "became" can mean begetting, so they do not show that the Son is a creature.

Two Greek letters on monastic life addressed to "the most blessed father Castor", transmitted under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria but not his work. They are a Greek abridgement of material from John Cassian's Institutes, which Cassian wrote around 420 for Castor, bishop of Apt, who had founded a new monastery in Gaul. The letters describe the rules of the coenobitic monasteries of Egypt and the Thebaid, beginning with how the monks pray together. Their date of composition is uncertain, and they show how Cassian's teaching reached Greek readers.

This short Greek confession of faith addressed to the Emperor Jovian circulated under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria. Modern scholarship generally credits it to Apollinaris of Laodicea, writing around 363, and it was handed down with other Apollinarian writings under orthodox names. It sets out baptismal Trinitarian faith and teaches that the Word is one Son even after the incarnation. It calls Mary Theotokos and confesses "one nature of God the Word incarnate". Cyril of Alexandria took that formula to be Athanasian, and it became central to later Christological controversy.

The Sermo contra omnes haereses ("Sermon against all heresies") is a Greek homily handed down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria but not considered his work. Its author is unknown and its date uncertain, perhaps between the fifth and seventh centuries. It takes the opening of John's Gospel, "In the beginning was the Word," as its text. It argues that the prophets foresaw salvation through Christ and the evangelists confirmed it, pairing Isaiah's sacrificial lamb with John the Baptist's "Behold the Lamb of God."

This short Greek treatise or sermon on the Trinity has come down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria, but it is not considered his work. Its real author is unknown, and it probably dates from the later fourth or fifth century. It opens by setting Christian faith apart from both Greek idolatry and Jewish denial of the Son. It then turns against the Sabellians, who merged Father and Son into one person, and argues that the Son and the Holy Spirit have always existed with God as distinct from the Father.

The Liber de definitionibus (Greek Peri horōn, "On Definitions") is a Greek handbook of theological and philosophical definitions. It is falsely attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria, and its date is uncertain, though it is probably from between the sixth and eighth centuries. It says its definitions are gathered from Clement and other holy Fathers in line with the faith of the catholic Church. It teaches that every question has three parts: what a thing is, why it bears its name and how many meanings that name has. It also calls God alone the "definition of definitions." It is meant as basic training for anyone who would defend orthodox doctrine.

De incarnatione Dei Verbi is a short Greek treatise in letter form, traditionally attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria but not regarded as his work. Its author and date are uncertain, though it is generally placed between the mid-fourth and fifth centuries. Written in reply to readers who had asked for a statement of the apostolic faith, it recalls the synod's condemnation of Paul of Samosata's innovations. Citing 1 Timothy 3:16, it urges believers to hold to the tradition they received and avoid curious speculation. It confesses that God was manifested in the flesh, sinless and pure.

De incarnatione Dei Verbi ("On the Incarnation of God the Word") is a Greek theological treatise that has come down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria. Editors class it as doubtful or spurious, so it belongs among the Pseudo-Athanasian writings. Its real author and date are unknown, though it is usually placed between the mid-fourth and late fifth centuries. Its subject is the incarnation of the divine Word, a central issue in the Trinitarian and Christological debates of that period. It is separate from Athanasius's authentic treatise On the Incarnation.

De sabbatis et circumcisione (On Sabbaths and Circumcision) is a short Greek treatise handed down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria but generally regarded as spurious. Its date is uncertain, probably between the mid-fourth and the fifth century. Starting from Exodus 31, it argues that the Sabbath marked the end of the first creation. Christians therefore honour the day of the Lord's resurrection, the start of the new creation, and look toward the eternal "Sabbath of Sabbaths". It treats circumcision in the same typological way.

De virginitate, or On Virginity (Greek Peri parthenias, also titled "On Ascetic Practice"), is a Greek treatise of practical guidance for a woman dedicated to virginity. It has been handed down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria, but most scholars think the attribution is doubtful or false. It is generally dated to the fourth century, and its exact origin is uncertain. The treatise opens with a creed affirming three hypostases and one Godhead. It then gives rules on fasting, prayer, psalmody, dress and daily conduct, which makes it a valuable witness to early Christian ascetic life among women.

The Five Dialogues on the Holy Trinity are a Greek theological work handed down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria. Its real author is unknown. It is usually dated to the late fourth century, after the time of Athanasius. In question-and-answer form, an Orthodox speaker argues against opponents of Nicene doctrine, beginning with an Anomoean, or radical Arian. The dialogues defend the full divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit, as well as the limits of human knowledge of God. They are a witness to the Trinitarian controversies after Nicaea.

The Disputatio contra Arium is an anonymous Greek dialogue falsely attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria. Its date is uncertain, but it is usually placed between the fifth and seventh centuries. Its title sets it as a debate with Arius, or an Arian, at the Council of Nicaea under Emperor Constantine and Pope Silvester. The narrator is asked about Christ's saying "The Father who sent me is greater than I" (John 14:28), which leads into a defence of the Son's full divinity. It is a late example of anti-Arian polemic written under Athanasius' name.

The Doctrina ad Antiochum ducem ("Teaching for Duke Antiochus") is a Greek instructional work falsely attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria. It is addressed to an otherwise unknown military commander named Antiochus. Its author and date are unknown, though it is generally placed somewhere between the sixth and ninth centuries. The work gives Christian teaching on questions of faith and nature in a simple style. Its discussion of the soul, for example, places it in the heart, the back of the head and the major veins, which together give life to the whole body.

The Epistula catholica is a short Greek encyclical letter that bears the name of Athanasius of Alexandria and his fellow bishops but is generally regarded as spurious. Its date and true author are uncertain, though it probably comes from the fourth or fifth century. It is addressed to orthodox bishops in Egypt, Syria, Cilicia, Phoenicia and Arabia. The letter urges them to separate from the Arians, who deny the one true Godhead of the Trinity and cause violence and disorder in the Church, and to stay in communion with one another.

This Greek homily tells of a miracle at Berytus (Beirut). It is falsely attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria and probably dates from the eighth century. In the story a Christian moves house and leaves behind an icon of Christ. Jews living nearby find it and mock and pierce it, re-enacting the Passion. Blood and water flow from the image and heal the sick, and the Jews convert. The legend was used in the defence of images during the Iconoclast controversy and was read at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787.

The History of Melchizedek is a short Greek narrative falsely attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria. Its date is uncertain, perhaps between the fifth and ninth centuries. It is an apocryphal legend that explains why Melchizedek is called "without mother, without genealogy" (Hebrews 7:3). In the story, Melchizedek is the son of Melchi, a pagan king of Salem who sacrifices to idols. While contemplating the heavens, the young man recognises the one Creator and refuses idolatry, and this sets him apart from his family. The work belongs to a wider body of Melchizedek legends found in several Eastern Christian traditions.

The Homily on the Sowing (Homilia de semente) is a Greek sermon handed down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria. It is generally regarded as spurious, and its author and exact date are unknown, though it is usually placed in late antiquity. The preacher speaks at a gathering held on the Sabbath and comments on the Gospel reading about Jesus' disciples plucking grain as they pass through the sown fields, and about the healing of the withered hand. Along the way he argues against Jewish Sabbath observance and says the Lord has transferred the Sabbath to the Lord's Day.

This is a group of Greek festal sermons that were handed down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria but are not by him. They cover feasts of the church year, including the Nativity of John the Baptist, the Annunciation, the Nativity of Christ, the Meeting of the Lord, Easter and the Ascension. The authors and dates are unknown, and the sermons probably come from different hands between the fifth and ninth centuries. The first sermon praises Elizabeth, who gave birth in old age after being barren, and contrasts her with Zechariah, who did not believe.

This Greek homily on Matthew 21:2 ("Go into the village… you will find a colt tied") has come down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria, but it is considered spurious. Its author and date are unknown; it is usually placed between the later fourth and fifth centuries. Using Ecclesiastes' "a time to seek, and a time to lose", the preacher presents Christ's coming as the time to seek lost humanity and free it from the devil's bonds. The homily is linked to Christ's entry into Jerusalem.

In passionem et crucem Domini (On the Passion and Cross of the Lord) is a Greek homily handed down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria. Scholars generally regard it as the work of an unknown later author. Its date is uncertain but probably falls between the mid-fourth and the fifth century. The sermon explains the Gospel account of the crucifixion at Golgotha (Matthew 27:33–36). It starts from Paul's statement that God cannot lie and contrasts the unchanging God with changeable creation. From there it builds a theological reading of Christ's suffering and the cross.

The Diatyposis, or Monasticae vitae institutio, is a short Greek rule for "those who wish to live in stillness" (hesychia). It is attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria in its title but is not his, and its author and date are unknown; it is perhaps from between the fifth and eighth centuries. It tells the monk to give up worldly business and cares and to keep only simple food and enough clothing. He should not seek wealth even to give alms, which it calls a snare of vainglory. Instead he should practise solitary quiet as a soldier of Christ.

This is a miscellany of short Greek writings that manuscripts attribute to Athanasius of Alexandria but that are not by him. It includes dialogues with a Macedonian "Pneumatomachian", who denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and a series of short chapters against various opinions. These chapters reject the formula of "one nature" in Christ, the claim that "God suffered impassibly", and refusals to examine the meaning of theological terms. Their concerns point to the Trinitarian and Christological controversies of the late fourth and fifth centuries. The authors and exact dates are unknown.

The Quaestiones ad Antiochum ducem (Questions to Antiochus the Governor) is a Greek work of questions and answers, or erotapokriseis, falsely attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria. It was probably written between the seventh and eighth centuries, though its exact date and author are unknown. Addressed to an official named Antiochus, it takes up a long series of difficulties in Scripture and Christian belief. It opens by asking how Christians can confess Father, Son and Holy Spirit as God without believing in three gods. It shows how Byzantine Christians taught doctrine in a popular form.

These are Greek writings preserved under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria but not his own work. Their real author or authors are unknown, and they are usually dated between the seventh and ninth centuries. The Questions on the Gospels discuss difficult passages of the Gospels in a question-and-answer format. The short fragment on images probably comes from the debates over icons in the Byzantine period. Material passed down with these texts includes a collection of Old Testament proof-texts against Judaism, ending with Daniel's vision of judgement and the defeat of the Antichrist.

This Greek collection of questions and answers on Scripture has come down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria, but it is not his work. Its author is unknown, and it is usually dated between the seventh and ninth centuries. In short catechetical exchanges it explains biblical passages, especially Gospel parables, through allegory. The king stands for God, the jar of water for baptism and the obedient son for the Gentiles. Other questions on various topics follow. It belongs to the Byzantine erotapokriseis genre of question-and-answer literature.

Quod unus sit Christus ("That Christ Is One") is a short Greek Christological treatise that has come down among the writings attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria but is not considered his. Its real author and date are uncertain; it probably belongs to the later fourth or fifth century. It urges converts from paganism and Judaism not to treat Christ as a mere man because of his body and sufferings. It also attacks those who use Greek philosophical reasoning to call the Son's begetting a creation. Against both, it defends the unity of the incarnate Word.

The Refutation of the Hypocrisy of Meletius and Eusebius of Samosata is a short Greek polemical treatise transmitted under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria but generally regarded as spurious. Its author and date are uncertain. It targets the party of Meletius of Antioch and Eusebius of Samosata and their acceptance of the Nicene homoousios. The author argues that being "like" something is not being identical with it: the Son is not merely like God, as humans are, but one in essence with the Father.

This is a Greek version of the Athanasian Creed, known from its Latin opening words as the Quicumque vult. The creed is attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria, but it was in fact composed in Latin, probably in southern Gaul in the late fifth or sixth century, by an unknown author. It sets out the doctrine of one God in three persons and of the two natures of Christ, and it warns that holding this faith is necessary for salvation. Greek translations appeared later, in the medieval period, and their dates are uncertain.

The Synopsis of Holy Scripture is an anonymous Greek handbook to the Bible. It was transmitted under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria, but he did not write it. Scholars have dated it to the fourth, fifth or sixth century, most often the sixth. It begins by saying that inspired Scripture is fixed in a canon. It then lists the books of the Old and New Testaments, quoting each book's opening words and summarizing its contents. The work is an important witness to how the biblical canon was understood and set out in the Greek East.

The Syntagma doctrinae is a short Greek handbook of Christian conduct, transmitted under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria but not his work. Its author and exact date are unknown; it is usually placed between the fourth and fifth centuries. Addressed to all Christians and especially to monks and ascetics, it lists precepts on chastity, speech, oaths, fasting, prayer and avoiding magic and pagan festivals. It draws on the "Two Ways" tradition of the Didache and is evidence for early ascetic discipline.

The Testimonia ex Scriptura sacra is a short Greek collection of biblical proof-texts on the Trinity. It has come down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria but is not his work, and its date is uncertain, probably between the later fourth and fifth centuries. Under numbered headings such as freedom, giving life and appointing ministers of the Church, it sets out passages that ascribe the same action to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The point is to show that the three share one essence. It belongs to the controversies over the Spirit's divinity that followed Nicaea.

The Life and Conduct of Saint Syncletica is a Greek hagiography of Syncletica of Alexandria, a fourth-century Egyptian ascetic and teacher of women living the monastic life. It was traditionally attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria, but it is the work of an unknown author and is usually dated to the fifth century. After a short account of her renunciation, most of the work records her long discourses on ascetic practice, the passions and spiritual struggle. It is an important early source for women's monasticism, and sayings ascribed to her also appear in the Apophthegmata Patrum.

Against Eunomius is a Greek polemical treatise in three books by Basil of Caesarea, usually dated to about 363–365, before he became bishop. It refutes the Apology of Eunomius, leader of the Heteroousian (Anomoean) party, who held that "unbegotten" defines God's essence, so the Son must be unlike the Father in substance. Basil answers with his account of names formed by human conception (epinoia), defends the full divinity of the Son and, in the third book, of the Holy Spirit. Two further books passed down with it are generally considered spurious. Eunomius replied, and Gregory of Nyssa answered that reply.

Adversus Eunomium IV–V is a Greek anti-Arian treatise in two books, handed down as a continuation of Basil of Caesarea's authentic three books against Eunomius. Its Basilian authorship was doubted even in antiquity and is now generally rejected. Modern scholars have often proposed Didymus the Blind as the author, though Apollinaris of Laodicea has also been suggested, and the question remains open. It probably dates from the later fourth century. Book IV sets out objections and replies from Scripture on the Son's divinity and his shared nature with the Father. Book V defends the divinity of the Holy Spirit.

The Homilies on the Psalms are a collection of Greek sermons by Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), preached in Cappadocia while he was a presbyter and later bishop. Each one explains a single psalm from a selection, among them Psalms 1, 14, 29, 33, 44 and 45. The homilies draw moral and spiritual lessons from the text rather than offering close technical exegesis. The opening homily on Psalm 1 is especially well known. It praises the Psalter as a medicine for every ailment of the soul, with teaching sweetened by melody as a physician sweetens a bitter cup with honey.

The Hexaemeron is a series of nine Greek homilies by Basil of Caesarea, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, on the six days of creation, working through Genesis 1:1–26. Basil preached them to his congregation in the 370s, possibly in 378. They pair a literal reading of the text with natural philosophy, describing the heavens, earth, plants and animals to show the Creator's wisdom. It was the first Christian work of its kind and shaped later hexaemeral writing, including Ambrose's Hexameron. Eustathius Afer translated it into Latin around 400.

This is a miscellaneous grouping of material from volume 29 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the first of the volumes given to the works of Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379). It brings together front matter, editorial notes and shorter pieces that have no separate entry. The material includes prefatory and biographical writing on Basil. This draws on Greek testimony such as Gregory of Nazianzus's funeral oration for him, which recalls their friendship and studies and praises Caesarea as a centre of learning. Because the material is mixed, it has no single author or date.

De hominis structura is a pair of Greek homilies on the creation of humankind, based on Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man in our image". They present themselves as paying an old debt by completing Basil of Caesarea's Hexaemeron, which ends before reaching the creation of man. Manuscripts attribute them to Basil or to Gregory of Nyssa, and their authorship is still disputed. They discuss the image and likeness of God, human dominion over creation and the formation of the body. They give an early Cappadocian account of human nature.

De paradiso oratio ("Oration on Paradise") is a Greek homily that has come down under the name of Basil of Caesarea, though its authenticity is doubted and it is generally classed among the pseudo-Basilian writings. Its date and true author are uncertain. Addressed to listeners, it explains Genesis 2:8: "And God planted a paradise in Eden eastward." It presents paradise as a garden that God himself planted, set on a high and safe place with a mild climate, free from storms and winter frost, and fit for humanity as his special creation.

On the True Integrity of Virginity is a Greek ascetic treatise addressed to Letoius, bishop of Melitene. It was handed down among the works of Basil of Caesarea, but modern scholars generally attribute it to Basil of Ancyra, the fourth-century homoiousian bishop and physician. That attribution is not certain, and the date is uncertain too. Rather than simply praising virginity, fasting or giving up possessions, the author explains what each practice is and how it serves true virtue. The treatise is an important early source for Christian thinking about consecrated virginity and the discipline of the body.

The Apology (Liber apologeticus) is a short Greek theological treatise by Eunomius, the leading Anomoean theologian, who was briefly bishop of Cyzicus. It was written around 359–361, during the controversies over Arianism. Presented as a defence against slander and as a confession of faith, it argues that God is by essence "unbegotten" (agennētos), so the begotten Son must differ from the Father in essence. It is a key document of later Arian thought. Basil of Caesarea refuted it in his Against Eunomius, and Eunomius answered him with a further Apology for the Apology.

These Greek homilies on Psalms 28, 37, 115 and 132 have come down among the works of Basil of Caesarea (d. 379), but scholars generally regard them as spurious. Their real author and date are unknown. In the manner of Basil's authentic psalm homilies, they explain the psalms verse by verse with a moral and spiritual focus. The homily on Psalm 28 reads the Lord's "holy court" as the Church, warns against schism and against making a god of the belly or of money, and collects scriptural passages to explain "the voice of the Lord upon the waters."

The Commentarius in Isaiam prophetam is a Greek commentary on the first sixteen chapters of the Book of Isaiah. It has come down under the name of Basil of Caesarea, but scholars have long doubted that he wrote it. Some have defended it as authentic, while others assign it to an anonymous author of the fourth century. The commentary works verse by verse and favours moral and spiritual readings. It draws on earlier Alexandrian exegesis and often uses examples from nature, such as the snake shedding its old skin, to teach about Christian conduct.

This is a set of miscellaneous material from volume 30 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, one of the volumes given to the writings of Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379). It brings together front matter, editorial notes and shorter pieces that are not listed as separate works. The surviving portion consists mainly of Latin and Greek scholarly annotations on Basil's homilies on the Hexaemeron, the six days of creation. These notes discuss the title of the work, cite ancient witnesses such as the Suda, Photius and Anastasius, and explain points of text and interpretation.

The Sermo de contubernalibus (Greek "Logos peri tōn syneisaktōn", "Discourse on the Women Brought In") is a Greek homily that has come down under the name of Basil of Caesarea. Its authenticity is generally rejected, so it is counted among the Pseudo-Basilian writings, and its real author and date are unknown. The sermon condemns the custom of the syneisaktoi, in which ascetic or clerical men lived with consecrated virgins in supposedly chaste partnerships. It urges self-restraint and complains that the warnings of Christ and the apostles go unheeded. It is evidence for early Christian debates about this practice.

This short Greek treatise by Basil of Caesarea is usually known in English as the Address to Young Men on the Right Use of Greek Literature. It was written in the mid- to late fourth century, and its exact date is uncertain. Basil addresses young relatives and advises them to read pagan poets, historians and philosophers selectively, as bees gather from flowers. They should take what encourages virtue and prepares them for Scripture, and leave the rest. The work became one of the most influential early Christian statements on classical education.

The Exhortation to Holy Baptism is a Greek sermon by Basil of Caesarea (d. 379), usually numbered among his homilies. Its exact date is uncertain. It opens by reworking Ecclesiastes' "a time to be born and a time to die": spiritual rebirth requires first dying to the flesh with Christ. Basil argues that a person's whole life is the right time for baptism. He urges catechumens not to put it off until old age or the deathbed. The homily is an important witness to the fourth-century practice of delaying baptism and to the Church's efforts to discourage it.

The Homily against Those Who Are Angry (Greek Κατὰ ὀργιζομένων) is a moral sermon by Basil of Caesarea, preached in Cappadocia in the 360s or 370s. Its exact date is unknown. Basil begins by comparing spiritual precepts to medical prescriptions, whose value is best shown by experience. He then draws on Proverbs, Paul's command to put away all anger, and Christ's warning about anger against a brother. He describes how anger overthrows reason and turns a person into a beast. The homily is one of the best-known early Christian treatments of the passions.

This is a group of Greek ascetical writings that have come down under the name of Basil of Caesarea (d. 379), and it belongs to the larger Basilian ascetic corpus. The Praevia institutio ascetica uses the image of the soldier of Christ to urge renunciation of home, property and family. The ascetic sermons give guidance on monastic life. De judicio Dei and De fide serve as prefaces to Basil's Moralia and monastic Rules. Scholars doubt that some of these pieces, especially the sermons, are really by Basil.

This Greek homily by Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379) is a sermon on the words "Give heed to yourself" (Deuteronomy 15:9). Its exact date is uncertain. Basil begins by reflecting on speech as the means by which the soul makes its hidden thoughts known, and asks his listeners for silence. He then expounds the brief scriptural command, urging watchfulness over one's own soul rather than over the body or outward possessions. He presents attention to oneself as a guard against sin and a path to knowing God. The homily became an influential text on Christian self-examination and the inner life.

The Ascetic Constitutions (Constitutiones asceticae, Greek Asketikai diataxeis) are a Greek treatise on the monastic life. They have come down under the name of Basil of Caesarea, but scholars generally regard them as the work of an unknown later writer. The date is uncertain. They are addressed to ascetics living both in community and alone. A prologue explains that the text was written at a disciple's request, and the chapters that follow give guidance on resisting bodily passions, guarding the mind and pursuing virtue. They show how far Basil's authority reached in shaping Greek monastic teaching.

This Greek homily by Basil of Caesarea defends Nicene Trinitarian doctrine against errors on two opposite sides. It likens the danger to Judaism and Hellenism, which oppose each other and both oppose Christianity. Sabellius merges Father and Son into one person, while Arius and the Anomoeans divide their substance and call the Son unlike the Father. Basil defends a middle course that keeps the persons distinct and their nature one. The homily belongs to his struggle against the later Arians of the 360s and 370s, and its exact date is unknown.

The Homilia de fide (Greek Περὶ πίστεως, "On Faith") is a Greek sermon by Basil of Caesarea, delivered sometime between his ordination and his death in 379. It begins by reflecting that remembering God is always pious, but speaking about God is daring, because the mind falls short of divine reality and words fall short of the mind. Basil cites the humility of Abraham and Moses, then sets out an account of faith in the Trinity. The sermon shows how he preached on theology and defended Nicene doctrine during the Trinitarian controversies.

The Homily on Thanksgiving is a Greek sermon by Basil of Caesarea, preached sometime between his ordination and his death in 379. It explains Paul's command to the Thessalonians: "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, in everything give thanks" (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18). Basil answers those who say the command is impossible, since grief and misfortune seem to rule out constant joy. He argues that the Christian can stay grateful and calm through suffering and bereavement. He warns against excessive mourning while still allowing natural sorrow, citing Christ's tears at the tomb of Lazarus.

The Homily on Humility is a Greek sermon by Basil of Caesarea, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, written in the decades before his death in 379. It opens with the fall of Adam. Humanity lost its true glory by grasping at a greater one, and Basil presents humility as the cure for that sickness and the way back. He then condemns pride in wealth, luxury, public office, eloquence and even virtue. He urges his hearers to seek glory from God alone rather than from themselves.

The Homily on Envy (De invidia) is a Greek sermon by Basil of Caesarea, one of his moral homilies, preached at Caesarea in Cappadocia at an uncertain date before his death in 379. Basil calls envy the most destructive of passions and says it harms the envious person most of all. He compares it to rust that eats away iron and to young vipers said to devour their mother's womb. The envious person is wounded by a neighbour's every success and finds relief only when that neighbour falls. The homily became a widely read work of early Christian moral teaching.

De jejunio homilia II is the second of two Greek sermons on fasting attributed to Basil of Caesarea, the Cappadocian bishop who died in 379. It opens with a verse from Isaiah, "Comfort the people, O priests." Basil compares himself to a general rallying soldiers or a trainer encouraging athletes. He urges Christians, as soldiers of Christ, to prepare through fasting and self-restraint for the struggle against invisible spiritual enemies. Fasting strengthens the soul the way oil strengthens an athlete's body.

This Greek homily by Basil of Caesarea (d. 379) is on Luke 12:18, where the rich fool says, "I will tear down my barns and build larger ones," and it also deals with avarice. Basil begins by naming two kinds of temptation: affliction, as in the case of Job, and prosperity. He then presents the rich man's abundance as a test he failed. He argues that wealth is held in trust for those in need and condemns hoarding. It is one of Basil's best-known sermons on wealth and poverty and is widely cited in discussions of early Christian social teaching.

This is a group of Greek homilies handed down among the works of Basil of Caesarea, though his authorship is doubted. Who wrote them and when is uncertain. If they are Basil's, they would come from the period of his career in the Trinitarian controversies, roughly 357 to 379. The opening homily is on the Holy Spirit. It argues that baptism into the Trinity shows the Father, Son and Spirit to be above creation. Citing Paul and John, it says the Spirit shares God's single activity and divine nature and is neither a creature nor a servant.

The first homily on fasting is a Greek sermon by Basil of Caesarea. It was evidently preached as a period of fasting began, probably at the start of Lent, though its exact date is unknown. Basil opens with the psalm verse "Blow the trumpet at the new moon" and draws on Isaiah's teaching on true fasting and on Christ's command not to look gloomy while fasting. He urges his hearers to fast cheerfully, describing fasting as a medicine that destroys sin and as a care for the soul rather than the stomach. A second homily on fasting goes with it.

The Homily on the Martyr Barlaam is a Greek panegyric sermon handed down under the name of Basil of Caesarea (d. 379), though its authenticity has been questioned. It was delivered at a festival in honour of Barlaam, a martyr venerated at Antioch. The preacher argues that since the cross, the deaths of the saints are no longer mourned but celebrated with joy, because death is a passage to a better life. He then praises Barlaam, a rustic man without learning, whose steadfast faith put the wise of this world to shame.

Homilia in divites ("To the Rich") is a Greek sermon by Basil of Caesarea, preached in Cappadocia some time before his death in 379. It takes up the Gospel story of the rich young man who asked Jesus how to inherit eternal life but went away grieving. Basil says that he already discussed this young man in an earlier sermon. He condemns the love of wealth, the hoarding of goods and luxury, and urges almsgiving to the poor. It is one of the main early Christian texts on wealth and social justice.

Homilia in ebriosos ("Against Drunkards") is a Greek sermon by Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. It belongs to his collection of moral homilies, and the exact date of delivery is uncertain. Basil attacks drunkenness and the disorderly revelry that went with it. He describes vividly how wine degrades body and mind, turns people into something less than rational beings, and leads them into lust and violence. He urges his congregation toward sobriety and repentance. The homily shows Basil as a moral preacher and gives a picture of popular festive customs in fourth-century Christian Cappadocia.

This Greek sermon by Basil of Caesarea was preached at Caesarea in Cappadocia during a severe drought and famine. It is usually linked to the famine of around 368, when Basil was still a presbyter and organised relief for the hungry. It opens with Amos 3:8 and takes up the prophet's call to repentance. Basil presents the drought as a consequence of the people's sins, condemns hoarding and greed, and urges prayer, repentance and generous almsgiving. It is an important witness to his social preaching and his concern for the poor.

This Greek homily by Basil of Caesarea, probably preached while he was priest or bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia (between about 357 and 379), was delivered at a martyr's festival at the shrine outside the city. It praises Gordius, a centurion of Caesarea who withdrew to the mountains during persecution. He later came into the crowded theatre during public games, openly confessed Christ, and was executed. Basil holds up his boldness and his scorn for worldly life as examples for the crowds who honoured his memory.

This Greek panegyric homily by Basil of Caesarea was delivered at the annual festival of Mamas, a shepherd martyred in Cappadocia in the third century and greatly venerated around Caesarea. Basil says he cannot do justice to so great a martyr. Instead he asks his listeners to recall from their own memory the saint's deeds and the help they have received from him. The homily belongs to Basil's festal preaching on martyrs, which shows the growth of the cult of local saints in fourth-century Cappadocia. Its exact date is uncertain.

This is a Greek homily by Basil of Caesarea, preached on the feast day of the martyr Julitta during his ministry in Cappadocia (c. 357–379). Its exact date is unknown. Basil tells the story of a wealthy woman whose property was seized by a powerful and greedy man. When she went to court to recover it, she was required to deny Christ, refused, and was put to death by fire. He praises her courage as proof that a woman's strength could overcome the devil. The homily also completes his earlier sermon on thanksgiving.

This is a Greek sermon by Basil of Caesarea (d. 379) on the opening verse of John's Gospel, "In the beginning was the Word." Basil calls John, the "son of thunder," the loftiest voice of the gospel. He notes that pagan thinkers admired the prologue and borrowed from it. He then examines the terms "beginning," "was" and "Word" to show that the Son is eternal and fully divine, against the Arian view that he came into being. The homily shows Basil defending Nicene theology in his preaching.

The Homily on the Beginning of Proverbs is a Greek sermon by Basil of Caesarea, the Cappadocian Father who was bishop of Caesarea from 370 until his death in 379. Its exact date is unknown. It is an exposition of the opening verses of the Book of Proverbs, which Basil reads as a guide to wisdom, instruction and moral understanding. It is one of the shorter homilies in which Basil gives moral teaching based on the Old Testament wisdom books.

This Greek panegyric homily by Basil of Caesarea (d. 379) was preached on the feast of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste. They were Christian soldiers who, by tradition, were put to death in the early fourth century by being left naked on a frozen lake. Basil praises their unity of faith and endurance. He tells how one soldier gave up and how a guard took his place, so that the number of forty stayed complete. The homily set the pattern for later veneration of these martyrs. It survives in several ancient translations.

The Moralia (Greek Ethika) is an ascetical handbook by Basil of Caesarea, compiled between his turn to the monastic life in the late 350s and his death in 379. It sets out eighty rules for Christian conduct. Each rule is a short statement backed only by New Testament quotations, starting with the call to repentance. Basil thus grounds Christian life entirely in Scripture. Usually linked with his ascetic writings, the work strongly influenced Greek monastic and moral teaching.

This is a miscellaneous grouping, not a single work. It collects introductory matter, editorial notes and short unindexed pieces from the volume of Migne's Patrologia Graeca that holds writings attributed to Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), chiefly his homilies. The Greek passages quoted with Latin commentary include lines from the homily on the martyr Barlaam and from sermons on wealth and on suffering. Basil's authorship of the Barlaam homily is disputed, and the notes discuss variant readings and attributions.

This Greek homily by Basil of Caesarea (d. 379) argues that God is not the cause of evil. It starts from Psalm 13 (12 in the Septuagint), "How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me?", and the fool who says there is no God. Basil separates true evil, which is sin and comes from the free choice of rational creatures, from suffering such as illness, poverty and death. He treats suffering as God's healing discipline. The homily was influential in early Christian thought on theodicy.

This Greek homily is attributed to Basil of Caesarea, the fourth-century Cappadocian bishop and theologian, and is usually counted among his moral sermons. Its title, "That one should not cling to worldly things, and on the fire that broke out outside the church", gives its theme. The preacher speaks of himself as a stranger to his audience and thanks them for welcoming his sharp rebukes. He warns against attachment to possessions and earthly concerns, and takes a recent fire near the church as an occasion for reflection. Its exact date and setting are uncertain.

The Shorter Rules is a Greek ascetic work by Basil of Caesarea (d. 379), written in question-and-answer form. Along with the Longer Rules, it makes up his Asceticon. In over three hundred brief answers, Basil deals with practical questions raised by Christians living in community: how Scripture should guide all action, how to correct a brother who sins, the signs of true repentance, obedience, prayer, work and the common life. The collection grew out of his direction of monastic communities in Pontus and Cappadocia. It deeply shaped Eastern communal monasticism.

The Regulae fusius tractatae, or Longer Rules, are a Greek work on monastic life by Basil of Caesarea, written between about 357 and his death in 379. Together with the Shorter Rules, they make up his Asketikon. After a prologue urging the gathered brethren to care for their souls, the work answers a series of questions about the ascetic life. Its topics include love of God and neighbour, renunciation, life in community, obedience, work and the role of the superior. The Longer Rules became foundational for Eastern communal monasticism, and Benedict of Nursia cited Basil's rule.

On the Holy Spirit is a Greek theological treatise by Basil of Caesarea, written around 374–375 and addressed to Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium. It began as a defence of Basil's use of the doxology "with the Holy Spirit" alongside "in the Holy Spirit". The treatise argues against the Pneumatomachians, opponents of the Spirit's divinity, that the Spirit shares the honour and glory of the Father and the Son. It is also known for its appeal to unwritten apostolic tradition. The work helped shape the teaching on the Spirit affirmed at the Council of Constantinople in 381.

This is the collected correspondence of Basil of Caesarea, about 365 Greek letters written between roughly 357 and his death in 379. The first, to the philosopher Eustathius, describes how Basil followed him from Athens through Syria and Egypt without catching up. The letters deal with friendship, monastic life, church administration and the Trinitarian disputes. They also include canonical letters to Amphilochius of Iconium, which became part of Eastern church law. Some letters are of doubtful authenticity. The collection is a major source for fourth-century church history and the Cappadocian Fathers.

This is a miscellaneous collection of editorial material from volume 32 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, part of the series given to the works of Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379). Volume 32 mainly holds Basil's treatise On the Holy Spirit and his letters. The material here includes front matter, editors' notes and short pieces not indexed separately. The notes are written in Latin and quote Greek passages. Many concern doctrine, for example the distinction between ousia (essence) and hypostasis, which was central to the fourth-century Trinitarian controversies.

The Twenty-Four Ethical Discourses are a Greek collection of moral sermons put together from the writings of Basil of Caesarea. They are attributed to Symeon Metaphrastes, the Byzantine official and hagiographer who died around 1000. Each discourse gathers and rearranges passages from Basil's homilies, letters and ascetic works around a single moral theme, such as virtue, vice and the Christian life. The first discourse stresses that all of Christ's commandments must be kept, not only some. The collection shows how Byzantine compilers reworked patristic authors for edifying reading.

The Catechetical Lectures are a series of eighteen Greek instructions by Cyril of Jerusalem, given during Lent around 350 to candidates preparing for baptism at Easter. They were delivered in Jerusalem, probably in Constantine's basilica at the Holy Sepulchre. The early lectures deal with repentance, baptism and faith. The rest explain the baptismal creed of Jerusalem one article at a time. They are one of the earliest surviving systematic courses of Christian instruction and an important witness to the creed, teaching and church life of fourth-century Jerusalem.

The Mystagogical Lectures are five Greek homilies given in Jerusalem to the newly baptized during Easter week. They follow and complete Cyril of Jerusalem's Catechetical Lectures. They explain the rites the neophytes have just received: the renunciation of Satan, baptism, anointing with chrism, the Eucharist and the eucharistic liturgy, including an early witness to the epiclesis. Their date is uncertain, and some scholars attribute them wholly or partly to Cyril's successor, John of Jerusalem. They are a key source for fourth-century sacramental theology and liturgical practice.

The Letter to the Emperor Constantius is a short Greek letter by Cyril of Jerusalem, written in 351, soon after he became bishop. It reports a luminous cross that appeared in the sky over Jerusalem in May 351, stretching from Golgotha to the Mount of Olives. Cyril presents the sign as heavenly favour on Constantius's reign and as fulfilling Gospel prophecy. The letter is an early witness to imperial-ecclesiastical relations and to the cult of the cross in Jerusalem. Its authenticity has sometimes been questioned, but it is generally accepted.

These Greek fragments are attributed to Cyril of Jerusalem, bishop of Jerusalem in the mid-fourth century. They survive as excerpts quoted by later writers. One comes from a homily on the Gospel account of Christ turning water into wine at Cana. It argues that Christ neither fully revealed nor fully hid his divinity. He let his flesh suffer to refute those who claimed his body was only an appearance. Their language of Christ's "twofold operation", divine and human, links them to later Christological debates. Their exact origin and authenticity are uncertain.

The Homily on the Paralytic is a Greek sermon attributed to Cyril of Jerusalem. It is generally thought to come from about the time of his Catechetical Lectures, around 340–350, perhaps before he became bishop of Jerusalem. It explains the Gospel story in John 5 of the man who had been ill for thirty-eight years and whom Jesus healed at the pool with five porticoes in Jerusalem. The sermon presents Christ as the physician of souls and bodies. It is one of the very few sermons by Cyril to survive outside his catechetical works.

The Metaphrasis Psalmorum is a Greek verse paraphrase of the whole Psalter, written in Homeric dactylic hexameters. Short iambic prefaces introduce many of the psalms. It has come down under the name of Apollinaris of Laodicea, the fourth-century bishop. Most scholars now reject that attribution and date the poem to the mid-fifth century, roughly 450–470, which is why its author is called Pseudo-Apollinaris. It is a significant example of late antique Christian epic poetry, which recast biblical texts in the language and metre of classical Greek verse.

This is a miscellaneous collection of material from volume 33 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the volume given to Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 313–386). It gathers front matter, editorial dissertations, notes and shorter pieces not indexed as separate works. Much of it is scholarly Latin commentary with Greek quotations. It covers Cyril's life, including his consecration as bishop, his conflict with Acacius of Caesarea and his repeated exiles, as reported by historians such as Socrates. It also discusses terms from his Catechetical Lectures, such as illumination (photismos) and the renunciation made before baptism.

This encyclical letter is by Peter II, bishop of Alexandria from 373 to 381 and a disciple and chosen successor of Athanasius, and is presented here with other fragments of his writings. Peter wrote the letter in Greek after he was driven from his see under the emperor Valens. It describes the violence of the prefect Palladius against Nicene Christians in Alexandria: the attack on the church of Theonas, the abuse of consecrated virgins and the installation of the Arian bishop Lucius. Much of the letter survives because Theodoret quoted it in his Ecclesiastical History.

The Procatechesis is the introductory address to the Catechetical Lectures of Cyril of Jerusalem. It was delivered in Greek around 348–351, probably before or soon after Cyril became bishop. He spoke it to candidates preparing for baptism at Easter, the "ones to be enlightened." Citing the example of Simon Magus, Cyril urges them to come with a sincere purpose and not merely in body. He stresses regular attendance, exorcisms and secrecy about the teaching given. It opens the eighteen pre-baptismal lectures, a key witness to fourth-century catechesis.

This is a group of Greek writings that were handed down under the name of Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem (c. 313–386), but are not considered his work. Their real authors are unknown, and they are generally dated to between the fifth and eighth centuries. The best known is a festal homily on the Presentation of the Lord in the Temple (the Hypapante) and on Symeon, who received Christ. It opens with a joyful address to Zion and Jerusalem. These texts show how later preachers drew on Cyril's authority.

The Canonical Answers are a short collection of questions and answers on church discipline attributed to Timothy I, bishop of Alexandria (381–384), who took part in the Council of Constantinople in 381. Each brief answer settles a practical pastoral case: the baptism of catechumens who are sick or possessed, who may receive communion, ritual purity, marital continence and the duties of clergy. The Quinisext Council of 692 approved the collection, and it became part of the canon law of the Byzantine and Eastern Orthodox churches.

The Apophthegmata is a Greek collection of sayings, anecdotes and short teachings attributed to Macarius of Egypt (c. 300–391), the founding figure of monastic life at Scetis. It belongs to the wider apophthegmatic tradition of the Desert Fathers, which was passed down orally before being written down, probably between the late fourth and fifth centuries. Its exact date and authenticity are uncertain. The pieces deal with ascetic practice and spiritual warfare. They include visions of angels and demons leading souls after death, and accounts of demons that make monks drowsy and distracted while reading Scripture.

The Lausiac History is a Greek collection of short accounts of the monks, hermits and holy women of early Christian monasticism. Palladius of Helenopolis, a disciple of John Chrysostom, wrote it around 419–420 and dedicated it to Lausus, a chamberlain at the court of Theodosius II, after whom it is named. It draws on his own years among the ascetics of Egypt, Palestine and Syria. It is a key source for the Desert Fathers and was widely translated and imitated.

The Fifty Spiritual Homilies are a collection of Greek sermons and spiritual discourses on the Christian ascetic life, traditionally attributed to Macarius of Egypt. Modern scholars hold that he did not write them. The anonymous author, known as Pseudo-Macarius, appears to have come from Upper Mesopotamia, probably in the late fourth or early fifth century. The homilies stress the indwelling Holy Spirit, inner prayer and the soul's struggle against sin. They strongly influenced Eastern Orthodox monasticism and hesychasm, and later Protestant pietism, notably John Wesley.

This is a set of seven short Greek ascetic treatises transmitted under the name of Macarius the Great of Egypt: On Guarding the Heart, On Perfection in the Spirit, On Prayer, On Patience, On the Elevation of the Mind, On Love and On the Freedom of the Mind. They belong to the Pseudo-Macarian tradition and are usually regarded as a later Byzantine reworking of the Macarian homilies, traditionally linked with Symeon Metaphrastes. Their date is uncertain. They teach inward purification of the heart, unceasing prayer and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, and they shaped Eastern monastic spirituality.

This is a collection of miscellaneous Greek material from volume 34 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca. That volume is devoted mainly to Macarius of Egypt, Macarius of Alexandria and the Lausiac History of Palladius of Helenopolis. The pieces gathered here include front matter, editorial notes, variant readings and short texts that are not indexed separately. Much of it concerns the Lausiac History and its account of the Egyptian desert monks, including John of Lycopolis, Pachomius and the Tabennesiots. Some passages tell stories about Macarius, Athanasius and Melania. The material has no single author or date.

This short Greek discourse is about the soul's departure from the body. Its heading ascribes it to Saint Macarius of Alexandria, but it is generally counted among the spurious writings circulating under the name Macarius, and its author and date (perhaps fifth to eighth century) are unknown. In the narrative, two angels walk with Macarius in the desert and explain how the souls of the righteous and of sinners leave the body and what they meet after death. It is a witness to Byzantine monastic teaching about death and the afterlife.

Oration 1 is a short sermon Gregory of Nazianzus gave at Easter, usually dated to 362. It is the first of his collected orations. His father, the bishop of Nazianzus, had ordained him a priest against his will, and Gregory had withdrawn for a while to Pontus. Back for the feast, he presents the Resurrection as the start of his ministry. He asks for mutual forgiveness and defends his "tardiness" by pointing to Moses and Jeremiah. The sermon introduces themes he develops at length in Oration 2, his defence of his flight.

Oration 10, "On Himself, to His Father and Basil," is a short Greek speech by Gregory of Nazianzus, usually dated to 372. Basil of Caesarea had consecrated him bishop of Sasima, and Gregory had fled to solitude. In this speech, given after his return to Nazianzus, he says he was overcome by "old age and friendship", meaning his aged father, Gregory the Elder, and Basil. He sets his longing for quiet contemplation, after the examples of Elijah and John the Baptist, against his acceptance of church duty. The speech is an important source on his strained friendship with Basil.

Oration 11 is a short Greek speech by Gregory of Nazianzus addressed to Gregory of Nyssa, Basil of Caesarea's younger brother. It is usually dated to 372, soon after Basil had consecrated Nazianzen as bishop of Sasima, and was delivered when Gregory of Nyssa visited him. It opens with the praises of the faithful friend from Sirach 6 and welcomes the guest with warm, rhetorically rich praise, comparing him to biblical figures such as Moses and Aaron. It also touches on Nazianzen's unease about his recent consecration, and it reflects the close friendship among the Cappadocian Fathers.

Oration 12 is a short Greek discourse by Gregory of Nazianzus, delivered in 372 when he agreed to act as coadjutor to his aged father, Gregory the Elder, bishop of Nazianzus. Earlier that year Basil of Caesarea had consecrated him bishop of Sasima during his dispute with Anthimus of Tyana, but Gregory never took up that see. Here he gives himself to the Holy Spirit and accepts the new duties only provisionally, without being bound to the see. The oration documents his lasting reluctance about church office and his strong preference for a contemplative life.

Oration 13 is a short Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus, preached at the consecration of Eulalius as bishop of Doara, a town in Cappadocia. It is usually dated to about 372–373, when Gregory was helping his father, the bishop of Nazianzus. Gregory asks his hearers to accept his modest words as a thanksgiving to God. He praises God for calming the storms and conflicts that had troubled the community and for giving it a new shepherd. The address also gives Eulalius advice on his pastoral duties.

Oration 14, "On Love for the Poor," is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus. Its date and setting are disputed. It is usually placed between about 365 and 375 and is often linked to Basil of Caesarea's charitable foundation for the sick and needy. Gregory first ranks the virtues and gives love the highest place. He then urges his hearers to show mercy to the poor, especially lepers, whose suffering he describes vividly. It is one of the most important early Christian texts on care for the poor and on how wealth should be used.

Oration 15, "In Praise of the Maccabees", is a festal sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus. Its date and place of delivery are uncertain. It is usually placed in the 360s or early 370s, though some link it to Constantinople. Gregory praises the aged Eleazar, the seven brothers and their mother, who were martyred under Antiochus IV, drawing especially on 4 Maccabees. He argues that martyrs who suffered before Christ deserve Christian honour, since they could not have been perfected without faith in the Word. It is a key witness to the early Christian cult of the Maccabean martyrs.

Oration 16 is a sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus, usually dated to 373. He gave it at Nazianzus while serving as coadjutor to his father, Gregory the Elder. The town had suffered a cattle plague, then a drought, and finally a hailstorm that ruined the ripened crops. The aged bishop was too overwhelmed to preach, so his son spoke in his place, largely without preparation. He interprets the disasters as divine chastisement, calls the people to repentance and almsgiving, and asks why God allows such suffering. The text that survives may have been revised after delivery.

Oration 17 is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus, usually dated to about 373. It was given at Nazianzus in Cappadocia while Gregory was helping his elderly father, the town's bishop. The citizens were in great fear, and the provincial governor was angry with them after some public disturbance. The sermon opens with Jeremiah's lament, "My bowels, my bowels." Gregory urges the frightened townspeople to repent and trust in God. He then appeals to the governor to show mercy, reminding him that he too will answer to God.

Oration 18 is a Greek funeral speech by Gregory of Nazianzus for his father, Gregory the Elder, bishop of Nazianzus. The elder Gregory died in 374, in about his hundredth year. Gregory delivered the speech that year in front of his mother, Nonna, and Basil of Caesarea. It tells how his father moved from the sect of the Hypsistarians to Christianity under Nonna's influence, and praises his work as bishop, his orthodoxy and his family life. The speech is one of the main sources of what is known about the Hypsistarians.

Oration 19, addressed to Julian, an official responsible for equalising tax assessments, is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus. It is usually dated to about 374, when Gregory was helping his aged father in the church of Nazianzus. Gregory begins by explaining his earlier silence and his wish for a retired life given to contemplation. He then speaks to Julian, a friend, during a church festival, and asks him to carry out the tax census fairly and mercifully. The oration shows how Cappadocian bishops intervened with civil officials for their communities.

Oration 2 is a long apologetic discourse by Gregory of Nazianzus, written around 362–363 and probably never meant to be delivered aloud. In it Gregory explains why he fled to Pontus after his father, Gregory the Elder, ordained him priest at Nazianzus against his will. Defending his conduct leads him into a wider reflection on the priesthood. He describes the pastor as a physician of souls and stresses how hard and dangerous the work of spiritual direction is. The oration became a classic treatise on pastoral ministry and influenced John Chrysostom's On the Priesthood and Gregory the Great's Pastoral Rule.

Oration 20, known as "On Theology and the Appointment of Bishops", is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus, generally dated to about 379, when he was leading the small Nicene community in Constantinople. Gregory first criticises the "theologians" of his day who claim wisdom overnight or hold their office only by ordination. He insists that only a soul purified by long discipline and contemplation should take on church leadership or speak about God. He then sets out an orthodox account of the Trinity. The oration anticipates themes of his later Theological Orations.

Oration 21 is a panegyric by Gregory of Nazianzus praising Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria who died in 373. Gregory delivered it at Constantinople, probably on an annual feast of the saint, in 379 or more likely 380. In it he portrays Athanasius as a model bishop and a steadfast defender of Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism. He recounts Athanasius' life, his exiles and his struggles with emperors and with church councils such as those of Seleucia and Constantinople. The oration is often considered a classic example of the Christian ecclesiastical panegyric.

Oration 22, the second Oration on Peace, is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus. He preached it in Constantinople around 379–380, while leading the small Nicene community there. Its heading says it addresses strife that had broken out among the people over disputed questions. The speech opens with a lyrical address to "beloved Peace," which Gregory laments as lost, comparing his grief to Jacob mourning Joseph and David mourning Jonathan and Absalom. He pleads for concord among Christians and warns against breaking agreements made before God. It belongs to his series of three orations on peace.

The Third Oration on Peace (Oration 23) is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus. He delivered it in Constantinople around 379–380, while leading the small Nicene community there. It celebrates a reconciliation among believers of the same faith after a period of internal division. Gregory opens by contrasting zeal with the gentleness of the Spirit and with love that binds people together. He warns against judging one another harshly and closes with a statement of orthodox Trinitarian doctrine. Together with Orations 6 and 22, it forms his series of three discourses on peace.

Oration 24, "In Praise of Cyprian", is a panegyric by Gregory of Nazianzus, usually dated to 379 in Constantinople, where it was delivered on the martyr's feast. Gregory opens by greeting his congregation after a period of retreat and then praises Cyprian. He merges the story of Cyprian of Antioch, the magician converted through the virgin Justina, with the life and martyrdom of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. The speech shows the cult of martyrs in the late fourth century and Gregory's skill in the classical rhetoric of praise.

Oration 25 is a panegyric by Gregory of Nazianzus, given in Constantinople around 379–380 while he led the small Nicene community there. It praises a Christian philosopher of Cynic dress, honoured as a confessor who had returned from three years of exile for the faith. The man is generally identified with Maximus the Cynic. Soon afterwards Maximus tried to have himself made bishop of Constantinople in Gregory's place, and the name "Hero" in the title is thought to have replaced his. The speech presents Christian life as the true philosophy.

Oration 26 is a Greek oration by Gregory of Nazianzus, given in Constantinople around 380. Gregory had briefly left the city after the affair of Maximus the Cynic, who had been secretly consecrated bishop in an attempt to take his place. In this speech, delivered on his return, he tells his small Nicene congregation how much he missed them and contrasts the noise of city life with the quiet he values. He also reflects on his own conduct and on how a philosopher should bear injustice. The oration is an important source for his troubled time in Constantinople.

Oration 3 is a short Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus, usually dated to around Easter 362. Gregory's father, the bishop of Nazianzus, had ordained him a priest against his will. Gregory then withdrew to the solitude he preferred, but he returned to take up his duties. In this oration he reproaches the people of Nazianzus: they had pressed him to come back, yet few came to hear him. He contrasts their eagerness to have him with their indifference to his teaching. The speech belongs with his first orations, which reflect his reluctant start in pastoral ministry.

Oration 4 is the first of two invectives by Gregory of Nazianzus against the emperor Julian, known in Christian tradition as the Apostate. It was written soon after Julian's death on the Persian campaign in June 363, probably in 363 or 364. Gregory celebrates the tyrant's fall and attacks his return to paganism and his measures against Christians, especially the edict barring Christians from teaching classical literature. He also defends the Christian claim to Greek learning and eloquence. Together with Oration 5, it is a major Christian response to Julian's reign and an important example of late antique polemical rhetoric.

The Second Invective against Julian is a Greek oration by Gregory of Nazianzus, written soon after the emperor Julian's death in 363, probably in 363 or 364. It follows the first invective (Oration 4) and moves from Julian's misdeeds to the judgments of God. Gregory narrates the failed attempt to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, Julian's disastrous Persian campaign and his death, and recalls the young Julian he had known as a student at Athens. Together the two orations form an important Christian polemical response to Julian's pagan revival.

The First Oration on Peace (Oration 6) is a Greek speech by Gregory of Nazianzus, usually dated to about 363–364. Gregory gave it at Nazianzus in the presence of his father, Bishop Gregory the Elder, to mark the end of a schism. Monks of the town had broken communion with the elder Gregory after he accepted a doctrinally compromising creed. Gregory explains why he stayed silent during the division, then praises peace and the unity of the Body of Christ. He warns that schism among Christians does the devil's work.

Gregory of Nazianzus gave this funeral oration for his younger brother Caesarius, a physician, probably in 369. In it he recounts Caesarius's studies at Alexandria, his medical career at the court of Constantius, and how he resisted Julian's efforts to turn him from Christianity. He then covers Caesarius's later service as a treasury official in Bithynia and his early death. The speech joins the classical Greek funeral speech with Christian consolation and reflections on how short human life is. It is the main source for Caesarius's life, and Jerome placed it first among Gregory's orations.

Gregory of Nazianzus gave this Greek funeral oration for his sister Gorgonia. Its exact date is uncertain. It came after the death of their brother Caesarius in 369 and before their father's death in 374. It was probably delivered in the city where she had lived her married life with her husband Alypius, traditionally said to be Iconium. Gregory praises her modesty, generosity, prayer and self-discipline as a married woman. He also describes her healing from illness and her peaceful death. The speech is an important portrait of a Christian laywoman and a source for the life of Gregory's family.

Oration 9, the Apologeticus ad patrem, is a short Greek speech by Gregory of Nazianzus, usually dated to 372. Gregory delivered it before his father, Gregory the Elder, bishop of Nazianzus, and Basil of Caesarea, who had just made him bishop of the small town of Sasima against his will. Opening with "Again unction and the Spirit upon me," he compares his reluctance to the awe of Isaiah, Manoah and Peter before God. The speech shows his deep unease about holding church office.

This is the miscellaneous material in volume 35 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the first volume of the works of Gregory of Nazianzus, the fourth-century Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It is not a single work. It brings together editorial front matter, prefaces, annotations and short pieces that are not catalogued separately. Much of it comments on Gregory's orations, for example those about his consecration as bishop of Sasima. The notes quote his autobiographical poems, mix Greek and Latin, and come from various hands and periods.

This short Greek text is falsely attributed to Gregory of Nazianzus, "the Theologian". It presents itself as a fragment from a speech against astronomers, and it is grouped with a piece titled On the Orthodox Faith. Its author and date are unknown. The surviving passage explains death in physiological terms. When the heat of the blood fails, the soul separates from the body, which is why births and deaths happen most often at night. It then describes the body's four elements separating after death, so that the reader can hold firm to the teaching on the resurrection.

The Liturgy of Saint Gregory is a Greek eucharistic liturgy traditionally attributed to Gregory of Nazianzus, though the attribution is generally regarded as pseudonymous. Its date and place of origin are uncertain; estimates fall roughly between the fifth and eighth centuries, and the text is usually linked with Egypt or Syria. Unusually, most of its anaphora is addressed to Christ rather than to the Father. A form of it remains in use in the Coptic Orthodox Church alongside the liturgies of Basil and Cyril.

The Metaphrasis in Ecclesiasten is a Greek paraphrase of the biblical book of Ecclesiastes, attributed to Gregory Thaumaturgus, the third-century bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus and a pupil of Origen. It was probably written between about 240 and 270. The work restates the sayings of Solomon in clearer, more continuous prose and draws out their moral and spiritual meaning for Christian readers. Some manuscripts attribute it to Gregory of Nazianzus, but Jerome assigns it to Thaumaturgus, and most scholars accept his attribution. It is an early example of Christian biblical paraphrase.
