Oration 27 is the first of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople in 380, while he led the small Nicene community there. It serves as an introduction to the series and is aimed at the Eunomians, radical Arians known for their skill in dialectic. Gregory does not yet discuss the Trinity itself. Instead he asks who may speak about God, when, before whom and how far, arguing that theology requires purity of life, quiet and restraint rather than clever debate.

Oration 28 is the second of the five Theological Orations by Gregory of Nazianzus. He preached them in Constantinople around 380, when he led the small Nicene community there against the Eunomians, who claimed that God's essence could be fully known. The first oration set out who may practise theology and under what conditions. This one argues that God's nature cannot be grasped by the human mind. Using the image of Moses on Sinai seeing only God's "back parts", Gregory shows that creation reveals that God exists, not what God is. The work is a classic statement of divine incomprehensibility.

The third of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople around 380 against the Eunomians and other Arian groups. After setting out the monarchy of the Father, Gregory defends the full divinity of the Son. He argues that the Son is eternally begotten without time or passion, and answers his opponents' arguments from the terms "begotten" and "unbegotten." The oration closes with a set of antitheses contrasting Christ's human lowliness with his divine glory. Oration 30 continues the argument with a fuller treatment of the disputed passages of Scripture.

Oration 30 is the fourth of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus delivered in Constantinople around 380 against the Eunomians and other Arians. It is his second discourse on the Son. Gregory answers, one by one, the scriptural texts his opponents used to make the Son subordinate, such as "The Lord created me" (Proverbs 8:22) and "the Father is greater than I." He assigns the exalted expressions to Christ's divinity and the lowly ones to his assumed humanity. The oration ends with a discussion of the titles of the Son.

Oration 31 is the last of the five Theological Orations that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople, probably in 380, against the Eunomians and the Pneumatomachi, who denied that the Holy Spirit is fully divine. Gregory openly calls the Spirit God and consubstantial with the Father and the Son. He separates the Spirit's procession from the Son's generation and answers the objection that Scripture is silent on the matter with a theory of progressive revelation. The oration was an important statement of Cappadocian Trinitarian theology shortly before the Council of Constantinople of 381.

Oration 32, On Moderation in Disputation (also called On Good Order in Discussions), is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus. He delivered it in Constantinople around 379–380, while leading the small Nicene community there. Gregory calls himself a poor and humble shepherd and urges a congregation torn by faction and quarrelsome debate to keep to order, restraint and humility. He argues that not everyone may speak about God, and not on every occasion. The sermon belongs to his effort to restore peace and orthodox teaching in the capital, and it is closely related in theme to his Theological Orations.

Oration 33 is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus. He delivered it at Constantinople, probably around 380, while leading the small Nicene congregation there at a time when the Arians held the city's churches. Gregory replies to opponents who mocked his flock for its poverty and small numbers, and who measured the Church by its size. He defends his own conduct and character and argues that true faith is not judged by numbers. He closes by affirming the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity. The speech mixes personal apology with polemic against the Arians.

Oration 34 is a sermon Gregory of Nazianzus preached at Constantinople in 380, during his leadership of the city's small Nicene community at the Anastasia church. It welcomes Egyptian sailors, probably crews of the grain fleet, who passed the many Arian-held churches to worship with Gregory. They came shortly after Peter of Alexandria's envoys had tried to consecrate the intruder Maximus in Gregory's place. Gregory praises Egypt and its Christian heritage, seeks reconciliation with Alexandria, and restates the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity.

This Greek sermon, "On the Martyrs and against the Arians", has come down among the orations of Gregory of Nazianzus as Oration 35. It is generally regarded as spurious, and its author and date are unknown. The preacher celebrates a festival of the martyrs, whose honours had long been neglected. The city, once a "mother of martyrs", now sees priests gather and spiritual festivities return. He attributes to the martyrs the end of strife and the scattering of the heresy, meaning Arianism, like a mist.

Oration 36 is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus, usually dated to around 380, during his time leading the Nicene community in Constantinople. In it Gregory answers critics who said he wanted the city's episcopal throne. He denies any personal ambition, plays down his own wisdom and eloquence, and says he did not bring the people a new teaching. Instead, he claims to follow Alexander of Constantinople, the bishop who had resisted Arius. The oration shows the church politics of the city in the years before the Council of 381.

Oration 37 is a sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus, preached in Constantinople around 380 during his time as bishop there. It is his only surviving exegetical homily, a commentary on Matthew 19:1–12. Gregory starts from Christ's humility in becoming "all things to all men" and then turns to the Pharisees' question about divorce. He defends the permanence of marriage and condemns the unequal civil laws that punished women's adultery while excusing men's. He also praises virginity and celibacy as a higher calling, with brief remarks on Trinitarian doctrine.

Oration 38 is a festal sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus, preached in Constantinople around the end of 380, during his brief time leading the church there. Scholars disagree whether it was delivered on 25 December 380 or 6 January 381, since "Theophany" could mean either Christmas or Epiphany. It opens with the words "Christ is born, glorify Him" and reflects on the Incarnation, the creation and fall of humanity, and God becoming human for our salvation. It is one of the earliest witnesses to the Christmas feast in the East.

Oration 39, "On the Holy Lights", is a festal sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus. He preached it in Constantinople on the Feast of the Epiphany (Theophany), usually dated to 6 January 381, and Oration 40 on Baptism followed the next day. The feast was then known as the "Holy Lights" because baptism was called illumination. The sermon reflects on Christ's baptism in the Jordan, sets out a Trinitarian theology of God as light and lists five kinds of baptism: those of Moses, John and Jesus, baptism by martyrdom and baptism by tears.

Oration 40 is a Greek sermon on baptism by Gregory of Nazianzus. He preached it at Constantinople during the Epiphany festival, the day after Oration 39 on the Holy Lights. It is usually dated to January 381, though some scholars prefer 380. Gregory distinguishes three births: natural birth, birth by baptism and birth by resurrection. He describes baptism as illumination and explains its benefits, and he strongly urges his hearers not to put it off. The oration ends with a confession of Trinitarian faith. It is one of the most important early Christian treatises on the sacrament.

Oration 41 is a festal sermon for Pentecost by Gregory of Nazianzus. He delivered it at Constantinople while he led the Nicene community there, between 379 and 381. The exact year is uncertain, though the Benedictine editors favoured 381. Gregory first compares how Jews, pagans and Christians keep their feasts. He then reflects on the mystical meaning of the number seven. His main theme is the full divinity of the Holy Spirit, defended against the Macedonians. Here he uses arguments different from those of his Fifth Theological Oration (Oration 31) on the same subject.

Oration 42 is the farewell speech of Gregory of Nazianzus, given in Constantinople in 381 during the First Council of Constantinople. Gregory was archbishop of the city and had been presiding over the council. Opposition from some bishops, including challenges to whether his appointment was legitimate, led him to resign. Speaking before the assembled bishops and his own congregation, he defends his ministry with restraint and recalls how he rebuilt the city's small Nicene community. He restates his Trinitarian faith and takes a moving leave of his church. It is a key source on the council and on Gregory's life.

Oration 43 is the funeral oration of Gregory of Nazianzus for his close friend Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, who died in 379. Illness and his duties at Constantinople kept Gregory from the funeral. He most likely delivered the speech after returning to Cappadocia in 381 or 382, though the exact date and occasion are uncertain. The longest of his orations, it surveys Basil's family, their shared studies at Athens, his ascetic life, charity, resistance to the Arian emperor Valens and teaching. It joins classical encomium with Christian praise and is a key source for Basil's life.

Oration 44, "On New Sunday", is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nazianzus for the Sunday after Easter, the feast of renewal. It is usually dated to about 383, after Gregory returned from Constantinople to Cappadocia. The sermon begins with the ancient custom of celebrating dedications, or "encaenia", and draws on Old Testament examples such as the tabernacle and David's kingship. It calls on believers to renew their souls in Christ. The oration is admired for its rhetorical skill, especially its long description of spring as an image of the resurrection.

Oration 45 is an Easter sermon in Greek by Gregory of Nazianzus. It is usually regarded as his last oration and is often dated to about 383, after he had retired to his estate at Arianzus near Nazianzus. It opens in biblical style with the watch of Habakkuk and the Angel of the Resurrection. Gregory then reads the ancient Passover allegorically, applying each of its details to Christ and the Christian life. Two passages repeat his Oration 38, on the Nativity, word for word. Byzantine readers knew the oration well and used it in the liturgy.

Three sets of Greek scholia on the orations of Gregory of Nazianzus are gathered here. The first is the "Collection and Explanation of Histories" attributed to Pseudo-Nonnus, a 6th-century commentator. It explains the mythological and historical allusions in four orations, beginning with the first invective against Julian. Next come the scholia of Basil the Minor (Basil Minimus), a 10th-century bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, followed by anonymous notes. The Pseudo-Nonnus commentary circulated widely and was translated into Syriac, Armenian and Georgian.

The Significatio in Ezechielem ("Meaning of Ezekiel") is a short Greek exegetical piece handed down among the works of Gregory of Nazianzus, though it is generally regarded as spurious. Its author and date are unknown. It reads the opening vision of Ezekiel allegorically. The four living creatures stand for the parts of the soul: the man is reason, the lion the spirited part, the calf desire, and the eagle conscience. The enthroned figure, spirit and cloud are taken as the Trinity. The piece also cites the alternative Greek renderings of Symmachus and Aquila.

This is a group of Greek poems by Gregory of Nazianzus, probably written in his retirement after leaving Constantinople in 381 and before his death around 390. In the traditional arrangement of his verse, they form the second section of the historical poems: pieces addressed to or about other people. Most are verse epistles of moral advice in classical metres and Homeric diction. They include an exchange between Nicobulus and his son on the value of education, and a poem to Olympias on how a Christian wife should live.

The Carmina de se ipso ("Poems about himself") are the autobiographical section of Gregory of Nazianzus's historical poems, conventionally numbered II.1. Most were written after he left Constantinople in 381 and retired to Cappadocia. The group contains about a hundred Greek poems in classical metres. They include prayers, laments over illness and old age, attacks on his enemies and reflections on his career. The best known is the long iambic De vita sua (II.1.11). Together they are a major source for his life and an early landmark of Christian autobiographical poetry.

This short Greek poem by Gregory of Nazianzus belongs to his dogmatic poems (Carmina dogmatica). It was probably written during his retirement in Cappadocia in the 380s. It warns readers against "malignant writings" and lists the books of Scripture to be read. Gregory counts twenty-two Old Testament books, matching the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and leaves out Esther and the deuterocanonical books. His New Testament list names the four Gospels, Acts, fourteen Pauline and seven Catholic epistles, but not Revelation. The poem is an important witness to how the biblical canon developed in the fourth-century Greek East.

The Carmina moralia ("Moral Poems") are a group of Greek poems by Gregory of Nazianzus. In the standard arrangement of his verse they form the second section of Book I, the theological poems. Most were probably written during his retirement in Cappadocia after he left Constantinople in 381. They are in classical metres, chiefly hexameters and elegiac couplets, and deal with Christian ethics and the ascetic life. The collection opens with a long poem in praise of virginity and also includes poems on virtue, human nature and the passions, and on the vanity of worldly life.

This is the collected Greek correspondence of Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390), written mostly between the 360s and his death. Gregory himself assembled a selection of his letters for his young relative Nicobulus and offered him advice on epistolary style. The letters include warm and sometimes teasing exchanges with Basil of Caesarea, personal and administrative business, and polished rhetorical pieces. The most influential are the two letters to the priest Cledonius (Epp. 101–102). They argue against Apollinarianism with the principle that "what has not been assumed has not been healed", and later councils cited them as authoritative Christology.

The Testament is the will of Gregory of Nazianzus, written in Greek in 381, while he was still bishop of the catholic Church of Constantinople. It follows the legal form of a Roman will. It is dated by the consuls of the year and was witnessed and signed by several bishops. In it Gregory leaves his property to the church of Nazianzus for the care of the poor and makes personal bequests to relatives, friends and dependants. It is a rare surviving will of a fourth-century bishop and gives evidence on church property, Christian charity and Roman inheritance practice.

The Epitaphs and Epigrams form a large group of short Greek poems by Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390), written mostly in elegiac couplets. Many probably date from his last years in Cappadocia, though the date of individual pieces is uncertain. They commemorate family and friends, including his brother Caesarius, his parents Gregory the Elder and Nonna, his sister Gorgonia, Basil of Caesarea and the Athenian sophist Prohaeresius. A long series also denounces tomb-robbers. The collection makes up Book VIII of the Greek Anthology and is an important example of Christian epigram in classical form.

This is a group of Greek poems by Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390), the Cappadocian Father and briefly archbishop of Constantinople, gathered under the name of the nineteenth-century philologist Dronke, who published them. Most likely they were written in Gregory's retirement after 381. The material centres on the Poemata Arcana, his hexameter poems on first principles, the Son, the Holy Spirit, the world, providence and rational beings. It comes with a Byzantine prose commentary explaining these difficult theological verses, and the commentator's identity is uncertain. These poems are a key source for Gregory's Trinitarian thought in verse.

Christus patiens ("Christ Suffering") is a Greek religious drama of about 2,600 verses on the Passion, Burial and Resurrection of Christ. Manuscripts attribute it to Gregory of Nazianzus, but its authorship and date are disputed. Many scholars place it in the Byzantine period, around the eleventh or twelfth century, while others argue for an earlier date. It is a cento: much of it is built from lines adapted from Euripides and other tragedians. The Virgin Mary is the chief speaker and mourns her Son. It is a rare surviving example of Christian drama in the classical tragic manner.

This Greek commentary collects and explains the historical, biblical and mythological stories that Gregory of Nazianzus alludes to in his poems. The title presents it as drawn "from the divinely inspired Scripture and from the outside poets and historians." It is attributed to "Cosmas of Jerusalem," who is traditionally identified with the eighth-century hymnographer Cosmas of Maiuma. That identification has been questioned. Written as a learned aid for readers of Gregory's verse, the work shows how classical and scriptural knowledge was taught in Byzantium.

This short Byzantine Greek paraphrase explains Gregory of Nazianzus's poem on the canonical books of Scripture, which lists the books of the Old and New Testaments to be read and warns against spurious writings. It quotes each verse of Gregory's hexameters and follows it with a simpler prose rendering and brief explanations, for example of how the four books of Kingdoms are counted as two. The heading attributes it to the "philosopher" Niketas David, an interpreter of Gregory's poems, though the attribution is uncertain. It probably dates from between the seventh and tenth centuries.

The Erotapokriseis ("Questions and Answers") is a Greek collection of questions with answers, arranged in four dialogues. Tradition ascribed it to Caesarius, the physician brother of Gregory of Nazianzus, who died in 368 or 369. Scholars now agree it is a pseudonymous work of the sixth century, usually dated to about 540–560. Its anonymous author covers a wide range of subjects: the Trinity and Christology, problems in biblical interpretation, cosmology and natural phenomena, and arguments against pagans, astrology and heresies. It is a valuable witness to the encyclopedic question-and-answer literature of the early Byzantine period.

This is a collection of the Greek writings of Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium from about 373 until his death in the 390s or early 400s, and a close associate of Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus. It brings together homilies, a synodal letter on the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and fragments of lost works, mostly from the controversies with the Arians, Eunomians and Macedonians. Some pieces are of doubtful authenticity. Among these is a legendary narrative of Amphilochius' call to the episcopate and his struggle against those heretics.

Contra Manichaeos (Against the Manichaeans) is a short Greek polemical treatise attributed to Didymus the Blind, the Alexandrian teacher who died around 398. Its date is uncertain. It argues philosophically against the Manichaean teaching of two opposed, unbegotten principles of good and evil, light and darkness. The treatise holds that contraries must share something prior to their opposition, such as substance and existence, so neither principle can truly be unbegotten. It is one of the few works of Didymus to survive in Greek.

De Trinitate is a Greek dogmatic treatise in three books on the Holy Trinity, traditionally attributed to Didymus the Blind of Alexandria. Its authorship has been disputed by modern scholars. It was probably written in the 380s or early 390s, after the Council of Constantinople. The work defends the full divinity and consubstantiality of the Son and the Holy Spirit against Arian and Pneumatomachian opponents. It relies heavily on scriptural proof-texts and is an important witness to late fourth-century Nicene Trinitarian theology.

This collection gathers fragments of lost works by Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), the Alexandrian teacher. They survive mainly as excerpts in exegetical catenae. Didymus was associated with Origen, and after Origen's condemnation in 553 his writings largely stopped being copied. The fragments are mostly short comments on biblical passages, beginning with Genesis. In them Didymus explains the creation of the luminaries through number symbolism and reads the thorns of the curse as bodily pleasures and cares. They are an important witness to his allegorical exegesis.

This is a miscellaneous grouping of material from volume 39 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca: front matter, editorial notes and shorter pieces not catalogued as separate works. The volume chiefly gathers Greek writers of the later fourth century, among them Didymus the Blind and Amphilochius of Iconium. The opening passage is a Greek note on the Iambics to Seleucus. It says the poem reflects the mind of Gregory the Theologian but was written by Amphilochius, the friend of Basil the Great. The authorship of the poem is still debated.

These five Greek homilies are by Asterius of Amasea, a former lawyer who became bishop of Amasea in Pontus in the late fourth century. They were probably preached between about 380 and 410, and they are moral sermons rather than doctrinal ones. The first takes the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus (Luke 16) as its starting point and attacks the waste and luxury of the wealthy. Asterius preached in a lively style and paid close attention to everyday customs, so his sermons are valued as evidence for social life and attitudes in late antique Asia Minor.

This is a collection of Greek ascetic writings by Evagrius Ponticus (345–399), the monk who lived in the Egyptian desert at Nitria and Kellia. It includes the Capita practica (Praktikos), whose prologue, addressed to Anatolius, explains the symbolism of the Egyptian monastic habit, and which analyses the eight evil thoughts. It also includes collections of sayings (Sententiae) and the Rerum monachalium rationes, on the foundations of the solitary life. Written in the 380s and 390s, these short texts shaped Eastern and Western monastic spirituality, partly through John Cassian.

This is a small group of Greek theological writings attributed to "the blessed Jerome." The author is an obscure Byzantine writer known as Jerome the Greek, who is not the same person as Jerome of Stridon. His date is uncertain and is usually placed between the seventh and ninth centuries. The main piece is a question-and-answer dialogue in which a Christian answers a Jew's objection that worshipping Father, Son and Holy Spirit contradicts God's oneness. Shorter texts follow, including one on the effects of baptism.

The Capita de ascesi et quiete ("Chapters on Asceticism and Stillness") is a short Greek collection of numbered sayings attributed to Abba Isaiah. He was a fifth-century monk who moved from Scetis in Egypt to the region of Gaza and died in the late 480s or around 490. Many chapters are built on sets of three virtues. They teach discernment, humility, obedience, forgiveness of those who do wrong, and restraint in eating. They also tell the monk to spend his time in the cell on handiwork, meditation and prayer. The collection belongs to the tradition of desert spirituality and hesychasm.

De natura hominis (On Human Nature) is a Greek treatise written around 390–400 by Nemesius, bishop of Emesa in Syria. It tries to build a Christian account of the human person from philosophy and medicine. It describes man as a rational soul joined to a body and as a link that binds together the whole of creation. Drawing on Plato, Aristotle, Plotinus and Galen, it covers the soul, the senses and mental faculties, the passions, free will and providence. The work was widely read in later Greek, Latin, Arabic and Armenian thought.

This is a set of miscellaneous material from volume 40 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca: front matter, editorial notes, prefaces and short pieces that are not indexed as separate works. Most of it is Greek with Latin translation and commentary. The surviving opening deals with Philo, bishop of Carpasia in Cyprus, whom Epiphanius is said to have ordained after a divine revelation. It also covers Philo's commentary on the Song of Songs and catena fragments, including those in the commentary on Luke compiled by Nicetas the deacon. The pieces have no single author or date.

This is a collection of monastic precepts and short writings from the Pachomian communities of Upper Egypt, attributed to Pachomius (d. 348), founder of cenobitic monasticism, and to his successors Horsiesi and Theodore. The Greek precepts are excerpts from the Pachomian Rule. They regulate everyday community life: going to the synaxis and praying there, silence and conduct at meals, care for sick brothers, and the admission of new monks. Together with Jerome's Latin version, these texts are an important witness to the earliest organised communal monasticism.

The Enarratio in Canticum canticorum is a Greek commentary on the Song of Songs by Philo, bishop of Carpasia in Cyprus, who was ordained by Epiphanius of Salamis in the late fourth century. Addressed to the presbyter Eustathius and the deacon Eusebius, it reads the Song allegorically. It begins by comparing the title "Song of Songs" with "Holy of Holies" and "Sabbath of Sabbaths", arguing that the book holds a deeper spiritual meaning and that readers must turn away from fleshly thoughts. It is Philo's principal surviving work and a witness to Cypriot exegesis around 400.

This is a short Greek chapter from the Amphilochia, the collection of questions and answers on theology and scholarship by Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople (858–867, 877–886). It asks how many men named Asterius there were and what each believed. Photius separates the Arian sophist Asterius from an orthodox contemporary of the same name, a monk taught by Julian Saba who later headed a monastery. He also argues that the author of the ekphrasis on the martyr Euphemia, Asterius of Amasea, was not the Arian.

This is a collection of the Greek writings of Serapion of Thmuis, a fourth-century Egyptian monk and bishop who was a disciple of Antony and an ally of Athanasius. It was probably written around the middle of the century. The main work is a treatise against the Manichaeans, which defends the goodness of creation and of the body against Manichaean dualism. The collection also contains letters, among them a letter praising monks for giving up worldly ties to seek God. These writings show the ascetic and anti-heretical concerns of Egyptian Christianity in Athanasius's time.

This is a short exchange of Greek letters from about 374–377 that stands at the head of the Panarion of Epiphanius of Salamis. Acacius and Paul, presbyters and heads of monasteries in Syria, wrote to Epiphanius praising him as a new apostle. They sent their letter with Marcellus, a recently instructed member of their community, and asked for his teaching on the heresies. Epiphanius's reply answers this request. The exchange explains why the Panarion, his great catalogue and refutation of eighty heresies, was written. Acacius later became bishop of Beroea.

This is editorial and supplementary material gathered in volume 41 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the volume that opens the works of Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310/20–403), bishop of Constantia in Cyprus. It includes front matter, notes and shorter pieces not indexed separately. Among them are catalogues of writings attributed to Epiphanius, both genuine and spurious. The genuine works include the Panarion against eighty heresies. Spurious or doubtful items include the Physiologus, a treatise on the prophets and writings against images. There are also ancient testimonies to his life, such as Sozomen's report of miracles at his tomb.

The Panarion ("medicine chest"), later known in Latin as Adversus haereses, is a Greek treatise against heresies by Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis (Constantia) in Cyprus. He began it around 374–375 at the request of the Syrian archimandrites Acacius and Paul and finished it about three years later. It describes and refutes eighty sects and schools of thought, from the time of Adam to the late fourth century. The work preserves many otherwise lost documents and reports, including fragments of Jewish-Christian gospels such as the Gospel of the Ebionites.

This Greek hagiographical Life tells the story of Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia (Salamis) in Cyprus, who died in 403. It claims to be written by John, a disciple of Epiphanius, and an appendix is attributed to Polybius, bishop of Rhinocorura. Both attributions are generally considered pseudonymous, and the date of composition is uncertain. It probably falls somewhere between the fifth and eighth centuries. The narrative is largely legendary. It covers Epiphanius's humble birth in Phoenicia, his early life, his miracles and his career as a monk and bishop. It is an important witness to how his memory was later venerated.

This is the closing part of the Panarion ("Medicine Chest"), the great treatise against heresies by Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis (Constantia) in Cyprus, written in Greek around 374–377. It covers heresies 65 to 80, mostly fourth-century movements. Among them are Paul of Samosata, the Manichaeans, the Hieracites, the Melitians, the Arians, the Photinians, the Pneumatomachi, the Anomoeans, the Apollinarians, the Antidicomarianites, the Collyridians and the Massalians. To each heresy Epiphanius offers an "antidote" in the form of a refutation. The work ends with the Expositio fidei (De fide), a summary of the orthodox faith of the catholic Church.

The Ancoratus ("The Well-Anchored") is a Greek doctrinal treatise by Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia (Salamis) in Cyprus. He wrote it around 374 at the request of presbyters in Syedra in Pamphylia, whose letters stand at its beginning. It explains Christian teaching from Scripture and tradition: the consubstantiality of the Trinity, the full incarnation of Christ, and the resurrection and judgment. It argues against pagans, Jews and heretics, and lists the eighty heresies that Epiphanius later treated in the Panarion. It ends with two creeds, one of which closely resembles the creed associated with the Council of Constantinople of 381.

De XII gemmis ("On the Twelve Stones") is a treatise by Epiphanius of Salamis, bishop in Cyprus, usually dated to about 394. It is addressed to a Diodore, generally identified as Diodore of Tarsus, and discusses the twelve gems set in the breastplate of the high priest Aaron (Exodus 28). For each stone it gives the name, colour, place of origin, medicinal uses, the tribe of Israel it represents, and a spiritual interpretation. The Greek survives only in part, but early translations, notably in Latin, Georgian and Armenian, preserve fuller versions.

On Weights and Measures is a treatise compiled in 392 at Constantia on Cyprus by Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis, reportedly at the request of a Persian priest. It is meant as an aid to reading Scripture. It covers the critical signs used in biblical manuscripts, the Greek translations of the Old Testament from the Septuagint to Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, and biblical weights and measures, along with some geography. Only fragments of the Greek survive. The complete text is preserved in Syriac, with partial Armenian and Georgian versions.

De vitis prophetarum is a Greek recension of the Lives of the Prophets, a collection of short notices on the Hebrew prophets. In the manuscripts it is ascribed to Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, but the attribution is spurious. Its date is uncertain and is often placed between the fifth and sixth centuries. Each entry gives a prophet's tribe and home town, some legendary details of his life, and how and where he died and was buried. The work's underlying tradition, which may be of early Jewish origin, matters for the history of tomb veneration and biblical legend.

This is a group of shorter Greek writings by Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, from the 390s. The tract On the Seventy Translators retells the legend of the Septuagint. In it, Ptolemy II Philadelphus founds the Alexandrian library, asks Jerusalem for the Hebrew Scriptures and pairs seventy-two translators in separate cells. The account is closely related to Epiphanius's On Weights and Measures. With it are two letters written during the Origenist controversy, one to Bishop John of Jerusalem and one to Jerome. Both survive among Jerome's correspondence in Latin translation.

This Greek homily for Holy Saturday, on the burial of Christ's body, has come down under the name of Epiphanius of Salamis. It is generally regarded as the work of a later anonymous preacher, and its date is uncertain, perhaps between the fifth and ninth centuries. It opens by mocking the defeat of those who plotted against Christ. It then contrasts the old Passover, now coming to an end, with Christ's new one, and proclaims his descent into Hades to raise those who had long slept. The homily was popular in Byzantine tradition and was translated into Church Slavonic.

The Paraphrase of the Gospel of John, often called the Metabole, is a retelling of the Fourth Gospel in Greek dactylic hexameters. It is attributed to Nonnus of Panopolis, the Egyptian poet who also wrote the Dionysiaca, and was probably composed in the mid-fifth century. It has twenty-one books, one for each chapter of John. It follows the gospel closely but expands it with Homeric diction and ornament. It is a major example of late antique Christian epic poetry. Scholars still debate how it relates to the Dionysiaca and which of the two came first.

This is a group of Greek writings falsely attributed to Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia (Salamis) in Cyprus, who died in 403. The main piece, On the Mysteries of Numbers, opens with short definitions of faith and of the Trinity. It then lists the persons, objects and events that Scripture groups in threes and other numbers, treating each number as a sign of divine mystery. With it go several homilies carried under Epiphanius's name. The real authors and dates are unknown; the pieces were probably written between the fifth and ninth centuries.

This short Greek treatise on what it means for humanity to be made "in the image of God and in his likeness" (Genesis 1:26) has come down among the works of Gregory of Nyssa, but it is generally regarded as spurious. Its author and date are uncertain. It opens with the image of a clear mirror and calls human creation a hidden mystery. It presents the human being as a mixed world, linking the invisible spiritual creation with the visible material world made of four elements. It then explores how human nature reflects its divine archetype.

Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, wrote these eight Greek homilies on the Beatitudes of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:3–10). Their exact date is uncertain, though they belong to his years as bishop in the later fourth century. Gregory treats the Beatitudes as a ladder of ascent, rising from the lowly ground of thought to the "mountain" of contemplation. Each homily explains one blessing as a step in growing virtue and likeness to God. The sixth homily, on purity of heart and seeing God, is especially influential in Christian mystical theology.

On the Making of Man (De hominis opificio) is a Greek theological treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, written around 379, soon after the death of his brother Basil of Caesarea. Gregory sent it to his brother Peter as an Easter gift and meant it to complete Basil's homilies on the Hexaemeron, which had not dealt with the creation of humanity. It discusses humanity as made in the image of God, the relation of soul and body, the passions, and the resurrection. It is a foundational work of Christian anthropology. In the sixth century Dionysius Exiguus translated it into Latin.

The Homilies on the Lord's Prayer are five sermons in Greek by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. They were written in the later fourth century, though the exact date is uncertain. The first homily argues that prayer is necessary at all, against people who put business and daily affairs ahead of it. The remaining homilies go through the Our Father petition by petition, combining moral exhortation with theological reflection on God as Father, the kingdom, daily bread and forgiveness. They are among the most important early Greek commentaries on the Lord's Prayer.

The Life of Moses, or On Perfection in Virtue, is a spiritual treatise by Gregory of Nyssa. He wrote it late in life, probably in the early 390s, after a younger friend asked him for advice on the perfect life. The work has two parts: a retelling of the life of Moses based on Exodus and Numbers, followed by an allegorical reading of its spiritual meaning. Gregory describes perfection as endless progress in virtue toward the infinite God. His account of Moses entering the divine darkness on Sinai deeply influenced later Christian mystical theology.

The Homilies on the Song of Songs are fifteen sermons by Gregory of Nyssa, one of the Cappadocian Fathers, written late in his life, probably in the early 390s. They were dedicated to the deaconess Olympias of Constantinople, who had asked for them. The prologue defends allegorical reading against those who held to the literal sense alone. The homilies read the Song as the soul's endless ascent toward God, an idea later called epektasis. They are central to Gregory's mystical theology and shaped later Christian contemplative exegesis.

The Homilies on Ecclesiastes are eight sermons by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. They were written in the later fourth century, though the exact date is uncertain. The homilies interpret Ecclesiastes 1:1 to 3:13. Gregory reads the book as a guide that leads the soul away from attachment to passing, material things and toward contemplation of God. The fourth homily is especially well known. Commenting on the acquisition of slaves (Ecclesiastes 2:7), Gregory condemns slavery itself as an offence against human nature and against God. It is one of the earliest known outright condemnations of the practice.

The Explicatio apologetica in Hexaemeron, also called the Apology on the Hexaemeron, is a Greek treatise by Gregory of Nyssa. He addressed it to his brother Peter, later bishop of Sebaste, and probably wrote it around 379, soon after the death of their brother Basil of Caesarea. At Peter's request, Gregory defends and supplements Basil's Homilies on the Hexaemeron. He tries to resolve apparent contradictions in the Genesis account of the six days of creation. In doing so he argues that God created all things at once in potential, and that they then unfolded in an ordered sequence.

This short exegetical treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, dates from the late fourth century. Its exact date is uncertain. It explains 1 Corinthians 15:28, "then the Son himself will also be subjected." Arian and Eunomian opponents used this verse to argue that the Son is inferior to the Father. Gregory answers that the subjection refers to humanity, which forms Christ's body. When all evil is removed and every creature is united to God, God becomes "all in all." The work is an important witness to Gregory's teaching on universal restoration.

On the Inscriptions of the Psalms is a Greek exegetical treatise in two books by Gregory of Nyssa. It was written at the request of an unnamed "man of God", probably during his years as bishop, though the exact date is uncertain. The first book considers the aim of the whole Psalter, which Gregory identifies as blessedness. He reads the five divisions of the book as stages in the soul's ascent through virtue toward likeness to God. The second book interprets the psalm titles themselves. The work is an important example of Gregory's spiritual, Origenist-influenced approach to Scripture.

De hominis structura is a pair of Greek homilies on the creation of humankind, based on Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man in our image". They present themselves as paying an old debt by completing Basil of Caesarea's Hexaemeron, which ends before reaching the creation of man. Manuscripts attribute them to Basil or to Gregory of Nyssa, and their authorship is still disputed. They discuss the image and likeness of God, human dominion over creation and the formation of the body. They give an early Cappadocian account of human nature.

This is a collection of introductory and supplementary material, not a single work. It belongs with the writings of Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian who was active about 370 to 395. It includes a bibliographical notice that lists Gregory's writings with their Greek titles, opening words and remarks on authenticity and manuscripts. Among the works it names are On the Making of Man, the Explanation of the Hexaemeron, the Life of Moses, Against Fate, Against Eunomius and On "Not Three Gods". There are also editorial notes and short pieces that were not catalogued separately.

On "Not Three Gods" is a short Greek theological treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, written as a letter to a younger correspondent named Ablabius. Its exact date is uncertain. Ablabius had asked why, if Peter, James and John share one human nature and are called three men, Father, Son and Holy Spirit should not be called three gods. Gregory answers that "man" properly names a single nature. He adds that every divine action comes from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, and is therefore one. The work is a key statement of Cappadocian teaching on the Trinity.

Ad Graecos ex communibus notionibus ("To the Greeks, from Common Notions") is a short Greek treatise on the Trinity by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It dates from the later fourth century, but its exact date is uncertain. Gregory argues from shared philosophical concepts that the word "God" names the divine essence, not the persons. Because Father, Son and Holy Spirit share one essence, Christians confess one God and not three. The treatise is closely related to his better-known Ad Ablabium (On Not Three Gods). Both defend Nicene doctrine against the charge of tritheism.

This is a short Greek letter by Gregory of Nyssa to his younger brother Peter, bishop of Sebasteia, printed with Peter's reply at the head of Gregory's treatise Against Eunomius. Gregory wrote it soon after the death of their brother Basil in 379. He explains that he answered only one of Eunomius' pamphlets, because he had the book for just seventeen days, and asks Peter whether he should publish his refutation. Peter answers by urging him to finish the defence of Nicene Trinitarian doctrine against Eunomius.

On the Faith (to Simplicius) is a short dogmatic treatise in Greek by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It is addressed to a certain Simplicius and was written sometime between about 370 and 395. Gregory argues against the Arian claim that the Son "once was not" and is a creature. He draws on scriptural commands against worshipping any "new" or "strange" god to show that the Only-begotten is eternal and shares the Father's nature. It is a concise example of the Nicene teaching on the Trinity that Gregory defended against Arian and Eunomian opponents.

A short Greek treatise against the Apollinarians by Gregory of Nyssa, written as a letter to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. Since Theophilus became bishop in 385 and Gregory died around 394, the work belongs to Gregory's last years. Gregory praises Alexandria as a source of true wisdom and asks Theophilus to oppose the followers of Apollinaris of Laodicea. They had accused Gregory and his allies of teaching "two Sons", and Gregory rejects the charge. He defends a Christology in which Christ's full humanity is united with the one divine Son.

Against Arius and Sabellius is a short Greek theological treatise transmitted among the works of Gregory of Nyssa, though its authenticity is doubted and its real author is uncertain. It probably dates from the late fourth century. Starting from Psalm 45:1, "My heart has poured forth a good word," it attacks two opposite errors: the Arian view that the Son is a creature, and the Sabellian merging of Father and Son into a single "Son-Father." Against both it defends the Son's distinct hypostasis and full divinity as the narrow middle way of orthodoxy.

On the Holy Spirit, Against the Macedonians is a Greek polemical treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, one of the Cappadocian Fathers. He wrote it in the later fourth century, probably around the time of the debates linked with the Council of Constantinople (381), but the exact date is uncertain. It answers the Pneumatomachi, or followers of Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is fully divine. Gregory argues that the Spirit shares the same rank, nature and activity as the Father and the Son. The treatise is an important witness to the development of Nicene teaching on the Trinity.

The Antirrheticus adversus Apollinarium is a Greek polemical treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It is generally dated to the later part of his career, probably the 380s, though the exact date is uncertain. In it Gregory refutes the Christology of Apollinarius of Laodicea, who taught that the divine Logos took the place of a human mind in Christ. Gregory argues that Christ assumed a complete human nature. The treatise quotes Apollinarius's Apodeixis at length, so it is also an important source for fragments of that otherwise lost work.

Against Eunomius is a long polemical treatise in Greek by Gregory of Nyssa, written around 380–383. It defends his late brother Basil of Caesarea against the Anomoean leader Eunomius of Cyzicus, whose "Apology for the Apology" had attacked Basil's earlier refutation. Gregory rejects the claim that "unbegotten" defines God's essence and that the Son is therefore unlike the Father. He argues for the Son's full divinity and for the infinity and incomprehensibility of God. The work was divided into differing numbers of books, and it is a major source for Cappadocian Trinitarian theology.

Contra fatum (Against Fate) is a short Greek treatise in the form of a letter by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. Its exact date is uncertain, but it falls within his active years in the late fourth century. Gregory writes at the request of an honoured correspondent and gives a brief account of a debate he held in Constantinople with a pagan philosopher. In it he argues against astrological determinism, the belief that the stars fix human lives. The work defends human free will and God's providence against the fatalism common in late antiquity.

De anima ("On the Soul") is a Greek philosophical treatise transmitted among the works of Gregory of Nyssa but not by him. Its text matches the chapter on the soul in Nemesius of Emesa's On the Nature of Man, written around 400, which circulated in part under Gregory's name. It opens by surveying ancient views of the soul, including those of Democritus, Epicurus, the Stoics, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Plato and Aristotle. It then refutes materialist accounts and defends the soul as an incorporeal, self-subsistent substance.

On the Medium (De pythonissa) is a short Greek letter by Gregory of Nyssa, the fourth-century Cappadocian bishop, to a Bishop Theodosius who had sent him questions about Scripture. Its main subject is 1 Samuel 28, where the medium of Endor appears to call up the dead Samuel for King Saul. Gregory rejects the view of some earlier interpreters that the prophet really appeared. He argues instead that a demon took Samuel's likeness to deceive Saul. Its exact date is unknown, and it is a notable patristic example of interpreting this disputed passage.

The Canonical Epistle to Letoius is a letter on penitential discipline by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, sent to Letoius, bishop of Melitene. It was written in the later fourth century, usually placed around 390. Gregory sorts sins by the parts of the soul they corrupt: reason, desire and anger. He then sets the length and stages of penance for apostasy, magic, fornication, adultery, murder, theft and grave-robbing. Its rulings were later received into Byzantine canon law and became part of the Orthodox canonical tradition.

The Great Catechism, or Catechetical Oration, is a Greek theological treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, usually dated to about 383–387. It was written as a guide for those who teach the faith, not for catechumens. It argues from reason as well as Scripture to defend Christian teaching against pagans, Jews and heretics. It covers the Trinity, creation and the fall, the incarnation and redemption, including the well-known image of the divine bait and fishhook, and baptism and the Eucharist. After Origen's On First Principles, it is among the earliest attempts at a systematic account of Christian doctrine.

"Against Those Who Resent Reproofs" (Greek "Pros tous achthomenous tais epitimesesi") is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. He wrote it during his time as bishop, in the later fourth century. It opens by praising reason and speech (logos) as God's gift. This gift sets human beings apart from the animals, lets them master beasts and cross the seas, and leads them to know and worship the Giver of reason. From there the sermon turns to those in his congregation who took offence at his rebukes. It defends the preacher's duty to correct.

Against Those Who Delay Baptism (Adversus eos qui baptismum differunt) is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. He preached it on a feast when baptism was given, sometime between about 370 and 395; the exact date is uncertain. It targets a common fourth-century habit: catechumens put off baptism until late in life or until they were dying. Gregory warns that death can come suddenly and urges his hearers to be baptized now. The sermon is an important witness to baptismal practice and pastoral preaching in the late fourth-century Greek Church.

Contra fornicarios is a short Greek homily attributed to Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, and dated to the later fourth century. Its Greek heading cites Paul's words that "he who commits fornication sins against his own body" (1 Corinthians 6:18). The sermon comments on Paul's command to "flee fornication". Using military imagery, it argues that some spiritual enemies must be faced head-on, while sexual temptation must be escaped by flight. It also explains why this sin, unlike others, harms the sinner's own body.

Contra Manichaeos syllogismi is a short Greek treatise against the Manichaeans, made up of twelve syllogisms and handed down under the name of Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–c. 394). Whether Gregory actually wrote it has been questioned. Using brief logical arguments, it rejects the Manichaean dualism that treats evil as an eternal principle. It argues that evil is a quality rather than a substance, that it is corruptible and therefore not unbegotten, and that the devil, whom Scripture describes as subject to punishment, cannot be unbegotten either.

Contra usurarios (Against Those Who Practise Usury) is a Greek homily by Gregory of Nyssa, bishop of Nyssa in Cappadocia. Its exact date is uncertain. Taking a prophet's condemnation of interest as its starting point, it attacks lending at interest as a form of greed that exploits the poor, and it urges generous lending without profit. At the start Gregory modestly admits that he follows an earlier famous speech on the same subject, generally taken to be Basil of Caesarea's. The homily is an important early Christian statement on wealth and usury.

On the Soul and the Resurrection is a philosophical dialogue in Greek by Gregory of Nyssa, written soon after the death of his sister Macrina in 379. It is set at her deathbed. Gregory, grieving for their brother Basil, questions her, and Macrina answers as his teacher, in a way consciously modelled on Plato's Phaedo. The dialogue argues that the soul is immaterial and survives death, and defends the resurrection of the body. It also explores the purification of souls and the final restoration of all things to God. It is a key source for Gregory's anthropology and eschatology.

This Greek sermon by Gregory of Nyssa is also called an encomium of the righteous Abraham. It is usually dated to about 383, probably when Gregory was in Constantinople. It defends the full divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit against those who denied it, following the Nicene faith of the Cappadocian Fathers. Gregory begins by comparing himself to a bee gathering from the meadow of Scripture. He then praises Abraham's faith and ends with a vivid account of the sacrifice of Isaac, a passage later quoted in debates about religious images.

On Infants' Early Deaths is a short theological treatise in Greek by Gregory of Nyssa, addressed to Hierius, a Cappadocian official. It was written late in Gregory's life, since he calls himself aged. It asks why God allows infants to die before they can do either good or evil, and what becomes of them afterwards. Gregory argues that such souls are neither punished nor rewarded like those who lived virtuously. Instead they share in the knowledge of God as far as their nature allows. The treatise is an important early Christian discussion of divine providence and of the fate of children who die young.

De instituto Christiano, also called On the Christian Mode of Life, is a Greek ascetic treatise attributed to Gregory of Nyssa. It is addressed to a community of ascetics who asked about the goal of piety. It describes the soul's natural longing for God, its purification from the passions and the virtues of common monastic life. The text is closely parallel to the Great Letter of Pseudo-Macarius. Most scholars now think it is an adaptation of that letter, so Gregory's authorship and the date are disputed.

De mortuis ("On the Dead") is a Greek discourse by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. Its exact date is uncertain. It is addressed to those who grieve for the departed. Gregory argues that people mourn death bitterly out of irrational habit rather than reasoned judgement. He sets out what is truly good, what is distinctive about bodily life, and what is hoped for in the life to come. The work presents death as passing into a better, bodiless existence and develops his teaching on the soul, the body and resurrection.

De occursu Domini ("On the Meeting of the Lord, and on the Theotokos") is a Greek festal homily for the Presentation of Christ in the Temple, known in the East as the Hypapante or "Meeting". It has come down under the name of Gregory of Nyssa, but its authenticity is disputed and it is widely thought to be later than his time. Its date is therefore uncertain. The sermon opens with a rhetorical praise of the apostle Paul, then turns to the feast, Simeon's encounter with the infant Christ and the role of the Virgin Mary as Theotokos.

The Oratio adhortatoria ad paenitentiam (Greek Protreptikos peri metanoias, "Exhortation to Repentance") is a short Greek sermon handed down under the name of Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian who died around 394. Its manuscript heading calls it a protreptic, or hortatory, discourse. It urges hearers to turn from sin and seek God's mercy through repentance, which was a common theme of late fourth-century preaching. Its exact date is unknown, and whether Gregory really wrote it has been questioned, as with several minor homilies that circulate under his name.

De pauperibus amandis I, also called On Good Works (De beneficentia), is the first of two Greek sermons on love for the poor by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop. It was preached during a fast, probably in Lent; its exact date is uncertain. Gregory moves from bodily fasting to a "bodiless" fast, abstaining from evil, and then urges his hearers to help the many destitute and homeless people of his day. It is an important witness to early Christian teaching on poverty and almsgiving.

De pauperibus amandis oratio II is the second of two Greek sermons "On the Love of the Poor" by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It was preached in the later fourth century, but its exact date is uncertain. The sermon is a commentary on Matthew 25:40, "Inasmuch as you did it to one of these." Gregory opens with a vivid picture of Christ's Last Judgment and goes on to urge compassion for the destitute sick, especially people suffering from leprosy. It is an important witness to early Christian teaching on charity and social care.

On Perfection is a short Greek ascetical treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. He addressed it to Olympius, a monk who had asked how one might become perfect through a life of virtue. Its exact date is uncertain. Gregory starts from the name "Christian" and argues that those who bear Christ's name should show his titles and attributes in their lives. Perfection is presented as a continual imitation of Christ, a theme central to Gregory's spiritual teaching.

De professione Christiana, also known as On What It Means to Call Oneself a Christian, is a short ascetic treatise in the form of a letter by Gregory of Nyssa, the fourth-century bishop and Cappadocian Father. It is addressed to Harmonius, a younger friend, and its exact date is uncertain. Gregory says the long letter makes up for the many he owes and stands in for their talks together. He argues that bearing Christ's name commits the believer to imitating the divine nature through a virtuous life.

This is a Greek homily for the feast of Pentecost by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It was written in the later fourth century, though its exact date is uncertain. It opens with David's harp and the psalm verse "Come, let us rejoice in the Lord." It then describes how humanity strayed into worshipping the elements, demons and idols. God led people back to the truth step by step, as physicians feed the starving gradually. The sermon presents Pentecost as the revelation of the Holy Spirit and reflects Gregory's defence of the Spirit's divinity.

De sancto Theodoro martyre is a panegyric sermon by Gregory of Nyssa, the fourth-century Cappadocian bishop and theologian. He delivered it at the shrine of the soldier-martyr Theodore, known as Theodore Tyro or "the Recruit," on the saint's feast before crowds of pilgrims gathered in winter. Gregory credits the martyr with turning back a "Scythian" invasion the year before. He then retells Theodore's confession and execution by fire and encourages devotion at his tomb. The exact year of delivery is disputed. The sermon is an important early witness to the cult of martyrs and the veneration of relics.

On Virginity (De virginitate) is a Greek treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, generally regarded as one of his earliest works and dated to the 370s. It praises consecrated virginity as the gateway to a holier life. Gregory argues that freedom from the cares of marriage and worldly life allows undistracted contemplation of God and restores the soul toward its divine likeness. He begins by praising virginity, then contrasts it with the troubles of ordinary life and ends with an exhortation. The work is an important early statement of Cappadocian ascetic and mystical thought.

De vita S. Ephraem Syri is a Greek encomium, or panegyric, on Ephrem the Syrian, the fourth-century deacon, poet and theologian of Nisibis and Edessa who died in 373. It has come down under the name of Gregory of Nyssa, but its authenticity is widely doubted, and its date and real author are uncertain. Opening with Christ's parable of the lamp on the lampstand, the speaker argues that Ephrem's life should not stay hidden. He then praises Ephrem's asceticism, virtues and writings. The work shaped the legendary picture of Ephrem in the Greek-speaking world.

This is the surviving correspondence of Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–c. 394), bishop of Nyssa and one of the Cappadocian Fathers, written in Greek between about 370 and 395, along with some fragments. The roughly thirty letters deal with church disputes, friendships and practical matters. One, to Flavian, protests the hostility of Helladius of Caesarea. Others discuss pilgrimage to Jerusalem, and one describes plans for building a martyr's church. Together the letters shed light on Gregory's life, his personality and church affairs in late fourth-century Asia Minor.

In ascensionem Christi is a short Greek festal sermon on Christ's Ascension by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It was delivered sometime between 370 and 395. Its heading notes that in Cappadocian local custom the feast was called the Episozomene. The homily is built around the Psalms of David. Psalm 23 is read as a picture of catechesis and baptism. Psalm 24, with its call to "lift up your gates," is read as the angels' welcome to the ascending Christ. It is an early witness to how the Ascension was celebrated.

Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, preached this Greek homily for the Feast of Lights (Epiphany or Theophany). The feast commemorated Christ's baptism in the Jordan and was a customary day for baptisms. Its exact date is uncertain but falls within Gregory's episcopate in the later fourth century. He begins by welcoming the crowded congregation, then explains baptism as a new birth through water and the Spirit and finds figures of it in the Old Testament. The sermon is an important witness to fourth-century Eastern teaching on baptism and to how the Epiphany feast was kept.

This Greek encomium by Gregory of Nyssa praises his elder brother Basil of Caesarea, who died in 378 or 379. It was delivered on Basil's annual commemoration, probably in the early 380s. The speech opens by placing the feast within the cycle that follows Christmas: Stephen, Peter, James, John and Paul are honoured first, then Basil as the "shepherd and teacher" who comes after the apostles. Gregory compares Basil with Paul, Moses and other biblical figures. The speech is an important witness to Basil's early cult and to Cappadocian festal oratory.

This is a collection of five Greek sermons for Easter that have come down under the name of Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian who died around 394. The orations celebrate Christ's resurrection and discuss the three days between his death and rising. They also present the paschal feast as fulfilling the blessings, laws, figures and prophecies of the Old Testament, and they hail the newly baptised as Abraham's promised offspring, shining like stars. Not all five orations are accepted as Gregory's own, and the authenticity of several of them is debated.

In diem natalem Christi is a Greek festal sermon on the Nativity of Christ by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian theologian and bishop. He preached it for the Christmas feast, probably in the 380s, although the exact date is uncertain. It opens with the psalm's call to "blow the trumpet" and presents the Incarnation as the true Feast of Tabernacles, in which Christ pitches a human tent and rebuilds humanity's dwelling that death had destroyed. The sermon also deals with the infants of Bethlehem killed by Herod. It is early evidence for the Nativity feast in the Greek East.

This is a Greek funeral oration by Gregory of Nyssa for Meletius, bishop of Antioch. Meletius died in Constantinople in 381 while presiding over the Council of Constantinople, and Gregory gave the speech there before the assembled bishops. In it he counts Meletius among the apostles and mourns the loss of a father and leader at a time when heresy threatened the Church. Like other Christian funeral speeches of the period, it draws on the forms of classical rhetoric.

The Funeral Oration on the Empress Flacilla is a Greek funeral speech by Gregory of Nyssa. He gave it in Constantinople around 386 for Aelia Flaccilla, wife of the emperor Theodosius I, who died in Thrace. Gregory opens by reflecting on the silence the bishop of the city first imposed on the mourning church. He then praises the empress's piety, humility, charity to the poor and loyalty to Nicene orthodoxy, and offers consolation drawn from Christian hope. It is one of his occasional speeches tied to the imperial court, along with his oration for her young daughter Pulcheria.

The Oratio consolatoria in Pulcheriam is a Greek funeral oration by Gregory of Nyssa. He gave it in Constantinople around 385 for Pulcheria, the young daughter of Emperor Theodosius I and Empress Flaccilla, who had died in early childhood. Gregory compares the city's grief to an earthquake, and his speech is meant to comfort the imperial family and the people. He draws on classical rhetoric of consolation and on Christian teaching about the innocence of children who die young and the hope of resurrection. It belongs with his funeral oration for Flaccilla, who died soon afterwards.

This is the first of two Greek homilies by Gregory of Nyssa on Stephen, the first Christian martyr. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa in Cappadocia, preached it in the late fourth century on Stephen's feast, the day after the celebration of Christ's Nativity. The sermon links the two feasts: Christ put on humanity for us, and Stephen put off his life for Christ. Using athletic imagery, it shows Stephen as a champion who opened the way for the martyrs while heaven watched.

The second Encomium on Saint Stephen the Protomartyr is a Greek festal sermon by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, composed in the later fourth century. It is the companion to his first encomium on Stephen and was likewise preached for the saint's feast in the Christmas season. Gregory presents Stephen as the first fruit of the Church after Christ. He plays on his name (stephanos, "crown"), contrasts him with the crown of thorns, and praises his care for widows, his fullness of the Spirit and his witness unto death.

In suam ordinationem ("On his own ordination") is a Greek sermon by Gregory of Nyssa, the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It is usually dated to 381 and linked to the Council of Constantinople. The exact occasion is disputed, because Gregory had already been a bishop since 372. In the opening, the preacher modestly calls himself a poor, grey-haired guest at a "spiritual feast" of eloquent speakers and asks his hearers to support him with their prayers. The sermon is a source for Gregory's preaching during the Trinitarian controversies.

This Greek panegyrical sermon by Gregory of Nyssa, bishop and Cappadocian Father, was preached in the late fourth century in honour of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste. These Christian soldiers were remembered for dying of exposure on a frozen lake under the emperor Licinius. Its two parts are conventionally labelled Ia and Ib. Gregory begins by rejoicing at the crowded congregation and asking which of the day's readings to take up. He then turns to the martyrs, whose cult was particularly honoured in his family. The sermon is an important witness to their early veneration in Cappadocia and Pontus.

This is the second of Gregory of Nyssa's Greek homilies in honour of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste. These were Roman soldiers who, by tradition, were put to death by exposure on a frozen lake under Licinius in the early fourth century. Gregory gave the sermon the day after an earlier address, during their festival at the start of March. He contrasts the soldiers' new-year military exercises with the spiritual contest of Christ's forty soldiers and praises hearing stories of virtue as moral formation. It is an important witness to the early cult of these widely venerated martyrs.

This is a miscellaneous body of Greek material in volume 46 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the volume devoted mainly to the writings of Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–c. 395). It brings together front matter, editorial notes and passages not catalogued as separate works. The surviving opening criticises the doctrine of transmigration, which held that souls fall from heavenly life into human, animal and plant bodies and climb back again. It argues that such an endless cycle would blur the line between good and evil. This critique matches Gregory's arguments about the soul.

The Testimonia adversus Judaeos (Selected Testimonies against the Jews) is a Greek collection of Old Testament proof texts. Manuscripts attribute it to Gregory of Nyssa, but his authorship is generally rejected, and the work is dated to the fourth or fifth century. It belongs to the early Christian testimonia tradition and arranges prophetic and scriptural passages, each with brief comments, to argue Christian doctrine against Jewish readings. It opens with the Trinity, arguing from Psalm 32(33):6 and other verses that God's Word and Spirit are real, personal beings, and goes on to Christological themes.

The Life of Gregory the Wonderworker is a Greek panegyric by Gregory of Nyssa, written in the late fourth century and delivered as a speech at a festal gathering in honour of the saint. It praises Gregory Thaumaturgus, the third-century bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, and draws on local oral traditions about his conversion, his study under Origen, his miracles and his missionary work. It matters as an early example of Christian hagiography. It also contains the earliest known account of a vision of the Virgin Mary, in which a creed is revealed to Gregory.

The Life of St Macrina is a Greek hagiography by Gregory of Nyssa, probably written around 380–383. It is framed as a long letter to the monk Olympius, whom Gregory met at Antioch. It tells the life of his elder sister Macrina the Younger: her education and her choice of consecrated virginity. It also covers the ascetic community she led on the family estate in Pontus and her death in 379, at which Gregory was present. It is a key early source for women's monasticism and for the family of the Cappadocian Fathers.

Ad Stagirium a daemone vexatum is a consolatory treatise in three books by John Chrysostom. It is addressed to Stagirius, a young ascetic friend who had fallen into severe despondency and seizures that were believed to be the work of a demon. It is usually dated to Chrysostom's early years in Antioch, around 380, before he became a priest. Kept at home by illness, Chrysostom writes to encourage his friend. He reflects on divine providence, the purpose of suffering and the overcoming of despair, which makes the work an important early witness to his ascetic and pastoral thought.

This early Greek work by John Chrysostom consists of two exhortations, a longer treatise and a shorter letter. It probably dates from his years as a young ascetic at Antioch. It is addressed to Theodore, a companion in the ascetic life who had left it to marry and return to worldly affairs. He is traditionally identified with the later Theodore of Mopsuestia. Chrysostom mourns Theodore's fall and urges him to repent, insisting that no sin is beyond God's mercy and warning against despair. The work became an important early Christian text on repentance.

This is a treatise in three books by John Chrysostom, written in Greek at Antioch, probably between about 376 and 386, before his ordination as priest. It defends monks and those who urged young men to take up the monastic life against hostility in the city. The first book answers the critics in general. The second addresses a pagan father whose son has become a monk, and the third a Christian father. The work argues that a monastic upbringing forms virtue better than worldly education, and it is an important early statement of Chrysostom's ascetic ideals.

The Comparison between a King and a Monk is a short Greek treatise attributed to John Chrysostom. Its exact date is uncertain, though it is often placed among his early writings from Antioch. It sets the wealth, power and glory of a ruler against the solitary life of the monk devoted to the worship of God. It argues that earthly rule is fleeting and dangerous, while the monastic "philosophy according to Christ" is open to everyone and wins lasting goods in this life and the next. The work shows Chrysostom's early enthusiasm for asceticism.

Two Greek treatises by John Chrysostom on one theme. The first is addressed to clerics and ascetic men who kept consecrated virgins in their homes as "spiritual sisters" (subintroductae, Greek syneisaktoi). The second warns women vowed to virginity not to live with men. Chrysostom calls the arrangement a recent and strange invention. He rejects the reasons its defenders gave and argues that it caused scandal, temptation and damage to the reputation of virginity. The exact date of the treatises is uncertain. They are important evidence for the practice of spiritual marriage, called syneisaktism, in the late fourth-century Church.

On Compunction is a Greek ascetical treatise in two books by John Chrysostom. The first book is addressed to a monk named Demetrius, who had pressed the author for discourses on the subject. The second is addressed to Stelechius. The exact date is uncertain, but the work is usually placed in Chrysostom's years at Antioch. It describes compunction, the heartfelt sorrow for sin that frees the soul from worldly cares and lifts it toward God. It draws on Scripture, especially the example of David, and is an important early Greek source on penitence and tears in Christian spirituality.

This is a miscellany of Greek material from the first volume of John Chrysostom's works in Migne's Patrologia Graeca: editorial front matter, notes and shorter pieces that are not catalogued separately. It opens with an excerpt from an encomium of Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople, ascribed to Martyrius of Antioch. The excerpt presents his exile and sufferings as a kind of martyrdom. Scholars now usually treat this funeral oration as the work of an anonymous partisan, written soon after Chrysostom's death in 407. Such testimonia are important early evidence for his life and the controversy that surrounded him.

The Dialogue on the Life of St John Chrysostom is a Greek biographical and apologetic work by Palladius of Helenopolis, a loyal supporter of Chrysostom, written around 407–408. It is set out as a conversation, modelled on Plato, between an Eastern bishop and a Roman deacon named Theodore. It tells the story of Chrysostom's career, his deposition at the Synod of the Oak and his exile, and defends him against the charges made against him. It sharply criticises Theophilus of Alexandria and the clerical ambition behind Chrysostom's downfall, and it is a major early source for his life.

The Letter to a Young Widow is a Greek consolatory treatise by John Chrysostom. It is usually dated to his early career at Antioch, around 380, before he became a priest, though dating varies. He addresses a young woman whose husband died after only a few years of marriage. He waits until her first grief has passed, then comforts her with Christian teaching on death, the resurrection and the passing nature of worldly honours. He also praises widowhood as an honourable state. With a companion treatise against second marriage, it is an important early example of Christian consolation literature.

The Adversus Judaeos are eight Greek homilies preached by John Chrysostom at Antioch around 386–387, while he was a presbyter there. Despite the title, they are aimed mainly at members of his own congregation who attended synagogue services, kept Jewish fasts and feasts, or sought healing from Jews. The first homily breaks off from his series on the incomprehensibility of God to deal with this urgent problem. The sermons are known for their harsh polemic against Judaism. They are important evidence for Jewish–Christian relations in late antique Antioch and have been much discussed for their later influence.

John Chrysostom wrote this Greek apologetic treatise, the "Demonstration to Jews and Greeks that Christ is God". Its exact date is uncertain, and it is usually placed in his years as a priest at Antioch. He deliberately writes briefly and plainly so that slaves, widows, shopkeepers, sailors and farmers can follow. Addressing pagans first, he argues that Christ is divine because the prophets foretold him and because his own predictions came true, above all the worldwide spread of the Church.

This Greek homily is transmitted under the name of John Chrysostom with the heading "That one must not anathematize the living or the dead". Its authenticity has been questioned. The preacher refers back to an earlier sermon on the incomprehensibility of God. He then rebukes people with no training in Scripture who dogmatize rashly and pronounce anathemas on things they do not understand, so that Christians become a laughing-stock to outsiders. He urges charity and restraint in condemning others, whether they are alive or dead.

This is a series of Greek homilies by John Chrysostom, also known as the homilies against the Anomoeans. Most were preached at Antioch while he was a presbyter, beginning around 386, and later ones at Constantinople after he became bishop there in 398. They oppose the radical Arian (Anomoean) followers of Eunomius, who claimed that God's essence could be fully known. Chrysostom argues that God's nature remains beyond the grasp of humans and even of angels. The homilies are a key witness to patristic apophatic theology and to the defence of the Son's equality with the Father.

This is a series of sermons on the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31), preached by John Chrysostom at Antioch while he was a presbyter there, probably around 388–389. Seven discourses survive under this title. The first opens just after the pagan New Year celebrations, attacking drunkenness and street revelry before turning to the parable. Across the series Chrysostom deals with wealth and poverty, almsgiving, providence, and judgement after death. The sermons are a key source for his social teaching on riches and care for the poor.

On the Priesthood is a treatise in six books by John Chrysostom, written in Greek, probably at Antioch. It is usually dated between about 386 and 391, though some scholars place it earlier. It takes the form of a dialogue between John and his close friend Basil. John had avoided ordination while letting Basil be ordained, and he defends that deception. He then sets out the dignity, responsibilities and dangers of the priestly office, including the care of souls and preaching. It became one of the most influential early Christian works on pastoral ministry.
