De virginitate (On Virginity) is a Greek treatise by John Chrysostom, probably written in Antioch in the late 370s or early 380s, before he became a priest. It praises virginity as a higher calling than marriage while defending marriage as good. Chrysostom denies that heretical groups who condemn marriage as evil practise true virginity, and much of the work is an extended reading of Paul's teaching in 1 Corinthians 7. It is one of the main early Greek statements of the Christian ascetic ideal.

In Kalendas is a Greek homily that John Chrysostom preached at Antioch as a presbyter under Bishop Flavian, usually dated to 1 January 387 or 388. It opens by noting the bishop's absence and recalling a recent sermon in praise of the apostle Paul. Chrysostom then attacks the popular New Year festivities of the Kalends, including drunken revelry, decorating doors, divination and the belief that the year's first day foretells its fortune. The homily is valuable evidence for how Christians in late antiquity dealt with pagan civic customs.

This is a miscellany of material from volume 48 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the volume given over to writings of John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), together with spurious works attributed to him. It gathers front matter, editorial notes and shorter Greek pieces that are not catalogued separately, so its authorship is mixed and partly uncertain. The opening passage defends the divinity of the Holy Spirit and of the Son. It cites Isaiah's vision, Acts and Paul, and rejects any talk of a "great" and a "lesser" God.

This Greek sermon is the first John Chrysostom preached after Bishop Flavian ordained him presbyter at Antioch in 386. Its heading says it concerns the preacher himself, the bishop and the people. Chrysostom opens by asking whether his sudden rise is real or only a dream, since a humble and lowly young man has been raised to such a high office before a great crowd. The sermon combines a show of personal humility with praise of Flavian. It is an early witness to the preaching career that made Chrysostom famous.

Spuria is a group of Greek writings that manuscripts attribute to John Chrysostom (died 407) but that scholars regard as spurious. They are printed among the doubtful and spurious works in volume 48 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca. Their authors are anonymous, and the pieces may date from anywhere between the fifth and tenth centuries. The collection opens with a short ascetic exhortation, "That the ascetic must not jest." Drawing on Paul, Job and Ecclesiastes, it warns monks that laughter and frivolous joking weaken self-control and the fear of God.

The Instructions to Catechumens are baptismal sermons by John Chrysostom. He preached them at Antioch as a presbyter, probably around 387–390, to candidates preparing for baptism at Easter, who were called "those about to be illuminated." The first instruction explains why baptism is called a laver of regeneration rather than simply of remission of sins. It also warns against both swearing falsely and taking oaths at all. The second deals with renouncing Satan and condemns superstitious practices such as amulets and omens. Together they are important evidence for baptismal teaching and practice in late fourth-century Antioch.

This Greek homily by John Chrysostom was preached for the feast of Epiphany, most likely at Antioch during his years as a presbyter there. It opens by contrasting the crowded church at the festival with the empty assemblies of ordinary days. Chrysostom criticises those who come to church only once or twice a year. He then turns to the baptism of Christ in the Jordan and explains why the feast is called Epiphany. He also warns against receiving communion unworthily, and compares people who leave the liturgy before the final prayer to Judas.

De coemeterio et de cruce ("On the Cemetery and the Cross") is a Greek homily by John Chrysostom. It was preached at a martyr's shrine in a cemetery outside the city, probably at Antioch, on a feast commemorating the Cross. Chrysostom explains why the congregation gathers outside the walls: Christ suffered "outside the gate," as the Letter to the Hebrews says. He reflects on the word "cemetery" as a "sleeping-place," which shows that for Christians death is a sleep awaiting resurrection. He then preaches on the Cross as the means of Christ's victory over death and the devil.

De cruce et latrone homilia I (On the Cross and the Thief, Homily 1) is a Greek sermon by John Chrysostom. It was preached on Good Friday, as its opening shows: "Today our Lord Jesus Christ is on the cross, and we keep a feast." The exact date and place are uncertain. Chrysostom presents the cross as a sign of honour and salvation rather than condemnation. He reflects on the penitent thief who received paradise, discusses Christ's second coming and urges constant prayer for one's enemies. A second homily on the same theme survives under his name.

This is the second of two Greek homilies "On the Cross and the Thief" by John Chrysostom, delivered during his preaching career between 386 and 407, traditionally on Good Friday. Chrysostom explains that Christ suffered outside the walls of Jerusalem, not in the Temple, so that his sacrifice would be understood as offered for the whole world. By his blood the whole earth was cleansed and became a place of prayer. The homily also reflects on the repentant thief crucified beside Christ.

The Three Homilies Concerning the Power of Demons (De diabolo tentatore) are a set of Greek sermons by John Chrysostom. They are generally thought to have been preached at Antioch during his years as a priest there. The first homily answers people who claimed that demons govern human affairs, or who were troubled by God's chastisements and by the wicked prospering while the just suffer. Across the series Chrysostom argues that the devil cannot force anyone to sin. The cause of evil lies in human free will and negligence, and God's providence guides all things for good.

The Homilies on Repentance are a collection of nine Greek sermons attributed to John Chrysostom. Most are thought to have been preached at Antioch while he was a presbyter there, probably in the late 380s. However, the collection is composite, and the dating and authenticity of some pieces have been questioned. Drawing on biblical examples, the sermons describe the many roads to repentance, including confession of sins, forgiveness of others, prayer, almsgiving, tears and humility. They also urge hearers not to despair of God's mercy. The collection is an important witness to early Christian teaching on penance.

This is the first of two Greek homilies by John Chrysostom on the betrayal of Judas, preached on Holy Thursday. It was probably delivered at Antioch, though the exact date is uncertain. The full title also names the Pascha, the institution of the Eucharist and the duty not to bear grudges. Chrysostom kept it short so the faithful could go on to communion. He calls them to weep for the traitor rather than for the betrayed Christ, and to approach the "awesome mysteries" with fear and reconciliation. The homily is often cited for its teaching on the Eucharist.

The second of two Greek homilies on the betrayal of Judas attributed to John Chrysostom. They are usually thought to have been preached at Antioch for Holy Thursday, and the second closely parallels the first. The preacher sets the treachery of Judas beside the patience and love of Christ, who is troubled and grieves for his disciple, keeps trying to turn him back, and warns that "one of you will betray me." He then calls listeners to weep for wrongdoers rather than for those who suffer wrong. The sermon also discusses the Passover and the institution of the Eucharist.

This is a series of twenty-one Greek sermons that John Chrysostom preached at Antioch in 387, while he was still a presbyter. That year, crowds angered by a new imperial tax tore down statues of Emperor Theodosius I and his family, and the city feared severe punishment. Bishop Flavian travelled to Constantinople to ask the emperor for mercy. Meanwhile, through Lent, Chrysostom comforted his frightened congregation, urged repentance, and attacked vices such as swearing oaths. The homilies are a vivid record of a civic crisis and of his preaching.

This is a Greek homily for the feast of Christ's Nativity by John Chrysostom, preached at Antioch while he was a presbyter there, usually dated to 25 December 386, though some scholars prefer a slightly later year. Chrysostom celebrates the Incarnation as the rising of the "sun of righteousness" in human flesh. He also notes that the December feast had been known in Antioch for less than ten years and had come from the West. This makes the homily key early evidence for how the Christmas feast spread to the Eastern churches.

Against the Drunkards and on the Resurrection is a Greek homily by John Chrysostom, preached on Easter Sunday. Its exact date and place are uncertain. It opens with the end of the Lenten fast, and Chrysostom urges his hearers to keep the fruit of that fast. Bodily fasting has ended, he says, but spiritual fasting, which means keeping away from sin, must continue. He warns against the drunkenness and excess that often came with the feast, and he reflects on the resurrection of Christ.

De beato Abraham ("On the Blessed Abraham") is a Greek homily that has come down under the name of John Chrysostom but is considered spurious. Its author and date are unknown. Estimates place it somewhere between the fifth and tenth centuries. The sermon praises Abraham as a noble athlete who, in extreme old age, stood firm against nature and paternal feeling, which points to his readiness to sacrifice Isaac. It contrasts the uselessness of old men in war, seafaring and farming with the Church, where aged faith flourishes and grey hair is an adornment.

This is a Greek panegyric homily by John Chrysostom honouring Babylas, the third-century bishop of Antioch who died as a martyr under the emperor Decius. It was preached at Antioch on the saint's feast, probably while Chrysostom was a priest there (386–397). He leaves Babylas's episcopate, his boldness before an emperor and his death to older teachers and to the bishop, whom he calls "our common father." He tells instead what the martyr did after burial in the suburb, a theme he develops more fully in his longer discourse on Babylas against Julian and the pagans.

This is an apologetic treatise in Greek by John Chrysostom, written at Antioch. Its date is debated, but it is usually placed in the late 370s or early 380s. It celebrates Babylas, the bishop of Antioch martyred under Decius, and argues that Christ's power continues to work through his saints. Its centrepiece is the episode at Daphne in 362. There the emperor Julian had the martyr's relics removed because the oracle of Apollo had fallen silent, and soon afterwards Apollo's temple was destroyed by fire. The work is an important witness to Christian responses to Julian's pagan revival.

This is a Greek encomiastic homily by John Chrysostom honouring the virgins Bernice and Prosdoce and their mother Domnina. They were Christians martyred during the Diocletianic persecution in the early fourth century. Rather than face violation after their arrest, they drowned themselves in a river. The sermon was most likely preached at Antioch, less than twenty days after the commemoration of the Cross at Easter. It presents the women's courage in the face of death as proof of Christ's resurrection and victory over the devil. It also takes up the question of whether such a voluntary death was legitimate.

This is a Greek panegyric homily attributed to John Chrysostom, titled in the manuscripts an encomium on the holy great-martyr Drosis and on the remembrance of death. It was probably delivered at Antioch, and its exact date is uncertain. The preacher compares himself to a shepherd leading his flock out to pasture after winter, since the congregation has gathered at a martyr's shrine among many tombs. He praises Drosis's courage and uses the setting to urge his hearers to think about death and lead virtuous lives.

De fato et providentia oratio I is a Greek homily handed down under the name of John Chrysostom. It is now regarded as spurious, and its author and date are unknown. It is the first in a series of discourses on fate and divine providence. The preacher notes that rich and poor, rulers and subjects, parents and the childless all complain alike. He argues that distress comes from our own attitude rather than from circumstances, and he defends God's providential ordering of human life against belief in blind fate.

De fato et providentia oratio II is a Greek sermon on fate and providence. It belongs to a series of orations once attributed to John Chrysostom, but it is now regarded as spurious, and its real author and date are unknown. The preacher begins with the Mosaic law that whoever curses father or mother must die, and argues that cursing God is far worse. He counts as blasphemers those who set the disorder and necessity of fate against God's wise providence. He is especially troubled by baptized Christians who fall back into this pagan belief.

De fato et providentia oratio III is a Greek sermon on fate and providence, the third in a series of six homilies on the subject that have come down under the name of John Chrysostom but are considered spurious. Its author and date are unknown. The preacher says he spoke on fate only recently and returns to it because of his hearers' carelessness. He argues that rejecting belief in fate needs no lengthy proof: like the commandments against murder and adultery, the prohibition is self-evident and needs only to be obeyed.

The fourth of six Greek sermons On Fate and Providence handed down under the name of John Chrysostom. Their authenticity is disputed, and the date of composition is uncertain. The homily warns against envying those who are wealthy without deserving it, against blaming God's providence, and against attributing events to fate. It uses the parable of Lazarus and the rich man as its model. Lazarus, though starving and sick, never complained or accused God, while the cruel rich man prospered. The series is part of early Christian writing against astrological fatalism.

The fifth of a series of six Greek discourses On Fate and Providence that have come down under the name of John Chrysostom but are considered spurious. The author and date are unknown. The sermon attacks the doctrine of fate (heimarmene) and astrological determinism (genesis) as blasphemous and morally ruinous. It argues that such a belief makes laws, judges, teaching, warnings, punishments and rewards pointless, and so undermines both human effort and the guidance God gives through nature, the prophets and holy men.

De fato et providentia oratio VI is the last of six Greek sermons on fate and providence handed down under the name of John Chrysostom (died 407). Its true author and date are unknown; it may have been written anywhere between the fifth and tenth centuries. It takes up the old question of why the wicked prosper while the righteous live in poverty. Its answer is that God's providence lets hardship win greater crowns for the patient. Prosperity misused, by contrast, adds to the guilt of those who will not repent.

This is the first of seven Greek homilies by John Chrysostom in praise of the apostle Paul. They are often thought to have been preached at Antioch, but their exact date is uncertain. The sermon calls Paul's soul a "meadow of virtues" and a "spiritual paradise." It argues that he gathered in himself, to a surpassing degree, every excellence shown by Abel, the patriarchs, prophets, apostles and martyrs. The series is a classic of Christian panegyric and reflects Chrysostom's lifelong devotion to Paul.

This is the second of John Chrysostom's seven Greek homilies In Praise of Saint Paul (De laudibus sancti Pauli apostoli). They are usually assigned to his years as a preacher at Antioch, though their exact date is uncertain. Here Chrysostom presents Paul as proof that a human being sharing ordinary nature can rival the angels. He rejects the claim that virtue is hard and vice easy, and praises Paul for counting his sufferings as light, loving virtue without seeking reward, and pressing forward with fresh zeal amid constant dangers.

This is the third of seven Greek homilies by John Chrysostom in praise of the apostle Paul. Their exact date and place are uncertain, though they are often linked to his preaching at Antioch. This sermon presents love as the virtue that brings people closest to God, since it is something humans share with him. It holds up Paul as its supreme example: he loved his enemies, did good to those who plotted against him and pitied those who persecuted him. The cycle shows Chrysostom's deep admiration for Paul.

The fourth of seven Greek homilies by John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) in praise of the apostle Paul, the series known as De laudibus sancti Pauli. It was probably preached at Antioch, though the exact date is uncertain. The homily focuses on Paul's conversion. Chrysostom argues that his blinding on the road to Damascus became the illumination of the world, and that his calling was not forced. To show this, he contrasts Paul with Judas, Simon Magus, Ananias and Sapphira and others who saw miracles yet turned back. The series is a leading example of Chrysostom's devotion to Paul.

This is the fifth of seven Greek homilies by John Chrysostom in praise of the apostle Paul, generally thought to have been preached at Antioch, though their exact date is uncertain. It answers those who blame death and the mortal, corruptible body as obstacles to virtue. Paul's achievements show that only a weak soul and a slack will stand in the way of goodness, and that wealth, eloquence, rank and power are worth nothing without virtue. The series is a key witness to Chrysostom's lifelong admiration for Paul.

This is the sixth of seven Greek homilies by John Chrysostom in praise of the apostle Paul. They were probably preached at Antioch, though their exact date is uncertain. This homily takes up the objection that Paul sometimes seemed afraid of suffering, for example when he was stretched out to be scourged. Chrysostom argues that Paul's ordinary human weakness actually makes his virtue greater. Although he feared pain, he scorned every danger for Christ, which shows that holiness is within reach of ordinary believers. The cycle is a key witness to Chrysostom's lifelong admiration for Paul.

This Greek sermon by John Chrysostom is the last of his seven panegyric homilies in praise of the apostle Paul. It was written between 386 and 407, and is usually placed in his years as a preacher at Antioch. The homily argues that Paul's chains, scourgings and hunger made him more glorious than kings in purple and diadem. It cites the healing power of his garments and presents his bearing of the cross as a model, quoting his call, "Be imitators of me." The series shaped later Christian devotion to Paul.

The first of John Chrysostom's Greek homilies on the Maccabean martyrs, a panegyric for their feast. It was probably preached at Antioch, where their relics were venerated, during his priesthood there (386–397); the exact date is uncertain. Chrysostom calls the day brighter than any other because the martyrs' remains light up the city. He praises the elderly Eleazar, the seven young brothers and their aged mother from 2 Maccabees, and treats these pre-Christian Jewish heroes as models of Christian martyrdom and endurance.

This is the second of John Chrysostom's Greek panegyric homilies on the Maccabean martyrs, the seven brothers and their mother whose deaths under Antiochus IV are told in 2 and 4 Maccabees. It was probably preached at Antioch during his priesthood. Chrysostom says no tongue can fully praise the martyrs, then recalls that the previous day's sermon was devoted to the mother alone. Here he turns to one of the sons. The homily shows early Christian veneration of these Jewish martyrs as saints.

De Maccabaeis homilia III is a Greek sermon attributed to John Chrysostom and placed in his preaching career between 386 and 407. It is a panegyric on the Maccabean martyrs: the aged Eleazar, the seven brothers and their mother, whose deaths under Antiochus IV are told in 2 Maccabees 6–7. It opens with an image of coinage. The emperor's likeness is stamped as clearly on bronze as on gold or silver. In the same way, the image of virtue shines in every kind of person. The homily belongs to a group of sermons on the Maccabees transmitted under Chrysostom's name.

This is a Greek panegyric homily by John Chrysostom honouring Pelagia of Antioch, a young virgin martyr. During the persecution of the early fourth century, she threw herself from a height to her death rather than risk being violated by the soldiers sent to arrest her. Chrysostom probably preached it at Antioch on her feast day while he was a presbyter there. He presents her as proof that Christ's victory over death lets even young girls scorn it, and he defends her choice to die before being brought to trial.

This is the first of two Greek homilies on Pentecost by John Chrysostom, preached on the feast probably during his years as a priest at Antioch or later as archbishop of Constantinople (386–407). He opens by praising the large festival crowd and then rebukes those who come to church only on feast days, leaving their mother the Church "naked". He compares them with Ham, who saw his father's nakedness. The homily also explains why miraculous signs no longer occur and warns that every deed and word is recorded.

This is a Greek sermon for the feast of Pentecost, one of two homilies on the feast attributed to John Chrysostom. It was probably preached at Antioch or Constantinople between 386 and 407. The preacher presents Pentecost as the culmination of the Church's feasts, following the cross, the resurrection and the ascension, and as the fulfilment of Christ's promise to send the Paraclete. He praises the gifts of the Holy Spirit, through whom believers receive freedom, adoption and every heavenly good.

This is a Greek homily by John Chrysostom honouring Phocas, a bishop-martyr from Pontus. Its full title says it is also directed against heretics and comments on Psalm 141 (LXX), "With my voice I cried to the Lord." It was preached the day after the martyr's relics had been carried through the city in procession, and the emperors themselves joined the celebration. Chrysostom urges everyone who missed it to escort the relics by sea to their shrine. He praises the power of the martyrs, which draws both ordinary people and rulers and puts pagans to shame.

De precatione oratio I is a Greek homily on prayer. It has come down under the name of John Chrysostom but is generally regarded as spurious, and its author and date are unknown. It is the first of two discourses on prayer transmitted together. The preacher praises God's servants who placed their hope of salvation in prayer and handed down their hymns in writing. He teaches that prayer is to the soul what the sun is to the body. Prayer is true conversation with God and the work of angels, and it even surpasses their dignity.

De precatione oratio II is the second of two short Greek discourses on prayer that have come down among the works of John Chrysostom but are generally judged spurious. The author and date are unknown. The sermon opens by calling prayer the summit of every good and the means to salvation and eternal life. It describes prayer as conversation with God, an honour greater even than that of the angels. Citing the reverent fear of the seraphim in the prophets, it urges believers to pray zealously and warns the careless not to neglect prayer.

This is a Greek homily by John Chrysostom, given in the city while its bishop was away in the countryside keeping a feast of martyrs. It is probably from his years as a presbyter at Antioch (386–397), though the exact date is uncertain. Chrysostom contrasts the "devilish" shows of the theatre and the horse races with the Christian feasts of the saints. He praises the country Christians, who speak a foreign tongue but share the faith of the city. He also urges his hearers to compunction (sorrow for sin) and to almsgiving.

De terrae motu ("On the Earthquake") is a short Greek homily by John Chrysostom, preached after an earthquake had struck his city. The exact date and place are uncertain, but it falls within his preaching career as a priest at Antioch and later as bishop of Constantinople (386–407). The preacher says illness had kept him from joining the congregation's procession and psalm-singing. He praises his hearers for turning to repentance after the brief shock and urges them to keep up that devotion once the fear has passed.

This Greek encomium (panegyric) honours Thecla, the disciple of Paul whom Eastern tradition calls protomartyr and "equal to the apostles." It has been handed down among the works of John Chrysostom but is considered spurious, and its author and date are unknown. The homily presents the saint's annual commemoration as a living icon of her deeds. It praises her twofold crown of virginity and martyrdom, treating her victory over bodily pleasures as a martyrdom before martyrdom, and draws on Paul's teaching that the unmarried woman cares for the things of the Lord.

This Greek homily by John Chrysostom was preached on the feast of Christ's Ascension. Its heading says it was delivered in the martyrium at Romanesia, a site outside Antioch. There the bodies of martyrs that had lain near the remains of heretics were raised and reburied on their own. This places it in Chrysostom's years as a priest at Antioch (386–397). The preacher explains that the feast was held outside the city to honour the martyrs. He then reflects on the Ascension, through which Christ raised human nature to heaven and reconciled humanity with God.

This Greek panegyric homily is attributed to John Chrysostom. It honours Barlaam, a martyr venerated at Antioch, on his feast day, and was probably preached there during Chrysostom's years as a priest in the city. Tradition holds that Barlaam let his hand burn over a pagan altar rather than drop the incense placed in it as an offering. Chrysostom tells his hearers that martyrs are honoured by imitation rather than by praise alone. Though the age of persecution has passed, he argues, believers can still be martyrs by struggling against the passions and temptations of daily life.

This Greek panegyric homily by John Chrysostom honours Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, a champion of the Nicene faith who was deposed by his opponents and died in exile. It was probably preached at Antioch on the saint's feast while Chrysostom was a priest there (386–397), though the exact year is uncertain. It opens with the wisdom saying "call no one blessed before death" (Sirach 11:28). Since Eustathius has died, Chrysostom argues, he can now be praised freely. The homily then praises his steadfastness and his lasting care for the Antiochene church.

This Greek panegyric homily by John Chrysostom honours Ignatius, the early second-century bishop of Antioch. Ignatius was taken to Rome and martyred there, and his relics were later brought back to Antioch. Chrysostom probably preached it at Antioch while he was a presbyter there, on the saint's feast, which came soon after that of the martyr Pelagia. He praises Ignatius as a model bishop and martyr and insists that the martyr's contest is open to men and women alike, since "in Christ there is neither male nor female."

This Greek homily on Luke 2:1, "There went out a decree from Caesar Augustus", deals with the census and the enrolment of the Theotokos, the Virgin Mary. It has come down under the name of John Chrysostom, but it is not his work, and its real author and date are unknown. The preacher argues that Augustus's decree, which reached the whole inhabited world, prepared the way for the universal preaching of the faith. He also explains that Augustus had his long reign, given as fifty-six years and four months, because Christ was born under him.

In sanctum Joannem Praecursorem is a Greek homily in honour of John the Baptist. It has come down under the name of John Chrysostom but is considered spurious, and its author and date are unknown. The preacher calls his hearers to celebrate the Forerunner, "greater than any born of women", whose highest honour was to baptize the Lord. He asks them to picture the Jordan flowing in their midst and Christ coming to his servant. Following Matthew 3:13, he then explains the Lord's baptism and the witness given there by Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

In sanctum Julianum martyrem is a Greek panegyric homily by John Chrysostom honouring Julian, a martyr of Anazarbus in Cilicia, whose relics were venerated near Antioch. It was probably preached at Antioch during Chrysostom's years as a presbyter there (386–397), though its exact date is uncertain. The sermon argues that God, as the martyrs' debtor, will reward those who shed their blood for Christ even more generously than the faithful honour them. It contrasts the martyrs, as athletes of piety, with competitors in worldly contests. It belongs to Chrysostom's series of homilies on the martyrs.

This is a Greek panegyric homily by John Chrysostom on Juventinus and Maximinus, two Christian soldiers put to death at Antioch under the emperor Julian the Apostate. It was probably preached at Antioch while Chrysostom was a presbyter there, shortly after a feast of the martyr Babylas, which the opening mentions. Chrysostom compares the two soldiers with older martyrs and presents them as fresh jewels of the Church. He tells how they resisted Julian's pagan measures and holds them up as examples of courage and steadfast faith.

This Greek homily by John Chrysostom honours Lucian of Antioch, the presbyter and biblical scholar martyred under Maximinus Daia in 312. It was most likely preached at Antioch while Chrysostom was a presbyter there (386–397), on the martyr's feast shortly after Epiphany. It opens by rebuking the many who came to church for the great feast but did not come back. Chrysostom compares the Church to Noah's ark, a refuge from the passions, and then praises Lucian's endurance under torture and his unwavering confession of faith.

In martyres homilia ("Homily on the Martyrs") is a Greek sermon by John Chrysostom, preached at a martyrs' festival sometime between his ordination as priest in 386 and his death in 407. Chrysostom praises the large crowd that came to the martyrs' shrines: slaves and masters, poor and rich, old people, women and officials. He argues that a true feast is kept through a pure conscience, citing Paul's call to celebrate with "the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." A believer can therefore honour the martyrs every day, even at home, by imitating their virtue.

In martyres Aegyptios is a Greek panegyric homily by John Chrysostom honouring martyrs from Egypt. It was probably delivered at Antioch, though its exact date is uncertain. It opens by blessing God that martyrs have come even from Egypt, a land once hostile to God and known for blasphemy. Chrysostom compares the Egyptians to a city with a surplus harvest that sends its goods abroad: they have spread their martyrs' relics and example throughout the world. The sermon reflects the late fourth-century cult of the martyrs and their relics.

This Greek encomiastic homily by John Chrysostom honours Meletius, bishop of Antioch, who died in Constantinople in 381 while presiding over the Council of Constantinople. Chrysostom preached it at Antioch, apparently in 386, early in his priesthood. He notes that five years have passed since Meletius's death. He praises the dead bishop, whose body lay in the city, and the great crowd that gathered at his feast, as proof of the affection Meletius left among his people. The sermon is valuable evidence for the cult of Meletius at Antioch and for Chrysostom's early preaching as a priest there.

This Greek homily for the feast of the Presentation of Christ in the Temple (the Hypapante, or Meeting of the Lord) is falsely attributed to John Chrysostom. Its real author and date are unknown; it is placed only loosely between the fifth and tenth centuries. The sermon begins with Christ's circumcision on the eighth day. It argues that by submitting to the Law in the flesh he confirmed his descent from David and left the Jews no excuse for unbelief. It then turns to the Theotokos and to Simeon, who received the child in the Temple.

This Greek homily, attributed to John Chrysostom, praises all the martyrs who suffered throughout the world. It probably dates from his years as a preacher at Antioch or as archbishop of Constantinople (386–407). The preacher argues that death, though a mark of human weakness, became an advantage. Without mortality there could be no martyrdom and no crown. He compares the martyrs' wounds to stars adorning the sky, and he draws on the Psalms and Paul. The homily is an early witness to the shared commemoration of all martyrs in the Greek-speaking Church.

This is a Greek homily on the angel's announcement to Zechariah and the conception of John the Baptist by Elizabeth (Luke 1). It has come down under the name of John Chrysostom but is considered spurious, and its author and date are unknown. The sermon begins by saying that nothing can resist the Lord's commands. It recalls how God's word made water flow from a dry rock, which prepares for the miraculous conception by the barren, aged Elizabeth. The text also praises the power of prayer through the examples of Samuel, David, Hezekiah and the Ninevites.

In Parasceven is a Greek homily for Good Friday that was handed down under the name of John Chrysostom but is considered spurious. Its author and date are unknown. The sermon reflects on Simeon's prophecy that a sword would pierce Mary's soul, which it reads as her trial and doubt when she sees her Son crucified. It also recalls Peter's denial and the flight of the disciples, and argues that the "sign spoken against" tests unbelief and proves the faithful, as persecution proved the martyrs. The homily was also translated into Church Slavonic.

In Petrum apostolum et in Eliam prophetam is a Greek sermon on the apostle Peter and the prophet Elijah. It has come down under the name of John Chrysostom, but it is counted among the spurious works of the Pseudo-Chrysostom corpus. Its true author and date are unknown. The preacher delivered it at a commemoration of martyrs held outside the city. He opens by rebuking the many who stayed away out of laziness. He then answers those who excused themselves as sinners, presenting the Church's sacrifice, prayers, fasts and martyr feasts as remedies for the soul's wounds.

In proditionem Judae ("On the Betrayal of Judas") is a Greek homily attributed to John Chrysostom. It was preached for the feast of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, probably during his years as a preacher at Antioch or later at Constantinople, between 386 and 407. The preacher says he is torn between hatred of the traitor and love for the Master. He then turns from Judas to praise Christ's love for humanity: Christ knowingly chose Judas as a disciple, warned him at the supper and tried to bring him to salvation. The homily survives in more than one version.

In quatriduanum Lazarum ("On Lazarus Four Days Dead") is a Greek sermon that has come down under the name of John Chrysostom. It is the second sermon on the raising of Lazarus in John 11, continuing an earlier springtime sermon that linked the season with resurrection. The preacher asks why only John records the miracle, then sets Christ's human acts beside his divine ones, such as fasting and hunger or stilling the sea, to show his two natures united in one person.

This is the first of two Greek panegyric homilies that John Chrysostom preached in honour of Romanus, a martyr who died at Antioch during the Diocletianic persecution. They were probably delivered at Antioch on the martyr's feast while Chrysostom was a presbyter there, though the exact date is uncertain. The sermon opens with Paul's image of the Church as one body. When one member is honoured, all rejoice: the martyrs are the head and the congregation the feet, and love joins them together. Chrysostom then praises Romanus's endurance and steadfast confession.

This Greek panegyric sermon is the second of two homilies on the martyr Romanus that are transmitted under the name of John Chrysostom. If genuine, it dates from his preaching career at Antioch or Constantinople (386–407), though its authenticity has been questioned. It celebrates Romanus, a deacon put to death at Antioch during the Diocletianic persecution. The sermon pictures the persecution as a storm striking the ship of the Church. It praises the martyr's endurance under torture and tells how he asked for a child from the marketplace to be brought to judge between Christ and the pagan gods.

In sancta Theophania ("On the Holy Theophany") is a Greek sermon for the feast of the Lord's baptism. It has come down under the name of John Chrysostom but is not considered his work, and its real author and date are unknown. The preacher begins by praising the Gospel as a never-failing spring. He then explains John the Baptist's words about the one coming after him, whose sandals he is not worthy to carry. He reads the sandals as the mystery of the Incarnation and supports this with the Psalms' images of the Lord's shoe and footstool.

In triduanam resurrectionem Domini ("On the Lord's Resurrection on the Third Day") is a short Greek Easter homily. It has come down under the name of John Chrysostom but is considered spurious; its real author and date are unknown. It opens with Paul's call to "rejoice in the Lord always" and proclaims Christ's resurrection as the defeat of the devil, death and Hades, quoting "O death, where is thy sting?" It praises the incarnate Word, of one substance with the Father, who freed humanity from slavery to sin. The homily also survives in Church Slavonic.

In venerabilem crucem sermo (Sermon on the Venerable Cross) is a Greek homily that was falsely handed down under the name of John Chrysostom. Its real author and date are unknown. The preacher calls his hearers sailors, helmsmen, disciples and teachers, and offers them a "spiritual table." He pictures the Church as a ship whose hull is the Old and New Testaments, whose rudder is the Cross and whose helmsman is Christ. The sermon was widely copied and translated into Armenian, Latin, Old Nubian, Old Russian and Syriac. Its Old Nubian version is the longest surviving text in that language.

Non esse ad gratiam concionandum is a Greek homily by John Chrysostom, preached during his career as a priest and bishop, between 386 and 407. Its full title says that speaking to please is dangerous for both preachers and hearers, and that accusing oneself of one's own sins is useful and a very great form of justice. Chrysostom says his previous sermon cut deep, so he now offers gentler remedies. Like a physician who both cuts and bandages, he argues, a teacher must mix rebuke with encouragement and consolation.

This is a miscellaneous body of material from volume 50 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the volume holding many of the homilies and panegyrics of John Chrysostom, preached at Antioch and Constantinople between 386 and 407. Rather than a single work, it gathers the volume's prefaces, editorial notes, variant readings and short pieces not catalogued separately. These include Greek passages quoted for comparison, such as Chrysostom's sermon openings and excerpts from later ecclesiastical letters. The material is mostly anonymous or editorial, and its contents are mixed.

This is a small group of Greek sermons by John Chrysostom honouring two martyr-bishops of Antioch. They were probably preached at Antioch while he was a presbyter there, in the late fourth century. The eulogy of Ignatius was delivered on his feast, shortly after that of the martyr Pelagia. It celebrates Ignatius's episcopate, his journey to martyrdom in Rome and the return of his relics to Antioch. The material on Babylas, who died during the Decian persecution, praises his courage. These sermons show how the cult of local martyrs was promoted through preaching in Antioch.

In commemorationem sancti Bassi is a Greek homily for the feast of Bassus, honoured in it as a martyr and bishop. It has come down among the works of John Chrysostom but is considered spurious, and its author and date are unknown. Its heading says it also treats Christ's words "Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart" (Matthew 11:29). The preacher says he speaks after other priests and teachers, despite a long illness and a weak voice. He presents the martyr as an intercessor whose contest won him the crown of incorruption.

These twenty-five Greek sermons by John Chrysostom each explain a particular passage of the New Testament. He preached them at different times between his ordination as priest at Antioch in 386 and his death in exile in 407. Later editors gathered them into one collection. The first sermon was given after an illness had kept him from preaching. It explains the parable of the servant who owed ten thousand talents (Matthew 18) and argues that holding on to past wrongs is worse than any other sin. The sermons show Chrysostom's careful moral reading of Scripture.

This is a collection of fifteen short Greek pieces, mostly homilies, by John Chrysostom. They were written during his time as archbishop of Constantinople, roughly 398 to 404, and deal with the political and church upheavals of those years. The collection opens with his famous sermon on the fallen eunuch and consul Eutropius, built around the text "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." Other pieces come from the crises that led to his deposition and exile. Together they are an important witness to Chrysostom's turbulent time in office and to life at the imperial court.

This is the collected correspondence of John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople, almost all of it written in Greek during his exile from 404 until his death in 407. It opens with his appeal to Pope Innocent I of Rome, which gives an account of the proceedings against him led by Theophilus of Alexandria. At its centre are seventeen letters to the deaconess Olympias, which reflect on suffering and despondency, along with many shorter letters to bishops, clergy and supporters. Together they are a major source for his deposition and his last years.

This is a group of Greek sermons and other pieces that were transmitted under the name of John Chrysostom (died 407) but are now considered spurious. They were printed together among the doubtful and inauthentic works in volume 52 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca. Their authors are anonymous, and they may date from anywhere between the fifth and tenth centuries. The opening piece is a homily on Christ's Ascension. It presents three wonders: the virgin birth, the resurrection on the third day and the bodily ascent into heaven. These works show how preaching circulated under Chrysostom's prestigious name.

The Homilies on Genesis are a series of sixty-seven Greek sermons by John Chrysostom, preached at Antioch while he was a presbyter there, probably in the later 380s; the exact year is disputed. The first homily opens the series as an exhortation at the start of Lent, which it presents as a remedy for the soul. The series works through the Book of Genesis verse by verse. It stresses the literal and moral sense of the text and adds ethical exhortation. It is the most extensive surviving Greek patristic commentary on Genesis.

This is a collection of miscellaneous Greek material from volume 53 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca: editorial front matter, notes, and passages not indexed as separate works. The volume belongs to the series devoted to John Chrysostom, preacher at Antioch and later archbishop of Constantinople, who was active between 386 and 407. Much of it consists of his homilies on Genesis. The surviving pieces include the end of a sermon urging the faithful to give to the poor rather than hoard gold and clothing. It closes with a standard Trinitarian doxology.

The Five Sermons on Hannah are a series of Greek homilies by John Chrysostom, usually dated to 387, while he was a priest at Antioch. They centre on Hannah (Anna), the mother of the prophet Samuel, as told in the First Book of Samuel. The first sermon opens just after Lent and urges hearers to remember the benefits of the fast rather than return to self-indulgence. The series then uses Hannah's barrenness, prayer and dedication of her son to teach about prayer, patience, the duties of parents and the Christian upbringing of children.

The Homilies on David and Saul are three Greek sermons by John Chrysostom, generally dated to 387, when he was a presbyter preaching at Antioch. They expound the narrative in 1 Samuel of David sparing Saul's life although his persecutor was in his power. Chrysostom presents David as a model of forbearance, meekness and love of enemies, and urges his congregation to forgive injuries and set aside revenge. The series also includes moral exhortation on wider matters of Christian conduct, typical of his Antiochene preaching.

The Homilies on Genesis are a series of sixty-seven Greek sermons that John Chrysostom preached while a priest at Antioch, usually dated to the later 380s. This second part continues the verse-by-verse exposition of Genesis. It opens with Homily 42, on Genesis 18:16, about Abraham's intercession for Sodom, and goes on through the patriarchal narratives. Chrysostom pairs a literal reading of the text with moral exhortation, presenting Abraham and the other patriarchs as models of hospitality, faith, humility and compassion for his congregation to follow.

The Sermons on Genesis are a series of Greek sermons by John Chrysostom. He preached them at Antioch as a presbyter during Lent, usually dated to 386. They are separate from his longer series of sixty-seven Homilies on Genesis. Starting from the opening chapters of Genesis, they treat the creation of the world and of humankind, human dominion over creation, sin and its consequences. The first sermon opens the Lenten season by praising fasting and almsgiving as the "spiritual spring" of the soul.

The Expositio in Psalmos is a Greek commentary on the Psalms by John Chrysostom, probably preached as homilies at Antioch during his priesthood (386–397), though the place and date are debated. It covers a selection of psalms, not the whole Psalter. It combines close reading of the text with moral exhortation, often drawing on the life of David. Some pieces transmitted with the collection are of doubtful authenticity. It is among the most substantial Greek patristic treatments of the Psalter.

This Greek homily on Psalm 50 (Psalm 51 in the Hebrew numbering), the Miserere, has come down under the name of John Chrysostom, but its authenticity is doubted. Its heading says it treats King David and the Apostle Paul, repentance, and verses of the Psalter that point to Christ, and urges hearers never to despair of salvation. The preacher reads David's plea for mercy as a model of penitence. He also treats David as a prophet who announced Christ's cross, burial, resurrection and the calling of the nations.

Spuria in Psalmos is a group of Greek writings on the Psalms that were handed down under the name of John Chrysostom but are not by him. Their authors are unknown, and they may date from anywhere between the fifth and the tenth century. The opening passage describes how David organised the Temple choirs under Asaph, Idithun, the sons of Korah, Ethan and others, and the instruments they used. It explains the term "diapsalma" as the point where one choir handed the rest of a psalm to another, citing Chronicles as evidence.

This Greek homily was preached by John Chrysostom as archbishop of Constantinople, usually dated to 399. In it he rebukes members of his congregation who stayed away from church to attend horse races in the hippodrome and shows in the theatre. Chrysostom describes the uproar of the crowds and warns that these spectacles corrupt the soul, especially through the lust aroused by watching actresses. He calls his hearers back to the church and to repentance. The sermon is an important witness to his long campaign against public entertainments and to daily life in the late antique city.

The Homilia de continentia is a Greek sermon on self-control and chastity (sōphrosynē). It has come down under the name of John Chrysostom, but it is regarded as spurious. Its real author and date are unknown. The preacher speaks to newly baptized Christians, who have "put on Christ" and received strength from the Spirit through the divine mysteries. He compares them to athletes going down into the stadium and urges them to value chastity above the other virtues as they enter the spiritual contest.

The Homily on the Lawgiver (De legislatore) is a Greek sermon attributed to Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria, who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. Like most of Severian's Greek homilies, it survived among the spurious works of his opponent John Chrysostom. It opens by praising the word of God as the true food and wealth of the soul, drawing on the Beatitudes and the Psalms of David. It then takes up the theme of the divine law and its giver. Its exact date is uncertain, but it probably belongs to Severian's years in Constantinople.

The Homily on Melchizedek is a Greek sermon that has come down under the name of John Chrysostom, though its authenticity has been questioned. It expounds the Apostle Paul's teaching on Melchizedek, the priest-king of Genesis 14 whom the Epistle to the Hebrews presents as a type of Christ's eternal priesthood. The preacher opens with an extended image of sailors at sea. Inexperienced passengers grow dizzy before the deep, while seasoned divers plunge in safely. He compares this to the soul tossed by passions and to the hearer facing the depths of apostolic thought.

The Homilia de perfecta caritate is a Greek sermon "on perfect love, on recompense according to the worth of deeds, and on compunction." It has come down among the works of John Chrysostom but is considered spurious, and its real author and date are unknown. It begins by calling every good deed the fruit of love, citing Christ and Paul. It then argues that God built mutual love into human life by making all people descend from one man and by giving different lands their own produce and different people their own skills, so that everyone depends on others.

Two Greek homilies by John Chrysostom, "On the Obscurity of the Prophecies", usually placed in his years as a preacher at Antioch, though their exact date is uncertain. Chrysostom compares studying Isaiah to sailing out onto open sea. He argues that the prophecies about Christ, the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews were deliberately left obscure, and that this served a purpose in God's plan. The homilies show how he thought about reading Scripture, especially the Old Testament prophets.

The Homily on the Serpent is a Greek sermon by Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. It follows a sermon given the day before, which had defended the glory of the Only-begotten Son against heretics. Severian now turns to Christ's prediction of his own cross. The title points to the bronze serpent that Moses lifted up in the wilderness, which Christ presented as a figure of his crucifixion. The homily shows Severian's Antiochene style of preaching and his concern with doctrinal controversy.

The Interpretatio in Danielem prophetam is a Greek commentary on the Book of Daniel that manuscripts attribute to John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople (died 407). Its authenticity is doubted, so it is usually listed among the works of Pseudo-Chrysostom, and its real author and date are uncertain. It goes through the biblical text chapter by chapter, starting with the young Hebrew captives at the Babylonian court. It explains the literal sense and draws moral lessons, contrasting outward physical beauty with the beauty of the soul that God seeks.

This is a Greek homily by John Chrysostom on Isaiah 45:7: "I the Lord God made light and darkness, making peace and creating evils." It was preached on a day of chariot races, and he praises the crowd for choosing church over the hippodrome. He follows another speaker who had addressed the congregation before him. Chrysostom contrasts the "spiritual theatre" of Scripture with the spectacles and celebrates God's wisdom in creation. He then explains the difficult verse, taking the "evils" God creates to mean calamities and afflictions rather than moral wickedness.

This Greek sermon by John Chrysostom is on John 5:19: "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do." Its opening says that it was preached after a bishop had given a brief address and then deliberately left the rest of the teaching to John. This points to his time as a presbyter at Antioch, though the exact date is uncertain. The homily defends the Son's full equality with the Father against Arian and Anomoean readings of the verse, which seemed to make the Son subordinate.

This is a Greek sermon by John Chrysostom on 2 Timothy 3:1, "This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come." It was preached at some point in his career as priest at Antioch and later archbishop of Constantinople (386–407). The exact date is uncertain. In the opening Chrysostom calls himself weak, poor and inexperienced in teaching. He praises his audience for its eagerness, comparing the listeners to young swallows waiting to be fed. He then turns to Paul's warning about the last days and the vices that mark them.

The Interpretatio in Isaiam prophetam is a Greek commentary on the Book of Isaiah by John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), the preacher of Antioch and later Archbishop of Constantinople. It probably dates from his years as a priest in Antioch, though the exact date is uncertain. The surviving Greek text explains the opening chapters of Isaiah verse by verse. It opens by praising the prophet's boldness of speech, his clear prophecy of Christ and his compassion for his people. It is a good example of the literal, moral approach to interpreting Scripture associated with Antioch.

This Greek sermon by John Chrysostom is on Jeremiah 10:23: "O Lord, I know that the way of man is not in himself; it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps." Its opening refers back to his earlier preaching on the quarrel between Peter and Paul at Antioch, which suggests it was delivered there during his years as a presbyter. Chrysostom compares hard passages of Scripture to steep, narrow roads that need careful attention. He explains the verse in a way that does not deny human free will.

The six homilies on the creation of the world are Greek sermons by Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria. He probably preached them in Constantinople around 400, while he was a popular preacher there. They follow the opening chapters of Genesis day by day, ending with the creation of humanity, and read the text in the literal manner of the Antiochene school, with extensive discussion of cosmology. Some manuscripts attribute them to John Chrysostom, and they were transmitted among his works. They are an important example of early Hexaemeron literature.

This is a Greek Christmas sermon handed down under the name of John Chrysostom. It opens with the words "I see a strange and novel mystery." Most scholars regard it as probably not authentic, though some have defended it, so its author and date are uncertain. In hymn-like prose it celebrates the Nativity at Bethlehem. Angels and shepherds sing together, heaven and earth seem to change places, and God becomes man without ceasing to be God. By his will and his love for humanity, he overcomes the order of nature.

This is a series of six Greek sermons attributed to John Chrysostom, probably preached between 386 and 407. They comment on Isaiah 6, where the prophet sees the Lord enthroned among the seraphim "in the year that King Uzziah died". The preacher praises his congregation's zeal at night vigils and urges order and reverence when singing God's praise, comparing it to the angels' hymn. He also treats Uzziah's presumption in burning incense and the dignity of the priesthood. Scholars have questioned whether some of the homilies are authentic.

This is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople around 400–404. It is dated roughly to 398–408. It takes as its theme the question the Jewish leaders put to Jesus in the temple: "By what authority are you doing these things?" (Matthew 21:23). The sermon opens by praising the fear of God and reverence for the divine law, which bring enlightenment. It then contrasts this humility with the arrogance of those who approached Christ "like tyrants" to challenge his authority.

This short Greek letter is addressed to Theodore of Mopsuestia and attributed to John Chrysostom, but it is considered spurious and is grouped among the Pseudo-Chrysostom writings. Its author and date are unknown. The writer, "sitting in solitude", thanks Theodore for the comfort his letter brought. He then reflects on virtue as the means of restoring the original beauty of the human being, made in God's image and likeness. Citing Genesis 1:31, he argues that no creature, not even the irrational animals, was created evil, though those who live without virtue come to resemble them.

The Synopsis Scripturae sacrae is an anonymous Greek overview of the books of the Bible. It has come down among the works of John Chrysostom but is generally regarded as spurious, and its date is uncertain. It opens by explaining why the New Testament is called "new" and argues that both Testaments share a single aim: the correction and amendment of humankind. It then goes through the scriptural books, summarising their contents and purpose. The work is an example of the introductory guides to the biblical canon written in the Greek Christian tradition.

The Homilies on the Gospel of Matthew are a series of ninety sermons in Greek by John Chrysostom. He preached them at Antioch around 390, while he was still a priest there. This part contains Homilies I–XLIV. The series works through Matthew's Gospel passage by passage, explaining its literal and historical sense and ending each sermon with moral exhortation, often about almsgiving, care for the poor and Christian conduct. It is the oldest complete patristic commentary on Matthew to survive. It was widely read in both East and West and remains one of Chrysostom's most important exegetical works.

This is a set of miscellaneous Greek material that goes with the homilies of John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) on the Gospel of Matthew, preached at Antioch around 390. It includes prefatory and editorial matter and short pieces not catalogued separately. One of these is an anonymous later preface. Its author notes that Chrysostom ended each exposition of a Gospel passage with a moral exhortation, and says he has placed short summaries of these ethical sections at the front so readers can grasp their substance quickly and easily.

This is the second half of John Chrysostom's ninety homilies on the Gospel of Matthew. He preached them at Antioch around 390, while he was still a priest there. Homilies XLV–XC run from the parable discourse of Matthew 13 to the end of the Gospel. Each homily explains the passage verse by verse, then ends with moral exhortation, often on almsgiving, wealth and care for the poor. It is the earliest complete patristic commentary on Matthew to survive, and it was widely read in both East and West.

The Homilies on the Gospel of John are a series of eighty-eight sermons in Greek by John Chrysostom. He preached them at Antioch around 390 to 392, while he was still a priest there and before he became archbishop of Constantinople. Working through the Fourth Gospel passage by passage, they explain its literal meaning and defend the full divinity of the Son against Arian (Anomoean) teaching. Each sermon usually ends with moral exhortation. The series is among the most important patristic commentaries on John, and it circulated widely in translation, including into Old Georgian.

This is a collection of miscellaneous material from volume 59 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca. That volume is devoted mainly to John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) and above all to his Homilies on the Gospel of John. The material includes editorial front matter, notes and shorter pieces that are not indexed separately. Among them are titles and opening words of homilies attributed to Chrysostom. One was preached at a martyr's shrine to a small winter congregation, urging people to attend church regularly and to repent. Others concern a night procession carrying martyrs' relics through Constantinople, attended by the empress and the emperor.

These spuria are a group of Greek sermons that were handed down under the name of John Chrysostom (died 407) but are not by him. Their authors are anonymous, and their dates are uncertain; they may come from anywhere between the fifth and tenth centuries. The surviving opening deals with the faith of the Canaanite woman of the Gospels. It contrasts her with unbelievers, who are no true children of Abraham, of Canaanites or even of stones. Such texts show how widely Chrysostom's authority was borrowed in Byzantine preaching.

The Homilies on the Acts of the Apostles are a series of fifty-five Greek sermons by John Chrysostom. He preached them at Constantinople while he was archbishop, around 400 to 401. In the first homily Chrysostom observes that many Christians hardly knew the book existed, and he sets out to make it known. He works through Acts in order, mixing explanation of the text with moral exhortation, and he gives particular attention to the work of the Holy Spirit in the apostles. The series is the only complete commentary on Acts to survive from the early Church.

This item collects the editorial and other material in volume 60 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca that is not indexed as separate works. The volume mainly contains John Chrysostom's homilies on the Acts of the Apostles and on Romans. The material includes prefaces, notes and short unindexed pieces. The opening is a Latin editorial notice on the fifty homilies on Acts. Quoting passages from the homilies themselves, it argues that Chrysostom preached them at Constantinople around the third year of his episcopate, about 400. It also discusses their style and how often they were delivered.

This is a group of Greek sermons that manuscripts attribute to John Chrysostom (died 407), but which are now considered spurious. Their authors are anonymous, and their dates are uncertain, possibly ranging from the fifth century into the Byzantine period. The group includes a series of homilies on fasting. Drawing on Christ's teaching in Matthew 6, they argue that true fasting means turning away from sin, slander, usury, envy and fornication, forgiving one's neighbour, and feeding the hungry. They also present the fast as a contest that prepares believers for Christ's coming.

The Homilies on First Corinthians are a series of forty-four Greek sermons by John Chrysostom that work through Paul's First Epistle to the Corinthians verse by verse. They are usually assigned to his years as a priest at Antioch (386–398), although their exact date is uncertain. An introductory "Argument" describes Corinth's wealth and learning and Paul's mission there. The homilies then deal with factions, pride in human wisdom, marriage, the Eucharist, spiritual gifts and the resurrection. Each one ends with moral exhortation, often on almsgiving. They are among the most complete early patristic expositions of the epistle.

The Homilies on Second Corinthians are a series of thirty Greek sermons by John Chrysostom that work through Paul's Second Epistle to the Corinthians. They are usually dated to his years as a presbyter at Antioch (386–398), although the exact date and place are uncertain. Each homily explains a passage of the letter, including its themes of divine consolation in suffering, Paul's defence of his apostleship and the collection for Jerusalem, and then ends with moral exhortation. The series is one of the main patristic commentaries on this epistle.

This is a collection of Greek sermons that were handed down under the name of John Chrysostom (died 407) but are now considered spurious. Their authors are mostly anonymous, and the pieces date from different periods, probably between the fifth century and the end of the first millennium. Many are festal homilies. One of them, on the Theophany, gives John the Baptist a speech at the Jordan in which he protests to Christ, "I have need to be baptized by you." The attribution to Chrysostom helped these works survive.

The Homilies on First Thessalonians are a series of eleven Greek sermons by John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), preacher at Antioch and later Archbishop of Constantinople. They work through Paul's First Epistle to the Thessalonians passage by passage. Chrysostom explains the text's literal sense, such as why Timothy is named in the greeting, and then turns to moral exhortation. Where and when they were preached, whether at Antioch or at Constantinople, is uncertain. The series belongs to his large body of exegetical homilies on the Pauline letters, which were widely read in both East and West.

This is a series of eighteen Greek homilies by John Chrysostom on Paul's First Epistle to Timothy. They were preached between 386 and 407, but scholars disagree on whether he gave them as a priest in Antioch or as archbishop of Constantinople. An introductory "Argument" presents Timothy as Paul's trusted disciple. The homilies then go through the letter in order, with moral exhortation throughout. They cover sound teaching, prayer, the qualifications of bishops and deacons, the care of widows, and the dangers of wealth. They are an important early witness to patristic thinking on church order and pastoral ministry.

The Homilies on Second Thessalonians are a series of five Greek sermons by John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), preacher at Antioch and later Archbishop of Constantinople. They expound Paul's Second Epistle to the Thessalonians verse by verse. Exactly when and where they were preached is uncertain. Chrysostom explains why Paul wrote again after his first letter and addresses the Thessalonians' confusion about the coming of Christ. He discusses the "man of sin" at length and takes the power restraining him to be the Roman Empire. Throughout, he joins this exegesis to moral exhortation, as in his other homilies on Paul's letters.

The Homilies on Colossians are a series of twelve sermons in Greek by John Chrysostom. They give a continuous, verse-by-verse commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Colossians. They are usually dated to his years as archbishop of Constantinople (398–404), though the exact date is uncertain. Chrysostom treats Colossians as one of the letters Paul wrote while imprisoned. He explains its teaching on Christ's supremacy and warns against false doctrine, and he draws out practical moral lessons for his congregation. The series belongs to his extensive cycle of homilies on the Pauline epistles.

The Homilies on Ephesians are a series of twenty-four Greek sermons by John Chrysostom explaining Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians verse by verse. They were preached at some point between his ordination as a priest at Antioch in 386 and his death in 407. Whether they belong to his Antioch or his Constantinople years is disputed. An introductory argument describes Ephesus and its learned culture. The homilies combine close reading of the text with moral exhortation, especially on church unity, Christian conduct, and marriage and household life.

The Homilies on Philippians are a series of fifteen sermons in Greek by John Chrysostom on Paul's Epistle to the Philippians. Like his other homilies on Paul, they work through the letter in order and pair close explanation of the text with moral exhortation. An introductory discourse on Philippi and Paul's imprisonment comes first. Scholars disagree about whether they were preached at Antioch or at Constantinople, so their date is uncertain. They are among the most important early Greek commentaries on the epistle, notably for their reading of the Christological hymn in chapter 2.

This is a group of anonymous Greek writings, mostly homilies, that were once attributed to John Chrysostom but are now considered spurious. They are gathered among the doubtful works in volume 62 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca. Their authors and dates are unknown, and they may come from anywhere between the fifth and the tenth centuries. The opening piece is a sermon on fasting. It argues that the soul should rule the body and uses biblical examples: Adam, who failed to abstain from a single tree; Esau, who sold his birthright for food; and Moses, who fasted forty days.

The Sermo de mansuetudine ("Sermon on Meekness") is a Greek homily that has come down under the name of John Chrysostom, the preacher and Archbishop of Constantinople who died in 407. Its date and authenticity are uncertain. The surviving text opens with an argument against heretics, apparently the Anomoeans, over the word "unbegotten" (agennētos) as a title for the Father. It argues that many things never brought into being are also called unbegotten, such as the beasts and the statue in Daniel's visions and Judas, of whom Christ said it would have been better if he had not been born.

The Eclogae ex diversis homiliis is a Greek collection of forty-eight homilies, or excerpts, transmitted under the name of John Chrysostom. Each piece is put together from passages of Chrysostom's genuine sermons, rearranged by theme. The compilation is usually ascribed to the tenth-century Byzantine writer Theodore Daphnopates, though its date and authorship are not certain. The section shown here praises the protomartyr Stephen as the first "athlete" to win a martyr's crown. The collection shows how Byzantine readers later reworked and passed on Chrysostom's preaching.

The Homiliae XI is a group of eleven Greek sermons by John Chrysostom, preached in Constantinople while he was archbishop there (398–404). They were delivered on different occasions, often in the city's martyria and churches. The first was given at the martyrium "at the Old Rock". In it Chrysostom rebukes those who stayed away from the gathering, attacks avarice, and urges his hearers to repent and not despair of salvation. The homilies are a useful source for his pastoral preaching and for church life in the capital during his time as archbishop.

John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople, preached this series of thirty-four Greek homilies on the Epistle to the Hebrews, probably in Constantinople in the last years of his episcopate. They were published only after his death, from notes taken by Constantine, a presbyter of Antioch. The series opens with an introduction that treats the letter as Paul's and asks why the Apostle of the Gentiles wrote to Hebrews. The sermons then go through the epistle in order, joining exegesis to moral exhortation. They remain one of the most important early commentaries on Hebrews.

A Greek sermon on the opening verse of the Gospel of John, "In the beginning was the Word", attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400. It continues a sermon given the previous day and calls the evangelist John a soaring eagle and a voice of thunder. Severian sets the Gospel's "was" against the heretics' claim that "there was when he was not", defending the eternal and passionless begetting of the Word against Arian teaching. Like most of Severian's Greek homilies, it has come down under the name of John Chrysostom.

The Homily on the Seals of the Books (De sigillis librorum) is a Greek sermon by Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. Like most of Severian's Greek homilies, it has come down among the spurious works attributed to his rival, John Chrysostom. It opens by praising the divine word as the soul's food and sets it against worldly, sophistic wisdom, citing Moses and Paul. It then turns to scriptural interpretation, explaining the sealed books of Scripture as mysteries opened by Christ.

De natura hominis ("On the Constitution of Man") is a Byzantine Greek treatise on human anatomy and physiology by Meletius the Monk. He describes himself as a monk of the Holy Trinity monastery near Tiberiopolis in the Opsikion theme. Its date is uncertain, with estimates ranging from the ninth to the eleventh century. The author presents it as a concise and complete synopsis. It draws on Hippocrates, Galen and the Church Fathers, including Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, John Chrysostom and Cyril, to describe the body's parts, faculties and activities within a Christian framework.

This is a miscellaneous group of Greek texts in volume 64 of the Patrologia Graeca, the final volume of the works of John Chrysostom (bishop of Constantinople, d. 407). It covers front matter, notes and pieces not separately indexed, many of them of doubtful or spurious attribution. The opening passage comes from a homily praising David and the Psalms. It shows how the Psalter speaks to every condition of life, including children, virgins, sinners, penitents and priests, and calls it a great lyre. Authorship and dates of the individual pieces vary and are often uncertain.

This is a collection of Greek homilies and fragments under the name of John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople (d. 407). It brings together pieces that were left out of Bernard de Montfaucon's standard edition of his works. Many of these texts are of doubtful or spurious authorship, and they may date from anywhere between the fifth and tenth centuries. The opening piece urges believers to hold to the faith handed down by Scripture and the Fathers rather than argue over it. It affirms that Christ will return in his risen body to judge the living and the dead.

The alphabetical collection of the Apophthegmata Patrum, or Sayings of the Desert Fathers, is an anonymous Greek compilation of brief sayings and anecdotes of the monks of Egypt's deserts, especially Scetis. It was probably put together in the later fifth century, possibly in Palestine, though its date and place are uncertain. A prologue explains its arrangement. Sayings are grouped under the names of individual abbas in Greek alphabetical order, beginning with Antony, Arsenius and Agathon. Anonymous material follows in a supplement arranged by theme. It is a foundational source for early monastic spirituality.

This is a small collection of Greek writings by Atticus, archbishop of Constantinople from 406 until his death in 425. It brings together a letter and fragments that survive mostly as quotations in later authors, church historians and conciliar records. Atticus, who opposed John Chrysostom and later the Pelagians, wrote little that survives whole. These pieces matter as evidence of the doctrine and church politics of Constantinople in the years before the Nestorian controversy, and of his reputation among his successors, including Proclus.

This Greek collection groups writings attributed to Diadochus, the fifth-century bishop of Photice in Epirus. Its best-known part, the Hundred Chapters on Spiritual Perfection (also called the Gnostic Chapters), is a set of short ascetic sayings on faith, love, discernment, the prayer of the heart and the experience of grace. The chapters were later included in the Philokalia and influenced Maximus the Confessor, John Climacus and the Hesychast tradition. The collection also contains a homily on the Ascension and polemic against Arian teaching on the eternity of the Word.

The Opuscula are the collected short Greek writings attributed to Mark the Hermit, also called Mark the Ascetic or Marcus Eremita, an ascetic author of the fifth century. Most of the treatises give practical guidance on monastic life. Among them are On the Spiritual Law and On Those Who Think They Are Justified by Works, both written as series of short numbered sayings on prayer, humility, grace, compunction and watchfulness over one's thoughts. Other pieces deal with repentance and baptism. Several of these writings were later included in the Philokalia and became influential in Eastern Christian spirituality.

The Historia monachorum in Aegypto, also called the "Paradise" of the Egyptian monks, is an anonymous Greek travel narrative written around the end of the fourth century. Its author was one of a small party of monks from a community on the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem who toured the monastic settlements of Egypt around 394–395. At his brethren's request he recorded the lives, sayings and miracles of the ascetics they met, beginning with John of Lycopolis. Rufinus of Aquileia made a Latin version, and the work is an important early source for Egyptian monasticism.

The Ecclesiastical History of Philostorgius (368–c. 439), a Cappadocian historian who followed the Anomoean teaching of Eunomius, was written in Greek in twelve books and appeared between about 425 and 433. It covered church history from the Arian controversy into the early fifth century from a non-Nicene point of view. The original is lost. It survives mainly through the epitome made by Photius of Constantinople in the ninth century. Photius summarised the work critically, but his epitome keeps a rare account of the period from the side of the losing party.

This is the collected homilies (orations) and letters of Proclus, archbishop of Constantinople from 434 to 446, written in Greek between about 426 and 446. The homilies are known for their rhetorical style and rich Marian imagery. The first homily, on the Virgin Mary as Theotokos ("God-bearer"), was preached at Constantinople in the presence of Nestorius and became an important text in the Nestorian controversy. Among the letters is the Tome to the Armenians, a key statement of Christology. Together these writings make Proclus one of the earliest major Marian theologians.

In theophaniam is a Greek homily for the feast of the Theophany, celebrating Christ's baptism and manifestation. It has come down under the name of John Chrysostom but is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400 and later opposed Chrysostom. Like many of Severian's sermons, it survived among Chrysostom's spurious works. In rhetorical style, the homily calls all creation to praise the coming of Christ and presents the Church as an earthly community taking part in the worship of the angels.

This is a set of short disciplinary rulings in Greek by Theophilus, Patriarch of Alexandria from 385 to 412. It brings together a prosphonesis (address) on how to keep the Epiphany fast when the feast falls on a Sunday, a commonitory (memorandum) given to Ammon, letters to Agatho and Menas, and a ruling on the Cathari (Novatianists). Among the questions they answer are the treatment of clergy who had communicated with Arians, unworthy ordinations, fasting and the reception of returning schismatics.
