The Council in Trullo (692) accepted these rulings into the Byzantine collection of canons of the Fathers.

This is a small group of Greek ascetic texts attributed to Arsenius the Great (c. 354–450). He was a Roman imperial tutor who became an anchorite at Scetis and later Troe in Egypt. The "Teaching and Exhortation" is addressed to monks. It argues that the purpose of leaving the world is to purify the soul, and that inner purity of mind matters as much as bodily discipline. The collection also contains his sayings from the Apophthegmata Patrum and a short piece, "To a Lawyer Who Tested Him". Whether Arsenius wrote all of these pieces is uncertain.

This is a miscellany of editorial material from volume 66 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the volume given mainly to Theodore of Mopsuestia and other Antiochene writers of the late fourth and early fifth centuries. It contains front matter, notes and short pieces not indexed separately. The Greek passages include references to Theodoret's Ecclesiastical History, which spans the 105 years from the Arian controversy to the deaths of Theodore and Theodotus. There are also excerpts from John Chrysostom's letters to the lapsed Theodore. It has no single author or unified subject.

This is the collected writings of Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–c. 414), a Neoplatonist philosopher and pupil of Hypatia who became bishop of Ptolemais around 410. It includes De regno, a speech on kingship addressed to the emperor Arcadius at Constantinople. Dion defends his ideal of the cultivated philosophical life. The Praise of Baldness is a playful rhetorical piece, and De providentia, also called the Egyptian Tale, is a political allegory. The collection also contains a treatise on dreams, a letter accompanying the gift of an astrolabe, about 150 letters, and hymns that blend Neoplatonic and Christian thought.

This is a collection of Greek fragments from the doctrinal writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia (c. 350–428). Most come from his treatise On the Incarnation, which survives only in quotations. In the opening passage, from its seventh book, Theodore asks how God dwells in human beings. He rejects indwelling by essence or by operation and argues instead for indwelling by divine good pleasure. Many of these excerpts were kept by hostile writers and by the Second Council of Constantinople (553), which condemned Theodore. They are central evidence for Antiochene Christology.

This is a collection of Greek fragments from the Old Testament commentaries of Theodore of Mopsuestia (c. 350–428), the leading exegete of the Antiochene school. It covers Genesis, the Psalms, Job and the Song of Songs. Theodore was condemned after his death at the Second Council of Constantinople in 553, and most of his works were then lost in Greek. These passages survive mainly as quotations in catenae and other later writings. They show his literal, historical method of interpretation, as in his explanation of the heavenly lights and the seventh day of creation.

These are fragments of New Testament commentaries by Theodore of Mopsuestia (c. 350–428), bishop of Mopsuestia and the leading exegete of the Antiochene school. They are short verse-by-verse explanations that survive mainly in Byzantine catenae, the chains of excerpts from earlier commentators. The opening passages cover Matthew's Gospel: the Holy Spirit's role in forming Christ's body, Herod's slaughter of the infants, the dove at the baptism, and the temptation. After Theodore's condemnation in 553, most of his Greek works were lost, so these fragments are important evidence for his literal, historical style of interpretation.

The Commentary on the Twelve Minor Prophets is a Greek biblical commentary by Theodore of Mopsuestia (c. 350–428), the leading exegete of the Antiochene school. It is usually counted among his earlier writings, but its exact date is uncertain. It works through Hosea to Malachi and reads the prophecies mainly in their historical setting in Israel's past. Theodore avoids allegory and keeps messianic readings to a minimum. Most of his works were lost after his condemnation in 553, but this commentary survives complete in Greek. That makes it a key witness to Antiochene method.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in seven books by Socrates of Constantinople, also called Socrates Scholasticus. It was written in the 440s and continues Eusebius's history, covering events from 305 to 439: Constantine's conversion, the Arian controversy, the councils, and the affairs of the churches of the eastern empire. Socrates aimed for a plain style and drew on documents and on eyewitnesses. Sozomen used the work as a source. In the sixth century it was put into Latin as part of the Historia Tripartita, which carried it into the medieval West.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in nine books by Sozomen, a lawyer at Constantinople. He wrote it around the 440s and dedicated it to Emperor Theodosius II. It was meant to continue the work of Eusebius and covers events from the 320s to the 420s. The ninth book seems unfinished and stops short of the end date the author announced. Sozomen drew heavily on Socrates Scholasticus but added much material of his own, especially on monasticism, missions and the Church outside the empire. It is a key source for fourth- and early fifth-century Christianity.

This exegetical treatise in seventeen books by Cyril of Alexandria, written in Greek, is generally dated to the early part of his episcopate, before the Nestorian controversy. It takes the form of a dialogue between Cyril and a certain Palladius. It reads selected passages of the Pentateuch spiritually, showing that the Mosaic law, the tabernacle, the priesthood and the sacrifices were types of Christ and the Church. It covers sin and repentance, justification in Christ, love of God and neighbour, and worship "in spirit and in truth". Its companion work is the Glaphyra.

This is supplementary material from volume 68 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the first of the volumes devoted to Cyril of Alexandria, bishop of Alexandria from 412 to 444. It includes the volume's front matter, editorial notes and shorter pieces not separately indexed. Among them is a bibliographical notice listing Cyril's writings, such as the Thesaurus on the Trinity, On Adoration in Spirit and Truth, the defences of the Twelve Chapters and the reply to Julian, together with their opening words and later testimonies praising him as a teacher of orthodox doctrine.

The Explanatio in Psalmos is a Greek commentary on the Book of Psalms attributed to Cyril of Alexandria, Patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444. Its exact date is uncertain. It survives only in fragments, chiefly preserved in exegetical catenae, and the authenticity of some passages is debated. A short prologue praises the study of Scripture and notes how much the Psalms are sung in the Church. The commentary then explains individual psalms, often reading them in reference to Christ and the Church, as is typical of Alexandrian exegesis.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments attributed to Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch from 412 to 444. They comment on the biblical canticles, namely the Songs of Moses in Exodus and Deuteronomy and the Song of Hannah, and on Proverbs and the Song of Songs. Such fragments survive mainly in catenae, and the authenticity of some is uncertain. The comments are brief, give a moral and spiritual reading, and defend proper language about God. One example explains that when Scripture calls God "jealous", this does not mean the divine nature is subject to passion.

The Fragmenta in libros Regnorum are Greek exegetical fragments on the Books of Kingdoms, the Septuagint name for the books of Samuel and Kings. They are attributed to Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch from 412 to 444, and survive as excerpts in catenae, the chains of patristic comments arranged around the biblical text. Some passages are explicitly drawn from Cyril's other works, such as his commentary on Matthew. The fragments discuss episodes such as Israel's demand for a king before Samuel, Saul's early career and Doeg the Edomite's betrayal of David. Their authenticity varies from fragment to fragment.

The Glaphyra ("Elegant Comments") is a Greek exegetical work by Cyril of Alexandria, generally dated to the early years of his episcopate, before the Nestorian controversy began around 429. In thirteen books, seven on Genesis and six on Exodus through Deuteronomy, it takes selected narratives and laws of the Pentateuch and reads them as figures of the mystery of Christ and the Church. It accompanies Cyril's earlier dialogue On Adoration in Spirit and Truth, and it is a major example of Alexandrian typological interpretation of the Old Testament.

This is a set of miscellaneous Greek material from volume 69 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the volume given to writings of Cyril of Alexandria, bishop from 412 to 444. It includes front matter, editorial notes and pieces not catalogued separately. The opening section heading states that the mystery of Christ is shown in hidden form throughout the writings of Moses, and then turns to Cain and Abel. This matches the start of Cyril's Glaphyra, his typological commentary on the Pentateuch, which reads Old Testament stories as pointing to Christ.

The Commentary on Isaiah is a Greek exegetical work by Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444. It is usually dated to the early part of his episcopate, before the Nestorian controversy began around 429. Working through the book of Isaiah, the commentary explains both the historical sense and the spiritual meaning of the prophecy. Its prologue presents Christ as the end of the law and the prophets. Cyril admits that earlier writers have commented on Isaiah but hopes to add new insight. The work is a major example of Alexandrian exegesis of the Old Testament.

The Fragmenta in Jeremiam, Baruch et Danielem is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the books of Jeremiah, Baruch and Daniel. They are attributed to Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch from 412 to 444, and survive mainly in the catenae, the medieval chains of patristic biblical commentary. The comments go through the prophetic text verse by verse. They attack Israel's idolatry on the hills and mountains, describe God's anger tempered by mercy toward Jerusalem, and read the prophecies in the light of Christ. As with many catena excerpts, the attribution of individual fragments is not always certain.

Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch from 412 to 444, wrote this Greek commentary on the twelve Minor Prophets, from Hosea to Malachi. It is usually dated to the earlier part of his episcopate, before the Nestorian controversy. The preface admits that many have already explained the prophets but argues that further interpretation still helps readers. Cyril reads each prophet first in its historical setting and then spiritually, as pointing to Christ and the Church. It is the fullest surviving patristic commentary on these books.

Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444, wrote a commentary on the Gospel of Luke as a series of homilies. It survives almost complete only in a Syriac translation. These Greek fragments are passages from the commentary preserved mainly in the exegetical anthologies called catenae. They follow the Gospel text verse by verse and stress Cyril's Christology: the unchangeable divine Word became flesh and was made visible and tangible. The fragments are important evidence for Cyril's preaching and his reading of Scripture.

These are Greek fragments of a commentary on the Gospel of Matthew attributed to Cyril of Alexandria, Patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444. The complete work is lost. What survives are excerpts preserved in the exegetical chains (catenae) of Byzantine manuscripts, so the extent and date of the original are uncertain. The passages explain the Gospel verse by verse, often reading it typologically. Abraham, for example, prefigures the Church drawn from both Jews and Gentiles, and David prefigures Christ as the second Adam. They are evidence of Cyril's lesser-known work on the New Testament.

Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch from 412 to 444, wrote this Greek commentary on the twelve Minor Prophets, from Hosea to Malachi. It is usually dated to the earlier part of his episcopate, before the Nestorian controversy. The preface admits that many have already explained the prophets but argues that further interpretation still helps readers. Cyril reads each prophet first in its historical setting and then spiritually, as pointing to Christ and the Church. It is the fullest surviving patristic commentary on these books.

Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444, wrote this Greek exegetical commentary on the Gospel of John. This part contains its first six books. The full work had twelve books, of which books seven and eight survive only in fragments. It is usually dated before the Nestorian controversy, around 425–429. Cyril reads the Gospel closely, verse by verse, and pays most attention to doctrine. He argues at length against Arian and Eunomian teaching that the Son is lesser than the Father. The commentary is one of the most important patristic studies of John.

The Fragments on the Acts of the Apostles are Greek exegetical passages attributed to Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444. They survive only as excerpts preserved under his name in catenae, the chains of patristic commentary on Scripture. It is not known whether they come from a full commentary on Acts or were taken from his other writings. The surviving comments include remarks on Pentecost and the gift of tongues, and on Joel's prophecy of signs in heaven. Cyril reads that prophecy as fulfilled in the darkness and portents at the crucifixion.

These are fragments of Greek commentary on the Catholic Epistles of James, 1 Peter and Jude, attributed to Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch from 412 to 444. Like much of Cyril's exegesis, they survive only in excerpts, probably preserved in catenae, and no complete commentary is known. The surviving passages argue for the divinity of the Son, who judges and rewards every person. They also urge offering God the "sacrifice of praise" from the lips rather than material offerings, citing the prophet Hosea.

This is a collection of Greek fragments from Cyril of Alexandria's exegetical commentaries on Paul's Epistles to the Romans, First and Second Corinthians and Hebrews. The complete commentaries are lost, and the surviving passages were preserved mainly in catenae, the chains of patristic comments arranged verse by verse. Their date is uncertain but falls within Cyril's episcopate (412–444). The comments explain Paul's text through Cyril's theology. They contrast Christ's sonship by nature with the believer's adoptive sonship received through the Spirit in baptism. Other topics include knowing God through creation and God's faithfulness despite human unbelief.

These are the second half of Cyril of Alexandria's Greek commentary on the Gospel of John, a verse-by-verse exposition in twelve books. It is generally dated to the years before the Nestorian controversy broke out in 429. Books 7 and 8 survive only in fragments, picking up at John 10. The later books carry the exposition through the end of the Gospel. Cyril stresses that Christ is God by nature, especially against Arian readings. The work is one of the most substantial patristic commentaries on the Fourth Gospel.

De incarnatione Domini (On the Incarnation of the Lord) is a Greek theological treatise by Theodoret of Cyrrhus. It was probably written around 429–431, as the Nestorian controversy began and before the Council of Ephesus. It was long transmitted under the name of Cyril of Alexandria, but modern scholarship has restored it to Theodoret. Beginning with the creation of humanity in God's image and Adam's fall, it sets out the divine plan of salvation. It then defends an Antiochene Christology that firmly distinguishes Christ's complete divine and human natures.

On the Incarnation of the Only-begotten is a Greek theological dialogue by Cyril of Alexandria, usually dated to about 429–431, during the early Nestorian controversy. Two speakers discuss the incarnation of the Word. Its opening presents it as a sequel to the speakers' earlier discussion of the Son's divinity, probably Cyril's seven Dialogues on the Trinity. The dialogue argues that Christ is one Lord, the Word made flesh, against teachings that divide him into two. Cyril later reworked the text into his dialogue That Christ Is One. It is a key witness to his Christology before the Council of Ephesus.

The Dialogues on the Holy and Consubstantial Trinity is a Greek theological treatise in seven dialogues by Cyril of Alexandria. It was written during his episcopate, before the Nestorian controversy, probably in the 420s. Cyril dedicates the work to a "brother Nemesinus." It takes the form of questions and answers between two speakers marked A and B, one of whom is named Hermias. The dialogues defend the full divinity and consubstantiality of the Son and the Holy Spirit against Arian and Eunomian arguments. Together with Cyril's Thesaurus, it is one of his main works on the Trinity.

De sacrosancta Trinitate is a Greek theological treatise on the Holy and life-giving Trinity, handed down under the name of Cyril of Alexandria but not by him. It opens by arguing that church teaching should be simple and instructive rather than dialectical, then sets out orthodox doctrine of God and the Trinity. Its date was long disputed, and some scholars once treated it as a source of John of Damascus. It has since been identified as an extract from the work of Joseph the Philosopher, a Byzantine scholar of the early fourteenth century.

That Christ is One is a Greek theological dialogue by Cyril of Alexandria, generally dated to the later 430s, after the Council of Ephesus. It is set as a conversation between Cyril and an interlocutor named Hermias. The work defends the unity of Christ as one incarnate Son against the teaching associated with Nestorius. Cyril upholds the title Theotokos for Mary and rejects a mere "connection" between the Word and a man. He then answers the scriptural objections drawn from Christ's human weaknesses. It is regarded as one of the most mature statements of his Christology.

The Scholia on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten is a Christological treatise by Cyril of Alexandria. It was written in Greek in the 1430s, probably soon after the Council of Ephesus of 431. It is made up of short numbered chapters. These explain the meaning of the title "Christ", the anointing of the Word made flesh and the union of divinity and humanity in one Son. Throughout, Cyril argues against the teaching of Nestorius. The Greek original survives only in part, and the full text is preserved in an early Latin translation, traditionally credited to Marius Mercator.

The Thesaurus on the Holy and Consubstantial Trinity is a Greek dogmatic treatise by Cyril of Alexandria. He wrote it in his early years as patriarch, before the Nestorian controversy, probably between about 412 and 425. It is dedicated to a fellow Christian named Nemesinus. The work is a large collection of arguments against the Arians and Eunomians, defending the full divinity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit and their consubstantiality with the Father. It draws heavily on Athanasius's writings against the Arians and is an important witness to Cyril's early Trinitarian theology.

Adversus anthropomorphitas ("Against the Anthropomorphites") is a Greek letter by Cyril of Alexandria, bishop of Alexandria from 412 to 444, addressed to Calosyrius, bishop of Arsinoe. Its exact date is unknown. Cyril had heard reports about monks of the mountain of Calamon in Egypt, and he rebukes some of them who argued that, because humanity was made in God's image, God must have a human form. Against this he holds that God is incorporeal, citing Christ's words "God is spirit." The letter is a witness to the anthropomorphite controversy among Egyptian monks in the late fourth and fifth centuries.

The Five Tomes against Nestorius is a polemical treatise in five books by Cyril of Alexandria, written around 430 on the eve of the Council of Ephesus. Cyril quotes passages from a published collection of Nestorius's sermons and refutes them one by one. He defends the title Theotokos ("Mother of God") for the Virgin Mary and insists that the Word truly became flesh in a single union of person, not by mere indwelling or conjunction. He appeals to Scripture and the Nicene Creed. The work is a key statement of Cyril's Christology.

The Apologeticus pro XII capitibus contra Orientales is a Greek treatise by Cyril of Alexandria, written around 431. In it he defends his Twelve Chapters, or anathemas, against Nestorius from the objections of the Eastern bishops associated with Antioch, chiefly Andrew of Samosata. Cyril takes each anathema in turn, quotes the Eastern criticism and answers it, arguing for the single subject of the incarnate Word. It is one of several defences of the anathemas he produced during the controversy around the Council of Ephesus. Others were addressed to Theodoret of Cyrus and to the council itself.

This is a Greek polemical treatise by Cyril of Alexandria, written around 431 in the form of a letter to his fellow bishop Euoptius. In it Cyril answers the critique that Theodoret of Cyrrhus had written against his Twelve Anathemas, the propositions directed at Nestorius. Cyril quotes Theodoret's objections to each anathema in turn and gives his reply. He defends the union of divine and human in the one Christ and rejects charges of Apollinarianism. The work is a key document of the controversy around the Council of Ephesus.

Against Julian is an apologetic treatise in Greek by Cyril of Alexandria, usually dated to the 430s or early 440s and dedicated to Emperor Theodosius II. It refutes the emperor Julian the Apostate's polemic Against the Galileans, which attacked Christianity. Cyril quotes Julian's arguments at length and answers them one by one, defending Scripture and Christian doctrine against Greek philosophy and pagan religion. Ten books survive complete, with fragments of later books. The work matters as the main source for reconstructing Julian's lost treatise.

This Greek treatise by Cyril of Alexandria was written around 430, during the Nestorian controversy. It is one of three treatises "On the True Faith" that Cyril sent to the court of Emperor Theodosius II: one to the emperor and two to the imperial women. This second address to the royal ladies, usually identified as the Augustae Pulcheria and Eudocia, collects arguments and patristic and scriptural testimonies for the unity of Christ as one incarnate Son. It also defends Mary's title Theotokos against Nestorius. Theodosius reportedly took offence at the separate appeals to his household.

The Explanation of the Twelve Chapters is a Greek treatise by Cyril of Alexandria, written at Ephesus in 431 at the time of the Council of Ephesus. According to its heading, the council asked Cyril to set out more clearly the meaning of his twelve anathemas against Nestorius. Cyril takes each chapter in turn, explaining and defending his teaching that the incarnate Word is one subject, against the charge that his propositions were heretical. It is a key source for understanding Cyril's Christology in the Nestorian controversy.

Fragmenta dogmatica is a modern editorial title for a group of short Greek theological excerpts attributed to Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch from 412 to 444. They survive as quotations by later writers and compilers rather than as complete works. One excerpt comes from a treatise against those who denied that prayers and the eucharistic offering should be made for the faithful departed. Cyril defends this practice of the Church. The surrounding material reads the name of Abraham as a figure of the Trinity. The authenticity of individual fragments varies and is not always certain.

This short Greek treatise, transmitted under the name of Cyril of Alexandria, is titled "Against those who do not wish to confess that the Holy Virgin is Theotokos". It belongs to the Nestorian controversy of the 420s–430s, though its authenticity has been questioned. It opens by comparing God to doctors and ship's pilots who foresee dangers, noting that Christ warned of false teachers. It then names the newest heresy as the "dregs" of earlier errors. It defends calling Mary Mother of God, a title that follows from the unity of Christ's person.

This is a collection of short treatises, homilies and letters by bishops caught up in the Nestorian controversy around the Council of Ephesus in 431. The contributors include Theodotus of Ancyra, Paul of Emesa, Acacius of Beroea, John of Antioch, Memnon of Ephesus, Acacius of Melitene, Rabbula of Edessa, Firmus of Caesarea and Amphilochius of Side. It opens with Theodotus's exposition of the Nicene Creed. These texts date from roughly 425 to 460. They show the arguments over Christ's person and the title Theotokos from both the Cyrillian and Antiochene sides, and record the steps toward the reunion of 433.

Cyril of Alexandria wrote this synodal letter, his third letter to Nestorius, in 430 on behalf of an Alexandrian synod. It ends with twelve anathemas, propositions that condemn anyone who rejects the full unity of Christ. They insist that the Word is united to flesh "in hypostasis", that Christ is one and not two persons, and that Mary is Theotokos, the Mother of God. Nestorius replied with counter-anathemas, and the dispute between Alexandria and Antioch led to the Council of Ephesus in 431. The anathemas were read into the council's acts and remained central to later Christological debate.

These two short Greek letters by Cyril, Patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444, deal with church discipline. The exact date of each is uncertain. In the first, Cyril asks Domnus, a metropolitan, to call a synod to rehear the case of a deposed bishop named Peter. Peter said he had been denied a fair defence, stripped of his property and frightened into resigning. The second warns the bishops of Libya and Pentapolis against ordaining men who had been turned down by their own bishops or expelled from monasteries. The Eastern Church later counted both letters among its canonical writings.

Homiliae diversae ("Various Homilies") is a collection of miscellaneous Greek sermons attributed to Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444. Unlike his annual Paschal (festal) letters, these homilies were delivered on different occasions. Several are associated with the Council of Ephesus in 431, among them a celebrated sermon in praise of the Virgin Mary as Theotokos. They deal with Christ's incarnation, passion and resurrection, and with Christian moral life. Cyril's authorship of some pieces in the collection is doubted.

The Paschal Homilies, also called the Festal Letters, are a series of Greek pastoral letters by Cyril of Alexandria, sent out as patriarch roughly between 414 and 442. Following Alexandrian custom, each letter announced the dates of Lent and Easter for the year to the churches of Egypt. The letters also urge spiritual renewal, fasting and virtue, and they read Scripture typologically. Many argue against Jewish and pagan positions, and some state Cyril's teaching on the Incarnation, making them important evidence for his preaching and theology.

This collection brings together Greek writings falsely attributed to Cyril of Alexandria, chief among them the treatise On the Holy Trinity (De sacrosancta Trinitate). The treatise sets out the doctrine of God systematically, starting from the claim that knowledge of God's existence is implanted in human nature. It closely parallels John of Damascus's Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith. It was once thought to be one of John's sources, but scholars now generally attribute it to Joseph the Philosopher, a much later author. Its date is therefore disputed.

This is the Greek correspondence of Isidore of Pelusium (c. 370–c. 450), an Egyptian ascetic who lived near Pelusium. It was arranged in five books and survives as a collection of about 2,000 letters, compiled in antiquity at the monastery of the "Sleepless" monks in Constantinople. Most letters are brief. They were addressed to monks, clergy, officials and others, including Cyril of Alexandria and Theodosius II. They offer moral and ascetic advice and explain difficult passages of Scripture, and they are valued for their biblical exegesis.

This is a miscellany of editorial and ancillary material from the Patrologia Graeca volume devoted to Isidore of Pelusium (died c. 450). Isidore was an Egyptian monk and priest near Pelusium who wrote a very large collection of Greek letters. The pieces include notes, variant readings, cross-references to his letters and short biographical testimonies. These describe his Alexandrian origin, his monastic life and his ties to Theophilus and Cyril of Alexandria. One quoted letter rebukes Cyril for his conduct at the Council of Ephesus (431). The material is not a single work and has no single author.

This is a Greek collection of letters in four books, attributed to Nilus of Ancyra, a monastic writer and disciple of John Chrysostom who died around 430. It contains more than a thousand letters, most of them short, offering spiritual and moral counsel and scriptural interpretation to monks, clergy and lay officials. Among them are letters reproaching the emperor Arcadius for exiling Chrysostom. Many items appear to be excerpts or adaptations from other authors, and the authenticity of parts of the collection is disputed.

A Greek ascetic treatise on the eight evil thoughts (logismoi) or passions, traditionally attributed to Nilus of Ancyra (also called Nilus of Sinai), who died in the early fifth century. Modern scholars generally assign it to Evagrius Ponticus. It treats gluttony, fornication, avarice, anger, sadness, acedia, vainglory and pride in turn, setting each vice against its opposing virtue and giving practical counsel on matters such as moderate fasting. The scheme of eight vices shaped later monastic teaching and the Western list of capital sins. The treatise is accompanied by fragments of Nilus's sermons preserved by Photius.

This is a collection of shorter Greek ascetic writings handed down under the name of Nilus of Ancyra, a monk and disciple of John Chrysostom who died around 430. It includes a eulogy of the monk Albianus, the Ascetic Discourse, the Peristeria, treatises on voluntary poverty and on the superiority of monks, a work addressed to Eulogius, and texts on the vices and on prayer, along with collections of sentences. Several of these texts, including On Prayer and On Evil Thoughts, are now generally credited to Evagrius Ponticus. Even so, they shaped later Byzantine monastic spirituality.

Interpretatio in Psalmos is a Greek commentary on the whole Psalter by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was probably written in the 440s. In its preface Theodoret says he had wanted to explain David's Psalms first, because monks, townspeople and country people alike sang them. Requests for commentaries on the Song of Songs, Daniel, Ezekiel and the Twelve Prophets came first, however. Working in the Antiochene tradition, he aims for a clear, concise reading that balances the Psalms' historical sense with their prophetic and christological meaning. It is one of the most important patristic commentaries on the Psalms.

The Quaestiones in Octateuchum is a Greek work of biblical exegesis by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, written late in his life, probably in the early 450s. It works through the first eight books of the Old Testament, Genesis to Ruth, as a series of questions and answers. Each answer explains a difficult or puzzling passage, using the restrained historical and literal approach of the Antiochene school. It is one of the major examples of the patristic question-and-answer genre and an important witness to the Antiochene reading of the Old Testament.

This is a biblical commentary in question-and-answer form by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, written late in his life, probably in the early 450s. It covers the four books of Kingdoms (1–2 Samuel and 1–2 Kings) and the two books of Chronicles (Paralipomenon), and it follows on from his similar Questions on the Octateuch. Theodoret works through difficulties in the text, such as Samuel's Levitical descent and Elkanah's two wives. He reads the text in the historical and literal manner of the Antiochene school, and the work is an important witness to the Antiochene Greek biblical text.

The Interpretatio in Baruch is a Greek commentary on the deuterocanonical Book of Baruch by Theodoret of Cyrrhus, the Antiochene theologian and bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It is usually dated between about 435 and 447 and belongs to his larger exposition of Jeremiah, which also covers Lamentations. Theodoret explains how Baruch went to Babylon and read Jeremiah's prophecy to the exiles and King Jechoniah. He sets the text in its historical context and links its prayer for foreign rulers to the Apostle Paul's command to pray for kings, showing the agreement of the Old and New Testaments.

This Greek commentary on the Song of Songs is by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It is usually dated to the 430s and is one of his earliest biblical commentaries. Theodoret wrote it at the request of a Bishop John and dedicated it to him. He reads the Song as a spiritual allegory of the love between Christ and the Church, or the soul, and rejects readings that treat it as a merely human love poem. The work is a notable example of Antiochene exegesis taking up allegorical interpretation.

The Commentary on the Visions of Daniel is a Greek biblical commentary by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was probably written in the 430s and is among his earliest exegetical works. Theodoret goes through the Book of Daniel, explaining its prophetic visions in the historical, restrained manner of the Antiochene school. He argues that Daniel should be counted among the prophets and reads the visions as foretelling the succession of empires and the coming of Christ. It is an important witness to early Christian interpretation of Daniel.

The Interpretation of Ezekiel is a Greek verse-by-verse commentary on the Book of Ezekiel by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It is usually dated to the late 430s or 440s and belongs to his series of commentaries on the Old Testament prophets. Its preface argues that the prophets seem obscure only to readers whose spiritual sight is clouded by unbelief. The commentary is a leading example of Antiochene exegesis. It reads the prophecies mainly against their historical setting and adds Christological interpretation where Theodoret thinks the text supports it.

This Greek commentary on the Book of Isaiah by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, was probably written between about 435 and 447. For centuries it survived only in excerpts preserved in exegetical catenae, which were collected under the title "interpretation by selection." A complete text was later found in a manuscript. The preface presents Isaiah as the clearest of the prophets on Christ's virgin birth, miracles, passion, resurrection and ascension, the calling of the nations and the fall of Jerusalem. In the Antiochene manner, Theodoret sets out to explain the prophecy's plain sense alongside its figurative passages.

The Interpretatio in Jeremiam is a Greek commentary on the Book of Jeremiah by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was probably written between the late 430s and the 440s, though the date is uncertain. It works through the prophetic text verse by verse in the historical, literal manner of the Antiochene school. It explains Jeremiah's oracles about the Babylonian siege, the destruction of the Temple and the return from exile, and also reads some passages as foretelling the New Covenant and the calling of the Gentiles.

The Interpretatio in Lamentationes is a Greek commentary on the biblical Book of Lamentations by Theodoret (c. 393–c. 458), bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It forms part of his larger exposition of Jeremiah, which also covers the Book of Baruch. It was probably written during the period of his commentaries on the prophets, roughly 435–447, though the exact date is uncertain. Theodoret follows the Antiochene method, reading the laments mainly in their historical setting: the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and the exile. He also draws moral lessons for Christian readers. The work is a typical example of Antiochene prophetic exegesis.

This is a Greek commentary on the twelve Minor Prophets, from Hosea to Malachi, by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was probably written between about 435 and 447. In the preface Theodoret admits that others have already explained these prophets, but he defends his own attempt by pointing to the widow's two coins. The commentary follows the Antiochene method of reading the text for its historical sense while also allowing for Christological prophecy. It is one of the most important surviving examples of Antiochene biblical interpretation.

This is a set of supplementary material from volume 81 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca. It is not a single work. The volume mainly contains Greek commentaries by Theodoret of Cyrus (d. c. 466) on the Prophets. The material gathered here includes editorial front matter, Latin notes on manuscripts and smaller unindexed pieces. Among them are descriptions of codices with their incipits and explicits, chapter summaries, prefatory headings to Jeremiah, Lamentations and Ezekiel, and references to related exegetical texts attributed to Hesychius of Jerusalem and John Chrysostom.

The Discourse on Divine and Holy Love is a short Greek treatise by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was written as the closing piece of his Religious History (Philotheos Historia), a collection of lives of Syrian ascetics composed around 440. Having described what the monks did, Theodoret asks what moved them to take up their way of life and how they reached the summit of "philosophy", meaning the ascetic life. His answer is love for God. That love, not bodily strength, let them go beyond the limits of human nature.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in five books by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was written around 449–450 and continues the history of Eusebius of Caesarea. It begins with the rise of Arianism under Constantine and ends in 429, with the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Theodoret writes from a firmly Nicene and Antiochene viewpoint and focuses on the struggle against Arianism. He quotes many letters, creeds and synodal documents in full. Along with the histories of Socrates Scholasticus and Sozomen, it is one of the main sources for fourth-century church history.

The Historia Religiosa, also called the Philotheos Historia ("History of the Lovers of God"), is a Greek hagiographical collection written by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, around 440. It gives thirty accounts of ascetics of Syria and Mesopotamia, beginning with Jacob of Nisibis. Among them is Symeon the Stylite, who was still living when Theodoret wrote. Theodoret knew many of these monks personally, and he tells of their hardships, miracles and teaching. A short treatise on divine love closes the work. It is a key source for early Syrian monasticism.

This Greek commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Romans by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, is the first part of his Interpretation of the Fourteen Epistles of Saint Paul, usually dated between about 430 and 448. It opens with an argument summarising the letter: Gentiles broke the natural law, Jews failed to keep the written law, and the gospel brings pardon and life to all. Following the Antiochene tradition, it explains the text concisely and literally, drawing heavily on John Chrysostom.

This is a collection of miscellaneous material from volume 82 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca: editorial front matter, notes and shorter pieces not indexed as separate works. The volume belongs to the works of Theodoret of Cyrus, the fifth-century Greek bishop and theologian, which include his commentaries on the Pauline epistles. Among the material is a scribe's colophon. In it a copyist named Peter Karneades, of Epidaurus, "now called Monemvasia", records that he copied the manuscript by his own hand.

This is a group of short Greek pieces credited to Theodoret of Cyrrhus, the fifth-century Antiochene bishop and theologian. It opens with a polemical tract against Nestorius addressed to Sporacius. The tract attacks Nestorius's background, his showy preaching and his teaching on the divinity of the Only-begotten. Theodoret defended Nestorius for years and condemned him only at Chalcedon in 451, so the harsh tone has led scholars to question whether he wrote the piece. Alongside it are summaries of arguments against various propositions and fragments on the Trinity, which together show something of his doctrinal writing.

The Ten Discourses on Providence (De providentia orationes X) are a series of Greek discourses by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, usually dated to the 430s. They defend divine providence against people who credit the world to chance or fate, or who deny that God cares for creation. The early discourses argue from the order of the heavens, the elements, the human body and the arts. Later ones consider wealth and poverty, slavery and the apparent prosperity of the wicked, and the series ends with the Incarnation. They are admired as a polished example of late antique Christian rhetoric and apologetic.

The Demonstrationes per syllogismos is a short Greek theological treatise by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus. It forms the closing section of his Eranistes, written about 447–448. After the three dialogues of that work, it restates their arguments as a series of brief syllogisms. These argue that God the Word is immutable, that his divinity and humanity remain unconfused in the one Christ, and that the divine nature did not suffer. The work belongs to the Antiochene response to the Christology that soon became associated with Eutyches, on the eve of the Council of Chalcedon.

The Letters of Theodoret of Cyrrhus (c. 393–c. 458), bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria from 423, form one of the largest surviving Greek letter collections of the fifth century. Over two hundred letters survive in several collections. They are addressed to bishops, monks, officials and friends, and cover consolation and friendship, the bishop's pleas for his poor diocese, and the Christological controversies that followed the Council of Ephesus (431). They also cover his deposition in 449 and his restoration at Chalcedon in 451. The letters are a major source for the church and society of the period.

The Eranistes ("Beggar" or "Collector"), also called Polymorphus ("Multiform"), is a Greek theological treatise by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, written around 447–448. It consists of three dialogues between Orthodoxos and Eranistes. Eranistes speaks for the emerging Eutychian position, which Theodoret presents as pieced together from older heresies. The dialogues argue that the divine Word is immutable, that Christ's two natures remain unconfounded, and that the Godhead is impassible. A syllogistic summary follows. Each dialogue includes collections of patristic quotations, which make the work an important witness to Christological debate on the eve of the Council of Chalcedon.

The Cure of Greek Maladies (Graecarum affectionum curatio) is a Greek apologetic treatise by Theodoret of Cyrrhus. Its date is disputed, though it is usually placed in the 420s or 430s. Its twelve discourses set Greek philosophical and religious opinions beside Christian teaching on faith, the first principle, angels and gods, matter and the cosmos, human nature, providence and other subjects. Theodoret quotes Plato, Plotinus and many other pagan authors, often drawing on Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius. The work is often regarded as one of the last great Christian apologies against paganism.

The Compendium of Heretical Fables is a Greek heresiological treatise by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, written around 452–453, shortly after the Council of Chalcedon. It is dedicated to Sporacius, a high-ranking official who had asked to learn about the paths that turn away from orthodox teaching. Its first four books survey heresies from Simon Magus to the Christological controversies of Theodoret's own time. The fifth book sets out orthodox doctrine in a systematic way. It is an important source for early Christian sects and for Theodoret's later theology.

This is a gathering of editorial material from volume 83 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the volume given to works of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus (c. 393–c. 458/466). It includes front matter, notes and short pieces not catalogued separately, along with older testimonies about Theodoret's writings. Among them are Photius's descriptions of the Eranistes, a dialogue in four parts on the unchangeable and impassible divine Word, and of the Compendium of Heretical Fables addressed to Sporacius. There are also cross-references to his treatises on Providence and his apologetic work against the Greeks.

The Auctarium of the French Jesuit Jean Garnier is a supplement of fragments and other pieces attributed to Theodoret of Cyrrhus, the fifth-century Antiochene bishop and biblical commentator. Its authenticity varies, and some pieces are doubtful. It opens with a "Method" said to come from Theodoret's commentaries. This piece introduces the Psalter. It explains how the book was put together, which writings mentioned in Scripture have been lost, and who translated the Psalms and when. It also describes the Psalms as a spiritual garden that teaches virtue, true faith and the movements of the soul.

This is a miscellany rather than a single work. It gathers the front matter, editorial notes and smaller unindexed pieces of volume 84 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, one of the volumes given to Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–c. 466) and to writings attributed to him. The material includes Latin prefaces and notes by earlier editors. Among them is a discussion of the catena on the Octateuch and Books of Kings published by Nicephorus Theotokis, a compilation that preserves Greek exegetical fragments. The pieces vary in date, authorship and authenticity.

Theophrastus is a Greek philosophical dialogue by Aeneas of Gaza, a Christian sophist of the rhetorical school of Gaza. It was written in the late fifth century, probably around 485–500. Modelled on Plato, it brings together Aegyptus of Alexandria, the Syrian Christian Axitheus and the Athenian Neoplatonist Theophrastus, and recalls their teacher Hierocles. Axitheus argues for the soul's immortality and the resurrection of the body. He also rejects the soul's pre-existence, transmigration and the eternity of the world. The dialogue is an important witness to how Christians engaged with late Neoplatonism.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments credited to Ammonius, a presbyter of Alexandria. He is usually dated to the later fifth or sixth century and should not be confused with the third-century philosopher Ammonius Saccas. His commentaries do not survive as complete works. Their passages were preserved in catenae, the anthologies of patristic comment arranged verse by verse. Most of the fragments explain the Gospel of John and the Acts of the Apostles, and some comment on the Psalms. They give evidence of Alexandrian biblical interpretation after Cyril.

This is a group of letters by Andrew, bishop of Samosata, written around 430 to 435 during the Nestorian controversy surrounding the Council of Ephesus (431). Andrew had written against Cyril of Alexandria's anathemas and supported the Eastern bishops. Illness kept him away from the council itself. The letters follow his opposition to Cyril, his correspondence with Theodoret and John of Antioch, and his part in working toward reconciliation. They were composed in Greek, but several survive mainly in Latin translation. They are a valuable source for the negotiations after Ephesus.

The Anonymi fragmenta historica are anonymous Greek historical fragments, usually assigned to the fifth century, although their date and authorship are uncertain. The surviving text describes the emperor Julian's campaign against Persia in 363: his march through Hierapolis and Carrhae, the boats built at Samosata, how he divided his army at Circesium, and his speech to the troops. It names the chronicler Magnus of Carrhae, who went on the campaign, as its source. The account runs very close to the chronicle of John Malalas.

This is a collection of Greek homilies and fragments attributed to Antipater, metropolitan bishop of Bostra in the Roman province of Arabia in the mid-fifth century. The homilies include a festal sermon on John the Baptist, which praises the forerunner who leapt in his mother's womb when the newly conceived Christ arrived at the Visitation. Other fragments survive mainly as quotations in later writers. They include material from Antipater's polemic against Origen, which made him one of Origen's leading critics. The collection shows Greek preaching and anti-Origenist controversy in the period after Chalcedon.

This Greek corpus is associated with Basil, archbishop of Seleucia in Isauria by 448, and dates from the mid-fifth century. Its first part is a series of sermons (Orationes) on Old and New Testament subjects. The first sermon, on the creation, opens with praise of fasting. The second part is the Life and Miracles of Saint Thecla, an expanded retelling of the Acts of Thecla with an account of 46 later miracles at her shrine near Seleucia. Although long attributed to Basil, this work is now thought to be by an anonymous contemporary whom Basil had once excommunicated.

The Fragmenta historica are the surviving remains of a Greek history in three books by Candidus the Isaurian, an Eastern Roman historian from Rough Isauria who served as secretary to leading Isaurians. The work covered events from the accession of Leo I in 457 to the proclamation of Anastasius in 491, giving prominence to Isaurian affairs under Zeno. It is known chiefly from Photius's summary, which describes Candidus as an orthodox Christian who praised the Council of Chalcedon but faults his overwrought, poetic style.

These are short Greek documents attributed to Dalmatius (died c. 440), archimandrite and leading monk of Constantinople, and preserved with the acts of the Council of Ephesus of 431. They include a letter to the bishops gathered at Ephesus, and another from Dalmatius and the clergy of Constantinople, welcoming Cyril of Alexandria's letters and accepting the deposition of Nestorius. They also include a defence, or apologia. Together they show the part Constantinople's monks played in the Nestorian controversy and in turning imperial support toward Cyril's side.

This is a Greek hagiographical poem in dactylic hexameters by the empress Aelia Eudocia (c. 400–460), wife of Theodosius II. She probably wrote it in her later years, after she had settled in Jerusalem. It retells the legend of Cyprian of Antioch, a pagan magician hired by a suitor, Aglaïdas, to win over the Christian virgin Justina. The demons he summons fail against her sign of the cross, and Cyprian converts. Only parts of the poem survive. Along with her Homeric centos, it shows how Christian narrative was recast in classical epic diction.

This is a Greek set of prologues, chapter lists and related aids to reading the Acts of the Apostles, the Catholic Epistles and the Letters of Paul. Known as the Euthalian Apparatus, it is attributed to Euthalius, described as a deacon and later a bishop. Who he was and when he wrote are disputed, and estimates range from the fourth to the seventh century. The apparatus divides the text into chapters and sense-lines and lists Old Testament quotations. It had a wide influence on Greek New Testament manuscripts and on how readers studied them.

This Greek church history in three books was written around 475 by an anonymous author, the son of a presbyter of Cyzicus, who worked in Bithynia. Following Photius, it was long misattributed to Gelasius of Cyzicus. Book I covers Constantine's reign up to 323, Book II the Council of Nicaea and Book III its aftermath. It draws on Eusebius, Rufinus and other historians, as well as on a parchment book that had belonged to Dalmatius of Cyzicus. The author aimed to show against the Eutychians that the Nicene Fathers did not teach Monophysite doctrine.

These are the surviving Greek writings of Gennadius I, patriarch of Constantinople from 458 to 471, gathered into one collection. Gennadius was a learned exegete who followed the literal method of the Antiochene school. His commentaries on books of the Old and New Testaments, including Genesis, Daniel and the Pauline epistles such as Galatians and Hebrews, survive only as fragments preserved in exegetical chains (catenae). The collection also contains an encyclical letter that he issued as patriarch, along with material on the anathematisms connected with the Christological controversies of the fifth century.

A Greek collection of one hundred short ascetic chapters by John of Carpathus, a bishop of the island of Karpathos who probably lived in the seventh century, though his dates are uncertain. He wrote them at the request of monks "in India", and where those monks actually lived is unclear. In a modest preface, John compares his gift to spring flowers that beggars offer to kings. The chapters encourage monks struggling with passionate thoughts, despondency and falls, urging repentance and trust in grace. The work was later included in the Philokalia.

This is a collection of miscellaneous material from Volume 85 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, a series of Greek Christian writings from late antiquity. It includes front matter, editorial notes and short pieces not catalogued as separate works. Much of it is Latin editorial commentary on Basil of Seleucia, a fifth-century bishop. The notes list the opening words of his sermons on Old and New Testament figures, record which ones Photius read, and discuss the Life and Miracles of Thecla attributed to him.

The Epistula ad Leonem imperatorem is a short letter to the Byzantine emperor Leo I (reigned 457–474) from Theotimus, bishop of Tomi on the Black Sea. It is usually dated to about 457–458. This Theotimus is a later bishop of Tomi, not the friend of John Chrysostom who held the see around 400. The letter belongs to the replies that bishops sent when Leo asked their views on the Council of Chalcedon and the disputed patriarch of Alexandria, Timothy Aelurus. Its surviving closing urges the emperor to keep a pure mind and an undefiled faith in God the Saviour.

Fragmenta is a small group of surviving Greek passages linked to two bishops of Berytus (Beirut). Timothy of Berytus was a late fourth-century follower of Apollinaris of Laodicea. Eustathius of Berytus was bishop in the mid-fifth century and took part in the Christological disputes around the Council of Chalcedon in 451. The passages deal with the person of Christ. One discusses how the Word governed the natural movements and sufferings of the flesh he took on. They are useful as rare remains of Apollinarian and fifth-century Christological debate, but which passages belong to which bishop is not always certain.

This collection brings together Greek writings of Zacharias of Mytilene, also called Zacharias Rhetor or Scholasticus (c. 465 – after 536), from the early sixth century. Ammonius, also known as De mundi opificio, is a philosophical dialogue set among students at Berytus. It argues against the Alexandrian Neoplatonist Ammonius's teaching that the world is eternal, and defends the Christian doctrine of creation. The Disputatio contra Manichaeos is a polemical refutation of Manichaean dualism. The historical fragments come from his Ecclesiastical History, whose Greek original is lost and which survives mainly through a later Syriac compilation.

The Capita admonitoria (Ekthesis) is a Greek "mirror for princes" by Agapetus, a deacon of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. He addressed it to the Emperor Justinian, probably around the time of his accession in 527. Its seventy-two short chapters form an acrostic whose initial letters spell a dedication to the emperor from "Agapetus the least deacon." In polished, rhetorical prose it urges the ruler to piety, justice, humility, self-knowledge and philanthropy, and presents imperial power as a likeness of God's heavenly rule. The work was widely read in later Byzantium and was much translated in later centuries.

This is a short Greek text in question-and-answer form, attributed to Barsanuphius of Gaza, the sixth-century hermit near Gaza. It belongs to the spiritual correspondence of Barsanuphius and John. A monk writes that he has been reading Origen, Didymus and the Gnostic Chapters of Evagrius. He is troubled by their teaching that souls existed beforehand as bodiless intellects and that all beings will finally be restored (apokatastasis), so he asks for the truth. The elder's reply rejects these ideas. The text shows monastic reactions to Origenism in Palestine before its condemnation in 553.

The Epistulae et sententiae are a small collection of Greek letters and synodal decisions attributed to Epiphanius, patriarch of Constantinople from 520 to 535. Epiphanius led the church in the years after the Acacian schism with Rome had ended, and he corresponded with Pope Hormisdas. The collection opens with a sentence of the resident synod (endemousa synodos) of Constantinople. It condemns Severus of Antioch and Peter of Apamea as apostates from the Catholic Church and the orthodox faith. The texts are evidence of anti-Miaphysite church policy under Justin I and Justinian.

The Letter to Timothy Scholasticus on the Two Natures is a Greek theological letter by Eustathius the Monk, usually dated to the mid-sixth century. Its full title calls it a work "against Severus", and it defends the Chalcedonian teaching that Christ exists in two natures against the miaphysite doctrine of Severus of Antioch. Eustathius wrote it at Timothy's request, following up on discussions they had held in person. He argues that the one-nature formula echoes Manichaean, Marcionite and Valentinian docetism, and he quotes Timothy Aelurus and Severus at length. These quotations preserve passages from Severus's writings.

The Laws of the Himyarites (Nomoi) and the Debate with the Jew Herban (Dialexis) are Greek texts attributed to Gregentios, said to have been archbishop of Ẓafār, capital of the South Arabian kingdom of Ḥimyar, in the mid-sixth century. Together with his Life, they form a hagiographical dossier probably compiled in the tenth century. The dossier is largely legendary. The Laws set out a Christian legal code for the kingdom under King Abraham, and the Debate stages a long disputation in which Christianity is defended against Judaism.

De cogitationibus (On Thoughts) is a short Greek ascetic treatise transmitted under the name of Isaac the Syrian (Isaac of Nineveh), the seventh-century Church of the East bishop and monastic writer. Isaac wrote in Syriac, and his works reached Greek readers in translation. The treatise says that thoughts arise from four causes: the natural will of the flesh, sense impressions of the world, the soul's prior dispositions, and demonic attacks. Struggle with them lasts until death. It urges purity of heart through unceasing remembrance of God.

This is the collected writings of John Maxentius, leader of the "Scythian monks", written around 519–523. It contains letters, professions of faith and the dialogues against the Nestorians. The works survive in Latin. They defend the theopaschite formula "One of the Trinity suffered in the flesh", which the Scythian monks argued for in Constantinople and Rome during the papacy of Hormisdas. The writings set out a strict Cyrillian Christology against what the monks saw as Nestorian readings of Chalcedon. They are an important witness to the theopaschite controversy, whose formula was later accepted under Justinian.

This is a collection of theological writings issued under the name of the Byzantine emperor Justinian I, who reigned from 527 to 565. It opens with his treatise against Origen, addressed in 543 to Patriarch Menas of Constantinople. In it the emperor condemns Origen's teachings as pagan, Arian and Manichaean and appends a list of anathemas. The collection also includes letters, edicts and treatises against the Monophysites. Together they show how Justinian tried to define Chalcedonian orthodoxy and impose it through imperial legislation, in the period leading up to the Second Council of Constantinople in 553.

This collection gathers Greek theological writings from the sixth century that have been traditionally grouped under the name of Leontius of Byzantium. Some are also linked to Leontius of Jerusalem. The works defend the Christology of the Council of Chalcedon against Nestorians, Eutychians, Apollinarians and Severus of Antioch. They are notable for applying Aristotelian logical terms such as essence, nature, hypostasis and person to the doctrine of Christ. De sectis presents itself as notes from the lectures of Abba Theodore. Its authorship, like that of several other pieces here, is disputed.

This collection of Greek excerpts preserves part of the Ecclesiastical History of Theodore Lector, a reader at Hagia Sophia in Constantinople in the early sixth century. Theodore's original history, probably composed around the 520s or 530s, is lost except for such fragments. It continued earlier church histories from the death of Theodosius II in 450 to the beginning of Justin I's reign in 518. The excerpts, attributed in their heading to Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, deal with emperors, the Council of Chalcedon and later Christological controversies. They matter because little other evidence survives for this period.

On Those Who Enter the Church, also called On the Reception of Heretics, is a Greek treatise by Timothy, a Chalcedonian presbyter in Constantinople, probably written around 600. It should not be confused with the patriarch Timothy I. Addressed to a fellow cleric named John, it is a handbook for admitting heretics into the Church. It sorts them into three classes: those who must be baptised, those who need only anointing with chrism, and those who need only anathematise their heresy. Each sect gets a short description, and the work is a valuable source on heresiology.

This is a collection of homilies and fragmentary writings attributed to Eulogius, the Chalcedonian Greek Patriarch of Alexandria from about 580 to 607 or 608 and a correspondent of Pope Gregory the Great. Most of his writings, many of them aimed against the Monophysites and other dissenting groups, are lost or survive only in pieces. The collection includes a festal discourse for Palm Sunday that celebrates Christ's royal entry into Jerusalem in rhythmic, exultant rhetoric. The surviving pieces are rare evidence of Greek Chalcedonian preaching and theology in Alexandria on the eve of the Arab conquest.

These are two Greek writings by Eutychius, Patriarch of Constantinople (552–565 and 577–582). The letter to Pope Vigilius dates from the start of his first patriarchate in 552. In it he professes his faith, accepts the four ecumenical councils and asks for a council to settle the Three Chapters controversy, which led to the Second Council of Constantinople in 553. The sermon on Pascha and the holy Eucharist deals with Christ's Passover and the Eucharistic mysteries. Its exact date is uncertain. Both texts are rare surviving examples of Eutychius's own theological writing.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in six books by Evagrius Scholasticus, a lawyer at Antioch and aide to Patriarch Gregory of Antioch. He completed it around 593–594. It continues the histories of Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret, covering the period from the First Council of Ephesus in 431 to the reign of Emperor Maurice. Written from a Chalcedonian standpoint, it is a major source for the Christological controversies after Chalcedon, for imperial and Persian affairs, and for the plague of the 540s, which Evagrius survived.

This short Greek theological fragment asks why the Son, and not the Father or the Holy Spirit, became incarnate. Its authorship is uncertain: it has been attributed both to Job the Monk and to Erechthius, bishop of Antioch in Pisidia, and it probably dates from the sixth or seventh century. The text says the manger itself reveals why the Word took flesh. It reads the ox and the ass of Isaiah 1:3 and Habakkuk 3:2 (Greek text) as Israel and the Gentiles, united through the Word's mediation, and it draws on Gregory of Nazianzus's Nativity oration.

The Homiliae are Greek sermons attributed to Modestus, who led the Church of Jerusalem while Patriarch Zacharias was held captive by the Persians after the city fell in 614. Modestus then served as patriarch himself from 632 to 634. The surviving opening urges the faithful to remember, with tears, their brothers and sisters carried off into captivity. It rebukes the wealthy for wearing silk and jewels while fellow Christians suffer in chains, and it teaches that riches are given so that captives may be ransomed. The authenticity of some pieces transmitted under Modestus's name is disputed.

This is a set of miscellaneous Greek material from the second part of volume 86 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, covering writers of roughly the sixth and early seventh centuries. It includes front matter, notes and shorter pieces not indexed separately. It opens with a short anti-Monophysite treatise attributed to the monk Leontius of Jerusalem. The treatise is a series of numbered logical arguments against those who call Christ one composite nature, and it closes with patristic testimonies. Its contents are mixed, so no single author or date applies to the whole.

Two Greek poems by Paul the Silentiary, a poet and official at the court of Justinian I in Constantinople. The Description of the Ambo is a hexameter poem with an iambic prologue. It is a companion to his longer ekphrasis of Hagia Sophia, written for the church's rededication in 562–563 after its dome was rebuilt. It describes in detail the great marble pulpit and the walkway linking it to the sanctuary. The second piece is a short poem on the hot springs at Pythia in Bithynia. Both are valuable examples of late antique Christian ekphrasis.

These Greek exegetical writings are attributed to Peter of Laodicea, a Christian scholar of the seventh or eighth century, probably a bishop of Laodicea, about whom almost nothing is known. They include an exposition of the Lord's Prayer and verse-by-verse commentaries on the Gospels. The commentaries draw heavily on earlier Greek interpreters. The surviving text on the Last Supper stresses that Christ said "This is my body", not "This is the symbol", and presents the Eucharist as the truth that fulfils the Passover type. The dating and attribution remain uncertain.

This is a group of Greek writings attributed to Symeon Stylites the Younger (521–596/597), the ascetic who lived on pillars on the Wondrous Mountain near Antioch. It contains ascetic sermons addressed to monks, a letter to the emperor Justin II and a passage on holy images. These writings survive mainly through later quotation and compilation, and some of the ascriptions to Symeon are uncertain. The texts on images and the letter to Justin were later used as patristic evidence in the Byzantine debates over the veneration of icons.

This short Greek pastoral letter is attributed to Zacharias, Patriarch of Jerusalem (609–632), who was carried into captivity after the Sasanian Persians took Jerusalem in 614. Writing as a "captive shepherd" to the church of Jerusalem, he grieves for Zion, Golgotha, the Holy Sepulchre and Bethlehem, drawing on Psalm 137. He warns those who escaped not to grow proud or self-indulgent, citing the parable of the rich man and Lazarus. It is transmitted with a brief anonymous account of the Persian captivity and is an early witness to the fall of Jerusalem.

The Commentarii in Octateuchum is a Greek exegetical commentary on the first eight books of the Bible, Genesis through Ruth. It was written by Procopius of Gaza, the Christian sophist and rhetorician, in the early sixth century. In its preface Procopius explains that he first gathered verbatim extracts from the Fathers and other interpreters. Because that collection grew too long, he condensed it into one continuous commentary. Points on which the authorities agreed are stated once, and differing views are summarised. The work is an important early example of the catena tradition.

Greek exegetical commentaries on the biblical books of Proverbs and the Song of Songs, attributed to Procopius of Gaza (c. 465–c. 528), the Christian rhetorician of the School of Gaza. They are usually dated to the early sixth century. Like his other biblical works, they draw on earlier interpreters in the manner of a catena, which gathers excerpts from several writers. The Proverbs commentary reads Solomon's figure of Wisdom as the Son and Word of God and also draws moral teaching from the text. Scholars debate how much of the material is authentically his.

The Scholia on the Books of Kingdoms and Chronicles is a Greek exegetical work attributed to Procopius of Gaza (c. 465–c. 528), the Christian rhetorician of the school of Gaza. It was probably written in the early sixth century. It comments on 1–4 Kingdoms (Samuel and Kings) and on Chronicles in short explanatory notes. These address questions such as who wrote the historical books, the genealogy of Samuel, and apparent contradictions in names and places. Like Procopius's other biblical commentaries, it reflects his practice of condensing and adapting earlier Greek exegesis.

The Epistulae are a collection of Greek letters by Procopius of Gaza (c. 465–528), the Christian sophist and teacher who led the Rhetorical School of Gaza. Written in an elegant Atticizing style, more than 160 letters survive, most of them probably from the late fifth and early sixth centuries. They are addressed to friends, former pupils, fellow rhetors and officials, and are full of classical allusion, praise and literary play. They matter as models of late antique epistolary art and as evidence for the intellectual and social life of Gaza and its links with Egypt and Palestine.

The Commentary on the Song of Songs is a Greek exegetical compilation attributed to Procopius of Gaza (c. 465–528), the Christian rhetorician of the Gaza school who is often credited with developing the catena form. Its heading calls it an "epitome of exegetical extracts." It arranges excerpts from earlier interpreters, including Gregory of Nyssa, Cyril of Alexandria, Origen, Apollinaris, Eusebius of Caesarea, Didymus, Isidore, Theodoret and Theophilus, into a running spiritual reading of the Song. It reads the Song as the soul's mystical marriage to God. It preserves fragments of commentaries that are otherwise lost.

The Commentary on Isaiah is a Greek verse-by-verse exposition of the Book of Isaiah by Procopius of Gaza (c. 465–c. 528), the Christian rhetorician of the School of Gaza, written in the early sixth century. Like his other biblical works, it is a compilation and digest of earlier Greek interpretations, with Eusebius of Caesarea and Cyril of Alexandria among its sources. It combines historical and Christological readings, notes on Hebrew terms and comparisons with other Greek versions. It is an important early example of the catena form of exegesis and preserves material from earlier commentators.

These are two Greek prose works attributed to Alexander the Monk, a Cypriot monk usually placed in the sixth century, though his date is uncertain. The first, on the finding of the Cross, was written at the request of his superiors. It traces sacred history from the Incarnation to the discovery of the True Cross under Constantine and Helena. The second is an encomium of the apostle Barnabas. It tells of his life and martyrdom on Cyprus and the later discovery of his relics, and it supports the Cypriot church's claim to ecclesiastical independence.

This group of Greek texts is falsely attributed to Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem (d. 638). The main piece, a liturgical commentary, claims to give a detailed account of everything performed in the Divine Liturgy. It traces the eucharistic rite to the apostles, inspired by the Holy Spirit, and to later Fathers such as Epiphanius, Basil and John Chrysostom. It is closely related to the Byzantine commentary tradition linked with Germanus of Constantinople. A prayer and an account of the labours of the apostles Peter and Paul go with it. Their date and authorship are uncertain.

The Pratum spirituale (Greek Leimōn or Leimonarion, "Spiritual Meadow") is a collection of edifying monastic tales by the Byzantine monk John Moschus (d. 619 or 634). He wrote it in the late sixth or early seventh century and dedicated it to his companion Sophronius, later patriarch of Jerusalem. It contains several hundred anecdotes, short biographies and sayings that the two gathered while travelling among the monasteries of Palestine, Egypt, Syria and elsewhere. It is a major source for Eastern monasticism and daily life on the eve of the Persian and Arab conquests.

This is a miscellany of Greek material from the third part of volume 87 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca. That part of the volume covers writers of the sixth and early seventh centuries. The collection holds front matter, editorial notes and shorter pieces that were not indexed separately. It opens with a panegyric addressed to the Emperor Anastasius I (491–518) by a "sophist of Gaza", normally identified as Procopius of Gaza. The speech praises the emperor's victories and his generosity to the orator's city. The pieces are by several different hands, so the collection has no single author or date.

The Anacreontica are a collection of Greek religious poems by Sophronius, monk and later Patriarch of Jerusalem (634–638). They were probably written in the early seventh century. The poems use the classical anacreontic metre and literary dialect for Christian subjects, chiefly the feasts of the Church, such as the Annunciation and the Nativity, as well as saints and the holy places of Jerusalem. One poem mourns the Persian capture of the city in 614. Some odes are arranged as alphabetic acrostics with refrains. The collection is an important example of learned Byzantine hymnography that adapts classical poetic forms.

The Synodical Letter to Sergius is a Greek profession of faith that Sophronius sent in 634, on becoming patriarch of Jerusalem, to Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople. As was customary for a new bishop, he set out his belief in detail. He covers the Trinity and then the Incarnation. Against the monenergism promoted by Sergius, he argues that Christ, one person in two natures, has two natural operations. The letter was later read at the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681), and it survives in that council's acts. It is a key document of the early Monothelite controversy.

This collection gathers Greek prose works by Sophronius, monk and Patriarch of Jerusalem (634–638). It opens with his homilies on feasts such as the Annunciation, which also set out Trinitarian and Christological teaching. The other pieces are treatises on the confession of sins and on the baptism of the apostles, and an encomium of the healing saints Cyrus and John. There is also an account of their miracles at their shrine in Menouthis near Alexandria. Finally, the Life of Saint Mary of Egypt is traditionally attributed to Sophronius, but scholars dispute that attribution.

This Greek liturgical poem is a triodion, a short canon of three odes rather than the full nine. It is attributed to Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem (died 638), though the attribution and date are uncertain. Written for the Lenten fast, it calls the soul to repentance, sobriety and tears. It asks Christ for enlightenment, turns from bodily pleasure to the "luxury" of fasting, and includes petitions to the Theotokos. Its troparia follow the model melodies of the biblical odes.

The Histories is a classicizing Greek history in five books by Agathias Scholasticus, the lawyer and poet from Myrina. It was written after Justinian's death, probably in the 570s, and continues Procopius. It covers the years 552 to 558: Narses' campaigns in Italy against the Goths, Franks and Alamanni, the Lazic War with Persia, the earthquake at Constantinople and the Kutrigur invasion. It includes long digressions on Persian religion and Sasanian kings. Agathias left it unfinished, and Menander Protector continued it.

The Liber ad pastorem ("To the Shepherd") is a short Greek treatise by John Climacus, the seventh-century monk of Mount Sinai. It was written for John, abbot of Raithu, as a companion to The Ladder of Divine Ascent, and the two works are usually transmitted together. It describes the duties of a monastic superior, who is pictured as a shepherd, a ship's pilot, a physician and a teacher. A good superior guides, corrects and heals the souls in his care, and his teaching should come from God rather than from books. Its date of composition is uncertain.

The Ladder of Divine Ascent, or Ladder of Paradise, is an ascetical treatise by John Climacus, monk and later abbot of Mount Sinai. He wrote it in the early seventh century at the request of John, abbot of Raithu. Their exchange of letters often accompanies the text. It is written in concise, aphoristic prose and has thirty "steps", recalling the thirty years of Christ's hidden life. These lead from renouncing the world to the virtues and finally to love. It became one of the most influential monastic texts of Eastern Christianity and drew commentaries and scholia from an early date.

The Life of John Climacus is a short Greek hagiography of John, abbot of Mount Sinai and author of the Ladder of Divine Ascent, who died around 649. It is attributed to Daniel, a monk of Raithu, and was probably written in the seventh century. The Life says it does not know John's birthplace. It describes how he entered monastic life at Sinai at about sixteen, his obedience and humility, and his years of solitude and spiritual guidance. It was often copied as a preface to the Ladder and was later translated into Georgian and Slavonic.

The Laudatio omnium martyrum is a Greek encomium in praise of all the martyrs, attributed to Constantine, a deacon of Constantinople. Little is known about him, and the work is usually dated to roughly the sixth or seventh century. In elaborate rhetorical prose, the panegyric describes the martyrs as an army standing against persecuting tyranny. It stresses how varied they were: men and women, children and elders, masters and slaves, and a long list of peoples from across the Roman world and beyond. The work shows how the Byzantine Church honoured the martyrs together as one body.

The Christian Topography is a Greek treatise on cosmology and geography by Cosmas Indicopleustes, an Alexandrian merchant who had sailed to Aksum and India. He wrote it around 545–550.
