It first had five books and was later expanded to ten and then twelve. Cosmas argues against the spherical cosmos of pagan astronomy. In its place he describes a flat earth inside a universe shaped like the Tabernacle of Moses. The work is valued for its early world maps and for its first-hand reports on trade, animals and Christian communities around the Indian Ocean.

The Doctrinae diversae, often called the Instructions or Discourses, is a collection of spiritual teachings by Dorotheus of Gaza. He was a sixth-century monk and abbot who trained at the monastery of Seridus under Barsanuphius and John. Written in Greek for monks, the talks deal with humility, obedience, giving up one's own will, conscience, the fear of God and not judging others. An anonymous prologue defends the author's orthodoxy. It separates him from a namesake who followed Severus and cites Theodore the Studite in his support. The work became a standard guide to monastic life in both East and West.

The Epistulae ad diversos are a short collection of Greek letters of spiritual direction by Dorotheus of Gaza, a sixth-century monk and abbot formed at the monastery of Seridus near Gaza. Addressed mostly to monks, whom he calls "child", they offer practical counsel. He urges them to entrust their affairs to God's providence instead of relying on their own reasoning, to endure afflictions with thanksgiving, and to resist troubling thoughts, and he draws on sayings of the desert fathers such as Abba Poemen. The letters are usually transmitted with his better-known Instructions on the ascetic life.

This Greek homily is attributed to Gregory, Patriarch of Antioch from about 570 to 593. Its full title says it is about the myrrh-bearing women, the burial of Christ, Joseph of Arimathea and the Lord's resurrection on the third day. The preacher praises the Church's custom of keeping the memory of Christ's three days in death among the tombs. He tells his crowded audience to see graves as resting places, where the dead wait for the trumpet of the resurrection. He then reflects on the mystery of the Saviour's voluntary death and burial.

The Concio ad exercitum is a Greek speech by Gregory, Chalcedonian patriarch of Antioch (571–593), addressed to Roman troops fighting the Persians on the eastern frontier who had mutinied under the emperor Maurice around 588. The emperor asked Gregory to mediate. In the speech he calls the soldiers "Romans in name and in deed," offers Maurice's promise of amnesty and urges them to return quickly to obedience, citing Proverbs on the king's heart being in God's hand. The speech is preserved in the Ecclesiastical History of Evagrius Scholasticus, Gregory's aide, and is an important source for the mutiny.

De baptismo Christi sermo I is a Greek homily on the baptism of Christ in the Jordan. It is attributed to Gregory, the Chalcedonian Patriarch of Antioch from about 570 to 593, who had earlier been a monk in Jerusalem and an abbot at Sinai. It is the first of his sermons on this feast and belongs to the few writings that survive under his name. The sermon ends with a prayer that Christ, who did not reject the sinful woman who touched his feet, would also receive unworthy believers. The prayer closes with a Trinitarian doxology.

De baptismo Christi sermo II is a Greek homily on the baptism of Christ, attributed to Gregory of Antioch, the sixth-century monk and abbot who was Patriarch of Antioch from about 570 to 593. The heading of the sermon calls its author a presbyter of Antioch. The preacher says he is continuing the sermon of the previous Sunday, which he had to break off for lack of time. That sermon dealt with Christ coming to John the Baptist. This one explains the Father's words from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

The Ordo et ritus confessionis is a Greek order of service for sacramental confession, attributed to John IV the Faster, patriarch of Constantinople from 582 to 595. Many scholars doubt the attribution and think the text may be considerably later. The priest stands the penitent before the altar and recites with him the Trisagion, penitential psalms and troparia. A prayer for forgiveness follows, recalling biblical penitents such as David, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Peter, the harlot and the tax collector. Penitential texts under John's name shaped Byzantine confessional practice.

This is a group of Greek penitential texts attributed to John IV the Faster, patriarch of Constantinople from 582 to 595. It contains a sermon on penance addressed to someone about to make confession, followed by excerpts from a Penitential and a Nomocanon. The sermon opens by recalling the law, angels, prophets, apostles and clergy that Christ gave to help sinners. It then gathers Old and New Testament passages urging repentance and confession. The attribution to John is disputed, and much of this material probably dates from later centuries. These texts were influential in Byzantine practice of confession and penance.

The Sermon on Repentance, Continence and Virginity is a Greek homily that manuscripts attribute to John IV the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople from 582 to 595. The attribution is not certain, so its date is uncertain too. It opens with a long praise of the Apostle Paul, who feared he might be "disqualified" after preaching to others despite all his achievements. From this it argues that ordinary Christians must keep watch and pray constantly. They should ask God for the kingdom of heaven rather than earthly wealth. The sermon then urges repentance, self-restraint and the life of virginity.

This short Greek work records a disputation between Photinus, a Manichaean, and Paul the Persian, a Christian. It is usually dated to about 527–530 and placed in Constantinople under Justinian. Photinus argues that because good and evil are opposites, both must exist as substances. Paul answers this dualist case with philosophical argument. The work ends with a list of Manichaean "blasphemies" for formal rejection. Its authorship is uncertain: one manuscript credits the refutation to Zacharias, bishop of Mytilene. It is a useful witness to Christian polemic against Manichaeism in the sixth century.

This Greek record of a public debate between Paul the Persian, a Christian, and Photinus, a Manichaean teacher, survives in more than one session. It was held in Constantinople on the orders of the co-emperors Justin I and Justinian, in the presence of the prefect Theodore, and so is usually dated around 527. Written as question and answer, it begins with the origin and creation of souls, then turns to Manichaean dualism and Christian teaching on God and creation. Whether this Paul is the philosopher of the same name at Khosrow I's court is debated.

The Propositiones christianae adversus Manichaeos is a short Greek anti-Manichaean treatise attributed to Paul the Persian and usually dated to around 527–530. It uses philosophical argument against the Manichaean teaching that the world comes from an eternal evil matter. It asks whether things arise from matter by nature, by art or by choice, and argues that none of these can explain how many different and opposing natures could come from a single matter. Whether this author is the same Paul who wrote philosophical works at the Sasanian court remains uncertain.

This is a collection of Greek theological writings attributed to Anastasius I, Chalcedonian Patriarch of Antioch (561–571 and 593–599). It brings together fragments against the Arians, including quoted extracts from Arius and Aetius on the will and nature of the Son, along with a disputation against the Jews and various orations and sermons on orthodox faith. The authorship of several pieces is uncertain. Some are assigned to his namesake successor, Anastasius II, or to other writers, and the disputation is widely considered spurious.

The Pandects of Holy Scripture is a Greek compilation of moral teaching in 130 chapters by Antiochus, a monk of the lavra of Mar Saba near Jerusalem. He wrote it in the early seventh century, between the Persian conquest of Palestine in 614 and Heraclius's reconquest. Eustathius, abbot of Attaline near Ancyra, had asked for it after his monks were driven from their home. It gathers sayings from Scripture and earlier Christian writers. It opens with the martyrdom of forty-four Sabaite monks and ends with a list of heretics.

The Oratio de sacra synaxi is a Greek homily attributed to Anastasius of Sinai, priest and abbot of the monastery on Mount Sinai, and probably composed in the late seventh century. Its heading also announces themes of not judging others and not bearing grudges. Drawing heavily on the Psalms, it urges Christians to give unceasing attention to prayer, the reading of Scripture and attendance at the liturgical assembly, or synaxis. The homily is a witness to Byzantine pastoral teaching on prayer, the liturgy and Christian conduct.

The Hodegos (Greek "Guide"; Latin Viae dux) is a Greek dogmatic and polemical handbook by Anastasius of Sinai, a monk of Mount Sinai. He probably wrote it in the late seventh century and added to it later. It is aimed chiefly at the Miaphysite followers of Severus of Antioch. The work gives definitions of theological terms, a short account of heresies and councils, and arguments from Scripture and the Fathers in defence of Chalcedonian Christology. It was meant as a practical guide for debate. Some manuscript headings wrongly call the author a bishop of Antioch.

The Anagogical Contemplations on the Hexaemeron is a Greek commentary in twelve books on the six days of creation in Genesis. It is attributed to Anastasius of Sinai, the monk and abbot of Mount Sinai, and probably dates from the late seventh century, although the attribution has been questioned. The work reads the creation narrative "anagogically", as a spiritual and allegorical account of Christ and the Church. It draws on earlier Fathers such as Irenaeus, Clement, Justin, Papias and Philo, which makes it valuable for preserving traces of early exegetical traditions.

This Greek homily on Psalm 6 is attributed to Anastasius of Sinai, the monk and abbot of Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai, who died after 700. It probably dates from the late seventh century. The sermon reads the psalm as a lesson in true repentance, covering humility, confession, tears, nightly prayer, forgiveness and the restoration of the sinner. It also interprets the psalm's title, "concerning the eighth," as pointing to the age beyond the present seven-day world. Passing references to Christ's two natures and energies place it within the debates over monotheletism.

The Quaestiones et responsiones is a Greek collection of questions and answers (erotapokriseis) attributed to Anastasius of Sinai, the monk and abbot of Mount Sinai. The core collection probably dates from the late seventh century. It answers practical and exegetical questions put by Christians living under early Islamic rule. Topics include puzzling passages of Scripture, fasting, vows, marriage, sin and forgiveness, and food eaten in times of need. The transmitted collection grew over time, and the authenticity of some questions is disputed. It is a valuable witness to pastoral concerns and popular belief in the late seventh-century Christian East.

The Quaestiones ad Thalassium (Questions to Thalassius) is a Greek work by Maximus the Confessor, written around 630–634, probably while he lived in North Africa. In it Maximus answers sixty-five questions on difficult passages of Scripture sent to him by Thalassius, a Libyan priest and abbot. His replies use spiritual and allegorical interpretation, as in his reading of Jonah as a figure of Christ. The work is one of Maximus's major writings. Its passages on the incarnation, the divine purpose of creation and deification (theosis) became central to later Byzantine theology.

The Chapters on Love (Capita de caritate) is a work of ascetic spirituality by Maximus the Confessor, usually dated to the 620s. It is addressed to a monk named Elpidius and sent together with Maximus's Ascetic Discourse. It has four hundred short maxims arranged in four "centuries", one for each Gospel. Maximus says he gathered the teaching of earlier Fathers rather than his own ideas. The chapters deal with love of God and neighbour, the passions, dispassion and pure prayer, and the work became a classic of Byzantine monastic literature.

The Chapters on Theology and the Incarnate Economy of the Son of God, also known as the Gnostic Chapters or Two Hundred Chapters on Knowledge, is a Greek work by Maximus the Confessor. It was probably written in the 620s or 630s. Its two "centuries" of short numbered paragraphs belong to the genre of ascetic chapters. The opening chapters set out God's transcendence beyond being, power and activity, and the work goes on to treat contemplation, Scriptural interpretation, the Incarnation and deification. It is one of Maximus's most influential spiritual writings and was later included in the Philokalia.

The Diversa capita ad theologiam et oeconomiam spectantia (Various Chapters on Theology and the Divine Economy, and on Virtue and Vice) is a Greek collection of short spiritual and doctrinal chapters arranged in "centuries", or groups of a hundred. It is traditionally ascribed to Maximus the Confessor (d. 662). It is now generally regarded as a later Byzantine compilation of uncertain date, drawn largely from his authentic writings. It opens with chapters on the incomprehensible Trinity and goes on to treat creation, the incarnation and the ascetic life. It was later included in the Philokalia.

This brief commentary on the Lord's Prayer was written in Greek by Maximus the Confessor, probably in the 620s or 630s. It is addressed to an unnamed "Christ-loving" correspondent and opens with a reflection on how fear and longing combine to form love. Maximus reads the Our Father as a compact summary of the divine mysteries accomplished in Christ. These include theology, adoption as children of God, the restoration of human nature and the overthrow of sin. The work is a concise statement of his spiritual and Christological theology and remains one of his most widely read shorter works.

The Ascetic Discourse (Liber asceticus, Greek Logos asketikos) is a Greek dialogue by Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662), generally counted among his early works and usually dated to the 620s. It is written as questions and answers between a brother and an elder. The elder begins by explaining that the purpose of the Lord's incarnation was human salvation. He then speaks about keeping Christ's commandments, love even of enemies, struggling against the passions, watchfulness, prayer and compunction. The work is a short, accessible summary of Maximus's spiritual teaching on monastic life.

This is a short Greek work by Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662), addressed to Theopemptus, a scholasticus, or lawyer, and published with other minor pieces. Its exact date is uncertain. Writing in reply to his correspondent's request, Maximus explains three Gospel passages: the "mammon of unrighteousness" (Luke 16:9), the command to turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:39), and the risen Christ's words "Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended" (John 20:17). His preface holds that knowledge must be confirmed by practice and leads toward deification by grace. The work shows his spiritual way of reading Scripture.

Two early Greek works by Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662), usually dated to roughly the 620s or 630s. The Quaestiones et dubia ("Questions and Doubts") is a collection of short questions and answers about difficult passages in Scripture and the Fathers, and about ascetic topics such as the virtues of soul and body and the ways people fall into sin. The Expositio in Psalmum LIX is a brief commentary on Psalm 59 (60) that reads the psalm allegorically and spiritually. Both show the exegetical method Maximus developed further in his later writings.

This anonymous Greek hagiographical dossier concerns Maximus the Confessor (d. 662), the monk and theologian who opposed Monothelitism. The Life and Contest (Vita ac certamen) praises his asceticism, learning and leadership of fellow monks, and recounts his struggle with imperial religious policy. Its date is uncertain; it is usually thought to be considerably later than his death. With it are documents about his trials and exile, notably the Relatio motionis, a record of his interrogation at Constantinople. Together they are central sources for the end of his life.

The Ambigua ("Difficulties") is a major theological work by Maximus the Confessor, written in Greek around 628–634. It explains obscure or disputed passages in Gregory of Nazianzus and Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite. It is made up of two collections, a longer early set addressed to John, bishop of Cyzicus, and a later set addressed to Thomas. Through these explanations Maximus refutes Origenist ideas, sets out his teaching on the divine logoi in creation and discusses deification and Christ's two natures. John Scotus Eriugena translated it into Latin in the ninth century.

The Disputation with Pyrrhus is a Greek theological dialogue recording a public debate held in North Africa, traditionally at Carthage, in 645. The debate was between Maximus the Confessor and Pyrrhus, the exiled former patriarch of Constantinople. Written as an exchange of questions and answers, it argues against Monothelitism. It holds that Christ, being both God and man, has two natural wills and two operations, one for each nature. Pyrrhus is recorded as accepting this position, though he later went back on it. The work is a key source for Maximus's Christology.

The Epistulae are the collected Greek letters of Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662), the Byzantine monk and theologian. They were written over several decades, roughly from the 620s until his final years of exile. Their recipients included monks, clergy and imperial officials. Some letters give spiritual counsel on love, the passions and the ascetic life. Others are doctrinal treatises defending Chalcedonian Christology. They explain how Christ's two natures remain undiminished in one hypostasis, and they argue against Monoenergism and Monothelitism. The letters are a major source for Maximus's thought and for the seventh-century Christological controversies.

The Hymni are a small group of Greek religious poems that have come down under the name of Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662), the Byzantine monk and theologian. They include a hymn of thanksgiving to God and other pieces of prayer and praise, written in short accentual verse. Their authenticity is uncertain, and scholars have often treated them as doubtful or spurious. In some printings they follow directly after Maximus's own writings on difficult passages in Gregory of Nazianzus. They are a minor part of the Maximian corpus, but they show the devotional poetry associated with his name.

The Loci communes, or Theological Chapters, is a Byzantine Greek florilegium falsely attributed to Maximus the Confessor. It was compiled in the late ninth or early tenth century and enlarged around 1000. Its 71 chapters, loosely grouped by theme, focus on ethics and human conduct rather than doctrine. Each chapter quotes the New Testament, the Old Testament, the Church Fathers and then pagan authors such as Plato, Aristotle and Menander. It was one of the most widely copied florilegia and was translated into Arabic in the eleventh century.

The Mystagogia is a Greek treatise by the monk Maximus the Confessor, usually dated to about 628–630. It interprets the church building and the rites of the Byzantine eucharistic liturgy (the synaxis) as symbols. Maximus says he is recording the teaching of an unnamed "great elder." He reads the church as an image of God, the cosmos, humanity and the soul. He then follows the stages of the liturgy, from the entrance to communion, as a path of ascent toward union with God. It is a foundational work of Byzantine liturgical commentary.

The Opuscula theologica et polemica are a collection of short Greek treatises, letters and doctrinal notes by Maximus the Confessor, mostly written during the Monothelite controversy of the 640s and after. They argue that Christ has two natural wills and two operations, divine and human. They also give careful philosophical definitions of terms such as will, choice (proairesis) and gnomic will. One piece, the letter to Marinus, is an early and much-cited comment on the Western Filioque. Together they are central to Maximus's Christology and to the teaching later upheld at the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681).

The Chapters on Love, Self-Control and Life in Accordance with the Intellect is a Greek collection of short ascetic sayings by Thalassius, a seventh-century abbot in the Libyan desert and a friend and correspondent of Maximus the Confessor. They are arranged in four "centuries" of one hundred chapters each and addressed to Paul the presbyter. The first letters of the chapters spell out an acrostic dedication. The chapters deal with love, self-control, passions, prayer and spiritual knowledge, and were later included in the Philokalia.

The Praeparatio (Greek Proparaskeue, "Preparation") is a Greek Christological treatise by Theodore of Raithu, a monk of Raithu in Sinai who was active in the late sixth or early seventh century. Writing as a Neo-Chalcedonian, he aims to prepare and train believers to understand the incarnation and to answer the followers of Eutyches and Dioscorus. The work has two parts. The first lists Christological heresies from Mani to Severus of Antioch, with refutations that include an attack on Julian of Halicarnassus. The second sets out Chalcedonian Christology philosophically, reconciling Cyril of Alexandria's terminology with Chalcedon.

The Akathistos Hymn is an anonymous Byzantine Greek kontakion addressed to the Theotokos, the Virgin Mary. It is usually dated between the late fifth and early seventh centuries. Romanos the Melodist, Patriarch Sergius and others have been proposed as its author, but none of these attributions is settled. Its twenty-four stanzas follow the Greek alphabet in an acrostic. They recount the Annunciation, the Nativity and the mystery of the Incarnation, with long chains of "Chaire" ("Hail") salutations. Congregations sing it standing, which gives it its name. It became the model for the whole genre of akathist hymns.

The Chronicon Paschale, or Paschal Chronicle, is an anonymous Greek world chronicle written in the seventh century, probably at Constantinople during the reign of Heraclius. Its author called it an epitome of the ages from Adam to the seventeenth year of Heraclius. Its name comes from its dating system, which follows the Christian Easter cycle. It opens with a discussion of the date of Easter that cites Philo and Peter of Alexandria. Although much of it draws on earlier works, it is an important independent source for events of the late sixth and early seventh centuries.

These are three historical panegyric poems in Greek iambic trimeter by George of Pisidia, a deacon at Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, written between about 622 and 630. They celebrate Emperor Heraclius during the war against Sasanian Persia. The Expeditio Persica recounts the emperor's campaign of 622. The Bellum Avaricum describes the Avar and Persian siege of Constantinople in 626 and credits the city's survival to the Virgin Mary. The Heraclias praises Heraclius's final victory over Khosrow II. The poems are important early Byzantine verse and a near-contemporary source for the war.

This is a collection of religious and moral poems by George of Pisidia, a Byzantine deacon and poet active in Constantinople under Emperor Heraclius in the early seventh century. It includes a poem on Christ's Resurrection that celebrates creation's renewal and the defeat of paganism. The Hexaemeron is a long poem on the six days of creation, and On the Vanity of Life is a moral reflection. Against Severus attacks the anti-Chalcedonian theologian Severus of Antioch. Various shorter poems complete the collection. George's polished twelve-syllable verse helped shape later Byzantine poetry.

This is a miscellaneous collection of Greek material from volume 92 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, a volume centred on seventh-century Byzantine writings, chiefly the Chronicon Paschale. It includes front matter, editorial notes and shorter pieces not indexed separately. The opening has chronological tables counting years from Adam, with landmark events such as the Exodus, the birth and baptism of Christ, and the councils of Nicaea and Constantinople. It also has a list of the seventy disciples of the Lord attributed to Dorotheus, bishop of Tyre, an attribution generally regarded as spurious.

The Homiliae are Greek sermons attributed to Hesychius of Jerusalem, a priest and biblical exegete active in the first half of the fifth century. Most were preached on Church feasts, such as the Nativity, the Presentation of Christ in the Temple, Easter and the commemorations of saints, and several honour the Virgin Mary as Theotokos. Some pieces carry chronological speculation, including a fragment on the Nativity that dates Christ's birth to the sixth millennium from Adam. Not every piece handed down under his name is certainly his.

This Greek exegetical aid is attributed to Hesychius, a priest of Jerusalem active in the first half of the fifth century. It sets out the Twelve Minor Prophets and Isaiah, with Daniel also named in some titles, in short sense-lines (stichoi) under chapter headings. Brief notes on difficult or ambiguous passages appear beside the lines. In the preface Hesychius cites the old practice of writing the Psalms, Proverbs, Job and the Song of Songs in lines. He argues that such division makes prophecy clearer to both unlearned and learned readers.

This is a Greek commentary on the Psalms attributed to Hesychius of Jerusalem, a priest and biblical exegete active in the first half of the fifth century, probably written around 430–450. It works through the Psalter verse by verse in brief explanatory notes. It reads the psalms morally and spiritually, often in a Christological or allegorical way. For example, it treats the "seat of the pestilent" as corrupt judges, false teachers and hypocrites. Hesychius's Psalm exegesis survives in more than one form, and parts of it circulated under other authors' names, so the exact attribution of some material is disputed.

The Collection of Difficulties and Solutions is a Greek work of questions and answers on apparent problems in the Gospels, attributed to Hesychius of Jerusalem, a priest and exegete of the first half of the fifth century. Its title presents it as a short selection drawn from a work on the agreement of the Gospels. It takes up puzzles such as why Mark ascribes to Isaiah a prophecy found in Malachi, and why John the Baptist denied being Elijah when Christ called him Elijah. Like earlier question-and-answer writings, it aims to reconcile apparent contradictions between the evangelists.

This is a Greek ascetic treatise in short numbered chapters arranged as "centuries", known in English as "On Watchfulness and Holiness". It is attributed to Hesychius the Sinaite, a priest and monk associated with Mount Sinai whose dates are uncertain, though he is usually placed between the eighth and ninth centuries. The work presents watchfulness (nepsis) as a spiritual method that frees the mind from passionate thoughts and leads to purity of heart. It stresses guarding the heart, inner stillness and calling on the name of Jesus. Its inclusion in the Philokalia made it an important text for Byzantine hesychasm.

This collection gathers the Greek writings of Leontius, bishop of Neapolis (Limassol) in Cyprus in the seventh century. It includes sermons and fragments of an apologia against the Jews that defends the Christian veneration of images. Passages from that apologia were later quoted by John of Damascus and at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787. The collection also contains his Life of John the Merciful, patriarch of Alexandria, and his Life of Symeon the Holy Fool of Emesa. Both saints' lives are valued for their vivid narrative and their glimpses of vernacular Byzantine Greek.

The Commentarii in Ecclesiasten is a Greek commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes by Olympiodorus, a deacon of Alexandria active in the early sixth century. It was probably written around 510–530, though the date is uncertain. It works through the biblical text verse by verse and pairs a literal, moral reading with a spiritual one. In one passage, for example, the city and its king stand for the soul and the mind. It is one of the few complete Greek patristic commentaries on Ecclesiastes to survive.

The Fragmenta in Jeremiam are exegetical comments on the Book of Jeremiah attributed to Olympiodorus, a deacon of Alexandria active in the first half of the sixth century. Olympiodorus wrote Bible commentaries, including a commentary on Ecclesiastes, and notes on Job and on Jeremiah with its related books. His Jeremiah material survives only as excerpts preserved in Greek catenae, the chains of patristic comment. The fragments mostly explain the literal and moral sense of the text. They show how Alexandrian biblical interpretation continued in the age of Justinian.

This is a set of Greek exegetical fragments on the biblical books of Lamentations and Baruch. They are attributed to Olympiodorus the Deacon, an Alexandrian biblical commentator of the sixth century, and survive mainly in catenae. The commentary reads the laments on three levels. Historically, they mourn Jerusalem's capture by Babylon. Prophetically, they point to its destruction by the Romans after the crime against Christ. Allegorically, they describe the soul that falls from virtue into vice. The work illustrates Alexandrian exegesis, which combined literal and spiritual interpretation.

On Heresies (De haeresibus) is the second part of the Fount of Knowledge by John of Damascus, the Greek monk and theologian of Mar Saba. It was probably written in the decade or so before his death around 749. The work is a short catalogue of about one hundred heresies. It begins with four "mother" heresies: Barbarism, Scythism, Hellenism and Judaism. Much of it is drawn from the Panarion of Epiphanius of Salamis and from later compilations. Later entries cover more recent movements, and the chapter on the "Ishmaelites" is one of the earliest Christian discussions of Islam.

Three Greek apologetic treatises by John of Damascus, a monk of Mar Saba near Jerusalem, against those who attacked holy images. They were written in response to the iconoclast policy of Emperor Leo III, beginning around 726–730, though their exact dates are uncertain. John argues that the Incarnation makes it lawful to depict Christ, and he distinguishes the worship owed to God alone from the veneration given to images. Each treatise ends with a florilegium of patristic testimonies. The work became a foundational defence of icons and informed the Second Council of Nicaea (787).

The Dialectica, or Philosophical Chapters, is the first part of the Fount of Knowledge by John of Damascus, a Greek monk of Mar Saba, written in the mid-eighth century. The whole work is dedicated to Cosmas, bishop of Maiuma. This part is a handbook of philosophical terminology. It draws on Aristotle, Porphyry's Isagoge and earlier Greek Fathers to define terms such as being, substance, nature, hypostasis, person, genus and species. These definitions prepare the reader for the treatise On Heresies and the Exposition of the Orthodox Faith that follow, and they shaped later Byzantine and Scholastic theological vocabulary.

The Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith is a systematic summary of Christian doctrine by John of Damascus. He wrote it in the first half of the eighth century at or near Mar Saba as the third part of his Fountain of Knowledge. Its hundred chapters cover God and the Trinity, creation, angels, humanity, providence, the Incarnation and the two natures of Christ, sacraments, icons, Scripture and the resurrection. It largely draws on earlier Greek Fathers and became a standard reference in the East. A twelfth-century Latin translation influenced Western scholastic theology.

This is a miscellany of supplementary material in volume 94 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, which opens the collected works of John of Damascus (c. 675–749), the Greek monk and theologian. It includes hagiographical texts about John, such as the close of a Greek Life of the saint and a menologion notice for his feast on 4 December. These describe his noble Damascene family and his career under the Isaurian emperors Leo III and Constantine V. The volume also contains editorial notes and minor pieces not catalogued separately. Authorship and dates vary from piece to piece.

The Vita S. Joannis Damasceni is a Greek hagiographical Life of John of Damascus, the 8th-century monk, theologian and defender of icons. It is attributed to a John, patriarch of Jerusalem, and is usually dated to the 10th or 11th century, though its author and date are uncertain. After a rhetorical prologue on the duty to honour saints in fitting words, it tells of John's Damascene origins, his education, the legend of his severed hand miraculously restored by the Virgin, and his monastic life at Mar Saba. It is a principal source for John's traditional biography.

This Greek exegetical work is a running commentary on the Epistles of Paul, attributed to John of Damascus, the eighth-century monk of Mar Saba. It goes through the letters verse by verse, explaining both their moral teaching and their doctrine. It is largely a compilation: much of it condenses John Chrysostom's homilies on Paul, with some material drawn from other Fathers. Its main value lies in preserving and passing on earlier Greek patristic exegesis. Its exact date and how much of it is original are uncertain.

This is a group of shorter Greek treatises attributed to John of Damascus, the eighth-century monk of Mar Saba. They include a question-and-answer catechism on the Trinity and the Incarnation, a letter on the Trisagion hymn, and ascetic pieces on fasting, the eight evil spirits, and virtues and vices. There is also an elementary introduction to theological terms, and polemical works against Monophysite and Monothelete Christology. Several pieces are of doubtful authenticity. The treatise on unleavened bread in particular is generally considered later and spurious.

The Sacra Parallela is a large Greek florilegium of quotations from Scripture and the Church Fathers, arranged by topic. It is traditionally attributed to John of Damascus in the first half of the eighth century, though his authorship and the history of the compilation are debated. In its prologue the work sets virtues side by side with their opposing vices, along with what Scripture and the Fathers say about each, to encourage keeping the divine commandments. It also preserves many patristic fragments that are otherwise lost.

This Greek hagiographical romance tells of the Indian prince Ioasaph. Kept from the world by his father, the king, he is converted by the hermit Barlaam and gives up his throne for the ascetic life. The story is a Christianised version of the legend of the Buddha. Manuscripts credit "John the monk" of Mar Saba, long taken to be John of Damascus. Most scholars now attribute it to Euthymius the Athonite, who adapted a Georgian version around 1000. It contains the text of Aristides' Apology and was widely translated in the Middle Ages.

This is a group of Byzantine liturgical canons in Greek, attributed in the manuscripts to "John the Monk". They honour Saint Basil the Great, Saint John Chrysostom and the Apostle Peter. Each canon is a sequence of odes sung to model melodies (heirmoi), with Theotokia addressed to the Virgin. The canon on Basil has the acrostic "With songs I sing Basil the Great." It praises his angelic life, his purified mind and his miracles. The author's identity is uncertain. Liturgical tradition sometimes identifies him with John of Damascus. The canons probably date from between the eighth and tenth centuries.

This is a collection of Greek liturgical poetry and prayers attributed to John of Damascus (c. 675–749), the monk and hymnographer associated with the monastery of Mar Saba near Jerusalem. It brings together canons and hymns for major feasts with several prayers. Among them are devotional prayers before Holy Communion, such as "Before the doors of your temple I stand", which are still used in Byzantine-rite worship. The works show John's important role in shaping Byzantine hymnography. Not every piece in the collection can be securely attributed to him.

The Disputatio Saraceni et Christiani is a short Greek dialogue between a Saracen (a Muslim) and a Christian, traditionally attributed to John of Damascus (d. c. 749). Its authorship is disputed, and part of the material is also associated with Theodore Abu Qurrah. In question-and-answer form, it gives the Christian answers to Muslim objections on the source of good and evil, free will and divine predestination, and on Christ as the Word of God. It is an important early witness to Christian–Muslim theological debate under early Islamic rule.

This is a collection of Greek sermons for church feasts attributed to John of Damascus, the monk of Mar Saba near Jerusalem who died around 749. It includes homilies on the Transfiguration, Holy Saturday, the Annunciation, and the Nativity and Dormition of the Virgin Mary, along with encomia of saints. The Transfiguration homily presents Moses and Peter on Mount Tabor as leaders of the Old and New Covenants. The three Dormition homilies became key witnesses to the tradition of Mary's bodily assumption. Scholars question whether John wrote some of the pieces.

The Sermones are Greek homilies by John of Euboea, who calls himself a monk and presbyter of Euboea and is usually dated to the mid-eighth century, the time of John of Damascus. The best known is a sermon on the conception of the Theotokos, meaning the conception of Mary by Joachim and Anna. It opens with the preacher confessing that he is unworthy to praise the Virgin and asking her help. The sermon is an important early witness to that feast and to Byzantine devotion to Mary. A homily on the Holy Innocents is also attributed to him.

De nativitate Domini is a Greek treatise in the form of a letter on the birth of Christ. It is attributed to John, archbishop of Nicaea, and addressed to Zacharias, Catholicos of Greater Armenia, which places it probably in the ninth century. It deals with the Nativity and Epiphany of Christ and with the reasons for the Church's practice of keeping the feast of the Nativity separately. It cites the apostolic ordinances ascribed to James, a homily attributed to John Chrysostom, and Epiphanius. The work is a witness to Byzantine–Armenian discussions over the liturgical calendar.

The Passio S. Artemii is a Greek hagiographical account of the martyrdom of Artemius, the military commander (dux) of Roman Egypt who was executed under Emperor Julian in 362. Manuscripts transmit it anonymously or under the name of a monk John, sometimes identified as John of Rhodes. It is usually dated between the eighth and ninth centuries. It tells of Artemius's confrontation with Julian at Antioch, his tortures and his death. It matters to historians because it drew heavily on the lost Church History of the Arian historian Philostorgius and preserves fragments of it.

The Sacra Parallela is a large Greek florilegium, an anthology of quotations from Scripture and the Church Fathers on moral and spiritual subjects. It is traditionally attributed to John of Damascus and dated to the first half of the eighth century, though his authorship is debated. The excerpts are grouped under numbered thematic headings, such as the divine oracles and the duty to hear and meditate on them. The collection survives in several recensions and preserves fragments of many patristic writings otherwise lost.

This is the collected Greek homilies and liturgical poetry of Andrew of Crete (c. 650–712 or later), a monk of Jerusalem who later became archbishop of Gortyna in Crete. His sermons are on the feasts of Christ and the Virgin, including the Nativity and Dormition of the Theotokos, and on saints. The opening sermon presents Mary's Nativity as the threshold between law and grace. The hymns include canons and idiomela, chief among them the penitential Great Canon. It is still sung during Great Lent and is a landmark in the development of the canon as a hymn form.

The Chronographia is a Greek world chronicle by John Malalas of Antioch, written in the sixth century. Its eighteen books run from Creation, through biblical, mythological and Roman history, to the reign of Justinian I. The surviving text breaks off in the 560s. It is written in a plain Greek close to the spoken language and pays particular attention to Antioch. It records earthquakes, buildings, games and the deeds of emperors. It is the earliest surviving Byzantine world chronicle. Later chroniclers drew heavily on it, and it was translated into Slavonic.

This is a miscellany of Greek and Latin material from volume 97 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca: front matter, editorial notes and short pieces that are not indexed as separate works. The surviving portion deals mostly with Andrew of Crete, the eighth-century archbishop and hymnographer. It lists the opening words of homilies attributed to him, taken from manuscript catalogues such as Bandini's and Nani's. These include encomia of Saint George, Saint Nicholas and Saint Patapius. It also quotes liturgical verses that ask for Andrew's intercession. The pieces date from different periods and have no single author.

The Opuscula are a collection of short Greek treatises and dialogues attributed to Theodore Abu Qurrah, the Melkite bishop of Harran (c. 750 – c. 825). They are usually dated to the late eighth or early ninth century. Many are written as disputations with Muslims ("Saracens"), Jews, Nestorians and Jacobites. They defend the Trinity, the Incarnation, the eternal Son and the Eucharist, deny that Muhammad's mission came from God, and set out philosophical terms. Some pieces are said to report the teaching of John of Damascus. Together they are important early evidence for Christian apologetic in the Islamic world.

This is a collection of Greek liturgical hymns, chiefly canons, by Cosmas of Maiuma. He was an eighth-century monk of Jerusalem, foster brother of John of Damascus and later bishop of Maiuma near Gaza. A canon is a sequence of odes modelled on the biblical canticles. Cosmas wrote canons for major feasts of the Lord and the Theotokos, often with acrostics. The best known is the Nativity canon, which opens "Christ is born, glorify him!", a phrase taken from Gregory of Nazianzus. Many of these canons are still sung in Byzantine-rite worship.

This is an anonymous Greek statement of faith, probably composed between the seventh and ninth centuries. Its heading presents it as the orthodox teaching handed down by the holy apostles, the Fathers and the ecumenical teachers. It opens with the Trinity, into which believers are baptized: one God in three hypostases. The three share one nature, will, energy and kingdom, and are told apart only by their properties of being unbegotten, begotten and proceeding. Like other Byzantine expositions of faith, it gathers standard patristic doctrine into a concise creedal summary. Its author and exact date are unknown.

This is the collected Greek writings of Germanus I, Patriarch of Constantinople from 715 to 730, who was removed from office at the start of Byzantine Iconoclasm under Leo III. The best-known piece is the Historia ecclesiastica et mystica contemplatio, a symbolic commentary on the Byzantine Divine Liturgy that remained influential for centuries. The collection also contains homilies, many in honour of the Virgin Mary; De haeresibus et synodis, a survey of heresies and councils; and letters, including several defending the veneration of icons.

The Explanatio in Ecclesiasten is a Greek commentary on the biblical book of Ecclesiastes. It is traditionally attributed to Gregory, a Sicilian who was bishop of Agrigento from 590 and corresponded with Pope Gregory I. Scholars have questioned the attribution, as well as whether this Gregory is the same person as the subject of the semi-legendary Greek lives of a saint of that name. If the attribution holds, the work dates from around the late sixth or early seventh century. It explains Solomon's sayings verse by verse and is a rare surviving example of Greek biblical exegesis from Byzantine Sicily.

The Isagoge in sacras Scripturas (Introduction to the Divine Scriptures) is a Greek handbook of biblical interpretation attributed to Hadrian (Adrian), an exegete of the Antiochene tradition. Little is known about him, and the work is usually dated to the fifth century. It sorts the figurative "idioms" of the Hebrew style into three kinds: those of sense, of wording and of arrangement. For example, it explains how Scripture speaks of God's actions through human limbs, senses and passions. Cassiodorus recommended it, and it is an important witness to Antiochene principles of reading Scripture.

The Life of Saint Gregory of Agrigento is a Greek saint's life about Gregory, bishop of Agrigento in Sicily in the late sixth century. Its author, Leontius, calls himself a presbyter, monk and abbot of the monastery of Saint Sabas in Rome. When it was written is uncertain, but it is usually dated to the eighth or early ninth century. The Life is largely legendary. It follows Gregory's travels to Jerusalem, Constantinople and Rome, his consecration as bishop, and his patience under false accusations and imprisonment. It is an important example of Greek hagiography from Byzantine Italy.

This is a group of Greek texts transmitted under the name of Tarasius, patriarch of Constantinople from 784 to 806. Its heading says the encomiastic oration was addressed to the holy synod by Epiphanius, deacon of Catania in Sicily, who represented Thomas, archbishop of Sardinia. It belongs to the acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (787), which Tarasius presided over, and it praises the bishops for clearing heretical "stones" from the road of faith. The letters come from Tarasius's patriarchate, when he worked to restore the veneration of icons and to enforce church discipline.

This Greek liturgical canon for the veneration of the Holy Cross is attributed to Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. It was written for the Byzantine Lenten observance in which the Cross is set out for veneration, a feast linked to the Third Sunday of Lent in the Triodion. Its hymns call the faithful to embrace the Cross joyfully and celebrate it as the source of light and salvation. They also proclaim Christ's resurrection, sing of the defeat of Hades, and present Moses' outstretched arms as a type of the Cross.

This Byzantine liturgical canon of thanksgiving celebrates the restoration of the holy icons in 843, the event later commemorated as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. Set in the plagal second mode, it praises God for raising up an Orthodox imperial power. It rejoices that the Church has received back its "garment" and shames the iconoclast leaders, including John the Grammarian and Antony. Manuscripts ascribe it to Theodore the Studite. However, he died in 826, before these events, so the attribution cannot be accepted as it stands. The canon is a hymnographic witness to the end of Byzantine iconoclasm.

This is a Greek penitential text attributed to Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople, with a set of related questions. It defines confession as recalling shameful words and thoughts without taking pleasure in them, and urges monks to disclose their sins to their abbot. Short chapters on faults such as rancour and slander then set out penances. They compare the canons of the Fathers, such as exclusion from communion, with monastic penalties like eating only dry food and making daily prostrations. Its authenticity and date are uncertain.

Adversus iconomachos capita septem ("Seven Chapters against the Iconoclasts") is a short Greek polemical treatise by Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. It probably dates from the second period of Byzantine iconoclasm, after 813. Theodore answers the charge that Christians who venerate images of Christ, the Theotokos and the saints are making gods of them. He contrasts pagan idolatry with Christian image veneration, citing biblical precedents such as the bronze serpent and the cherubim that Moses made.

The Catechesis chronica, or Chronological Catechesis, is an instruction in Greek addressed to the monks of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. It is attributed to Theodore the Studite (759–826), the monastery's abbot. Unlike his many other catecheses, it explains how the yearly cycle of feasts and fasts should be kept. It starts from the Mosaic festivals and grounds its teaching in the canons of the apostles and the Fathers. It was meant both to guide the faithful and to refute heretics. Its exact date is uncertain.

This is a Greek letter by Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople, to his uncle and spiritual father Plato of Sakkoudion. Its date is uncertain. Plato had asked how the holy icon of Christ should be venerated, and Theodore answers that the image is a likeness of its prototype. Citing Pseudo-Dionysius and Basil the Great, he argues that whoever venerates an icon honours the person depicted, not the material. The letter is a short statement of the Studite case against iconoclasm.

The Epistulae are the collected letters of Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. More than five hundred survive, written to monks, clergy, officials, emperors and many women, often during his several exiles. They give spiritual direction, encourage his scattered community, and defend his positions in the controversies of his time, especially his opposition to iconoclasm. The collection is a major source for Byzantine monasticism, church politics and the second period of iconoclasm.

This short Greek treatise explains the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts. It is attributed to Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople, though the attribution is not certain. Written as instruction to a "child", it explains that this rite is celebrated in a veiled and mournful manner, unlike other liturgies. It then takes the priest step by step through the service: the opening "Blessed is God", the lamplighting prayers, the gradual psalms, the entrance without the Gospel, the readings and "Let my prayer arise". It is valuable evidence for Byzantine Lenten liturgical practice.

The Hypotyposis is a Greek monastic rule setting out the customs of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. It is traditionally attributed to Theodore the Studite (759–826). The text itself says it was written down by his followers, who recorded the tradition "received from our great Father and confessor Theodore," so it probably dates from the period after his death. It regulates the liturgical cycle from Easter onward, the night offices, the signals that call the monks to prayer, meals and discipline. The rule had a lasting influence on later Byzantine and Slavonic monastic typika.

The Iambi de variis argumentis ("Iambics on various subjects") is a collection of short Greek verse epigrams by Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. They were probably written in the late eighth or early ninth century and use the Byzantine twelve-syllable iambic line. The poems cover many subjects, among them the relics of martyrs, the monk's cell, the offices and duties of monastic life, saints and holy images. Several defend icon veneration against iconoclasm. The collection shows Theodore's part in reviving classical literary forms in Byzantium.

The Laudatio S. Arsenii anachoretae is a Greek encomium of Arsenius the Great, the celebrated anchorite of the Egyptian desert. It is attributed to Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. It was composed for the saint's annual feast. The author remarks that, unlike other holy men, Arsenius had no written life, only scattered anecdotes. He gathers these sayings and stories and weaves them into a continuous account of his ascetic virtues, especially his humility and compunction. The work shows the Middle Byzantine monastic revival's interest in the desert fathers.

This Greek funeral oration was written by Theodore the Studite for his maternal uncle and spiritual father, Plato of Sakkoudion. Plato was the abbot who led Theodore into monastic life, and he died in 814. Theodore opens by contrasting the showy eloquence of rhetoricians and sophists with a speech that aims only at truth. He presents the eulogy as a debt owed to the man who formed him. The oration traces Plato's life, ascetic virtues and humility, and it is an important source for his biography and for the early history of the Studite monastic movement.

This is a short anonymous Greek account of the "Moechian" (adulterine) schism. The schism divided Theodore the Studite and his followers from the patriarchs of Constantinople, Tarasius and Nicephorus. It tells how Emperor Constantine VI put away his wife and remarried, and how the priest Joseph performed the marriage. Theodore broke communion with Tarasius for failing to oppose it, and later with Nicephorus when Joseph was restored under Emperor Nicephorus I. The account treats both patriarchs and Theodore as saints. It probably dates from between the ninth and tenth centuries, but its date is uncertain.

This Greek encyclical letter was written by Naucratius, a disciple of Theodore the Studite who later succeeded him as abbot of the Stoudios monastery. Addressed to the scattered Studite monks and fathers who were being persecuted during the second period of Iconoclasm, it reports Theodore's death in 826 and mourns him as their common spiritual father. It also describes his last days and praises his confession of the faith. The letter is an important early witness to Theodore's death and to how the Studite community remembered him.

The Capitula quatuor ("Four Chapters") is a short Greek ascetic text attributed to Theodore the Studite (759–826), the Byzantine abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. It defines the monastic life as mastery of the passions, watchfulness over thoughts and constant struggle against invisible enemies. Addressed to "brothers", it urges sobriety and attention of heart to guard the mind against evil images and desires. It also describes how the devil advances step by step, from a first suggestion to inner assent and finally to the death of sin, and recommends tears, prayer and compunction as defences.

The Refutation of the Iconoclast Poems is a Greek polemical treatise by Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. It was probably written during the second period of Byzantine iconoclasm, after 815, and answers iambic verses written by opponents of icons. Theodore quotes each verse in turn and rebuts it in prose. He rejects the claim that an image of Christ is a mute idol made of base matter, and defends icons by appeal to the Incarnation, Scripture and the Church's councils. The work is a key text of iconophile theology.

The funeral oration for his mother Theoctista is a Greek speech by Theodore the Studite, the Byzantine abbot and opponent of iconoclasm. It was probably composed around the turn of the ninth century, though the exact date is uncertain. Theodore addresses his monks to announce the death of Theoctista, sister of the abbot Plato of Sakkoudion. He offers her life as instruction, praising her piety, her household discipline and her later monastic life. The speech is an important source for Theodore's family and for the lives of devout Byzantine women.

The Orationes are a collection of Greek discourses by Theodore the Studite (759–826), the abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople and a leading opponent of iconoclasm. They include sermons and addresses written for monastic and liturgical settings. In the opening piece Theodore speaks to his monks as "my children" and urges restraint in spring, when the flesh grows restless. He sets measures for bread and wine and allows exceptions for feasts, heavy labour, illness and travel. The addresses show his concern for ascetic discipline and his role in the revival of Byzantine monasticism.

This is a miscellaneous group of Greek material from volume 99 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, the volume given chiefly to the writings of Theodore the Studite (759–826), the Constantinopolitan abbot and defender of icons. It brings together prefatory matter, editorial notes and short pieces that are not catalogued separately. Among them are excerpts drawn from Theodore's various letters. The dates assigned to the material match the period of his monastic leadership and the second Iconoclast controversy.

The Parva Catechesis, or Small Catechesis, is a collection of short spiritual addresses by Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. It is a companion to his longer Great Catechesis. Each talk opens with "Brothers and Fathers" and was given to his monks, probably in the early ninth century. The addresses urge obedience, humility, repentance and endurance. They often draw on feasts, the seasons and the lives of earlier saints. Later Byzantine monasteries read them aloud, and they shaped Studite monastic spirituality.

The Poenae monasteriales (Greek epitimia, "penances") is a Byzantine Greek collection of monastic penalties attributed to Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. It sets out short, numbered penances for faults in the common life of a monastery, such as arriving late to or missing parts of the divine office. Typical penalties include dry eating of bread and water, and set numbers of prostrations. An opening note distinguishes this daily monastic discipline from the canons of the nomocanon. The collection reflects the strict communal order of the Studite reform, which shaped later Byzantine monastic rules.

Problemata ad iconomachos (Problems Put to the Iconoclasts) is a short Greek polemical treatise by Theodore the Studite, abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. It probably dates from the second period of Byzantine iconoclasm, which began in 815. It is a series of numbered questions and syllogisms. They argue that Christ, being perfect in two natures, must be circumscribable, and therefore can be depicted, according to his humanity. Denying this, Theodore argues, mixes or confuses the natures. The work is one of Theodore's contributions to the Christological defence of icons.

This short Greek scholion is attributed to Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople. It defends Basil of Caesarea's authorship of the Ascetica, pointing to their elevated style and their agreement with Basil's other ascetic writings. Against doubters it compares the case with Hebrews, 2 Peter and Revelation, which were also once disputed but are accepted by the Church. It also cites Gregory of Nazianzus's mention of Basil's written and unwritten rules for monks, and the use of the work by Saint Theodosius.

The Testament of Theodore the Studite (759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople, is his spiritual will. It was written during his final illness and read aloud before his death in 826. Because illness kept him from gathering his monks from their scattered monasteries, he set down his last words for them. The text opens with a detailed confession of faith in the consubstantial Trinity and the Incarnation. It goes on to name his successor as abbot and to lay down rules for monastic life, urging the community to stay united and at peace.

The Orationes are a collection of Greek sermons by George of Nicomedia, a ninth-century Byzantine churchman. He was a cleric of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople and later became metropolitan of Nicomedia; he was a close associate of Patriarch Photios. The homilies were preached on church feasts and are mostly about the Virgin Mary, including her conception, nativity and presentation in the Temple, and her presence at the Cross. They are written in an elaborate rhetorical style. They are important evidence for Marian devotion and the development of feast-day preaching in middle Byzantine Constantinople.

The Opuscula are a group of short Greek writings attributed to Methodius I, Patriarch of Constantinople from 843 to 847, who restored the veneration of icons after the second period of Byzantine Iconoclasm. The best-known piece is a disciplinary ordinance on receiving back into the Church people who had denied the faith. It sets different penances by age and by circumstance, such as capture in childhood, ignorance or torture. These include fasting, prostrations and prayers, along with anointing with chrism.

The Epistulae are a small group of Greek letters by Nicephorus, chartophylax (archivist and legal officer) of the church of Constantinople. The best known is addressed to Theodosius, a monk and recluse at Corinth. It answers his questions on church discipline, drawing on the canonical collections. Its topics include who may be ordained, who may receive communion, penance, and whether monks who are not priests may hear confessions and reconcile penitents without their bishop's authority. Nicephorus's dates are uncertain: he has traditionally been placed around 800, but some scholars put him later.

These are two historical works by Nikephoros I, Patriarch of Constantinople (806–815). The Breviarium, or Short History, is a concise Greek narrative of Byzantine affairs from the death of Emperor Maurice in 602 to 769. It was probably written before he became patriarch, and alongside Theophanes it is a key source for the seventh and eighth centuries. The Chronographia brevis is a chronological outline running from Adam to the author's own day. It lists rulers and bishops, and its list of canonical and apocryphal books is often cited.

This is a collection of Greek writings by Nicephorus I, Patriarch of Constantinople from 806 until Emperor Leo V deposed him in 815. Most of them defend the veneration of icons during the second period of Byzantine Iconoclasm. They include an account of his exile, including a dialogue between the patriarch and the emperor, and his synodical letter to Pope Leo III. The core works are the three Antirrhetici, which answer the iconoclast arguments of Emperor Constantine V, along with the Apologeticus and demonstrations on sacred images. Canons attributed to him are also included.

This is a miscellaneous group of material from volume 100 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca that is not indexed as separate works. It includes front matter, editorial notes and shorter pieces. The volume centres on Nicephorus I, Patriarch of Constantinople (806–815), and on the Iconoclast controversy of the early ninth century. Its contents include ecclesiastical canons attributed to Nicephorus and patristic florilegia arguing that Christ, as fully human, can be circumscribed and therefore depicted. The pieces differ in authorship and date.

The Life of Saint Stephen the Younger is a Greek hagiography written in the early ninth century, about 806–810, by Stephen the Deacon, a cleric of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. It tells the life, ascetic career, miracles and death of Stephen the Younger, a monk of Mount Auxentius near Chalcedon. He opposed the iconoclast policy of Emperor Constantine V and was killed in 765. The opening defends the honouring of saints through both images and written accounts. The work is a major source for the first period of Byzantine Iconoclasm and for iconophile polemic.

This is a grouping of short Greek writings by three Byzantine churchmen of the early ninth century. It includes encomia and minor pieces. It opens with a festal encomium on the apostle and evangelist Mark by Procopius, deacon and chartophylax. The speech praises Mark as Peter's disciple, the writer of a Gospel and the first bishop of the see of Alexandria. Alongside it are minor works attributed to Gregory of Decapolis, a monk, and to Christopher, a patriarch of Alexandria. Their dating to roughly 800–850 is approximate.

The Life of Saint Nicephorus is a Greek hagiography by Ignatius the Deacon, skeuophylax of Hagia Sophia, who calls himself a disciple of its subject. It was written in the 840s, after icon veneration was restored in 843. Nicephorus was patriarch of Constantinople from 806 to 815. He was deposed for opposing iconoclasm and died in exile in 828. The Life opens as a lament and praises Nicephorus as a defender of orthodoxy. It is an important source for the second period of Byzantine iconoclasm.

The Amphilochia is a Greek collection of questions and answers by Photius, patriarch of Constantinople. It is addressed to Amphilochius, metropolitan of Cyzicus, who had sent him some three hundred difficulties to resolve. Most of it is usually dated to Photius's exile after his first deposition in 867, the "time of trials" mentioned in its preface. The answers mostly deal with difficult passages of Scripture and points of theology, but some also take up philosophy, grammar and secular learning. Together with the Bibliotheca, it is a major witness to Photius's wide learning and to Byzantine scholarship in the ninth century.

This is a supplementary group of questions and answers attached to the Amphilochia of Photius, patriarch of Constantinople (c. 815–893). The Amphilochia is a large collection of answers to theological, exegetical and philosophical questions, addressed to Amphilochius, metropolitan of Cyzicus. It was probably compiled during Photius's period out of office. Like the main collection, these additional pieces explain difficult passages of Scripture. The opening section comments on Paul's words in Galatians 5:13, that Christians are called to freedom but should serve one another through love.

These Greek exegetical fragments on the New Testament are attributed to Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople (858–867 and 877–886) and the leading scholar of ninth-century Byzantium. They do not survive as a continuous commentary. They are short comments preserved under his name in catenae, the chains of excerpts from biblical interpreters. The fragments on Matthew's Gospel begin with the genealogy, arguing that the Gentile Church is Abraham's true seed through faith in Christ. They then explain Joseph's perplexity and the conception "of the Holy Spirit". The fragments show how Photius explained Scripture, alongside his better-known Amphilochia.

This is a collection of miscellaneous material from volume 101 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, which is devoted to the writings of Photius, patriarch of Constantinople in the ninth century. It brings together prefatory matter, editorial notes and shorter pieces without their own index entry. The opening preface quotes a Byzantine account, apparently the hostile Life of Patriarch Ignatius, describing how Photius, a learned lay official, was raised to the patriarchate after Ignatius was removed. The material is anonymous or editorial and varies in date and origin.

The Carmina are a small group of Greek poems and hymns attributed to Photios, patriarch of Constantinople (858–867 and 877–886) and the leading scholar of the ninth-century Byzantine revival. The pieces are liturgical and occasional. They include a festal hymn celebrating Patriarch Methodios, the restorer of icon veneration, and the collection also carries a short prose appraisal of Athanasios's writings addressed to Photios's brother Tarasios. Their exact dates are uncertain. They show a side of Photios's learning less familiar than his Bibliotheca and his theological works.

Against the Manichaeans is a Greek polemical treatise in four books attributed to Photius, patriarch of Constantinople (858–867, 877–886). Its target is the Paulicians, a dualist movement that Byzantine writers saw as a revival of Manichaeism. The first book tells the history of the sect: its origins near Samosata, its leaders and how it spread. The remaining books refute its teachings with theological arguments. The text is an important source on the Paulicians. Scholars still debate its composition, how it relates to Peter of Sicily's history of the sect, and how much of it Photius actually wrote.

The Epistulae are the collected letters of Photios I, Patriarch of Constantinople (858–867 and 877–886), written in Greek during his career as churchman and scholar. They are addressed to popes, emperors, rulers, bishops, monks and officials. Among them are his enthronement letter to Pope Nicholas I, the encyclical of 867 to the Eastern patriarchs and a letter of instruction to the newly baptized Bulgarian ruler Boris-Michael. Other letters take up questions of theology, scriptural interpretation and spiritual counsel. The collection is an important source for ninth-century Byzantine church politics, the Photian schism and Byzantine learning.

The Homiliae are a collection of Greek sermons by Photius, patriarch of Constantinople (858–867 and 877–886) and the leading scholar of the ninth-century Byzantine revival. Most were preached in Constantinople during his patriarchates. Some are festal homilies, such as a sermon on the Nativity of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God. Others deal with public events, among them the attack of the Rus' on the city in 860 and the unveiling of the image of the Virgin in Hagia Sophia in 867. They are valuable for Byzantine preaching, Marian devotion and the history of the period.

The Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit is a Greek theological treatise by Photius, patriarch of Constantinople. He wrote it late in life, in the mid-880s, around the time of his second removal from office. It argues against the Latin teaching that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father (the Filioque). Photius holds that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, drawing on Scripture, the Fathers, councils and earlier popes, and on reasoning about the Trinity. It is the first systematic Byzantine refutation of the Filioque and shaped later Eastern polemic against Rome.

Codex 119 of the Bibliotheca, the ninth-century collection of book reviews by Photius, patriarch of Constantinople, describes a twelve-book work by Pierius, a presbyter of Alexandria. Pierius was said to have headed the Alexandrian school and taught the martyr Pamphilus. Photius praises his clear, easy style and wealth of argument. He also notes opinions that stray from later Church teaching: his talk of "two substances" in Father and Son, which Photius reads as meaning persons, and a view of the Holy Spirit as lower in glory. The entry is a key witness to Pierius's lost writings.

This is a collection of front matter, editorial notes and shorter unindexed pieces from volume 103 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca. The volume is devoted to the writings of Photius, patriarch of Constantinople (858–867 and 877–886), chiefly his Bibliotheca. Among the prefatory texts is a Greek address by Maximus Margunios, the sixteenth-century bishop of Cythera, praising Photius's learning. He commends Photius's festal homilies, his letters, his scriptural exegesis in the Amphilochia, and his skill in history and literary criticism. The pieces vary in date and authorship.

This is the closing section, codices 250 to 280, of the Bibliotheca or Myriobiblon, a ninth-century Greek work by Photius, later patriarch of Constantinople. The whole Bibliotheca is a set of reviews and summaries of books Photius had read, addressed to his brother Tarasius. When he wrote it is disputed. The section opens with excerpts from Agatharchides' work on the Erythraean (Red) Sea. Like most of the later codices, it gives longer extracts rather than brief notices. The Bibliotheca preserves much of what is known about many classical and Christian writings that are now lost.

The Elenchus et confutatio Agareni (Refutation of the Hagarene) is a Greek polemical treatise against Islam by Bartholomew of Edessa, a Christian monk who calls himself "the monk of Edessa". Its date is uncertain. Older scholarship placed it as early as the ninth century, but it is now usually assigned to the thirteenth. Addressed to a Muslim opponent and citing the Qur'an, it answers Muslim objections to the divinity and crucifixion of Christ, the title Theotokos for Mary, the eternal generation of the Son and the Trinity. It also attacks Muhammad and Islamic teaching.

The Ten Questions with as Many Answers is a short Greek canonical work in question-and-answer form, attributed to Photius, patriarch of Constantinople (858–867 and 877–886). Drawing on synodal and historical precedents, it deals with bishops, metropolitans and related matters of church order. Several answers point to failings of Roman bishops, including Liberius's acceptance of a creed issued at Antioch, the conduct of Felix, and Honorius's support for Monothelitism. Others ask which patriarchs Rome had refused to recognise. The work reflects the conflicts between Constantinople and Rome in the ninth century.

The Syntagma canonum is a Byzantine Greek collection of church canons, closely tied to the Nomocanon in Fourteen Titles. It gathers canons of the Apostles, the ecumenical and local councils, and the Fathers, and arranges them by subject, beginning with theology and orthodox faith, baptism and ordination. Tradition ascribes it to Patriarch Photius of Constantinople, but this attribution is disputed. The collection was probably revised around 883. It became a foundational source of canon law in the Greek Church.

This is a miscellany of front matter, editorial notes and shorter unindexed pieces from a volume of the Greek Patrologia devoted mainly to Byzantine canon law connected with Photius of Constantinople (ninth century). The material includes prefaces and tables to the Nomocanon in Fourteen Titles, which grouped the canons of the councils under subject headings. It also includes collections of Justinianic civil legislation from the Code, Digest, Institutes and Novels concerning bishops, clergy, monks, church property, Jews and heretics. These collections illustrate how imperial law and ecclesiastical canons were brought together in Byzantium.

These two Greek prose works are attributed to Peter, bishop of Argos, a Byzantine saint active in the late ninth and early tenth centuries. The first is a festal oration on the conception of the Theotokos by Saint Anne. It celebrates the event as the first sign of humanity's reconciliation with God, using springtime and paradise imagery for the Virgin. The second is a hagiographical life of Athanasius, bishop of Methone in the Peloponnese. Both texts witness to Byzantine Marian devotion and to the church in southern Greece at that time.

This is a Greek anti-heretical treatise attributed to Peter of Sicily, a Byzantine official. Under Emperor Basil I, around 869–870, he spent several months at Tephrike, the Paulician stronghold, to negotiate an exchange of prisoners. The History describes the Paulicians, whom it calls "Manichaeans": their supposed origins, their leaders and their dualist teachings. It is usually transmitted with three sermons against them. The work is a key source for the Paulician movement, though scholars dispute its date, its authorship and how it relates to other Byzantine anti-Paulician texts.

The Encomium on All Saints is a Byzantine Greek festal sermon in praise of all the saints, probably from the late ninth or early tenth century. Its authorship is uncertain. It has been grouped with the works of Niketas David Paphlagon, but its heading names a monk called Theognostos as the author. The preacher says that the subject is too great for his words. He praises a countless multitude of martyrs and holy ascetics across the whole world. No human can count them, but God, who numbers every hair of the head, knows each one.

This is a collection of Greek liturgical poetry attributed to Joseph the Hymnographer (c. 816–886), a Byzantine monk and one of the most prolific hymn writers of the Orthodox Church. The Mariale brings together canons, the nine-ode hymns sung chiefly at Matins, in honour of the Theotokos. It opens with verses for the feast of her Nativity, praising Anna's child as the temple of the King. A praise of the Apostle Bartholomew is included with it. Joseph is often confused with the earlier Joseph of Thessalonica, so the authorship of individual hymns is sometimes uncertain.

These are polemical treatises by Nicetas of Byzantium, a Byzantine philosopher and theologian of the ninth century, written at imperial request between about 842 and 886. The refutation answers a letter from an Armenian ruler that attacked Chalcedonian orthodoxy and the Fourth Ecumenical Council. It was composed in the name of the patriarch of Constantinople and defends the doctrine of Christ's two natures. The confutation of Muhammad's doctrines is a detailed critique of the Qur'an and one of the most substantial Byzantine anti-Islamic works.

This is a collection of Greek writings by Niketas David Paphlagon, a Byzantine author and pupil of Arethas of Caesarea who was active in the late ninth and early tenth centuries. It includes encomiastic orations on the apostles and on feasts such as the Nativity of the Theotokos, and his Life of Patriarch Ignatios, probably written in the 910s, which also serves as a polemic against Photios. It also contains fragments of a commentary on Luke and an exegesis of the poems of Gregory of Nazianzus.

This is a collection of miscellaneous material from volume 105 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca: editorial front matter, notes and shorter pieces not indexed as separate works. The volume mainly covers Byzantine Greek writers of the late ninth and tenth centuries, above all Nicetas David the Paphlagonian, author of a Life of Patriarch Ignatius of Constantinople, as well as homilies and commentaries. Its title page also names Theodore Daphnopates, Joseph Genesius and others. The pieces vary in authorship and date and have no single author.

This Greek petition (libellus) to Pope Nicholas I was written in the name of Patriarch Ignatius of Constantinople, who had been deposed in 858 and replaced by Photius. Its author was Theognostus, a monk who was archimandrite and exarch of Constantinople for the Roman Church. It presents itself as coming from Ignatius together with ten metropolitans, fifteen bishops and many abbots, priests and monks. It describes the wrongs done to Ignatius and asks Rome to intervene. The petition is an important source for the Photian controversy and for relations between Rome and Constantinople in the ninth century.

This Greek hagiographical Life of Joseph the Hymnographer (d. 886), the Sicilian-born monk and prolific composer of liturgical canons, is ascribed to John the Deacon. It was probably written in the late ninth or early tenth century.
