It tells of Joseph's flight from Sicily to the Peloponnese, and of his capture by pirates and imprisonment on Crete while travelling to Rome during the Iconoclast controversy. It then covers his release after Emperor Theophilos died, the church he built for apostolic relics, and a vision that gave him the gift of hymnody. It is a principal source for his life.

This anonymous Greek saint's life honours Nicholas the Studite (d. 868), a confessor and hegumen of the Stoudios monastery in Constantinople. It was written some time between his death and the mid-tenth century. Nicholas was a disciple of Theodore the Studite and suffered during the second period of Byzantine iconoclasm. Later he was removed as abbot for refusing to recognise the patriarch Photius. The author contrasts the rhetorical praise given to Olympic victors with a truthful account of a saint's virtues, written to rescue his deeds from oblivion for the benefit of readers.

This Greek commentary on the Book of Revelation is by Andrew, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and dates from the late sixth or early seventh century. It explains the Apocalypse verse by verse, mainly through spiritual and moral readings, and often draws on and corrects the earlier commentary of Oecumenius. Andrew divided it into twenty-four discourses and seventy-two chapters. It became the standard Greek interpretation of Revelation and helped the book gain acceptance in the Eastern Church. It also shaped how the Greek text of Revelation was handed down.

This is a Greek commentary on the Book of Revelation attributed to Arethas, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia in the early tenth century and a leading Byzantine scholar. It relies heavily on the earlier commentary of Andrew of Caesarea, which it abridges, supplements and sometimes corrects. It works through the Apocalypse in numbered sections, beginning with the prologue, the letters to the seven churches and the opening of the seals. Its interpretation is mainly spiritual and ecclesial. The work is a witness to how Revelation was received in the Byzantine Church.

The Hypomnesticon ("Book of Memoranda") is a Greek Christian handbook of biblical knowledge attributed to an otherwise unknown Joseppus (Josephus). Its date and place of origin are uncertain; it is commonly placed between the late fourth and fifth centuries, though some scholars argue for a later date. Arranged as short chapters of lists and questions, it covers genealogies from Adam to Christ, kings, prophets, priests and other figures and matters of the Old and New Testaments. It is a valuable witness to early Christian biblical learning and to the catechetical reference works of its time.

This is a group of anonymous Byzantine Greek writings, probably dating from between the eighth and tenth centuries. The main piece is an epitome on Genesis. Its heading presents it as interpretations of Genesis drawn from various Fathers and links it with a "Leo the Patrician". In short excerpts it takes up questions about creation, such as when the angels were made, the nature of darkness, and whether the Spirit moving over the waters means air or the Holy Spirit. A fragment attributed to a Jacob the Jacobite follows, with short exegetical and liturgical pieces.

This is not a single work. It gathers the miscellaneous Greek material in volume 106 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca that is not catalogued as a separate text: title pages, editorial prefaces, notes and short unindexed pieces. The volume is mainly given over to Byzantine exegetes linked with the see of Caesarea in Cappadocia, above all the commentary on the Apocalypse by Andrew of Caesarea. The fragments include remarks on biblical chronology reckoned from Adam within a six-thousand-year scheme of world history. Their authors and dates vary and are mostly uncertain.

This is a grouped collection of Byzantine Greek orations, hymns and encomia from roughly the eighth to the tenth century. Most of the pieces are attributed to John Geometres, a tenth-century poet, soldier and monk. Others are assigned to Cosmas Vestitor, and some are anonymous. Among them are orations on the Edessene martyrs Samonas, Gurias and Abibus and a discourse on evil. There is also a festal address on the Annunciation that opens with the angel's greeting "Rejoice." The collection also contains hymns in honour of the Theotokos. Together these texts reflect Middle Byzantine Marian devotion and rhetoric.

This collection brings together the writings of Leo VI the Wise, Byzantine emperor from 886 to 912 and noted for his learning. It includes his orations and homilies, many preached on church feasts such as the Nativity of the Theotokos; letters; the Tactica, a major treatise on Byzantine warfare; Notitiae listing the ranks of episcopal sees; and religious poems. It also contains the Paraeneses, admonitory chapters attributed to his father Basil I and addressed to Leo. Together these texts show the literary and religious culture of the Macedonian court.

The Oracles of Leo the Wise are a Byzantine collection of short prophetic verses, each paired with a symbolic picture, together with an old prose paraphrase that explains them. They are attributed to Emperor Leo VI the Wise (reigned 886–912), whose interest in astrology and divination later gave him a reputation as a prophet. The attribution is spurious, and the collection probably took shape between the tenth and thirteenth centuries. In riddling images the oracles foretell the fates of emperors and of Constantinople. They were widely copied and reinterpreted in later Byzantine and post-Byzantine apocalyptic thought.

This is a set of miscellaneous Greek material from volume 107 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, a volume mainly devoted to the Byzantine emperor Leo VI the Wise (reigned 886–912). It includes editorial front matter, notes and shorter pieces not indexed separately. Among them are the Admonitory Chapters (Kephalaia parainetika), attributed to the emperor Basil I and addressed to his son and co-emperor Leo. These are sixty-six short exhortations linked by an acrostic, covering education, faith and the virtues proper to a Christian ruler. Their authorship is disputed, and they may have been composed in Basil's circle, possibly by Photius.

The Chronographia is a Greek world chronicle by the Byzantine monk Theophanes the Confessor, written around 810–815. It continues the chronicle of George Synkellos and covers events from the accession of Diocletian in 284 to 813. It is arranged as annals by year of the world, and each entry gives the regnal years of the Roman emperors, of Persian kings or Arab caliphs, and of the leading bishops. It is a key source for seventh- and eighth-century Byzantine history, the early Arab conquests and iconoclasm. In the ninth century Anastasius Bibliothecarius translated it into Latin.

The Chronographia is a Byzantine Greek chronicle that carries the name of Leo the Grammarian, about whom almost nothing else is known. A colophon dates the copy to 1013. The work is one version of the chronicle tradition linked with Symeon Logothete and depends closely on that text rather than being an independent composition. Its section on the "new emperors" begins with Leo V the Armenian in 813. It covers imperial reigns, iconoclasm and wars with the Bulgarians and Arabs, and runs to the mid-tenth century. It is a significant witness to ninth- and tenth-century Byzantine history.

This anonymous Byzantine Greek historical fragment is conventionally known as the Scriptor Incertus de Leone Armenio and was probably written in the early ninth century. It covers events from the accession of Michael I Rangabe in 811 into the reign of Leo V the Armenian. Its subjects include the wars against the Bulgars under Krum and Leo's seizure of power, and it is hostile to Leo and his revival of iconoclasm. Its author is unknown, and scholars disagree about whether it formed part of a larger lost chronicle. It is a valuable near-contemporary source for this period.

This is a collection of anonymous Greek hagiographical and liturgical material on Saint Theophanes the Confessor (died c. 817/818). Theophanes was abbot of the monastery of Megas Agros near Sigriane and the author of the Chronographia. He opposed the iconoclast policy of Emperor Leo V and died in exile. The material combines a Life with a liturgical office for his feast, and probably dates from the ninth century. Its exact date and authorship are uncertain. It belongs to the body of literature that honoured opponents of iconoclasm as confessors.

This anonymous Greek polemical treatise defends the veneration of icons against the iconoclast policy of the Byzantine emperor Constantine V (741–775). Its opponents mocked Constantine as "Caballinus". It is usually dated to the third quarter of the eighth century, probably after the iconoclast Council of Hieria in 754. Some manuscripts attribute it to John of Damascus, but the attribution is generally rejected. Its title presents it as a public denunciation, "posted up" against the iconoclasts. It is an important witness to monastic resistance during the first period of Byzantine Iconoclasm.

The "Lives of the New Emperors" is an anonymous Byzantine Greek chronicle that continues the Chronicle of George the Monk (George Hamartolos). For this reason it is usually called Georgius Monachus Continuatus. It was probably written in the mid-tenth century and covers Byzantine history from the accession of Leo V the Armenian in 813 to about 948. It is closely related to the chronicle of Symeon the Logothete. The account is strongly hostile to the iconoclast emperors and presents Leo V's persecution of the Church and his exile of the patriarch Nikephoros as apostasy, comparing him to King Saul.

An anonymous Greek hagiographical extract associated with the Miracles of Saint Demetrius, the patron martyr of Thessalonica. That collection of miracle accounts was compiled in the seventh century and is an important source for the city's history. The passage itself tells how a caliph, here called Yazid, was persuaded by a Jewish false prophet to order the destruction of images in all Christian churches under his rule. It also describes the caliph's sudden death and the restoration of the icons. The same story was read at the Second Council of Nicaea (787) in defence of images.

This is a miscellany rather than a single work: the front matter, editorial notes and shorter unindexed pieces in volume 109 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca. The volume is devoted to tenth-century Byzantine historiography, especially the chronicles known as Theophanes Continuatus. The material includes Latin prefaces and annotations, along with Greek headings and notices. Among them is the title of the Life of Basil I, written by his grandson, Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos. Another note marks where the chronicle of George the Monk ends and the continuation by the Logothete begins.

This anonymous tenth-century Greek history is usually known as the Basileiai, or "On the Reigns of the Emperors", and is traditionally attributed to Joseph Genesios. Despite the title "Patria", it is not the topographical Patria of Constantinople. It was written at the command of Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos, son of Leo VI. In four books it covers Byzantine history from the accession of Leo V the Armenian in 813 to the reign of Basil I. It is an important source for ninth-century Byzantium and draws on oral reports as well as written accounts.

Theophanes Continuatus is the conventional name for an anonymous Byzantine Greek collection of histories that continues the chronicle of Theophanes the Confessor. It was compiled in the mid-tenth century under Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos, who commissioned it. The collection covers the emperors from Leo V the Armenian (813) to the reign of Romanos II. Its first four books run from Leo V to Michael III. The fifth book, the Vita Basilii, is a laudatory biography of Constantine's grandfather Basil I the Macedonian. It is often attributed to Constantine himself. The collection is a major source for ninth- and tenth-century Byzantium.

This is an excerpt from the Greek Life of Saint Basil the Younger, a holy man who lived in Constantinople and died in the mid-tenth century. Its author calls himself Gregory, Basil's disciple, and it was probably written in the later tenth century. The passage opens in the reign of Leo VI and Alexander. Imperial officials arrest Basil in Asia Minor as a suspected spy and have him questioned by the patrician Samonas. The full Life is best known for its visions of the soul's passage through the aerial toll-houses and of the Last Judgment.

The Chronicon is a Byzantine Greek world chronicle compiled by George the Monk, who called himself "Hamartolos" ("the sinner"). He wrote it in Constantinople in the reign of Michael III, probably around 866–867. Gathered from earlier chroniclers and commentators, it runs from Adam to the death of Emperor Theophilos in 842. It gives special attention to church history and monasticism and is strongly hostile to iconoclasm. A later continuation carries the narrative to 948. The work was very widely copied and was translated into Old Church Slavonic, where it shaped early Slavic historical writing.

This is a set of miscellaneous Greek material in volume 110 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca: front matter, notes and shorter pieces that are not indexed separately. The volume is given over to the Chronicle of George the Monk, also called Hamartolos. He was a ninth-century Byzantine monk who wrote a world history running from Creation to 842. The opening heading describes the Chronicle as "compiled and composed from various chroniclers and interpreters." The pieces gathered here help a reader understand that work and how it has been handed down.

This Greek prologue introduces a commentary on the twelve Minor Prophets. It is attributed to Basil, metropolitan of Neai Patrai (Neopatras, modern Hypati in Thessaly), and is usually dated, though not securely, to the first half of the tenth century. The author says that divine grace has explained to him mysteries in the prophets that are obscure and hard to grasp, and that the earlier Fathers had left many of them unexplained. He presents his work as a reply to the Jews, who he says mock Christians and mislead the simpler faithful.

This is an anonymous Greek historical fragment on the bishops of Rome, headed "On the popes, from the chronicle." It probably dates from the tenth century. It gives short notices of the late ninth-century popes, beginning with Formosus, formerly bishop of Porto, and going on to Boniface VI, Stephen VI and Theodore II. For each it records the length of the pontificate, the pope's origin and his main acts. It is notable as a Greek witness to the conflict over Formosus's ordinations and to the posthumous trial of his corpse, the so-called Cadaver Synod, under Stephen VI.

This Greek encomium praises the 318 holy Fathers of the Council of Nicaea (325) and the emperor Constantine the Great. It is attributed to Gregory, a presbyter of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and its date is uncertain, though it is usually placed in the Middle Byzantine period. The author says he wrote it at the request of a superior, for presentation to the church of Nicaea. Beginning with Constantine's rise after the persecuting emperors, it gives a brief account of the council and its defence of orthodoxy against Arius.

This short Greek treatise on the conduct of life is addressed to the protos, the head of the monks of the Holy Mountain (Athos). It is attributed to Nicholas I Mystikos, Patriarch of Constantinople (901–907 and 912–925). Its author says the recipient repeatedly urged him to write a brief, easily surveyed booklet on how to live rightly until death. It is set out in numbered chapters, like a rule (typikon). It begins with faith, love of God and neighbour and the commandments, and goes on to give moral and spiritual counsel.

This Greek homily by Nicholas I Mystikos, Patriarch of Constantinople, survives only as a fragment. Its heading says it was preached from the ambo of the Great Church, Hagia Sophia. It responds to the sack of Thessalonica in 904, when Arab raiders took the city. The preacher laments the slaughter of the men and the abuse of women and consecrated virgins. He mourns the desecrated altars and relics, and asks Saint Demetrios, the city's patron, why he let it fall. The homily is a rare contemporary church response to the disaster.

The Epistulae are the collected letters of Nicholas I Mystikos, Patriarch of Constantinople (901–907 and 912–925). They were written in Greek during his two terms as patriarch and his years of influence at court. They deal with church affairs and with diplomacy. They include his long correspondence with Simeon I of Bulgaria during the Byzantine–Bulgarian war, letters to the pope, and a letter to the emir of Crete. They are a major source for Byzantine politics, church disputes and foreign relations in the early tenth century.

This is a miscellany rather than a single work: the front matter, editorial notes and shorter pieces in volume 111 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca that are not indexed as separate works. The volume covers Byzantine Greek writing of the late ninth and tenth centuries. Among the pieces are an acclamation to Emperor Leo VI marking the ordination of Nicholas as patriarch of Constantinople and a confession of faith condemning Monothelitism, the one-will teaching of Sergius, Pyrrhus and Cyrus. Authorship differs from piece to piece, and much of the editorial apparatus is in Latin.

The Life of Saint Andrew the Fool (Andreas Salos) is a Greek hagiographical work attributed to Nikephoros, who presents himself as a presbyter of Hagia Sophia and an eyewitness. It recounts the life of a Scythian slave in Constantinople who feigned madness for Christ, and it is set in the fifth century. Most scholars date it to the tenth century, though some have argued for an earlier date. Its visions and apocalyptic passages proved influential. They include the appearance of the Virgin at Blachernae spreading her protecting veil, the source of the feast of the Pokrov.

This anonymous Greek saint's life tells the story of Luke the Younger, also called Steiriotes, a hermit and wonderworker of central Greece who died around 953. It was written in the decades after his death, probably by a monk connected with his shrine. It traces his family's flight from Aegina during Arab raids, his ascetic life in Phocis and his prophecies and miracles. The text is an important source for tenth-century Byzantine Greece and for the origins of the monastery of Hosios Loukas.

De cerimoniis aulae Byzantinae, often called the Book of Ceremonies, is a Greek handbook of court protocol compiled in Constantinople in the mid-tenth century. It was made under Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus and is attributed to him, and some material was added after his death in 959. The preface explains that setting down imperial order keeps the dignity of the throne. The book describes processions, receptions, feasts, coronations and church festivals. It draws on older documents, some from the sixth century, which makes it an important source for Byzantine court life, administration and liturgy.

This is a miscellany of editorial and supplementary material from the Patrologia Graeca volume devoted to the writings of the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos, who reigned from 913 to 959. It includes front matter and notes, among them a bibliographical survey drawn from Johann Albert Fabricius. The survey lists the emperor's works, such as his oration on the return of John Chrysostom's relics to Constantinople. It also covers the historical excerpt collections made at his command, naming the ancient and Byzantine historians they draw on.

De administrando imperio ("On Imperial Administration") is a Greek manual written by the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus around 948–952. He addressed it to his son and successor, Romanos II, and its Greek heading is "To my own son Romanos". The emperor offers guidance on domestic and foreign policy. He describes the peoples bordering the empire, including Pechenegs, Rus', Magyars, Bulgars, Croats, Serbs and Arabs, giving their origins, lands and dealings with the Romans, and advises how each might be used or resisted. It is a key source for tenth-century history and an important example of Byzantine encyclopaedism.

De thematibus ("On the Themes") is a Greek treatise attributed to the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (reigned 913–959). It describes the themes, the military and administrative provinces of the empire, in two books, one on the East and one on the West. For each theme it explains where the name came from and what it means. The work draws heavily on older geographical writers such as Hierocles' Synecdemus and Stephanus of Byzantium, so it is often antiquarian rather than up to date. Even so, it remains an important source for Byzantine provincial organization and historical geography.

This is a composite collection of Byzantine Greek texts from the eighth to tenth centuries, mostly legal and imperial writings. It includes the Ecloga, a short law code issued by the iconoclast emperors Leo III and Constantine V around 726 or 741, together with imperial novels (new laws) and other short works. Among these is the Narratio de imagine Edessena, attributed to Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus. It tells the story of the Mandylion, the image of Christ "not made by hands" said to have been sent to King Abgar of Edessa, and of its transfer to Constantinople in 944.

This is a miscellaneous group of material from volume 113 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca: front matter, editorial prefaces and notes, and short pieces not catalogued separately. The volume mainly contains Greek writings connected with the tenth-century Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos (reigned 913–959). These include his treatise On the Themes, which explains the origin of the names of the empire's provinces, and the guide to foreign peoples and diplomacy addressed to his son Romanos, known as De administrando imperio. Latin introductions and critical annotations accompany the texts.

This is part of the Greek menologion compiled by Symeon Metaphrastes, a Byzantine official and hagiographer who died around 1000. The menologion is a large collection of saints' lives arranged by feast day across the church year. Symeon collected older hagiographical texts and often rewrote them in a more polished, elevated Greek style. This section opens with the Life of Euphrosyne of Alexandria, set under Theodosius II. The Metaphrastic collection became the standard menologion of the Byzantine Church. Its success meant that many earlier versions of these lives were copied far less often.

This is a grouping of minor Greek texts connected with Symeon Metaphrastes, the tenth-century Byzantine official and hagiographer best known for his menologion of rewritten saints' lives. It opens with a liturgical office in his honour. Its canon carries the acrostic "I sing of you who wrote the metaphrases." Next come writings attributed to Symeon himself: an oration on the lament of the Mother of God at the Cross, iambic verses, moral sayings arranged alphabetically and a summary of church canons. Some of these attributions are uncertain.

This is a set of miscellaneous material from volume 114 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, which belongs to the series of volumes devoted to Symeon Metaphrastes, the tenth-century Byzantine compiler of the Menologion, a collection of reworked saints' lives. It includes editorial front matter, notes and shorter pieces not catalogued separately. Among them is Metaphrastes' account of a visit to Paros during a naval expedition against the Arabs of Crete. There are also bibliographical notes on later vernacular Greek translations of his saints' lives, such as those made by the Cretan monk Agapios.

This is part of a Greek collection of saints' lives associated with Symeon Metaphrastes, a Byzantine official and hagiographer who died around 1000. His menologion, compiled in the later tenth century, rewrote older accounts of the saints in a more polished literary style. The lives are arranged by feast day across the church year. This section opens with an encomium of Theophanes the Confessor of Sigriane, who defended icons against iconoclast emperors. The Metaphrastic collection became the standard Byzantine menologion and largely replaced earlier versions of many saints' lives.

The Acta S. Demetrii martyris is an anonymous Greek hagiographical account of Demetrius of Thessalonica, one of the most venerated military martyrs of the Byzantine world. It probably dates from between the seventh and ninth centuries, though the date is uncertain. It tells how Demetrius brought others to Christ through his teaching and was tortured and put to death under the emperor Maximian for refusing to give up his faith. It is one of several Greek versions of his passion that helped spread his cult, which centred on Thessalonica.

This is a Greek hagiographical account of the martyrs of Edessa. It is included in the menologion of Symeon Metaphrastes, the tenth-century Byzantine collection of saints' lives that he reworked and compiled. It tells how Shamuna and Guria, two Christians raised at Edessa, were denounced, tortured and executed during the persecution under Diocletian. It also tells of the later martyrdom of the deacon Habib. The text reworks earlier Syriac traditions about these saints and shows how the cults of Edessene martyrs reached the Greek-speaking Byzantine church.

This is a miscellaneous grouping of Greek material from volume 116 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca: front matter, notes and pieces not indexed separately. The volume belongs to the series of volumes devoted to the saints' lives collected or reworked by Symeon Metaphrastes in the late tenth century. The opening piece is a martyr narrative of Acindynus, Pegasius and Anempodistus. Under the Persian king Shapur (Sapor), they were denounced for teaching the Christian faith and were interrogated before him. The pieces vary in authorship and date.

The Novellae constitutiones are the Greek legislative decrees ("novels") issued by the Byzantine emperor Basil II, who reigned from 976 to 1025. One of them repealed the law of Nikephoros II Phokas that had banned the founding of new monasteries, hostels and homes for the elderly. Basil's other novels, notably that of 996, limited the growth of large estates held by the powerful landowning families. The texts survive partly through canonists such as Theodore Balsamon. They are an important source for Byzantine law, church property and the relationship between church and state.

This is a group of Greek writings attributed to Ignatius the Deacon, a Byzantine churchman and man of letters of the early ninth century. Its main piece is a short verse drama in iambic lines on the fall of Adam. The poem retells how the envious serpent, once fallen himself, tricked the first parents in Eden and brought about their downfall, with the characters speaking in dialogue. The group also contains other verses, an alphabetic sequence of iambic poems and a letter. Together they are evidence for learned Byzantine poetry in the period of Iconoclasm.

The History in ten books is a Greek historical narrative by the Byzantine deacon Leo, probably written in the 990s. It runs from the death of Constantine VII in 959 to the death of John I Tzimiskes in 976, covering mainly the reigns of Romanos II, Nikephoros II Phokas and Tzimiskes. Its subjects include the reconquest of Crete and the wars against the Arabs, Bulgarians and Sviatoslav of Kiev. Written in a classicizing style and drawing partly on eyewitness experience, it is a key source for tenth-century Byzantium.

The Menologium Basilii II, or Menologion of Basil II, is an anonymous Byzantine Greek collection of short notices on saints and feasts, arranged by day according to the liturgical calendar. It belongs to the synaxarion tradition. It was compiled for Emperor Basil II (reigned 976–1025), whom an opening dedicatory poem praises as "lord of all the earth" and "sun of the purple". Its date is disputed, with estimates ranging from the 980s to around 1000. It is an important witness to middle Byzantine hagiography and the cult of the saints.

The Suda (Latin Suidae Lexicon) is a large Byzantine Greek encyclopedic lexicon compiled anonymously in the late tenth century. It was once wrongly attributed to an author called Suidas or Soudas. Its roughly 30,000 entries are arranged in a modified alphabetical order and combine word definitions, grammatical notes, proverbs and biographies of ancient and Christian writers. Its compilers drew on earlier lexica, scholia and historical excerpts, many of them now lost. That makes the Suda an important source for classical literature, Byzantine learning and the history of the early Church.

This is a miscellaneous group of Greek texts from the tenth century, as printed in the Patrologia Graeca. It brings together a letter attributed to the Byzantine emperor John I Tzimiskes (reigned 969–976) and several short anonymous fragments gathered by the eighteenth-century Italian editor Andrea Gallandi. One fragment closes a military treatise on ambushes in mountain passes, ending with "the end of the Tactica". Another is a short chronological note that counts the years from Adam to Christ and then traces the early life of Jesus. Authorship and dating of the individual pieces are uncertain.

This is a Greek commentary on the Acts of the Apostles and the Pauline Epistles, in the form of a catena: a chain of short explanations drawn mainly from earlier Fathers, especially John Chrysostom. It was long attributed to Oecumenius, thought to have been bishop of Trikka in Thessaly around the tenth century. That attribution is now doubted, so the compiler is often called Pseudo-Oecumenius, and the date is uncertain. Its preface praises the compiler for gathering the best of earlier interpreters, like a bee collecting honey from many flowers, into a brief and clear exposition.

This is not a single work but a grouping of miscellaneous material from volume 118 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca: editorial front matter, notes, scholia and short pieces not catalogued separately. The volume is largely given over to Greek catena-style commentaries on the New Testament, traditionally attributed to Oecumenius. These commentaries compile and summarise earlier patristic exegesis, especially that of John Chrysostom. The fragments here are anonymous or of uncertain authorship and are usually placed in the tenth century, though that date is approximate.

This is a collection of synodal decrees and canonical letters issued by patriarchs of Constantinople, attributed here chiefly to Michael I Cerularius (patriarch 1043–1059) and his successor Constantine III Leichoudes (1059–1063). It also includes pieces under other patriarchs' names, beginning with a ruling headed "of Nicholas the Old". That ruling banned the doorkeeper of the patriarchal archive from charging fees for patriarchal letters and gave him a yearly salary instead. The texts deal with church discipline, administration and canon law, and they document how the Byzantine patriarchate governed itself in the tenth and eleventh centuries.

This is a miscellaneous grouping of material from volume 119 of Migne's Patrologia Graeca, a series of Greek Christian writings. It holds front matter, notes and shorter pieces that are not indexed as separate works. Most of it is anonymous and probably dates from the Middle Byzantine period. The opening passage defends the inspiration and authenticity of the Apocalypse of John against those who called it spurious. To support this, it cites Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, Methodius of Olympus, Cyril of Alexandria and Hippolytus of Rome, and it presents the book as a prophecy of things past, present and to come.

This Greek commentary on the seven Catholic Epistles (James, 1–2 Peter, 1–3 John and Jude) has come down under the name of Oecumenius. Its author is uncertain, and it is now usually called Pseudo-Oecumenius. It was long linked with a tenth-century bishop of Trikka in Thessaly, but the various commentaries carrying that name are no longer thought to come from one person. The work divides each epistle into chapters with summary headings and explains the text in a compiled, catena-like style that draws on earlier Greek interpreters.

This Greek commentary on the Pauline epistles, covering Colossians through Hebrews, has come down under the name of Oecumenius. It was once credited to a tenth-century bishop of Trikka in Thessaly, but its authorship is uncertain, so the writer is often called Pseudo-Oecumenius. It is a catena-style work that draws heavily on earlier Greek interpreters, especially John Chrysostom. Each epistle opens with an introductory summary of its occasion and argument, followed by verse-by-verse exposition. It is a useful witness to Byzantine exegesis of Paul.

This is a group of eleventh-century Greek documents on the breach between Rome and Constantinople. It includes the synodal edict issued at Constantinople in 1054 under Patriarch Michael Cerularius, which condemned the papal legates led by Humbert of Silva Candida after they excommunicated the patriarch. It also contains letters exchanged between Cerularius and Peter III, patriarch of Antioch, who urged moderation over disputed Latin practices. The last piece is a short treatise by Nicetas, chartophylax of Nicaea, that lists earlier schisms between the two churches and their causes. Together these texts are key Byzantine evidence for the events of 1054.

This collection contains Greek writings by Epiphanius, a monk and priest of the Kallistratos monastery in Constantinople in the eighth or ninth century. Its main text is a Life of the Virgin Mary, one of the earliest Byzantine attempts at a full narrative of her birth, upbringing, life and death. Epiphanius criticises earlier accounts, including the Protevangelium of James and Dormition narratives attributed to John of Thessalonica and to John the Theologian. He says he gathered only reliable material, from Eusebius and other writers. The collection also includes a Life of the Apostle Andrew and shorter pieces.

These Greek polemical letters by Leo, Archbishop of Ohrid (1037–1056), attack Latin liturgical practices. The best-known was written about 1053 to John, bishop of Trani in Apulia. Through him it was meant to reach all the bishops of the "Franks" and the pope. Leo condemns the Western use of unleavened bread (azymes) in the Eucharist and fasting on Saturdays, calling both Jewish observances that Christ's new Passover had ended. Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida translated the letter into Latin and wrote a reply. The letter helped start the controversy that led to the break of 1054 between Rome and Constantinople.

The Orationes et carmina gather the speeches and poems of John Mauropous (c. 1000–c. 1080), a Byzantine scholar, teacher of Michael Psellos and metropolitan of Euchaita. They are written in learned Greek and include sermons for church feasts, such as an oration on the Dormition of the Theotokos introduced by verse, along with religious and occasional poems and pieces addressed to the imperial court. Taken together, the collection is an important witness to the literary, religious and intellectual culture of eleventh-century Constantinople.

This collection gathers Greek writings of Niketas Stethatos (c. 1005–c. 1090), a monk and priest of the Stoudios monastery in Constantinople and disciple of Symeon the New Theologian. Its centrepiece is three "centuries" of chapters on the practical, natural and gnostic stages of the spiritual life. They trace the ascent from ascetic struggle through contemplation of creation to mystical theology, and they were later included in the Philokalia. The volume also contains his polemic against the Latins, written around the schism of 1054, which attacks practices such as unleavened bread in the Eucharist, together with shorter theological treatises.

This is a collection of Greek writings by or attributed to Symeon the New Theologian (c. 949–1022), the Byzantine monk and abbot of Saint Mamas in Constantinople. It contains his discourses (orationes) to monks on repentance, tears, obedience and the vision of God, and his Hymns of Divine Love. It also has the Practical and Theological Chapters, short ascetic maxims later included in the Philokalia, and a dialogue. The treatise On the Three Methods of Prayer, an early description of hesychast prayer, is also included, though Symeon's authorship of it is widely doubted.

The Life of Saint Nilus the Younger is a Greek hagiography of Nilus of Rossano (c. 910–1004), the Calabrian monk who founded the monastery of Grottaferrata near Rome. It was written in the first half of the eleventh century, probably at Grottaferrata. It is traditionally attributed to his disciple Bartholomew, though this attribution is uncertain. The Life follows Nilus's ascetic career among the Greek monastic communities of southern Italy and his travels northward. It is a key source for Italo-Greek monasticism and for the history of Byzantine and Lombard southern Italy around the year 1000.

The Homiliae are a collection of Greek sermons from eleventh-century Byzantium that follow the feasts and Sundays of the church year. They are transmitted under the name John Xiphilinus. Some attribute them to Patriarch John VIII Xiphilinus (died 1075), but they are more commonly assigned to his nephew, John Xiphilinus the Younger, a monk known as a preacher and as the epitomator of Cassius Dio. One homily, for the Third Sunday of Lent and the veneration of the Cross, presents Moses' rod as a type of the Cross and its saving power.

The Apology of al-Kindī is an Arabic Christian apologetic work written as an exchange of letters and set at the court of the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn (813–833). In it a Muslim, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ismāʿīl al-Hāshimī, courteously invites his Christian friend ʿAbd al-Masīḥ ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī to accept Islam. Al-Kindī replies at length, defending the Trinity and the Incarnation and criticising Islam. Its author and date are disputed, with estimates ranging from the ninth to the tenth century. A twelfth-century Latin translation shaped medieval European views of Islam.

The History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria is a collection of biographies of the patriarchs of the Coptic Church, written in Arabic. It was traditionally attributed to Severus ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, bishop of al-Ashmunein in the tenth century. Modern scholars credit Mawhub ibn Mansur ibn Mufarrij with compiling it in the late eleventh century, partly from earlier Coptic sources. This first part opens with Saint Mark the Evangelist, the church's founder and martyr in Alexandria. It continues through his successors to Theonas, who died in 300. The work is a central source for Egyptian church history.

The History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria is an Arabic collection of biographies of the heads of the Coptic Church. Tradition attributes it to the tenth-century bishop Severus ibn al-Muqaffaʿ. Modern scholarship credits its compilation, around the late eleventh century, to the Alexandrian deacon Mawhub ibn Mansur ibn Mufarrij, who drew on earlier Coptic sources. This section begins with Peter I, martyred under Diocletian in 311, and ends with Benjamin I (d. 661). It covers the Arian controversy, the Christological disputes after Chalcedon and the Arab conquest of Egypt. It is a key source for Egyptian church history.

This section of the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria is an Arabic collection of the lives of the Coptic (Miaphysite) patriarchs. It was traditionally credited to Severus ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, but it was largely put together in the late eleventh century, chiefly by Mawhub ibn Mansur ibn Mufarrij, from earlier Coptic biographies. This part runs from Agathon (661–677) to Michael I, who died in the 760s. It covers church life in Egypt under early Islamic rule, Umayyad taxation and persecution, and the change to Abbasid rule. It is a key source for Egyptian Christian and early Islamic history.

This section of the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria, the chief chronicle of the Coptic Orthodox Church, covers the patriarchs from Mennas I (767–774) to Joseph I (d. 849). That was a period of early Abbasid rule in Egypt, with heavy taxation, unrest and revolts. Its anonymous author says he took up the work after a holy monk saw a dream, and that he continued earlier biographers. The collection was traditionally credited to Severus ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, but it was compiled in Arabic from older Coptic material, largely in the late eleventh century.

1 Chronicles is the first half of the Book of Chronicles, a Hebrew scriptural history that the Septuagint divided into two books and called Paralipomenon. Tradition ascribed it to Ezra. Modern scholars instead attribute it to an anonymous priestly author, "the Chronicler," writing in Jerusalem in the Persian or early Hellenistic period. It opens with genealogies from Adam to the exiles who returned from Babylon. It then narrates the death of Saul and the reign of David, stressing the ark, the Levites and the preparations for the Temple.

1 Kings is the first half of the Book of Kings in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint and Vulgate tradition calls it 3 Kingdoms (Regnorum III). The anonymous work belongs to the Deuteronomistic history. Scholars generally date a first edition to the late seventh century BC and a final edition to the mid-sixth. It tells of David's death and Solomon's accession and reign, including the building of the Jerusalem Temple. It then covers the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam and Jeroboam and the later kings of Israel and Judah, ending with Elijah's conflict with Ahab.

1 Samuel is the first half of the Book of Samuel in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint calls it 1 Kingdoms and the Vulgate 1 Kings. It is anonymous. Jewish tradition credits it to the prophet Samuel, with additions by Gad and Nathan. Modern scholars see it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, put together from older sources around the seventh to sixth centuries BC. It tells of Samuel's birth to Hannah and his career as a prophet, the fortunes of the Ark of the Covenant, Saul's anointing and rejection as Israel's first king, and David's rise.

2 Chronicles is the second half of the Book of Chronicles in the Hebrew Bible, which was divided into two books in the Septuagint. Greek and Latin tradition calls it Paralipomenon. It is anonymous. Tradition credited it to Ezra, but scholars attribute it to an unknown "Chronicler" writing in the Persian or early Hellenistic period. It tells the story of Solomon's reign and the building of the Temple, then follows the kings of Judah to the Babylonian exile. It ends with the edict of Cyrus allowing the exiles to return.

2 Kings is the second half of the Book of Kings in the Hebrew Bible. In the Septuagint and later Greek and Latin tradition it is called 4 Kingdoms. The anonymous work closes the Deuteronomistic history. It runs from Elijah's last days and Elisha's ministry through the fall of Samaria to Assyria and the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah. It ends with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and Jehoiachin's release in exile. Scholars generally date a first edition to the late seventh century BC and a final edition to the mid-sixth.

2 Samuel is the second half of the Book of Samuel in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint and Vulgate count it as the second Book of Kingdoms or Kings. It tells of David's reign, from his lament for Saul and Jonathan to his rule over Judah and Israel, his capture of Jerusalem, God's promise of a lasting dynasty, his sin with Bathsheba, and Absalom's revolt. Jewish tradition credits it to Samuel, Gad and Nathan. Modern scholars treat it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, compiled about 630–540 BC from older sources.

Amos is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is the third of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew order and the second in the Septuagint. It is attributed to Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah. He preached in the northern kingdom of Israel around 760–750 BC, under Jeroboam II and Uzziah. Its nine chapters announce oracles against the surrounding nations and then against Israel itself. They condemn oppression of the poor, empty worship and injustice. Scholars debate how much of the book's account of the prophet is historical.

The Book of Daniel is a biblical apocalypse set during the Babylonian exile in the 6th century BC. Most scholars date its final form to about 167–163 BC, during the persecution under Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Its six court tales (chapters 1–6), written mostly in Aramaic, tell of Daniel and his companions at the Babylonian and Persian courts. Four visions follow (chapters 7–12), written mainly in Hebrew. The Greek versions, the Old Greek and Theodotion, add Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, and the Prayer of Azariah. Daniel strongly shaped Jewish and Christian apocalyptic thought.

Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Torah and of the Christian Old Testament, is presented as Moses' farewell speeches to Israel on the plains of Moab before they enter the Promised Land. It reviews the wilderness wanderings, restates the law, and calls Israel to stay faithful to God. It ends with the Song and Blessing of Moses and his death. Tradition credited Moses with writing it, but most scholars date it to the 7th–5th centuries BC. It contains the Shema (6:4), which Jesus quoted as the greatest commandment.

Ecclesiastes (Hebrew Qoheleth, "the Preacher" or "Teacher") is a book of wisdom literature in the Ketuvim of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. Tradition attributes it to Solomon, but most scholars date it to roughly the fifth to second centuries BC, partly because of its late Hebrew and Persian loanwords. Its speaker reflects on how fleeting and "vain" human toil, wisdom and pleasure are "under the sun," since death comes to all. He recommends enjoying life's simple gifts from God, and the book closes by urging the reader to fear God and keep his commandments.

Esther is an anonymous book of the Hebrew Bible, one of the Five Scrolls (Megillot) among the Writings, and part of the Christian Old Testament. Its date is uncertain, usually placed in the Persian or early Hellenistic period. Set at the court of the Persian king Ahasuerus, it tells how the Jewish queen Esther and her cousin Mordecai foil Haman's plot to destroy the Jews, and it explains the origin of the festival of Purim. The Hebrew text never names God explicitly. The Greek version adds several passages, including prayers, that are accepted as canonical in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

Exodus is the second book of the Bible and of the Pentateuch. Tradition ascribes it to Moses, but modern scholars think it took shape from earlier sources and oral traditions during and after the Babylonian exile, with final revision in the Persian period. It tells how the Israelites were enslaved in Egypt and freed under Moses. It goes on to describe the covenant and the giving of the Law at Mount Sinai, and the building of the Tabernacle. Passover and the crossing of the Red Sea became central images for Jewish and Christian interpreters alike.

The Book of Ezekiel is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It follows Isaiah and Jeremiah among the major prophets. It presents itself as the visions and oracles of Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, dated between about 593 and 571 BC, though its final form reflects a longer process of composition. It has three main parts: judgment on Israel, oracles against the nations and promises of restoration. These include the valley of dry bones and the new Temple. Its throne-chariot vision shaped later Jewish mysticism and Christian apocalyptic and exegetical tradition.

The Book of Ezra is a book of the Hebrew Bible and Christian Old Testament, written in Hebrew and Aramaic and originally joined with Nehemiah as a single work. Its author is unknown; tradition credits Ezra himself. It tells how Cyrus allowed the exiles to return from Babylon in 538 BC and how the Temple in Jerusalem was rebuilt and dedicated in 515 BC. It then follows the scribe and priest Ezra's mission to reform the community, including his campaign against marriages with non-Jews.

Genesis is the first book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, and the opening book of the Torah, or Pentateuch. Tradition names Moses as its author. Most modern scholars instead see it as an anonymous composite work that took its final form during or after the Babylonian exile, perhaps in the fifth century BC. Its first part (chapters 1–11) tells of the creation, the fall, the flood and the early history of humanity. Its second part (chapters 12–50) follows the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. Church Fathers wrote many commentaries and homilies on it.

The Book of Habakkuk is the eighth of the Twelve Minor Prophets of the Hebrew Bible. It is attributed to the prophet Habakkuk and is usually dated to the late seventh century BC, probably during the reign of Jehoiakim of Judah (609–597 BC). In the first two chapters the prophet speaks with God about injustice and the coming Chaldean (Babylonian) invasion. The third chapter is a liturgical prayer, and scholars disagree about whether it has the same author. Habakkuk 2:4, "the just shall live by his faith," became central to Christian thought through Paul's letters.

The Book of Haggai is a short prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible. It is the tenth of the Twelve Minor Prophets. Its two chapters contain oracles that the prophet Haggai delivered in Jerusalem in 520 BC, the second year of the Persian king Darius I. Haggai addresses the governor Zerubbabel, the high priest Joshua and the people who had returned from exile in Babylon. He urges them to rebuild the ruined Temple and blames the land's poor harvests on their neglect of it. He also promises future glory for the Temple and for Zerubbabel.

The Book of Hosea is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is traditionally first among the Twelve Minor Prophets and is attributed to Hosea son of Beeri, an eighth-century BC prophet of the northern Kingdom of Israel. Its fourteen chapters condemn Israel's worship of other gods. They compare the people's unfaithfulness to Yahweh with the infidelity of Hosea's wife Gomer, and they promise eventual reconciliation. Much of the book probably dates to the time of Jeroboam II, though scholars dispute how far later editors shaped it.

The Book of Isaiah is the first of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the first of the major prophets in the Christian Old Testament. It is attributed to Isaiah son of Amoz, an eighth-century BC prophet in Jerusalem. Most scholars think much of it was written later, during and after the Babylonian exile. Its oracles of judgment and restoration focus on Judah, Jerusalem and the nations. Christian writers read its prophecies of Immanuel and the Suffering Servant as foretelling Christ, and quoted it more often than almost any other book.

The Book of Jeremiah is the second of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and one of the major prophets of the Christian Old Testament. It collects the oracles, laments and life story of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, a priest from Anathoth, who preached in Judah from the reign of Josiah until the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC. Jeremiah's followers, perhaps including his scribe Baruch, and later editors expanded the book. It warns of judgment for idolatry and promises a new covenant. It survives in two forms: the Hebrew text and a shorter Greek Septuagint version.

The Book of Job is an anonymous book of the Hebrew Bible. It belongs to the Ketuvim (Writings) and is the first of the Poetic Books of the Christian Old Testament. Its language points to composition in the Persian period, though the date is uncertain. A prose prologue and epilogue frame poetic dialogues between the righteous Job, who has lost his wealth, children and health, and his friends, followed by Elihu's speeches and God's reply from the whirlwind. The book's treatment of innocent suffering and divine justice made it a major subject of Jewish and Christian theology and exegesis.

The Book of Joel is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and one of the Twelve Minor Prophets. It names its author as "Joel the son of Pethuel", of whom nothing else is known. Its date is disputed. Many scholars place it in the Persian period, partly because it alludes so often to earlier prophetic texts. Starting from a devastating locust plague, it calls the people to repentance and announces the coming Day of the Lord. It also foretells the outpouring of God's Spirit on all people, a prophecy Peter quotes in his Pentecost sermon in Acts 2.

The Book of Jonah is an anonymous Hebrew narrative and one of the twelve Minor Prophets in the Jewish and Christian Old Testament. It tells of the prophet Jonah, son of Amittai, who flees God's command to preach against Nineveh. A great fish swallows him during a storm. After he is released he preaches, the city repents, and God spares it. Most scholars date the book to the postexilic period. Jesus' "sign of Jonah" led early Christian writers to read Jonah as a type of Christ's death and resurrection.

Joshua is the sixth book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It tells how Joshua son of Nun succeeded Moses and led the Israelites across the Jordan. It narrates their campaigns to conquer Canaan, the division of the land among the twelve tribes, and Joshua's closing call to remain faithful to the Law. Jewish tradition attributes the book to Joshua himself. Modern scholars treat it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, with an early form probably written in the late seventh century BC and completed during or after the Babylonian exile.

Judges is the seventh book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is anonymous: Jewish tradition attributed it to Samuel, while modern scholars see it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, with the main editing often dated to the 7th century BC and later. It covers the period between Joshua's conquest and the monarchy. The book follows a repeated cycle in which Israel is unfaithful, is oppressed, repents and is rescued by a leader. These leaders include Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson. Its closing chapters look ahead to the coming of kingship.

Lamentations is a book of the Hebrew Bible made up of five poems mourning the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians in 586 BC. Four are alphabetic acrostics. Tradition ascribes them to the prophet Jeremiah, and in Christian Bibles the book follows his. Most modern scholars reject this authorship but date the poems to shortly after the city's fall. The poems personify Zion as a bereaved widow and present the people's sin as the cause of divine judgment. Jews read the book on Tisha B'Av, and Christians read it during Holy Week.

Leviticus is the third book of the Torah (Pentateuch) and of the Old Testament, traditionally ascribed to Moses. Its anonymous text probably developed over a long period, and many scholars think it reached its present form in the Persian period, though this is disputed. Set at Mount Sinai, it consists mostly of divine instructions given to Moses for the Israelites and the Aaronic priests. These cover sacrifices, priestly ordination, purity laws, the Day of Atonement and the Holiness Code (chapters 17–26). Christian interpreters read its sacrifices and priesthood typologically.

Malachi is the last of the Twelve Minor Prophets and, in Christian Bibles, the final book of the Old Testament. Its author is unknown: "Malachi" means "my messenger" and may not be a personal name, and Jewish tradition identified the writer with Ezra. The book mostly dates from the Persian period, perhaps around 500–450 BC. It is written as disputes between God and the people, and it rebukes careless priests, corrupt sacrifice, divorce and unpaid tithes. Christians long read its promise of a coming messenger and the return of Elijah as foretelling John the Baptist.

The Book of Micah is the sixth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is attributed to Micah of Moresheth, a Judean prophet active in the late 8th century BC under kings Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. Its seven chapters alternate oracles of doom against Samaria and Jerusalem with promises of restoration. Micah condemns corrupt leaders and defends the poor. Christians read 5:2 as foretelling the Messiah's birth in Bethlehem. Scholars debate when the book reached its final form, possibly in the Persian or Hellenistic period.

The Book of Nahum is the seventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It has three chapters and is attributed to the prophet Nahum the Elkoshite. In vivid poetry it foretells the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, as God's judgement on an oppressor of Judah. Its date is debated. Many place it between the sack of Thebes in 663 BC and Nineveh's fall in 612 BC, though other dates have been proposed. The book survives in the Septuagint, the Peshitta and other ancient versions.

Nehemiah is a book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, written in Hebrew. In Jewish tradition it originally formed a single book with Ezra. Much of it is a first-person memoir by Nehemiah, the Jewish cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes. He was appointed governor of Judah and, around 445 BC, led the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls despite local opposition. The book also covers the public reading of the Law under Ezra, the renewal of the covenant, and Nehemiah's religious and social reforms. Its final form probably dates from the late fifth or fourth century BC.

Numbers is the fourth book of the Hebrew Bible and of the Pentateuch, traditionally attributed to Moses. Scholars think it has a long, complex history, and its final form probably comes from a Priestly editing in the early Persian period. It is named after the two censuses of Israel that it records. The book follows the Israelites from Sinai through their wanderings in the wilderness. It tells of their rebellions, the sending of the spies and the Balaam episode, and ends on the plains of Moab before Canaan.

The Book of Obadiah is the fourth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible. Tradition attributes it to the prophet Obadiah, of whom nothing else is known. It is a single chapter of 21 verses, the shortest book of the Hebrew Scriptures. It announces divine judgment on Edom for its pride and its betrayal of Judah, and it foresees the restoration of Israel on the day of the Lord. Most scholars date it shortly after the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC. Others think it took shape through later editing during the Persian period.

The Book of Proverbs is a book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, and a classic example of biblical wisdom literature. Tradition ascribes it to King Solomon. Scholars instead see it as a "collection of collections" from different periods, with the final redaction often placed in the Persian or Hellenistic era. In short sayings and longer discourses it sets wise conduct against folly. It teaches that "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge" and personifies Wisdom as present at creation. Christian writers widely read Proverbs 8 in a Christological sense.

The Book of Psalms, or Psalter, is an anthology of Hebrew religious poetry in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It has 150 psalms in Jewish and Western usage, with a few more in Eastern churches, and is divided into five books. It includes hymns of praise, laments, royal psalms and thanksgivings. Many psalms are traditionally attributed to David, but scholars doubt this. They were composed over several centuries, before and after the Exile. The Psalms were central to Jewish and Christian worship, and early Christian writers commented on them extensively.

The Book of Ruth is a short anonymous Hebrew narrative in the Hebrew Bible. It is one of the Five Megillot in the Writings, while the Greek and Christian canons place it after Judges. The date is uncertain, but many scholars assign it to the Persian period. It tells how Ruth, a Moabite widow, stays loyal to her mother-in-law Naomi, goes with her to Bethlehem and marries their kinsman Boaz. Their son Obed became David's grandfather. Ruth appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, and the book is read in synagogues at Shavuot.

The Song of Songs, also called the Song of Solomon or Canticle of Canticles, is a book of Hebrew love poetry, one of the five megillot in the Ketuvim. Its superscription links it to Solomon, but its real author is unknown and its date is debated; many scholars place it in the Persian or Hellenistic period. In dialogues, dreams and rich imagery, a woman and her beloved express their desire. Jewish tradition reads it as an allegory of God and Israel. Christian commentators, from Origen onward, read it as an allegory of Christ and the Church or the soul.

The Book of Zechariah is the eleventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is attributed to Zechariah, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, a prophet active from about 520 BC under the Persian king Darius I. Chapters 1–8 contain eight night visions and oracles urging the returned exiles to repent and rebuild the Temple. Chapters 9–14, often assigned by scholars to later authors, hold oracles about a coming king and the future of Jerusalem. Christian writers frequently read these passages as messianic prophecy.

The Book of Zephaniah (Latin Sophonias) is the ninth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible, a short prophetic book of three chapters. It is attributed to Zephaniah, who prophesied in the reign of Josiah of Judah (640–609 BC). Many scholars date it to that period, though others think an original core was later expanded. It announces the coming "day of the Lord" as a day of judgement on Judah and the nations, and ends with promises that a humble remnant will be restored. Its imagery inspired the medieval hymn Dies irae.

This Arabic Christian commentary explains the Nicene Creed phrase by phrase. It is attributed to a priest called Abū al-Majdalus, about whom little is known, and its date is uncertain. The text calls the Creed the work of the 318 fathers of Nicaea and says Christ himself sat among them as a 319th member. It tries to show that each article of the faith comes from the Law of Moses and the prophets, beginning with "We believe in one God" and the Shema.

On Knowledge and Miracles (Fī al-ʿilm wa-al-muʿjiz) is a short Arabic treatise by Abū al-Faraj ʿAbdallāh ibn al-Ṭayyib (died 1043). He was a priest, physician and philosopher of the Church of the East in Baghdad, and the text calls him secretary of the Catholicos. The treatise argues that in Christianity rational proof ranks above miracles. Reasoned argument persuades the learned through the intellect, while miracles persuade ordinary people through the senses. To support this ranking, the author cites Paul's list of gifts in 1 Corinthians 12:28. The work reflects his effort to bring Aristotelian philosophy together with Christian theology.

The Book of the Councils (Kitāb al-majāmiʿ) is an Arabic theological and historical work attributed to Severus ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, the tenth-century Coptic bishop of Hermopolis (al-Ashmunein) in Egypt. Writing from the Coptic Orthodox (non-Chalcedonian) position, the author reviews the church councils and defends Miaphysite teaching. This fragment, preserved at Cairo, collects supposed prophecies of Christ by pagan sages such as Hermes, including the eclipse at the crucifixion and the fall of the idols' temples. Such testimonies were a common feature of Christian apologetic writing.

This short Arabic treatise by Yaḥyā ibn ʿAdī (893/4–974), the Jacobite (Syriac Orthodox) Christian philosopher and theologian of Baghdad, deals with apparent discrepancies between the four Gospels. It first separates the senses of "difference": real contradiction, which it holds impossible in inspired books; one evangelist reporting what others omit; and different words with the same meaning. It argues that the evangelists, made free from error by the Holy Spirit, each wrote what was useful when need arose. The treatise defends the Gospels' reliability against charges of inconsistency.

This is a short Arabic theological treatise by Yaḥyā ibn ʿAdī (893/4–974), the Miaphysite Christian philosopher and translator active in Baghdad. Written in reply to questions from fellow Christians, it explains the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed's clause that Christ "became incarnate of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary." It grounds the phrase in the infancy narrative of Matthew and in Paul's letter to the Galatians, and it builds on an earlier essay of his on the same subject. It is an example of Christian theology written in Arabic and using philosophical argument in the tenth-century Abbasid world.

This short Arabic apologetic treatise is by Yaḥyā ibn ʿAdī (893/4–974), a Miaphysite (Jacobite) Christian philosopher, theologian and translator in Baghdad. Its exact date is unknown. It defends the truth of the Gospel by reasoning rather than by appeal to scriptural authority. Peoples far apart, of different religions and aims, could not have conspired to accept the Gospel. Ibn ʿAdī lists the motives that lead people to embrace falsehood, such as fear, power, wealth, pleasure and lax law. He argues that the Gospel demands the opposite of each, so its acceptance must rest on its truth.

This Arabic Christian commentary explains the Nicene Creed phrase by phrase. It is attributed to a priest called Abū al-Majdalus, about whom little is known, and its date is uncertain. The text calls the Creed the work of the 318 fathers of Nicaea and says Christ himself sat among them as a 319th member. It tries to show that each article of the faith comes from the Law of Moses and the prophets, beginning with "We believe in one God" and the Shema.
