"In pretiosam et vivificam crucem" ("On the Precious and Life-giving Cross") is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala. He was a Syrian bishop and popular preacher in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. Severian delivered the sermon after another speaker and opens by praising that preacher's treatment of the cross and of virginity. He then praises the cross as weak in word but great in power. Its effects, he says, appear in deeds: sinners are converted, paradise is opened, and the world turns to chastity. Severian also links the cross to its "root", the virgin birth.

The Homily on Peace is a Greek sermon by Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria and a popular preacher in Constantinople in the early fifth century. It is usually dated to about 401–404 and linked to Severian's brief reconciliation with John Chrysostom, after their quarrel had divided the city's church. It opens by echoing the angels' message to the shepherds and goes on to praise peace as the name of Christ and the glory of the Church, set against the turmoil of the heretics. Like most of Severian's homilies, its Greek text was handed down among the works of Chrysostom.

The Homily on Peace is a Greek sermon by Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria and a popular preacher in Constantinople in the early fifth century. It is usually dated to about 401–404 and linked to Severian's brief reconciliation with John Chrysostom, after their quarrel had divided the city's church. It opens by echoing the angels' message to the shepherds and goes on to praise peace as the name of Christ and the glory of the Church, set against the turmoil of the heretics. Like most of Severian's homilies, its Greek text was handed down among the works of Chrysostom.

This Greek homily is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 401 and 404. Its subject is Christ's prayer in Gethsemane, "Father, let this cup pass from me" (Matthew 26:39). The opening praises the listeners' eagerness for an earlier sermon on almsgiving and hospitality. It compares God's word to rain on dry ground and the hearers to bees gathering from Scripture. Like many of Severian's sermons, it also survives in an Armenian translation.

This Greek homily is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 401 and 404. Its subject is Christ's prayer in Gethsemane, "Father, let this cup pass from me" (Matthew 26:39). The opening praises the listeners' eagerness for an earlier sermon on almsgiving and hospitality. It compares God's word to rain on dry ground and the hearers to bees gathering from Scripture. Like many of Severian's sermons, it also survives in an Armenian translation.

The Homilia de lotione pedum is a Greek sermon on the washing of the feet, the episode in John 13 where Christ washes his disciples' feet. It is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. The sermon opens with a reflection on God's love for humankind as seen in creation. Drawing on the Psalms, it argues that God's mercy and justice belong together: justice moves the hearer to fear judgment, and mercy invites repentance. It then turns to Christ's humility as an expression of that love.

This Greek homily survives only as a fragment and is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. It divides the course of the world into five ages, each with its own founding "father": Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and finally Christ according to the flesh. Severian argues that each period had its own order, rules and laws. He compares these changes to the seasons of the year, all of them governed by one divine providence.

A Greek homily by Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the early fifth century. It was probably delivered between about 401 and 404. It opens with an image of snow whitening the earth, as Scripture whitens the soul. It then turns to the Gospel reading of the centurion whose faith Christ praised. Severian argues from the centurion's recognition of Christ's authority against heretics who make the Son subordinate to the Father, and he asserts that power belongs in common to the divine essence. As the title indicates, he also attacks Manichaean and Apollinarian errors.

This Greek homily by Severian of Gabala is thought to have been preached at Constantinople around 401–404, when he was a popular preacher in the city. The order of his sermon series called for a discussion of Noah, but Severian puts that subject off because the evening is short. He turns instead to Hosea's words, "Sow for righteousness, and harvest the fruit of life." He reads them as the giving back of the life Adam lost when he was barred from the tree of life and driven out of paradise. The title also lists the cherubim as a subject.

This Greek homily, attributed to Severian of Gabala, is a polemical sermon against Jews, pagans and heretics. It probably dates from Severian's preaching in Constantinople around 401–404, and, like most of his surviving homilies, it may have come down under the name of John Chrysostom. The sermon calls the heretics of its own day "new Jews." It says they are worse than those who crucified Christ's body because they deny his Godhead and his divine knowledge. Using texts from the Psalms, it argues for the Son's full divinity, a typical anti-Arian theme of Antiochene preaching at the time.

This is a Greek homily by Severian of Gabala on Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness." It was preached in Constantinople, probably between 401 and 404. Severian refers back to an earlier sermon on creation that a noisy crowd had interrupted. He asks his audience for silence, restates that God created matter itself out of nothing, and goes on to discuss what it means for humanity to be made in God's image. Like many of his sermons, it survives in Greek mainly among works attributed to John Chrysostom.

De caeco et Zacchaeo ("On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus") is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 401 and 404. It begins by praising the single source of all Scripture, the Holy Spirit. It then turns to the Gospel stories of the blind man healed near Jericho and of the tax collector Zacchaeus. Severian marvels that the blind man recognised Christ without having read the Law, the prophets or the Gospels. Like most of Severian's Greek sermons, it was handed down among works ascribed to John Chrysostom.

This Greek homily on 1 Corinthians 15:28, "When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected", is attributed to Severian of Gabala, who preached in Constantinople in the early 400s. It follows a sermon given the day before on the endless kingdom of Christ. The homily answers the objection that Paul's words imply the Son's subordination or that his reign will end, and defends his equal dignity with the Father. Like many of Severian's sermons, it has come down among the works attributed to John Chrysostom.

This Greek homily is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople from about 400 until 404. Its subject is the phrase "Brood of vipers," spoken by John the Baptist (Luke 3:7) and by Christ (Matthew 23:33). It opens by praising the Scriptures as springs of salvation from which hidden meanings must be laboriously "drawn" from the depths. Like most of Severian's Greek sermons, it survives among works wrongly attributed to John Chrysostom.

The Homily on Noah and the Ark is a Greek sermon attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It was delivered at the midpoint of the Lenten fast. Severian compares that midpoint to the height of a battle or of noon, and calls the Scriptures the fast's bright rays. He then turns to the story of Noah, presenting the deeds of the ancients as examples for his hearers to imitate. Like most of his sermons, it reflects the Antiochene tradition of preaching on Scripture.

This is a Greek sermon on Genesis by Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria, who was a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. Like most of his homilies, it survived among the works wrongly attributed to John Chrysostom. Starting from the "meadows of piety", it treats humanity as made in the image and likeness of God. Severian argues that virtue keeps that likeness intact, while vice drags people down to the level of the irrational animals. He also insists that the animals themselves are not evil, since God called all of creation "very good".

This Greek homily is the first in a series of sermons on the biblical figure Job, attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the early fifth century. Like many of Severian's sermons, it has come down mainly under the name of John Chrysostom, so its authorship has been debated. The preacher hails Job, whose story was read in church every year, as the "athlete of the whole world". He calls Job a champion often struck by the devil and vindicated by God, and says no human eloquence can praise him as he deserves.

In Iob sermo 2 is a Greek homily on the trials of Job, attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. The preacher begins by admitting that he is unequal to so great a subject, then explains the opening words of the Book of Job phrase by phrase, starting with "There was a man in the land of Ausitis." He argues that Scripture first stresses Job's ordinary human nature so that hearers will admire how his endurance and virtue went beyond the human condition.

This is the third in a series of Greek sermons on the Book of Job, attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. Like many of his homilies, it probably survives among the works of John Chrysostom. Preached in the evening as a continuation of the Job story, it holds up Job's endurance on the dunghill as a rebuke to a lazy congregation. It argues that only the blameless, righteous and God-fearing person is truly a "man," because he keeps the divine image intact.

This Greek homily is the fourth in a series of sermons on the biblical Job. It was handed down among the works of John Chrysostom and is now attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 401 and 404. The preacher returns to Job's story and argues that although Job lost all his possessions, he kept his virtue, which was the root of his good fortune. He holds up Job's endurance as a model, praising the courage of the soul while admitting that the body truly suffered.

De tribus pueris sermo is a Greek sermon on the three Hebrew youths of Daniel 3, attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. It retells how Nebuchadnezzar, portrayed as an arrogant tyrant who wished to be worshipped as a god, had the youths thrown into the fiery furnace. The sermon praises them as martyrs whose confession of faith the fire could not overcome. Like many of Severian's homilies, it has come down among the works attributed to John Chrysostom. Its exact date is uncertain.

De caeco nato ("On the Man Born Blind") is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the first years of the fifth century. It is probably from about 401–404. The sermon takes as its subject the Gospel account of Christ healing the man blind from birth (John 9). It begins with a reflection on the word of God as light that makes believers "sons of light," while ignorance and unbelief are darkness. Like many of Severian's sermons, it has come down among the writings attributed to John Chrysostom.

This Greek sermon in praise of the martyrs is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the early fifth century. It was probably delivered between about 401 and 404. Preached at a martyrs' festival, it teaches that honouring the martyrs honours Christ, to whom they bore witness. It sets the precious death of the righteous against the death of the ungodly, citing the Psalms. The martyrs are praised so that hearers will imitate their zeal and self-control.

This is a Greek homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. It was delivered in the last week of the Lenten fast. Severian takes the psalm heading "To the end: do not destroy" as a call to bring a good beginning to a good end. He urges his hearers to finish the fast with eager longing rather than mere toil, because fasting frees the soul to contemplate divine things and curbs desire. The alternative title links the sermon's theme of the end to the Last Judgement.

In ascensionem Domini is a Greek homily for the feast of the Ascension, attributed to Severian of Gabala. Like many of his sermons, it has come down among the works once ascribed to John Chrysostom. It was probably preached while Severian was active in Constantinople, around 401–404, though the exact date is uncertain. The sermon celebrates the Ascension as the exaltation of human nature: Christ, the eternal Word, needs no elevation, but takes mortal humanity up above the angels and frees Adam from the ancient condemnation.

De cruce et latrone ("On the Cross and the Thief") is a Greek sermon for Good Friday. It has come down among the works of John Chrysostom but is attributed here to Severian of Gabala, who preached in Constantinople around 401–404. The authorship is not settled. The homily opens with a series of "Today…" acclamations celebrating the cross as the victory over death and the demons. It reads the darkness and earthquake at the crucifixion as signs, sets the Jews against the believers in polemical terms, and turns to the penitent thief's confession.

De cruce et latrone ("On the Cross and the Thief") is a Greek sermon for Good Friday. It has come down among the works of John Chrysostom but is attributed here to Severian of Gabala, who preached in Constantinople around 401–404. The authorship is not settled. The homily opens with a series of "Today…" acclamations celebrating the cross as the victory over death and the demons. It reads the darkness and earthquake at the crucifixion as signs, sets the Jews against the believers in polemical terms, and turns to the penitent thief's confession.

The Oratio de exaltatione Crucis is a Greek sermon on the cross attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. The homily opens by calling on the apostle Paul and building on his saying that "the word of the cross" is folly to those who are perishing but the power of God to the saved. It praises the cross as the power that silenced orators and philosophers, overthrew idols and oracles, drove out demons and destroyed death.

This Greek homily on the temptation of Christ in the desert is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. Commenting on the gospel account, the preacher stresses that Christ hid his divine rank and fought the devil "as in the person of humanity". He answered the tempter as a man, so that human nature itself might win the victory and the crown. The sermon shows the Antiochene concern with Christ's real humanity. Like most of Severian's homilies, it is probably dated to his years in Constantinople.

This Greek homily on the temptation of Christ in the desert is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. Commenting on the gospel account, the preacher stresses that Christ hid his divine rank and fought the devil "as in the person of humanity". He answered the tempter as a man, so that human nature itself might win the victory and the crown. The sermon shows the Antiochene concern with Christ's real humanity. Like most of Severian's homilies, it is probably dated to his years in Constantinople.

This is the first of six Greek homilies on the creation account in Genesis by Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria. He preached them in Constantinople, probably in the early 400s, and they survived among the works wrongly attributed to John Chrysostom. In the opening sermon, Severian says that all Scripture aims at the salvation of souls and calls the book of creation the foundation of the Law and the Prophets. He also defends adding his own interpretation to those of earlier Fathers. The series is an important example of Antiochene literal exegesis of the six days of creation.

This is the second of six Greek homilies on the creation account of Genesis by Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria. He preached them in Constantinople, probably between about 401 and 404, while he was a popular preacher in the capital. The series came down to us among the works attributed to John Chrysostom. The sermon opens by comparing the word of God to a whetstone that cleans, sharpens and brightens the soul, then continues its line-by-line reading of the six days of creation. The series is an important example of Antiochene literal exegesis and of early Christian cosmology.

This Greek sermon is the third of six homilies on the creation account in Genesis by Severian of Gabala. He preached them in Constantinople, probably in the early 400s. Like most of Severian's sermons, the series survived among the writings attributed to his rival John Chrysostom. This homily recalls the work of the first two days and then turns to the third: the waters gathered together, dry land appearing and the earth producing plants. Severian combines a literal, Antiochene-style reading of creation with moral and Christological applications, urging his hearers to wonder at the works and worship their maker.

This is the fourth in a series of six Greek sermons on the creation account of Genesis by Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop and popular preacher in Constantinople. He delivered them around 401–404. Like most of his Greek works, the homilies survive among the writings attributed to John Chrysostom. The preacher first asks his hearers to pray for him, then resumes his account of the creation days in order. His exegesis is literal and follows the Antiochene tradition.

This is the fifth of six Greek homilies on the creation account of Genesis by Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople in the early 400s. Like most of his sermons, it survives among the works wrongly attributed to John Chrysostom. The homily turns to the creation of man. It opens by praising Scripture as God's greatest gift and defends the study of nature against hearers who wanted theology alone. It reflects the literal, Antiochene style of reading Genesis.

This Greek sermon is the last of six homilies on the creation account in Genesis by Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It goes back to the subject of paradise. It discusses Adam's dwelling there, the land outside it, and his expulsion, and it aims to answer believers' questions and refute unbelievers using Scripture alone. Like most of Severian's sermons, it survived in Greek among works wrongly attributed to John Chrysostom. It is a witness to Antiochene literal exegesis.

De incarnatione ("On the Incarnation") is a homily attributed to Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria, a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404 and an opponent of John Chrysostom. Severian preached in Greek, but this sermon survives in an ancient Armenian translation, like several of his homilies whose Greek text is lost. It opens with an extended contrast between light and darkness. Drawing on Psalm 43:3 ("Send out your light and your truth") and John 1:9, it presents Christ as the true light and the sun of righteousness who drives away the darkness of ignorance.

De dogmate baptismoque ("On Doctrine and Baptism") is a homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. It survives in an ancient Armenian translation and is one of the Severian sermons published from Armenian by J. B. Aucher in 1827. The preacher begins by recalling an earlier sermon on Christ's Ascension, which he says raised human nature to heaven. He then explains Paul's contrast between the earthy and the heavenly man (1 Corinthians 15:47–49) before moving to doctrine and baptism.

De apostolis ("On the Apostles") is a homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople between about 400 and 404. Several of his sermons are lost in Greek and survive only in Armenian translation, and this text has come down in Armenian. It opens by recalling the previous day's sermon on the body and its "lamp", the eye. It then sets out a series of lamps: the evening lamp, the divine law and the gospel. It goes on to John the Baptist as a lamp who baptized Christ in obedience to God's command.

De pascha, deque catharis ("On the Pascha and on the Cathari") is a homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople around 400–404. It is among the sermons that survive in an ancient Armenian translation, and Severian would have preached it in Greek. The preacher begins by praising the presiding bishop, whom he calls the head of the fathers, and the earlier speakers. He then turns to the Paschal feast and argues against the Cathari, the rigorist Novatianist party. The homily shows how Severian preached in the capital.

This is a homily attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It was probably delivered in Greek but survives in an ancient Armenian translation. Its title refers to Daniel 7:10, "the books were opened." The opening, however, explains John 4:46 and following, where Jesus returns to Cana of Galilee. The preacher contrasts Christ's movement from place to place in the body with his divinity, which is present everywhere. He presents Christ as the single source of life, light and healing for both soul and body.

This festal homily in honour of the martyr Acacius is attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop who was a popular preacher in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It was presumably composed in Greek but survives in an Armenian translation. The sermon was preached the day after a feast of the apostles. It uses rich imagery of stars, crowns and lamps to celebrate the martyrs as a light and a rampart for the Church. It is one of several homilies by Severian that are preserved mainly or only outside Greek.

This is a homily on Christ's entry into Jerusalem riding a colt, attributed to Severian of Gabala, the Syrian bishop who preached in Constantinople from about 400 to 404. It survives in an ancient Armenian translation. The sermon reads Zechariah's prophecy of the king coming on the colt of an ass as a sign that Christ defeats pride and the devil through meekness and humility, not through chariots and warhorses. It belongs to the group of Severian's sermons that were preserved in translation into other languages.

These Greek exegetical fragments on the letters of Paul are attributed to Severian of Gabala, a Syrian bishop and popular preacher at Constantinople around 400–404 who became an opponent of John Chrysostom. They do not survive as a continuous commentary. They are known only as excerpts preserved in the catenae, the medieval chains of patristic comment. The opening passages, on Romans, discuss Paul's apostolic calling, Christ's divinity and the true prophets, and argue against heretical readings. The fragments reflect the literal, historically minded exegesis of the Antiochene school. Their exact date is uncertain.

The Homilies on Colossians are a series of twelve sermons in Greek by John Chrysostom. They give a continuous, verse-by-verse commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Colossians. They are usually dated to his years as archbishop of Constantinople (398–404), though the exact date is uncertain. Chrysostom treats Colossians as one of the letters Paul wrote while imprisoned. He explains its teaching on Christ's supremacy and warns against false doctrine, and he draws out practical moral lessons for his congregation. The series belongs to his extensive cycle of homilies on the Pauline epistles.

Contra Marcellum ("Against Marcellus") is a Greek polemical treatise in two books by Eusebius of Caesarea, written about 336–338. It followed the deposition of Marcellus of Ancyra at a synod in Constantinople in 336. Eusebius attacks Marcellus's only treatise, which had criticised Asterius and other eastern bishops, both living and dead. He charges Marcellus with Sabellian views that denied the distinct existence of the Son. Eusebius soon followed it with his Ecclesiastical Theology. The work matters because it quotes Marcellus at length, and these quotations preserve much of his otherwise lost writing.

De ecclesiastica theologia (On Ecclesiastical Theology) is a Greek polemical treatise in three books by Eusebius of Caesarea, written in the last years of his life, around 337–339. It is dedicated to Flacillus, bishop of Antioch. It follows Eusebius's two books Against Marcellus, which mostly quoted Marcellus of Ancyra's own words. This work goes further and refutes them. Eusebius rejects Marcellus's teaching that the Word has no distinct existence from God and defends the Son as a real, distinct being. The treatise is an important source for the fragments of Marcellus and for the Trinitarian debates after Nicaea.

The Commentary on Isaiah is a Greek exegetical work by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. He wrote it late in life, probably after the Council of Nicaea in 325 and before his death in 339. It works through the Book of Isaiah, and its preface sets out a method that separates passages to be read literally from those that speak through symbols. Eusebius combines historical explanation with figurative and Christological reading. The commentary is an important witness to Christian biblical scholarship at Caesarea after Origen.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in five books by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was written around 449–450 and continues the history of Eusebius of Caesarea. It begins with the rise of Arianism under Constantine and ends in 429, with the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Theodoret writes from a firmly Nicene and Antiochene viewpoint and focuses on the struggle against Arianism. He quotes many letters, creeds and synodal documents in full. Along with the histories of Socrates Scholasticus and Sozomen, it is one of the main sources for fourth-century church history.

This exegetical treatise in seventeen books by Cyril of Alexandria, written in Greek, is generally dated to the early part of his episcopate, before the Nestorian controversy. It takes the form of a dialogue between Cyril and a certain Palladius. It reads selected passages of the Pentateuch spiritually, showing that the Mosaic law, the tabernacle, the priesthood and the sacrifices were types of Christ and the Church. It covers sin and repentance, justification in Christ, love of God and neighbour, and worship "in spirit and in truth". Its companion work is the Glaphyra.

The Glaphyra ("Elegant Comments") is a Greek exegetical work by Cyril of Alexandria, generally dated to the early years of his episcopate, before the Nestorian controversy began around 429. In thirteen books, seven on Genesis and six on Exodus through Deuteronomy, it takes selected narratives and laws of the Pentateuch and reads them as figures of the mystery of Christ and the Church. It accompanies Cyril's earlier dialogue On Adoration in Spirit and Truth, and it is a major example of Alexandrian typological interpretation of the Old Testament.

The Commentarius magnus in Psalmos, or Great Commentary on the Psalms, is a Greek exegetical work attributed to Hesychius of Jerusalem, a priest and biblical interpreter active in the first half of the fifth century. It is the most extensive of several works he wrote on the Psalter. It reads the psalms mainly as prophecies of Christ and the Church. The prologue presents Christ as Malachi's "sun of righteousness", who makes plain the hidden meaning of Scripture. The commentary does not survive complete, and parts of it are known only from fragments.

The Exhortation to Martyrdom is a Greek treatise by Origen of Alexandria, generally dated to about 235, during the persecution under the emperor Maximinus Thrax. It is addressed to his patron Ambrose and to Protoctetus, a presbyter of Caesarea, who were both facing arrest. Drawing heavily on Scripture, Origen urges them to stand firm, to reject idolatry and apostasy, and to see suffering for Christ as a contest that leads to glory. It is one of the most important early Christian writings on the meaning of martyrdom.

On Prayer (Peri euchēs) is a Greek treatise by Origen of Alexandria, usually dated around 233–234 and addressed to his patron Ambrose and to Tatiana. It is the earliest surviving systematic Christian study of prayer. Origen asks why prayer is worthwhile if God already knows all things, explains the kinds of prayer named in 1 Timothy 2:1, and argues that prayer in the strict sense should be offered to the Father through the Son. He gives a long commentary on the Lord's Prayer and ends with advice on posture, place and times for prayer.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in nine books by Sozomen, a lawyer at Constantinople. He wrote it around the 440s and dedicated it to Emperor Theodosius II. It was meant to continue the work of Eusebius and covers events from the 320s to the 420s. The ninth book seems unfinished and stops short of the end date the author announced. Sozomen drew heavily on Socrates Scholasticus but added much material of his own, especially on monasticism, missions and the Church outside the empire. It is a key source for fourth- and early fifth-century Christianity.

The Epistula synodalis is a Greek synodal letter issued in the name of a synod of bishops presided over by Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, probably in the mid-370s. It replies to a joint letter of questions sent by a distant church whose bishops were suffering for their faith. The letter regrets that Basil of Caesarea could not attend because he was ill, and it directs the recipients to his treatise written on the same subject. It upholds the Nicene faith and the full divinity of the Holy Spirit, and it shows how closely Amphilochius worked with the Cappadocian Fathers.

Against the Heathen (Contra Gentes) is a Greek apologetic treatise by Athanasius of Alexandria, addressed to a certain Macarius. It forms the first half of a two-part work completed by On the Incarnation. Its date is disputed: some scholars place it before the Arian controversy, around 318, and others in the 330s. Athanasius answers pagan mockery of the Cross by attacking idolatry and the worship of nature. He argues that the soul, being rational and immortal, and the order of creation both lead to knowledge of the one God through his Word.

On the Incarnation of the Word is a Greek theological treatise by Athanasius of Alexandria. It is the second part of a double work that opens with Against the Pagans, and both are addressed to a certain Macarius. Its date is disputed: some place it before the Arian controversy, around 318, while others place it in the 330s. It explains why the divine Word, through whom the world was made, took a human body to restore humanity from corruption and death. It also answers Jewish and pagan objections and remains a classic of Christian thought on the incarnation.

De Decretis is a Greek treatise in the form of a letter by Athanasius of Alexandria, usually dated to the 350s. It is written to an unnamed correspondent who had argued with supporters of Arius, including friends of Eusebius. Athanasius answers the Arian objection that the Council of Nicaea (325) used unscriptural terms, "of the essence" and "one in essence" (homoousios). He argues that these words express the meaning of Scripture about the Son's true divinity. The work is a major early defence of the Nicene formula. It also preserves documents connected with the council.

On the Opinion of Dionysius is a Greek letter by Athanasius of Alexandria, usually dated to the 350s. It answers Arian claims that Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria in the third century, had shared their view that the Son of God is a creature. Athanasius argues that the disputed phrases came from letters against Sabellianism and referred to Christ's human nature. He quotes Dionysius's later Refutation and Defence to show that Dionysius held the Son to be eternal and of one being with the Father. The letter preserves important fragments of Dionysius's writings.

The Apology to the Emperor Constantius is a Greek defence written by Athanasius of Alexandria and usually dated to 356–357, during his third exile. Addressed to Constantius II, it answers political charges brought against him: that he had turned the emperor's brother Constans against him, corresponded with the usurper Magnentius, used a new church in Alexandria before it was dedicated, and disobeyed an imperial summons. It also describes the armed attack on his church in 356 and his flight. The work is an important source for the Arian controversy and for relations between church and empire.

This is a short Greek letter by Athanasius of Alexandria to John and Antiochus, two presbyters who had written to him from Jerusalem. It dates from his last years, after Basil became bishop of Caesarea in 370. He tells them to avoid people who quarrel over words and want to add to or take away from the confession of faith of the Nicene fathers. Instead they should help the brethren keep God's commandments. He also defends Basil against his critics, calling him a true servant of God. The letter shows how the aged Athanasius supported Basil.

This short Greek letter was written by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, to the presbyter Palladius late in his life, probably around 371–372. Palladius had told him that monks at Caesarea in Cappadocia were opposing their bishop, Basil. Athanasius defends Basil as an orthodox bishop and "a glory to the Church." He urges the monks to obey him as children obey a father, and explains Basil's caution in his teaching as wise accommodation to the weak. The letter shows the elderly Athanasius supporting Basil's leadership of the Nicene cause.

This Greek letter was written by Athanasius of Alexandria around 354–355 to Dracontius, the head of a monastic community. Dracontius had been chosen unanimously as a bishop in the region of Alexandria but fled to avoid ordination, partly because the Church was under pressure at the time. Athanasius rebukes him and argues that his flight would harm the faithful and the pagans who had promised to convert. He gives examples of monks who became bishops to show that the monastic life is compatible with pastoral office. The letter is an important source for relations between Egyptian monasticism and the episcopate.

The Letter to the Bishops of Africa is a Greek synodal letter issued by about ninety bishops of Egypt and Libya under Athanasius of Alexandria, who wrote it, probably between about 367 and 372. It warns the African churches against attempts to set the Council of Ariminum (359) above the Council of Nicaea. The letter defends the Nicene creed and the term homoousios, and cites the condemnation of Auxentius, Ursacius and Valens by Pope Damasus and Western synods. It is one of Athanasius's last anti-Arian writings.

The Tomus ad Antiochenos is a synodal letter issued by Athanasius of Alexandria and the council he held at Alexandria in 362, after Julian allowed exiled bishops to return. It is addressed to bishops including Eusebius of Vercelli, Lucifer of Cagliari and Asterius of Petra. It aimed to heal the schism at Antioch and set lenient terms for receiving former Arians who accepted the Nicene faith. It also accepted both "one hypostasis" and "three hypostases" as orthodox when properly understood, an important step toward settling Trinitarian terminology.

This is a short doctrinal letter by Athanasius of Alexandria to the Emperor Jovian, written between 363 and 364. It comes with Jovian's own brief letter, which praises Athanasius's steadfastness and recalls him from the exile imposed under Julian. Jovian had asked to learn the true faith. In reply, Athanasius sets out the Nicene Creed as the faith of the whole Church and defends the full divinity of the Son against Arian teaching. The exchange shows the brief return of imperial favour to the Nicene party after Julian's death.

The Petitions of the Arians is a short Greek record of the appeals that Lucius, Bernicianus and other Arians of Alexandria made at Antioch to the emperor Jovian, probably in late 363. They sought a bishop of their own and accused Athanasius by pointing to his earlier depositions and exiles. The record is preserved among Athanasius' writings as an appendix to his letter to Jovian. Its author is unknown. It reports Jovian's sharp refusals and his support for Athanasius, and is a vivid source for church politics after Julian's death.

The Fragmenta are the surviving remains of the writings of Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra (died c. 374), a supporter of the Council of Nicaea and opponent of Arianism. Most come from his treatise against Asterius the Sophist, written around the early 330s. They survive almost entirely as quotations in Eusebius of Caesarea's polemical works against him, with a few more in Epiphanius's Panarion 72. The fragments set out Marcellus's theology of the Word, which his critics condemned as Sabellian, and they are central to the history of the Arian controversy.

De sabbatis et circumcisione (On Sabbaths and Circumcision) is a short Greek treatise handed down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria but generally regarded as spurious. Its date is uncertain, probably between the mid-fourth and the fifth century. Starting from Exodus 31, it argues that the Sabbath marked the end of the first creation. Christians therefore honour the day of the Lord's resurrection, the start of the new creation, and look toward the eternal "Sabbath of Sabbaths". It treats circumcision in the same typological way.

De sabbatis et circumcisione (On Sabbaths and Circumcision) is a short Greek treatise handed down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria but generally regarded as spurious. Its date is uncertain, probably between the mid-fourth and the fifth century. Starting from Exodus 31, it argues that the Sabbath marked the end of the first creation. Christians therefore honour the day of the Lord's resurrection, the start of the new creation, and look toward the eternal "Sabbath of Sabbaths". It treats circumcision in the same typological way.

On the Lord's Day is a Greek homily in the collection attributed to Eusebius of Alexandria, a fictional bishop whose sermons were probably written by John the Notary, perhaps in the sixth century. It is a dialogue in which the disciple Alexander asks why Sunday must be kept free from work. Eusebius answers that the day is a memorial of the Eucharist and of the resurrection, and the first day of creation. The homily circulated in several versions and was widely used to teach Sunday rest.

On the Lord's Day is a Greek homily in the collection attributed to Eusebius of Alexandria, a fictional bishop whose sermons were probably written by John the Notary, perhaps in the sixth century. It is a dialogue in which the disciple Alexander asks why Sunday must be kept free from work. Eusebius answers that the day is a memorial of the Eucharist and of the resurrection, and the first day of creation. The homily circulated in several versions and was widely used to teach Sunday rest.

On the Lord's Day is a Greek homily in the collection attributed to Eusebius of Alexandria, a fictional bishop whose sermons were probably written by John the Notary, perhaps in the sixth century. It is a dialogue in which the disciple Alexander asks why Sunday must be kept free from work. Eusebius answers that the day is a memorial of the Eucharist and of the resurrection, and the first day of creation. The homily circulated in several versions and was widely used to teach Sunday rest.

On the Lord's Day is a Greek homily in the collection attributed to Eusebius of Alexandria, a fictional bishop whose sermons were probably written by John the Notary, perhaps in the sixth century. It is a dialogue in which the disciple Alexander asks why Sunday must be kept free from work. Eusebius answers that the day is a memorial of the Eucharist and of the resurrection, and the first day of creation. This Greek church history in three books was written around 475 by an anonymous author, the son of a presbyter of Cyzicus, who worked in Bithynia. Following Photius, it was long misattributed to Gelasius of Cyzicus. Book I covers Constantine's reign up to 323, Book II the Council of Nicaea and Book III its aftermath. It draws on Eusebius, Rufinus and other historians, as well as on a parchment book that had belonged to Dalmatius of Cyzicus. The author aimed to show against the Eutychians that the Nicene Fathers did not teach Monophysite doctrine.

The Commentary on Daniel is a Greek exegetical work in four books attributed to Hippolytus of Rome. It is usually dated to the early third century and is often called the oldest Christian biblical commentary to survive in substantial form. It covers the Book of Daniel, including the story of Susanna. Hippolytus reads the narratives typologically, seeing Daniel and Susanna as prefigurations of Christ and the Church. He interprets the visions of the four kingdoms and of the Antichrist in terms of history and the end times. The commentary is also an important early witness to Christian chronology.

The Shepherd of Hermas is an early Christian apocalyptic and moral work written in Greek at Rome, probably in the first half of the second century. The Muratorian fragment attributes it to Hermas, brother of Bishop Pius of Rome. It is divided into Visions, Mandates and Similitudes, and in it an angel in the form of a shepherd teaches about repentance after baptism, simplicity and Christian conduct. Some early Christians treated it as scripture, and it is included in Codex Sinaiticus. It is counted among the Apostolic Fathers.

This is an anonymous Greek paraenetic sermon on the observance of Sunday, the Lord's Day. Manuscripts attribute it to John Chrysostom, but it is not his work, and its date is unknown. The preacher lists events said to have happened, or yet to happen, on a Sunday: the Annunciation to the Mother of God, God's appearance to Moses in the burning bush, Christ's baptism, the Resurrection and the Last Judgement. He contrasts the Christian Lord's Day with the Jewish sabbath and urges the faithful to honour it. The sermon survives in two versions, A and B.

This is an anonymous Greek paraenetic sermon on the observance of Sunday, the Lord's Day. Manuscripts attribute it to John Chrysostom, but it is not his work, and its date is unknown. The preacher lists events said to have happened, or yet to happen, on a Sunday: the Annunciation to the Mother of God, God's appearance to Moses in the burning bush, Christ's baptism, the Resurrection and the Last Judgement. He contrasts the Christian Lord's Day with the Jewish sabbath and urges the faithful to honour it. The sermon survives in two versions, A and B.

This is an anonymous Greek sermon on Sunday, the Lord's Day. Some manuscripts attribute it to Basil of Caesarea and others to John Chrysostom, but neither is its author, and its date is uncertain. The preacher rebukes those who dishonour the day God has honoured. He urges hearers to leave field and vineyard work and hurry to the churches and martyrs' shrines. Taking the repentant tax collector of the Gospel as a model, he calls for prayer and penitence. It is a witness to the growing insistence on Sunday rest and worship in Greek preaching.

This anonymous Greek hagiography tells the life and miracles of Saint Conon of Bidana, a village in the Taurus highlands of Isauria in southern Asia Minor. Its date is uncertain, but it is usually placed in late antiquity. It begins by describing the region's devotion to idols and how the apostle Paul passed it by. It then introduces Conon's father, Nestor, and tells of Conon's chaste life, his help from the Archangel Michael, his power over demons and his work converting the Isaurians. Versions also circulated in Church Slavonic.

This anonymous Greek catena on Paul's Epistle to the Colossians is a running commentary built from excerpts of earlier patristic interpreters, arranged verse by verse. Its compiler and exact date are unknown, though such catenae belong to the Byzantine period. The opening passage draws on John Chrysostom's homilies on Colossians. It discusses the letter as one Paul wrote in captivity and places it in sequence with Romans, Philemon, Philippians and Timothy. Catenae like this one matter because they preserve fragments of patristic exegesis, some of which survive nowhere else.

This Greek letter is the confession of faith that Arius and the Alexandrian presbyters and deacons who supported him sent to Bishop Alexander of Alexandria. It was written around 320, early in the Arian controversy. It describes God as alone unbegotten and eternal. The Son is called a perfect creature of God, brought into being by the Father's will before the ages, and rival views such as those of Valentinus, Mani, Sabellius and Hieracas are rejected. Athanasius and Epiphanius preserved the letter, and it remains a key primary source for Arius's own teaching.

This pair of documents comes from Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, at the start of the Arian controversy. In a short covering letter, he asks the clergy of Alexandria and the Mareotis to endorse the deposition of the presbyter Arius and his supporters. It is followed by an encyclical, beginning "Since there is one body of the Catholic Church", that tells bishops everywhere of the condemnation and refutes Arius's teaching that the Son is a creature. Usually dated around 319–324, it survives through Athanasius and Socrates and is a key early source for the dispute.

This is a brief Greek summary of a circular letter sent by a synod of bishops in Bithynia in the early stages of the Arian controversy, around 320–322. The bishops wrote to their colleagues everywhere that Arius and his followers held orthodox views and should be received into communion, and that Alexander of Alexandria should be persuaded to do the same. The letter itself is lost. The summary survives in the Church History of Sozomen and is numbered Urkunde 5 among Hans-Georg Opitz's documents of the Arian controversy.

This Greek letter was written by Eusebius of Nicomedia to Paulinus, bishop of Tyre, around 320–322, early in the Arian controversy. Theodoret's Church History preserves it. Eusebius praises the zeal of Eusebius of Caesarea for Arius's cause and rebukes Paulinus for keeping silent, urging him to write. He holds that there is one unbegotten God and one Son truly made by him, not from his substance, and cites Proverbs 8:22. It is a key early statement of the pro-Arian position.

This Greek fragment preserves hostile reports of a letter, or possibly several letters, by Paulinus, bishop of Tyre, an early supporter of Arius in the 320s. The reports come from Marcellus of Ancyra's polemic against Asterius the Sophist and survive through Eusebius of Caesarea's Contra Marcellum. Marcellus accuses Paulinus, whom he calls Asterius's "father", of calling Christ a "second god" and a creature, and of citing Origen instead of the Gospels and the apostles. The fragment is one of the documents collected on the early Arian controversy.

This short Greek fragment comes from a letter by George, then a presbyter of Alexandria living in Antioch and later bishop of Laodicea, to Bishop Alexander of Alexandria. It was written early in the Arian controversy, around 320. George urges Alexander not to condemn Arius's followers for saying "there was when the Son of God was not." He compares the case to Isaiah, son of Amos, who did not exist before he was born. Athanasius preserved the fragment in De synodis. It is numbered Urkunde 12 among the documents of the Arian controversy.

This short Greek fragment comes from a letter by George, then a presbyter in Alexandria and later bishop of Laodicea, to supporters of Arius. It dates from the early years of the Arian controversy, probably the early 320s, and survives because Athanasius quoted it in his polemic. George urges the Arians not to fault Bishop Alexander for saying the Son is "from the Father." Citing Paul's words that "all things are from God," he argues that the Son, though a creature, can be called "from God" in the same sense as all created things.

This brief Greek summary records two documents from the early Arian controversy, probably from the early 320s. Neither survives in full; both are known only through the account of the church historian Sozomen. Arius, who was in conflict with Bishop Alexander of Alexandria, appealed to Paulinus of Tyre, Eusebius of Caesarea and Patrophilus of Scythopolis, possibly by letter. A synod of Palestinian bishops then allowed Arius and his followers to keep holding services as presbyters, while remaining subject to Alexander and seeking peace and communion with him.

This is a fragment of a Greek letter from Eusebius of Caesarea to Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, written in the early years of the Arian controversy, around 320. Eusebius defends Arius and his supporters, arguing that Alexander had misrepresented them. He quotes their confession that the Son is "a perfect creature of God, but not as one of the creatures" and questions Alexander's objections to their teaching. The fragment survives because it was quoted as evidence against Eusebius at the Second Council of Nicaea (787). Hans-Georg Opitz numbered it Urkunde 7 in his collection of documents on the controversy.

This is a set of Greek fragments from a letter by Eusebius of Caesarea to Euphration, bishop of Balaneae in Syria and a supporter of Arius. It was probably written around 320, early in the Arian controversy. Eusebius argues that the Son does not coexist with the Father, who exists before him and causes his being. Citing "the Father is greater than I" and "the only true God," he calls the Son God but not "true God" in the Father's sense. The surviving passages were read out at the Second Council of Nicaea (787) as evidence of Eusebius's subordinationist views.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Syriac church history by John of Ephesus (c. 507–c. 588), a Miaphysite bishop and one of the earliest major historians writing in Syriac. It was originally composed in three parts. The first is lost and the second survives mainly in excerpts preserved by later chroniclers. The third part, largely extant, gives an eyewitness account of events from about 571 to the mid-580s, especially the persecution of anti-Chalcedonians under Justin II and Tiberius II, some of which John suffered himself. It is a key source for sixth-century Byzantine and Syriac history.

The Old Alemannic Psalms are fragments of an anonymous interlinear translation of the Latin Psalter into Old High German in its Alemannic dialect. They are usually dated to the first half of the ninth century. The surviving pieces render parts of several psalms word by word beneath the Latin. Among them are passages from Psalms 107–108 and 113–114 in the Vulgate numbering, such as "Deus locutus est in sancto suo" and "Dilexi quoniam exaudiet." They are an early witness to how Scripture was translated in Carolingian monasteries, and their vocabulary is valuable evidence for the language.

The Augsburg Prayer (Augsburger Gebet) is a short anonymous Old High German prayer from the later ninth century, named after Augsburg, where it was preserved. It gives the Latin collect "Deus, cui proprium est misereri semper et parcere" followed by a free German verse rendering in rhymed long lines, in the end-rhymed style associated with Otfrid of Weissenburg. The prayer asks God, whose nature is always to show mercy, to loosen the chains of sin. It is a small but notable example of early vernacular liturgical verse.

This short Old Saxon homily for the feast of All Saints was written in the later tenth century. It is a free vernacular rendering of a Latin homily traditionally attributed to Bede, though the attribution is uncertain. It tells how Pope Boniface asked the emperor for the Pantheon in Rome, once a temple of all the idols, and dedicated it to Mary and all the martyrs. It explains that a yearly commemoration of all God's saints on 1 November grew out of this dedication. The homily is one of the few surviving prose texts in Old Saxon.

The Rule of Saint Benedict is a Latin guide to monastic life written by Benedict of Nursia, probably around the 530s or 540s at Monte Cassino. It opens with "Ausculta, o fili" ("Listen, my son") and has a prologue followed by 73 short chapters. The Rule covers obedience, humility, silence, the abbot's authority, the daily round of communal prayer, manual work and reading. It draws heavily on the earlier Rule of the Master and on John Cassian, but is noted for its moderation. It later became the standard rule of Western monasticism.

The Rule of Saint Benedict is a Latin guide to monastic life written by Benedict of Nursia, probably around the 530s or 540s at Monte Cassino. It opens with "Ausculta, o fili" ("Listen, my son") and has a prologue followed by 73 short chapters. The Rule covers obedience, humility, silence, the abbot's authority, the daily round of communal prayer, manual work and reading. It draws heavily on the earlier Rule of the Master and on John Cassian, but is noted for its moderation. It later became the standard rule of Western monasticism.

The Carmen ad Deum is an anonymous Old High German interlinear rendering of a Latin rhythmical prayer that begins "Sancte sator, suffragator". The Latin poem is generally thought to be of Insular, probably Hiberno-Latin, origin, and its author is unknown. The German version dates from the later ninth century. It translates the Latin word by word and calls on God as Father, helper and lawgiver to protect the speaker against the devil with Christ's shield. It is a small but valuable witness to early German religious vocabulary.

Christus und die Samariterin (Christ and the Samaritan Woman) is a short anonymous Old High German poem, usually dated to the late ninth or early tenth century. It retells the meeting of Jesus and the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well from John 4 in rhyming long lines, the verse form also used by Otfrid of Weissenburg. Its lively dialogue covers the request for water, the promise of living water and the woman's recognition of a prophet. The poem survives only as a fragment and breaks off mid-sentence. It is a notable early example of German biblical verse.

The Cologne Baptismal Vow is a short anonymous baptismal formula in Old Saxon, usually dated to the later tenth century. In a series of questions and answers, the candidate renounces the devil, his works and will, and all heathen practices, sacrifices and idols. The candidate then professes faith in the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, the Church, the communion of saints, the resurrection of the flesh and eternal life. A Latin rubric follows, directing an exorcism by breathing on the candidate's face. It is a valuable record of early vernacular liturgy in the Christianization of the Saxons.

The Exhortatio ad plebem christianam is a short anonymous sermon-like admonition preserved in Old High German alongside its Latin original. It dates from the early ninth century and is generally linked to Bavaria. It tells Christian lay people that every believer must learn the Creed and the Lord's Prayer by heart. It also stresses that godparents must teach both texts to the children they sponsor at baptism, or answer for their neglect on Judgement Day. The work reflects the Carolingian push for basic religious instruction and is an important early witness to German prose.

The Frankish Baptismal Vow is a short anonymous baptismal formula in Old High German, usually dated to around 800. It takes the form of questions and answers. The candidate first renounces the devil, his works and will, and the blood sacrifices, offerings and gods of the heathens. He then professes faith in the Father, Son and Holy Spirit as one God, in the holy Church, the forgiveness of sins through baptism, and life after death. It reflects Carolingian efforts to teach Christianity in the vernacular and is among the earliest surviving German texts.

The Frankish Prayer (Fränkisches Gebet) is a short anonymous prayer in Old High German from the early ninth century, and one of the earliest surviving prayers in the German vernacular. In it the speaker asks the Lord God for help and for wisdom, right faith, love of God, a good will, health, prosperity and divine grace. A Latin version follows the German text. Its Franconian dialect gives the prayer its modern name. It is valued as early evidence of Carolingian efforts to teach Christian devotion in the vernacular.

The Freising Lord's Prayer (Freisinger Paternoster) is an anonymous Old High German translation and exposition of the Lord's Prayer in the Bavarian dialect, usually dated to the early ninth century. It survives in two related versions, of which this is A. Each petition is given first in Latin, then in German translation, and is followed by a short explanation. For example, the bread petition is applied both to bodily needs and to the Eucharist. It is an early example of vernacular catechetical instruction in the Carolingian period.

The Freising Lord's Prayer (Freisinger Paternoster) is an anonymous Old High German translation and explanation of the Lord's Prayer, written in the Bavarian dialect in the early ninth century. It is associated with Freising and survives in two versions, of which this is the second. Each Latin petition is followed by a German rendering and a short commentary. The commentary covers baptismal innocence, God's reign in the soul, the Eucharist as daily bread, and the forgiveness of debts. It is an important early witness to German-language catechetical teaching.

The Fulda Confession is an anonymous Old High German formula of general confession, named for its association with the monastery of Fulda and usually dated to the tenth century. The penitent confesses to God, all the saints and the priest a long list of sins of thought, word and deed. These include perjury, theft, drunkenness, neglect of church, fasting and almsgiving, and failing to keep Sundays and feasts. It ends with a short prayer. It belongs to a group of related vernacular confessions and is important evidence for early German pastoral practice and language.

The Old Saxon Genesis is an anonymous alliterative poem in Old Saxon that retells episodes from the Book of Genesis. It was composed in the first half of the ninth century, probably in the same milieu as the Heliand. Only three fragments survive. They cover Adam and Eve's lament after the Fall, the story of Cain and Abel and their descendants, and the destruction of Sodom. Along with the Heliand, it is the only major surviving Old Saxon poetry. Part of it was translated into Old English as Genesis B.

The Georgslied is an anonymous Old High German poem on Saint George, usually dated to the late ninth century. It survives incomplete and is one of the earliest saint's lives in German verse. Written in short rhymed lines with recurring refrains, it follows the eastern legend of George's martyrdom. He defies many kings, works healing miracles in prison and is repeatedly tortured and killed by the furious ruler Tacianus, rising again each time to preach and convert pagans. The poem is valued for showing early vernacular devotion to the saint.

The Gernrode Psalm Commentary is an anonymous fragment of Old Saxon biblical exegesis, usually dated to the later tenth century and associated with the religious foundation at Gernrode in the Harz. It survives only in damaged form and covers parts of Psalms 4 and 5. Latin lemmata such as "Verba mea" and "Introibo in domum tuam" are followed by allegorical explanation in the vernacular, drawing on the Latin patristic tradition of commentary on the Psalms. It is one of the few surviving prose texts in Old Saxon.

The Heliand ("Saviour") is an anonymous Old Saxon epic of about 6,000 alliterative lines, composed in the first half of the ninth century, probably around 830–850. It retells the life of Christ in the style of Germanic heroic poetry and draws mainly on a gospel harmony derived from Tatian's Diatessaron. Christ appears as a mighty lord and his disciples as loyal retainers. A Latin preface links the poem's commission to a King Louis, either Louis the Pious or Louis the German. It is the largest surviving work in Old Saxon and an important witness to the Christianization of the Saxons.

De fide catholica contra Iudaeos is a Latin treatise in two books by Isidore of Seville, written in the early seventh century and dedicated to his sister Florentina, a head of a community of nuns, at her request. It gathers Old Testament prophecies about Christ's divine birth, incarnation, passion, death, resurrection, kingdom and judgement. Isidore presents them as proofs of the Catholic faith against Jewish objections. The work was widely read in the Middle Ages. An Old High German translation made in the late eighth century is one of the earliest major prose texts in German.

The Lorsch Confession (Lorscher Beichte) is an anonymous Old High German confessional formula, usually dated to the second half of the ninth century and associated with the monastery of Lorsch. The penitent speaks in the first person to God, the saints and the priest ("God's man") and admits a long, formulaic list of sins: envy, perjury, gluttony, drunkenness and murder, failing to honour parents, lords and godchildren, and neglecting Sunday, Mass, tithes and works of mercy. It is one of the earliest vernacular German witnesses to the practice of confession.

The Ludwigslied, or Song of Ludwig, is an anonymous Old High German poem of 59 rhyming couplets. It celebrates the victory of the West Frankish king Louis III over Viking raiders at Saucourt-en-Vimeu on 3 August 881. Because it speaks of Louis as still living, it was probably composed before his death in August 882. The poem is deeply Christian: the Northmen are sent by God to punish Frankish sins, and Louis rides out at God's command. It survives in a single manuscript from Saint-Amand, alongside the Old French Sequence of Saint Eulalia.

The Mainz Confession (Mainzer Beichte) is an anonymous Old High German formula of general confession from the later tenth century. The penitent confesses to Almighty God, to all angels and saints, and to the priest. It goes on to list sins of word, deed and thought. These include gluttony, drunkenness, perjury, theft and killing, broken fasts, neglect of church and Sundays, failure to give alms, and failure to love one's neighbour. It is one of a group of related vernacular confessions and is important evidence for pastoral practice and for the early German language.

This is an Old High German translation of Augustine of Hippo's Sermon 76, made around 800. It survives among the Monsee (Mondsee) Fragments, a group of early German prose translations of religious texts that also includes parts of the Gospel of Matthew and Isidore of Seville's De fide catholica. Augustine's sermon comments on Matthew 14, where Christ walks on the water and Peter sinks through doubt. He treats Peter as a figure of the Church and discusses his confession of Christ. The translation is an important early witness to German theological prose.

De vocatione gentium ("On the Calling of the Gentiles") is an anonymous Old High German sermon. It survives in the Monsee (Mondsee) Fragments, a Bavarian manuscript of about 800 from Mondsee Abbey. The manuscript also holds early German versions of the Gospel of Matthew and Isidore of Seville's treatise against the Jews. The sermon is translated from Latin and is only partly preserved. It reflects on the many languages of humankind, God's knowledge of all thoughts, and the call of the nations to faith, quoting Solomon and Paul. It is among the earliest examples of German theological prose.

This is an anonymous Old High German homily that survives only in fragments. It belongs to the Monsee (Mondsee) Fragments, a group of translations of Latin religious texts made around 800, probably in a Bavarian scriptorium. The same group includes parts of the Gospel of Matthew and of Isidore's De fide catholica. What survives of the homily speaks of the angel sent to the Virgin and of God's coming in the Incarnation. It ends with a prayer for grace and eternal life in God's kingdom. It is valuable as early evidence of vernacular German preaching prose.

De fide catholica contra Iudaeos is a Latin treatise in two books by Isidore of Seville, written in the early seventh century and dedicated to his sister Florentina, a head of a community of nuns, at her request. It gathers Old Testament prophecies about Christ's divine birth, incarnation, passion, death, resurrection, kingdom and judgement. Isidore presents them as proofs of the Catholic faith against Jewish objections. The work was widely read in the Middle Ages. An Old High German translation made in the late eighth century is one of the earliest major prose texts in German.

The Mondsee (or Monsee) Fragments of the Gospel of Matthew are an anonymous Old High German translation of Matthew's Gospel. They were made around 800 and survive only in part, in pieces of a manuscript from Mondsee Abbey in Bavaria. The translation belongs to the so-called Isidor group, linked to the Old High German version of Isidore's De fide catholica, and was copied in a Bavarian form. It is one of the earliest Gospel translations into any German language, with this passage covering Matthew 8:34–9:8. The fragments matter greatly for the history of early German prose.

The Murbach Hymns are a cycle of anonymous Latin hymns for the Divine Office, sung at the night and day hours, such as "Mediae noctis tempore" and "Deus, qui caeli lumen es". They belong to the early medieval hymn tradition that followed Ambrose, and individual hymns probably date from between the fifth and eighth centuries. The cycle takes its name from the abbey of Murbach in Alsace. It is best known because it survives with an interlinear Old High German translation from the early ninth century, an important witness to early German religious language.

The Murbach Hymns are a cycle of anonymous Latin hymns for the Divine Office, sung at the night and day hours, such as "Mediae noctis tempore" and "Deus, qui caeli lumen es". They belong to the early medieval hymn tradition that followed Ambrose, and individual hymns probably date from between the fifth and eighth centuries. The cycle takes its name from the abbey of Murbach in Alsace. It is best known because it survives with an interlinear Old High German translation from the early ninth century, an important witness to early German religious language.

Muspilli is an anonymous Old High German poem in alliterative verse, probably composed in the ninth century. It survives incomplete, about 103 lines, in a Bavarian manuscript. Its subject is Christian eschatology. It describes the struggle of angels and devils for the soul just after death, the contest between Elijah and Antichrist, the burning of the world, and the Last Judgment. The poem's modern title comes from an obscure word in the text. Scholars still dispute that word's meaning, the poem's unity and its possible pre-Christian echoes.

The Consolation of Philosophy is a Latin work in alternating prose and verse by the Roman statesman and philosopher Boethius. He wrote it around 523–524 while imprisoned and awaiting execution under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric. Across five books, Lady Philosophy visits the grieving author. She leads him from complaints against Fortune to reflection on true happiness, the supreme good, providence, fate and free will. It was one of the most widely read books of the Middle Ages. Notker Labeo of St Gall translated it into Old High German with a commentary.

These Old High German translations with commentary were made by Notker Labeo, monk and teacher at the Abbey of Saint Gall, in the early eleventh century, before his death in 1022. They come after his Psalter and cover the biblical canticles used in the liturgy, such as the Song of Isaiah, as well as the Lord's Prayer and the creeds. Notker mixes Latin and German: each Latin verse is followed by a German rendering and explanation, often drawing on patristic interpretation. The texts are important witnesses to early German religious prose and to monastic teaching.

Notker's Psalter is an Old High German translation of the Book of Psalms with a running commentary. It was made by Notker Labeo (c. 950–1022), a Benedictine monk and teacher at the Abbey of Saint Gall, probably in the early eleventh century. Each Latin verse is followed by a German rendering and an explanation, in a mixed German and Latin prose that draws chiefly on Augustine's Enarrationes in Psalmos and on Cassiodorus. It is among the largest and most important surviving prose texts in Old High German.

The Old Bavarian Confession (Altbairische Beichte) is an anonymous confessional formula in Old High German, usually dated to the first half of the ninth century. It is written in the Bavarian dialect and addressed to the Lord ("Truhtin"). The penitent confesses sins of word, deed and thought, committed knowingly or unknowingly, waking or sleeping, including perjury, lying, greed, fornication and excess in food and drink. It then asks for pardon and grace, and for repentance in this life. It is one of the earliest vernacular German confessions and shows how the Carolingian Church used the vernacular in penitential practice.

The Old Saxon Confession is an anonymous formula of general confession in Old Saxon, usually dated to the tenth century. The penitent confesses to almighty God, the saints and the priest all sins of thought, word and deed. These are then listed one by one: envy, hatred, slander, perjury, lying, gluttony, drunkenness, failing to honour parents, the poor, Sundays and the Mass, and receiving the Eucharist without due awe and love. It is one of the few surviving prose texts in Old Saxon. It also shows how vernacular penitential practice worked in early medieval Germany.

The Old Saxon Creed is a short anonymous statement of faith in Old Saxon, the early medieval language of northern Germany. Its date is uncertain, but it is usually placed in the tenth or early eleventh century. It is set out as questions and answers, in the style of a baptismal interrogation. The person is asked whether they believe each article of faith, including the resurrection of the flesh on Judgement Day and life after death. It is one of the few surviving religious texts in Old Saxon.

The Evangelienbuch (Liber evangeliorum) is a gospel harmony in rhyming verse by Otfrid, a monk of Weissenburg Abbey in Alsace. It was written in the South Rhine Franconian dialect of Old High German and completed between about 863 and 871. In five books, it retells the life of Christ and adds passages of allegorical and moral interpretation. Otfrid dedicated it to King Louis the German and to others, and in a Latin letter to Archbishop Liutbert of Mainz he defended writing in Frankish. It is the first major German poem to use end rhyme rather than alliteration.

Ad Liutbertum is a Latin dedicatory letter by Otfrid of Weissenburg, monk and priest, addressed to Liutbert, archbishop of Mainz. It accompanied Otfrid's Old High German gospel harmony, the Evangelienbuch, written between about 863 and 871, and submitted the poem for the archbishop's approval. Otfrid says that brethren and a noble lady named Judith asked him to write it, so that it might replace secular songs. He notes that Virgil, Lucan and Ovid, and Christian poets such as Juvencus, Arator and Prudentius, wrote in their own languages. The letter is a key early statement on writing Christian literature in German.

Othloh's Prayer is a prose prayer in Old High German by Othloh (Otloh), a Benedictine monk of St Emmeram's in Regensburg, written around the middle of the eleventh century. A heading calls it a German version of a Latin prayer that comes before it, which Othloh also wrote. The speaker asks God to light up his heart and give him repentance, strength in service, faith, love, humility and purity, appealing to the events of Christ's life, beginning with his birth. It is one of the latest surviving Old High German texts.

The Palatine Confession is a short anonymous confessional formula in Old High German, usually dated to the tenth century. Spoken in the first person, it confesses sins to almighty God, all God's saints and the priest. It lists faults of word, deed and thought: lying, cursing, theft, killing, perjury and broken fasts. It also confesses neglect of church, Mass, almsgiving and care for the poor. It belongs to a group of related vernacular confessions and is evidence for early medieval penitential practice and the religious vocabulary of Old High German.

The Petruslied is an anonymous Old High German hymn to Saint Peter, usually dated to the second half of the ninth century and written in a Bavarian dialect. Its three short strophes, each of two rhyming long lines, say that Christ has given Peter power to save those who hope in him and to open the gates of heaven. They end with a plea for his mercy. Each strophe closes with a Kyrie eleison refrain. Copied with neumes, it is among the earliest surviving German songs with musical notation.

This short anonymous Old High German text is usually dated to the tenth century. It survives only as a fragment. It is an interlinear gloss: Old High German words are set beside the Latin phrases of a liturgical prayer. The surviving lines render part of the anamnesis of the Roman Canon of the Mass, recalling Christ's resurrection from the dead and glorious ascension and offering gifts to the divine majesty. It is evidence of early efforts to make the Latin liturgy understandable in the vernacular.

The Priests' Oath (Priestereid) is a short anonymous formula in Old High German, usually dated to the tenth century. A newly ordained or appointed priest used it to swear loyalty to his bishop, whose name was left blank as "N." The priest promises to be faithful, obedient and steadfast within the diocese, to serve the bishop's will as far as his strength and skill allow, and to prevent harm, as the canons require. It is a rare vernacular witness to church discipline and to the swearing of oaths in the period.

The Old High German Psalm 138 is a short anonymous verse paraphrase of the biblical psalm "Domine probasti me" (Psalm 139 in Hebrew numbering). It was probably composed in Bavaria in the late ninth or early tenth century. Written in end-rhymed long lines like those of Otfrid of Weissenburg, it presents David as the speaker. It freely retells the psalmist's praise of God's knowledge and presence everywhere, along with his rejection of evildoers. It is one of the few surviving vernacular German biblical poems of the Carolingian period.

The Reichenau Confession is an anonymous Old High German confession formula from the late tenth century, named after the monastery of Reichenau on Lake Constance. Spoken by a penitent, it confesses sin before God, the Virgin Mary, Saint Michael, Saint Peter, all the saints and the priest. It lists sins of thought, word and deed, including adultery, theft, slander, envy, anger, gluttony, drunkenness and swearing. It also lists failures to keep Sundays and feasts, attend services, receive communion worthily, and perform the works of mercy. It is a valuable witness to vernacular penitential practice in medieval Germany.

The Rhenish Franconian Canticles are an anonymous Old High German translation of Old Testament canticles used in the Divine Office. They survive only as fragments and are usually dated to the first half of the tenth century. The surviving text renders the end of the Canticle of Hezekiah (Isaiah 38), the Song of Hannah (1 Samuel 2) and the start of the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32). The translation closely follows the Latin wording. The fragments matter as a rare witness to Rhenish Franconian dialect and to early vernacular biblical and liturgical translation in Germany.

The Saxon Baptismal Vow is a short anonymous baptismal formula in an early form of Old Saxon. Its dialect is debated, and it shows Frankish features. It dates from the late eighth century and is usually linked to Charlemagne's campaigns to convert the Saxons. In question-and-answer form, the person being baptised renounces the devil, all idol worship and the devil's works. They also renounce by name the pagan gods Thunaer, Woden and Saxnot, then profess faith in the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It is valued as a rare witness to Germanic pagan religion and to early vernacular Christian texts.

Sigihart's Prayers are two short rhymed prayers in Old High German, dating from the early tenth century, roughly 902–906. They are named after Sigihart, a priest at Freising who wrote them at the end of his copy of Otfrid of Weissenburg's Gospel Book, made for Bishop Waldo of Freising. It is uncertain whether Sigihart composed them or only copied them. Each prayer asks Christ, the heavenly Lord, for grace and a place in his kingdom. Their end-rhymed long lines imitate Otfrid's verse. They are among the few surviving examples of early German vernacular devotional poetry.

The St. Emmeram Prayer is an anonymous Old High German confessional prayer in the Bavarian dialect, usually dated to the first half of the ninth century and associated with the Benedictine abbey of St. Emmeram in Regensburg. It survives in two related versions, and this is version A. The speaker confesses to the Lord all sins of word, deed and thought, committed knowingly or unknowingly, asleep or awake. He asks for grace, forgiveness and repentance in this life, and entrusts his heart, will, body and works to Christ's mercy. It is one of the earliest pieces of German devotional prose.

The St. Emmeram Prayer is an anonymous Old High German confessional prayer in the Bavarian dialect, usually dated to the first half of the ninth century. It survives in two related versions, known as A and B, and is associated with the monastery of St. Emmeram at Regensburg. The speaker confesses to the Lord all sins of word, deed and thought, whether done knowingly or unknowingly, waking or sleeping, and asks for forgiveness, true faith and good will in God's service. It is among the earliest German prayers of confession.

The St. Gall Creed is an anonymous Old High German translation of the Apostles' Creed, dated to the late eighth century, probably between about 770 and 800.
