Written in the Alemannic dialect and associated with the monastery of St. Gall, it renders the Latin creed article by article: belief in God the almighty Father, in Jesus Christ his only Son, and in the Holy Spirit, the Church, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection and eternal life. It ranks among the earliest Christian texts in German and was likely made for catechetical instruction.

The St. Gall Lord's Prayer is an anonymous Old High German translation of the Pater noster, made in the Alemannic dialect in the late eighth century, around 770 to 800. It is preserved at the abbey of St. Gall alongside a German version of the Apostles' Creed. It is one of the oldest surviving texts in the German language. Its literal, sometimes awkward wording shows early efforts to render basic Christian prayers in the vernacular for teaching the laity, as Carolingian church reform required.

This Latin gospel harmony combines the four gospels into a single continuous narrative of the life of Christ, following the order of Tatian's second-century Diatessaron. Its text, however, is largely that of the Vulgate. It goes back to the harmony preserved in the Codex Fuldensis, which was prepared for Bishop Victor of Capua around 541–546. It opens with Luke's prologue, followed by the prologue of John. Around 830, at the Abbey of Fulda under Rabanus Maurus, it was copied alongside an Old High German translation. This bilingual version is one of the most important prose monuments of early German.

This Latin gospel harmony combines the four gospels into a single continuous narrative of the life of Christ, following the order of Tatian's second-century Diatessaron. Its text, however, is largely that of the Vulgate. It goes back to the harmony preserved in the Codex Fuldensis, which was prepared for Bishop Victor of Capua around 541–546. It opens with Luke's prologue, followed by the prologue of John. Around 830, at the Abbey of Fulda under Rabanus Maurus, it was copied alongside an Old High German translation. This bilingual version is one of the most important prose monuments of early German.

The Vorauer Beichte is an anonymous Old High German confession formula, probably from the tenth century. It takes its name from Vorau in Styria, where the manuscript is kept. It opens with questions on faith in the Trinity, then has the penitent confess a long list of sins: failing to honour parents, love neighbours, family and clergy, keep Sundays and Mass, visit the sick and comfort the sorrowful, as well as theft, false oaths and sinful thoughts. The surviving text is fragmentary.

The Weissenburg Catechism is an anonymous collection of basic Christian texts in Old High German, generally dated to the late eighth or early ninth century and named after the abbey of Weissenburg (Wissembourg) in Alsace. It contains the Lord's Prayer with a phrase-by-phrase vernacular explanation, a list of capital sins, the Apostles' and Athanasian Creeds, and the Gloria. Probably connected with Carolingian efforts to have clergy teach the essentials of the faith in the vernacular, it is a key early witness to German religious prose.

The Wessobrunn Prayer is an anonymous Old High German text from around 800, and one of the earliest surviving poetic works in German. It is named after the Bavarian abbey of Wessobrunn, where its manuscript was kept. It opens with a short passage of alliterative verse describing the nothingness that came before creation: no earth, heaven, tree, mountain, sun, moon or sea, only the almighty God. A prose prayer follows, asking for true faith, good will, wisdom and strength to resist the devil. Scholars often compare its cosmological opening with Cædmon's Hymn and the Old Norse Völuspá.

The Würzburg Confession is an anonymous Old High German confession formula, usually dated to the second half of the ninth century and named after Würzburg. Written for use in penance, it has the penitent confess to almighty God, his saints and the priest every sin committed since baptism, in thought, word and deed. It then gives a long, detailed list of sins, including anger, envy, gluttony, idle speech in church, unbelief, theft, perjury and sexual offences. It is among the earliest surviving vernacular German texts of Christian worship and pastoral care.

The Younger Bavarian Confession is an anonymous Old High German confession formula of uncertain date, usually placed around the late tenth or early eleventh century. The penitent addresses Almighty God, Saint Mary, the angels, the saints and the priest. He confesses every sin of deed, thought and word committed since baptism, then works through a long catalogue of vices, including unbelief, sorcery, pride, envy, perjury, murder, theft and gluttony. He also admits to neglecting the works of mercy. Like related Bavarian confessions, it is valuable evidence for vernacular penitential practice and for early German religious vocabulary.

The Sibylline Oracles are a collection of prophetic oracles in Greek hexameter verse. They are attributed to the Sibyls, the inspired prophetesses of Greek and Roman tradition. The surviving twelve books were written by Jewish and Christian authors over several centuries, roughly from the second century BC to the early centuries AD. Their contents mix apocalyptic prophecy, sacred history, moral teaching and attacks on idolatry. Early Christian writers such as Lactantius quoted them widely as pagan witnesses to Christian truth.

The First Epistle to the Corinthians is a letter of the New Testament written in Greek by the apostle Paul, with Sosthenes named as co-sender, to the church he had founded at Corinth. It was probably written from Ephesus around 53–57. Paul responds to reports of factions and to questions from the community about sexual morality, marriage, food offered to idols, conduct in worship, the Lord's Supper and spiritual gifts. It includes the celebrated hymn to love (chapter 13) and the earliest extended teaching on the resurrection (chapter 15).

The First Epistle of John is a New Testament writing in Greek, the first of the three Johannine epistles. It names no author. Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is disputed, and many scholars place it within the Johannine community around 85–100. It reads more like a homily than a letter. It teaches that God is light and God is love, and that believers must confess their sins and love one another. It also rejects those who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. Its theology of love and fellowship has strongly shaped Christian thought.

The First Epistle of Peter is a letter in the New Testament, one of the Catholic Epistles. Its author presents himself as the apostle Peter, writing from "Babylon", probably meaning Rome. Many scholars, however, think it came from a Roman Christian circle linked to Peter, sometime around 60–90. It is addressed to Christians scattered across Asia Minor who were suffering persecution. The letter urges them to keep hope, holiness and patient endurance, modelled on the sufferings of Christ. It also gives household instructions and contains a famous passage on Christ preaching to the "spirits in prison".

The First Epistle to the Thessalonians is a letter of the New Testament sent by the apostle Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, to the Christian community he had founded at Thessalonica in Macedonia. It was probably written around 50–52, most likely from Corinth. Scholars widely accept it as authentic, and it is often regarded as the earliest surviving Christian writing. Paul gives thanks for the converts' faith under persecution and defends his own conduct among them. He urges them to live holy lives and addresses the fate of believers who have died before the Lord's return.

The First Epistle to Timothy is a New Testament letter written in Greek and addressed by the apostle Paul to his co-worker Timothy, who had been left at Ephesus. With 2 Timothy and Titus it forms the Pastoral Epistles. It warns against false teachers, gives directions on prayer and worship, and sets out qualifications for bishops and deacons and rules on widows and elders. Pauline authorship is disputed. Many scholars date it to the late first or early second century. It was important for later teaching on church order and ministry.

The Second Epistle to the Corinthians is a New Testament letter written in Greek by the apostle Paul, with Timothy named as co-sender. It is addressed to the church at Corinth and the Christians of Achaia, and is usually dated about 55–57. Paul writes about comfort in suffering and defends his apostolic ministry. He also urges a collection for the church in Jerusalem and confronts rival "super-apostles." Many scholars think it combines parts of several letters. It was translated early into Syriac, Latin, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian and Georgian.

The Second Epistle of John is a short New Testament letter. Its author calls himself "the elder" and writes to "the elect lady and her children", which most readers take to mean a local church. Tradition ascribes it to the apostle John, but the authorship is disputed. It is usually dated to the late first century. The letter urges mutual love and obedience to the commandments. It warns against deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh and forbids welcoming them.

The Second Epistle of Peter is a short letter in the New Testament. Its author presents himself as the apostle Simon Peter, but most modern scholars consider it pseudonymous and date it to roughly 80–120, which may make it the latest New Testament book. It urges believers to grow in virtue and become "partakers of the divine nature," warns against false teachers, and defends the expectation of Christ's return. It overlaps closely with the Epistle of Jude, and its place in the canon was disputed in the early Church.

The Second Epistle to the Thessalonians is a short letter of the New Testament. It names Paul, Silvanus and Timothy as its senders and is addressed to the Christian community at Thessalonica in Macedonia. It encourages believers suffering persecution and promises God's just judgement when the Lord Jesus is revealed. It corrects the claim that the day of the Lord has already come, describing a "man of lawlessness" who must appear first. It also warns against idleness. Scholars disagree about whether Paul wrote it. Dates proposed range from about 50 to near the end of the first century.

The Second Epistle to Timothy is a New Testament letter. It is one of the three Pastoral Epistles and is presented as written by the apostle Paul to his co-worker Timothy. Many scholars think it was written by a later follower of Paul in the late first century, while others accept that Paul wrote it during his final imprisonment in Rome. It is framed as Paul's last charge: Timothy should endure hardship, guard sound teaching and resist false teachers. It contains the statement that all Scripture is inspired by God, and Paul's farewell, "I have fought the good fight."

The Third Epistle of John is the shortest book of the New Testament. It is a private letter from an author who calls himself "the elder" to a Christian named Gaius. Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is debated, and it is usually dated to the late first century. The elder praises Gaius for welcoming travelling missionaries and condemns Diotrephes for refusing to receive them and for seeking preeminence. He also recommends Demetrius. The letter sheds rare light on authority and hospitality in the early church. Some early churches questioned whether it belonged in the canon.

The Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament. It forms the second half of a two-volume work with the Gospel of Luke and is addressed, like that Gospel, to Theophilus. Tradition names Luke, a companion of Paul, as its author, though scholars disagree about this; it is usually dated around 80–90. Acts begins with Christ's ascension and Pentecost and describes the early Jerusalem church. It then follows the spread of the gospel to the Gentiles, mostly through Paul's missionary journeys, and ends with his imprisonment in Rome.

The Epistle to the Colossians is a New Testament letter addressed to the Christian community at Colossae in Phrygia, Asia Minor. It names Paul and Timothy as senders, but many scholars doubt that Paul wrote it, and its date is uncertain. It is usually placed between about 58 and 80. The letter presents Christ as supreme over all creation and powers. It warns against a local "philosophy" involving ascetic and ritual practices and gives instructions for Christian households. Its close parallels with Ephesians have long attracted scholarly attention.

The Epistle to the Ephesians is a New Testament letter written in Greek and addressed under the name of the apostle Paul to Christians at Ephesus. The words "at Ephesus" are missing from some early manuscripts. Many scholars think a later disciple wrote it, perhaps around 80–90, while others hold that Paul wrote it during his imprisonment around 60–62. Its main themes are God's eternal plan to unite all things in Christ, the Church as Christ's body, and the reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles. It ends with moral teaching, including household codes and the image of the "armour of God."

The Epistle to the Galatians is a letter of the apostle Paul to the churches of Galatia in Asia Minor, written in Greek around the middle of the first century. Its exact date and the location of its recipients are disputed. Paul defends his apostolic authority and his gospel against teachers who urged Gentile converts to be circumcised and keep the Mosaic law. He argues that people are justified through faith in Christ, not works of the law. A central text for Christian ideas of grace and freedom, it was translated early into Syriac, Latin, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian and Georgian.

The Epistle to the Hebrews is a New Testament book written in highly polished Greek, usually dated between about 65 and 90. It does not name its author. It was long attributed to Paul the Apostle and placed among his letters, though this was doubted in antiquity and most modern scholars regard the author as unknown. Its sermon-like argument presents Christ as the Son, superior to the angels and Moses, and as the eternal high priest of a new covenant. It urges its readers to persevere in faith despite persecution.

The Epistle of James is a New Testament letter written in Greek and addressed "to the twelve tribes which are of the Dispersion." It names its author as James, traditionally identified with James the brother of the Lord, who led the church in Jerusalem. That attribution is disputed, and proposed dates run from the mid-first century to its end or later. Written in the manner of wisdom literature, it urges endurance in trials, care for the poor and control of the tongue, and teaches that faith without works is dead. Early Christians long debated whether it belonged in the canon.

The Gospel of John is the fourth of the canonical Gospels of the New Testament. Tradition attributes it to the apostle John, though modern scholars dispute who wrote it. It is usually dated to about 90–100. It opens with a prologue on the divine Word (Logos) made flesh. It then tells of Jesus' signs, long discourses, farewell teaching to his disciples, passion and resurrection. Its strong emphasis on Christ's divinity made it central to early Trinitarian and Christological debate. Origen, John Chrysostom, Augustine and Cyril of Alexandria all wrote major commentaries on it.

The Epistle of Jude is a short letter of 25 verses and the penultimate book of the New Testament. It names its author as Jude, "brother of James," traditionally taken to be a brother of Jesus. Its date and authorship are disputed, though it is usually placed in the late first century. The letter urges readers to contend for the faith against false teachers. It recalls examples of divine judgment and quotes the Book of Enoch, and it alludes to a dispute over the body of Moses. It closes with a well-known doxology.

The Gospel according to Luke is the third of the canonical Gospels of the New Testament, written in Greek, probably around 75–90. Tradition attributes it to Luke, companion of Paul, who also wrote the Acts of the Apostles, but the work itself is anonymous. Addressed to Theophilus, it tells of Jesus from the births of John the Baptist and Jesus to the resurrection and ascension. It is noted for its infancy narratives, its parables, and its concern for the poor and outcast.

The Gospel according to Mark is the second book of the New Testament and is generally thought to be the earliest of the four canonical gospels. Most scholars date it to about 65–75. Tradition attributes it to John Mark, a companion of Peter, but the authorship is uncertain. Written in Greek, it is a short, fast-moving account that runs from John the Baptist's preaching through Jesus' ministry in Galilee to his passion in Jerusalem and the empty tomb. Matthew and Luke drew heavily on it. It was soon translated into Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian, Georgian and Slavonic.

The Gospel of Matthew is the first book of the New Testament and one of the three Synoptic Gospels. It was written in Greek, probably between about 70 and 100, and is traditionally attributed to the apostle Matthew, although its author is unknown. It opens with Jesus' genealogy from Abraham and goes on to tell of his birth, ministry, teaching, death and resurrection. It includes the Sermon on the Mount and stresses Jesus as the fulfilment of Jewish scripture. In the early Church it was the most widely cited gospel.

The Epistle to the Philippians is a letter of the New Testament written by the apostle Paul, with Timothy named as co-sender, to the Christian community at Philippi in Macedonia. Paul wrote it while imprisoned, possibly in Rome around 60–62, though Ephesus and Caesarea have also been proposed. Its central themes are joy, partnership in the gospel and humility. It thanks the Philippians for their gift and warns against opponents. It is especially valued for the Christ hymn (2:6–11), which describes Christ's self-emptying and exaltation and was central to later Christological debate.

The Epistle to Philemon is a short letter in the New Testament written by the apostle Paul, with Timothy named as co-sender, while Paul was in prison. It is usually dated to the late 50s or early 60s, but the place of writing is disputed. Paul addresses Philemon, a Christian whose house was used for church meetings, and asks him to receive back his slave Onesimus as a beloved brother. Onesimus had become a Christian while with Paul. Its authenticity is almost universally accepted. The letter has been central to Christian discussions of slavery, reconciliation and fellowship.

Revelation, also called the Apocalypse, is the last book of the New Testament and its only full apocalyptic work. Its author calls himself John and says he received his visions on the island of Patmos. Tradition identifies him with John the Apostle, but this has been disputed since antiquity. It is usually dated to about 95, under Domitian, though some scholars prefer an earlier date. It contains letters to seven churches in Asia and visions of judgement, the defeat of evil and the New Jerusalem. Its place in the canon was long contested, especially in the East.

The Epistle to the Romans is a letter of the apostle Paul to the Christian community at Rome and is part of the New Testament. Paul probably wrote it from Corinth around 55–58, before a planned visit to Rome and a journey on to Spain. It is the longest and most systematic of his letters. It sets out his teaching on sin, justification by faith, the place of Israel in God's plan, and Christian conduct. Romans has deeply shaped Christian theology, from Origen and Augustine to the Reformation. It was translated early into Syriac, Latin, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian and Georgian.

The Epistle to Titus is a short New Testament letter written in Greek. It presents itself as Paul's letter to his co-worker Titus, whom he had left in Crete to organise the church there. Whether Paul wrote it is disputed: many scholars see it as a later pastoral letter, dated anywhere from the 60s to around 100. It sets out qualifications for elders and bishops, warns against false teachers, and urges sound doctrine and godly conduct. Together with 1 and 2 Timothy, it is one of the Pastoral Epistles.

The Sacramentary or Prayer-Book of Sarapion is a collection of about thirty Greek liturgical prayers for a bishop's use, from Egypt in the mid-fourth century. It is attributed to Sarapion, bishop of Thmuis in Lower Egypt and a friend of Antony and Athanasius, though how much of it he wrote himself is disputed. It contains a eucharistic anaphora and prayers for baptism, ordination, the blessing of oils and burial. It is valued as an early witness to Egyptian worship and contains the earliest recorded use of the Sanctus.

This is a small anonymous collection of Syriac fragments preserved as quotations in later books. They are attributed to the teaching that Addai (Addaeus), the legendary apostle of Edessa, is said to have given before King Abgar and the assembly of the city. The passages deal with Christ's voluntary death and resurrection, his divine power under a human appearance, and the survival of souls after death. They belong to the Abgar legend, which was also told in the Doctrine of Addai. Their date is uncertain, but they are probably from the fifth or sixth century.

The Acts of Sharbil is an anonymous Syriac martyr narrative from Edessa. It tells of Sharbil, chief priest of the city's pagan cult, who is converted to Christianity by the bishop Barsamya during a great festival to Nebu, Bel and other gods. He is then tortured and executed under a persecution set in the fifteenth year of Trajan. The text belongs to a cycle of Edessene martyr acts and was probably composed in the fourth or fifth century. Its historical value is doubtful, but it offers evidence of Edessa's pagan religion and of how the city's Christians remembered their past.

This short apologetic discourse survives in Syriac and is attributed to Ambrose, described as a leading man of Greece who became a Christian, faced the outcry of his fellow senators, and fled. It is a version of the Greek Oratio ad Graecos (Discourse to the Greeks), traditionally but doubtfully ascribed to Justin Martyr. Its date and authorship are uncertain, perhaps the second or third century. The speaker explains why he left paganism, mocks the immoral gods and heroes of Homer and Greek myth, and urges the Greeks to turn to the divine Word.

The Book of the Laws of Countries is a Syriac philosophical dialogue from the early third century, among the oldest surviving original works of Syriac literature. It records the teaching of Bardaisan of Edessa and is traditionally credited to his disciple Philip rather than to Bardaisan himself. Bardaisan answers the questions of a pupil, Avida, on human free will, nature and fate. To show that the stars do not determine human conduct, he surveys the differing laws and customs of many peoples. Eusebius quoted parts of it in Greek.

The Ecclesiastical History is a ten-book account of Christianity from the time of Christ to the early fourth century, written in Greek by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. He completed it in stages, with the final edition dating to around 324–326. It traces the succession of bishops in the major sees, Christian writers, heresies, the fate of the Jews and the persecutions, ending with Constantine's victory. Eusebius quotes many earlier documents that are otherwise lost, which makes the work the foundation of later church historiography. It was translated early into Latin, Syriac and Armenian.

A Syriac metrical homily (memra) by Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), the Syriac poet and later bishop of Batnan. It retells the legend of King Abgar of Edessa, who wrote to Christ asking him to come to the city. Jacob uses the story as an allegory: Edessa, the "daughter of the peoples," gives up her idols and calls the Bridegroom away from Zion, which had rejected him. He draws on the imagery of the Song of Songs. The poem shows how the Abgar tradition shaped Edessa's sense of itself as a Christian city from early on.

This is an extract from a Syriac verse homily (memra) on the fall of idols by Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), the Miaphysite poet and bishop of Batnan known for his large body of metrical homilies. The passage draws on the Edessene legend of the apostle Addai and King Abgar, picturing apostle and king building the church together in Edessa while Satan flees to Babylon and the Chaldeans. It shows how the Abgar tradition was taken up in later Syriac preaching about Christianity overcoming paganism.

The Homily on Guria and Shamuna is a Syriac verse homily (memra) attributed to Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), a Syriac poet and bishop. It celebrates Guria and Shamuna, two elderly Christians of Edessa who were martyred during the Roman persecutions of the early fourth century. Jacob calls them "salt of our land", "candlesticks of gold" and "bulwarks" against error and war. He presents them as patrons and protectors of the region and praises their endurance under torture. The homily is a good example of the Syriac tradition of preaching on local martyrs.

This verse homily (mimra) was composed in Syriac by Jacob of Serugh (c. 452–521), one of the leading poets of the Syriac tradition. It honours Habib, a deacon of Edessa who was burned to death in the persecution of the early fourth century. Jacob writes as though the martyr calls to him from the flames, asking to be portrayed among the glorious. He then compares Habib with the three youths in the fiery furnace of Daniel, who were not burned. The poem is a good example of Jacob's metrical homilies and of the Edessene cult of martyrs.

This Syriac letter of moral advice was written by Mara bar Serapion, a philosopher of Stoic outlook from Samosata, to his young son Serapion. Mara apparently wrote it as a captive after the Romans annexed his city in AD 72. Its date is uncertain and is placed anywhere from shortly after 73 to the late second century. In urging the boy to pursue wisdom, the letter cites the unjust treatment of Socrates, Pythagoras and "the wise king" of the Jews. That last phrase is often read as an early non-Christian reference to Jesus.

The Martyrdom of Barsamya is an anonymous Syriac hagiographical text. It tells of Barsamya, bishop of Edessa, who was accused of converting the pagan priest Sharbil. The story is set in the fifteenth year of Trajan's reign and is dated to the Seleucid year 416. Barsamya is tried before the judge Lysinus and suffers torture. The text is a companion to the Acts of Sharbil. It was probably composed in the fourth or fifth century, and it is generally treated as legendary. Its account may reflect a later bishop of Edessa who was persecuted around 250 but not martyred.

The Martyrdom of Habib the Deacon is an anonymous Syriac hagiographical text about Habib, a deacon from the village of Telzeha near Edessa. It is set during the persecution under the emperor Licinius, while Cona was bishop of Edessa. It tells how Habib secretly ministered in village churches, read the Scriptures and encouraged Christians to stand firm. He was then arrested and burned to death at Edessa. The date and reliability of the account are disputed, but scholars accept Habib's martyrdom as historical. Habib is venerated as Abibus of Edessa.

This is a Greek hagiographical account of the martyrs of Edessa. It is included in the menologion of Symeon Metaphrastes, the tenth-century Byzantine collection of saints' lives that he reworked and compiled. It tells how Shamuna and Guria, two Christians raised at Edessa, were denounced, tortured and executed during the persecution under Diocletian. It also tells of the later martyrdom of the deacon Habib. The text reworks earlier Syriac traditions about these saints and shows how the cults of Edessene martyrs reached the Greek-speaking Byzantine church.

This passage comes from Book II of the History of the Armenians by Movses Khorenatsi (Moses of Khoren), written in Armenian. The work's date is disputed: it is placed either in the fifth century or between the seventh and ninth. The section tells the story of King Abgar of Edessa, whom Movses presents as an Armenian ruler. It covers his conflicts with Herod and Rome, his exchange of letters with Christ, and the conversion of Edessa through the apostle Thaddeus (Addai). It adapts the Syriac Abgar legend, which Eusebius had also recorded, into Armenian national and Christian history.

The Teaching of Addai is an anonymous Syriac narrative, usually dated to around 400, though estimates range from the fourth to the early fifth century. It develops the legend of King Abgar of Edessa, an earlier form of which Eusebius records. Abgar writes to Jesus and receives a reply. After the Ascension, the apostle Addai heals the king, preaches and converts the city. The work also contains the Protonike legend of the finding of the Cross. It is a key source for how the Edessene church understood its own apostolic origins.

The Teaching of Simon Cephas in the City of Rome is an anonymous apocryphal text that survives in Syriac. It is usually dated to the fourth or fifth century, though its date is uncertain. It describes the apostle Peter leaving Antioch in the third year of Claudius and preaching on his way to Rome. There it gives his sermon to the people, which tells of Christ's incarnation, miracles, death and resurrection, and recounts the miracles he performed in the city. It belongs to the Syriac apostolic legends brought together in collections of early Syriac documents.

The Teaching of the Apostles (Doctrina Apostolorum) is an anonymous Syriac church order, usually dated to the fourth or early fifth century, though its exact date is uncertain. It begins with Christ's ascension and the apostles receiving the Spirit at Pentecost. It then sets out a series of ordinances on worship, the Sunday assembly, fasting, clergy and church discipline, presented as decisions made by the apostles. It closes by listing the regions each apostle evangelised and how ordination to the priesthood passed to various lands. It is a witness to early Syriac traditions about church order and apostolic succession.

The Liturgy of Saint James is a Eucharistic liturgy traditionally attributed to James the Just, the "brother of the Lord" and first leader of the Jerusalem church. The attribution is traditional, not historical. The text took shape between roughly the fourth and sixth centuries and reflects the rite of the Jerusalem church. It was originally written in Greek and later also used in Syriac. It was the main liturgy of Jerusalem and Antioch before the liturgies of Basil and John Chrysostom displaced it in Byzantine use. It remains the principal anaphora of the West Syriac churches.

This is a selection from the Latin correspondence of Ambrose, bishop of Milan from 374 to 397, written mostly between about 384 and 396. The letters go to emperors, bishops, clergy and friends. Among them are his appeals to Valentinian II against Symmachus's petition to restore the Altar of Victory in the Senate, and accounts of his clash with the imperial court over the basilicas of Milan. Others are addressed to Theodosius I. Besides scriptural and pastoral teaching, the letters are a key source for relations between church and empire in the late fourth century.

This group of Latin letters by Ambrose, bishop of Milan from 374 to 397, makes up what the Benedictine editors called the "second class" of his correspondence. It gathers letters with no clear internal evidence of date and arranges them by subject instead of chronologically. The first are expositions of passages of Scripture, such as the opening letter to Irenaeus presenting Christ's Body as the true manna. Next come discussions of mainly doctrinal questions, and the group ends with brief letters of friendship. Together they show Ambrose's allegorical exegesis and his pastoral guidance.

These five Greek homilies are by Asterius of Amasea, a former lawyer who became bishop of Amasea in Pontus in the late fourth century. They were probably preached between about 380 and 410, and they are moral sermons rather than doctrinal ones. The first takes the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus (Luke 16) as its starting point and attacks the waste and luxury of the wealthy. Asterius preached in a lively style and paid close attention to everyday customs, so his sermons are valued as evidence for social life and attitudes in late antique Asia Minor.

This short Greek treatise by Basil of Caesarea (d. 379), the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, is addressed to young men, traditionally his nephews. Writing as an older man, apparently late in life, Basil advises them on how to read pagan poets, historians and philosophers such as Hesiod and Homer. They should take what supports virtue and reject the rest, as bees gather only what is useful from flowers. The work became a classic Christian statement on the value of classical education. Renaissance humanists in particular read and promoted it.

This is the prologue to the Latin tractates, or sermons, on the Gospel of Matthew by Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia from about 388 until his death around 407. It introduces the commentary by setting out the gospel as the special vessel of the mystery of salvation. It then names the four evangelists and the order in which they wrote. According to the prologue, Matthew wrote first and John last, after his exile on Patmos, to answer rising heresies. It also stresses that Matthew and John were apostolic eyewitnesses. The collection of tractates survives only in part.

The Chronicle of Edessa is an anonymous Syriac history of the city of Edessa, generally dated to about 540–550. Its manuscript title is "Histories of Events in Brief." In short dated entries, it covers the period from the founding of the kingdom of Osrhoene in 133/132 BC to 540. It draws mainly on Edessan royal archives and church records and is considered historically reliable. Its account of the Daisan flood of 201 mentions a Christian church building and is one of the earliest pieces of evidence for Christianity in Edessa. Only an abridged version survives.

This anonymous Syriac chronicle was written around 506–507 by an eyewitness living at Edessa, at the request of Sergius, a priest and abbot. It records the disasters that struck Edessa, Amida and Mesopotamia, including locusts, famine, plague and earthquake, and above all the Roman–Persian war of 502–506. It survives only because it was copied into the Chronicle of Zuqnin, and its old attribution to Joshua the Stylite is now rejected. It is one of the earliest and most reliable histories in Syriac and is admired for how it analyses causes.

The Liberian Catalogue is an anonymous Latin list of the bishops of Rome. It forms part of the Chronography of 354, a collection compiled in Rome in that year. Beginning with Peter and ending with Liberius (bishop 352–366), after whom it is named, it gives the length of each episcopate in years, months and days, with the consuls and emperors of the time. Its early sections are thought to draw on older lists, possibly including one by Hippolytus. It is the earliest surviving papal list of this kind, and the later Liber Pontificalis drew on it.

This Greek homily was preached by John Chrysostom as archbishop of Constantinople, usually dated to 399. In it he rebukes members of his congregation who stayed away from church to attend horse races in the hippodrome and shows in the theatre. Chrysostom describes the uproar of the crowds and warns that these spectacles corrupt the soul, especially through the lust aroused by watching actresses. He calls his hearers back to the church and to repentance. The sermon is an important witness to his long campaign against public entertainments and to daily life in the late antique city.

This is a series of sermons on the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31), preached by John Chrysostom at Antioch while he was a presbyter there, probably around 388–389. Seven discourses survive under this title. The first opens just after the pagan New Year celebrations, attacking drunkenness and street revelry before turning to the parable. Across the series Chrysostom deals with wealth and poverty, almsgiving, providence, and judgement after death. The sermons are a key source for his social teaching on riches and care for the poor.

In Kalendas is a Greek homily that John Chrysostom preached at Antioch as a presbyter under Bishop Flavian, usually dated to 1 January 387 or 388. It opens by noting the bishop's absence and recalling a recent sermon in praise of the apostle Paul. Chrysostom then attacks the popular New Year festivities of the Kalends, including drunken revelry, decorating doors, divination and the belief that the year's first day foretells its fortune. The homily is valuable evidence for how Christians in late antiquity dealt with pagan civic customs.

This is a Greek Christmas sermon handed down under the name of John Chrysostom. It opens with the words "I see a strange and novel mystery." Most scholars regard it as probably not authentic, though some have defended it, so its author and date are uncertain. In hymn-like prose it celebrates the Nativity at Bethlehem. Angels and shepherds sing together, heaven and earth seem to change places, and God becomes man without ceasing to be God. By his will and his love for humanity, he overcomes the order of nature.

The Christian Topography is a Greek treatise on cosmology and geography by Cosmas Indicopleustes, an Alexandrian merchant who had sailed to Aksum and India. He wrote it around 545–550. It first had five books and was later expanded to ten and then twelve. Cosmas argues against the spherical cosmos of pagan astronomy. In its place he describes a flat earth inside a universe shaped like the Tabernacle of Moses. The work is valued for its early world maps and for its first-hand reports on trade, animals and Christian communities around the Indian Ocean.

The Five Tomes against Nestorius is a polemical treatise in five books by Cyril of Alexandria, written around 430 on the eve of the Council of Ephesus. Cyril quotes passages from a published collection of Nestorius's sermons and refutes them one by one. He defends the title Theotokos ("Mother of God") for the Virgin Mary and insists that the Word truly became flesh in a single union of person, not by mere indwelling or conjunction. He appeals to Scripture and the Nicene Creed. The work is a key statement of Cyril's Christology.

Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444, wrote this Greek exegetical commentary on the Gospel of John. This part contains its first six books. The full work had twelve books, of which books seven and eight survive only in fragments. It is usually dated before the Nestorian controversy, around 425–429. Cyril reads the Gospel closely, verse by verse, and pays most attention to doctrine. He argues at length against Arian and Eunomian teaching that the Son is lesser than the Father. The commentary is one of the most important patristic studies of John.

These are the second half of Cyril of Alexandria's Greek commentary on the Gospel of John, a verse-by-verse exposition in twelve books. It is generally dated to the years before the Nestorian controversy broke out in 429. Books 7 and 8 survive only in fragments, picking up at John 10. The later books carry the exposition through the end of the Gospel. Cyril stresses that Christ is God by nature, especially against Arian readings. The work is one of the most substantial patristic commentaries on the Fourth Gospel.

That Christ is One is a Greek theological dialogue by Cyril of Alexandria, generally dated to the later 430s, after the Council of Ephesus. It is set as a conversation between Cyril and an interlocutor named Hermias. The work defends the unity of Christ as one incarnate Son against the teaching associated with Nestorius. Cyril upholds the title Theotokos for Mary and rejects a mere "connection" between the Word and a man. He then answers the scriptural objections drawn from Christ's human weaknesses. It is regarded as one of the most mature statements of his Christology.

The Scholia on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten is a Christological treatise by Cyril of Alexandria. It was written in Greek in the 1430s, probably soon after the Council of Ephesus of 431. It is made up of short numbered chapters. These explain the meaning of the title "Christ", the anointing of the Word made flesh and the union of divinity and humanity in one Son. Throughout, Cyril argues against the teaching of Nestorius. The Greek original survives only in part, and the full text is preserved in an early Latin translation, traditionally credited to Marius Mercator.

This anonymous apocryphal narrative tells of the death, or "departure", of the apostle John at Ephesus. It is a Syriac version of the account known in Greek as the Metastasis, which closes the apocryphal Acts of John. On a Sunday, John urges the assembled brethren to stay faithful and celebrates the Eucharist. He then has a grave dug, prays, and lies down in it to die in peace. Its date of composition is uncertain, perhaps the fourth or fifth century. It shaped later traditions about John's end.

The Celestial Hierarchy is a Greek treatise in the Corpus Dionysiacum. It is addressed to "Timothy" by an author writing as Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul's Athenian convert. In fact it was written by an anonymous Christian Neoplatonist, probably in Syria, around 485–530. The treatise reads the symbolic images of angels in Scripture and arranges the heavenly beings into nine orders grouped in three triads. Through these orders, divine light passes down to purify, illuminate and perfect. It became the basis of medieval angelology in both East and West.

The Divine Names is a Greek theological treatise in thirteen chapters belonging to the Corpus Areopagiticum. It was written in the late fifth or early sixth century by an anonymous author who presents himself as Dionysius the Areopagite, the Athenian convert of Paul. Addressed to Timothy, it interprets the names Scripture gives to God, such as Good, Light, Beauty, Love, Being, Life and Wisdom. It holds that God is beyond every name and includes an influential account of evil as privation. Drawing on Proclus, the work shaped later Byzantine and medieval Latin theology.

The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy is a Greek treatise in the Corpus Dionysiacum. Its author wrote under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul's Athenian convert, but was probably a Syrian monk of the late fifth or early sixth century. Addressed to "Timothy", it pairs with the Celestial Hierarchy. It interprets the Church's rites as sacred symbols: baptism, the Eucharistic synaxis, the consecration of myron, ordination, monastic tonsure and funeral rites. It also describes the ordered ranks of clergy, monks and laity through which divine light leads believers toward deification. The treatise deeply influenced Byzantine liturgical commentary and medieval Western theology.

The Letters are a collection of ten short Greek epistles that form part of the Corpus Areopagiticum. They were written in the late fifth or early sixth century by an anonymous author, probably in Syria, who presented himself as Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul's Athenian convert. Their addressees are figures from the apostolic age, among them the monk Gaius, Bishop Polycarp, Titus and John the Evangelist on Patmos. The letters return to the corpus's main themes: God's unknowability beyond being, the "divine darkness", the interpretation of scriptural symbols and the right ordering of the church hierarchy.

The Mystical Theology is a short Greek treatise in five chapters belonging to the Corpus Dionysiacum. Its anonymous author wrote under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul's Athenian convert, probably in Syria around 485–530. Addressed to Timothy, it opens with a prayer to the Trinity. It then describes the soul's ascent beyond sense and intellect into the "divine darkness," where God is known by unknowing. By contrasting affirmative with negative theology, it became a founding text of Christian apophatic mysticism in both East and West.

The Prose Refutations are a group of polemical discourses in Syriac by Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), the deacon and theologian of Nisibis and Edessa. They are aimed at the three main rival teachings of his region: Mani, Marcion and Bardaisan. The first discourse is a letter to a certain Hypatius. In it Ephrem argues against dualist ideas about light and darkness, matter and the body, and defends free will and the goodness of creation. The work is a rare example of Ephrem's prose. It is also an important witness to early Manichaean, Marcionite and Bardaisanite thought.

The Life of St Severinus is a Latin hagiography written around 511 by Eugippius, Severinus's disciple and later abbot of the monastery at Castellum Lucullanum near Naples. Eugippius dedicated it, with a prefatory letter, to the deacon Paschasius. It describes the ascetic life, miracles and public work of Severinus (died 482) in the Danubian province of Noricum as Roman rule collapsed there. It also covers his dealings with the Rugians and Odoacer, and the later move of the Roman population and his relics to Italy. It is a key historical source for the end of Roman rule along the Danube.

The first book of the Chronicle by Eusebius of Caesarea was probably compiled in the early fourth century. Sometimes called the Chronographia, it sets out the chronologies of the Chaldeans, Assyrians, Hebrews, Egyptians, Greeks and Romans through extracts from earlier historians. Eusebius uses these to place the biblical patriarchs and prophets, especially Moses, alongside the history of other nations, and he warns that exact chronology cannot be achieved. It prepared the way for the dated tables of book 2. The Greek original is lost except for quotations in later writers, but the book survives largely in an Armenian translation.

Against Hierocles is a short Greek polemical treatise traditionally attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea, although some scholars have questioned this attribution. It probably dates from the early fourth century, around the time of the Great Persecution. It answers the Lover of Truth (Philalethes), an anti-Christian work generally identified with the Roman official Sossianus Hierocles, which compared Apollonius of Tyana with Jesus. The treatise leaves Hierocles' other arguments to Origen's reply to Celsus. Instead, it attacks Philostratus' Life of Apollonius, the account on which the comparison relied, and argues that its miracle stories are unreliable.

The Proof of the Gospel (Demonstratio evangelica) is an apologetic treatise in Greek by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, probably written in the 310s. It is dedicated to Theodotus, bishop of Laodicea, and follows his fifteen-book Preparation for the Gospel. Eusebius uses the Hebrew prophecies to argue that Christ and the Church fulfil the Scriptures, and explains why Christians follow the faith of the patriarchs rather than the Mosaic Law. Of the original twenty books, only the first ten survive, along with a fragment of the fifteenth. It is a major source for early Christian interpretation of prophecy.

The Preparation for the Gospel is a Greek work of Christian apologetics in fifteen books by Eusebius of Caesarea. He began it around 313 and dedicated it to Bishop Theodotus of Laodicea. It argues that Christians were right to give up pagan religion and philosophy for the Hebrew Scriptures. It surveys Phoenician, Egyptian and Greek theology and claims that Greek philosophers owed a debt to the Hebrews. It was written as a companion to the Demonstration of the Gospel, and it is valued for preserving many passages from authors whose works are otherwise lost.

The Theophania, or "Divine Manifestation", is an apologetic treatise in five books by Eusebius of Caesarea. It was probably written in the later years of his life, though its exact date is disputed. The Greek original survives only in fragments, but a complete early Syriac translation is extant. The work argues against atheism and polytheism and presents the divine Word as creator and governor of the world. It then treats the incarnation, Christ's teaching and miracles, and the fulfilment of prophecy. Much of its material overlaps with Eusebius's Demonstratio Evangelica and his oration in praise of Constantine.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in six books by Evagrius Scholasticus, a lawyer at Antioch and aide to Patriarch Gregory of Antioch. He completed it around 593–594. It continues the histories of Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret, covering the period from the First Council of Ephesus in 431 to the reign of Emperor Maurice. Written from a Chalcedonian standpoint, it is a major source for the Christological controversies after Chalcedon, for imperial and Persian affairs, and for the plague of the 540s, which Evagrius survived.

De excidio Britanniae is a Latin sermon in the form of a letter by the British monk Gildas. It was written in the late fifth or sixth century; the exact date is disputed. It has three parts. The first tells British history from the Roman conquest to the author's own day and mentions Ambrosius Aurelianus and the victory at Mons Badonicus. The second condemns five contemporary kings, Maelgwn Gwynedd among them. The third attacks the British clergy. The work's history is not reliable, but it is the only major source for sub-Roman Britain written by a near-contemporary.

The Dialogues are a Latin hagiographical collection in four books, traditionally attributed to Pope Gregory the Great and usually dated to about 593–594. Their authorship has been questioned by some modern scholars. Written as a conversation between Gregory and his deacon Peter, the first three books tell of the miracles and holy lives of Italian saints. The second book, on Benedict of Nursia, is the fullest early source for his life. The fourth book argues for the soul's survival and the afterlife. The work's wide influence led Eastern Christians to call Gregory "the Dialogist".

Oration 4 is the first of two invectives by Gregory of Nazianzus against the emperor Julian, known in Christian tradition as the Apostate. It was written soon after Julian's death on the Persian campaign in June 363, probably in 363 or 364. Gregory celebrates the tyrant's fall and attacks his return to paganism and his measures against Christians, especially the edict barring Christians from teaching classical literature. He also defends the Christian claim to Greek learning and eloquence. Together with Oration 5, it is a major Christian response to Julian's reign and an important example of late antique polemical rhetoric.

The Second Invective against Julian is a Greek oration by Gregory of Nazianzus, written soon after the emperor Julian's death in 363, probably in 363 or 364. It follows the first invective (Oration 4) and moves from Julian's misdeeds to the judgments of God. Gregory narrates the failed attempt to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, Julian's disastrous Persian campaign and his death, and recalls the young Julian he had known as a student at Athens. Together the two orations form an important Christian polemical response to Julian's pagan revival.

The Life of St Macrina is a Greek hagiography by Gregory of Nyssa, probably written around 380–383. It is framed as a long letter to the monk Olympius, whom Gregory met at Antioch. It tells the life of his elder sister Macrina the Younger: her education and her choice of consecrated virginity. It also covers the ascetic community she led on the family estate in Pontus and her death in 379, at which Gregory was present. It is a key early source for women's monasticism and for the family of the Cappadocian Fathers.

The Life of St Benedict is the second of the four books of the Dialogues by Pope Gregory the Great, written in Latin around 593–594. Like the rest of the work, it is a conversation between Gregory and his deacon Peter. It tells of Benedict of Nursia: his studies at Rome, his time as a hermit at Subiaco, the founding of Monte Cassino, his miracles and prophecies, his sister Scholastica and his death. Gregory names Benedict's disciples as his informants. The book is the fullest early source for Benedict's life and shaped later Western hagiography and monastic tradition.

The History of John, the Son of Zebedee is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal narrative about the apostle John, probably composed in the fifth century. It tells how, after Pentecost, the apostles dispersed to preach and John went to Ephesus, where he preached, worked wonders, baptised and turned the city from pagan worship to Christianity. Its heading claims Eusebius of Caesarea as author and says it was translated from a Greek book, but this attribution is not credited. The work is a witness to Syriac traditions about John and his Ephesian ministry.

The History of Philip, the Apostle and Evangelist is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal narrative, probably composed between the fifth and seventh centuries; its exact date is uncertain. It tells how Christ appears to Philip in a night vision at Jerusalem and sends him to preach in "Carthage, which is in Azotus." There he drives out Satan's power and converts the city through wonders and preaching. The work blends Philip the Apostle with Philip the Evangelist of Acts, and it reflects the Syriac tradition of legendary apostolic acts.

The Hymn of the Soul, also called the Hymn of the Pearl, is an anonymous Syriac poem preserved in the apocryphal Acts of Thomas. There the apostle Thomas sings it in prison in India. It tells of a prince sent from his father's kingdom in the East to bring back a pearl guarded by a serpent in Egypt. He forgets his mission until a letter reminds him, then returns to receive his glorious robe. It is widely read as an allegory of the soul's exile and redemption. It may be older than the Acts, and some have attributed it to Bardaisan, but its authorship and date are uncertain.

The Chronicon, often called the Chronica maiora, is a Latin universal chronicle by Isidore, bishop of Seville (c. 560–636). It summarises history from the Creation to the reigns of the emperor Heraclius and the Visigothic king Sisebut, and a later revised version carries the account a few years further. Isidore follows the tradition of Julius Africanus, Eusebius, Jerome and Victor of Tunnuna, and arranges events in six ages of the world. Its compact scheme of world history was widely copied and used by early medieval chroniclers.

The Chronicle is a universal chronicle that Jerome wrote in Latin at Constantinople around 380–381. It translates and expands the chronological tables in the second book of Eusebius of Caesarea's Greek Chronicon, adding material on Roman history, and carries the record on from 325 to 378. In its preface, addressed to Vincentius and Gallienus, Jerome discusses how hard it is to translate faithfully. Although it contains errors, the work preserves Eusebius's tables, whose Greek original is lost. Later chroniclers such as Prosper of Aquitaine and Victor of Tunnuna wrote continuations of it.

Jerome wrote this Latin commentary on the Book of Daniel in one book at Bethlehem, around 407. It goes through the prophecy verse by verse, and its prologue answers the pagan philosopher Porphyry. Porphyry had argued that Daniel was written in the time of Antiochus IV Epiphanes and recorded past events rather than predicting future ones. Jerome holds that no prophet spoke more clearly of Christ. He reads the fourth kingdom as Rome and gives an account of the seventy weeks. The work matters most because it preserves much of Porphyry's lost argument.

The Bazaar (or Book) of Heracleides is a theological and autobiographical apology attributed to Nestorius, the archbishop of Constantinople deposed at the Council of Ephesus in 431. He wrote it in exile late in his life, around 451–452. The Greek original is lost, and the work survives only in a Syriac translation preserved by the Church of the East and rediscovered in the nineteenth century. In it Nestorius defends his Christology against Cyril of Alexandria and recounts the events of his condemnation. The work has prompted scholars to reassess his actual teaching.

This is a dossier of Latin documents from the early Donatist controversy in Roman North Africa, preserved as an appendix to the anti-Donatist treatise of Optatus of Milevis (late fourth century). It includes the acts of the proceedings that cleared Felix of Aptunga, who consecrated Caecilian as bishop of Carthage, of handing over the Scriptures during the Diocletianic persecution. It also includes letters of the emperor Constantine and records of councils. These official records are key evidence for how the schism began and for the early church's dealings with the emperor.

This Latin polemical treatise by Optatus, bishop of Milevis in Numidia, replies to Parmenian, the Donatist bishop of Carthage. It was first written around 366–367, and a seventh book was added later, probably in the 380s. Optatus traces the North African schism back to accusations of betraying the Scriptures (traditio) during the Diocletianic persecution. He treats the Donatists as schismatics rather than heretics and argues for the unity of the Catholic Church, its communion with the see of Peter, and the validity of sacraments whatever the worthiness of the minister. The work strongly shaped Augustine's later anti-Donatist writings.

The Philocalia is a Greek anthology of extracts from the writings of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). The Greek text names Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen as its compilers, probably working in Pontus around 358–362. This attribution is widely accepted, though some scholars question it. It has twenty-seven chapters with titles added by the compilers, dealing with the inspiration and interpretation of Scripture, free will and providence. About a fifth comes from Contra Celsum. Because many of Origen's works are lost, the anthology also preserves Greek passages of On the First Principles.

The Letters to Sympronian are three Latin letters by Pacian, bishop of Barcelona, written in the second half of the fourth century to Sympronian, a follower of the rigorist Novatianist movement. Pacian defends the name "Catholic" and the Church's power to forgive grave sins committed after baptism through penance and episcopal absolution, both of which the Novatianists denied. The first letter contains the famous phrase "Christian is my name, Catholic my surname." The letters are important evidence for the controversy over penance and for the church in Roman Hispania.

The Dialogue on the Life of St John Chrysostom is a Greek biographical and apologetic work by Palladius of Helenopolis, a loyal supporter of Chrysostom, written around 407–408. It is set out as a conversation, modelled on Plato, between an Eastern bishop and a Roman deacon named Theodore. It tells the story of Chrysostom's career, his deposition at the Synod of the Oak and his exile, and defends him against the charges made against him. It sharply criticises Theophilus of Alexandria and the clerical ambition behind Chrysostom's downfall, and it is a major early source for his life.

The Lausiac History is a Greek collection of short accounts of the monks, hermits and holy women of early Christian monasticism. Palladius of Helenopolis, a disciple of John Chrysostom, wrote it around 419–420 and dedicated it to Lausus, a chamberlain at the court of Theodosius II, after whom it is named. It draws on his own years among the ascetics of Egypt, Palestine and Syria. It is a key source for the Desert Fathers and was widely translated and imitated.

The Ecclesiastical History of Philostorgius (368–c. 439), a Cappadocian historian who followed the Anomoean teaching of Eunomius, was written in Greek in twelve books and appeared between about 425 and 433. It covered church history from the Arian controversy into the early fifth century from a non-Nicene point of view. The original is lost. It survives mainly through the epitome made by Photius of Constantinople in the ninth century. Photius summarised the work critically, but his epitome keeps a rare account of the period from the side of the losing party.

The Ascetic Discourses are a collection of thirteen Syriac discourses on the Christian and monastic life by Philoxenus of Mabbug (died 523), the Miaphysite bishop of Hierapolis. They were written in the late fifth or early sixth century, though the exact date is uncertain. The work sets out a gradual path of discipleship that starts from faith and simplicity and moves through the fear of God and renunciation of the world. It then turns to the struggle against gluttony and fornication, with spiritual love and perfection as the goal. It is among the most important works of early Syriac spirituality.

De excidio Hierosolymitano is an anonymous Christian Latin history in five books, usually dated to around 370. It is a free adaptation of the Jewish War of Flavius Josephus and covers events from the Maccabees to the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple by Titus in AD 70. The author treats the city's fall as divine punishment of the Jews. The work was once ascribed to Ambrose of Milan, but this remains uncertain. The name "Hegesippus" probably comes from a corruption of "Iosippus", a form of Josephus's name. The book was widely read in the Middle Ages.

The Admonitions to Monks is a short set of disciplinary rules in Syriac attributed to Rabbula, bishop of Edessa (Urhay) from about 411 to 435/6. It governs life in the monasteries of his diocese. Its numbered precepts ban women from entering monasteries and limit monks' contact with villages and lay households to an appointed "Visitor". They also forbid drinking wine and restrict ascetic practices such as wearing long hair, iron chains or hair garments outside the monastery. The text is important evidence for early Syrian monasticism and for Rabbula's efforts to bring it under church discipline.

De Gubernatione Dei is a Latin treatise in eight books by Salvian, a priest of Marseilles. He wrote it in the 440s and dedicated it to Bishop Salonius. Christians in Gaul were asking why God allowed the barbarian invasions. Salvian answers that God still governs the world and that the Romans' sufferings are a just punishment for their sins. He sets Roman vice, injustice and oppression of the poor against the comparative virtues of Goths, Vandals and other peoples. The work is an important source for society in fifth-century Gaul.

This is the first of six Greek homilies on the creation account of Genesis by Severian, bishop of Gabala in Syria. He probably preached them in Constantinople during his time there, around 401 to 404. The Greek text survives among the works wrongly attributed to John Chrysostom. This sermon covers the first day of creation. It presents Genesis as the foundation of the Law and the Prophets and acknowledges earlier Fathers who wrote on the subject. The series is a notable example of literal Antiochene exegesis and of late fourth-century Christian cosmology.

The Letters of Sidonius Apollinaris, the Gallo-Roman aristocrat who became bishop of Clermont, are a collection of about 147 letters in nine books. He revised them and published them in stages, probably during the 470s and early 480s. The opening letter, addressed to his friend Constantius, places the collection in the tradition of Pliny and Symmachus. Written in an ornate, allusive Latin, the letters describe aristocratic life, the Church and politics in Gaul as Roman rule gave way to the Visigoths and Burgundians. They are a major source for the fifth-century West.

The third Relatio of Quintus Aurelius Symmachus is an official petition sent in 384, while he was prefect of Rome. It was addressed to the emperors Valentinian II, Theodosius I and Arcadius, though it was really meant for Valentinian. Speaking for the Senate, Symmachus asked for the Altar of Victory to be restored to the senate house and for the funds of the Vestals and priesthoods to be returned. He appealed to ancestral custom and religious tolerance. Ambrose of Milan wrote letters rebutting it, and the request was refused.

This Greek commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Romans by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, is the first part of his Interpretation of the Fourteen Epistles of Saint Paul, usually dated between about 430 and 448. It opens with an argument summarising the letter: Gentiles broke the natural law, Jews failed to keep the written law, and the gospel brings pardon and life to all. Following the Antiochene tradition, it explains the text concisely and literally, drawing heavily on John Chrysostom.

The Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament. It forms the second half of a two-volume work with the Gospel of Luke and is addressed, like that Gospel, to Theophilus. Tradition names Luke, a companion of Paul, as its author, though scholars disagree about this; it is usually dated around 80–90. Acts begins with Christ's ascension and Pentecost and describes the early Jerusalem church. It then follows the spread of the gospel to the Gentiles, mostly through Paul's missionary journeys, and ends with his imprisonment in Rome.

The Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament. It forms the second half of a two-volume work with the Gospel of Luke and is addressed, like that Gospel, to Theophilus. Tradition names Luke, a companion of Paul, as its author, though scholars disagree about this; it is usually dated around 80–90. Acts begins with Christ's ascension and Pentecost and describes the early Jerusalem church. It then follows the spread of the gospel to the Gentiles, mostly through Paul's missionary journeys, and ends with his imprisonment in Rome.

The Gospel of John is the fourth of the canonical Gospels of the New Testament. Tradition attributes it to the apostle John, though modern scholars dispute who wrote it. It is usually dated to about 90–100. It opens with a prologue on the divine Word (Logos) made flesh. It then tells of Jesus' signs, long discourses, farewell teaching to his disciples, passion and resurrection. Its strong emphasis on Christ's divinity made it central to early Trinitarian and Christological debate. Origen, John Chrysostom, Augustine and Cyril of Alexandria all wrote major commentaries on it.

The Gospel according to Luke is the third of the canonical Gospels of the New Testament, written in Greek, probably around 75–90. Tradition attributes it to Luke, companion of Paul, who also wrote the Acts of the Apostles, but the work itself is anonymous. Addressed to Theophilus, it tells of Jesus from the births of John the Baptist and Jesus to the resurrection and ascension. It is noted for its infancy narratives, its parables, and its concern for the poor and outcast.

The Gospel according to Mark is the second book of the New Testament and is generally thought to be the earliest of the four canonical gospels. Most scholars date it to about 65–75. Tradition attributes it to John Mark, a companion of Peter, but the authorship is uncertain. Written in Greek, it is a short, fast-moving account that runs from John the Baptist's preaching through Jesus' ministry in Galilee to his passion in Jerusalem and the empty tomb. Matthew and Luke drew heavily on it. It was soon translated into Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian, Georgian and Slavonic.

The Gospel of Matthew is the first book of the New Testament and one of the three Synoptic Gospels. It was written in Greek, probably between about 70 and 100, and is traditionally attributed to the apostle Matthew, although its author is unknown. It opens with Jesus' genealogy from Abraham and goes on to tell of his birth, ministry, teaching, death and resurrection. It includes the Sermon on the Mount and stresses Jesus as the fulfilment of Jewish scripture. In the early Church it was the most widely cited gospel.

Revelation, also called the Apocalypse, is the last book of the New Testament and its only full apocalyptic work. Its author calls himself John and says he received his visions on the island of Patmos. Tradition identifies him with John the Apostle, but this has been disputed since antiquity. It is usually dated to about 95, under Domitian, though some scholars prefer an earlier date. It contains letters to seven churches in Asia and visions of judgement, the defeat of evil and the New Jerusalem. Its place in the canon was long contested, especially in the East.

It is usually dated to about 90–100. It opens with a prologue on the divine Word (Logos) made flesh. The First Epistle of John is a New Testament writing in Greek, the first of the three Johannine epistles. It names no author. Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is disputed, and many scholars place it within the Johannine community around 85–100. It reads more like a homily than a letter. It teaches that God is light and God is love, and that believers must confess their sins and love one another. It also rejects those who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. Its theology of love and fellowship has strongly shaped Christian thought.

The First Epistle of Peter is a letter in the New Testament, one of the Catholic Epistles. Its author presents himself as the apostle Peter, writing from "Babylon", probably meaning Rome. Many scholars, however, think it came from a Roman Christian circle linked to Peter, sometime around 60–90. It is addressed to Christians scattered across Asia Minor who were suffering persecution. The letter urges them to keep hope, holiness and patient endurance, modelled on the sufferings of Christ. It also gives household instructions and contains a famous passage on Christ preaching to the "spirits in prison".

The Second Epistle of John is a short New Testament letter. Its author calls himself "the elder" and writes to "the elect lady and her children", which most readers take to mean a local church. Tradition ascribes it to the apostle John, but the authorship is disputed. It is usually dated to the late first century. The letter urges mutual love and obedience to the commandments. It warns against deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh and forbids welcoming them.

The Second Epistle of Peter is a short letter in the New Testament. Its author presents himself as the apostle Simon Peter, but most modern scholars consider it pseudonymous and date it to roughly 80–120, which may make it the latest New Testament book. It urges believers to grow in virtue and become "partakers of the divine nature," warns against false teachers, and defends the expectation of Christ's return. It overlaps closely with the Epistle of Jude, and its place in the canon was disputed in the early Church.

The Third Epistle of John is the shortest book of the New Testament. It is a private letter from an author who calls himself "the elder" to a Christian named Gaius. Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is debated, and it is usually dated to the late first century. The elder praises Gaius for welcoming travelling missionaries and condemns Diotrephes for refusing to receive them and for seeking preeminence. He also recommends Demetrius. The letter sheds rare light on authority and hospitality in the early church. Some early churches questioned whether it belonged in the canon.

The Epistle of James is a New Testament letter written in Greek and addressed "to the twelve tribes which are of the Dispersion." It names its author as James, traditionally identified with James the brother of the Lord, who led the church in Jerusalem. That attribution is disputed, and proposed dates run from the mid-first century to its end or later. Written in the manner of wisdom literature, it urges endurance in trials, care for the poor and control of the tongue, and teaches that faith without works is dead. Early Christians long debated whether it belonged in the canon.

The Epistle of Jude is a short letter of 25 verses and the penultimate book of the New Testament. It names its author as Jude, "brother of James," traditionally taken to be a brother of Jesus. Its date and authorship are disputed, though it is usually placed in the late first century. The letter urges readers to contend for the faith against false teachers. It recalls examples of divine judgment and quotes the Book of Enoch, and it alludes to a dispute over the body of Moses. It closes with a well-known doxology.

The Second Epistle of Peter is a short letter in the New Testament. Its author presents himself as the apostle Simon Peter, but most modern scholars consider it pseudonymous and date it to roughly 80–120, which may make it the latest New Testament book. It urges believers to grow in virtue and become "partakers of the divine nature," warns against false teachers, and defends the expectation of Christ's return. It overlaps closely with the Epistle of Jude, and its place in the canon was disputed in the early Church.

The Third Epistle of John is the shortest book of the New Testament. It is a private letter from an author who calls himself "the elder" to a Christian named Gaius. Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is debated, and it is usually dated to the late first century. The elder praises Gaius for welcoming travelling missionaries and condemns Diotrephes for refusing to receive them and for seeking preeminence. He also recommends Demetrius. The letter sheds rare light on authority and hospitality in the early church. Some early churches questioned whether it belonged in the canon.

The Epistle of James is a New Testament letter written in Greek and addressed "to the twelve tribes which are of the Dispersion." It names its author as James, traditionally identified with James the brother of the Lord, who led the church in Jerusalem. That attribution is disputed, and proposed dates run from the mid-first century to its end or later. Written in the manner of wisdom literature, it urges endurance in trials, care for the poor and control of the tongue, and teaches that faith without works is dead. Early Christians long debated whether it belonged in the canon.

The Epistle of Jude is a short letter of 25 verses and the penultimate book of the New Testament. It names its author as Jude, "brother of James," traditionally taken to be a brother of Jesus. Its date and authorship are disputed, though it is usually placed in the late first century. The letter urges readers to contend for the faith against false teachers. It recalls examples of divine judgment and quotes the Book of Enoch, and it alludes to a dispute over the body of Moses. It closes with a well-known doxology.

The First Epistle of John is a New Testament writing in Greek, the first of the three Johannine epistles. It names no author. Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is disputed, and many scholars place it within the Johannine community around 85–100. It reads more like a homily than a letter. It teaches that God is light and God is love, and that believers must confess their sins and love one another. It also rejects those who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. Its theology of love and fellowship has strongly shaped Christian thought.

The First Epistle of Peter is a letter in the New Testament, one of the Catholic Epistles. Its author presents himself as the apostle Peter, writing from "Babylon", probably meaning Rome. Many scholars, however, think it came from a Roman Christian circle linked to Peter, sometime around 60–90. It is addressed to Christians scattered across Asia Minor who were suffering persecution. The letter urges them to keep hope, holiness and patient endurance, modelled on the sufferings of Christ. It also gives household instructions and contains a famous passage on Christ preaching to the "spirits in prison".

The Second Epistle of John is a short New Testament letter. Its author calls himself "the elder" and writes to "the elect lady and her children", which most readers take to mean a local church. Tradition ascribes it to the apostle John, but the authorship is disputed. It is usually dated to the late first century. The letter urges mutual love and obedience to the commandments. It warns against deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh and forbids welcoming them.

Its author presents himself as the apostle Simon Peter, but most modern scholars consider it pseudonymous and date it to roughly 80–120, which may make it the latest New Testament book. It urges believers to grow in virtue and become "partakers of the divine nature," warns against false teachers, and defends the expectation of Christ's return. It overlaps closely with the Epistle of Jude, and its place in the canon was disputed in the early Church.

That attribution is disputed, and proposed dates run from the mid-first century to its end or later.
