The Gospel of John is the fourth of the canonical Gospels of the New Testament. Tradition attributes it to the apostle John, though modern scholars dispute who wrote it. It is usually dated to about 90–100. It opens with a prologue on the divine Word (Logos) made flesh. It then tells of Jesus' signs, long discourses, farewell teaching to his disciples, passion and resurrection. Its strong emphasis on Christ's divinity made it central to early Trinitarian and Christological debate. Origen, John Chrysostom, Augustine and Cyril of Alexandria all wrote major commentaries on it.

The Gospel according to Luke is the third of the canonical Gospels of the New Testament, written in Greek, probably around 75–90. Tradition attributes it to Luke, companion of Paul, who also wrote the Acts of the Apostles, but the work itself is anonymous. Addressed to Theophilus, it tells of Jesus from the births of John the Baptist and Jesus to the resurrection and ascension. It is noted for its infancy narratives, its parables, and its concern for the poor and outcast.

The Gospel according to Mark is the second book of the New Testament and is generally thought to be the earliest of the four canonical gospels. Most scholars date it to about 65–75. Tradition attributes it to John Mark, a companion of Peter, but the authorship is uncertain. Written in Greek, it is a short, fast-moving account that runs from John the Baptist's preaching through Jesus' ministry in Galilee to his passion in Jerusalem and the empty tomb. Matthew and Luke drew heavily on it. It was soon translated into Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian, Georgian and Slavonic.

The Gospel of Matthew is the first book of the New Testament and one of the three Synoptic Gospels. It was written in Greek, probably between about 70 and 100, and is traditionally attributed to the apostle Matthew, although its author is unknown. It opens with Jesus' genealogy from Abraham and goes on to tell of his birth, ministry, teaching, death and resurrection. It includes the Sermon on the Mount and stresses Jesus as the fulfilment of Jewish scripture. In the early Church it was the most widely cited gospel.

The Odes are a collection of biblical canticles, or songs of praise, attached to the Psalter in some Greek Bible manuscripts and in related Syriac and other traditions. The anonymous collection gathers Old Testament songs such as the two Songs of Moses (Exodus 15 and Deuteronomy 32), the prayers of Hannah, Habakkuk, Isaiah and Jonah, and the Song of the Three Young Men. New Testament canticles such as the Magnificat, Benedictus and Nunc dimittis are also included. It took shape for liturgical use, and its contents and order vary between traditions.

The Book of Psalms, or Psalter, is an anthology of Hebrew religious poetry in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It has 150 psalms in Jewish and Western usage, with a few more in Eastern churches, and is divided into five books. It includes hymns of praise, laments, royal psalms and thanksgivings. Many psalms are traditionally attributed to David, but scholars doubt this. They were composed over several centuries, before and after the Exile. The Psalms were central to Jewish and Christian worship, and early Christian writers commented on them extensively.

On the Faith (De fide) is a short doctrinal treatise that survives in Old Georgian. Its heading names it a discourse of Saint Hippolytus, though the work has also been linked to the Armenian tradition associated with Agathangelos. Its authorship and date are uncertain. It confesses faith in the Trinity into which believers are baptized: the unbegotten Father, the begotten Son and the Holy Spirit, each fully God and sharing one essence, nature and will. It also stresses that human language and the bodily senses cannot fully describe God.

On Devotion is an Old Georgian version of an ascetic homily by Aphrahat, the fourth-century Syriac writer known as the Persian Sage. Its content matches his sixth Demonstration, addressed to the "sons of the covenant", early Syriac ascetics. In the Georgian tradition, its heading attributes the work to "Hippolytus the archbishop". It urges readers to stay watchful for the coming Bridegroom and to live by prayer, mercy, humility and detachment from the world, drawing on Gospel parables. The date of the Georgian translation is uncertain.

The Conversion of Kartli (Mokcevay Kartlisay) is an anonymous Old Georgian historical and hagiographical compilation, and one of the earliest surviving works of Georgian historiography. This version is preserved in the tenth-century Shatberdi codex. It begins with a short chronicle of Kartli's legendary origins, starting with Alexander the Great and King Azo, and its pagan kings. It then tells how Saint Nino converted King Mirian and Iberia to Christianity in the fourth century, and it includes lists of rulers and bishops. Its date of composition is uncertain. The core may go back to the seventh century, with later additions.

On the Twelve Stones (De gemmis) is a treatise by Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, written late in his life, probably in the 390s. It is addressed as a letter to a fellow bishop and discusses the twelve precious stones on the high priest's breastplate described in Exodus. Epiphanius gives each stone's name, appearance, origin and supposed properties, and draws allegorical meanings from them. The complete text survives only in Georgian and Armenian versions. Greek and Latin survive only in abridgements and fragments.

On Weights and Measures is a treatise compiled by Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, around 392. It was written at the request of a Persian priest. Despite its title, it covers biblical canon and versions, Hebrew and Greek weights and measures, and biblical geography. It survives complete only in Syriac, with Greek fragments and partial Armenian and Georgian versions. This Old Georgian excerpt opens with a dedication and then lists the works God created on each of the six days of creation, beginning with the heavens, the waters and the angels.

On the Making of Man (De hominis opificio) is a Greek theological treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, written around 379, soon after the death of his brother Basil of Caesarea. Gregory sent it to his brother Peter as an Easter gift and meant it to complete Basil's homilies on the Hexaemeron, which had not dealt with the creation of humanity. It discusses humanity as made in the image of God, the relation of soul and body, the passions, and the resurrection. It is a foundational work of Christian anthropology. In the sixth century Dionysius Exiguus translated it into Latin.

On the Blessings of Isaac and Jacob is an exegetical treatise attributed to Hippolytus, the early third-century Christian theologian traditionally linked with Rome. It reads the patriarchal blessings of Genesis typologically, in particular Jacob's blessing of the twelve patriarchs. It treats the patriarchs and the story of Joseph as figures of Christ, the apostles and the Church. Parts of the work survive in Greek, and fuller versions survive in Armenian and Georgian. The Old Georgian translation was probably made between the eighth and tenth centuries. The work is an important witness to early Christian allegorical reading of the Old Testament.

This is an exegetical treatise attributed to Hippolytus, the theologian of the early third century, which explains the blessings Moses gave the twelve tribes of Israel in Deuteronomy 33. It follows on from his commentary on the blessings of Isaac and Jacob. It begins by recalling those earlier blessings and giving a short account of Moses' life, then reads each blessing as a prophecy fulfilled in Christ. The Greek original is lost. The work survives in an Old Georgian translation of uncertain date, probably made sometime between the eighth and tenth centuries.

The Chronicle is a world chronicle attributed to Hippolytus of Rome and usually dated to about 234–235. It runs from Creation to the author's own time. Taking its figures mainly from the biblical genealogies, it lists the patriarchs from Adam through Noah, the Flood, Abraham and the Exodus, and adds up the years between key events. It also includes geographical material on the division of the earth among Noah's descendants. The Greek original survives only partly. It was translated and adapted in Latin, Armenian and Georgian, which shows its importance for early Christian chronography.

The Treatise on Christ and Antichrist is a Greek treatise on the end times by Hippolytus of Rome, usually dated to the early third century, around 200. It is addressed to a "beloved brother Theophilus" and draws largely on Scripture, especially Daniel, Isaiah, the Gospels, 2 Thessalonians and Revelation. It contrasts Christ with the Antichrist, who is expected to come from the tribe of Dan, and reads the four kingdoms of Daniel as a sequence ending in Rome. It is among the earliest surviving Christian works devoted entirely to the Antichrist.

On David and Goliath is a short exegetical treatise attributed to Hippolytus, the early third-century Christian theologian and biblical commentator. Its Greek original is lost, and it survives only in an Old Georgian translation, whose date is uncertain. Drawing on the story in 1 Samuel, it praises David as both king and prophet. It reads his life typologically: the shepherd secretly anointed, who overthrows Goliath, is persecuted by Saul and flees into the desert, prefigures Christ, who fulfils the Law and the Prophets. It is a witness to early Christian typological exegesis of the Old Testament.

This commentary on the Song of Songs is attributed to Hippolytus of Rome and was composed in Greek in the early third century. It is among the earliest surviving Christian commentaries on the Song. It reads the poem allegorically as the love between Christ and the Church, and between Christ and the believing soul. It opens by linking Solomon's three books, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song, to the work of the Trinity. The Greek original survives only in fragments. The fullest witness is an Old Georgian version, probably made through Armenian, which breaks off partway through the Song.

The Life of Jacob of Nisibis is an anonymous Old Georgian hagiography, dated only roughly to between the eighth and late tenth centuries. Its subject is Jacob, the fourth-century first known bishop of Nisibis, a city on the Roman–Persian frontier. A rhetorical prologue compares the saint's virtues to those of Moses, Abel, Enoch, Noah, Melchizedek, Abraham and Job. The narrative then tells of Jacob's monastic life from youth, his episcopate and his miracles. It may depend on earlier Greek or Syriac traditions about the saint.

The Physiologus is an anonymous early Christian didactic text, first compiled in Greek, probably in Alexandria, sometime between the 2nd and 4th centuries. It describes animals, birds and fabulous creatures, telling a story about each and drawing a moral or Christological lesson from it. The Old Georgian version was translated from Greek and is attributed in its heading to Basil of Caesarea. Its date is uncertain, probably between the 8th and 10th centuries. It belongs to a widely translated tradition that shaped medieval animal symbolism and the later bestiaries.

This is an excerpt from an Old Georgian commentary on the Psalms. It is listed under Theodoret of Cyrrhus, the fifth-century Antiochene exegete, but the translator's prefatory letter attributes it to Epiphanius of Cyprus, so the authorship is uncertain. The letter is signed by one Dachi and addressed to Bishop Stephen of Mtbevari, which places it around the tenth century. Dachi says he could not find the work in Georgian and could not manage the Greek. He therefore translated it from an Armenian version, sending only a sample of the Psalms for the bishop's approval.

The Hexaemeron is a series of nine Greek homilies by Basil of Caesarea, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, on the six days of creation, working through Genesis 1:1–26. Basil preached them to his congregation in the 370s, possibly in 378. They pair a literal reading of the text with natural philosophy, describing the heavens, earth, plants and animals to show the Creator's wisdom. It was the first Christian work of its kind and shaped later hexaemeral writing, including Ambrose's Hexameron. Eustathius Afer translated it into Latin around 400.

The first of two homilies on fasting by Basil of Caesarea, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia (d. 379), preached in Greek at the start of Lent. It opens with the psalm verse "Blow the trumpet at the new moon" and, drawing on Isaiah and Christ's command to anoint the head and wash the face, calls for joyful rather than gloomy fasting. Basil presents fasting as medicine against sin that purifies the soul. The homily was widely read and translated, including into Old Georgian around the turn of the eleventh century.

On Fasting II is the second of two homilies on fasting by Basil of Caesarea, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia (d. 379), probably preached at the start of Lent. It opens with Isaiah's call, "Comfort my people, O priests; speak to the heart of Jerusalem." Basil compares himself to generals and athletic trainers who encourage their men before a contest. He presents Christians as soldiers of Christ fighting invisible enemies, and fasting as the discipline that strengthens the soul, defeats the devil and draws the guardian angels closer. The homily was later translated into Old Georgian.

This is a homily by Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, written in Greek in the fourth century. It expounds Moses' command "Give heed to thyself" (Deuteronomy 15:9). Basil begins by reflecting on speech as the means by which hidden thoughts are shared. He then urges his hearers to watch over their souls rather than their bodies or possessions, and to know their own nature, dignity and weaknesses. The homily was widely read and translated, including into Old Georgian, and is a classic early Christian treatment of self-examination and spiritual vigilance.

On Giving Thanks is a homily by Basil of Caesarea (d. 379), the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, originally preached in Greek. It expounds Paul's command to the Thessalonians: "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, in everything give thanks" (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18). Basil answers those who call these precepts impossible, given life's constant trials and griefs. He argues that the Christian's joy and gratitude do not depend on outward fortune. The homily survives in an Old Georgian version that probably dates from the late tenth or early eleventh century.

On the Martyr Julitta is a homily by Basil of Caesarea (d. 379), written in Greek and preached at Caesarea on the feast of Julitta. She was a wealthy local Christian woman who was martyred under Diocletian. A powerful man had seized her property, and when she brought the case to court she was denied a hearing because she was a Christian. She chose to be burned rather than deny her faith. Basil praises her courage, which overcame what he calls a woman's natural weakness. He also finishes his earlier sermon on giving thanks to God in all things.

This homily by Basil of Caesarea, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, was composed in Greek in the fourth century and later translated into Old Georgian and other languages. It starts from the Psalms and from those who doubt God's providence when they suffer. Basil argues that God is not the author of evil. Moral evil comes from the misuse of free will. Evil has no existence of its own but is a lack of good. Hardships such as sickness or poverty can serve as correction. The homily is a key early Christian treatment of theodicy.

Against the Angry (Adversus iratos) is a moral homily by Basil of Caesarea, the fourth-century bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, originally written in Greek. Basil draws on Proverbs, Paul's command to put away all wrath, and Christ's warning against anger toward a brother. He shows how anger darkens reason and turns people into beasts that bark like dogs and bite like snakes, and he urges self-control and meekness. The homily also circulated in an Old Georgian translation made around the late tenth or early eleventh century.

On Envy (De invidia) is a moral homily by Basil of Caesarea, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia (d. 379). He composed it in Greek in the fourth century, and it later circulated in translation, including Old Georgian. Basil sets God, who is good and gives good things freely, against the devil, the author of envy. He defines envy as grief at a neighbour's good fortune and says it destroys the soul that harbours it, as rust eats iron. The homily belongs to Basil's widely read sermons on the virtues and vices.

This is a homily by Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), written in Greek in the fourth century, on the parable of the rich fool in Luke 12:16–21. Basil says that temptation comes in two forms: affliction, which Job withstood, and prosperity. God gave the rich man abundant harvests out of patience and kindness, but he chose to hoard them instead of sharing. The sermon is one of Basil's best-known attacks on greed. It urges generosity to the poor and is central to his social teaching on wealth. It also circulated in an Old Georgian translation.

Against the Rich (In divites) is a Greek homily by Basil of Caesarea (d. 379), preached in Cappadocian Caesarea. Basil says he had spoken before about the rich young man of the Gospel, who asked Christ how to gain eternal life and went away grieving when told to sell his possessions and give to the poor. He praises the young man's question but faults his attachment to wealth. Basil then condemns greed and hoarding and urges almsgiving as true use of riches. It is one of his best-known sermons on social ethics and circulated in translations, including Old Georgian.

This sermon by Basil of Caesarea was preached at Caesarea in Cappadocia during a severe drought and famine, usually dated to about 368, before he became bishop. It opens with Amos 3:8, "The lion roars; who will not fear?", and presents the cloudless sky and failing harvest as a divine warning. Basil calls his hearers to repentance, prayer and generous almsgiving, and condemns those who hoard grain. The homily belongs to his sermons on wealth and social duty. This version is an Old Georgian translation made from the Greek, probably around the late tenth or early eleventh century.

On the Beginning of Proverbs is a homily attributed to Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), first composed in Greek and later translated into Old Georgian. It explains the opening verses of the Book of Proverbs. The preacher says he took up the task out of obedience to a senior churchman. He then sets out the different purposes of Solomon's three books: Proverbs teaches moral conduct, Ecclesiastes shows that worldly things are vain, and the Song of Songs portrays the soul's union with the divine Word. He defines a proverb as a useful saying whose deeper meaning lies hidden.

This homily by Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, urges listeners not to put off baptism. In his day many catechumens delayed it until late in life. Basil reverses Ecclesiastes' "a time to be born and a time to die": in spiritual rebirth, dying to the flesh comes first and new life follows. Unlike other activities, he says, baptism has no special season, because the whole of life is the right time for it. The homily is an important witness to fourth-century baptismal practice and preaching.

On Faith (De fide) is a homily by Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), the Cappadocian bishop and theologian. It was written in Greek in the fourth century and later translated into other languages, including Old Georgian. It opens by stating that remembering God is always good but that speaking about God is bold, because both mind and speech fall short of the divine. Basil cites Abraham and Moses as examples of this humility. He then sets out the Church's faith in the Holy Trinity as far as human capacity allows. The homily reflects his defence of Nicene Trinitarian doctrine.

This is a homily attributed to Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), the Cappadocian bishop and theologian, on the opening verse of John's Gospel, "In the beginning was the Word." Basil holds that the Gospel of John, the "son of thunder," surpasses all other teaching. He notes that pagan philosophers admired these words, and he warns that the Word's eternal being is beyond human understanding, much as the sun dazzles anyone who stares at it. The homily defends the Son's eternity against Arian teaching. The Old Georgian translation dates from the late tenth or early eleventh century.

On the Holy Spirit is a short sermon on the Trinity attributed to Basil of Caesarea, the fourth-century bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. It survives in an Old Georgian version, probably from around the late tenth or early eleventh century. It is not Basil's long treatise of the same name. Its opening follows passages from Gregory of Nazianzus's Fifth Theological Oration very closely, so Basil's authorship is doubtful. The sermon argues that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are coeternal and equally divine: "light and light and light," yet one light and one God.

This Greek panegyric homily by Basil of Caesarea (d. 379) was preached on the feast of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste. They were Christian soldiers who, by tradition, were put to death in the early fourth century by being left naked on a frozen lake. Basil praises their unity of faith and endurance. He tells how one soldier gave up and how a guard took his place, so that the number of forty stayed complete. The homily set the pattern for later veneration of these martyrs. It survives in several ancient translations.

Against Drunkards is a Greek homily by Basil of Caesarea, preached at Caesarea in Cappadocia in the 370s. Basil gave it the day after a feast that ended in drinking and dancing, in which women of the congregation took a prominent part. He complains that his teaching through Lent had come to nothing. Recalling Jeremiah, he says he speaks only because he fears to keep silent. He then describes vividly how drunkenness harms body and soul. The sermon was widely read and was translated into other languages, including Old Georgian.

The Homily Delivered in Lakizoi is a sermon transmitted under the name of Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Its authenticity has been questioned. It was originally composed in Greek and later translated into Old Georgian, probably around the late tenth or early eleventh century. The preacher urges his hearers to keep their minds on the Scripture readings of the day. He describes the devil's many temptations and offers the words of Scripture as remedies for particular passions, including envy, anger, avarice and pride.

On Humility is a homily by Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. It was written in Greek in the fourth century and later translated into other languages, including Old Georgian. Basil argues that humanity was made to share in the glory God gives, but lost it by reaching for something greater. Humility is the remedy that restores the first honour. He warns against pride in wealth, fine living, servants and public office, comparing arrogance to an unhealthy swelling of the soul. He urges Christians to seek glory from God alone.

This is a homily by Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, known in Latin as Quod rebus mundanis adhaerendum non sit. It was preached after a fire broke out in Caesarea. Basil tells his congregation that the devil, whose own power has been bound by Christ, can harm people only through their own desires. He compares him to robbers lying in wait for travellers, and urges his hearers to let go of worldly attachments. Composed in Greek, the sermon also circulated in an Old Georgian translation made around the late tenth or early eleventh century.

The Life of John Climacus is a short Greek hagiography of John, abbot of Mount Sinai and author of the Ladder of Divine Ascent, who died around 649. It is attributed to Daniel, a monk of Raithu, and was probably written in the seventh century. The Life says it does not know John's birthplace. It describes how he entered monastic life at Sinai at about sixteen, his obedience and humility, and his years of solitude and spiritual guidance. It was often copied as a preface to the Ladder and was later translated into Georgian and Slavonic.

This is a short Old Georgian preface by Euthymius the Athonite (c. 957–1024) to his translation of the Ladder of Divine Ascent by John Climacus. It explains that "Klimax" is the book's title, Greek for "ladder", and not its author's name, which was John. The work is called a ladder because it rises step by step from lowly practices to the higher virtues. Euthymius says an earlier abridged Georgian version was faulty and incomplete, so he made a new translation from the Greek at the command of his father John. He asks readers to pray for John, for John the Synkellos and for himself. He also tells copyists to reproduce the text and its red chapter headings exactly.

On the Making of Man (De hominis opificio) is a Greek theological treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, written around 379, soon after the death of his brother Basil of Caesarea. Gregory sent it to his brother Peter as an Easter gift and meant it to complete Basil's homilies on the Hexaemeron, which had not dealt with the creation of humanity. It discusses humanity as made in the image of God, the relation of soul and body, the passions, and the resurrection. It is a foundational work of Christian anthropology. In the sixth century Dionysius Exiguus translated it into Latin.

On Virginity (De virginitate) is a Greek treatise by Gregory of Nyssa, generally regarded as one of his earliest works and dated to the 370s. It praises consecrated virginity as the gateway to a holier life. Gregory argues that freedom from the cares of marriage and worldly life allows undistracted contemplation of God and restores the soul toward its divine likeness. He begins by praising virginity, then contrasts it with the troubles of ordinary life and ends with an exhortation. The work is an important early statement of Cappadocian ascetic and mystical thought.

The Homilies on the Song of Songs are fifteen sermons by Gregory of Nyssa, one of the Cappadocian Fathers, written late in his life, probably in the early 390s. They were dedicated to the deaconess Olympias of Constantinople, who had asked for them. The prologue defends allegorical reading against those who held to the literal sense alone. The homilies read the Song as the soul's endless ascent toward God, an idea later called epektasis. They are central to Gregory's mystical theology and shaped later Christian contemplative exegesis.

The Homilies on the Gospel of John are a series of eighty-eight sermons in Greek by John Chrysostom. He preached them at Antioch around 390 to 392, while he was still a priest there and before he became archbishop of Constantinople. Working through the Fourth Gospel passage by passage, they explain its literal meaning and defend the full divinity of the Son against Arian (Anomoean) teaching. Each sermon usually ends with moral exhortation. The series is among the most important patristic commentaries on John, and it circulated widely in translation, including into Old Georgian.

To the Shepherd (Liber ad pastorem) is a short treatise by John Climacus, the seventh-century monk of Sinai. He wrote it as a companion to his Ladder of Divine Ascent, and it is usually copied alongside that work. Both were written at the request of John, abbot of Raithu. Where the Ladder guides monks, this text is addressed to the superior of a monastic community. Through images of the shepherd, helmsman, physician and teacher, it describes the duties, discernment and personal holiness required of a spiritual guide. It survives in Greek and in translations including Old Georgian.

The Ladder of Divine Ascent, or Ladder of Paradise, is an ascetical treatise by John Climacus, monk and later abbot of Mount Sinai. He wrote it in the early seventh century at the request of John, abbot of Raithu. Their exchange of letters often accompanies the text. It is written in concise, aphoristic prose and has thirty "steps", recalling the thirty years of Christ's hidden life. These lead from renouncing the world to the virtues and finally to love. It became one of the most influential monastic texts of Eastern Christianity and drew commentaries and scholia from an early date.

The Questions to Thalassius is a major exegetical and theological work by Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662), written around 630–633 in reply to questions sent by the Libyan monk Thalassius about difficult passages of Scripture. Its sixty-five answers read the Bible spiritually and develop Maximus's teaching on the passions, deification and the fall. This fragment, preserved in Old Georgian translation, comes from the introduction. It defines evil as ignorance of God, the cause of all beings, which leads humanity to serve the senses and the creature instead of the Creator.

On Repentance, Continence and Virginity is a homily that survives in Old Georgian and is attributed to John Chrysostom, though it is not considered his work. It belongs to the large body of Pseudo-Chrysostomic sermons. The Georgian text is tentatively dated to the mid-eleventh century, and its original author and date are unknown. It opens by praising the apostle Paul and recalls his fear of being found unworthy. From this it urges vigilance, constant prayer and seeking the kingdom of heaven rather than earthly riches. It also praises the virgin, whose joy is in the Lord.

The Scholia on the Ladder are anonymous explanatory notes in Old Georgian on the Ladder of Divine Ascent, the seventh-century ascetical treatise of John Climacus. They probably date from the late tenth or early eleventh century, though the date is uncertain. Each note, introduced as an "interpretation", explains a difficult passage. Topics include renouncing a nature corrupted by the passions, the difference between spiritual and bodily passions, and the kind of guide each needs. The scholia show how Georgian monks studied and absorbed Byzantine ascetic teaching.

On the Letters is a short Old Church Slavonic treatise attributed to Chernorizets Hrabar ("Hrabar the Monk"), a writer linked to the Preslav Literary School in the First Bulgarian Empire. It is usually dated to the late ninth or early tenth century. The work defends the Slavic alphabet created by Constantine-Cyril the Philosopher and argues that it is equal in dignity to the Hebrew, Greek and Latin scripts. It also describes how the letters were made in imitation of Greek. It is a key early witness to Slavic literacy and to the Cyrillo-Methodian mission.

The Euchologium Sinaiticum is an anonymous Old Church Slavonic prayer book (euchologion), mostly translated from Greek liturgical sources. It is preserved in a Glagolitic manuscript kept at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai, usually dated to the eleventh century, though the translations may be older. Besides sacramental and penitential material, it contains many occasional blessings for daily life. Examples include prayers for planting a vineyard, blessing grapes and restoring wine that has turned sour. It is one of the most important witnesses to early Slavonic liturgical language and practice.

The Kiev Missal, also called the Kiev Folios, is an anonymous Old Church Slavonic manuscript written in Glagolitic script. It is usually held to be the oldest and most archaic Old Church Slavonic manuscript and is dated no later than the second half of the tenth century. Its seven small parchment folios contain Mass prayers of the Roman rite translated from a Latin sacramentary, among them propers for Saint Clement and Saint Felicity. It is important evidence for early Slavonic use of the Western liturgy.

The Book of Psalms, or Psalter, is an anthology of Hebrew religious poetry in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It has 150 psalms in Jewish and Western usage, with a few more in Eastern churches, and is divided into five books. It includes hymns of praise, laments, royal psalms and thanksgivings. Many psalms are traditionally attributed to David, but scholars doubt this. They were composed over several centuries, before and after the Exile. The Psalms were central to Jewish and Christian worship, and early Christian writers commented on them extensively.

This Typikon is a Greek liturgical rulebook of the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople, setting out the order of services for the church year in the Byzantine Rite. It was prepared in the late nineteenth century by a five-member synodal committee. The committee included the metropolitans of Ainos, Samos, Caesarea and Mytilene and Georgios Violakis, Protopsaltes of the Great Church. It revised and corrected the earlier Typikon of Konstantinos the Protopsaltes, for example on the timing of the hours and on dismissals at Vespers. It remains the standard parish Typikon in Greek-speaking Orthodox churches.

The Würzburg Glosses on 1 Corinthians are anonymous explanatory notes, mostly in Old Irish mixed with Latin, written between the lines and in the margins of the Latin text of Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians. They belong to the larger body of Würzburg glosses on the Pauline epistles, usually dated to the eighth century. The glosses explain words, Paul's arguments and his moral teaching, often drawing on earlier Latin commentators. They are among the oldest substantial surviving texts in Old Irish and a key source for the language and for early Irish biblical scholarship.

The Würzburg Glosses on 1 Thessalonians are anonymous Old Irish and Latin explanatory notes written between the lines and in the margins of the Latin text of Paul's First Letter to the Thessalonians. They belong to the larger body of Würzburg Glosses on the Pauline epistles, usually dated to the eighth century. The glosses explain words and phrases, paraphrase Paul's meaning and add brief theological comments, for instance on faith, love and imitation of the apostle. The collection is one of the earliest substantial witnesses to the Old Irish language and to early Irish biblical scholarship.

This is the part of the Würzburg Glosses that covers Paul's First Letter to Timothy. The Würzburg Glosses are a body of anonymous Old Irish and Latin notes written between the lines and in the margins of the Latin Pauline epistles, usually dated to the eighth century. They are named after Würzburg, where they are kept. The glosses explain single words, paraphrase Paul's argument and point out moral lessons. They are among the most important early sources for the Old Irish language and for Irish biblical scholarship.

These are the anonymous Old Irish and Latin glosses on Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians, part of the Würzburg Glosses. They were written between the lines and in the margins of an eighth-century Latin manuscript of the Pauline epistles kept at Würzburg. The comments explain individual words, supply grammatical help, and draw moral and theological lessons, often based on earlier Latin commentaries. Together with the rest of the collection, they are among the oldest substantial witnesses to the Old Irish language and to early Irish biblical scholarship.

These are the anonymous Old Irish and Latin glosses on Paul's Second Letter to the Thessalonians. They belong to the Würzburg Glosses, a set of notes on the Pauline epistles usually dated to the eighth century. Written between the lines and in the margins of the Latin text, they explain individual words and phrases. They paraphrase Paul's meaning and draw out themes such as endurance under persecution, divine judgement, the Second Coming and the Antichrist. The Würzburg Glosses are among the oldest substantial sources for the Old Irish language. They also show how early Irish scholars studied and taught Scripture.

The Würzburg Glosses on 2 Timothy are short anonymous explanatory notes, mostly in Old Irish, written between the lines and in the margins of the Latin text of Paul's Second Letter to Timothy. They belong to the wider body of Würzburg glosses on the Pauline epistles, usually dated to the eighth century. The glosses paraphrase and expand single words or phrases, drawing out Paul's meaning, his affection for Timothy, and moral lessons on endurance and faith. With the other Würzburg glosses, they are among the earliest substantial witnesses to the Old Irish language and to Irish biblical scholarship.

These are anonymous interlinear and marginal glosses on the Latin text of Paul's Epistle to the Colossians. They belong to the Würzburg glosses, one of the most important early bodies of Old Irish writing, usually dated to the eighth century. Written mostly in Old Irish mixed with Latin, the short notes explain words and phrases. They paraphrase the text, clarify doctrine and offer moral or spiritual readings. They show how Irish scholars studied Scripture, and they are a key source for the early Irish language.

These are anonymous explanatory notes on Paul's Letter to the Ephesians. They form part of the Würzburg Glosses, a large body of Old Irish and Latin comments on the Pauline epistles written by Irish scholars, usually dated to the eighth century. The brief glosses sit beside words of the Latin text and explain their meaning. Here they deal with election, redemption through Christ's blood, which is also linked to the Eucharist, grace and salvation. The glosses are among the most important early witnesses to the Old Irish language and to Irish biblical scholarship.

The Würzburg Glosses on Galatians are anonymous explanatory notes, mostly in Old Irish with some Latin, written between the lines and in the margins of the Latin text of Paul's Letter to the Galatians. They belong to the larger Würzburg collection of glosses on the Pauline epistles, usually dated to the eighth century. Brief and often paraphrasing, they explain Paul's argument about the Gospel, the Law and Christian freedom, drawing on earlier Latin exegesis. They are among the oldest substantial texts in the Irish language and are a key source for Old Irish grammar.

These are anonymous Old Irish and Latin glosses on the Epistle to the Hebrews. They form part of the Würzburg Glosses, a continuous series of notes on the Pauline epistles, usually dated to the eighth century. The brief comments explain words of the Latin text. They stress Christ's divine sonship by nature and his one substance with the Father, and they distinguish his Godhead from his Manhood. Together the Würzburg Glosses are among the earliest substantial sources for Old Irish. They matter both for Celtic philology and for the history of Irish biblical exegesis.

These are anonymous Old Irish glosses on Paul's Letter to the Philippians, part of the Würzburg Glosses, which comment on the Latin text of the Pauline epistles. Irish scholars wrote them, probably in the eighth century, between and beside the lines of the Latin text. The short notes explain words, paraphrase Paul's meaning and add theological comments on his love for the Philippians, his imprisonment and the spread of the gospel. With the other Würzburg glosses, they are among the earliest substantial sources for the Old Irish language and for early medieval Irish biblical study.

This is the section of the Würzburg Glosses that comments on Paul's Epistle to Philemon. The Würzburg Glosses are anonymous Old Irish and Latin explanatory notes on the Latin text of the Pauline epistles, usually dated to the eighth century. They are among the most important early witnesses to the Old Irish language. The glosses on Philemon are brief. They explain the background of the letter, Onesimus's flight from Philemon to Paul, and paraphrase Paul's plea that Philemon freely receive Onesimus back as a brother.

The Würzburg Glosses on Romans are anonymous explanatory notes on Paul's Epistle to the Romans. They are part of the larger body of Würzburg Glosses, which comment on the Pauline epistles and are written in Old Irish mixed with Latin. Irish scholars, usually dated to the eighth century, added the glosses between the lines and in the margins of the Latin biblical text. They paraphrase words, clarify grammar and give brief theological explanations, often drawing on earlier commentators such as Pelagius. They are among the most important early witnesses to the Old Irish language and to Irish biblical scholarship.

These anonymous Old Irish glosses explain the Latin text of Paul's Epistle to Titus. They belong to the Würzburg Glosses on the Pauline epistles, which are usually dated to the eighth century and are among the earliest substantial records of the Irish language. Short notes written between the lines and in the margins paraphrase and expand individual Latin words. They discuss the qualifications and conduct of a bishop, ordination, sound teaching and false teachers. They matter both as early Irish biblical exegesis and as key evidence for Old Irish grammar.

The Würzburg Glosses on 1 Corinthians are anonymous explanatory notes, mostly in Old Irish mixed with Latin, written between the lines and in the margins of the Latin text of Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians. They belong to the larger body of Würzburg glosses on the Pauline epistles, usually dated to the eighth century. The glosses explain words, Paul's arguments and his moral teaching, often drawing on earlier Latin commentators. They are among the oldest substantial surviving texts in Old Irish and a key source for the language and for early Irish biblical scholarship.

The Würzburg Glosses on 1 Thessalonians are anonymous Old Irish and Latin explanatory notes written between the lines and in the margins of the Latin text of Paul's First Letter to the Thessalonians. They belong to the larger body of Würzburg Glosses on the Pauline epistles, usually dated to the eighth century. The glosses explain words and phrases, paraphrase Paul's meaning and add brief theological comments, for instance on faith, love and imitation of the apostle. The collection is one of the earliest substantial witnesses to the Old Irish language and to early Irish biblical scholarship.

This is the part of the Würzburg Glosses that covers Paul's First Letter to Timothy. They are named after Würzburg, where they are kept. The glosses explain single words, paraphrase Paul's argument and point out moral lessons. They are among the most important early sources for the Old Irish language and for Irish biblical scholarship.
